senses.definition: recognition for having tried to do something even if it was not successful.
examples: The plan didn’t work, but I’ll give you an A for effort for trying so hard.
Bobby played his violin in the concert and got an A for effort. It sounded terrible.

senses.definition: an apologetic way of saying that one is experiencing something new or participating in something new and is therefore ineffective or inept.
examples: I’m sorry I’m slow. I’m a little new to all this.
She’s new to this. She needs practice.

senses.definition: to follow the rules of something; to obey someone’s orders.
examples: John felt that he had to abide by his father’s wishes.
All drivers are expected to abide by the rules of the road.

senses.definition: able to relax and recover from a busy or stressful time; able to catch one’s breath.
senses.notes: Also literal. Able to can be replaced with can.
examples: Now that the lion has been caught, we’ll be able to breathe freely again.
Now that the annual sale is over, the sales staff will be able to breathe again.
Final exams are over, so I can breathe easily again.

altForms: able to do something standing on one’s head

senses.definition: able to do something easily and quickly, possibly without even looking.
senses.notes: Informal. Able to can be replaced with can.
examples: Bill boasted that he could pass his driver’s test blindfolded.
Mary is very good with computers. She can program blindfolded.
Dr. Jones is a great surgeon. He can take out an appendix standing on his head.

headword: able to do something with one’s eyes closed

senses.definition: able to do something very easily, even without having to think about it or look at it.
senses.notes: Also literal. Also with can. Always affirmative.
examples: It’s easy. I can do it with my eyes closed.
I can clean the house with my eyes closed! It’s easy!

senses.definition: alive, even if just barely.
senses.notes: Usually jocular. Refers to the use of a small mirror placed under one’s nose to tell if one is breathing or not.
examples: Look, I don’t need an athlete to do this job. Anybody able to fog a mirror will do fine!
I’m so tired this morning, I feel like I’m hardly able to fog a mirror.

senses.definition: to be able to accept ridicule good-naturedly; to be the object or butt of a joke willingly.
senses.notes: Able to can be replaced with can.
examples: Let’s play a trick on Bill and see if he’s able to take a joke.
Better not tease Ann. She can’t take a joke.

headword: able to take just so much

senses.definition: able to endure only a limited amount of discomfort.
senses.notes: Able to can be replaced with can.
examples: Please stop hurting my feelings. I’m able to take just so much before I get angry.
I can take just so much.

senses.definition: more than is required.
examples: Her efforts were above and beyond. We appreciate her time.
All this extra time is above and beyond her regular hours.

headword: (above and) beyond the call of duty

senses.definition: in addition to what is required; more than is required in one’s job.
examples: We didn’t expect the police officer to drive us home. That was above and beyond the call of duty.
The English teacher helped students after school every day, even though it was beyond the call of duty.

senses.definition: higher or better than the average.
examples: Max’s grades are always above average.
His intelligence is clearly above average.

senses.definition: better than average or normal.
examples: His work is above par, so he should get paid better.
Your chances of winning the game are a little above par.

senses.definition: not deserving of blame or criticism.
examples: Some politicians behave as though they are above reproach.
You must accept your punishment. You are not above reproach.

senses.definition: honest enough that no one would suspect you; to be in a position where you could not be suspected.
examples: The general is a fine old man, completely above suspicion.
Mary was at work at the time of the accident, so she’s above suspicion.

senses.definition: in the open; visible to the public; honest.
senses.notes: Especially with keep, as in the examples below.
examples: Don’t keep it a secret. Let’s make sure that everything is aboveboard.
You can do whatever you wish, as long as you keep it honest and aboveboard.
The inspector had to make sure that everything was open and aboveboard.

senses.definition: absent from a military unit without permission; absent from anything without permission.
senses.notes: AWOL is an abbreviation. This is a serious offense in the military.
examples: The soldier was taken away by the military police because he was absent without leave.
John was AWOL from school and got into a lot of trouble with his parents.

senses.definition: from all the reports; everyone is saying.
examples: According to all accounts, the police were on the scene immediately.
According to all accounts, the meeting broke up over a very minor matter.
By all accounts, it was a very poor performance.

senses.definition: according to the rules; in keeping with the way it is normally done.
senses.notes: Refers to the rules for playing games. Edmond Hoyle wrote a book about games. This expression is usually used for something other than games.
examples: That’s wrong. According to Hoyle, this is the way to do it.
The carpenter said, “This is the way to drive a nail, according to Hoyle.”

senses.definition: according to the way one believes; according to the way one’s conscience or inclinations lead one.
examples: People must act on this matter according to their own lights.
John may have been wrong, but he did what he did according to his own lights.

senses.definition: as said or indicated by someone or something.
examples: According to the weather forecast, this should be a beautiful day.
According to my father, this is a very good car to buy.
It’s too cold to go for a walk, according to the thermometer.

senses.definition: in proportion to something.
examples: You will get paid according to the number of hours that you work.
The doctor charges patients according to their ability to pay.

senses.definition: used to or comfortable with someone or something; accepting of someone or something as common and usual.
examples: We were accustomed to wearing shoes.
They aren’t accustomed to paying a visit without bringing a gift.
I’ll never become accustomed to you.

senses.definition: the feeling of distress because of love that is lost or has faded away, described as being in the heart, where love is said to reside.
examples: I try to tell my aching heart that I don’t love him.
There is no medicine for an aching heart.

senses.definition: a test whose findings are beyond doubt or dispute.
senses.notes: Refers to a chemical test that shows whether a metal is gold.
examples: Her new husband seems generous, but the acid test will be if he lets her mother stay with them.
The senator isn’t very popular just now, but the acid test will be if he gets reelected.

senses.definition: to inform the sender that what was sent was received.
examples: In a letter to a shoe company, Mary wrote, “I’m happy to acknowledge receipt of four dozen pairs of shoes.”
John acknowledged receipt of the bill.
The package hasn’t arrived, so I’m unable to acknowledge receipt.

senses.definition: to admit or state that someone is correct about something.
examples: Mary acknowledged Bill to be right about the name of the store.
Bill said that the car was useless, and the mechanic acknowledged him to be right.

senses.definition: to develop a liking for food, drink, or something else; to learn to like something.
examples: One acquires a taste for fine wines.
Many people are never able to acquire a taste for foreign food.
Mary acquired a taste for art when she was very young.

senses.definition: equally for everyone or everything.
examples: The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.
Congress cut the budget by reducing the money for each department 10 percent across the board.

senses.definition: to perform in the capacity of someone, temporarily or permanently.
examples: I’ll act as your supervisor until Mrs. Brown returns from vacation.
This is Mr. Smith. He’ll act as manager from now on.

senses.definition: to act proud and powerful.
examples: Why does the doctor always have to act so high-and-mighty?
If Sally wouldn’t act so high-and-mighty, she’d have more friends.

senses.definition: an act or deed demonstrating religious faith; an act or deed showing trust in someone or something.
examples: He lit candles in church as an act of faith.
For him to trust you with his safety was a real act of faith.

senses.definition: an occurrence (usually an accident) for which no human is responsible; a dramatic act of nature such as a storm, an earthquake, or a windstorm.
examples: My insurance company wouldn’t pay for the damage because it was an act of God.
The thief tried to convince the judge that the diamonds were in his pocket due to an act of God.

senses.definition: an international act of violence for which war is considered a suitable response; any hostile act between two people.
examples: To bomb a ship is an act of war.
Can spying be considered an act of war?
“You just broke my stereo,” yelled John. “That’s an act of war!”

senses.definition: to behave more maturely; to act as grown-up as one really is.
senses.notes: This is frequently said to a child.
examples: Come on, John, act your age. Stop throwing rocks.
Mary! Stop picking on your little brother. Act your age!

senses.definition: to perform an imaginary event as if one were in a play.
examples: Bill always acted his anger out by shouting and pounding his fists.
The psychiatrist asked Bill to act out the way he felt about getting fired.

senses.definition: It is better to do something about a problem than just talk about it.
examples: Mary kept promising to get a job. John finally looked her in the eye and said, “Actions speak louder than words!”
After listening to the senator promising to cut federal spending, Ann wrote a simple note saying, “Actions speak louder than words.”

senses.definition: to make a problem worse; to say or do something that makes a bad situation worse; to make an angry person even more angry.
examples: To spank a crying child just adds fuel to the fire.
Bill was shouting angrily, and Bob tried to get him to stop by laughing at him. Of course, that was just adding fuel to the flame.

senses.definition: to make a bad situation worse; to hurt the feelings of a person who has already been hurt.
examples: First, the basement flooded, and then, to add insult to injury, a pipe burst in the kitchen.
My car barely started this morning, and to add insult to injury, I got a flat tire in the driveway.

senses.definition: to total up to a particular amount.
examples: The bill added up to $200.
These groceries will add up to almost sixty dollars.
These numbers just won’t add up.

senses.definition: to mean something; to signify or represent something; to result in something.
examples: All this adds up to trouble!
I don’t understand. What does all this add up to?
If you think about it carefully, these facts add up perfectly.

senses.definition: to talk to or write to a person, using a particular title.
examples: They addressed Abraham Lincoln as “Mr. President.”
A physician is usually addressed as “Doctor.”

senses.definition: to treat a person you are talking with in a particular manner.
examples: You should address him as your equal.
Do not address me as your superior.

senses.definition: to suggest that something not be done.
examples: I advised against quitting work early.
Lisa always advises against hasty actions.

senses.definition: to supply someone with a suggestion of not doing something.
examples: I advised Bill against quitting his job.
Lisa advised Tom against doing it.

headword: an affinity for someone or something

senses.definition: a strong preference for something; a strong liking for something.
examples: Cats have an affinity for seafood.
Mary’s affinity for classical music accounts for her large collection of recordings.

senses.definition: easily frightened; always frightened, timid, or suspicious.
examples: After Tom was robbed, he was even afraid of his own shadow.
Jane has always been a shy child. She has been afraid of her own shadow since she was three.

senses.definition: in a manner that is just barely adequate; poorly.
examples: He thanked me—after a fashion—for my help.
Oh, yes, I can swim, after a fashion.

senses.definition: anyway; in spite of what had been decided.
senses.notes: Often refers to a change in plans or a reversal of plans.
examples: Mary had planned to go to the bank first, but she came here after all.
It looks like Tom will go to law school after all.

senses.definition: remember; consider the fact that.
examples: Don’t punish Tommy! After all, he’s only three years old!
After all, we really didn’t hurt anyone!

headword: after all is said and done

senses.definition: when everything is settled or concluded; finally.
senses.notes: See also when all is said and done.
examples: After all was said and done, it was a lovely party.
After all is said and done, it will turn out just as I said.

senses.definition: after the regular closing time; after any normal or regular time, such as one’s bedtime.
examples: John was arrested in a bar after hours.
The soldier was caught sneaking into the barracks after hours.
John got a job sweeping floors in the bank after hours.

senses.definition: after something has happened; after something, especially a crime, has taken place.
examples: John is always making excuses after the fact.
Remember to lock your car whenever you leave it. If it’s stolen, there is nothing you can do after the fact.

headword: after the fashion of someone or something

senses.definition: in the manner or style of someone or something.
examples: She walks down the street after the fashion of a grand lady.
The church was built after the fashion of an English cathedral.

senses.definition: repeatedly; again and even more.
examples: I like going to the beach, and I will go back again and again.
He knocked on the door again and again until I finally answered.

senses.definition: without a person’s consent or agreement.
examples: You cannot force me to come with you against my will!
Against their will, the men were made to stand up against the wall and be searched.

senses.definition: in a race with time; in a great hurry to get something done before a particular time.
examples: Bill set a new track record, running against the clock. He lost the actual race, however.
In a race against the clock, they rushed the special medicine to the hospital.

senses.definition: having ideas or attitudes that are too advanced to be acceptable to or appreciated by the society in which one is living.
examples: People buy that artist’s work now, but his paintings were laughed at when he was alive. He was ahead of his time.
Mary’s grandmother was ahead of her time in wanting to study medicine.

senses.definition: having done something before the time listed on the schedule.
examples: I want to be able to finish the job ahead of schedule.
We don’t have to rush because we are ahead of schedule.

senses.definition: being early; having an advantage over a situation; having done more than necessary.
examples: Whenever we go to a movie, we show up ahead of the game and have to wait.
Bill has to study math very hard to keep ahead of the game.
Bob does extra work so he’s always ahead of the game.

senses.definition: beforehand; before the announced time.
examples: If you show up ahead of time, you will have to wait.
Be there ahead of time if you want to get a good seat.

senses.definition: to help someone; to incite someone to do something that is wrong.
examples: He was scolded for aiding and abetting the boys who were fighting.
It’s illegal to aid and abet a thief.

senses.definition: to mean to do something; to intend to do something in the future.
examples: I aim to paint the house as soon as I can find a brush.
He aims to take a few days off and go fishing.

senses.definition: Isn’t that just the way it is?; I agree with you completely.
examples: A: Things aren’t the way they used to be in the good old days. B: Ain’t it the truth?
A: You just can’t buy good shoes anymore. B: Ain’t it the truth?

headword: air one’s dirty linen in public
altForms: wash one’s dirty linen in public

senses.definition: to discuss private or embarrassing matters in public, especially when quarreling.
senses.notes: This linen refers to sheets and tablecloths or other soiled cloth.
examples: John’s mother had asked him repeatedly not to air the family’s dirty linen in public.
Mr. and Mrs. Johnson are arguing again. Why must they always air their dirty linen in public?
Jean will talk to anyone about her financial problems. Why does she wash her dirty linen in public?

senses.definition: to complain; to make a public complaint.
examples: I know how you feel, John, but it isn’t necessary to air your grievances over and over.
I know you’re busy, sir, but I must air my grievances. This matter is very serious.

senses.definition: well and healthy.
examples: JANE: How is Bill? MARY: Oh, he’s alive and kicking.
The last time I saw Tom, he was alive and well.

senses.definition: covered with, filled with, or active with people or things.
examples: Look! Ants everywhere. The floor is alive with ants!
When we got to the ballroom, the place was alive with dancing.
The campground was alive with campers from all over the country.

senses.definition: everyone; one and all.
examples: Cold drinks were served to all and sundry.
All and sundry came to the village fair.

senses.definition: going somewhere not by a direct route; going way out of the way [to get somewhere]; by a long and circuitous route.
examples: We had to go all around Robin Hood’s barn to get to the little town.
She walked all around Robin Hood’s barn looking for a shop that sold Finnish glassware.

senses.definition: suddenly.
examples: All at once the chair broke, and Bob fell to the floor.
All at once she tripped on a stone.

senses.definition: all at the same time.
examples: The entire group spoke all at once.
They were trying to cook dinner, clean house, and paint the closet all at once.

senses.definition: confused; lost and bewildered.
examples: Mary is all at sea about getting married.
When it comes to higher math, John is totally at sea.

senses.definition: troubled; confused; in a mess.
examples: Look at you! You’re really all balled up!
John is all balled up because his car was stolen.
Of course this typewriter won’t work. It’s all balled up.

senses.definition: all fun and pleasure; easy and pleasant.
senses.notes: Skittles is the game of ninepins, a game similar to bowling.
examples: Life isn’t all beer and skittles, you know!
For Sam, college was beer and skittles. He wasted a lot of time and money.

senses.definition: improved; cured.
examples: My leg was sore, but it’s all better now.
I fell off my tricycle and bumped my knee. Mommy kissed it, and it’s all better now.

senses.definition: throughout the day; during the entire day.
examples: We waited for you at the station all day long.
I can’t keep smiling all day long.

senses.definition: dressed in one’s best clothes; dressed formally.
examples: We’re all dressed up to go out to dinner.
I really hate to get all dressed up just to go somewhere to eat.

senses.definition: good in spite of the way it seems now; better than you think.
senses.notes: Often said when someone dies after a serious illness.
examples: I’m very sorry to hear of the death of your aunt. Perhaps it’s for the best.
I didn’t get into the college I wanted, but I couldn’t afford it anyway. It’s probably all for the best.

senses.definition: used up; finished; over with.
examples: Oh, the strawberry jelly is all gone.
We used to have wonderful parties, but those days are all gone.

senses.definition: part of what is expected; typical or normal.
examples: I don’t particularly like to cook, but it’s all in a day’s work.
Putting up with rude customers isn’t pleasant, but it’s all in a day’s work.
Cleaning up after other people is all in a day’s work for a chambermaid.

senses.definition: at some future time; in good time; soon.
senses.notes: This phrase is used to encourage people to be patient and wait quietly.
examples: When will the baby be born? All in good time.
MARY: I’m starved! When will Bill get here with the pizza? TOM: All in good time, Mary, all in good time.

senses.definition: spoken rapidly, usually while one is very excited.
examples: Ann said all in one breath, “Hurry, quick! The parade is coming!”
Jane was in a play, and she was so excited that she said her whole speech in one breath.
Tom can say the alphabet all in one breath.

senses.definition: safely; without damage.
examples: Her son come home from school all in one piece, even though he had been in a fight.
The package was handled carelessly, but the vase inside arrived all in one piece.

senses.definition: restricted to one’s own family, as with private or embarrassing information.
examples: Don’t tell anyone else. Please keep it all in the family.
He only told his brother because he wanted it to remain in the family.

senses.definition: being serious for a moment; in all seriousness.
examples: I know I laugh at him but, joking aside, he’s a very clever scientist.
I know I threatened to leave and go round the world, but, joking aside, I need a vacation.

headword: all kinds of someone or something

senses.definition: a great number of people or things; a great amount of something, especially money.
examples: There were all kinds of people there, probably thousands.
The Smith family has all kinds of money.

headword: all manner of someone or something

senses.definition: all types of people or things.
examples: We saw all manner of people there. They came from every country in the world.
They were selling all manner of things in the country store.

senses.definition: throughout the whole night.
examples: I couldn’t sleep all night long.
John was sick all night long.

senses.definition: suddenly.
examples: All of a sudden, lightning struck the tree we were sitting under.
I felt a sharp pain in my side all of a sudden.

senses.definition: everything or nothing at all.
examples: Sally would not accept only part of the money. She wanted all or nothing.
I can’t bargain over trifles. I will have to have all or nothing.

senses.definition: time to choose to do something or not to do it.
examples: It was all or nothing. Tim had to jump off the truck or risk drowning when the truck went into the water.
Jane stood at the door of the airplane and checked her parachute. It was all or nothing now. She had to jump or be looked upon as a coward.

senses.definition: a very good and thorough effort.
senses.notes: See also make an all-out effort.
examples: We need an all-out effort to get this job done on time.
The government began an all-out effort to reduce the federal budget.

senses.definition: total war, as opposed to small, warlike acts or threats of war.
examples: We are now concerned about all-out war in the Middle East.
Threats of all-out war caused many tourists to leave the country immediately.

senses.definition: starting over completely again; going through something completely yet another time.
examples: Do I have to go through this all over again?
Please start over again for those who came in late.

senses.definition: essentially decided and concluded.
senses.notes: An elaboration of all over, which means “finished.”
examples: The last goal was made just as the final whistle sounded. Tom said, “Well, it’s all over but the shouting.”
Tom worked hard in college and graduated last month. When he got his diploma, he said, “It’s all over but the shouting.”

senses.definition: everywhere.
examples: Grass grows all over the earth.
It’s the same way all over the world.

senses.definition: everywhere; in all parts of a particular location.
examples: Tom, stop leaving your dirty clothes all over the place.
We keep finding this kind of problem all over the place.

senses.definition: everywhere in town.
examples: Our dog got loose and ran all over town.
Jane looked all over town for a dress to wear to the party.

senses.definition: known to everyone.
examples: Now keep this a secret. I don’t want it all over town.
In a short time the secret was known all over town.

senses.definition: well, good, or okay, but not excellent.
senses.notes: Informal. This phrase has all the uses that okay has.
examples: I was a little sick, but now I’m all right.
His work is all right, but nothing to brag about.
All right, it’s time to go.

senses.definition: beyond a doubt; as the evidence shows.
examples: The dog’s dead all right. It hasn’t moved at all.
The train’s late all right. It hasn’t been late in months.

senses.definition: hooray.
senses.notes: An exclamation of joy or encouragement.
examples: The Bears won! All right!
All right! That’s the way to do it!

senses.definition: That’s it for you!; That’s the last chance for you!
senses.notes: Juvenile and informal. Usually said by a child who is angry with a playmate.
examples: All right for you, John. See if I ever play with you again.
All right for you! I’m telling your mother what you did.

senses.definition: agreeable to someone.
examples: If you want to ruin your life and marry Tom, it’s all right with me.
I’ll see if it’s all right with my father.

senses.definition: ready to begin; okay.
senses.notes: See also (all) set to do something.
examples: TOM: Is everything all right? JANE: Yes, we are all set.
We are ready to leave now. Are you all set?

senses.definition: prepared or ready to do something.
examples: Are you set to cook the steaks?
Yes, the fire is ready, and I’m all set to start.

senses.definition: totally ruined.
examples: My car is all shot to hell and can’t be depended on.
This knife is shot to hell. I need a sharper one.

senses.definition: very sweet, innocent, and helpful.
examples: She was mad at first, but after a while, she was all sweetness and light.
At the reception, the whole family was all sweetness and light, but they argued and fought after the guests left.

senses.definition: everything is ready.
senses.notes: Informal. Originally said when preparing to launch a rocket.
examples: The rocket is ready to blast off—all systems are go.
TOM: Are you guys ready to start playing? BILL: Sure, Tom, all systems go.

senses.definition: talking about doing something, but never actually doing it.
examples: The car needs washing, but Bill is all talk and no action on this matter.
Bill keeps saying he’ll get a job soon, but he’s all talk and no action.
Bill won’t do it. He’s just all talk.

headword: All that glitters is not gold.

senses.definition: Many attractive and alluring things have no value.
examples: The used car looked fine but didn’t run well at all. “Ah, yes,” thought Bill, “all that glitters is not gold.”
When Mary was disappointed about losing Tom, Jane reminded her, “All that glitters is not gold.”

senses.definition: throughout the whole day.
examples: They kept at their work all the livelong day.
Bob just sat by the creek fishing, all the livelong day.

senses.definition: in current fashion.
examples: A new dance called the “floppy disc” is all the rage.
Wearing a rope instead of a belt is all the rage these days.

senses.definition: nevertheless; anyhow.
examples: They were told not to bring presents, but they brought them all the same.
His parents said no, but John went out just the same.

senses.definition: of no consequence to someone; immaterial to someone.
examples: It’s all the same to me whether we win or lose.
If it’s just the same to you, I’d rather walk than ride.
If it’s all the same, I’d rather you didn’t smoke.

senses.definition: throughout a specific period of time.
examples: Bill was stealing money for the last two years, and Tom knew it all the time.
Throughout December and January, Jane had two jobs all the time.

senses.definition: at all times; continuously.
examples: Your blood keeps flowing all the time.
That electric motor runs all the time.

senses.definition: repeatedly; habitually.
examples: She keeps a handkerchief in her hand all the time.
She hums softly all the time.

senses.definition: from the beginning to the end; the entire distance, from start to finish.
senses.notes: See also go all the way (with someone).
examples: The ladder reaches all the way to the top of the house.
I walked all the way home.

senses.definition: awkward and clumsy, especially with one’s hands.
examples: Poor Bob can’t play the piano at all. He’s all thumbs.
Mary is all thumbs when it comes to gardening.

senses.definition: totaled up; including all parts.
examples: All told, he earned about $700 last week.
All told, he has many fine characteristics.

senses.definition: for the best; for one’s benefit.
examples: He missed the train, but it was all to the good because the train had a wreck.
It was all to the good that he died without suffering.

senses.definition: tired out; worn out.
examples: Poor John worked so hard that he’s all tuckered out.
Look at that little baby sleeping. She’s really tuckered out.

senses.definition: all social, economic, and ethnic groups.
examples: We saw people there from all walks of life.
The people who came to the art exhibit represented all walks of life.

senses.definition: good; desirable.
examples: It’s well and good that you’re here on time. I was afraid you’d be late again.
It’s all well and good that you’re passing English, but what about math and science?

senses.definition: mistaken; wrongheaded; on the wrong track.
examples: It’s not that way, John. You’re all wet.
If you think that prices will come down, you’re all wet.

headword: all wool and a yard wide

senses.definition: genuine; genuinely warmhearted and friendly.
senses.notes: Informal and folksy. Refers to cloth that is 100 percent wool and exactly one yard wide.
examples: Old Bob is a true gentleman—all wool and a yard wide.
The banker, hardly all wool and a yard wide, wouldn’t give us a loan.

headword: All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy.

senses.definition: One should have recreation as well as work.
senses.notes: Proverb. Jack does not refer to anyone in particular. The phrase can be used for persons of either sex.
examples: Stop reading that book and go out and play! All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy.
The doctor told Mr. Jones to stop working on weekends and start playing golf, because all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy.

senses.definition: excited and agitated about something.
senses.notes: See also get worked up (over something).
examples: Tom is all worked up over the threat of a new war.
Don’t get all worked up about something that you can’t do anything about.
Bill is all worked up again. It’s bad for his health.

senses.definition: throughout all the seasons of the year; during the entire year.
examples: The public swimming pool is enclosed so that it can be used all year round.
In the South they can grow flowers all year round.

senses.definition: to plan on having enough of something (such as food, space, etc.) for someone.
examples: Mary is bringing Bill on the picnic, so be sure to allow for him when buying the food.
Allow for an extra person when setting the table tonight.

senses.definition: to plan on the possibility of something.
examples: Allow for a few rainy days on your vacation.
Be sure to allow for future growth when you plant the rosebushes.

senses.definition: An event that has a good ending is considered good, even if some things went wrong along the way.
senses.notes: Proverb. This is the name of a play by Shakespeare.
examples: I’m glad you finally got here, even though your car had a flat tire on the way. Oh, well. All’s well that ends well.
The groom was late for the wedding, but everything worked out all right. All’s well that ends well.

senses.definition: the U.S. dollar, worshiped as a god; money, viewed as more important and powerful than anything else.
examples: Bill was a slave to the almighty dollar.
It’s the almighty dollar that drives the whole country.

senses.definition: having been so angry or distraught as to nearly lose one’s temper, composure, or control.
examples: I was so mad, I almost lost it.
When he saw the dent in his fender, he almost lost it.

senses.definition: in addition to someone or something; together with someone or something.
examples: Jane went to the mall along with David.
I ate some chocolates along with some fruit.

senses.definition: as compared to a person or a thing.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. The things being compared need not be beside one another.
examples: Our car looks quite small alongside of theirs.
My power of concentration is quite limited alongside of yours.

senses.definition: both the beginning and the end; the essentials, from the beginning to the end; everything, from the beginning to the end.
senses.notes: Refers to the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.
examples: He was forced to learn the alpha and omega of corporate law in order to even talk to the lawyers.
He loved her deeply; she was his alpha and omega.

senses.definition: to be or to become valuable or successful.
examples: Most parents hope that their children will amount to something.
I put $200 in the bank, and I hope it will amount to something in twenty years.

senses.definition: to be the same as something; to have the same effect as something.
examples: Borrowing can be the same as stealing. If the owner does not know what you have borrowed, it amounts to the same thing.
Beer, wine. They come to the same thing if you drink and drive.

senses.definition: plus between 1 and 99 cents more.
examples: The book cost $12.49. That’s twelve dollars and change.
Subway fare is now one dollar and change.

senses.definition: continuing talking in the same way; and so on.
examples: She told me everything about her kids and so on and so forth.
I heard about problems at work and so forth.

senses.definition: with extra left over; with more than is needed.
senses.notes: With something, time, room, money, plenty, etc.
examples: I had as much flour as I needed with something to spare.
Fred said he should have enough cash to last the week—with money to spare.

senses.definition: and similar things or people.
examples: I eat hamburgers, hot dogs, and the like.
I bought shirts, pants, socks, and the like.

senses.definition: and even more; more than has been mentioned.
examples: John is going to have to run like a deer and then some to win this race.
The cook put the amount of salt called for into the soup and then some.

senses.definition: a catch phrase said when someone makes a comment or interrupts.
examples: Jane and Bill were discussing business when Bob interrupted to offer an opinion. “Another country heard from,” said Jane.
In the middle of the discussion, the baby started crying. “Another country heard from,” said Tom.

headword: (another) nail in someone’s or something’s coffin

senses.definition: something that will harm or destroy someone or something.
examples: Every word of criticism that Bob said about the boss was a nail in his coffin.
Losing the export order was the final nail in the company’s coffin.

senses.definition: to assume responsibility for something.
examples: John had to answer for the theft of the bicycle since it was found at his house.
Someday we’ll all have to answer for our wrongdoings.

senses.definition: to fit or suit someone’s purpose.
examples: This piece of wood will answer my purpose quite nicely.
The new car serves our purpose perfectly.

senses.definition: to go to the door to see who is there.
senses.notes: [after hearing the doorbell or a knock]
examples: Would you please answer the door? I am busy.
I wish someone would answer the door. I can’t wait all day.

senses.definition: to explain to someone; to justify one’s actions to someone.
examples: If John cannot behave properly, he’ll have to answer to me.
The car thief will have to answer to the judge.

senses.definition: When one is in difficulties one must accept any way out, whether one likes the solution or not.
examples: I don’t want to live with my parents, but it’s a case of any port in a storm. I can’t find an apartment.
He hates his job, but he can’t get another. Any port in a storm, you know.

senses.definition: to act a certain part in a play, opera, etc.
examples: Madame Smith-Franklin appeared as Carmen at the City Opera last season.
The actor refused to appear as a villain in the play.

senses.definition: to appear suddenly, without warning.
senses.notes: Almost the same as come out of nowhere.
examples: A huge bear appeared out of nowhere and roared and threatened us.
A butler appeared out of nowhere and took our coats.

senses.definition: someone’s favorite person or thing; a boyfriend or a girlfriend.
examples: Tom is the apple of Mary’s eye. She thinks he’s great.
John’s new stereo is the apple of his eye.

senses.definition: a pair of people or things representing two entities that are not similar.
examples: You can’t talk about Fred and Ted in the same breath! They’re apples and oranges.
Talking about her current book and her previous best-seller is like comparing apples and oranges.

headword: arguing for the sake of arguing
altForms: arguing for the sake of argument

senses.definition: simply arguing to be difficult or contrary.
examples: You are just arguing for the sake of arguing. You don’t even know what the issue is.
He is annoying, because he is always arguing for the sake of argument.

senses.definition: linked or hooked together by the arms.
examples: The two lovers walked arm in arm down the street.
Arm in arm, the line of dancers kicked high, and the audience roared its approval.

senses.definition: said of an armed person who is suspected of a crime and has not been captured and who is likely to resist arrest.
senses.notes: This is a warning to police officers.
examples: Max is at large, presumed to be armed and dangerous.
The suspect has killed once and is armed and dangerous.

senses.definition: heavily armed with deadly weapons.
examples: The bank robber was armed to the teeth when he was caught.
There are too many guns around. The entire country is armed to the teeth.

senses.definition: continuously for twenty-four hours at a time; all day and all night.
examples: The priceless jewels were guarded around the clock.
Grandfather was so sick that he had to have nurses round the clock.

senses.definition: constant; day and night.
examples: Grandfather required around-the-clock care.
I tuned into the around-the-clock news station.

senses.definition: to plan an event so as to include another person or persons.
examples: Jane arranged a meeting with Ann.
Bill arranged to go to the station with Tom and Mary.
forms: arrange to do something with someone

senses.definition: to get someone’s consent for something.
examples: Mary arranged the entire affair with her employer.
The new mother arranged the christening with the pastor.

headword: as a duck takes to water

senses.definition: easily and naturally.
examples: She took to singing just as a duck takes to water.
The baby adapted to bottle-feeding as a duck takes to water.

senses.definition: usually; almost always.
examples: He can be found in his office as a general rule.
As a general rule, Jane plays golf on Wednesdays.
As a rule, things tend to get less busy after supper time.

senses.definition: as the last choice; if everything else fails.
examples: Call the doctor at home only as a last resort.
As a last resort, she will perform surgery.

headword: as alike as (two) peas in a pod

senses.definition: very similar.
senses.notes: Compare this with like (two) peas in a pod.
examples: The twins are as alike as two peas in a pod.
These two books are as alike as peas in a pod.

senses.definition: normally; as a normal procedure.
examples: The nurse takes your temperature as a matter of course.
You are expected to make your own bed as a matter of course.

senses.definition: actually; in addition to what has been said; in reference to what has been said.
examples: As a matter of fact, John came into the room while you were talking about him.
I’m not a poor worker. As a matter of fact, I’m very efficient.

senses.definition: as a comment; as a comment that is not supposed to be heard by everyone.
examples: At the wedding, Tom said as an aside, “The bride doesn’t look well.”
At the ballet, Billy said as an aside to his mother, “I hope the dancers fall off the stage!”

senses.definition: because of something that has happened.
examples: As a result of the accident, Tom couldn’t walk for six months.
We couldn’t afford to borrow money for a house as a result of the rise in interest rates.

senses.definition: symbolic of something, especially of gratitude; as a memento of something.
examples: He gave me a rose as a token of the time we spent together.
Here, take this $100 as a token of my appreciation.
I can’t thank you enough. Please accept this money as a token.

headword: (as) awkward as a cow on a crutch
altForms: (as) awkward as a cow on roller skates

senses.definition: very awkward.
examples: When Lulu was pregnant, she was awkward as a cow on a crutch.
Tom will never be a gymnast. He’s as awkward as a cow on roller skates!

senses.definition: as bad as reported; as bad as it seems.
examples: Come on! Nothing could be as bad as all that.
Stop crying. It can’t be as bad as all that.

senses.definition: completely bald.
examples: If Tom’s hair keeps receding like that, he’ll be bald as a coot by the time he’s thirty.
FRED: Now, I’ll admit my hair is thinning a little on the top, but— JANE: Thinning? You’re not thinning, you’re as bald as a baby’s backside!

senses.definition: promising evil; very threatening.
examples: The wind’s moan was as baleful as death.
His voice sounded baleful as death.

senses.definition: very big, usually referring to a space of some kind.
examples: You should see Bob’s living room. It’s as big as all outdoors.
The new movie theater is as big as all outdoors.

altForms: (as) big as life and twice as ugly

senses.definition: an exaggerated way of saying that a person or a thing appeared in a particular place.
senses.notes: Folksy. The second phrase is slang.
examples: The little child just stood there as big as life and laughed very hard.
I opened the door, and there was Tom as big as life.
I came home and found this cat in my chair, as big as life and twice as ugly.

senses.definition: black.
examples: I don’t want to go down to the cellar. It’s as black as a skillet down there.
The bruise turned black as a skillet.

headword: (as) black as a stack of black cats

senses.definition: very black.
examples: I’m scared to go into that closet. It’s as black as a stack of black cats in there.
Her hair was black as a stack of black cats.

senses.definition: extremely dirty.
senses.notes: The sweep is a chimney sweep.
examples: After playing in the mud all morning, the children were as black as sweeps.
When Jane came in from working on her car, Alan told her, “Wash before you come to the dinner table. You’re black as a sweep!”

senses.definition: completely black.
examples: Mark’s eyes were as black as coal.
The stranger’s clothes were all black as coal.

senses.definition: very dark and black.
examples: The ink in this pen is black as night.
During the eclipse, my room was as black as night.

senses.definition: as evil as described.
examples: The landlord is not as black as he is painted. He seems quite generous.
Young people are rarely black as they are painted in the media.

senses.definition: very black; very dark.
examples: The night was as black as pitch.
The rocks seemed black as pitch against the silver sand.

headword: (as) black as the ace of spades

senses.definition: very black.
examples: The car was long and shiny and black as the ace of spades.
Jill’s shoes are black as the ace of spades.

senses.definition: with imperfect sight; blind.
examples: My grandmother is as blind as a bat.
I’m getting blind as a bat. I can hardly read this page.

senses.definition: very bold; bold to the point of rudeness.
examples: Lisa marched into the manager’s office, bold as brass, and demanded her money back.
The tiny kitten, as bold as brass, began eating the dog’s food right in front of the dog’s nose.

senses.definition: intelligent; quickminded.
examples: Why, Mrs. Green, your little girl is as bright as a button.
You can’t fool Mandy. She may be only six years old, but she’s bright as a button.

senses.definition: bright and clean; shiny.
examples: After Nora cleaned the house, it was as bright as a new pin.
My kitchen floor is bright as a new pin since I started using this new floor wax.

senses.definition: very broad.
examples: Jim’s backside is as broad as a barn door.
The weight-lifter’s chest was broad as a barn door.

senses.definition: very busy.
examples: I don’t have time to talk to you. I’m as busy as a beaver.
You don’t look busy as a beaver to me.
Whenever there is a holiday, we are all as busy as bees getting things ready.

headword: (as) busy as a cat on a hot tin roof

senses.definition: full of lively activity; very busy.
examples: I’m afraid I can’t go to lunch with you on Saturday; I’ll be busy as a cat on a hot tin roof, between working overtime and the two parties I have to go to.
Jerry’s three parttime jobs kept him as busy as a cat on a hot tin roof.

senses.definition: not busy at all.
examples: TOM: I can’t go with you. I’m busy. JANE: Yeah. You’re as busy as a hibernating bear.
He lounged on the sofa all day, busy as a hibernating bear.

senses.definition: very busy.
examples: My boss keeps me as busy as a one-armed paperhanger.
I’ve got plenty of work. I’m busy as a one-armed paperhanger.

senses.definition: very busy; crowded with customers or other people.
senses.notes: Refers to Grand Central Station in New York City.
examples: This house is as busy as Grand Central Station.
When the tourist season starts, this store is busy as Grand Central Station.

headword: (as) busy as popcorn on a skillet

senses.definition: very active.
examples: She rushed around, as busy as popcorn on a skillet.
Prying into other folks’ business kept him busy as popcorn on a skillet.

headword: (as) calm as a toad in the sun

senses.definition: very calm and content.
examples: She smiled, as calm as a toad in the sun.
Nothing ruffles him. He’s calm as a toad in the sun.

senses.definition: very clean.
senses.notes: Clean can mean “innocent,” as in the first example.
examples: John had faith that he would not be convicted for the robbery, since he had been clean as a hound’s tooth since getting out of prison.
After his mother scrubbed him thoroughly, James was as clean as a hound’s tooth.

senses.definition: very clean.
examples: The wound isn’t infected. It’s clean as a whistle.
I thought the car would be filthy, but it was as clean as a whistle.

senses.definition: very clear and easy to hear.
examples: I fixed the radio, so now all the stations come in clear as a bell.
Through the wall, I could hear the neighbors talking, just as clear as a bell.

senses.definition: very clear; transparent.
examples: The stream was as clear as crystal.
She cleaned the windowpane until it was clear as crystal.

senses.definition: very clear; easy to understand.
examples: The explanation was as clear as crystal.
Her lecture was not clear as crystal, but at least it was not dull.

senses.definition: not understandable.
examples: Your explanation is as clear as mud.
This doesn’t make sense. It’s clear as mud.

senses.definition: very clear.
examples: The weather is as clear as vodka.
The river wasn’t exactly as clear as vodka because it had just rained.

senses.definition: very understandable.
examples: Everything he said is as clear as vodka.
I understand what John said, but everything you say is clear as vodka.

headword: (as) close as two coats of paint

senses.definition: close and intimate.
examples: When Tom and Mary were kids, they were as close as two coats of paint.
All their lives, the cousins were close as two coats of paint.

headword: (as) cocky as the king of spades

senses.definition: boastful; overly proud.
examples: He’d challenge anyone to a fight. He’s as cocky as the king of spades.
She strutted in, cocky as the king of spades.

senses.definition: very cold; chilling.
examples: The wind was as cold as a witch’s caress.
She gave me a look as cold as a witch’s caress.

senses.definition: Very cold indeed.
senses.notes: Used to describe a person who is either physically or emotionally cold.
examples: Raymond took Joanna’s hand. It was cold as marble.
No one ever got a smile out of Caroline, who was as cold as marble.

senses.definition: very comfortable; very comforting and familiar.
examples: This old house is fine. It’s as comfortable as an old shoe.
That’s a great tradition—comfortable as an old shoe.

senses.definition: low class; uncouth.
examples: That trashy girl is just as common as an old shoe.
Jim may have money, but he’s common as an old shoe.

senses.definition: vulgar; ill-mannered.
examples: FRED: Did you notice Mr. Jones blowing his nose into the linen napkin at dinner? ELLEN: I’m not surprised. Everyone knows that the Joneses are as common as dirt.
Despite Jane’s efforts to imitate the manners of the upper class, the town’s leading families still considered her common as dirt.

senses.definition: very conceited; vain.
examples: Ever since he won that award, he’s been as conceited as a barber’s cat.
She’s stuck up all right—conceited as a barber’s cat.

senses.definition: calm and not agitated; with one’s wits about one.
examples: The captain remained as cool as a cucumber as the passengers boarded the lifeboats.
During the fire the homeowner was cool as a cucumber.

senses.definition: loony.
examples: TOM: Susan says she’s really the Queen of England. BILL: She’s crazy as a betsy bug.
Ever since his wife left him, Joe’s been acting as crazy as a betsy bug.

senses.definition: very silly; completely insane.
examples: If you think you can get away with that, you’re as crazy as a loon.
Poor old John is crazy as a loon.

senses.definition: loony.
examples: What’s wrong with Jim? He’s acting as crazy as a peach-orchard boar.
Mary’s been standing out on the street corner telling everybody the world’s about to end. Poor thing—she’s crazy as a peach-orchard boar.

headword: (as) crooked as a barrel of fishhooks

senses.definition: dishonest.
examples: Don’t play cards with him. He’s as crooked as a barrel of fishhooks.
After Jane cheated a few folks, word got around that she was crooked as a fishhook.

headword: (as) crooked as a dog’s hind leg

senses.definition: dishonest.
examples: Don’t trust John. He’s as crooked as a dog’s hind leg.
Mary says all politicians are crooked as a dog’s hind leg.

senses.definition: dead; no longer in existence.
examples: Yes, Adolf Hitler is really dead—as dead as a dodo.
That silly old idea is dead as a dodo.

senses.definition: dead.
examples: This fish is as dead as a doornail.
John kept twisting the chicken’s neck even though it was dead as a doornail.

senses.definition: very deaf; profoundly deaf.
examples: He can’t hear a thing you say. He’s as deaf as a post.
Our old dog is deaf as a post and he can’t see much either.

senses.definition: completely different.
examples: Although Bobby and Billy are twins, they are as different as night and day.
Birds and bats appear to be similar, but they are different as night and day.

senses.definition: very drunk.
examples: He came home drunk as a lord again.
She was as drunk as a lord by the time they left here.

senses.definition: completely dry.
examples: During the drought, the soil was as dry as a bone.
The dog’s water dish was dry as a bone.

senses.definition: very dry.
examples: The bread is as dry as dust.
When the leaves are dry as dust, they break into powder easily.

senses.definition: very dull; very boring.
examples: This book is as dry as dust. I am going to stop reading it.
Her lecture was dry as dust—just like her subject.

senses.definition: very uninteresting.
examples: I’m not surprised that he can’t find a partner. He’s as dull as dishwater.
Mr. Black’s speech was as dull as dishwater.

senses.definition: very easy.
examples: Making apple pie is as easy as ABC.
Calculus is easy as ABC.

senses.definition: very easy.
examples: Mountain climbing is as easy as pie.
Making a simple dress out of cotton cloth is easy as pie.

senses.definition: very easy; requiring no effort.
senses.notes: Informal. When a duck is cooked, it releases a lot of fat and juices, making a “soup” without effort.
examples: Finding your way to the shopping center is easy as duck soup.
Getting Bob to eat fried chicken is as easy as duck soup.

headword: (as) easy as falling off a log
altForms: (as) easy as rolling off a log

senses.definition: very easy.
examples: Passing that exam was as easy as falling off a log.
Getting out of jail was easy as rolling off a log.

senses.definition: very, very dull.
examples: This book is about as exciting as watching paint dry.
Listening to you is exciting as watching the paint dry.

senses.definition: to the limits of anyone’s knowledge.
senses.notes: Informal. The anyone can be replaced with a more specific noun or pronoun.
examples: As far as anyone knows, this is the last of the great herds of buffalo.
Far as I know, this is the best one.
These are the only keys to the house so far as anyone knows.

senses.definition: as much as something does, covers, or accomplishes.
senses.notes: Usually said of something that is inadequate.
examples: Your plan is fine as far as it goes. It doesn’t seem to take care of everything, though.
As far as it goes, this law is a good one. It should require stiffer penalties, however.

senses.definition: as much as possible; to whatever degree is possible.
examples: We must try, as far as possible, to get people to stop smoking in buses.
As far as possible, the police will issue tickets to all speeding drivers.
I’ll follow your instructions so far as possible.

headword: (as) far as someone or something is concerned
altForms: so far as someone or something is concerned

senses.definition: for all that someone cares; if someone is to make the decision.
examples: You can take your old dog and leave as far as I’m concerned.
Far as I’m concerned, you can get out and never come back.
So far as I’m concerned, you’re okay.

senses.definition: having to do with something; pertaining to something; as for something.
examples: This bill? As far as that’s concerned, the committee will have to take care of it.
As far as the roof’s concerned, it will just have to last another year.

senses.definition: exceptionally fat; grotesquely fat.
examples: If I don’t stop eating this cake, I’ll be fat as a pig!
You really ought to go on a diet; you’re as fat as a pig.

senses.definition: healthy and physically fit.
examples: Mary is as fit as a fiddle.
Tom used to be fit as a fiddle. Look at him now!

senses.definition: very flat.
senses.notes: Also used to describe someone’s chest or abdomen, referring to well-developed abdominal muscles or to small or absent breasts or pectoral development—in either sex.
examples: Jane was flat as a board until she was sixteen, when she suddenly blossomed.
The terrain in that part of the country is as flat as a board.

senses.definition: very flat.
examples: The punctured tire was as flat as a pancake.
Bobby squashed the ant flat as a pancake.

senses.definition: carefree; completely free.
examples: Jane is always happy and free as a bird.
The convict escaped from jail and was as free as a bird for two days.
In the summer I feel free as a bird.

senses.definition: completely free; without obligations or responsibilities.
examples: The day I got out of the army, I felt as free as air.
No, I’m not married. I don’t even have a girlfriend. I’m free as the air.

senses.definition: very fresh; fresh and alert.
examples: The morning dew was as fresh as a daisy.
Sally was fresh as a daisy and cheerful as could be.

senses.definition: very full of food or drink.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to a tick that has filled itself full of blood.
examples: Little Billy ate and ate until he was as tight as a tick.
Our cat drank the cream until he became full as a tick.

headword: (as) funny as a barrel of monkeys
altForms: more fun than a barrel of monkeys

senses.definition: very funny.
senses.notes: Almost the same as as much fun as a barrel of monkeys.
examples: Todd was as funny as a barrel of monkeys.
The entire evening was funny as a barrel of monkeys.
The party was more fun than a barrel of monkeys.

senses.definition: not funny at all.
examples: Your trick is about as funny as a crutch. Nobody thought it was funny.
The well-dressed lady slipped and fell in the gutter, which was funny as a crutch.

senses.definition: gaudy; colorful.
examples: Marie looked as gaudy as a butterfly in her new dress.
Michael’s scarf is gaudy as a butterfly.

senses.definition: very gentle.
examples: Don’t be afraid of Mr. Smith. He may look fierce, but he’s as gentle as a lamb.
Lisa was gentle as a lamb when dealing with children.

senses.definition: the same as being done; almost done.
senses.notes: Other past participles can replace done in this phrase: cooked, dead, finished, painted, typed, etc.
examples: This job is as good as done. It’ll just take another second.
Yes, sir, if you hire me to paint your house, it’s as good as painted.
When I hand my secretary a letter to be typed, I know that it’s as good as typed right then and there.

senses.definition: genuine; authentic.
examples: Mary’s promise is as good as gold.
Yes, this diamond is genuine—good as gold.

senses.definition: obedient to one’s promise; dependable in keeping one’s promises.
examples: He was as good as his word. He lent me the books as promised.
She said she would baby-sit and she was as good as her word.

senses.definition: very graceful.
examples: The boat glided out onto the lake as graceful as a swan.
Jane is graceful as a swan.

senses.definition: gruff; curt and unsociable.
examples: I hate to ask Erica questions; she’s always gruff as a bear.
I’m always as gruff as a bear before I’ve had my first cup of coffee.

senses.definition: happy and content.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples. Sometimes with additional phrases, such as in butter sauce or at high tide.
examples: Tom sat there smiling, as happy as a clam.
There they all sat, eating corn on the cob and looking happy as clams.

senses.definition: visibly happy and cheerful.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: Sally walked along whistling, as happy as a lark.
The children danced and sang, happy as larks.

senses.definition: very happy.
examples: We are both as happy as can be.
Bob was happy as can be when he won the lottery.

senses.definition: very hard.
examples: This cake is as hard as a rock!
I can’t drive a nail into this wood. It’s hard as stone.

senses.definition: very hard; cold and cruel.
senses.notes: Refers to the nails that are used with a hammer.
examples: The old loaf of bread was dried out and became as hard as nails.
Ann was unpleasant and hard as nails.

senses.definition: very high.
examples: The tree grew as high as a kite.
Our pet bird got outside and flew up high as the sky.

senses.definition: drunk or drugged.
examples: Bill drank beer until he got as high as a kite.
The thieves were high as the sky on drugs.

senses.definition: hoarse.
examples: After shouting at the team all afternoon, the coach was as hoarse as a crow.
JILL: Has Bob got a cold? JANE: No, he’s always hoarse as a crow.

senses.definition: very hot; burning hot.
examples: I’m afraid Betsy has a high fever. Her forehead is hot as fire.
In the summertime, the concrete sidewalks feel as hot as fire.

senses.definition: very hot.
examples: It’s as hot as hell outside. It must be near 100 degrees.
I hate to get into a car that has been parked in the sun. It’s hot as hell.

senses.definition: very hungry.
examples: I’m as hungry as a bear. I could eat anything!
Whenever I jog, I get hungry as a bear.

senses.definition: very hungry.
examples: Is there anything to eat? I’ve been out hoeing my garden all morning, and I’m as hungry as a hunter!
We’d better have a big meal ready by the time Tommy gets home; he’s always hungry as a hunter after soccer practice.

senses.definition: guiltless; naive.
examples: “Hey! You can’t throw me in jail,” cried the robber. “I’m innocent as a lamb.”
Look at the baby, as innocent as a lamb.

senses.definition: as one might say.
senses.notes: Sometimes used to qualify an assertion that may not sound reasonable.
examples: He carefully constructed, as it were, a huge sandwich.
The Franklins live in a small, as it were, exquisite house.

senses.definition: in person; actually, and sometimes surprisingly, present at a place.
examples: I thought Jack was away, but there he was as large as life.
Jean was not expected to appear, but she turned up large as life.

senses.definition: of little weight.
examples: Sally dieted until she was as light as a feather.
Of course I can lift the box. It’s light as a feather.

senses.definition: probably; with an even chance either way.
examples: He will as likely as not arrive without warning.
Likely as not, the game will be canceled.

senses.definition: since; because.
examples: As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread.
So long as you’re here, please stay for dinner.

senses.definition: if; only if.
examples: You may have dessert so long as you eat all your vegetables.
You can go out this evening as long as you promise to be home by midnight.

senses.definition: for a specified length of time.
examples: You may stay out as long as you like.
I didn’t go to school as long as Bill did.

senses.definition: of equal length.
examples: Is this one as long as that one?
This snake is as long as a car!

senses.definition: by good or bad luck; as it turned out; by chance.
examples: As luck would have it, we had a flat tire.
As luck would have it, the check came in the mail today.

senses.definition: crazy.
senses.notes: From the crazy character called the Hatter in Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.
examples: Poor old John is as mad as a hatter.
All these screaming children are driving me mad as a hatter.

senses.definition: angry.
senses.notes: This is a misunderstanding of mad in the first sense. Folksy. The first as can be omitted.
examples: You make me so angry! I’m as mad as a hatter.
John can’t control his temper. He’s always mad as a hatter.

senses.definition: angry.
examples: You make me so angry. I’m as mad as a hornet.
Jane can get mad as a hornet when somebody criticizes her.

senses.definition: crazy.
senses.notes: From the name of a character in Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.
examples: Sally is getting as mad as a March hare.
My Uncle Bill is mad as a March hare.

senses.definition: angry.
examples: Bob was screaming and shouting—as mad as a wet hen.
What you said made Mary mad as a wet hen.

senses.definition: very angry.
examples: He made his wife as mad as hell.
Those terrorists make me mad as hell.

senses.definition: meek; quiet and docile.
examples: Only an hour after their argument, Joe went to Elizabeth and, meek as a lamb, asked her to forgive him.
Betsy terrorizes the other children, but she’s as meek as a lamb around her elders.

senses.definition: cheerful.
examples: Mary is as merry as a cricket whenever she has company come to call.
George is such a pleasant companion; he’s usually merry as a cricket.

headword: (as) merry as the day is long

senses.definition: very happy and carefree.
examples: The little children are as merry as the day is long.
Only on vacation are we merry as the day is long.

headword: as much fun as a barrel of monkeys

senses.definition: a great deal of fun.
senses.notes: Almost the same as (as) funny as a barrel of monkeys.
examples: Roger is as much fun as a barrel of monkeys.
The circus was as much fun as a barrel of monkeys.

senses.definition: naked.
examples: “Billy,” called Mrs. Franklin, “get back in the house and get some clothes on. You’re as naked as a jaybird.”
Tom had to get naked as a jaybird for the doctor to examine him.

senses.definition: neat and orderly.
examples: Brad is such a good housekeeper; his apartment is always as neat as a pin.
Joanne certainly is well-organized. Her desk is neat as a pin.

senses.definition: silly; crazy.
senses.notes: Slang. A fruitcake usually has lots of nuts in it.
examples: Whenever John goes to a party, he gets as nutty as a fruitcake.
Sally has been acting as nutty as a fruitcake lately.

senses.definition: very old.
examples: The children think their mother’s as old as the hills, but she’s only forty.
That song’s not new. It’s old as the hills.

senses.definition: extremely pale.
senses.notes: The reference to death gives this phrase ominous connotations.
examples: Rita was as pale as death when she came out of the doctor’s office.
What’s the matter? You’re pale as death!

senses.definition: very patient.
senses.notes: Refers to a character in the Bible.
examples: If you want to teach young children, you must be as patient as Job.
The director who is working with that temperamental actor must have the patience of Job.

senses.definition: phony; bogus.
examples: This guy’s as phony as a three-dollar bill.
The whole deal stinks. It’s as phony as a three-dollar bill.

senses.definition: obvious; very clear.
examples: JILL: Why does the Senator always vote for measures that would help the tobacco industry? JANE: It’s as plain as a pikestaff—because there are a lot of tobacco growers in his district, and he wants them to vote for him.
FRED: I have a suspicion that Marcia is upset with me. ALAN: A suspicion? Come on, Fred, that’s been plain as a pikestaff for quite some time!

senses.definition: very plain and simple.
examples: Although his face was as plain as day, his smile made him look interesting and friendly.
Our house is plain as day, but it’s comfortable.

senses.definition: clear and understandable.
examples: The lecture was as plain as day. No one had to ask questions.
His statement was plain as day.

headword: (as) plain as the nose on one’s face

senses.definition: obvious; clearly evident.
examples: What do you mean you don’t understand? It’s as plain as the nose on your face.
Your guilt is plain as the nose on your face.

senses.definition: very pleased; very pleased with oneself.
senses.notes: Refers to the character Punch in [English] Punch and Judy puppet shows. Punch is sometimes capitalized.
examples: Wally was as pleased as punch when he won the prize.
She seems pleased as punch, but she knows she doesn’t deserve the award.

senses.definition: very poor.
examples: My aunt is as poor as a church mouse.
The Browns are poor as church mice.

senses.definition: very pretty.
examples: Sweet little Mary is as pretty as a picture.
Their new house is pretty as a picture.

senses.definition: very proud; haughty.
examples: John is so arrogant. He’s as proud as a peacock.
The new father was proud as a peacock.

senses.definition: pure and virginal.
examples: JILL: Sue must have gone to bed with every man in town. JANE: And I always thought she was as pure as the driven snow.
Robert was notoriously promiscuous, but tried to convince all his girlfriends that he was pure as the driven snow.

senses.definition: very strange.
examples: Today I saw a woman pushing a lawn mower down the street and singing to it as she went. I thought she was queer as a three-dollar bill.
JILL: In all the years I’ve known him, Mike has never had a suit and he goes barefoot. FRED: That’s because he’s as queer as a three-dollar bill.

senses.definition: very quickly.
examples: As quick as a wink, the thief took the lady’s purse.
I’ll finish this work quick as a wink.
The dog grabbed the meat as quick as a flash.
The summer days went by quick as a flash.

senses.definition: very quickly; very fast.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also like greased lightning.
examples: Jane can really run. She’s as quick as greased lightning.
Quick as greased lightning, the thief stole my wallet.

senses.definition: very quiet; shy and silent.
examples: Don’t yell; whisper. Be as quiet as a mouse.
Mary hardly ever says anything. She’s quiet as a mouse.

senses.definition: very quiet; silent.
examples: The house is as quiet as the grave when the children are at school.
This town is quiet as the grave now that the offices have closed.

senses.definition: bright red.
examples: When the children came in from ice-skating, Clara’s nose was as red as a cherry.
When Lester proposed marriage, Nancy blushed as red as a cherry.

senses.definition: bright red.
senses.notes: Usually used to describe someone blushing.
examples: You must be embarrassed—you’re as red as a poppy!
When her boss praised her in front of the whole office, Emily turned red as a poppy.

senses.definition: intensely red.
examples: Bill blushed as red as a rose when we teased him.

senses.definition: deep red.
senses.notes: Often used to describe a person’s lips.
examples: Linda has a beautiful face, with big blue eyes and lips as red as rubies.

senses.definition: completely red; deep red.
senses.notes: The reference to blood gives this expression sinister connotations.
examples: The magician’s cape was lined with satin as red as blood.
I want to have my car painted red as blood.

senses.definition: dependably regular.
examples: She comes into this store every day, as regular as clockwork.
Our tulips come up every year, regular as clockwork.

senses.definition: correct; genuine.
examples: Your answer is as right as rain.
John is very dependable. He’s right as rain.

senses.definition: very scarce or nonexistent.
senses.notes: An exaggeration. Chickens don’t have teeth.
examples: I’ve never seen one of those. They’re as scarce as hens’ teeth.
I was told that the part needed for my car is scarcer than hens’ teeth, and it would take a long time to find one.

senses.definition: very sharp.
examples: The penknife is sharp as a razor.
The carving knife will have to be as sharp as a razor to cut through this meat.

senses.definition: very sharp-witted or intelligent.
examples: The old man’s senile, but his wife is as sharp as a razor.
Don’t say too much in front of the child. She’s as sharp as a razor.

senses.definition: intellectually bright.
examples: Melissa doesn’t say very much, but she’s sharp as a tack.
Sue can figure things out from even the slightest hint. She’s as sharp as a tack.

senses.definition: very sick; sick and vomiting.
examples: We’ve never been so ill. The whole family was sick as dogs.
Sally was as sick as a dog and couldn’t go to the party.

senses.definition: completely silent.
senses.notes: Has ominous connotations because of the reference to death. Usually used to promise someone that you will be silent and therefore not betray a secret.
examples: I knew something was wrong as soon as I entered the classroom; everyone was silent as the dead.
Jessica is as silent as the grave on the subject of her first marriage.
If you tell me what Katy said about me, I promise to be as silent as the grave.

senses.definition: very foolish.
examples: Edith is as silly as a goose. She thinks that reading aloud to her houseplants will help them grow.

JILL: The ad in the newspaper said this lotion would make my hair grow faster, but I’ve been using it for a whole month and my hair is still the same length. JANE: You’re as silly as a goose! Do you believe everything you read in newspaper ads?

senses.definition: quickly and cleanly; quickly and skillfully.
examples: Tom took a broom and a mop and cleaned the place up as slick as a whistle.
Slick as a whistle, Sally pulled off the bandage.

senses.definition: devious; undependable.
examples: Tom can’t be trusted. He’s as slippery as an eel.
It’s hard to catch Joe in his office because he’s slippery as an eel.

senses.definition: slow.
examples: Can’t you get dressed any faster? I declare, you’re as slow as molasses in January.
The traffic on the way to the concert was slower than molasses in January.

senses.definition: smart and clever.
examples: My nephew is as sly as a fox.
You have to be sly as a fox to outwit me.

senses.definition: smooth and shiny.
senses.notes: Often used to describe calm bodies of water.
examples: The bay is as smooth as glass, so we should have a pleasant boat trip.
Eugene polished the floor until it was smooth as glass.

senses.definition: very smooth.
examples: This pudding is smooth as silk.
Your skin is as smooth as silk.

headword: (as) snug as a bug in a rug

senses.definition: cozy and snug.
senses.notes: Informal. The kind of thing said when putting a child to bed.
examples: Let’s pull up the covers. There you are, Bobby, as snug as a bug in a rug.
What a lovely little house! I know I’ll be snug as a bug in a rug.

senses.definition: very formal, somber, or stuffy.
examples: You certainly look gloomy, Bill. You’re sober as a judge.
Tom’s as sober as a judge. I think he’s angry.

senses.definition: not drunk; alert and completely sober.
examples: John’s drunk? No, he’s as sober as a judge.
You should be sober as a judge when you drive a car.

senses.definition: very soft and smooth to the touch.
examples: This cloth is as soft as a baby’s bottom.
No, Bob doesn’t shave yet. His cheeks are soft as a baby’s bottom.

senses.definition: soft to the touch.
senses.notes: Refers to the softness of goose or duck down.
examples: The kitten’s fur was as soft as down.
The baby’s skin was soft as down.

senses.definition: very soft.
examples: This fabric is as soft as silk.
Your touch is soft as silk.

senses.definition: very soft to the touch.
examples: The horse’s nose felt as soft as velvet.
This lotion will make your skin soft as velvet.

senses.definition: very solid; dependable.
examples: Jean has been lifting weights every day, and her arm muscles are solid as a rock.
This company builds typewriters that are as solid as a rock.

senses.definition: at the moment that; at the time that; when.
examples: I fell asleep as soon as I lay down.
John ate dinner as soon as he came home.

senses.definition: at the earliest time.
examples: I’m leaving now. I’ll be there as soon as possible.
Please pay me as soon as possible.

senses.definition: very secure and dependable.
examples: This investment is as sound as a dollar.
I wouldn’t put my money in a bank that isn’t sound as a dollar.

senses.definition: sturdy and well-constructed.
examples: This house is as sound as a dollar.
The garage is still sound as a dollar. Why tear it down?

senses.definition: sour and disagreeable.
examples: The old man greeted us illnaturedly, his face as sour as vinegar.
JILL: Is Mary in a bad mood today? JANE: Yes, sour as vinegar.

senses.definition: very steady and unmovable; very stable.
examples: His hand was steady as a rock as he pulled the trigger of the revolver.
You must remain as steady as a rock when you are arguing with your supervisor.

senses.definition: rigid and inflexible; stiff and awkward.
examples: This guy’s dead. He’s cold and as stiff as a poker.
John is not a very good dancer; he’s stiff as a poker.

senses.definition: immobile; completely still.
senses.notes: The reference to death gives this expression ominous connotations.
examples: George sat as still as death all afternoon.
When the storm was over, everything was suddenly still as death.

senses.definition: very straight.
examples: The road to my house is as straight as an arrow, so it should be very easy to follow.

senses.definition: honest or forthright.
examples: Tom is straight as an arrow. I’d trust him with anything.

senses.definition: very strong.
examples: JILL: My car broke down; it’s sitting out on the street. JANE: Get Linda to help you push it; she’s as strong as a horse.
The athlete was strong as a horse. He could lift his own weight with just one hand.

senses.definition: very strong.
examples: See if you can get Melissa to help us move our furniture. She’s as strong as a lion.
The football player was strong as a lion.

senses.definition: very strong.
examples: Tom lifts weights and is as strong as an ox.
Now that Ann has recovered from her illness, she’s strong as an ox.

senses.definition: very stubborn.
examples: My husband is as stubborn as a mule.
Our cat is stubborn as a mule.

senses.definition: the way something is; as someone or something is.
examples: I cannot accept your manuscript as such. It needs revisions.
You are new here, and as such, I will have to train you.

senses.definition: sure; very certain.
examples: As political tension increased, it became more and more apparent that war was coming, as sure as death.
JILL: Is the company definitely going to lay people off? JANE: Sure as death.

senses.definition: very sweet.
examples: These little cakes are as sweet as honey.
This fruit juice is as sweet as honey.

senses.definition: charming; very nice and friendly.
examples: She is as sweet as honey whenever she talks to me.
He seems sweet as honey, but he is really mean.

senses.definition: very fast.
examples: The new intercity train is swift as an arrow.
My week of vacation sped by as swift as an arrow.

senses.definition: very fast.
examples: This new car is as swift as the wind.
Joe ran swift as the wind, trying to get home in time.

senses.definition: extremely fast.
examples: Thanks to modern communication devices, news can now travel almost as swift as thought.
You won’t have to wait for me long; I’ll be there, swift as thought.

senses.definition: straight across the land, as opposed to distances measured on a road, river, etc.
examples: It’s twenty miles to town on the highway, but only ten miles as the crow flies.
Our house is only a few miles from the lake as the crow flies.

senses.definition: very thick.
examples: This fog is as thick as pea soup.
Wow, this coffee is strong! It’s thick as pea soup.

senses.definition: very close-knit; friendly; allied.
examples: Mary, Tom, and Sally are as thick as thieves. They go everywhere together.
Those two families are thick as thieves.

senses.definition: stretched tight.
examples: Julia stretched the upholstery fabric over the seat of the chair until it was as tight as a drum.

senses.definition: sealed tight.
examples: Now that I’ve caulked all the windows, the house should be tight as a drum.

senses.definition: very stingy.
examples: He won’t contribute a cent. He’s as tight as a drum.

senses.definition: very tight.
examples: I’ve got to lose some weight. My belt is as tight as Dick’s hatband.
This window is stuck tight as Dick’s hatband.

senses.definition: very tough.
examples: This meat is tough as an old boot.
Bob couldn’t eat the steak. It was as tough as an old boot.

senses.definition: very strong; not easily moved by feelings such as pity.
examples: Margaret is never off work. She’s as tough as an old boot.
Don’t expect sympathy from the boss. She’s tough as an old boot.

senses.definition: very loyal and dependable.
examples: Through all my troubles, my husband has been as true as steel.
Pedro was a staunch friend, true as steel.

senses.definition: very ugly.
examples: Maria may be a beautiful woman, but when she was a child she was as ugly as a toad.
The shopkeeper was ugly as a toad, but he was kind and generous, and everyone loved him.

senses.definition: very ugly.
examples: The new building is as ugly as sin.
