The old woman is ugly as sin, but she dresses beautifully.

senses.definition: as is the normal or typical situation.
examples: John ordered eggs for breakfast as usual.
He stood quietly as usual, waiting for the bus to come.

senses.definition: very warm and cozy.
examples: The baby will be warm as toast in that blanket.
We were as warm as toast by the side of the fire.

senses.definition: physically very weak.
examples: Six weeks of illness left the athlete as weak as a baby.
Hot, humid weather like this always makes me feel weak as a baby.

senses.definition: weak; weak and sickly.
examples: John is as weak as a kitten because he doesn’t eat well.
Oh! Suddenly I feel weak as a kitten.

senses.definition: also; in addition.
examples: Could I have some more potatoes as well?
I’m feeling tired, and dizzy as well.

senses.definition: in addition to someone or something.
examples: Mary and Jane are coming to the party, as well as Tom.
I’m studying biology and chemistry, as well as history.

senses.definition: to the same high degree as someone or something; as much as.
examples: Mary’s parents treated me as well as they treated her.
I did as well as you on the test.

senses.definition: very pale.
examples: His face is as white as a ghost.
He turned pale as a ghost when he saw his injured leg.

senses.definition: very pale.
examples: Jane was white as a sheet for weeks after her illness.
Mary went as white as a sheet when she heard the news.

senses.definition: very white.
examples: I like my bed sheets to be as white as the driven snow.
We have a new kitten whose fur is white as the driven snow.

senses.definition: very wise.
examples: Grandfather is as wise as an owl.
My goal is to be wise as an owl.

senses.definition: very wise.
senses.notes: Refers to a character in the Bible.
examples: If you are in trouble, get Chris to advise you. He’s as wise as Solomon.
This is a difficult problem. You’d need to be as wise as Solomon to be able to solve it.

senses.definition: not including someone or something.
examples: Aside from a small bank account, I have no money at all.
Aside from Mary, I have no friends.

senses.definition: to do something that will cause trouble.
examples: Don’t talk to me that way! You’re really asking for it.
Anyone who acts like that is just asking for a good talking to.

senses.definition: to ask for too much; to make great demands.
examples: When you’re trying to get a job, it’s unwise to ask for the moon.
Please lend me the money. I’m not asking for the moon!

senses.definition: to seem to be trying to get into trouble; to do something that would cause trouble; to do or say something that will cause trouble.
examples: Stop talking to me that way, John. You’re just asking for trouble.
The guard asked me to leave unless I was looking for trouble.
Anybody who threatens a police officer is just asking for trouble.
You’re looking for trouble if you ask the boss for a raise.

senses.definition: not attending to one’s job; failing to do one’s duty at the proper time.
examples: The guard was asleep at the switch when the robber broke in.
If I hadn’t been asleep at the switch, I’d have seen the stolen car.

senses.definition: a violent attack [upon someone] followed by a beating.
examples: Max was charged with two counts of assault and battery.
Dave does not go out at night because he does not want to be a victim of assault and battery.

senses.definition: to be very loud or persistent.
examples: That loud music assaults the ears!
I can’t hear with all that talk assaulting my ears.

senses.definition: to accept the responsibility for paying a cost.
examples: Mr. Smith assumed liability for his son’s student loans.
The store assumed liability for the injured customer’s hospital bill.

senses.definition: regardless of the difficulty or cost; no matter what.
examples: I intend to have that car at all costs.
I’ll get there by six o’clock at all costs.
Mary was going to get that job at any cost.

senses.definition: constantly; continuously.
examples: You must keep your passport handy at all times when you are traveling in a foreign country.
When you’re in a crowd, you must watch your child at all times.

senses.definition: unable to speak; speechless; befuddled.
examples: I was so surprised that I was at a loss for words.
Tom was terribly confused—really at a loss.

senses.definition: soon; some day soon.
examples: The note said, “Please call me at an early date.”
You’re expected to return the form to the office at an early date.

senses.definition: anyway.
senses.notes: Informal. Frequently used as an introduction to a conclusion or a final statement.
examples: At any rate, we had a nice time at your party. We are grateful that you asked us.
It’s not much, at any rate, but it’s the best we can do.

senses.definition: at a high price; priced high because of something special.
examples: Sally bought the shoes at a premium because they were of very high quality.
This model of car is selling at a premium because so many people want to buy it.

senses.definition: at a particular time; at an assigned time.
examples: Each person has to show up at a set time.
Do I have to be there at a set time, or can I come whenever I want?

senses.definition: at one time; during one period.
senses.notes: Refers to an activity that takes place while a person is seated.
examples: The restaurant could feed only sixty people at a sitting.
I can read about 300 pages at a sitting.

senses.definition: very slowly.
examples: When you watch a clock, time seems to move at a snail’s pace.
You always eat at a snail’s pace. I’m tired of waiting for you.

senses.definition: continuously; without stopping.
examples: We all had to do eight hours of duty at a stretch.
The baby doesn’t sleep for more than three hours at a stretch.

senses.definition: at a distance.
examples: I have to keep the bill collectors at bay until I get my check.
The wolves will not remain at bay for very long.

senses.definition: in the best view; in the most positive judgment; as the best one can say.
examples: I believe her to be totally negligent. Her actions were careless at best.
At best we found their visit pleasantly short.
The dinner was not at all pleasant. At best the food was not burned.
At most she was careless, but not criminal.
We found their visit pleasingly short at most.

senses.definition: very near; in close proximity.
senses.notes: Usually used in regard to shooting.
examples: The hunter fired at the deer at close range.
The powder burns tell us that the gun was fired at close range.

senses.definition: with opposing purposes; with goals that interfere with each other.
examples: We are arguing at cross-purposes. We aren’t even discussing the same thing.
Bill and Tom are working at cross-purposes. They’ll never get the job done right.

senses.definition: near death.
examples: I was so ill that I was at death’s door.
The family dog was at death’s door for three days, and then it finally died.

senses.definition: relaxed and comfortable.
examples: I don’t feel at ease driving when there is a lot of traffic.
Mary is most at ease when she’s near the sea.

senses.definition: everywhere; everywhere one looks.
examples: There is a new problem at every turn.
Life holds new adventures at every turn.

senses.definition: from outward appearance; from what something first appears to be.
senses.notes: From the value printed on the “face” of a coin or bank note.
examples: Don’t just accept her offer at face value. Think of the implications.
Joan tends to take people at face value and so she is always getting hurt.

senses.definition: initially; at the beginning.
examples: He was shy at first. Then he became more friendly.
At first we chose the red one. Later we switched to the blue one.

senses.definition: when first examined; at an early stage.
examples: At first glance, the problem appeared quite simple. Later we learned just how complex it really was.
He appeared quite healthy at first glance.
At first blush, she appeared to be quite old.

senses.definition: using full power; as loudly as possible.
examples: The neighbors had their televisions on at full blast.
The car radio was on full blast. We couldn’t hear what the driver was saying.

senses.definition: as fast as possible.
examples: The motor was running at full speed.
John finished his running at full speed.
Things are now operating at full tilt.

senses.definition: halfway up or down.
senses.notes: Primarily referring to flags. Can be used for things other than flags as a joke.
examples: The flag was flying at half-mast because the general had died.
Americans fly flags at half-mast on Memorial Day.
The little boy ran out of the house with his pants at half-mast.

senses.definition: close by.
senses.notes: Used with both time and distance. See also close at hand; near at hand.
examples: I don’t happen to have your application at hand at the moment.
With the holiday season at hand, everyone is very excited.

senses.definition: risked; in danger; at risk.
examples: He is not willing to have much of his money at hazard in the stock market.
Your entire life is at hazard unless you wear a helmet when you ride your bicycle.

senses.definition: at or in one’s dwelling.
examples: Is Mary at home, or is she still at work?
What time will she be at home?

headword: at home with someone or something

senses.definition: comfortable with someone or something; comfortable doing something.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also feel at home.
examples: Tom is very much at home with my parents.
Sally seems to be very much at home with her car.
Mary seems to be at home with her job.

senses.definition: doing something again.
examples: I asked Tom to stop playing his trumpet, but he’s at it again.
They are at it again. Why are they always fighting?

senses.definition: free; uncaptured.
senses.notes: Usually said of criminals running loose.
examples: At noon the day after the robbery, the thieves were still at large.
There is a murderer at large in the city.

senses.definition: in general; according to a general sample.
examples: Truck drivers at large don’t like the new law.
Students at large felt that the rule was too strict.

senses.definition: representing the whole group rather than its subsections.
senses.notes: Always refers to a special kind of elective office.
examples: He ran for representative at large.
She represented shareholders at large on the governing board.

senses.definition: no less than; no fewer than.
examples: There were at least four people there that I knew.
I want to spend at least three weeks in Mexico.

senses.definition: anyway; in spite of difficulties.
examples: At least we had a good evening, even though the afternoon was rainy.
At least we came away with some of our money left.

senses.definition: resting; not working.
examples: What do you usually do when you are at leisure?
During the summer when you are at leisure, you ought to play golf.

senses.definition: at one’s convenience.
examples: Choose one or the other at your leisure.
Please drop by at your leisure.

senses.definition: after some time; finally.
examples: At length, the roses bloomed and the tomatoes ripened.
And at length, the wizard spoke.

senses.definition: for quite a long time.
examples: He spoke on and on at some length.
He described the history of his village at length.

senses.definition: free; unrestrained.
examples: The criminal was set at liberty by the judge.
You’re at liberty to go anywhere you wish.
I’m not at liberty to discuss the matter.

senses.definition: in opposition; at an impasse; in a quarrel.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Franklin have been at loggerheads for years.
The two political parties were at loggerheads during the entire legislative session.
She was at loggerheads with him for years.

senses.definition: after a long wait; finally.
examples: At last the hostages were released.
Sally earned her diploma at long last.

senses.definition: restless and unsettled; unemployed.
examples: Just before school starts, all the children are at loose ends.
When Tom is home on the weekends, he’s always at loose ends.
Jane has been at loose ends ever since she lost her job.

senses.definition: during the night.
examples: Most people sleep at night.
Mary studies at night.

senses.definition: in opposition to someone; at loggerheads (with someone).
examples: Mary is always at odds with her father about how late she can stay out.
John and his father are always at odds too.

senses.definition: immediately; at this very moment.
examples: John, come here at once!
Bring me my coffee at once!
Shall I do it at once or wait until morning?

senses.definition: in a single incident; as a single event.
senses.notes: This phrase preserves the old word fell, meaning “terrible” or “deadly.”
examples: The party guests ate up all the snacks at one fell swoop.
When the stock market crashed, many large fortunes were wiped out in one fell swoop.

senses.definition: at the limits of one’s mental resources.
examples: I’m at my wit’s end with this problem. I cannot figure it out.
Tom could do no more. He was at his wit’s end.

senses.definition: peaceful; relaxed; happy.
examples: I am always at peace when I sit in my rocking chair.
When the warm breeze is blowing, I am at peace.

senses.definition: dead.
examples: It was a long illness, but she is at peace now.
At last, Uncle Tom is at peace.

senses.definition: involved in playing.
examples: The children are at play, and I am doing household chores.
Whether I am at work or at play, I try to be pleasant to people.

senses.definition: now; at this point in time.
examples: We are not able to do any more at present.
We may be able to lend you money next week, but not at present.

senses.definition: without sequence or order.
examples: Sally picked four names at random from the telephone book.
The gunman walked into the crowded restaurant and fired at random.
Jane will read almost anything. She selects four novels at random at the library each week and reads them all.

senses.definition: at points that are equal in distance apart.
examples: You will find service stations at regular intervals along the highway.
There are streetlights at regular intervals on the main street of town.

senses.definition: not moving; not active.
examples: After the hectic day, the office was finally at rest by midnight.
Do not remove your seat belt until the plane is at rest.

senses.definition: in a situation where there is risk or hazard; in danger.
examples: I refuse to put my family’s welfare at risk by quitting my job.
Your whole future is at risk if you don’t stop smoking.

senses.definition: on the sea; away on a voyage on the ocean.
examples: The ship is at sea now, and you can’t disembark.
I spent many happy days at sea on my cruise.

senses.definition: located at the bottom of the sea.
examples: It is easier to breathe at sea level than in the mountains.
Boats on the ocean are at sea level, but those on rivers are not.

senses.definition: disorderly; lost and bewildered; at loose ends.
examples: Mrs. Smith is at sixes and sevens since the death of her husband.
Bill is always at sixes and sevens when he’s home by himself.

senses.definition: ready to obey someone.
examples: What makes you think I wait around here at your beck and call? I live here too, you know!
It was a fine hotel. There were dozens of maids and waiters at our beck and call.

senses.definition: in someone’s care; as someone’s responsibility.
examples: Why do you always have to lay your problems at my doorstep?
I shall put this issue on someone else’s doorstep.
I don’t want it on my doorstep.

senses.definition: as soon as it is easy or convenient for someone.
senses.notes: This is also a polite way of saying immediately.
examples: Please stop by my office at your earliest convenience.
Bill, please have the oil changed at your earliest convenience.

senses.definition: ready to help someone in any way.
examples: The count greeted me warmly and said, “Welcome to my home. Just let me know what you need. I’m at your service.”
The desk clerk said, “Good morning, madam. We are always at your service.”

senses.definition: exactly at a named time.
examples: You must be here at noon sharp.
The plane is expected to arrive at seven fortyfive sharp.

senses.definition: to be won or lost; at risk; hanging in the balance.
examples: That’s a very risky investment. How much money is at stake?
I have everything at stake on this wager.

senses.definition: in that manner; at that speed.
examples: If things keep progressing at that rate, we’ll be rich by next year.
At that rate we’ll never get the money that is owed us.

senses.definition: at the announced or assigned time.
examples: The cab pulled up in the driveway at the appointed time.
We all met at the hotel at the appointed time.

headword: at the bottom of the hour

senses.definition: on the half hour; the opposite of at the top of the hour.
senses.notes: Typically heard on television or the radio. Refers to the minute hand on a clock.
examples: Hear the news on WNAG at the bottom of the hour.
We will have an interview with Harry Smith at the bottom of the hour.

headword: at the bottom of the ladder

senses.definition: at the lowest level of pay and status.
examples: Most people start work at the bottom of the ladder.
When Ann got fired, she had to start all over again at the bottom of the ladder.

senses.definition: at the time of the earliest light of the day.
examples: Jane was always up at the crack of dawn.
The birds start singing at the break of dawn.

headword: at the drop of a hat

senses.definition: immediately and without urging.
examples: John was always ready to go fishing at the drop of a hat.
If you need help, just call on me. I can come at the drop of a hat.

senses.definition: at the last possible moment.
examples: She always turned her term papers in at the eleventh hour.
We don’t worry about death until the eleventh hour.

senses.definition: at a remote place; at some distance from civilization.
examples: They live way out in the country at the end of nowhere.
The police will never find us here at the end of nowhere.

headword: at the end of one’s rope
altForms: at the end of one’s tether

senses.definition: at the limits of one’s endurance.
examples: I’m at the end of my rope! I just can’t go on this way!
These kids are driving me out of my mind. I’m at the end of my tether.

headword: at the end of the day

senses.definition: when everything else has been taken into consideration.
examples: At the end of the day you will have to decide where you want to live.
The committee interviewed many applicants for the post, but at the end of the day made no appointment.

headword: at the expense of someone or something

senses.definition: to the detriment of someone or something; to the harm of someone or something.
examples: He had a good laugh at the expense of his brother.
He took a job in a better place at the expense of a larger income.

senses.definition: the most important place; the place of greatest activity.
examples: I interviewed Max Brown, the director who is in the forefront of the movie industry.
The university I go to is at the forefront of computer technology.

senses.definition: at the most intense or forceful aspect of something.
examples: At the height of his career, Tom was known around the world.
At the height of the party, there were 50 people present.

senses.definition: in the position of being in control of something.
senses.notes: Also literal for ships and boats.
examples: The president is at the helm of the company.
Things will go well with Anne at the helm.

senses.definition: at the very last; at the last chance; at the last minute.
senses.notes: Refers to someone’s last breath before death.
examples: She finally showed up at the last gasp, bringing the papers that were needed.
We got there at the last gasp, just before our names were called.

senses.definition: at the last possible chance.
senses.notes: Compare this with at the eleventh hour.
examples: Please don’t make reservations at the last minute.
Why do you ask all your questions at the last minute?

senses.definition: no later than.
examples: Please pay this bill in ten days at the latest.
I’ll be home by midnight at the latest.

senses.definition: under the control of someone; without defense against someone.
examples: We were left at the mercy of the arresting officer.
Mrs. Franklin wanted Mr. Franklin at her mercy.

senses.definition: at the beginning.
examples: It seemed like a very simple problem at the outset.
At the outset, they were very happy. Then they had money problems.

senses.definition: now; at present.
senses.notes: Used often as a wordy replacement for now.
examples: We don’t know the location of the stolen car at the present time.
The tomatoes are doing nicely at the present time.
At this point in time, we feel very sad about his death.
Yes, it’s sad, but there is nothing we can do at this point.

senses.definition: located at the back part of something.
examples: I keep my tools at the rear of my garage.
There’s a creek at the rear of my property.

senses.definition: nevertheless; however.
examples: Bill was able to make the car payment. At the same time, he was very angry about the bill.
We agree to your demands. At the same time, we object strongly to your methods.

headword: at the top of one’s voice
altForms: at the top of one’s lungs

senses.definition: with a very loud voice.
examples: Bill called to Mary at the top of his voice.
How can I work when you’re all talking at the top of your lungs?

headword: at the top of the hour

senses.definition: at the exact beginning of the hour.
senses.notes: Typically heard on television or the radio. See also at the bottom of the hour. Refers to the minute hand on a clock.
examples: Every class in my school starts at the top of the hour.
Our next newscast will be at the top of the hour.

senses.definition: at the very most.
examples: The car repairs will cost $300 at the outside.
I’ll be there in three weeks at the outside.

senses.definition: in the worst view; in the most negative judgment; as the worst one can say about something.
examples: At worst, Tom can be seen as greedy.
Ann will receive a ticket for careless driving, at the worst.

senses.definition: at the highest point of something; at the pinnacle of something.
examples: At the zenith of his career, the teacher died suddenly.
The scientist was at the zenith of her career when she made her discovery.

senses.definition: at this point in time; at this pause.
examples: There is little more that I can say at this juncture.
We can, if you wish, at this juncture, request a change in venue.

senses.definition: at this speed.
senses.notes: Compare this with at any rate and at that rate.
examples: Hurry up! We’ll never get there at this rate.
At this rate, all the food will be gone before we get there.

headword: at this stage of the game

senses.definition: at the current point in some event; currently.
examples: We’ll have to wait and see. There isn’t much we can do at this stage of the game.
At this stage, we are better off not calling the doctor.

senses.definition: sometimes; occasionally.
examples: I feel quite sad at times.
At times, I wish I had never come here.

senses.definition: whenever one wants; freely.
examples: You’re free to come and go at will.
The soldiers were told to fire their guns at will.
You can eat anything you want at will.

senses.definition: working (at something); busy (with something).
examples: Tom is at work on his project. He’ll be finished in a minute.
Don’t disturb me when I’m busy at work.

senses.definition: at one’s place of work.
examples: I’m sorry to call you at work, but this is important.
She’s at work now. She’ll be home at supper time.

senses.definition: fond of something or something.
examples: John is really attached to his old-fashioned ideas.
I’m really attached to this old house.

senses.definition: to cause someone to take notice; to get someone’s attention.
examples: I called and waved to attract Ann’s attention.
A small yellow flower attracted my attention.

headword: augur well for someone or something

senses.definition: to indicate or predict good things for someone or something.
examples: This latest message does not augur well for the hostages.
I am afraid that this does not augur well for the outcome of the election.

senses.definition: the pathway or route along which someone or something escapes.
examples: The open window was the bird’s only avenue of escape from the house.
Bill saw that his one avenue of escape was through the back door.

headword: avoid someone or something like the plague

senses.definition: to avoid someone or something totally.
examples: What’s wrong with Bob? Everyone avoids him like the plague.
I don’t like opera. I avoid it like the plague.

senses.definition: not available for a telephone conversation; not available to be seen.
senses.notes: Sometimes said by the person who answers a telephone in an office. It means that the person whom the caller wants is not immediately available due to personal or business reasons.
examples: I’m sorry, but Ann is away from her desk just now. Can you come back later?
Tom is away from his desk, but if you leave your number, he will call you right back.

senses.definition: a naive or innocent person; an inexperienced person.
examples: Bill is a babe in the woods when it comes to dealing with plumbers.
As a painter, Mary is fine, but she’s a babe in the woods as a musician.

senses.definition: to act indecisively; to change one’s direction repeatedly; to reverse one’s course.
senses.notes: Originally nautical, referring to alternately filling the sails with wind and releasing the wind.
examples: The president spent most of his speech backing and filling on the question of taxation.
The other candidate was backing and filling on every issue, depending on whom she was addressing.

senses.definition: backwards and forwards; first one way and then another way.
senses.notes: Compare this with to and fro.
examples: The young man was pacing back and forth in the hospital waiting room.
The pendulum on the clock swung back and forth.

senses.definition: to yield to a person or a thing; to fail to carry through on a threat.
examples: Jane backed down from her position on the budget.
It’s probably better to back down from someone than to have an argument.
John agreed that it was probably better to back down than to risk getting shot.
Bill doesn’t like to back off from a fight.
Sometimes it’s better to back off than to get hurt.

senses.definition: to or from the eastern United States, often the northeastern or New England states.
senses.notes: See also down South, out West, and up North. This is used even by people who have never been in the East.
examples: Sally felt that she had to get back East for a few days.
Tom went to school back East, but his brother attended college in the Midwest.

senses.definition: available to the public again.
senses.notes: [for a thing to be] Said especially of things that are said to circulate, such as money, library books, and magazines.
examples: I’ve heard that gold coins are back in circulation in Europe.
I would like to read War and Peace. Is it back in circulation, or is it still checked out?

senses.definition: socially active again; dating again after a divorce or breakup with one’s lover.
examples: Now that Bill is a free man, he’s back in circulation.
Tom was in the hospital for a month, but now he’s back in circulation.

senses.definition: the most remote place; somewhere very remote.
examples: John hardly ever comes to the city. He lives at the back of the beyond.
Mary likes lively entertainment, but her husband likes to vacation in the back of the beyond.

senses.definition: to order something that is not in stock and then make delivery to the customer when the goods become available.
senses.notes: [for a merchant] The merchant may hold your money until the order is filled.
examples: The store didn’t have the replacement part for my vacuum cleaner, so the manager back ordered it for me.
The shop had to back order some of the items on my list.

senses.definition: to withdraw from something you have agreed to do; to break an agreement.
examples: The buyer tried to back out of the sale, but the seller wouldn’t permit it.
Please don’t back out of our date.
Mary backed out at the last minute.

senses.definition: to support someone or something; to concur with someone.
examples: Please back me up in this argument.
I would like you to back up John in this discussion.

senses.definition: to support someone or something that cannot win or succeed.
senses.notes: Also literal, as in horse racing.
examples: I don’t want to back the wrong horse, but it seems to me that Jed is the better candidate.
Fred backed the wrong horse in the budget hearings.

senses.definition: adjacent and touching backs.
examples: They started the duel by standing back-to-back.
Two people who stand back-to-back can manage to see in all directions.

senses.definition: following immediately.
examples: The doctor had appointments set up back-to-back all day long.
I have three lecture courses back-to-back every day of the week.

senses.definition: back to the beginning.
senses.notes: Also literal with a board game. See also the following entry.
examples: Negotiations have broken down, and it’s back to square one.
We lost the appeal of the court case, so it’s back to square one.

senses.definition: time to start over again; it is time to plan something over again.
senses.notes: Also literal. Note the variation in the examples.
examples: It didn’t work. Back to the drawing board.
I flunked English this semester. Well, back to the old drawing board.

senses.definition: time to return to work, school, or something else that might be unpleasant.
senses.notes: As if the speaker were a slave who works in the salt mines.
examples: It’s eight o’clock. Time to go to work! Back to the salt mines.
School starts in the fall, and then it’s back to the salt mines again.

senses.definition: unpleasant feelings or animosity between people.
examples: There is bad blood between Fred and Jim. They cannot be civil to one another.
There is no bad blood between us. I don’t know why we should quarrel.

senses.definition: to say bad things about someone or something.
examples: Mr. Smith was always badmouthing Mrs. Smith. They didn’t get along.
John bad-mouths his car constantly because it doesn’t run.

senses.definition: with one’s luggage; with all one’s possessions.
senses.notes: Informal. See also part and parcel (of something).
examples: Sally showed up at our door bag and baggage one Sunday morning.
All right, if you won’t pay the rent, out with you, bag and baggage!
Get all your stuff—part and parcel—out of here!

senses.definition: a collection of special techniques or methods.
examples: What have you got in your bag of tricks that could help me with this problem?
Here comes Mother with her bag of tricks. I’m sure she can help us.

senses.definition: to jump out of an airplane (with a parachute).
examples: John still remembers the first time he bailed out of a plane.
When we get to 8,000 feet, we’ll all bail out and drift down together. We’ll open our parachutes at 2,000 feet.

senses.definition: to abandon a situation; to get out of something.
examples: John got tired of school, so he just bailed out.
Please stay, Bill. You’ve been with us too long to bail out now.

senses.definition: to deposit a sum of money that allows someone to get out of jail while waiting for a trial.
examples: John was in jail. I had to go down to the police station to bail him out.
You kids are always getting into trouble. Do you really expect me to bail out the whole gang of you every time you have a problem?

senses.definition: to remove water from the bottom of a boat by dipping or scooping.
examples: Tom has to bail the boat out before we get in.
You should always bail out a boat before using it.

senses.definition: to rescue someone or something from trouble or difficulty.
examples: The proposed law was in trouble, but Todd bailed it out at the last minute.
I was going to be late with my report, but my roommate lent a hand and bailed me out at the last minute.

senses.definition: a deceptive merchandising practice where one product is advertised to get people’s attention [the bait], but pressure is applied to get the customer to purchase a more expensive item.
examples: Walter described the appliance store as bait and switch, since they never seemed to have in stock the bargains that they advertised.
Max accused the merchant of bait and switch and stalked out of the store.

senses.definition: to determine through accounting that accounts are in balance, that all money is accounted for.
examples: Jane was up all night balancing the accounts.
The cashier was not allowed to leave the bank until the manager balanced the books.

senses.definition: to get even [with someone].
examples: Tom hit Bob. Bob balanced the accounts by breaking Tom’s toy car.
Once we have balanced the accounts, we can shake hands and be friends again.

senses.definition: a person’s special burden; a job.
senses.notes: Usually considered slang. Prisoners are sometimes fettered with a chain attached to a leg on one end and a heavy metal ball on the other.
examples: Tom wanted to quit his job. He said he was tired of that old ball and chain.
Mr. Franklin always referred to his wife as his ball and chain.

senses.definition: a very active and energetic person who always succeeds.
examples: Sally is a real ball of fire—she works late every night.
Ann is no ball of fire, but she does get the job done.

senses.definition: the bottom part of the feet just under the toes.
examples: Mary got blisters on the balls of her feet from playing tennis.
The dancer balanced on the balls of his feet.

senses.definition: to count on something; to rely on something.
examples: The weather service said it wouldn’t rain, but I wouldn’t bank on it.
My word is to be trusted. You can bank on it.

senses.definition: a first experience of something, usually something difficult or unpleasant.
examples: My son’s just had his first visit to the dentist. He stood up to the baptism of fire very well.
Mary’s had her baptism of fire as a teacher. She was assigned to the worst class in the school.

senses.definition: the smallest amount of something possible.
examples: Bob did the bare minimum of work to pass the class.
Food, clothing, and shelter are the bare necessities of life.

senses.definition: to plan for something; to expect something.
examples: We knew it would be difficult, but we didn’t bargain for this kind of trouble.
I bargained on an easier time of it than this.

senses.definition: to break in on someone or something; to interrupt someone or something.
examples: Oh! I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to barge in on you.
They barged in on the church service and caused a commotion.
You can’t just barge in like that!

senses.definition: to make the wrong choice; to ask the wrong person; to follow the wrong course.
senses.notes: Refers to a hunting dog’s error.
examples: If you think I’m the guilty person, you’re barking up the wrong tree.
The baseball players blamed their bad record on the pitcher, but they were barking up the wrong tree.

senses.definition: to prepare for difficult times.
senses.notes: A nautical expression, meaning, literally, to seal the hatches against the arrival of a storm.
examples: Here comes that contentious Mrs. Jones. Batten down the hatches!
Batten down the hatches, Congress is in session again.

senses.definition: to argue something to a conclusion; to fight something to a conclusion.
examples: The Senate and the House disagree on the bill, so they will have to battle a compromise out.
The two young toughs went into the alley to battle out their disagreement.

senses.definition: to scold someone in a loud voice.
examples: The teacher bawled the student out for arriving late.
Teachers don’t usually bawl out students.

headword: be a heartbeat away from something

senses.definition: to be the next ruler upon the final heartbeat of the current ruler.
senses.notes: [for someone] Especially in reference to U.S. presidential succession.
examples: The vice president is just a heartbeat away from being president.
The prince was only a heartbeat away from being king.

senses.definition: something that is the very best or most important; something so good that it will end the search for something better.
examples: Finishing the building of his boat became the be-all and end-all of Roger’s existence.
Sally is the be-all and the end-all of Don’s life.

senses.definition: listening eagerly and carefully.
examples: Well, hurry up and tell me. I’m all ears.
Be careful what you say. The children are all ears.

senses.definition: to be alert for something to happen; to wait eagerly for something to happen or for someone or something to appear.
examples: There they were, sitting at the table, all eyes. The birthday cake was soon to be served.
Nothing can escape my notice. I’m all eyes and ears.

headword: be all things to all men
altForms: be all things to all people

senses.definition: to be liked or used by all people; [for someone or something] to be everything that is wanted by all people.
examples: You simply can’t be all things to all people.
The candidate set out to be all things to all men and came off looking very wishywashy.

senses.definition: to be distracted and daydreaming; not to be paying attention.
examples: You were a million miles away while I was talking to you.
Most of the class was a million miles away in the hot spring afternoon.

headword: be a new one on someone

senses.definition: to be something one has not heard before and that one is not ready to believe.
senses.notes: Informal. The someone is often me.
examples: Jack’s poverty is a new one on me. He always seems to have plenty of money.
The city’s difficulties are a new one on me.

headword: be curtains for someone or something

senses.definition: to be the death, end, or ruin of someone or something.
senses.notes: Informal. From the lowering or closing of the curtains at the end of a stage performance.
examples: If the car hadn’t swerved, it would have been curtains for the pedestrians.
If they can’t get into the export market, it’s curtains for the whole company.

senses.definition: to be very harmful to something.
examples: The salt they put on the roads in the winter is death on cars.
That teacher is death on slow learners.

senses.definition: said of a task that is easier to talk about than to do.
examples: Yes, we must find a cure for cancer, but it’s easier said than done.
Finding a good job is easier said than done.

senses.definition: to be very successful in one’s ambitions; to obtain an important or powerful position.
senses.notes: Also literal. Often with the implication that this will not last very long.
examples: The government is flying high just now, but wait until the budget is announced.
He’s flying high these days, but he comes from a very poor family.

senses.definition: to be in a state of euphoria.
senses.notes: From good news, success, or drugs.
examples: Wow! Todd is really flying high. Did he discover a gold mine?
Sally is flying high. What’s she on?

senses.definition: to require proof; to have to be shown [something].
senses.notes: Also literal. From the nickname for the state of Missouri, the “Show Me” State.
examples: You’ll have to prove it to me. I’m from Missouri.
She’s from Missouri and has to be shown.

senses.definition: to be ready for action; to be agreeable to participating in something.
examples: “I’m game,” David replied when I suggested we go bowling.
We’re going to the park to play football. Are you game?

headword: be off on the wrong foot
altForms: be off to a bad start

senses.definition: to have started something with negative factors.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to marching. See also get off on the wrong foot; get off to a bad start; start off on the wrong foot.
examples: I’m sorry we are off to a bad start. I tried to be friendly.
I hope that we won’t be off to a bad start after our little argument.

senses.definition: to help someone; to serve someone.
senses.notes: A phrase often used by salesclerks. See also be at someone’s service.
examples: Good morning, madam. May I be of service to you?
Welcome to the Warwick Hotel. Can I be of service?

headword: be of the persuasion that something is so

senses.definition: to hold a belief that something is true or is in existence.
examples: Anne is of the persuasion that supports that candidate for mayor.
The paranoid was of the persuasion that aliens lived among us.

senses.definition: to be unwilling to do something.
examples: David was reluctant to admit his mistakes.
The witness was reluctant to testify and was ordered to do so by the judge.

senses.definition: to vomit.
senses.notes: Euphemistic. Also with get, as in the examples. Also literal, meaning “to suffer from an illness.”
examples: Mommy, Billy just got sick on the floor.
Oh, excuse me! I think I’m going to be sick.
Bob was sick all over the carpet.

senses.definition: to be engulfed by an excess of something, as if it were a flood.
examples: The war-torn city was swimming in blood.
I am just swimming in paperwork.

senses.definition: even if what you say is true.
examples: I am sorry to hear that, but, be that as it may, you still must carry out your responsibilities.
Be that as it may, I still cannot help you.

senses.definition: to be true; to be an actual situation.
examples: I think Bill is a vegetarian, and if that is the case, we should not serve him meat.
Susie believes trees can talk, but that is not the case.

senses.definition: be my ruin, death, or downfall.
examples: This cold will be the death of me.
All these problems will be the death of me yet.

altForms: be the straw that broke the camel’s back

senses.definition: to be the final thing.; to be the last little burden or problem that causes everything to collapse.
senses.notes: From the image of a camel being loaded down with much weight, one straw at a time. Finally, at some point, when one is adding straw after straw, one straw will finally be too much and the camel’s back will break.
examples: When Sally came down sick, that was the straw that broke the camel’s back.
When she showed up late, that was the straw that broke the camel’s back.

headword: be the spit and image of someone
altForms: be the spitting image of someone

senses.definition: to look very much like someone; to resemble someone very closely.
senses.notes: Folksy. The second version is a frequent error.
examples: John is the spit and image of his father.
I’m not the spit and image of anyone.
At first, I thought you were saying spitting image.

senses.definition: accustomed to something; comfortable with something because it is familiar.
examples: We are used to cooking our own food.
I lived in Alaska so long that I am used to the cold.

senses.definition: to have an old resentment for someone; to be continually angry at someone.
senses.notes: See also nurse a grudge (against someone).
examples: She bears a grudge against the judge who sentenced her.
I have a grudge against my landlord for overcharging me.
How long can a person hold a grudge? Let’s be friends.

senses.definition: to yield results; to give results.
senses.notes: Also literal for fruit-bearing plants and trees.
examples: I hope your new plan bears fruit.
We’ve had many good ideas, but none of them has borne fruit.

headword: bear in mind that something is so

senses.definition: to remember that something is so; to consider that something is so.
senses.notes: See also keep someone or something in mind.
examples: Bear in mind that the trip will be expensive.
I asked the teacher to bear in mind that I am just a beginner.

senses.definition: to carry or bear one’s burden; to endure one’s difficulties.
senses.notes: This is a Christian biblical theme. It is always used figuratively except in the biblical context.
examples: It’s a very bad disease, but I’ll bear my cross.
I can’t help you with it. You’ll just have to carry your cross.

senses.definition: to demonstrate or prove that something is right.
examples: I hope that the facts will bear your story out.
I’m sure that the facts will bear out my story.

senses.definition: to withstand the worst part or the strongest part of something, such as an attack.
examples: I had to bear the brunt of her screaming and yelling.
Why don’t you talk with her the next time? I’m tired of bearing the brunt.

senses.definition: to need watching; to deserve observation or monitoring.
examples: This problem will bear watching.
This is a very serious disease, and it will bear watching for further developments.

senses.definition: to be patient with someone or something; to endure someone or something.
examples: Please bear with me while I fill out this form.
Please bear with my old car. It’ll get us there sooner or later.

headword: beard the lion in his den

senses.definition: to face an adversary on the adversary’s home ground.
examples: I went to the tax collector’s office to beard the lion in his den.
He said he hadn’t wanted to come to my home, but it was better to beard the lion in his den.

senses.definition: to continue fighting a battle that has been won; to continue to argue a point that is settled.
senses.notes: A dead horse will not run no matter how hard it is beaten.
examples: Stop arguing! You have won your point. You are just beating a dead horse.
Oh, be quiet. Stop beating a dead horse.

senses.definition: to retreat or withdraw very quickly.
examples: We went out into the cold weather, but beat a retreat to the warmth of our fire.
The dog beat a hasty retreat to its own yard.

headword: beat a path to someone’s door

senses.definition: to come to someone in great numbers.
senses.notes: [for people] So many people will wish to come and see you that they will wear down a pathway to your door.
examples: I have a product so good that everyone is beating a path to my door.
If you really become famous, people will beat a path to your door.

senses.definition: to avoid answering a question; to stall; to waste time.
examples: Stop beating around the bush and answer my question.
Let’s stop beating about the bush and discuss this matter.

headword: beat one’s brains out (to do something)

senses.definition: to work very hard (to do something).
examples: I beat my brains out to solve the problem.
That’s the last time I’ll beat my brains out trying to cook a nice dinner for you.

headword: beat one’s head against the wall
altForms: bang one’s head against a brick wall

senses.definition: to waste one’s time trying to accomplish something that is completely hopeless.
examples: You’re wasting your time trying to fix up this house. You’re just beating your head against the wall.
You’re banging your head against a brick wall trying to get that dog to behave properly.

senses.definition: to make a person more humble, possibly by beating.
senses.notes: See also cut someone down (to size).
examples: If you keep acting so arrogant, someone is going to beat you down to size.
It’s time someone knocked you down to size.
I’ll try to be more thoughtful. I don’t want anyone to beat me down.

senses.definition: to do something before someone else does it.
examples: I wanted to have the first new car, but Sally beat me to the punch.
I planned to write a book about computers, but someone else beat me to the draw.

senses.definition: to force someone to learn something, possibly through violence.
senses.notes: This can be a threat of violence and should not be used casually.
examples: I studied for hours. I have never beat so much stuff into my head in such a short time.
You’re going to learn this math if I have to beat it into your head.

senses.definition: to do something before a deadline; to finish before the time is up.
examples: Sam beat the clock, arriving a few minutes before the doors were locked.
They were afraid they would be late and hurried in order to beat the clock.

senses.definition: to manage to do something before the ending signal.
senses.notes: Originally from sports, referring to making a goal in the last seconds of a game. See also jump the gun.
examples: The ball beat the gun and dropped through the hoop just in time.
Tom tried to beat the gun, but he was one second too slow.

headword: beat the living daylights out of someone
altForms: beat the stuffing out of someone
beat the tar out of someone
whale the tar out of someone

senses.definition: to beat or spank someone, probably a child.
senses.notes: Folksy. These are all threats to do violence and should not be used casually.
examples: If you do that again, I’ll beat the living daylights out of you.
The last time Bobby put the cat in the refrigerator, his mother beat the living daylights out of him.
If you continue to act that way, I’ll beat the tar out of you.
He wouldn’t stop, so I beat the stuffing out of him.
He threatened to whale the tar out of each of them.

senses.definition: to beat someone severely.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to physical violence, not the removal of someone’s pants.
examples: The thugs beat the pants off their victim.
If you do that again, I’ll beat the pants off you.

senses.definition: to win out over someone.
senses.notes: Informal. This has nothing to do with violence or removing pants.
examples: In the footrace, Sally beat the pants off Jane.
Tom beats the pants off Bob when it comes to writing poetry.

senses.definition: to escape conviction and punishment (for a crime).
examples: He was charged with drunk driving, but he beat the rap.
The police hauled Tom in and charged him with a crime. His lawyer helped him beat the rap.

senses.definition: Looks are only superficial.
examples: BOB: Isn’t Jane lovely? TOM: Yes, but beauty is only skin-deep.
I know that she looks like a million dollars, but beauty is only skin-deep.

senses.definition: complimentary to someone; enhancing one’s good looks.
senses.notes: Refers to clothing and other personal ornaments.
examples: The dress you wore last night is not becoming on you.
That color is becoming on you.

senses.definition: complimentary to someone; enhancing one’s good looks.
senses.notes: Refers to hairstyle and things that add to one’s good looks. See also becoming on someone.
examples: Your new fur coat is becoming to you.
That hairstyle is very becoming to you.

senses.definition: a situation or way of life that is always happy and comfortable.
examples: Living with Pat can’t be a bed of roses, but her husband is always smiling.
Being the boss isn’t exactly a bed of roses. There are so many problems to take care of.

senses.definition: to make something stronger; to supplement something.
examples: The government decided to beef the army up by buying hundreds of new tanks.
Okay, let’s beef up the opening song. Please, everyone, sing louder!

senses.definition: soon.
examples: Billy will be grown-up before long.
Before long, we’ll be without any money if we keep spending so much.

headword: before you can say Jack Robinson

senses.definition: almost immediately.
examples: And before you could say Jack Robinson, the bird flew away.
I’ll catch a plane and be there before you can say Jack Robinson.

senses.definition: almost immediately.
examples: I’ll be there before you know it.
If you keep spending money like that, you’ll be broke before you know it.

senses.definition: to ask to be released from something; to refuse an invitation.
examples: I’m sorry. I’ll have to beg off on your invitation.
I have an important meeting, so I’ll have to beg off.

senses.definition: to carry on a false argument where one assumes as proved the very point that is being argued, or more generally, to evade a principled discussion of the issue at hand.
senses.notes: Essentially a criticism of someone’s line of argument.
examples: Stop talking in circles. You’re begging the question.
A: Why do two lines that are equidistant from one another never meet? B: Because they are parallel. A: You are begging the question.

senses.definition: to invite the (following) question.
senses.notes: This erroneous reinterpretation of beg the question is becoming increasingly popular and widespread.
examples: His complaints beg the question: Didn’t he cause all of his problems himself?

senses.definition: to disagree with someone; to state one’s disagreement with someone in a polite way.
senses.notes: Usually used in a statement made to the person being disagreed with.
examples: I beg to differ with you, but you have stated everything exactly backwards.
If I may beg to differ, you have not expressed things as well as you seem to think.

senses.definition: to defy description; to be unable to be described.
examples: The house was a mess. The place beggared description.
Our reaction to the proposal beggars description. We were deeply disturbed for days.

senses.definition: One should not criticize something one gets for free.
examples: I don’t like the old hat that you gave me, but beggars can’t be choosers.
It doesn’t matter whether people like the free food or not. Beggars can’t be choosers.

senses.definition: to begin to foresee the end of a long task.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also see the light (at the end of the tunnel).
examples: I’ve been working on my thesis for two years, and at last I’m beginning to see daylight.
I’ve been so busy. Only in the last week have I begun to see daylight.

senses.definition: to begin to understand (something).
examples: My algebra class is hard for me, but I’m beginning to see the light.
I was totally confused, but I began to see the light after your explanation.

senses.definition: the start of the final phase of something or of someone’s death.
examples: When he stopped coughing and remained still, I knew it was the beginning of the end.
The enormous federal deficit marked the beginning of the end as far as our standard of living is concerned.

senses.definition: in secret; away from observers, reporters, or intruders.
senses.notes: Refers to being in a private room with the doors closed.
examples: They held the meeting behind closed doors, as the law allowed.
Every important issue was decided behind closed doors.

senses.definition: late with something; late in doing something.
examples: I’m behind in my car payments.
She’s behind on her work.

senses.definition: having failed to do something by the time listed on the schedule.
examples: We have to hurry and finish soon because we are behind schedule.
The project is behind schedule. Very late, in fact.

senses.definition: in secret; without someone’s knowledge.
examples: Please don’t talk about me behind my back.
She sold the car behind his back.

senses.definition: in a difficult or awkward position.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to billiards, a game played with numbered balls.
examples: Bob broke his wife’s crystal vase and is really behind the eight ball.
I ran over the neighbor’s lawn with my car, so I’m really behind the eight ball.

senses.definition: privately; out of public view.
examples: The people who worked behind the scenes are the real heroes of this project.
I worked behind the scenes in the play.
We don’t usually thank the people who are behind the scenes.

senses.definition: old-fashioned.
examples: Sarah is a bit behind the times. Her clothes are quite old-fashioned.
Our legislature is a bit behind the times.

senses.definition: Watch out behind you!; There is danger behind you!
examples: Behind you! That car almost hit you.
There are snakes everywhere! Behind you! Look out!

senses.definition: to spend too much time on a point of discussion.
examples: I don’t want to belabor the point, but the sooner we get these things settled, the better.
If the speaker would agree not to belabor the point further, I will place it on the agenda for the next meeting.

senses.definition: to choose to believe something or not.
senses.notes: Indicating that an assertion may be hard to believe.
examples: Believe it or not, I just got home from work.
I’m over fifty years old, believe it or not.

senses.definition: symbols of witchcraft.
examples: Look, I can’t work miracles! Do you expect me to show up at your house with bell, book, and candle, and make everything right? You have to take charge of your own destiny!
On the top shelf of the tiny used-book store, Jim saw a bell, book, and candle sitting in a row, and he knew he was going to find some very interesting reading material.

senses.definition: lower or worse than average.
examples: Tom’s strength is below average for a child his size.
Dad asked why my grades are below average.

senses.definition: not as good as average or normal.
examples: I feel a little below par today. I think I am getting a cold.
His work is below par, and he is paid too much money.

senses.definition: to sing or play a song loudly and with spirit.
examples: When she’s playing the piano, she really belts the music out.
She really knows how to belt out a song.

senses.definition: to talk to someone, perhaps annoyingly.
examples: Tom is over there, bending Jane’s ear about something.
I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to bend your ear for an hour.

senses.definition: determined to do something.
examples: Jane was bent on having her own apartment.
Her mother was bent on keeping her at home.

senses.definition: in an extreme state of some emotion.
examples: I was beside myself with joy.
Sarah could not speak. She was beside herself with anger.
I laughed so hard I was beside myself.

senses.definition: irrelevant; of no importance.
examples: That’s very interesting, but beside the point.
That’s beside the point. You’re evading the issue.
Your observation is beside the question.

senses.definition: one’s best clothing.
examples: I always wear my best bib and tucker on Sundays.
Put on your best bib and tucker, and let’s go to the city.

headword: the best-laid plans of mice and men
altForms: the best-laid schemes of mice and men

senses.definition: the best thought-out plans of anyone.
examples: If a little rain can ruin the best-laid plans of mice and men, think what an earthquake might do!
The best-laid schemes of mice and men are often disturbed by any small matter.

senses.definition: almost all of something; a large part of something; the major part of something.
examples: The discussion took the best part of an hour.
The best part of the meeting was taken up by budgetary matters.

senses.definition: to be quite certain (about something).
senses.notes: Both are informal and folksy. A bottom dollar is the last dollar.
examples: I’ll be there. You bet your bottom dollar.
I bet my bottom dollar you can’t swim across the pool.
You bet your life I can’t swim that far.
I bet my life on it.

senses.definition: better to do something late than not at all.
examples: I wish you had come here sooner, but better late than never.
She bought a house when she was quite old. Better late than never.

headword: between a rock and a hard place
altForms: between the devil and the deep blue sea

senses.definition: in a very difficult position; facing a hard decision.
examples: I couldn’t make up my mind. I was caught between a rock and a hard place.
He had a dilemma on his hands. He was clearly between the devil and the deep blue sea.

senses.definition: in a position where living or dying is an even possibility.
examples: And there I was on the operating table, hovering between life and death.
The mountain climber hung by his rope, caught between life and death.

headword: between you, me, and the lamppost

senses.definition: confidentially, just between you and me.
examples: Just between you, me, and the lamppost, Fred is leaving school.
Now don’t tell anyone else. This is just between you, me, and the lamppost.

senses.definition: between (people or things).
examples: I liked the soup and the dessert and all that came betwixt and between.
I sat betwixt and between all the actors who weren’t on stage.

senses.definition: undecided.
examples: I wish she would choose. She has been betwixt and between for three weeks.
Tom is so betwixt and between about getting married. I don’t think he’s ready.

senses.definition: almost without any doubt.
examples: The jury decided beyond a reasonable doubt that she had committed the crime.
She was also found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

senses.definition: more than can be measured; in a very large amount.
examples: They brought in hams, turkeys, and roasts, and then they brought vegetables and salads beyond measure.
They thanked all of us beyond measure.

senses.definition: in water that is too deep.
senses.notes: See also in over one’s head.
examples: Sally swam out beyond her depth.
Jane swam out to get her even though it was beyond her depth, too.

senses.definition: beyond one’s understanding or capabilities.
examples: I’m working beyond my depth in algebra class.
Poor John was involved in a problem that seemed really beyond his depth.

senses.definition: more than one can afford.
senses.notes: See also live beyond one’s means.
examples: I’m sorry, but this house is beyond our means. Please show us a cheaper one.
They felt that a Caribbean cruise is beyond their means.

senses.definition: unacceptable; outlawed; over the top.
examples: Your behavior is simply beyond the pale.
Because of Tom’s rudeness, he’s considered beyond the pale and is never asked to parties anymore.

headword: beyond the shadow of a doubt

senses.definition: completely without doubt.
senses.notes: Said of a fact, not a person. See also beyond a reasonable doubt.
examples: We accepted her story as true beyond the shadow of a doubt.
Please assure us that you are certain of the facts beyond the shadow of a doubt.

senses.definition: more than one can say.
senses.notes: Especially with grateful, shocked, and thankful.
examples: Sally was thankful beyond words.
I don’t know how to thank you. I’m grateful beyond words.

headword: bid adieu to someone or something

senses.definition: to say good-bye to someone or something.
senses.notes: This adieu is French for good-bye and should not be confused with ado.
examples: Now it’s time to bid adieu to all of you gathered here.
He silently bid adieu to his favorite hat as the wind carried it down the street.

senses.definition: to wait patiently.
examples: I’ve been biding my time for years, just waiting for a chance like this.
He’s not the type just to sit there and bide his time. He wants some action.

senses.definition: large and capable of getting attention.
examples: The lettering on the book’s cover was big and bold, and it got lots of attention, but the price was too high.
She wore a brightly colored dress. The pattern was big and bold and the skirt was very full.

headword: a big frog in a small pond

senses.definition: an important person in the midst of a less important setting.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: I’d rather be a big frog in a small pond than the opposite.
The trouble with Tom is that he’s a big frog in a small pond. He needs more competition.

altForms: the moment everyone has been waiting for

senses.definition: the special time that everyone has been waiting for.
examples: The big moment has come. I will now announce the winner.
This is the big moment that you all have been waiting for!

senses.definition: generous of someone; kind or forgiving of someone.
examples: He gave me some of his apple. That was very big of him.
It was big of Sally to come over and apologize like that.

senses.definition: to overeat and then vomit, over and over.
senses.notes: A symptom of the condition called bulimia.
examples: She had binged and purged a number of times before she finally sought help from a doctor.
Terry had been bingeing and purging for a number of years and was very, very thin.

headword: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

senses.definition: Something you already have is better than something you might get.
examples: Bill has offered to buy my car for $4,000. Someone else might pay more, but a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
I might be able to find a better price, but a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

senses.definition: human reproduction.
senses.notes: A euphemistic way of referring to human sex and reproduction.
examples: My father tried to teach me about the birds and the bees.
He’s twenty years old and doesn’t understand about the birds and the bees.

senses.definition: a view seen from high above.
senses.notes: Refers to the height of a flying bird.
examples: We got a bird’s-eye view of Cleveland as the plane began its descent.
From the top of the tower you get a splendid bird’s-eye view of the village.

senses.definition: a brief survey of something; a hasty look at something.
senses.notes: Refers to the smallness of a bird’s eye.
examples: The course provides a bird’s-eye view of the works of Mozart, but it doesn’t deal with them in enough detail for your purpose.
All you need is a bird’s-eye view of the events of World War II to pass the test.

headword: Birds of a feather flock together.

senses.definition: People of the same type seem to gather together.
examples: Bob and Tom are just alike. They like each other’s company because birds of a feather flock together.
When Mary joined a club for redheaded people, she said, “Birds of a feather flock together.”

headword: bite off more than one can chew

senses.definition: to take (on) more than one can deal with; to be overconfident.
senses.notes: This is used literally for food and figuratively for other things, especially difficult projects.
examples: Billy, stop biting off more than you can chew. You’re going to choke on your food someday.
Ann is exhausted again. She’s always biting off more than she can chew.

senses.definition: to be nervous or anxious; to bite one’s nails from nervousness or anxiety.
examples: I spent all afternoon biting my nails, worrying about you.
We’ve all been biting our nails from worry.

senses.definition: to struggle not to say something that you really want to say.
senses.notes: Used literally only to refer to an accidental biting of one’s tongue.
examples: I had to bite my tongue to keep from telling her what I really thought.
I sat through that whole conversation biting my tongue.

senses.definition: to speak sharply and angrily to someone.
examples: There was no need to bite Mary’s head off just because she was five minutes late.
The boss has been biting everybody’s head off since his accident.

senses.definition: to put up with or endure (something).
examples: I didn’t want to go to the doctor, but I bit the bullet and went.
John, you just have to bite the bullet and do what you’re told.

senses.definition: to fall to defeat; to die.
senses.notes: Typically heard in movies about the old western frontier.
examples: A bullet hit the sheriff in the chest, and he bit the dust.
Poor old Bill bit the dust while mowing the lawn. They buried him yesterday.

headword: bite the hand that feeds one

senses.definition: to harm someone who does good things for you.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to a dog, cat, or other animal.
examples: I’m your mother! How can you bite the hand that feeds you?
She can hardly expect much when she bites the hand that feeds her.

senses.definition: an unpleasant fact that has to be accepted.
examples: It was a bitter pill for her brother to swallow when she married his enemy.
We found his deception a bitter pill to swallow.

senses.definition: bruised; showing signs of having been physically harmed.
examples: The child was black-and-blue after having been struck.
She was black-and-blue all over after falling out of the tree.

senses.definition: to faint or pass out.
examples: Sally blacked out just before the crash.
I was so frightened that I blacked out for a minute.

headword: the black sheep of the family

senses.definition: the worst member of the family.
examples: Mary is the black sheep of the family. She’s always in trouble with the police.
He keeps making a nuisance of himself. What do you expect from the black sheep of the family?

senses.definition: to shoot into the sky.
examples: What time does the rocket blast off?
It won’t blast off today. It has been canceled.

senses.definition: ) to create and develop a new area of study or development.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to creating and marking a trail.
examples: In the area of conservation, Wright and Walters blazed a trail in the use of technology to preserve topsoil.
Professor Williams blazed a trail in the study of physics.

senses.definition: to replace a word or phrase in a radio or television broadcast with some sort of musical tone.
senses.notes: This is sometimes done to prevent a bad word or other information from being broadcast.
examples: He tried to say the word on television, but they bleeped it out.
They tried to bleep out the whole sentence.

senses.definition: something that turns out to be fortunate and advantageous after seeming to be the opposite at first.
examples: Our missing the train was a blessing in disguise. It was involved in a crash.
It was a blessing in disguise that I didn’t get the job. I was offered a better one the next day.

senses.definition: having to do with a situation where people who don’t know how to do something try to explain it to other people.
examples: Tom doesn’t know anything about cars, but he’s trying to teach Sally how to change the oil. It’s a case of the blind leading the blind.
When I tried to show Mary how to use a computer, it was the blind leading the blind.

senses.definition: People who are related have stronger obligations to each other than to people outside the family and are expected to endure family problems.
examples: My friends invited me to go camping on Saturday, but I have to go to my cousin’s wedding instead. Blood is thicker than water, after all.
If you ever need help, don’t ask your friends. Come home and ask us, your family. Blood is thicker than water.

senses.definition: the signs of great personal effort.
examples: There will be much blood, sweat, and tears before we have completed this project.
After years of blood, sweat, and tears, Timmy finally earned a college degree.

senses.definition: showing signs of a struggle, but not bowed in defeat.
examples: Liz emerged from the struggle, her head bloody but unbowed.
We are bloody but unbowed and will fight to the last.

senses.definition: to burn out a fuse.
examples: The microwave oven blew a fuse, so we had no power.
You’ll blow a fuse if you use too many appliances at once.

senses.definition: to become very angry; to lose one’s temper.
examples: I was so mad I almost blew a gasket.
I’ve never heard such a thing. I’m going to blow a fuse.
I blew my cork when he hit me.
I was so mad I could have blown my top.
I makes me so mad I could blow my stack.

senses.definition: a detailed description (of an event) given as the event takes place.
senses.notes: This referred originally to boxing or other combat.
examples: I want to listen to a blow-by-blow account of the prizefight.
The lawyer got the witness to give a blow-by-blow description of the argument.

senses.definition: to be changeable or uncertain (about something).
examples: He keeps blowing hot and cold on the question of moving to the country.
He blows hot and cold about this. I wish he’d make up his mind.

senses.definition: to vomit.
examples: The accident was so horrible I almost blew my lunch.
Don’t run so hard, or you’ll blow your cookies.

senses.definition: to drive mucus and other material from the nose using air pressure from the lungs.
examples: Excuse me, I have to blow my nose.
Bill blew his nose into his handkerchief.

senses.definition: to go away without causing harm.
examples: If we are lucky, the storm will blow over.
Given time, all this controversy will blow over.

senses.definition: to kill or destroy someone or something.
examples: He drew his gun and blew the thief away.
His bad attitude blew away the whole deal.

senses.definition: to overcome someone emotionally.
examples: The bad news really blew me away.
Your news just blew me away! How exciting!

senses.definition: to neglect or bumble something.
examples: He would do better in school if he didn’t blow his math class off.
He blew off his homework.

senses.definition: to deceive or cheat someone.
examples: She really blew me off on the question of grades. She was really failing all the time.
She blew off the teacher by cheating on the test.

headword: blow someone or something to smithereens

senses.definition: to explode someone or something into tiny pieces.
examples: The bomb blew the ancient church to smithereens.
The mortar blew the entire squad to smithereens.

senses.definition: to reveal someone’s true identity or purpose.
examples: The spy was very careful not to blow her cover.
I tried to disguise myself, but my dog recognized me and blew my cover.

senses.definition: to destroy the function of one’s brain.
examples: It was a terrible experience. It nearly blew my mind.
She blew her mind on drugs.

senses.definition: to overwhelm someone; to excite someone.
examples: It was so beautiful, it nearly blew my mind.
The music was so wild. It blew my mind.

senses.definition: to ruin or waste something.
examples: I had a chance to do it, but I blew it.
He blew the whole five dollars on candy.

headword: blow something out of all proportion

senses.definition: to cause something to be unrealistically proportioned relative to something else.
senses.notes: The all can be left out.
examples: The press has blown this issue out of all proportion.
Let’s be reasonable. Don’t blow this thing out of proportion.

senses.definition: to reveal something, especially wrongdoing; to make wrongdoing public.
examples: The police blew the lid off the smuggling ring.
The government is glad that they blew the lid off.

senses.definition: to report someone’s wrongdoing to someone (such as the police) who can stop the wrongdoing.
examples: The citizens’ group blew the whistle on the street gangs by calling the police.
The gangs were getting very bad. It was definitely time to blow the whistle.

senses.definition: to fall apart or get ruined.
examples: The whole project blew up. It will have to be canceled.
All my planning was blown up this afternoon.

senses.definition: to get angry at someone; to lose one’s temper and yell at someone.
examples: I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to blow up.
You’d blow up, too, if you’d had a day like mine.

senses.definition: to blow up or explode suddenly.
examples: The bomb blew up in the terrorist’s face.
The firecracker blew up in his face and injured him.

senses.definition: to get ruined while someone is working on it.
examples: All my plans blew up in my face.
It is terrible for your life to get ruined and blow up in your face.

senses.definition: the blood [heredity] of a noble family; aristocratic ancestry.
examples: The earl refuses to allow anyone who is not of blue blood to marry his son.
Although Mary’s family is poor, she has blue blood in her veins.

senses.definition: to confuse someone; to overwhelm someone; to blow someone’s mind.
examples: The size of the house boggles my mind.
She said that his arrogance boggled her mind.

senses.definition: to reduce to something; to come down to something; to be essentially something.
examples: It all boils down to whether you wish to buy a car.
It boils down to a question of good health.

senses.definition: to summarize something; to make information more concise.
senses.notes: Also literal in reference to liquids.
examples: I don’t have time to listen to the whole story. Please boil it down for me.
Please boil down the report so I can read it on the plane.

senses.definition: the subject or point of an argument; an unsettled point of disagreement.
examples: We’ve fought for so long that we’ve forgotten what the bone of contention is.
The question of a fence between the houses has become quite a bone of contention.

senses.definition: to study something thoroughly; to review the facts about something.
examples: I have to bone up on the state driving laws because I have to take my driving test tomorrow.
I take mine next month, so I’ll have to bone up, too.

senses.definition: to bore someone very much.
senses.notes: Stiff is an old slang word meaning “dead.”
examples: The play bored me stiff.
The lecture bored everyone to death.

senses.definition: very bored; completely bored.
examples: I was bored silly at the lecture.
The dull speaker left me bored to distraction.
I am bored to tears. Let’s go home.

senses.definition: very bored.
examples: The children were bored to death.
I’ve never been so bored to death in my life.

senses.definition: born and nurtured through childhood, usually in a specific place.
examples: She was born and raised in a small town in western Montana.
Freddy was born and bred on a farm and had no love for city life.

senses.definition: born to an unmarried mother.
examples: The child was born out of wedlock.
In the city many children are born out of wedlock.

headword: born with a silver spoon in one’s mouth

senses.definition: born with many advantages; born to a wealthy family.
examples: Sally was born with a silver spoon in her mouth.
I’m glad I was not born with a silver spoon in my mouth.

senses.definition: to worry needlessly; to make trouble for oneself.
examples: Worrying too much about death is just borrowing trouble.
Do not get involved with politics. That’s borrowing trouble.

senses.definition: to give orders to someone; to keep telling someone what to do.
examples: Stop bossing me around. I’m not your employee.
Captain Smith bosses around the whole crew. That’s his job.

senses.definition: to constrict something as if it were put in a bottle.
examples: The patrol boats bottled the other boats up at the locks on the river.
The police bottled up the traffic while they searched the cars for the thieves.

senses.definition: to hold one’s feelings within; to keep from saying something that one feels strongly about.
examples: Let’s talk about it, John. You shouldn’t bottle it up.
Don’t bottle up your problems. It’s better to talk them out.

senses.definition: the last figure on a financial balance sheet representing net profit or loss.
examples: What’s the bottom line? How much do I owe you?
Don’t tell me all those figures! Just tell me the bottom line.

senses.definition: the result; the final outcome.
examples: I know about all the problems, but what is the bottom line? What will happen?
The bottom line is that you have to go to the meeting because no one else can.

senses.definition: to reach the lowest point.
examples: The price of wheat bottomed out last week. Now it’s rising again.
My interest in school bottomed out in my junior year, so I quit and got a job.

senses.definition: Everyone should drink now!
senses.notes: Said at the end of a drinking toast.
examples: Here’s to the bride and groom. Bottoms up!
Bottoms up! Drink hearty!

senses.definition: determined.
examples: We were bound and determined to get there on time.
I’m bound and determined that this won’t happen again.

senses.definition: on the way to somewhere; planning to go to somewhere.
examples: I’m bound for Mexico. In fact, I’m leaving this afternoon.
I’m bound for the bank. Do you want to go, too?

senses.definition: with hands and feet tied up.
examples: The robbers left us bound hand and foot.
We remained bound hand and foot until the maid found us and untied us.

senses.definition: to be certain to do something.
