examples: They are bound to come home soon. They always come home early.
Oh, yes. They are bound to.

senses.definition: to be very humble and subservient.
examples: Please don’t bow and scrape. We are all equal here.
The salesclerk came in, bowing and scraping, and asked if he could help us.

senses.definition: to quit and depart; to resign; to retire.
examples: I’ve done all that I can do. Now is the time to bow out.
Most workers bow out at the normal retirement age.

senses.definition: to surprise or overwhelm someone.
examples: The news bowled me over.
The details of the proposed project bowled everyone over.

senses.definition: That’s the kind of thing that boys seem to do.; That’s the kind of silly behavior that boys and men exhibit.
examples: They really messed up the living room, but boys will be boys.
Boys will be boys, but they can be trained.

senses.definition: a letter or note written to follow up on a visit; a thankyou note.
examples: When I got back from the sales meeting, I took two days to write bread-and-butter letters to the people I met.
I got sort of a bread-and-butter letter from my nephew, who wants to visit me next summer.

senses.definition: the most minimal meal possible; a prison meal.
senses.notes: Also literal. Refers to the stereotypical prison meal.
examples: Max knew that if he got in trouble again it would be at least a year on bread and water.
This dinner is terrible again. I would rather have bread and water! Why don’t we ever have pizza?

senses.definition: to figure out a code; to decipher a code.
examples: The intelligence agents finally broke the enemy’s code.
When they broke the code, they were able to decipher messages.

senses.definition: to end a habit.
examples: I was not able to break the habit of snoring.
It’s hard to break a habit that you have had for a long time.

senses.definition: to fail to obey a law; to act contrary to a law.
examples: Lisa broke the law when she drove the wrong way on a one-way street.
If you never break the law, you will never get arrested.

senses.definition: Good luck!
senses.notes: Also literal. Theatrical slang. This is said to actors before a performance instead of Good luck.
examples: Before the play, John said to Mary, “Break a leg!”
Saying “Break a leg!” before a performance is an old theatrical tradition.

senses.definition: to surpass a previously set high record of achievement by setting a new one.
examples: The athlete broke all the school records in swimming.
The record was broken after thirty years.

senses.definition: to close down a campsite; to pack up and move on.
examples: Early this morning we broke camp and moved on northward.
Okay, everyone. It’s time to break camp. Take those tents down and fold them neatly.

senses.definition: to fall apart; [for something] to stop operating.
senses.notes: [for something] See also break someone or something down.
examples: The air-conditioning broke down, and we got very warm.
The car broke down in the parking lot.

senses.definition: to lose control of one’s emotions; [for one] to have a nervous collapse.
examples: He couldn’t keep going. He finally broke down and wept.
I was afraid I’d break down.

senses.definition: for income to equal expenses.
senses.notes: This implies that money was not earned or lost.
examples: Unfortunately my business just managed to break even last year.
I made a bad investment, but I broke even.

senses.definition: to start digging the foundation for a building.
examples: The president of the company came to break ground for the new building.
This was the third building this year for which this company has broken ground.
When will they break ground?

senses.definition: Stop fighting!; Stop it!
senses.notes: Said to two or more people causing a disturbance.
examples: All right! Break it up, you guys!
Stop your talking! Break it up and get back to work.

senses.definition: to get away from a person or a thing that is holding one.
senses.notes: Compare this with cut loose (from someone or something).
examples: The criminal broke loose from the police officer.
It’s hard to break loose from home.
I was twenty years old before I could break loose.

senses.definition: to begin to do something that no one else has done; to pioneer (in an enterprise).
examples: Dr. Anderson was breaking new ground in cancer research.
They were breaking new ground in consumer electronics.

senses.definition: to end a friendship with someone, especially a boyfriend or a girlfriend.
examples: Tom has finally broken off with Mary.
I knew it couldn’t last. He was bound to break off.

senses.definition: to work very hard to do something.
examples: I broke my neck to get here on time.
That’s the last time I’ll break my neck to help you.
There is no point in breaking your back. Take your time.

senses.definition: not to do what one said one would do; not to keep one’s promise.
senses.notes: The opposite of keep one’s word.
examples: Don’t say you’ll visit your grandmother if you can’t go. She hates people who break their word.
If you break your word, she won’t trust you again.

senses.definition: to burst forth suddenly, as with a fire, a riot, giggling, shouting, etc.
examples: A fire broke out in the belfry.
A round of giggling broke out when the teacher tripped.
A riot almost broke out when the police came.

senses.definition: to erupt in pimples.
examples: Bob’s face has started breaking out badly.
My face breaks out when I eat a lot of chocolate.

headword: break out in a cold sweat

senses.definition: to perspire from fever, fear, or anxiety; to begin to sweat profusely or suddenly.
examples: I was so frightened I broke out in a cold sweat.
The patient broke out in a cold sweat.

senses.definition: to erupt with something such as a rash, a cold sweat, or pimples.
examples: After being in the woods, I broke out in a rash. I think it’s poison ivy.
I hate to break out like that.
When I eat chocolate, I break out in pimples.
I was so frightened I broke out in a cold sweat.
The patient broke out in a cold sweat.

senses.definition: to start crying suddenly.
examples: I was so sad that I broke out into tears.
I always break into tears at a funeral.
It’s hard not to break out in tears under those circumstances.

senses.definition: to escape from something, often by destructive means.
senses.notes: Especially from prison, but also in figurative senses.
examples: The convicts plotted to break out of prison.
You don’t have the guts to break out of jail!
Don finally broke out of the depression that had held him captive for so long.
The lion broke out of its cage.

senses.definition: to force someone to give up and tell secrets or agree to do something.
examples: After threats of torture, they broke the spy down.
They broke down the agent by threatening violence.

senses.definition: to tear something down; to destroy something.
examples: They used an ax to break the door down.
We broke down the wall with big hammers.

senses.definition: to train someone to do a job; to supervise a new person learning a new job.
examples: It takes time to break a new worker in.
Are they hard to break in?
I have to break in a new worker.

senses.definition: to make something fit by wearing or using it.
examples: I’ll be glad when I’ve finished breaking in these shoes.
Yes, it takes time to break them in.
They are easy to break in, though.
The car will run better after I break it in.

senses.definition: to cause a person to laugh, perhaps at an inappropriate time.
examples: John told a joke that really broke Mary up.
The comedian’s job was to break up the audience by telling jokes.

senses.definition: to destroy something.
examples: The storm broke the docks up on the lake.
The police broke up the gambling ring.

senses.definition: to put an end to something.
examples: The police broke the fight up.
Walter’s parents broke up the party at three in the morning.

senses.definition: to cushion a falling person; to lessen the impact of a falling person.
examples: When the little boy fell out of the window, the bushes broke his fall.
The old lady slipped on the ice, but a snowbank broke her fall.

senses.definition: to cause someone emotional pain.
examples: It just broke my heart when Tom ran away from home.
Sally broke John’s heart when she refused to marry him.

senses.definition: to explain something to someone in simple terms or in an orderly fashion.
examples: She doesn’t understand. You will have to break it down for her.
I can help. This is a confusing question. Let me break it down for you.

senses.definition: to divide something into smaller parts; to divide something into its component parts.
examples: Please break this paragraph down into sentences.
The chemist broke down the compound into a number of elements.
Walter broke the project down into five tasks and assigned them to various people.

senses.definition: to shatter something.
examples: I broke my crystal vase to pieces.
I dropped a glass and broke it to pieces.

senses.definition: to tell bad news to someone.
examples: I hated to break the news to Dad about his car.
Bill broke it to his employees gently.

senses.definition: to end the domination of something; to reduce the power of something.
examples: The government has worked for years to break the back of organized crime.
This new medicine should break the back of the epidemic.

senses.definition: to use up all one’s money.
senses.notes: As in casino gambling where a gambler wins more money than the house has on hand.
examples: It will hardly break the bank if we go out to dinner just once.
Buying a new dress at that price won’t break the bank.

senses.definition: to initiate social interchanges and conversation; to get something started.
examples: Tom is so outgoing. He’s always the first one to break the ice at parties.
It’s hard to break the ice at formal events.
Sally broke the ice by bidding $20,000 for the painting.

senses.definition: to tell someone some important news, usually bad news.
examples: The doctor had to break the news to Jane about her husband’s cancer.
I hope that the doctor broke the news gently.

senses.definition: to overcome something nonphysical, such as a barrier caused by law, regulation, prejudice, attitude, etc.
examples: Tom was able to break through racial barriers.
The scientists broke through the mystery surrounding the disease and found the cause.

senses.definition: to end a love affair or a romance.
examples: Tom finally broke up with Mary.
I thought they would break up. He has been so moody lately.

senses.definition: the crime of forcing one’s way into a place.
examples: Max was charged with four counts of breaking and entering.
It was not an act of breaking and entering. The thief just opened the door and walked right in.

senses.definition: air that is not stale or smelly.
examples: I feel faint. I think I need a breath of fresh air.
You look ill, John. What you need is a breath of fresh air.

senses.definition: air that is not (figuratively) contaminated with unpleasant people or situations.
senses.notes: This is a sarcastic version of sense 1.
examples: You people are disgusting. I have to get out of here and get a breath of fresh air.
I believe I’ll go get a breath of fresh air. The intellectual atmosphere in here is stifling.

senses.definition: a new, fresh, and imaginative approach (to something).
examples: Sally, with all her wonderful ideas, is a breath of fresh air.
New furniture in this room is like a breath of fresh air.

senses.definition: to keep close watch on someone; to watch someone’s activities.
senses.notes: Also literal. Refers to standing very close behind a person.
examples: I can’t work with you breathing down my neck all the time. Go away.
I will get through my life without your help. Stop breathing down my neck.

senses.definition: to try to hurry someone along; to make someone get something done on time.
senses.notes: The subject does not have to be a person. See the second example.
examples: I have to finish my taxes today. The tax collector is breathing down my neck.
I have a deadline breathing down my neck.

senses.definition: to assume a relaxed state after a stressful period.
examples: After all this is over, I’ll be able to breathe easy again.
He won’t be able to breathe easy until he pays off his debts.

senses.definition: to die; to breathe one’s last breath in the process of dying.
examples: Mrs. Smith breathed her last this morning.
I’ll keep running every day until I breathe my last.

senses.definition: to plot something; to make a plot.
examples: The children brewed an evil plot to get revenge on their teacher.
We brewed a plot so that we would not have to help with dinner.

senses.definition: buildings.
senses.notes: The buildings referred to can be constructed out of anything.
examples: The new president of the college preferred to invest in new faculty members rather than bricks and mortar.
Sometimes people are happy to donate millions of dollars for bricks and mortar, but they never think of the additional cost of annual maintenance.

senses.definition: very early.
examples: Yes, I’ll be there bright and early.
I want to see you here on time tomorrow, bright and early, or you’re fired!

senses.definition: very cheerful and eager.
senses.notes: Refers to the twinkling eyes and quick, energetic movements of a squirrel.
examples: She appeared at the top of the stairs, bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, ready to start the day.
I am awake, but I am hardly bright-eyed and bushy-tailed.

senses.definition: full of some kind of happy behavior.
examples: The volunteer worker was brimming with goodwill.
The giggling children were brimming with joy.

senses.definition: full to the point of overflowing.
examples: Tom’s glass was brimming with milk.
The pool was brimming with water.

senses.definition: to excite a theatrical audience to laughter or applause or both.
examples: Her performance didn’t bring down the house—it emptied it.
This is a great joke. The last time I told it, it brought the house down.

senses.definition: to earn a salary.
examples: I’ve got to get to work if I’m going to bring home the bacon.
Go out and get a job so you can bring home the bacon.

headword: bring people or other creatures out in droves

senses.definition: to lure or draw out someone or some creature in great number.
examples: The availability of free drinks brought people out in droves.
The fresh grass sprouts brought the deer out in droves.

senses.definition: to bring someone for a visit; to bring someone for someone (else) to meet.
examples: Please bring your wife around sometime. I’d love to meet her.
You’ve just got to bring the doctor around for dinner.

senses.definition: to bring someone to consciousness.
examples: The doctor brought Tom around with smelling salts.
The boxer was knocked out, but the doctor brought him around.

senses.definition: to persuade someone (to accept something); to manage to get someone to agree (to something).
examples: The last debate brought a lot of voters around to our candidate.
I knew I could bring her around if I just had enough time to talk to her.

senses.definition: to mention a person or a thing.
examples: I’m sorry. I won’t bring him up again.
Please don’t bring up that matter again.
Please don’t bring up John Jones’s name again.

senses.definition: to raise a child or an animal.
examples: Her uncle brought her up.
It’s difficult to bring up a pet monkey.

senses.definition: to make someone or something more modern.
senses.notes: See also bring someone up-to-date (on someone or something).
examples: Let’s buy some new furniture and bring this room up-to-date.
John tried to bring himself up-to-date by changing his hairstyle, but he still looked like the same old John.

headword: bring someone up-to-date (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to tell someone the news about something.
examples: Please bring me up-to-date on the Middle East situation.
Please bring me up-to-date on John. I want to hear all the news.
And bring me up-to-date, too.

senses.definition: to make something happen.
examples: Is she clever enough to bring it about?
Oh, yes, she can bring about anything she wants.

senses.definition: to destroy something that one has built; to destroy something that one has a special interest in.
examples: She brought her whole life crashing down around her.
Bob’s low grade in English brought everything crashing down when his parents grounded him.

senses.definition: to cause someone to realize the truth of something.
examples: Seeing the starving refugees on television really brings home the tragedy of their situation.
It wasn’t until she failed her test that the importance of studying was brought home to her.

senses.definition: to question something; to raise a question about something.
examples: It was necessary to bring your part in this matter into question.
The city council brought the building project into question.

senses.definition: to make something happen; to produce a great event.
examples: She managed to bring the party off with no difficulty.
She brought off a similar party last season.

senses.definition: to cause something to come to the point when a decision has to be made or an action taken.
examples: The latest disagreement between management and the union has brought matters to a head. There will be an all-out strike now.
It’s a relief that things have been brought to a head. The disputes have been going on for months.

senses.definition: to make something known; to discover something.
examples: The scientists brought their findings to light.
We must bring this new evidence to light.

senses.definition: to make someone aware of something; to mention or show something to someone.
examples: I would like to bring this problem to your attention.
If there is something I should know about, please bring it to my attention.

senses.definition: to move along behind everyone else; to be at the end of the line.
examples: Here comes John, bringing up the rear.
Hurry up, Tom! Why are you always bringing up the rear?

senses.definition: with wide hips or large buttocks.
senses.notes: From a nautical expression for a wide ship.
examples: I am getting a little broad in the beam. It’s time to go on a diet.
John is just naturally broad in the beam.

senses.definition: to review something, especially a school subject.
examples: I think I should brush up on my Spanish before I go to Mexico.
I’ve heard you speak Spanish. You need to do more than brush up.

senses.definition: to aim, try, or strike for a goal.
senses.notes: Originally referred to trying to get a higher military rank.
examples: Bill acts that way because he’s bucking for corporal.
Tom is bucking for a larger office.

senses.definition: cheer up.
examples: Buck up, old friend! Things can’t be all that bad.
I know I have to buck up. Life must go on.

senses.definition: to leave; to pack up and get out.
examples: It’s time to bug out. Let’s get out of here.
I just got a call from headquarters. They say to bug out immediately.

senses.definition: to irritate someone; to bother someone.
examples: Go away! Stop bugging me!
Leave me alone. Go bug someone else.

senses.definition: to put together the evidence needed to make a legal or disciplinary case against someone.
examples: The police easily built a case against the drunken driver.
As soon as we gather the case against her, we will arrest her.

senses.definition: to do something to make someone else start doing something.
examples: The teacher built a fire under the students, and they really started working.
Somebody built a fire under Bill, so he finally went out and got a job.

senses.definition: to daydream; to make plans that can never come true.
examples: Ann spends most of her time building castles in Spain.
I really like to sit on the porch in the evening, just building castles in the air.

senses.definition: to make someone or something stronger or bigger.
examples: Tom is eating lots of fresh fruits and vegetables to build himself up for basketball.
Tom needs to build up.
Tom needs to build himself up.
The farmer built up his stone fences where they had weakened.

senses.definition: to advertise, praise, or promote someone or something.
examples: Theatrical agents work very hard to build up their clients.
An advertising agency can build up a product so much that everyone will want it.

senses.definition: to build something especially for the customer who ordered it.
senses.notes: See also make something to order.
examples: Our new car was built to order just for us.
My company builds computers to order. No two are alike.

senses.definition: to lead up to something; to work up to something.
examples: You could tell by the way she was talking that she was building up to something.
The sky was building up to a storm.

headword: a bull in a china shop

senses.definition: a very clumsy or wild person around breakable things; a thoughtless or tactless person.
examples: Look at Bill, as awkward as a bull in a china shop.
Get that big dog out of my garden. It’s like a bull in a china shop.
Bob is so rude, a regular bull in a china shop.

senses.definition: to chance on someone; to meet someone by chance.
examples: Guess who I bumped into downtown today?
I ran into Bob Jones yesterday.

senses.definition: to kill someone.
examples: They tried to bump her off, but she was too clever and got away.
The crooks bumped off the witness to the crime.
They tried to knock them all off.

senses.definition: someone who is very nervous and anxious.
examples: Mary was a bundle of nerves until she heard that she passed the test.
You always seem to be such a bundle of nerves.

senses.definition: to make decisions that cannot be changed in the future.
examples: If you drop out of school now, you’ll be burning your bridges behind you.
You’re too young to burn your bridges that way.

senses.definition: to be unpleasant in a situation that you are leaving, ensuring that you’ll never be welcome to return.
examples: If you get mad and quit your job, you’ll be burning your bridges behind you.
No sense burning your bridges. Be polite and leave quietly.

senses.definition: to cut off the way back to where you came from, making it impossible to retreat.
examples: The army, which had burned its bridges behind it, couldn’t go back.
By blowing up the road, the spies had burned their bridges behind them.

headword: burn one’s bridges in front of one

senses.definition: to create future problems for oneself.
senses.notes: A play on burn one’s bridges (behind one).
examples: I made a mistake again. I always seem to burn my bridges in front of me.
I accidentally insulted a math teacher whom I will have to take a course from next semester. I am burning my bridges in front of me.

senses.definition: to do something so long and so intensely that one gets sick and tired of doing it and can no longer do it well.
examples: I burned myself out as an opera singer. I just cannot do it anymore.
Tom burned himself out playing golf. He can’t stand it anymore.
Tom burned out too young.

senses.definition: to break down and become useless.
examples: I hope the light bulb in the ceiling doesn’t burn out. I can’t reach it.
The motor burned out.

senses.definition: to set fire to a person tied to a post (as a form of execution).
examples: They used to burn witches at the stake.
Look, officer, I only ran a stop sign. What are you going to do, burn me at the stake?

senses.definition: to chastise or denounce someone severely, but without violence.
examples: Stop yelling. I made a simple mistake, and you’re burning me at the stake for it.
Sally only spilled her milk. There is no need to shout. Don’t burn her at the stake for it.

senses.definition: to burn a dummy or other figure that represents a hated person.
senses.notes: See also hang someone in effigy.
examples: For the third day in a row, they burned the king in effigy.
Until they have burned you in effigy, you can’t really be considered a famous leader.

senses.definition: to make someone very angry.
examples: People like that just burn me up!
It burns me up to hear you talk that way.
His answers really burned up the committee members.

headword: burn the candle at both ends

senses.definition: to work very hard and stay up very late at night.
examples: No wonder Mary is ill. She has been burning the candle at both ends for a long time.
You can’t keep on burning the candle at both ends.

senses.definition: to stay up working, especially studying, late at night.
senses.notes: Refers to working by the light of an oil lamp.
examples: I have to go home and burn the midnight oil tonight.
If you burn the midnight oil night after night, you’ll probably become ill.

headword: burn with a low blue flame

senses.definition: to be very angry.
senses.notes: Refers to the imaginary heat caused by extreme anger. A blue flame is a hot flame.
examples: By the time she showed up three hours late, I was burning with a low blue flame.
Whenever Ann gets mad, she just presses her lips together and burns with a low blue flame.

senses.definition: burned very badly.
examples: I stayed out in the sun too long, and I am burned to a cinder.
This toast is burnt to a cinder.

senses.definition: very angry.
examples: I’ve never been so burned up in my life.
I’m really burned up at Bob.

senses.definition: to “explode” (figuratively) with pride or laughter.
examples: Tom nearly burst at the seams with pride.
We laughed so hard we just about burst at the seams.

headword: burst in on someone or something

senses.definition: to enter a room, interrupting someone or some activity.
senses.notes: [for someone] Often without knocking or seeking permission to enter.
examples: Tom burst in on his sister and her boyfriend while they were kissing.
I must ask you not to burst in on a board meeting again. Whatever it is can wait.

senses.definition: to catch fire suddenly; to ignite all at once.
examples: Suddenly, the car burst into flames.
It was so hot in the forest fire that a few trees literally burst into flames.

senses.definition: to begin to cry suddenly.
examples: After the last notes of her song, the audience burst into tears, such was its beauty and tenderness.
The brother and sister burst into tears on hearing of the death of their dog.
Some people find themselves bursting out crying for no reason at all.

senses.definition: to appear suddenly in a location.
examples: When Charles burst onto the scene, no one was prepared for the news he brought.
The police suddenly burst onto the scene and arrested everyone present.

senses.definition: to begin to laugh suddenly.
examples: The entire audience burst out laughing at exactly the wrong time, and so did the actors.
Every time I think of you sitting there with a lap full of noodle soup, I burst out laughing.

senses.definition: to destroy someone’s illusion or delusion; to destroy someone’s fantasy.
examples: I hate to burst your bubble, but Columbus did not discover Canada.
Even if I am completely wrong, please don’t burst my bubble.

senses.definition: to be full to the bursting point with happiness.
senses.notes: See also burst at the seams.
examples: When I got my grades, I could have burst with joy.
Joe was not exactly bursting with joy when he got the news.

senses.definition: to be full to the bursting point with pride.
senses.notes: See also burst at the seams.
examples: My parents were bursting with pride when I graduated from college.
I almost burst with pride when I was chosen to go up in the space shuttle.

headword: bury one’s head in the sand
altForms: hide one’s head in the sand

senses.definition: to ignore or hide from obvious signs of danger.
senses.notes: Refers to an ostrich, which we picture with its head stuck into the sand or the ground.
examples: Stop burying your head in the sand. Look at the statistics on smoking and cancer.
And stop hiding your head in the sand. All of us will die somehow, whether we smoke or not.

senses.definition: to stop fighting or arguing; to end old resentments.
examples: All right, you two. Calm down and bury the hatchet.
I wish Mr. and Mrs. Franklin would bury the hatchet. They argue all the time.

senses.definition: having things go along as usual.
examples: Right after the flood, it was business as usual in all the stores.
Please, everyone, business as usual. Let’s get back to work.

senses.definition: the part or end of something that actually does the work or carries out the procedure.
examples: Keep away from the business end of the electric drill to avoid getting hurt.
Don’t point the business end of that gun at anyone. It might go off.

senses.definition: leisure time spent doing something similar to what one does at work.
examples: Tutoring students in the evening is too much of a busman’s holiday for our English teacher.
It’s a bit of a busman’s holiday to ask her to be wardrobe mistress for our amateur production in the summer. She’s a professional dressmaker.

senses.definition: to work very hard; to strain oneself to do something.
senses.notes: Slang. Gut is considered impolite in some circumstances. Bust is an informal form of burst.
examples: I don’t intend to bust a gut to get there on time.
I busted a gut to get there the last time, and I was the first one there.

senses.definition: if it were not for someone or something.
examples: But for the railing, I’d have fallen down the stairs.
But for the children, Mrs. Smith would have left her husband years ago.

senses.definition: to interrupt someone or something.
examples: Pardon me for butting in on your conversation, but this is important.
John butted in on Tom and Jane to tell them that the mail had come.
That’s a strange reason to butt in. What was in the mail?

senses.definition: to praise and flatter someone, usually with the intention of requesting a favor.
examples: I believe my landlady prefers for me to butter her up rather than getting the rent on time.
If I butter up the teacher, will he give me a good grade?

senses.definition: to get quiet and stay quiet.
examples: All right now, let’s button our lips and listen to the story.
Button your lip, Tom! I’ll tell you when you can talk.

headword: buy a pig in a poke

senses.definition: to purchase or accept something without having seen or examined it.
senses.notes: Poke means “bag.” Compare this with buy something sight unseen.
examples: Buying a car without test-driving it is like buying a pig in a poke.
He bought a pig in a poke when he ordered a diamond ring by mail.

senses.definition: to bribe someone; to win someone over by gifts or favors.
examples: It’s not hard to buy politicians off.
They bought off the whole city council with campaign contributions.

senses.definition: to believe someone; to accept something to be a fact.
examples: It may be true, but I don’t buy it.
I just don’t buy the idea that you can swim that far.

senses.definition: to buy something cheaply.
examples: No one else wanted it, so I bought it for a song.
I could buy this house for a song, because it’s so ugly.

senses.definition: to purchase something now and pay for it later (plus interest).
senses.notes: See also sell something on credit.
examples: Almost everyone who buys a house buys it on credit.
I didn’t have any cash with me, so I used my credit card and bought a new coat on credit.

senses.definition: to buy something without seeing it first.
senses.notes: Compare this with buy a pig in a poke.
examples: I bought this land sight unseen. I didn’t know it was so rocky.
It isn’t usually safe to buy something sight unseen.

senses.definition: to purchase food to take out; to make a purchase of cooked food to be taken elsewhere to be eaten.
examples: Let’s stop here and buy six hamburgers to go.
I didn’t thaw anything for dinner. Let’s stop off on the way home and get something to go.
No, I don’t want to sit at a table. I’ll just have a cup of coffee to go.

senses.definition: just barely; by a very small distance.
examples: I just missed getting on the plane by a hair’s breadth.
I made it by a hair!
The arrow missed the deer by a whisker.

senses.definition: apparently; according to what one sees.
examples: She is, by all appearances, ready to resume work.
By all appearances, we ought to be approaching the airport.

senses.definition: certainly; yes; absolutely.
senses.notes: Compare this with by any means.
examples: I will attempt to get there by all means.
BOB: Can you come to dinner tomorrow? JANE: By all means. I’d love to.

senses.definition: using every possible manner of something to do something.
examples: People will be arriving by all means of transportation.
The surgeon performed the operation by all means of instruments.

senses.definition: by a great distance.
senses.notes: Also literal. An exaggeration in this case.
examples: You missed the target by a mile.
Your estimate of the budget deficit was off by a mile.

senses.definition: generally; usually.
examples: I find that, by and large, people tend to do what they are told to do.
By and large, rosebushes need lots of care.

senses.definition: by any way possible.
examples: I need to get there soon by any means.
I must win this contest by any means, fair or unfair.
It cannot be done by any means.

senses.definition: a vote expressed by people raising their hands.
examples: We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands.
Bob wanted us to vote on paper, not by a show of hands, so that we could have a secret ballot.

senses.definition: accidentally; randomly; without planning.
examples: I found this book by chance at a book sale.
We met by chance in a class in college.

senses.definition: by using a check.
examples: He paid for the book by check.
You will be paid by check.

senses.definition: due to conscious choice; on purpose.
examples: I do this kind of thing by choice. No one makes me do it.
I didn’t go to this college by choice. It was the closest one to home.

senses.definition: by an accidental and strange similarity; by an unplanned pair of similar events or occurrences.
examples: We just happened to be in the same place at the same time by coincidence.
By coincidence, the circus was in town when I was there. I’m glad because I love circuses.

senses.definition: during the day; during the night.
examples: By day, Mary worked in an office; by night, she took classes.
Dave slept by day and worked by night.

senses.definition: because of something; due to the efforts of something.
senses.notes: Dint is an old word meaning “force,” and it is never used except in this phrase.
examples: They got the building finished on time by dint of hard work and good organization.
By dint of much studying, John got through college.

senses.definition: irregularly; unevenly; with much stopping and starting.
examples: Somehow, they got the job done by fits and starts.
By fits and starts, the old car finally got us to town.

senses.definition: by luck; with the help of God.
senses.notes: Folksy. Golly is a disguise of God.
examples: They managed to get the shed built by guess and by golly.
I lost my ruler and had to install the new floor tile by guess and by golly.

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: She hates to go to strange places by herself.
She sat by herself at a table big enough for six people.

senses.definition: with the help of no one else.
examples: She can do it by herself.
Susan is unable to get there by herself.

senses.definition: alone; with no one else present.
examples: He is home by himself tonight.
He hates to eat by himself. It makes him feel lonely.

senses.definition: with the help of no one else.
examples: Can he do it by himself?
The twoyear-old boy can get dressed by himself.

senses.definition: by any means, legal or illegal.
examples: I’ll get the job done by hook or by crook.
I must have that house. I intend to get it by hook or crook.

senses.definition: with the help of nothing else; without the addition of anything else.
examples: Will this be enough by itself?
Can the dog get out of the house by itself?

senses.definition: rapidly; by large movements forward.
examples: Our garden is growing by leaps and bounds.
The profits of my company are increasing by leaps and bounds.

senses.definition: using something; with the use of something.
examples: I opened the bottle by means of a bottle opener.
I was able to afford a car by means of a loan.

senses.definition: in error; accidentally.
examples: I’m sorry. I came into the wrong room by mistake.
I chose the wrong road by mistake. Now we are lost.

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: I sat at the table by myself.
I will not be at the party. I will be at home by myself tonight.

senses.definition: without the help of anyone else.
examples: I did it all by myself.
Do you think I can eat this whole pie by myself?

senses.definition: absolutely not; certainly not.
examples: I’m by no means angry with you.
BOB: Did you put this box here? TOM: By no means. I didn’t do it, I’m sure.

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: Do we have to sit here by ourselves? Can’t we sit with Mary and Max?
We like to eat by ourselves, so we can talk about private matters.

senses.definition: with the help of no one else.
examples: We can do it by ourselves.
Can we lift this by ourselves, or do we need some help?

senses.definition: by a subsequent mailing (back to the sender).
senses.notes: A phrase indicating that an answer is expected soon, by mail.
examples: Since this bill is overdue, would you kindly send us your check by return mail?
I answered your request by return mail over a year ago. Please check your records.

senses.definition: by foot.
senses.notes: Shank refers to the shank of the leg. Folksy. See also go (somewhere) by shank’s mare.
examples: My car isn’t working, so I’ll have to travel by shank’s mare.
I’m sore because I’ve been getting around by shank’s mare.

senses.definition: one day at a time.
examples: I don’t know when I’ll have to leave town, so I rent this room by the day.
Sally is in such distress. She manages to live only by the day.

senses.definition: twelve at a time; in a group of twelve.
senses.notes: Almost the same as the following entry.
examples: I purchase socks by the dozen.
Eggs are usually sold by the dozen.
Around here we have problems by the dozen.

senses.definition: many; by some large, indefinite number.
senses.notes: Similar to but less than hundreds. Almost the same as the previous entry.
examples: Just then people began showing up by the dozens.
I baked cakes and pies by the dozens.

senses.definition: in measurements equal to a handful; lots.
examples: Billy is eating candy by the handful.
People began leaving by the handful at midnight.

senses.definition: at each hour; after each hour.
examples: It kept growing darker by the hour.
I have to take this medicine by the hour.
The illness is getting worse by the hour.

senses.definition: one month at a time.
examples: Not many apartments are rented by the month.
I needed a car for a short while, so I rented one by the month.

senses.definition: with help from no one else.
examples: Do you think they can do it by themselves?
Mike and Max cannot lift the piano by themselves.

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: They are sitting there by themselves. Let’s sit with them.
They enjoy spending the evening at home by themselves.

headword: by the nape of the neck

senses.definition: by the back of the neck.
senses.notes: Mostly found in real or mock threats.
examples: He grabbed me by the nape of the neck and told me not to turn around if I valued my life. I stood very still.
If you do that again, I’ll pick you up by the nape of the neck and throw you out the door.

senses.definition: according to the rules.
examples: He always plays the game by the numbers. He never cheats.
I want all my people to go by the numbers. This place is totally honest.
We always go by the book in matters like this.

senses.definition: in the same way; reciprocally.
examples: Tom must be good when he comes here, and, by the same token, I expect you to behave properly when you go to his house.
The mayor votes for his friend’s causes. By the same token, the friend votes for the mayor’s causes.

headword: by the seat of one’s pants

senses.definition: by sheer luck and very little skill.
examples: I got through school by the seat of my pants.
The jungle pilot spent most of his days flying by the seat of his pants.

headword: by the skin of one’s teeth

senses.definition: just barely; by an amount equal to the thickness of the (imaginary) skin on one’s teeth.
examples: I got through that class by the skin of my teeth.
I got to the airport late and missed the plane by the skin of my teeth.

headword: by the sweat of one’s brow

senses.definition: by one’s efforts; by one’s hard work.
examples: Tom raised these vegetables by the sweat of his brow.
Sally polished the car by the sweat of her brow.

senses.definition: incidentally; in addition; while I think of it.
examples: By the way, I’m not going to the bank today.
Oh, by the way, your shoes need polishing.

senses.definition: one week at a time.
examples: I plan my schedules by the week.
Where can I rent a room by the week?

senses.definition: one year at a time.
examples: Most apartments are available by the year.
We budget by the year.

senses.definition: because of something; due to something.
examples: She’s permitted to vote by virtue of her age.
They are members of the club by virtue of their great wealth.

senses.definition: passing through something; via something.
examples: He came home by way of Toledo.
She went to the bank by way of the drugstore.

senses.definition: in illustration; as an example.
examples: By way of illustration, the professor drew a picture on the board.
He read them a passage from Shakespeare by way of example.

senses.definition: by speaking rather than writing.
examples: I learned about it by word of mouth.
I need it in writing. I don’t trust things I hear about by word of mouth.

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: Do you want to sit here by yourself, or can I sit here too?
Don’t sit at home by yourself. Come to the movie with me.

senses.definition: with the help of no one else.
examples: Can you really do this by yourself?
Bill, can you lift this by yourself?

senses.definition: with no one else present; alone.
examples: Are you two going to sit here by yourselves all evening?
Don’t sit home by yourselves. Come to the party.

senses.definition: with the help of no one else.
examples: Can you do this by yourselves?
Can all of you get to the meeting by yourselves?

senses.definition: to ask that people assemble for a meeting; to request that a meeting be held.
examples: The mayor called a meeting to discuss the problem.
I’ll be calling a meeting of the town council to discuss the new building project.

senses.definition: to call something by its right name; to speak frankly about something, even if it is unpleasant.
examples: Well, I believe it’s time to call a spade a spade. We are just avoiding the issue.
Let’s call a spade a spade. The man is a liar.

senses.definition: to arrive to collect or pick up a person or a thing.
senses.notes: Used especially when you are to pick someone up and are acting as an escort.
examples: I will call for you about eight this evening.
The messenger will call for your reply in the morning.

senses.definition: to need, require, or demand something or the services of someone.
examples: The recipe calls for two cups of flour.
This job calls for someone with good eyesight.

senses.definition: to quit work and go home; to say that a day’s work has been completed.
examples: I’m tired. Let’s call it a day.
The boss was mad because Tom called it a day at noon and went home.

senses.definition: to end what one is doing at night and go [home] to bed.
examples: At midnight, I called it a night and went to bed.
Guest after guest called it a night, and at last we were alone.

senses.definition: to quit; to resign from something; to announce that one is quitting.
examples: Okay! I’ve had enough! I’m calling it quits.
Time to go home, John. Let’s call it quits.

senses.definition: the need to go to the lavatory.
examples: Stop the car here! I have to answer the call of nature.
There was no break in the agenda to take account of the call of nature.

senses.definition: to visit someone.
examples: I have to call on my aunt this Sunday.
Bill called on his brother in the hospital.

senses.definition: to shout to someone.
examples: Mike called out to Tom that there was a telephone call for him.
I heard someone call out, but I could see no one.

senses.definition: to reprimand a person; to bawl someone out.
examples: The teacher had to call Sally down in front of everybody.
“I wish you wouldn’t call me down in public,” cried Sally.

senses.definition: to call a person unpleasant or insulting names.
senses.notes: Usually viewed as a juvenile act.
examples: Mommy! John is calling me names again!
We’ll never get anywhere by calling one another names.

senses.definition: to reprimand a person.
senses.notes: The phrase presents images of a person called into the boss’s carpeted office for a reprimand.
examples: One more error like that and the boss will call you on the carpet.
I’m sorry it went wrong. I really hope he doesn’t call me on the carpet again.

headword: call someone or something into question

senses.definition: to cause someone or something to be evaluated; to examine or reexamine the qualifications or value of someone or something.
examples: Because of her poor record, we were forced to call Dr. Jones into question.
We called Dr. Jones’s qualifications into question.
They called the whole project into question.
I cannot call into question the entire medical profession.

senses.definition: to demonstrate that a person is or is not being deceptive, usually by demanding that the person prove a claim or carry out a threat.
examples: All right, I’ll call your bluff. Show me you can do it!
Tom said, “I’ve got a gun here in my pocket, and I’ll shoot if you come any closer!” “Go ahead,” said Bill, calling his bluff.

senses.definition: to stop threatening, chasing, or hounding (a person).
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Note the variation in the examples.
examples: All right, I surrender. You can call your dogs off.
Tell the sheriff to call off the dogs. We caught the robber.
Please call off your dogs!

senses.definition: to start a meeting officially; to announce that the meeting has started.
examples: The president called the meeting to order shortly after noon.
We cannot do anything until someone calls the meeting to order.

senses.definition: to call the names of people on the rolls, expecting them to reply if they are present.
examples: After I call the roll, please open your books to page 12.
I will take roll, and then we will do arithmetic.

senses.definition: to make the decisions; to decide what is to be done.
examples: Sally always wants to call the shots, and Mary doesn’t like to be bossed around. They don’t get along well.
Sally always wants to call the tune.
Look here, friend, I’m calling the shots. You just be quiet.

headword: can take it to the bank

senses.definition: able to depend on the truthfulness of my statement: it is not counterfeit or bogus; to be able to bank on something.
examples: Believe me. What I am telling you is the truth. You can take it to the bank.
This information is as good as gold. You can take it to the bank.

senses.definition: Can you believe that?; Imagine that!
examples: She wore jeans to the dance. Can you imagine?
Billy was eating the houseplant! Can you imagine?

senses.definition: to destroy the effect of something; to balance something.
examples: This last payment cancels out my debt.
Yes, your last payment cancels it out.
Bob’s two good grades canceled out his two failing grades.

senses.definition: not able to refrain from doing something; not able not to do something.
examples: Anne is such a good cook, I can’t help eating everything she makes.
Since John loves to shop, he can’t help spending money.

senses.definition: unable to sing a simple melody; lacking musical ability.
senses.notes: [to be] Almost always negative. Also with cannot.
examples: I wish that Tom wouldn’t try to sing. He can’t carry a tune.
Listen to poor old John. He really cannot carry a tune.

headword: can’t do anything with someone or something

senses.definition: not [to be] able to manage or control someone or something.
examples: Bill is such a problem. I can’t do anything with him.
My hair is such a mess. I just can’t do anything with it.

senses.definition: unable to choose any but one course of action.
examples: Her parents live nearby, so she can’t help but go there on holidays.
Bob is a tennis fan and can’t help but travel to Wimbledon each year.

headword: can’t hold a candle to someone

senses.definition: not [to be] equal to someone; unable to measure up to someone.
examples: Mary can’t hold a candle to Ann when it comes to auto racing.
As for singing, John can’t hold a candle to Jane.

headword: can’t make heads or tails (out) of someone or something

senses.definition: unable to understand someone or something.
examples: John is so strange. I can’t make heads or tails of him.
Do this report again. I can’t make heads or tails out of it.

headword: can’t see beyond the end of one’s nose

senses.definition: unaware of the things that might happen in the future; not farsighted; self-centered.
examples: John is a very poor planner. He can’t see beyond the end of his nose.
Ann can’t see beyond the end of her nose. She is very self-centered.

headword: can’t see one’s hand in front of one’s face

senses.definition: unable to see very far, usually due to darkness or fog.
examples: It was so dark that I couldn’t see my hand in front of my face.
Bob said that the fog was so thick he couldn’t see his hand in front of his face.

headword: can’t stand (the sight of) someone or something

senses.definition: unable to tolerate someone or something; disliking someone or something extremely.
examples: I can’t stand the sight of cooked carrots.
Mr. Jones can’t stand the sight of blood.
None of us can stand this place.
Nobody can stand Tom when he smokes a cigar.
I can’t stomach your foul language.
I just can’t stomach Mr. Smith.

senses.definition: to be unable to endure the wait for something to happen.
examples: I am so anxious for my birthday to come. I just can’t wait.
Tom can’t wait for Mary to arrive.

senses.definition: unable to endure the wait until it is possible to do something.
examples: I’m glad it’s almost summertime—I just can’t wait to go swimming!
Jimmy can’t wait to go to school tomorrow.

senses.definition: the academic cap or mortarboard and the robe worn in academic ceremonies.
examples: We all had to rent cap and gown for graduation.
I appeared wearing my cap and gown, but I had shorts on underneath because it gets so hot at that time of year.

senses.definition: having the ability to do something.
examples: Do you think Tom is capable of lifting 200 pounds?
No one I know is capable of such a crime!

senses.definition: an entertaining and clever person who says or does funny things.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: He is such a card. Always making jokes.
Mary is a card, and someone is going to have to deal with her!

headword: the cards are stacked against one

senses.definition: luck is against one.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to playing cards. See also have the cards stacked against one; stack the cards (against someone or something).
examples: I have the worst luck. The cards are stacked against me all the time.
How can I accomplish anything when the cards are stacked against me?

senses.definition: excited or moved to (extreme) action (by someone or something).
examples: The crowd got carried away and did a lot of damage to the park.
I know that planning a party is fun, but don’t get carried away.

headword: carry (a lot of) weight (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to be very influential with someone or some group of people.
examples: Your argument does not carry a lot of weight with me.
The senator’s testimony carried a lot of weight with the council.
Her opinion carries weight with most of the members.

headword: carry a secret to the grave
altForms: carry a secret to one’s grave

senses.definition: to avoid telling a secret, even to the day of one’s death.
examples: John carried our secret to his grave.
Trust me, I will carry your secret to the grave!

senses.definition: to be in love with someone who is not in love with you; to brood over a hopeless love affair.
examples: John is carrying a torch for Jane.
Is John still carrying a torch?
Yes, he’ll carry the torch for months.

senses.definition: to do something unnecessary; to do something that is redundant or duplicative.
senses.notes: Newcastle is an English town from which coal was shipped to other parts of England.
examples: Taking food to a farmer is like carrying coals to Newcastle.
Mr. Smith is so rich he doesn’t need any more money. To give him money is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

senses.definition: to make a great fuss over someone or something; to cry and become out of control about someone or something.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples below.
examples: Billy, stop carrying on about your tummy ache like that.
Billy, you must stop carrying on so.
The child carried on endlessly about his mother.

senses.definition: to do one’s share; to earn one’s keep.
examples: Tom, you must be more helpful around the house. We all have to carry our own weight.
Bill, I’m afraid that you can’t work here anymore. You just haven’t been carrying your weight.
If you would just pull your weight, we would finish this by noon.

senses.definition: to manage to continue somehow, in spite of problems.
examples: Even though we did not have a lot of money, we managed to carry on somehow.
Don’t worry about us. We will carry on somehow.

senses.definition: to continue with something.
examples: Can I please carry on with my work now?
Yes, please carry on.

senses.definition: to behave improperly with someone; to be affectionate in public.
examples: Look at Jane carrying on with Tom. They ought to be ashamed.
Jane, stop carrying on like that!

senses.definition: to extend into another time period or location.
examples: I don’t like for bills to carry over into the next month.
Please do not let the paragraph carry over.

senses.definition: to make a planned event—especially a joke or deception— work out successfully.
senses.notes: Also literal, meaning to take something away. See also pull something off.
examples: It was a huge party, but the hostess carried it off beautifully.
The magician carried off the trick with great skill.

senses.definition: to perform a task; to perform an assignment.
senses.notes: Also literal meaning to remove something.
examples: “This is a very important job,” said Jane. “Do you think you can carry it out?”
The students didn’t carry out their assignments.

senses.definition: to let something like a bill extend into another period of time; to extend to another location.
examples: We’ll carry the amount of money due over into the next month.
Yes, please carry over the balance.
We’ll have to carry this paragraph over to the next page.

senses.definition: to be the player holding the ball, especially in football when a goal is made.
examples: It was the fullback carrying the ball.
Yes, Tom always carries the ball.

senses.definition: to be in charge; to make sure that a job gets done.
examples: We need someone who knows how to get the job done. Hey, Sally! Why don’t you carry the ball for us?
John can’t carry the ball. He isn’t organized enough.

senses.definition: to be successful; to win a competition, argument, etc.
senses.notes: Originally meaning to win a battle.
examples: Our team didn’t play well at first, but we won the day in the end.
Hard work won the day and James passed his exams.

senses.definition: to uphold a set of goals; to lead or participate in a (figurative) crusade.
examples: The battle was over, but John continued to carry the torch.
If Jane hadn’t carried the torch, no one would have followed, and the whole thing would have failed.

headword: carry the weight of the world on one’s shoulders

senses.definition: to appear to be burdened by all the problems in the whole world.
examples: Look at Tom. He appears to be carrying the weight of the world on his shoulders.
Cheer up, Tom! You don’t need to carry the weight of the world on your shoulders.

senses.definition: an example of what one is talking about.
examples: Now, as a case in point, let’s look at nineteenth-century England.
Fireworks can be dangerous. For a case in point, look what happened to Bob Smith last week.

senses.definition: the incorrect identification of someone.
examples: It is simply a case of mistaken identity.
I am not the criminal you want to arrest. This is a case of mistaken identity.

senses.definition: a method of buying and selling goods at the retail level where the buyer pays cash for the goods and carries the goods away.
senses.notes: As opposed to paying on credit or having something delivered.
examples: Sorry, we don’t accept credit cards. This is strictly cash-and-carry.
I bought the chair cash-and-carry before I realized that there was no way to get it home.

senses.definition: to die.
senses.notes: Also literal. Slang. From an expression used in gambling, chiefly poker.
examples: Bob cashed in his chips yesterday.
I’m too young to cash in my chips.

senses.definition: to earn a lot of money at something; to make a profit at something.
examples: This is a good year for farming, and you can cash in on it if you’re smart.
It’s too late to cash in on that particular clothing fad.

senses.definition: money paid for something when it is purchased; money paid at the time of sale.
examples: I don’t extend credit. It’s cash on the barrelhead only.
I paid $12,000 for this car—cash on the barrelhead.

senses.definition: either by paying cash or by putting the charges on a credit account.
examples: When Fred had all his purchases assembled on the counter, the clerk asked, “Cash or credit?”
That store does not give you a choice of cash or credit. They want cash only.

headword: cast around for someone or something
altForms: cast about for someone or something

senses.definition: to seek someone or something; to seek a thought or an idea.
senses.notes: Refers to a type of person rather than a specific person.
examples: John is casting around for a new cook. The old one quit.
Bob is casting about for a new car.
Mary cast about for a way to win the contest.

senses.definition: to make a rude and insulting remark.
examples: I resent your casting aspersions on my brother and his ability!
It is rude to cast aspersions on people in general.

senses.definition: to cause someone or something to be doubted.
examples: The police cast doubt on my story.
How can they cast doubt? They haven’t looked into it yet.
The city council cast doubt on John and his plan.
They are always casting doubts.

senses.definition: very similar.
examples: The two sisters are cast in the same mold— equally mean.
All the members of the family are cast in the same mold and they all end up in prison.

headword: cast one’s lot in with someone

senses.definition: to join in with someone and accept whatever happens.
examples: Mary cast her lot with the group going to Spain. They had a wonderful time.
I decided to cast in my lot with the home team this year.

senses.definition: to waste something good on someone who doesn’t care about it.
examples: To sing for them is to cast pearls before swine.
To serve them French cuisine is like casting one’s pearls before swine.

senses.definition: to vote; to place one’s ballot in the ballot box.
examples: The citizens cast their votes for president.
The wait in line to cast one’s vote was almost an hour.

senses.definition: to make the first criticism; to be the first to attack.
examples: Well, I don’t want to be the one to cast the first stone, but she sang horribly.
John always casts the first stone. Does he think he’s perfect?

senses.definition: Why do you not speak?; Speak up and answer my question!
examples: Answer me! What’s the matter, cat got your tongue?
Why don’t you speak up? Cat got your tongue?

senses.definition: the best one can do with whatever is available.
examples: We went hitchhiking for a week and lived catch-as-catch-can.
There were ten children in our family, and every meal was catch-as-catch-can.

senses.definition: to contract a cold (the disease).
examples: Please close the window, or we’ll all catch cold.
I take cold every year at this time.

senses.definition: to begin to burn; to ignite.
examples: If the wood were not so wet, it would catch fire more easily.
The curtains blew against the flame of the candle and caught fire.

senses.definition: to take a nap; to get some sleep.
examples: I’ll just catch forty winks before getting ready for the party.
Tom always tries to catch some Zs before going out for a late evening.
I think I’ll go to bed and take forty winks. See you in the morning.
Why don’t you go take forty winks and call me in about an hour?

senses.definition: to get into trouble and receive punishment.
senses.notes: Informal. See also get the devil.
examples: I know I’m going to catch it when I get home.
Bob hit Billy in the face. He really caught it from the teacher.

senses.definition: to resume one’s normal breathing after exertion; to return to normal after being busy or very active.
examples: I don’t have time to catch my breath.
I ran so fast that it took ten minutes to catch my breath.

senses.definition: to contract a cold; to catch a serious cold.
examples: If I go out in this weather, I’ll catch my death of cold.
Dress up warm or you’ll take your death of cold.
Put on your raincoat or you’ll catch your death.

headword: catch one with one’s pants down

senses.definition: to catch someone doing something, especially something that ought to be done in secret or in private.
senses.notes: Informal. Use with caution. This refers to having one’s pants down in the bathroom.
examples: John couldn’t convince them he was innocent. They caught him with his pants down.
Did you hear that John took the camera? The store owner caught him with his pants down.

senses.definition: to ignite and burn with flames.
examples: Keep your coat away from the flames, or it will catch fire.
Lightning struck the prairie, and the grass caught on fire.

senses.definition: to figure someone or something out; to solve a puzzle; to see through an act of deception.
examples: Mary caught on to Bob and his tricks.
Ann caught on to the woman’s dishonest plan.
The woman thought that Ann wouldn’t catch on.

headword: catch sight of someone or something

senses.definition: to see someone or something briefly; to get a glimpse of someone or something.
examples: I caught sight of the rocket just before it flew out of sight.
Ann caught sight of the robber as he ran out of the bank.

headword: catch someone in the act (of doing something)

senses.definition: to catch a person doing something illegal or private.
senses.notes: See also in the act (of doing something).
examples: They know who set the fire. They caught someone in the act.
I caught Tom in the act of stealing a car.

senses.definition: to find someone unprepared.
examples: The enemy soldiers caught our army napping.
The thieves caught the security guard napping.

senses.definition: to catch a person who is not prepared; to surprise someone.
examples: Sorry I acted so flustered. You caught me off balance.
The robbers caught Ann off balance and stole her purse.

senses.definition: to catch a person at a time of carelessness.
senses.notes: Compare this with catch someone off-balance.
examples: Tom caught Ann off guard and frightened her.
She caught me off my guard, and I told the location of the jewels.

senses.definition: to catch a person in the act of doing something wrong.
examples: Tom was stealing the car when the police drove by and caught him red-handed.
Mary tried to cash a forged check at the bank, and the teller caught her red-handed.

senses.definition: to establish eye contact with someone.
senses.notes: Also with have, as in the example.
examples: Tom got Mary’s eye and waved to her.
When Tom had her eye, he smiled at her.

senses.definition: to appear and attract someone’s interest.
examples: A small red car passing by caught my eye.
One of the books on the top shelf caught my eye, and I took it down to look at it.

senses.definition: to move faster in order to reach someone or something ahead, moving in the same direction.
examples: The red car caught up with the blue one.
Bill caught up with Ann, and they walked to the bank together.
He had to run to catch up to her.

senses.definition: seen doing something illegal or private.
examples: Tom was caught in the act.
She’s guilty. She was caught in the act.

senses.definition: caught between two arguing people or groups, making it difficult to remain neutral.
examples: The cook and the dishwasher were having an argument, and Tom got caught in the middle. All he wanted was his dinner.
Mr. and Mrs. Smith tried to draw me into their argument. I don’t like being caught in the middle.
Bill and Ann were arguing, and poor Bobby, their son, was caught in the cross fire.

senses.definition: caught in the act of doing something wrong.
examples: Tom was caught red-handed.
Many car thieves are caught red-handed.

senses.definition: to be without something you need, especially money.
examples: I needed eggs for my cake, but I was caught short.
Bob had to borrow money from John to pay for the meal. Bob is caught short quite often.

senses.definition: surprised and unprepared.
examples: Sorry. You startled me when you came up behind me. I was caught unaware.
The clerk was caught unawares, and the robber emptied out the cash register before the clerk could sound the alarm.

senses.definition: to cause people to become agitated; to cause trouble in a group of people; to shock or alarm people.
examples: When Bob appeared without his evening jacket, it caused a stir in the dining room.
The dog ran through the church and caused quite a commotion.

senses.definition: to shock people; to surprise and dismay people.
examples: John caused eyebrows to raise when he married a poor girl from Toledo.
If you want to cause some eyebrows to raise, just start singing as you walk down the street.

senses.definition: to cause people to gossip; to give people something to gossip about.
examples: The way John was looking at Mary will surely cause some tongues to wag.
The way Mary was dressed will also cause tongues to wag.

senses.definition: to yield and give in to someone else or to something.
senses.notes: [for someone] Also literal in reference to the collapse of caves, tunnels, ceilings, etc.
examples: Mr. Franklin always caves in to Mrs. Franklin.
It’s easier to cave in than to go on fighting.
Tom caved in to the pressure of work.

senses.definition: to stop doing something and stay stopped.
examples: The judge ordered the merchant to cease and desist the deceptive practices.
When they were ordered to cease and desist, they finally stopped.

senses.definition: to recognize something as the cause of something else.
examples: We chalked her bad behavior up to her recent illness.
I had to chalk up the loss to experience.
I chalked up my defeat to my impatience.

senses.definition: to be ready and anxious to do something.
examples: The kids were champing at the bit to get into the swimming pool.
The dogs were champing at the bit to begin the hunt.

senses.definition: to risk doing something; to try doing something.
examples: I don’t usually ride horses, but this time I will chance it.
Bob didn’t have reservations, but he went to the airport anyway, chancing a cancellation.

senses.definition: to be sold or passed from owner to owner.
examples: How many times has this house changed hands in the last ten years?
We built this house in 1920, and it has never changed hands.

headword: change horses in the middle of the stream

senses.definition: to make major changes in an activity that has already begun; to choose someone or something else after it is too late.
examples: I’m already baking a cherry pie. I can’t bake an apple pie. It’s too late to change horses in the middle of the stream.
The house is half-built. It’s too late to hire a different architect. You can’t change horses in the middle of the stream.

senses.definition: an addition of some variety in one’s life.
examples: Going to the beach on the weekend will be a change of pace.
The doctor says I need a change of pace.

senses.definition: a move to a different place, where the scenery is different or where things in general are different.
examples: I thought I would go to the country for a change of scenery.
A change of scenery would help me relax and organize my life.

senses.definition: to cause a person to think differently (about someone or something).
examples: Tom thought Mary was unkind, but an evening out with her changed his mind.
I can change my mind if I want to. I don’t have to stick with an idea.

senses.definition: to change the manner of a person, usually from bad to good, or from rude to pleasant.
examples: The teller was most unpleasant until she learned that I’m a bank director. Then she changed her tune.
“I will help change your tune by fining you $150,” said the judge to the rude defendant.

senses.definition: to begin talking about something different.
examples: They changed the subject suddenly when the person whom they had been discussing entered the room.
We’ll change the subject if we are embarrassing you.

senses.definition: detailed, in reference to sources of information.
senses.notes: A reference to the method of referring to biblical text.
examples: He gave chapter and verse for his reasons for disputing that Shakespeare had written the play.
The suspect gave chapter and verse of his associate’s activities.

senses.definition: to get someone excited and enthusiastic.
examples: The speaker charged up the crowd to go out and raise money.
Mrs. Smith tried to charge her husband up about getting a job.

senses.definition: to restore a charge to an electrical storage battery.
examples: They charged up the battery overnight.
My car charges the battery whenever the engine runs.

senses.definition: excited; enthusiastic
examples: The crowd was really charged up.
Tom is so tired that he cannot get charged up about anything.

senses.definition: full of electrical power.
examples: The battery is completely charged up.
If the battery isn’t charged, the car won’t start.

senses.definition: to use charming behavior to persuade someone to do something.
examples: She is so nice. She just charms the pants off of you.
He will try to charm the pants off you, but you can still refuse to take the job if you don’t want to do it.

senses.definition: to commit adultery; to be unfaithful to one’s lover.
examples: “Have you been cheating on me?” cried Mrs. Franklin.
“No, I haven’t been cheating on you,” said Mr. Franklin.

senses.definition: to be verified or authenticated.
examples: I spent all afternoon working with my checkbook, trying to get the figures to check out.
The police wouldn’t believe that I am who I say I am until they made a few telephone calls to see if my story checked out.

senses.definition: a system where power is kept in control and balance among the various branches of government.
examples: The newspaper editor claimed that the system of checks and balances built into our Constitution has been subverted by party politics.
We depend on checks and balances in government to keep despots from seizing control of the government.

senses.definition: side by side; close together.
examples: The pedestrians had to walk cheek by jowl along the narrow streets.
The two families lived cheek by jowl in one house.

senses.definition: to give words or shouts of encouragement to someone who is trying to do something.
examples: John was leading in the race, and the whole crowd was cheering him on.
Sally was doing so well in her performance that I wanted to cheer her on.

senses.definition: to make a sad person happy.
examples: When Bill was sick, Ann tried to cheer him up by reading to him.
Interest rates went up, and that cheered up all the bankers.

senses.definition: to become more happy.
examples: Things are bad for you now, but you’ll cheer up when they get better.
Cheer up, Tom! Things can’t be that bad.

senses.definition: bored; depressed; annoyed.
examples: He was cheesed off with his job.
She was cheesed off when she missed the bus.

senses.definition: to scold someone; to bawl someone out thoroughly.
senses.notes: Informal. Used much in the military.
examples: The sergeant chewed the corporal out; then the corporal chewed the private out.
The boss is always chewing out somebody.
The coach ate out the entire football team because of their poor playing.

senses.definition: to have a chat with someone; to talk very informally with one’s close friends.
examples: Hi, old buddy! Come in and let’s chew the fat.
They usually just sat around and chewed the rag. They never did get much done.

senses.definition: to withdraw from something due to fear or cowardice.
examples: Jane was going to go parachuting with us, but she chickened out at the last minute.
I’d never chicken out of parachute jumping, because I’d never agree to do it in the first place!

headword: The chickens have come home to roost.

senses.definition: All the problems have returned to the person who caused them and that person must now solve them or take the blame.
senses.notes: Literal for chickens whose home is a chicken house. See also come home (to roost).
examples: You took on too much credit card debt and now you are broke. The chickens have finally come home to roost.
Your car broke down because you never changed the oil. The chickens have come home to roost.

senses.definition: something very easy to do.
examples: The test was child’s play to her.
Finding the right street was child’s play with a map.

senses.definition: very cold.
examples: I was chilled to the bone in that snowstorm.
The children were chilled to the bone in the unheated room.

senses.definition: to add one’s voice to something; to add something to the discussion, usually by interrupting.
examples: Billy chimed in by reminding us to come to dinner.
Everyone chimed in on the final chorus of the song.

senses.definition: a special weakness that provides a means for attacking or impressing someone otherwise invulnerable.
examples: His love for his child is the chink in his armor.
Jane’s insecurity is a chink in her armor.

senses.definition: to contribute a small amount of money to a fund that will be used to buy something.
examples: Would you care to chip in on a gift for the teacher?
Yes, I’d be happy to chip in.
Could you chip in a dollar on the gift, please?

headword: a chip off the old block

senses.definition: a person (usually a male) who behaves in the same way as his father or resembles his father.
examples: John looks like his father—a real chip off the old block.
Bill Jones, Jr., is a chip off the old block. He’s a banker just like his father.

senses.definition: potato chips, or some other kind of crisply fried substance, and a sauce or dressing to dip them into before eating them.
examples: There were tons of chips and dip and all kinds of cold pop available for everyone.

senses.definition: to cheat someone to get money or belongings.
examples: The company tried to chisel the government out of taxes it owed.
Bill chiseled his little sister out of her allowance.

senses.definition: to make a person become overemotional and speechless; to make a person begin to cry.
examples: The sight of all those smiling people choked Bob up, and he couldn’t go on speaking.
The funeral procession choked up the whole family.

senses.definition: to stifle something; to force something to an end.
examples: The car ran over the hose and choked the water off.
The president choked off the debate.

senses.definition: to form into two opposing teams by having a leader or captain take turns choosing players.
examples: Let’s choose up sides and play baseball.
When I choose up sides, all the best players don’t end up on the same team.

senses.definition: to take the life of someone.
examples: The killer tornado claimed the lives of six people at the trailer park.
The athlete’s life was claimed in a skiing accident.

senses.definition: to become strict with someone; to become strict about something.
examples: Because Bob’s grades were getting worse, his parents clamped down on him.
The police have clamped down on speeders in this town.
Things have already gone too far. It’s too late to clamp down.

headword: clap eyes on someone or something

senses.definition: to see someone or something, perhaps for the first time; to set eyes on someone or something.
examples: I wish she had never clapped eyes on her fiancé.
I haven’t clapped eyes on a red squirrel for years.

senses.definition: to make a great profit.
examples: John won at the races and really cleaned up.
Ann cleaned up by taking a job selling encyclopedias.

senses.definition: to reform one’s conduct; to improve one’s performance.
senses.notes: Informal. Originally referred to polishing one’s stage performance.
examples: Since Sally cleaned her act up, she has become very productive.
If you don’t clean up your act, you’ll be sent home.

senses.definition: without touching something; away from something.
examples: Please stand clear of the doors while the train is moving.
Make sure the dog moves clear of the driveway before backing the car up.

senses.definition: to get out (of a place); to leave.
examples: All right, you people, clear out of here now.
I knew right then that it was time to clear out.

senses.definition: progress made without any difficulty; an easy situation.
examples: Once you’ve passed that exam, it will be clear sailing.
Working there was not all clear sailing. The boss had a very bad temper.

senses.definition: to prove that someone is not guilty of a crime or misdeed.
examples: I was accused of theft, but I cleared my name.
The student was accused of cheating, but her name was cleared.

senses.definition: to explain something; to solve a mystery.
examples: I think that we can clear this matter up without calling in the police.
First we have to clear up the problem of the missing jewels.

senses.definition: to cure a disease or a medical condition.
examples: There is no medicine that will clear pimples up.
The doctor will give you something to clear up your cold.

senses.definition: to get rid of doubts or hard feelings.
senses.notes: Also literal. Sometimes this is said about an argument or other unpleasantness.
examples: All right, let’s discuss this frankly. It’ll be better if we clear the air.
Mr. and Mrs. Brown always seem to have to clear the air with a big argument before they can be sociable.

senses.definition: get out of the way; get out of this area.
senses.notes: From a naval expression, “Clear the decks for action!” urging seaman to prepare for battle or other action.
examples: Clear the decks! Here comes the teacher.
Clear the decks and take your seats.

senses.definition: to remove the dishes and other eating utensils from the table after a meal.
senses.notes: The opposite of set the table.
examples: Will you please help clear the table?
