After you clear the table, we’ll play cards.

senses.definition: to become solved.
examples: This matter won’t clear up by itself.
The confusion cleared up very quickly when I explained.

senses.definition: to cure itself or run its course.
examples: I told you your pimples would clear up without special medicine.
My rash cleared up in a week.

senses.definition: to join others in supporting someone or something.
senses.notes: See also get on the bandwagon, jump on the bandwagon.
examples: Come join us! Climb on the bandwagon and support Senator Smith!
Look at all those people climbing on the bandwagon! They don’t know what they are getting into!

senses.definition: to do something desperate when one is extremely anxious, bored, or excited.
examples: I’m so upset I could climb the wall.
The meeting was so long and the speaker so boring that most of the audience wanted to climb the wall.

senses.definition: to restrain someone; to reduce or put an end to a teenager’s privileges.
examples: You had better learn to get home on time, or I will clip your wings.
My mother clipped my wings. I can’t go out tonight.

senses.definition: involving secrecy and plotting.
examples: A great deal of cloak-and-dagger stuff goes on in political circles.
A lot of cloak-and-dagger activity was involved in the appointment of the director.

senses.definition: within reach; handy.
examples: I’m sorry, but your letter isn’t close at hand. Please remind me what you said in it.
When you’re cooking, you should keep all the ingredients close at hand.

senses.definition: fairly close or accurate.
examples: I can do math pretty well. Close enough for government work anyway.
This isn’t quite right, but it’s close enough for government work.

senses.definition: to overwhelm or surround someone or something.
examples: My problems are closing in on me.
The wolves closed in on the elk.
They howled as they closed in.

senses.definition: to ignore something; to pretend that something is not really happening.
examples: You can’t close your eyes to hunger in the world.
I just closed my eyes to the problem and pretended that it wasn’t there.

senses.definition: to move closer together in a military formation.
senses.notes: See also close ranks (behind someone or something); close ranks (with someone).
examples: The soldiers closed ranks and marched on the enemy.
All right! Stop that talking and close ranks.

senses.definition: to support someone or something; to back someone or something.
examples: We will close ranks behind the candidate.
She needs our help. Let’s close ranks behind her and give her the support she needs.

senses.definition: to join with someone.
examples: We can fight this menace only if we close ranks.
Let’s all close ranks with Ann and adopt her suggestions.

senses.definition: to make something stop operating; to put something out of business.
examples: The police closed the factory down.
The manager shut down the factory for the holidays.
The city council closed down the amusement park.

headword: close the books (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to put an end to a matter that concerns someone or something.
senses.notes: The books here refers to financial accounting records.
examples: It’s time to close the books on the Franklin case.
Yes, let’s close the books on Mr. Franklin.
You closed the books too soon. Here is some new information.

senses.definition: affecting one personally and intimately.
examples: Her remarks were a bit too close to home. I was afraid she was discussing me!
She’s got me figured out all right. She knows where I live.
Every criticism she made of the performance hit a little too close to home for my comfort. I didn’t know I was so bad!
When you go through an experience like that and see the horror of a hurricane face to face, that sort of gets you where you live!

senses.definition: fond of someone; very good friends with someone.
examples: Tom is very close to Mary. They may get married.
Mr. Smith isn’t exactly close to Mrs. Smith.

senses.definition: to quit working, for the day or forever.
examples: It’s five o’clock. Time to close up shop.
I can’t make any money in this town. The time has come to close up shop and move to another town.

senses.definition: to get cloudy, as if it were going to rain.
examples: All of a sudden it clouded up and began to rain.
It usually clouds up at sunset.

senses.definition: to grow very sad, as if to cry.
senses.notes: [for someone] See also turn on the waterworks.
examples: The baby clouded up and let out a howl.
Whenever Mary got homesick, she’d cloud up. She really wanted to go home.

senses.definition: to inform someone of something.
examples: Please clue me in on what’s going on.
Yes, clue her in.

senses.definition: to continue to seek solutions, ideas, or hopes that are insubstantial.
examples: When you talk of inheriting money, you are just clutching at straws.
That is not a real solution to the problem. You are just clutching at straws.

senses.definition: There is no visible danger.
examples: I’m going to stay hidden here until the coast is clear.
You can come out of your hiding place now. The coast is clear.

senses.definition: from the Atlantic to the Pacific Oceans (in the continental U.S.A.); all the land between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
examples: My voice was once heard on a coast-to-coast radio broadcast.
Our car made the coast-to-coast trip in eighty hours.

senses.definition: a jacket or sports coat and necktie.
senses.notes: [for men] A standard of dress between casual and a suit.
examples: My brother was not wearing a coat and tie, and they would not admit him into the restaurant.
I always carry a coat and tie in my car just in case I have to dress up a little for something.

senses.definition: a silly, made-up story; a story that is a lie.
examples: Don’t give me that cock-and-bull story.
I asked for an explanation, and all I got was your ridiculous cock-and-bull story!

senses.definition: someone who acts more important than others in a group.
examples: The deputy manager was cock of the walk until the new manager arrived.
He loved acting cock of the walk and ordering everyone about.

senses.definition: a cup of coffee and a Danish sweet roll.
examples: A few of us like to have coffee and Danish before we start work.
Coffee and Danish is not my idea of a good breakfast!

senses.definition: a book that is more suitable for display than for reading, typically, an illustrated book left on the coffee table for visitors to examine.
examples: This book is more of a coffee-table book than an art book. I prefer something more scholarly.
We purchased a coffee-table book for Jan’s birthday.

senses.definition: a choice of beverage.
senses.notes: Originally used by airline personnel when offering something to drink to the passengers.
examples: She asked me if I wanted coffee, tea, or milk, and I chose just plain water.
Would you prefer coffee, tea, or milk to go with your meal?

senses.definition: no comfort or consolation at all.
examples: She knows there are others worse off than she is, but that’s cold comfort.
It was cold comfort to the student that others had failed as badly as he did.

senses.definition: a person who is distant and unfeeling.
senses.notes: Informal or slang. Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Bob is so dull—a real cold fish.
She hardly ever speaks to anyone. She’s a cold fish.

senses.definition: cash, not checks or promises.
examples: I want to be paid in cold, hard cash, and I want to be paid now!
Pay me now! Cash on the barrelhead—cold, hard cash.

senses.definition: to have a misfortune; to fail.
senses.notes: From an expression meaning to fall off one’s horse.
examples: Bob invested all his money in the stock market just before it fell. Boy, did he come a cropper.
Jane was out all night before she took her tests. She really came a cropper.

senses.definition: to find someone or something; to discover someone or something.
examples: John came across a book he had been looking for.
Where did you run across that lovely skirt?

senses.definition: Come back.; Return some other time.
examples: I’m so glad you enjoyed our party. Please come again sometime.
The store clerk gave me my change and my purchase and said, “Thank you. Come again.”

senses.definition: Say it again. I did not hear you.
examples: TOM: Hello, Grandfather. GRANDFATHER: Come again? You’ll have to talk louder.
The farmer looked at me and said, “Come again?”

senses.definition: already arrived and already departed.
examples: No, Joy is not here. She’s come and gone.
Sorry, you are too late for your appointment. The doctor has come and gone.

senses.definition: suddenly to lose one’s emotional self-control.
senses.notes: Informal. From the literal sense referring to something falling apart. See also burst at the seams; fall apart at the seams.
examples: Bill was so upset that he almost came apart at the seams.
I couldn’t take anymore. I just came apart at the seams.

senses.definition: finally to agree or consent (to something).
examples: I thought he’d never agree, but in the end he came around.
She came round only after we argued for an hour.

senses.definition: to return to consciousness; to wake up.
examples: He came around after we threw cold water in his face.
The boxer was knocked out, but came round in a few seconds.

senses.definition: not to be surprising [for someone] to learn [something].
examples: It will come as no surprise for you to learn that the company is losing money this year.
It came as no surprise that the president had been lying.

senses.definition: to return without anything.
examples: All right, go gambling. Don’t come away empty-handed, though.
Go to the bank and ask for the loan again. This time don’t come away empty-handed.

senses.definition: to be completely honest with someone; to confess (everything) to someone.
examples: The lawyer said, “I can help you only if you come clean with me.”
All right, I’ll come clean. Here is the whole story.

senses.definition: to descend (to someone) through inheritance.
examples: All my silverware came down to me from my great-grandmother.
The antique furniture came down through my mother’s family.

headword: come down hard on someone or something

senses.definition: to attack vigorously; to scold someone severely.
examples: Tom’s parents really came down hard on him for coming home late.
Yes, they came down on him hard.

senses.definition: to lose one’s social position or financial standing.
examples: Mr. Jones has really come down in the world since he lost his job.
If I were unemployed, I’m sure I’d come down in the world, too.

senses.definition: to become realistic; to become alert to what is going on around one.
examples: You have very good ideas, John, but you must come down to earth. We can’t possibly afford any of your suggestions.
Pay attention to what is going on. Come down to earth and join the discussion.

senses.definition: to be reduced to something; to amount to no more than something.
senses.notes: Informal. Similar to boil down to something.
examples: It comes down to whether you want to go to the movies or stay at home and watch television.
It came down to either getting a job or going back to college.

senses.definition: to become ill with some disease.
examples: I’m afraid I’m coming down with a cold.
I’ll probably come down with pneumonia.

senses.definition: to come from many different places.
examples: Everyone was there. They came from far and wide.
We have foods that come from far and wide.

senses.definition: to come as a surprise with no warning.
examples: The dogs came from nowhere and attacked my cat.
The whole set of problems came from nowhere. There was no way we could have foreseen them.

senses.definition: to return to the original position or state of affairs.
examples: The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now.
The employer’s power was reduced by the unions at one point, but matters have come full circle again.

senses.definition: no matter what happens.
examples: I’ll be there tomorrow, come hell or high water.
Come hell or high water, I intend to have my own home.

senses.definition: to return to cause trouble [for someone].
senses.notes: [for a problem] See also The chickens have come home to roost.
examples: As I feared, all my problems came home to roost.
Yes, problems all come home eventually.

senses.definition: to become apparent to someone; to be realized by someone.
examples: The truth of the matter suddenly came home to me.
It all came home to me while I was taking a bath. Suddenly I understood everything.

senses.definition: to arrive as a group.
examples: All the guests came in a body.
Things become very busy when everyone arrives in a body.

senses.definition: to be useful or convenient.
examples: A small television set in the bedroom would come in handy.
A good hammer always comes in handy.
A nice cool drink would come in handy about now.

headword: come in out of the rain

senses.definition: to become alert and sensible; to come down to earth.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also not know enough to come in out of the rain.
examples: Pay attention, Sally! Come in out of the rain!
Bill will fail if he doesn’t come in out of the rain and study.

senses.definition: to reach an age when one is old enough to own property, get married, and sign legal contracts.
examples: When Jane comes of age, she will buy her own car.
Sally, who came of age last month, entered into an agreement to purchase a house.

senses.definition: to win second place or worse; to lose out to someone else.
examples: John came off second-best in the race.
Why do I always come off second-best in an argument with you?

senses.definition: to approach people in a wild and exciting manner; to seem very active and pushy when approaching people.
examples: Why is she so unpolished? She comes on like gangbusters and frightens people away.
The people in this town come on like gangbusters and they seem very rude at first.

senses.definition: to appear as having certain characteristics to other people.
senses.notes: Informal. Especially with strong, which means “intensely.” See also the previous entry.
examples: Jane comes on like a very unpleasant person.
She really comes on strong.
John doesn’t care how he comes on.

senses.definition: to appear in a certain area or place.
senses.notes: Used in particular in police reports or dramatizations of police reports.
examples: What time did the picnickers come on the scene?
The witness arrived on the scene at about 7:13 in the evening.

senses.definition: to end up with a profit; to improve one’s situation.
examples: I hope you come out ahead with your investments.
It took a lot of money to buy the house, but I think I’ll come out ahead.

senses.definition: to work out all right.
senses.notes: Informal. This means that problems or difficulties will go away as dirt goes away in the process of washing.
examples: Don’t worry about that problem. It’ll all come out in the wash.
This trouble will go away. It’ll come out in the wash.

senses.definition: to come from an unexpected place.
examples: This new problem came out of left field. We were really surprised.
Your remarks came out of left field. I can’t understand your complaint.

senses.definition: to appear suddenly.
senses.notes: Almost the same as appear out of nowhere.
examples: Suddenly, a truck came out of nowhere.
Without warning, the storm came out of nowhere.

senses.definition: to become more friendly; to be more sociable.
senses.notes: Refers to a turtle that sticks its head and legs out of its shell when it feels safe.
examples: Ann, you should come out of your shell and spend more time with your friends.
Come out of your shell, Tom. Go out and make some friends.

senses.definition: to appear suddenly as if falling from the sky.
senses.notes: The blue refers to the blue sky.
examples: This idea came out of the blue, and I think it is a good one.
Sally showed up at the party even though no one told her where it was. She just came out of the blue.

senses.definition: to come to someone.
examples: I wish a large sum of money would come my way.
I hope that no bad luck comes my way.

senses.definition: to do what one is expected to do, especially under difficult conditions.
examples: You can depend on Jane. She’ll always come through.
We thought that there would be no food, but Tom came through at the last minute with everything we needed.

senses.definition: to be approved; [for something] to gain approval.
examples: Our mortgage loan application finally came through!
Your papers came through, and you can be sure that the matter has been taken care of.

headword: come through something with flying colors

senses.definition: to survive something quite well.
examples: Todd came through the test with flying colors.
Mr. Franklin came through the operation with flying colors.

senses.definition: to have a disaster, perhaps one that is deserved or expected; to die an unfortunate death.
examples: My old car came to a bad end. Its engine burned up.
The evil merchant came to a bad end.

senses.definition: to come to an absolute stopping point.
examples: The building project came to a dead end.
The street came to a dead end.
We were driving along and came to a dead end.

senses.definition: to come to a crucial point; to come to a point when a problem must be solved.
examples: Remember my problem with my neighbors? Well, last night the whole thing came to a head.
The battle between the two factions of the city council came to a head yesterday.

senses.definition: to stop; to finish.
examples: The party came to an end at midnight.
Her life came to an end late yesterday.

senses.definition: to come to an early death.
examples: Poor Mr. Jones came to an untimely end in a car accident.
Cancer caused Mrs. Smith to come to an untimely end.

senses.definition: to develop into a bad, unfortunate, or difficult situation.
examples: Things have come to a pretty pass when people have to beg in the streets.
When parents are afraid of their children, things have come to a pretty pass.

senses.definition: to stop, temporarily or permanently.
examples: The building project came to a standstill because the workers went on strike.
The party came to a standstill until the lights were turned on again.

senses.definition: to stop moving or happening.
examples: The bus finally came to a stop so I could get off.
The loud noise finally came to a stop.

senses.definition: to become increasingly angry and begin to fight about something, usually by striking blows, or verbally.
examples: They got excited about the accident, but they never actually came to blows over it.
Yes, they aren’t the kind of people who come to blows.

senses.definition: to fail; to have trouble or grief.
examples: The artist wept when her canvas came to grief.
The wedding party came to grief when the bride passed out.

senses.definition: to face something; to comprehend something.
examples: He found it difficult to come to grips with his grandmother’s death.
Many students have a hard time coming to grips with algebra.

senses.definition: to become alive or lively.
senses.notes: Usually used in a figurative sense.
examples: The party came to life about midnight.
As the anesthetic wore off, the patient came to life.

senses.definition: to become known.
examples: Some interesting facts about your past have just come to light.
If too many bad things come to light, you may lose your job.

senses.definition: to enter into one’s consciousness.
senses.notes: [for a thought or idea] Compare this with cross someone’s mind.
examples: Do I know a good barber? No one comes to mind right now.
Another idea comes to mind. Why not cut your own hair?

senses.definition: to amount to nothing; to be worthless.
examples: So all my hard work comes to nothing.
Yes, the whole project comes to naught.

senses.definition: to wake up; to become conscious; to start thinking clearly.
examples: John, come to your senses. You’re being quite stupid.
In the morning I don’t come to my senses until I have had two cups of coffee.

senses.definition: to happen.
examples: When did all of this come to pass?
When will this event come to pass?

senses.definition: to stop moving.
examples: When the car comes to rest, you can get in.
The leaf fell and came to rest at my feet.

headword: come to terms with someone or something

senses.definition: to come to an agreement with someone.
examples: I finally came to terms with my lawyer about his fee.
Bob, you have to come to terms with your father’s wishes.

senses.definition: to learn to accept someone or something.
senses.notes: See also come to grips with something.
examples: She had to come to terms with the loss of her sight.
It’s time you came to terms with your boss and her unreasonable demands.

senses.definition: to become prominent; to become important.
examples: The question of salary has now come to the fore.
Since his great showing in court, my lawyer has really come to the fore in city politics.

senses.definition: to get to the important part (of something).
examples: He has been talking a long time. I wish he would come to the point.
Quit wasting time! Get to the point!
We are talking about money, Bob! Come on, get to the point.

senses.definition: I just remembered [something].
examples: Come to think of it, I know someone who can help.
I have a screwdriver in the trunk of my car, come to think of it.

senses.definition: actually to happen.
examples: When I got married, all my dreams came true.
Coming to the big city was like having my wish come true.

senses.definition: to lose emotional control; to have a mental breakdown; to break out into tears or laughter.
examples: When Sally heard the joke, she almost came unglued.
When the bank took away my car, I came unglued and cried and cried.

senses.definition: to improve one’s status or situation in life.
examples: Since Mary got her new job, she has really come up in the world.
A good education helped my brother come up in the world.

senses.definition: to end up looking good or respectable after being involved in some difficult or notorious affair.
examples: It was a nasty political campaign, but both candidates came up smelling like roses.
I was not surprised that my congressional representative came up smelling like roses after his colleagues investigated him.

senses.definition: no matter what might happen.
examples: I’ll be home for the holidays, come what may.
Come what may, the mail will get delivered.

headword: come within an inch of doing something
altForms: come within an ace of doing something

senses.definition: almost to do something; to come very close to doing something.
examples: I came within an inch of going into the army.
I came within an inch of falling off the roof.
She came within an ace of buying the house.

senses.definition: to be expected under circumstances like this.
senses.notes: Refers to the details and difficulties attendant to something like the assignment of a specific sales territory to a salesperson. When one accepts the assignment, one accepts the problems.
examples: There is a lot of paperwork in this job. Oh, well, I guess it comes with the territory.
There are problems, but that comes with the territory.

senses.definition: to memorize something.
examples: We all committed the Gettysburg Address to memory.
I committed to memory the whole list of names and numbers.

senses.definition: to trick someone out of money or something of value.
examples: Anne conned her little sister out of her allowance.
Dave conned me out of my autographed baseball.

senses.definition: to tell secrets or personal matters to someone.
examples: Sally always confided in her sister Ann.
She didn’t feel that she could confide in her mother.

senses.definition: to collapse as from exhaustion.
examples: I was so tired I just went home and conked out.
I was afraid I would conk out while I was driving.

senses.definition: to break down; to quit running.
examples: My car conked out finally.
I hope my computer doesn’t conk out.

senses.definition: to have one’s absence (from an event) noticed.
examples: We missed you last night. You were conspicuous by your absence.
How could the bride’s father miss the wedding? He was certainly conspicuous by his absence.

senses.definition: a statement containing a seeming contradiction.
examples: A wealthy pauper is a contradiction in terms.
A straight-talking politician may seem a contradiction in terms.

senses.definition: in spite of something; regardless of something.
examples: Contrary to what you might think, I am neat and tidy.
Contrary to public opinion, my uncle is well and healthy.

senses.definition: to be in charge of the money in a business or a household.
examples: I control the purse strings at our house.
Mr. Williams is the treasurer. He controls the purse strings.

senses.definition: to damage or ruin someone.
examples: I cooked my own goose by not showing up on time.
Sally cooked Bob’s goose for treating her the way he did.

senses.definition: to cook something perfectly.
examples: John cooked my steak to perfection.
The entire dinner was cooked to perfection!

senses.definition: to plot something; to improvise something.
examples: Mary cooked an interesting party up at the last minute.
Let me see if I can cook up a way to get you some money.

senses.definition: to cheat in bookkeeping; to make the accounts appear to balance when they do not.
examples: Jane was sent to jail for cooking the accounts of her mother’s store.
It’s hard to tell whether she really cooked the accounts or just didn’t know how to add.

senses.definition: doing things the right way.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. From an advertising slogan.
examples: That’s great. Now you’re cooking with gas.
Things are moving along nicely with the project. The entire staff is really cooking with gas.

senses.definition: Calm down!; Take it easy!
examples: Don’t get mad, Bob. Cool it!
Cool it, you guys! No fighting around here.

senses.definition: to lose or reduce heat.
examples: I wish my soup would cool off. I’m hungry.
It’ll cool down this evening, after dusk.

senses.definition: to let one’s anger die away.
examples: I’m sorry I got angry. I’ll cool off in a minute.
Cool off, Tom. There is no sense getting so excited.

senses.definition: to let one’s passion or love die away.
examples: TED: Is Bob still in love with Jane? BILL: No, he’s cooled off a lot.
TED: I thought that they were both cooling down.

senses.definition: to wait (for someone).
examples: I spent all afternoon cooling my heels in the waiting room while the doctor talked on the telephone.
All right. If you can’t behave properly, just sit down here and cool your heels until I call you.

senses.definition: to reduce someone’s anger.
examples: I just stared at him while he was yelling. I knew that would cool him down.
The coach talked to them for a long time. That cooled them off.

senses.definition: to reduce someone’s passion or love.
examples: When she slapped him, that really cooled him down.
Dating Mary was too intense, so Bill cooled himself off by dating Sally for a while.

senses.definition: to plead guilty to a crime in hopes of receiving a lighter punishment.
examples: The robber copped a plea and got only two years in jail.
When you cop a plea, it saves the court system a lot of money.

senses.definition: to get out of a difficult situation; to sneak out of a difficult situation.
examples: At the last minute she copped out on us.
Things were going badly for Senator Phillips, so he copped out by resigning.

senses.definition: a person who copies or mimics what someone else does.
senses.notes: Usually juvenile. Can be preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Sally wore a pink dress just like Mary’s. Mary called Sally a copycat.
Bill is such a copycat. He bought a coat just like mine.

headword: cost an arm and a leg

senses.definition: to cost too much.
examples: It cost an arm and a leg, so I didn’t buy it.
Why should a little plastic part cost an arm and a leg?

senses.definition: to cost a lot of money.
examples: I’ll bet that diamond cost a pretty penny.
You can be sure that house cost a pretty penny. It has seven bathrooms.

senses.definition: to produce something unwillingly (that someone has requested).
examples: All right, Bill. Cough the stolen diamonds up or else.
Okay, okay. I’ll cough them up.
Bill had to cough up forty dollars to pay for the broken window.

senses.definition: satisfactory, but capable of improvement.
examples: The pie’s okay, but could be better.
Q: How do you feel? A: Could be better.

senses.definition: satisfactory, but not as bad as it could be.
examples: Q: How are things? A: Could be worse.
Things could be worse, and in a little while, they probably will be.

headword: could do with someone or something

senses.definition: to want or need someone or something; to benefit from someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with go for someone or something.
examples: I could do with a nice cool drink right now.
I could do with some help on this project.
This house could do with some cleaning up.
They said they could do with John to help them finish faster.
My car could do with a bigger engine.

senses.definition: completely satisfactory.
examples: I feeling great and couldn’t be better.
We had a wonderful time and our vacation couldn’t have been better.

senses.definition: totally happy.
examples: We are delighted. Couldn’t be happier.
They both couldn’t be happier since they got married.

senses.definition: unable to care at all.
senses.notes: Informal. Could care less is almost slang.
examples: John couldn’t care less whether he goes to the party or not.
So she won first place. I couldn’t care less.
I could care less if I live or die.

senses.definition: to count people.
examples: I’ll tell you how many people are here after I count noses.
Everyone is here. Let’s count noses so we can order hamburgers.

headword: count one’s chickens before they hatch

senses.definition: to plan how to utilize good results before they have occurred.
examples: You’re way ahead of yourself. Don’t count your chickens before they hatch.
You may be disappointed if you count your chickens before they hatch.

senses.definition: to rely on someone or something.
examples: Can I count on you to be there at noon?
I want to buy a car I can count on in winter weather.

senses.definition: to include someone in something.
senses.notes: Compare this with count someone out (for something).
examples: If you’re looking for a group to go mountain climbing, count me in on it.
I would like to count in your entire family, but there isn’t enough room.
Please count me in.

senses.definition: to exclude someone from something.
senses.notes: Compare this with count someone in (on something).
examples: Please count me out for the party next Saturday. I have other plans.
You should count the whole family out. We are going to the beach for the weekend.

senses.definition: two; two or three; a few; some; not many.
examples: Bill grabbed a couple of beers from the refrigerator.
I hung a couple of pictures on the wall.

senses.definition: the procedures or sequence of actions that someone will follow to accomplish a goal.
examples: I plan to take a course of action that will produce the best results.
The committee planned a course of action that would reduce costs and eliminate employees.

senses.definition: to travel over a great distance; to investigate a wide expanse of land.
examples: The prospectors covered a lot of ground, looking for gold.
My car can cover a lot of ground in one day.

senses.definition: to deal with much information and many facts.
examples: The history lecture covered a lot of ground today.
Mr. and Mrs. Franklin always cover a lot of ground when they argue.

senses.definition: to make excuses for someone; to conceal someone’s errors.
examples: If I miss class, please cover for me.
If you’re late, I’ll cover for you.

senses.definition: to handle someone else’s work.
examples: Dr. Johnson’s partner agreed to cover for him during his vacation.
I’m on duty this afternoon. Will you please cover for me? I have a doctor’s appointment.

senses.definition: to conceal one’s trail; to conceal one’s past activities.
examples: She was able to cover her tracks up so that they couldn’t find her.
It’s easy to cover up your tracks if you aren’t well known.
The robber failed to cover his tracks.

senses.definition: to conceal something.
examples: They covered up the truth about the crime.
We’ll cover this little matter up and make up a story for the press.

senses.definition: to deal with many things, much space, or much information from many points of view.
examples: That lecture really covered the waterfront. I could hardly follow it.
Why can’t she stick to the point? She has to cover the territory every time she talks.

senses.definition: to be extra friendly with someone, perhaps in hope of special favors in return.
examples: Look at that lawyer cozying up to the judge!
Lawyers who cozy up like that usually get into big trouble.

senses.definition: to open a book to study.
senses.notes: Slang. Almost always in the negative.
examples: I passed that test with an A, and I didn’t even crack a book.
If you think you can get through college without cracking a book, you’re wrong.

senses.definition: to tell a joke.
examples: She’s never serious. She’s always cracking jokes.
As long as she’s cracking jokes, she’s okay.

senses.definition: to smile a little, perhaps reluctantly.
examples: She cracked a smile, so I knew she was kidding.
The soldier cracked a smile at the wrong time and had to march for an hour as punishment.

senses.definition: to be hard on someone or something; to enforce a rule or law more strenuously.
examples: They are cracking down on speeding around here.
It’s about time they cracked down.

senses.definition: to open a bottle; to remove the cork or seal from a bottle, usually a bottle of an alcoholic drink.
examples: They cracked open a bottle to celebrate her arrival.
Let’s crack open a bottle of champagne and celebrate.

senses.definition: to crash something; to destroy something (in an accident).
examples: The driver cracked the car up in an accident.
The pilot cracked up the plane.

senses.definition: to make someone laugh.
examples: She told a joke that really cracked us up.
I cracked up my history class with a silly remark.

senses.definition: to expose and reveal some great wrongdoing.
examples: The police cracked the drug ring wide open.
The newspaper story cracked the trouble at city hall wide open.

senses.definition: to crash.
examples: The plane cracked up in the storm.
The boat cracked up on the rocks.

senses.definition: to break out in laughter.
examples: The audience really cracked up during the second act.
The class cracked up when I told my joke, but the teacher didn’t like it.

senses.definition: to go crazy.
examples: The mayor cracked up after only a year in office.
I was afraid the mayor would crack up because of too much work.

senses.definition: to limit someone in some way.
examples: I hope this doesn’t cramp your style, but could you please not hum while you work?
To ask him to keep regular hours would really be cramping his style.

senses.definition: to produce something; to make something in a casual and mechanical way.
examples: John can crank a lot of work out in a single day.
That factory keeps cranking out cars even though no one buys them.

senses.definition: to fail spectacularly.
senses.notes: Also literal, as with a car or a plane.
examples: Poor Chuck really crashed and burned when he made his presentation at the sales meeting.
Mary just knew that the whole project would crash and burn if she didn’t keep a close watch on it.

senses.definition: very fond of someone or something.
examples: Ann is crazy about John.
He’s crazy about her, too.
I’m mad about their new song.
Our whole family is nuts about homemade ice cream.

senses.definition: the best of all.
examples: This particular car is the cream of the crop.
The kids are very bright. They are the cream of the crop.

senses.definition: to cause an outburst or sensation.
examples: The dog got into church and made an uproar.
Her poodle created an uproar in the restaurant.
Why did you make such an uproar?

senses.definition: to make a major issue out of something; to make much over something; to make a lot of complaints and criticisms about something.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with make a federal case out of something.
examples: Tom created a stink about Bob’s remarks.
Why did he make a stink about that?
Tom is always trying to raise a stink.

senses.definition: things that make people comfortable.
examples: The hotel room was sparse, but all the creature comforts were there.
The entire country of Adonia seemed to lack the expected creature comforts.

headword: a credit to someone or something

senses.definition: someone or something that is of value or benefit.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, or seem like.
examples: I always want to be a credit to my school.
John is not what you would call a credit to his family.

senses.definition: a twisted or cramped place in the back that causes pain.
examples: I can’t move! I’ve got a crick in my back!
I had a crick in my back all night and I couldn’t sleep.

senses.definition: a twisted place or a cramp in the neck that causes pain.
examples: I got a crick in my neck from sleeping in a draft.
When I read on the plane, I get a crick in my neck.

headword: cross a bridge before one comes to it

senses.definition: to worry excessively about something before it happens.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: There is no sense in crossing that bridge before you come to it.
She’s always crossing bridges before coming to them. She needs to learn to relax.

headword: cross a bridge when one comes to it

senses.definition: to deal with a problem only when one is faced with the problem.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: Please wait and cross that bridge when you come to it.
He shouldn’t worry about it now. He can cross that bridge when he comes to it.

senses.definition: to ask someone questions in great detail; to question a suspect or a witness at great length.
examples: The police cross-examined the suspect for three hours.
The lawyer plans to cross-examine the witness tomorrow morning.

headword: cross one’s heart (and hope to die)

senses.definition: to pledge or vow that the truth is being told.
examples: It’s true, cross my heart and hope to die.
It’s really true—cross my heart.

senses.definition: to give money to someone in payment for a service.
senses.notes: A fortune-teller might ask for a potential customer to cross her palm with silver. Used in that sense or jocularly for something like tipping a porter.
examples: I crossed his palm with silver, but he still stood there.
You will find that things happen much faster in hotels if you cross the staff’s palms with silver fairly often.

senses.definition: to give someone trouble; to defy or betray someone.
examples: You really crossed me up when you told Tom what I said.
Please don’t cross me up again.

senses.definition: to enter into an argument with someone.
examples: I don’t want to cross swords with Tom on this matter.
The last time we crossed swords, we had a terrible time.

senses.definition: to do something that inevitably commits one to following a certain course of action.
senses.notes: The crossing of the River Rubicon by Julius Caesar inevitably involved him in a war with the senate in 49 b.c.
examples: Jane crossed the Rubicon by signing the contract.
Find another job before you cross the Rubicon and resign from this one.

senses.definition: demoralized; with hurt feelings.
examples: The whole family was completely crushed by the news.
I was just crushed by your attitude. I thought we were friends.

senses.definition: the central issue of the matter.
senses.notes: Crux is an old word meaning “cross.”
examples: All right, this is the crux of the matter.
It’s about time that we looked at the crux of the matter.

senses.definition: to cry or complain before one is injured.
examples: Bill always cries before he’s hurt.
There is no point in crying before one is hurt.

senses.definition: to scream as if something very serious has happened.
examples: Now that Bill is really hurt, he’s crying bloody murder.
There is no point in crying bloody murder about the bill if you aren’t going to pay it.

senses.definition: to cry very hard.
examples: When we heard the news, we cried our eyes out with joy.
She cried her eyes out after his death.

senses.definition: to be unhappy about something that cannot be undone.
examples: I’m sorry that you broke your bicycle, Tom. But there is nothing that can be done now. Don’t cry over spilled milk.
Ann is always crying over spilled milk.

senses.definition: to cry or complain about something when nothing is really wrong.
examples: Pay no attention. She’s just crying wolf again.
Don’t cry wolf too often. No one will come.

senses.definition: a very unfortunate situation; a real shame.
examples: It’s a crying shame that people cannot afford adequate housing.
That everyone could not attend the concert was a crying shame.

senses.definition: to frighten or disgust someone severely.
examples: The story was scary enough to curdle your blood.
The terrible scream was enough to curdle my blood.

senses.definition: It is dangerous to be curious.
examples: Don’t ask so many questions, Billy. Curiosity killed the cat.
Curiosity killed the cat. Mind your own business.

senses.definition: to frighten or alarm someone; to shock someone with sight, sound, or taste.
examples: Don’t ever sneak up on me like that again. You really curled my hair.
The horror film made my hair curl.

senses.definition: to retreat and die.
examples: When I heard you say that, I could have curled up and died.
No, it wasn’t an illness. She just curled up and died.

senses.definition: to try to win favor from someone.
examples: The lawyer tried to curry favor with the judge.
It’s silly to curry favor. Just be yourself.

headword: a cut above someone or something

senses.definition: a measure or degree better than someone or something else.
senses.notes: Especially with average, as in the examples.
examples: Your shirt is beautiful, but mine is a cut above yours.
John isn’t the best mechanic in town, but he’s a cut above average.

senses.definition: to reach beyond something; to embrace a wide variety; to slice across a figurative boundary or barrier.
examples: His teaching cut across all human cultures and races.
This rule cuts across all social barriers.

senses.definition: to look good; to look elegant.
senses.notes: Formal. Usually said of a male.
examples: Tom really cuts a fine figure on the dance floor.
Bill cuts a fine figure since he bought some new clothes.

senses.definition: fixed; determined beforehand; usual and uninteresting.
examples: I find your writing quite boring. It’s too cut-and-dried.
The lecture was, as usual, cut-and-dried. It was the same thing we’ve heard for years.

senses.definition: to cut something out of paper with scissors and paste it onto something else.
examples: The teacher told the little children that it was time to cut and paste, and they all ran to the worktables.
Mary made a tiny house by cutting and pasting little strips of paper.

senses.definition: something trivial, simple, or childish.
examples: I hate this job. It’s nothing but cut and paste.
I don’t mind doing things that have to be done, but I hate to waste my time on cut and paste.

senses.definition: to get free and run away.
senses.notes: Slang. As in cutting loose the rope on a ship’s or boat’s anchor and sailing away in a hurry.
examples: Max decided to cut and run when he heard the police sirens.
As soon as I finish what I am doing here, I’m going to cut and run. I’ve got to get home by six o’clock.

senses.definition: to seem important; to attract a lot of attention.
examples: In social matters, Mrs. Smith cuts a wide swath.
Bob cuts a big swath whenever he appears in his military uniform.

senses.definition: to reduce one’s use of something; to use less of something.
examples: The government has to cut back on its spending.
It’s very difficult for the government to cut back.

senses.definition: to affect both sides of an issue equally.
examples: Remember that your suggestion that costs should be shared cuts both ways. You will have to pay as well.
If our side cannot take along supporters to the game, then yours cannot either. The rule has to cut both ways.

senses.definition: to skip going to class.
examples: If Mary keeps cutting classes, she’ll fail the course.
I can’t cut that class. I’ve missed too many already.

senses.definition: to reduce efforts or expenditures; to do things poorly or incompletely.
examples: You cannot cut corners when you are dealing with public safety.
Don’t cut corners, Sally. Let’s do the job right.

senses.definition: sharing a lot of similarities; seeming to have been created, reared, or fashioned in the same way.
examples: She and her brother are cut from the same cloth. They both tell lies all the time.
They are made from the same mold and even sound alike on the telephone.

senses.definition: Stop doing that!
examples: That’s enough! Cut it out!
Stop doing that. It hurts! Cut it out!

senses.definition: to break away from someone or something; to break ties with someone or something; to act in a free manner.
senses.notes: Also literal. Compare this with break loose (from someone or something).
examples: Jane is finding it hard to cut loose from her family.
Cutting loose is part of growing up.
When those farm boys get to town, they really cut loose from convention.
They sure are wild when they cut loose.

senses.definition: to fail to change the mind of someone; to have no influence on someone.
examples: What you just said will cut no ice with the manager.
All that may be true, but it cuts no ice with me.
That idea cuts no ice. It won’t help at all.
It cuts no ice that your mother is the mayor.

senses.definition: to stop by itself or oneself.
examples: The machine got hot and cut off.
Bob cut off in midsentence.

headword: cut off one’s nose to spite one’s face

senses.definition: to harm oneself while trying to harm another person.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: Billy loves the zoo, but he refused to go with his mother because he was mad at her. He cut off his nose to spite his face.
Find a better way to be angry. It is silly to cut your nose off to spite your face.

senses.definition: to have done something since one was very young; to have much experience at something.
examples: Do I know about cars? I cut my eyeteeth on cars.
I cut my eyeteeth on Bach. I can whistle everything he wrote.

senses.definition: to reduce someone’s losses of money, goods, or other things of value.
examples: I sold the stock as it went down, thus cutting my losses.
He cut his losses by putting better locks on the doors. There were fewer robberies.
The mayor’s reputation suffered because of the scandal. He finally resigned to cut his losses.

senses.definition: to experience certain failure; to do damage to oneself.
examples: If I were to run for office, I’d just be cutting my throat.
Judges who take bribes are cutting their own throats.

senses.definition: well-suited for something; with a talent for something.
senses.notes: Compare this with cut out to be something.
examples: Tom was not cut out for banking.
Sally was cut out for the medical profession.

senses.definition: to remove unproductive persons from employment.
senses.notes: Also literal as in pruning away dead branches or deadwood.
examples: This company would be more profitable if management would cut out the deadwood.
When we cut out the deadwood, all our departments will run more smoothly.

senses.definition: well-suited for a particular role or a particular occupation.
senses.notes: Compare this with cut out for something.
examples: Tom was not cut out to be a banker.
Sally was cut out to be a doctor.

senses.definition: to write a check; to have a computer print a check.
examples: We will cut a check for the balance due you later this afternoon.
We will cut you a check as soon as possible.

senses.definition: to ignore someone totally.
examples: Joan was just about to speak to James when he cut her dead.
Jean cut her former husband dead.

senses.definition: to make a person humble; to put one in one’s place.
senses.notes: See also beat someone down (to size).
examples: John’s remarks really cut me down to size.
Jane is too conceited. I think her new boss will take her down to size.
The boss’s angry stare will really cut her down.

senses.definition: to give someone a share of something.
examples: Shall we cut Bill in on this deal?
I don’t think we should cut anybody in.
Pretty soon we’ll have to cut in the whole town.

headword: cut someone off without a penny

senses.definition: to end someone’s allowance; to fail to leave someone money in one’s will.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Franklin cut their son off without a penny after he quit school.
They cut off both of their sons without a penny.
We learned, when Uncle Sam’s will was read, that he cut off his own flesh and blood without a penny.

headword: cut someone or something to the bone

senses.definition: to slice flesh or meat deep to the bone.
examples: The knife cut John to the bone. He had to be sewed up.
Cut each slice of ham to the bone. Then each slice will be as big as possible.

senses.definition: to cut down severely (on something).
examples: We cut our expenses to the bone and are still losing money.
Congress had to cut the budget to the bone in order to balance it.

senses.definition: to criticize someone or something severely.
examples: Jane is such a gossip. She was really cutting Mrs. Jones up.
The professor really cut up my essay.

senses.definition: to hurt someone’s feelings very badly.
examples: Your criticism cut me to the quick.
Tom’s sharp words to Mary cut her to the quick.

senses.definition: to grow teeth.
examples: Billy is cranky because he’s cutting teeth.
Ann cut her first tooth this week.

headword: cut the ground out from under someone

senses.definition: to destroy the foundation of someone’s plans or someone’s argument.
examples: The politician cut the ground out from under his opponent.
Congress cut out the ground from under the president.

senses.definition: to get to the important matters.
examples: Let’s stop all this chatter and cut to the chase.
I like the way you cut to the chase and don’t waste my time.

senses.definition: to act wildly; to show off and be troublesome; to act like a clown.
senses.notes: Slang. See also cut someone or something up.
examples: Tom, Billy! Stop cutting up, or I’ll send you to the principal’s office.
If you spent more time studying than cutting up, you’d get better grades.

senses.definition: everyday work routine.
examples: I’m getting very tired of the daily grind.
When my vacation was over, I had to go back to the daily grind.

headword: damn someone or something with faint praise

senses.definition: to criticize someone or something indirectly by not praising enthusiastically.
examples: The critic did not say that he disliked the play, but he damned it with faint praise.
Mrs. Brown is very proud of her son’s achievements, but damns her daughter’s with faint praise.

senses.definition: to shift to a different kind of behavior; to change one’s behavior or attitude.
senses.notes: See also change someone’s tune; sing a different tune.
examples: After being yelled at, Ann danced to another tune.
A stern talking-to will make her dance to another tune.

senses.definition: to attempt to do something that is very risky.
examples: The crossing of the border into Adonia was like dancing with death.
You are dancing with death in your effort to cross that narrow ledge.

senses.definition: to challenge someone to do something.
examples: Sally dared Jane to race her to the corner.
You wouldn’t do that, would you? I dare you.

senses.definition: someone or something whose abilities, plans, or feelings are little known to others.
examples: It’s difficult to predict who will win the prize—there are two or three dark horses in the tournament.
Everyone was surprised at the results of the election. The dark horse won.

senses.definition: to come to someone’s door seeking entry.
senses.notes: [for an unwelcome person] As if the unwelcome visitor were casting a shadow on the door. Formal or jocular.
examples: Who is this who has come to darken my door?
Is that you, John, darkening my door again? I thought you were out of town.
The heroine of the drama told the villain never to darken her door again.
She touched the back of her hand to her forehead and said, “Go, and never darken my door again!”

senses.definition: to dart quickly between two things, or into a number of things, and move away again.
examples: On the highway, a small car was darting in and out of the two right lanes of traffic.
A small bird darted in and out of the bush, probably going into a nest inside.

senses.definition: to send something off, usually quickly.
examples: I’ll dash a quick note off to Aunt Mary.
Ann just dashed off a message to her parents.

senses.definition: to extend back to a particular time; to have been alive at a particular time in the past.
examples: My late grandmother dated back to the Civil War.
This record dates back to the sixties.
How far do you date back?

senses.definition: the bottom of the sea, especially when it is a grave.
senses.notes: From the seamen’s name for the evil spirit of the sea. See also go to Davy Jones’s locker.
examples: They were going to sail around the world, but ended up in Davy Jones’s locker.
Most of the gold from that trading ship is in Davy Jones’s locker.

senses.definition: to occur to someone; to cross someone’s mind.
examples: It just dawned on me that I forgot my books.
When will it dawn on him that his audience is bored?

senses.definition: every day; daily; all the time.
examples: He wears the same clothes day after day.
She visits her husband in the hospital day after day.

senses.definition: all the time; around the clock.
examples: The nurse was with her day and night.
The house is guarded night and day.

senses.definition: on every day; for each day.
examples: She smokes day in and day out.
They eat nothing but vegetables, day in, day out.

senses.definition: daily; everyday; common.
examples: They update their accounts on a day-to-day basis.
Just wear your regular day-to-day clothing.

senses.definition: the practice of blatantly or grossly overcharging.
examples: It’s daylight robbery to charge that amount of money for a hotel room!
The cost of renting a car at that place is daylight robbery.

senses.definition: days in a series; months in a series; etc.
examples: I had a bad cold for 5 days running.
For two years running, I brought work home from the office every night.

senses.definition: straight ahead; directly ahead.
examples: Look out! There is a cow in the road dead ahead.
The farmer said that the town we wanted was dead ahead.

senses.definition: gone forever.
senses.notes: Refers literally to persons and figuratively to ideas and other things.
examples: Now that memories of Uncle Bill are dead and buried, we can throw away his old boots.
That kind of thinking is dead and buried.

senses.definition: dead and buried, and probably forgotten.
examples: John is dead and gone. There is no reason to fear him anymore.
Her husband is dead and gone, but she is getting along fine.

senses.definition: someone or something that is failed, finished, or nearly dead.
examples: He missed the exam. He’s a dead duck.
Yes, John’s a dead duck. He drove his car into a tree.

headword: dead in someone’s or something’s tracks

senses.definition: stopped exactly where someone or something is at the moment.
senses.notes: This does not usually have anything to do with death. The phrase is often used with stop.
examples: Her unkind words stopped me dead in my tracks.
When I heard the rattlesnake, I stopped dead in my tracks.
The project came to a halt dead in its tracks.

senses.definition: a piece of mail that is returned to the post office as both undeliverable and unreturnable.
examples: At the end of the year, the post office usually has bushels of dead letters.
Some of the dead letters are opened to see if there is an address inside.

senses.definition: an issue, law, or matter that is no longer important or that no longer has force or power.
senses.notes: Usually a dead letter. Could also be used for a person.
examples: His point about the need for education reform is a dead letter. It is being done now.
This point of law is a dead letter since the last Supreme Court ruling on this matter.

senses.definition: a total loss.
examples: My investment was a dead loss.
This car is a dead loss. It was a waste of money.

senses.definition: exhausted; worn out; no longer useful.
examples: Ann is so tired. She’s really dead on her feet.
He can’t teach well anymore. He’s dead on his feet.
This inefficient company is dead on its feet.

headword: dead set against someone or something

senses.definition: totally opposed to someone or something.
senses.notes: See also one’s heart is (dead) set against something.
examples: I’m dead set against the new tax proposal.
Everyone is dead set against the mayor.

senses.definition: tired; exhausted; sleeping soundly.
senses.notes: Compare this with dead on one’s feet.
examples: I’ve had such a hard day. I’m really dead to the world.
Look at her sleep. She’s dead to the world.

senses.definition: unable to hear or speak.
senses.notes: Used without any intended malice, but no longer considered polite. Sometimes euphemized as “hearing and speech impaired.”
examples: Fred objected to being called deaf and dumb.
Aunt Clara—she was deaf and dumb, you know—lived to be over 100.

senses.definition: to buy and sell something.
examples: My uncle is a stockbroker. He deals in stocks and bonds.
My aunt deals in antiques.

senses.definition: death, which is inevitable, and the payment of taxes, which is unavoidable.
senses.notes: A saying that emphasizes the rigor with which taxes are collected.
examples: There is nothing as certain on this old planet as death and taxes.
Max said he could get out of anything except death and taxes.

senses.definition: very effective in acting against someone or something.
examples: This road is terribly bumpy. It’s death on tires.
The sergeant is death on lazy soldiers.

senses.definition: accurate or deadly at doing something requiring skill or great effort.
examples: John is death on curve balls. He’s our best pitcher.
The boxing champ is really death on those fast punches.

headword: decide in favor of someone or something

senses.definition: to determine that someone or something is the winner.
examples: The judge decided in favor of the defendant.
I decided in favor of the red one.

senses.definition: to believe that something is necessary.
examples: Mary deemed that it was necessary to leave town that night.
Lisa deemed it necessary to go home.

senses.definition: to get rid of someone or something; to dispose of someone or something.
senses.notes: Slang. To bury someone or something six feet deep, the standard depth for a grave.
examples: Take this horrible food out and deep-six it.
That guy is a pain. Deep-six him so the cops will never find him.

senses.definition: a place filled with wickedness.
examples: The town was a den of iniquity and vice was everywhere.
Police raided the gambling house, calling it a den of iniquity.

senses.definition: to leave a place, a person, or a situation when things become difficult or unpleasant.
senses.notes: Rats are said to be the first to leave a ship that is sinking.
examples: I hate to be the one to desert a sinking ship, but I can’t stand it around here anymore.
There goes Tom. Wouldn’t you know he’d leave a sinking ship rather than stay around and try to help?

senses.definition: a very casual attitude; a worry-free or carefree attitude.
examples: You must get rid of your devil-may-care attitude if you want to succeed.
She acts so thoughtlessly with her devil-may-care manner.

senses.definition: the most difficult task.
examples: We had a devil of a job fixing the car.
It was the devil’s own job finding a hotel with vacancies.

senses.definition: a valuable or potentially excellent person or thing hidden by an unpolished or rough exterior.
examples: Ann looks like a stupid woman, but she’s a fine person—a real diamond in the rough.
That piece of property is a diamond in the rough. Someday it will be valuable.

senses.definition: to die by disease or old age rather than by violence or foul play.
examples: I hope to live to 100 and die a natural death.
The police say she didn’t die a natural death, and they are investigating.

senses.definition: to fade away or die down.
examples: I expect that all this excitement about computers will die a natural death.
Most fads die a natural death.

senses.definition: to go down fighting; to die in some fashion other than in bed; to die fighting.
senses.notes: A cliché popularized by western movies. The villains of these movies said they preferred death by gunshot or hanging to dying in bed. See also go down fighting.
examples: I won’t let him get me. I’ll die in my boots.
He may give me a hard time, but I won’t be overcome. I’ll fight him and die with my boots on.

senses.definition: some process is past the point of no return.
senses.notes: This die is one of a pair of dice. This cast means “thrown.”
examples: After that speech favoring reform of the education system, the die is cast. This is now a campaign issue.
The die is cast. There is no turning back on this point.

senses.definition: to meet one’s death laughing—in good spirits, revenge, or irony.
examples: Sally is such an optimist that she’ll probably die laughing.
Bob tried to poison his rich aunt, who then died laughing because she had taken Bob out of her will.

senses.definition: to laugh very long and hard.
examples: The joke was so funny that I almost died laughing.
The play was meant to be funny, but the audience didn’t exactly die laughing.

senses.definition: to die of emotional distress.
examples: I was not surprised to hear of her death. They say she died of a broken heart.
In the movie, the heroine appeared to die of a broken heart, but the audience knew she was poisoned.

senses.definition: to suffer from emotional distress, especially from a failed romance.
examples: Tom and Mary broke off their romance and both died of broken hearts.
Please don’t leave me. I know I’ll die of a broken heart.

senses.definition: to suffer from boredom; to be very bored.
examples: No one has ever really died of boredom.
We sat there and listened politely, even though we almost died of boredom.

senses.definition: to eat a meal; to begin eating a meal.
senses.notes: Informal. See also Come and get it!
examples: Dinner’s ready, Tom. Sit down and dig in.
The cowboy helped himself to some beans and dug in.

senses.definition: to apply oneself to a task; to tackle (something) vigorously.
examples: Sally looked at the big job ahead of her. Then she rolled up her sleeves and dug in.
“Tom,” hollered Mrs. Smith, “you get to that pile of homework and dig in this very minute.”

senses.definition: to refuse to alter one’s course of action or opinions; to be obstinate or determined.
examples: The student dug her heels in and refused to obey the instructions.
I’m digging in my heels. I’m not going back.

senses.definition: to be responsible for one’s own downfall or ruin.
examples: The manager tried to get rid of his assistant, but he dug his own grave. He got fired himself for trying.
The committee has dug its own grave with the new tax bill.

headword: dig some dirt up on someone

senses.definition: to find out something bad about someone.
examples: If you don’t stop trying to dig some dirt up on me, I’ll get a lawyer and sue you.
The citizens’ group dug up some dirt on the mayor and used it against her at election time.

senses.definition: to understand something; to relate to a person or a thing.
examples: I really dig Tom. He’s a special guy.
I really dig rock music.

senses.definition: to go to great effort to find someone or something.
senses.notes: There is an implication that the thing or person dug up is not the most desirable, but is all that could be found.
examples: Mary dug a date up for the dance next Friday.
I dug up a recipe for roast pork with pineapple.
I dug up a carpenter who doesn’t charge very much.

senses.definition: to work hard to locate something and bring it forth.
examples: They dug the contract out of the file cabinet.
I dug this old suit out of a box in the attic.
I dug out an old dress and wore it to the fifties party.

senses.definition: abundant; cheap and common.
examples: People who can write good books are not a dime a dozen.
Romantic movies are a dime a dozen.

senses.definition: to take or borrow from a supply of something, especially a supply of money.
examples: I had to dip into my savings account to pay for the car.
I hate to dip in like that.
She put out her hand and dipped into the chocolate box.

senses.definition: extremely cheap.
examples: Buy some more of those plums. They’re dirt cheap.
In Italy, the peaches are dirt cheap.

senses.definition: an older man who is excessively interested in sex.
examples: Tell your daughter to stay away from him. He’s a dirty old man and might attack her.
There were several dirty old men looking at pornographic magazines in the park.

senses.definition: unpleasant or uninteresting work.
examples: My boss does all the traveling. I get all the dirty work to do.
She’s tired of doing all the dirty work at the office.

senses.definition: dishonest or underhanded actions; treachery.
examples: She knew there was some dirty work going on when she saw her opponents whispering together.
The company seems respectable enough, but there’s a lot of dirty work that goes on.

senses.definition: to cause the enemy to split into two or more warring factions, and then move in to conquer all of them.
examples: Mary thought she could divide and conquer the board of directors, but they had survived such tactics many times, and her efforts failed.
Sam led his men to divide and conquer the enemy platoon, and his strategy succeeded.

senses.definition: to divide something into two equal parts.
examples: Tommy and Billy divided the candy fifty-fifty.
The robbers split the money fifty-fifty.

senses.definition: to react with surprise; to have to look twice to make sure that one really saw correctly.
examples: When the boy led a goat into the park, everyone did a double take.
When the nurse saw that the man had six toes, she did a double take.

senses.definition: to make a sudden reversal of opinion.
examples: Without warning, the government did a flip-flop on taxation.
It had done an about-face on the question of deductions last year.

headword: do a job on someone or something

senses.definition: to damage someone or something; to mess up someone or something.
examples: The robbers really did a job on the bank guard. They beat him when they robbed the bank.
The puppy did a job on my shoes. They are all chewed to pieces.

senses.definition: to defecate on something.
senses.notes: [with something] Informal and euphemistic. Note the variation in the second example.
examples: The puppy did a job on the living-room carpet.
It’s supposed to do its job on the newspapers in the basement.

senses.definition: to do a large amount of business in a short period of time.
examples: The ice cream shop always does a land-office business on a hot day.
The tax collector’s office did a land-office business on the day that taxes were due.

headword: do a number on someone or something

senses.definition: to damage or harm someone or something.
examples: The teacher did a number on the whole class. That test was terrible.
Tom did a number on Mary when he went out with Ann.

headword: do a snow job on someone

senses.definition: to deceive or confuse someone.
examples: Tom did a snow job on the teacher when he said that he was sick yesterday.
I hate it when someone does a snow job on me. I find it harder and harder to trust people.

headword: do away with someone or something

senses.definition: to kill someone; to dispose of someone or something.
examples: The crooks did away with the witness.
I was there, too. I hope they don’t try to do away with me.

senses.definition: to get rid of something; to dispose of something.
examples: This chemical will do away with the stain in your sink.
The time has come to do away with that old building.

senses.definition: to add to the reputation of someone.
examples: Your new job really does credit to you.
Yes, it really does you credit.

headword: Do I need to paint you a picture?

senses.definition: It is so very simple, so why do you require more explanation to understand it?
examples: What is so difficult? Do I need to paint you a picture?
I’ve explained it every way I can. Do I need to paint you a picture?

senses.definition: to do something well; to represent or portray something accurately.
examples: Sally did justice to the contract negotiations.
This photograph doesn’t do justice to the beauty of the mountains.

senses.definition: to eat or drink a great deal.
examples: Bill always does justice to the turkey on Thanksgiving.
The party didn’t do justice to the roast pig. There were nearly ten pounds left over.

headword: do not have a care in the world

senses.definition: being free and casual; being unworried and carefree.
senses.notes: Do not have can be replaced with be without.
examples: I really feel good to-day—as if I didn’t have a care in the world.
Ann always acts as if she doesn’t have a care in the world.

headword: do not have a leg to stand on

senses.definition: to have no support.
senses.notes: [for an argument or a case] Informal. Do not have can be replaced with be without.
examples: You may think you’re in the right, but you don’t have a leg to stand on.
My lawyer said I didn’t have a leg to stand on, so I shouldn’t sue the company.

headword: do not have all one’s marbles

senses.definition: do not have all one’s mental capacities.
examples: John acts as if he doesn’t have all his marbles.
I’m afraid that I don’t have all my marbles all the time.

senses.definition: to do one’s job; to do what is expected of one.
examples: Please don’t thank me. I’m just doing my duty.
Soldiers who fight in wars are doing their duty.

senses.definition: to make oneself proud.
senses.notes: [for one] Folksy. See also do credit to someone.
examples: Well, Bill really did himself proud in the horse race.
You did yourself proud by raising that fine-looking, prizewinning hog.

senses.definition: to do (something) as well as one can.
examples: Just do your level best. That’s all we can ask of you.
Tom isn’t doing his best. We may have to replace him.

senses.definition: to do what one likes or what one pleases.
examples: Tom doesn’t like being told what to do. He prefers to do his own thing.
When you do your thing, you have no one but yourself to blame if things don’t work out.

senses.definition: to do one’s share of the work; to do whatever one can do to help.
examples: All people everywhere must do their part to help get things under control.
I always try to do my bit. How can I help this time?

senses.definition: to do something or die trying.
senses.notes: Refers to an attitude adopted when one must do something whether one wants to or not. Occurs as a noun or an adjective.
examples: It was do or die. There was no turning back now.
He simply had to get to the airport on time. It was a case of do or die.

senses.definition: to treat someone in a particular manner.
senses.notes: Informal. Do not confuse this with a passive construction. The someone is not the actor but the object.
examples: Tom did all right by Ann when he brought her red roses.
I did badly by Tom. I fired him.

senses.definition: to do something that is helpful to someone.
examples: My neighbor did me a good turn by lending me his car.
The teacher did me a good turn when he told me to work harder.

senses.definition: to do a kind deed for a person.
examples: My neighbor did me a kindness when he cut my grass.
I am always happy to have the opportunity of doing someone a kindness.

senses.definition: to harm someone.
examples: I hope she doesn’t plan to do me damage.
They did us damage by telling the whole story to the newspapers.

senses.definition: to benefit someone.
examples: A nice hot bath really does me good.
A few years in the army would do you good.

senses.definition: to do what is requested by someone.
examples: The servant grumbled but did his employer’s bidding.
Am I expected to do your bidding whenever you ask?

senses.definition: to make someone feel good emotionally.
examples: It does my heart good to hear you talk that way.
When she sent me a get-well card, it really did my heart good.

senses.definition: to do something with one’s hands rather than with a machine.
examples: The computer was broken so I had to do the calculations by hand.
All this tiny stitching was done by hand. Machines cannot do this kind of work.

senses.definition: to do something fairly.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also fair and square.
examples: He always plays the game fair and square.
I try to treat all people fair and square.

senses.definition: to do some kind of work to earn enough money to live.
examples: John paints houses for a living.
What do you do for a living?

senses.definition: to do something easily and without opposition.
examples: The mayor won the election hands down.
She was the choice of the people hands down.

senses.definition: to do something almost immediately.
examples: If I had the money, I would go back to college in a heartbeat.
Just tell me that you need me and I’ll come there in a heartbeat.

senses.definition: to appear somewhere and do something oneself rather than sending someone else or doing it over the telephone, or by mail.
examples: I know the money should be in his account. I saw him put it there in person.
The famous actor came to the hospital and greeted each patient in person.

senses.definition: to do something where anyone looking could see it.
examples: You should dress neatly when you appear in public.
I wish that you wouldn’t talk to me so rudely in public.
Bob, you must behave properly in public.

senses.definition: to do something with no result; to do something that fails.
examples: They rushed her to the hospital, but they did it in vain.
We tried in vain to get her there on time.

senses.definition: to do something while one is moving; to do something (to something that is in motion).
senses.notes: Slang. This has nothing to do with actual flight.
examples: We can’t stop the machine to oil it now. You’ll have to do it on the fly.
We will have to find the break in the film on the fly—while we are showing it.

senses.definition: to do something while one is moving hurriedly; to do something while one is going rapidly from one place to another.
examples: I was very busy today and had to eat on the run.
I didn’t have time to meet with Bill, but I was able to talk to him on the run.

senses.definition: to accomplish something in the most difficult manner, rather than by an easier way.
examples: I made it to this job the hard way. I came up through the ranks.
She did it the hard way. She had no help from her parents.

senses.definition: to do something the wrong way.
examples: No, you can’t pound in nails like that. You’re doing it the hard way.
I’m sorry. I learn things the hard way.

senses.definition: to do too much of something; to consume too much of something.
examples: Anne often drinks to excess at parties.
John smokes to excess when he works.

senses.definition: to do something just right.
senses.notes: Folksy. Refers to cooking something until it has just the right amount of brownish color.
examples: Of course I can do it right. I’ll really do it up brown.
Come on, Bob. Let’s do it right this time. I know you can do it up brown.

senses.definition: to do something with vigor; to do something energetically as if one were angry with it.
examples: Bob is building that fence with a vengeance.
Mary is really weeding her garden with a vengeance.

senses.definition: to wash and dry dishes, glasses, cups, knives, forks, etc., after a meal.
examples: Bill, you cannot go out and play until you’ve done the dishes.
Why am I always the one who has to do the dishes?

senses.definition: to act as host or hostess and serve one’s guests by pouring drinks, slicing meat, making (drinking) toasts, etc.
examples: All the guests were seated, and a huge, juicy turkey sat on the table. Jane Thomas turned to her husband and said, “Bob, will you do the honors?” Mr. Jones smiled and began slicing thick slices of meat from the turkey.

The mayor stood up and addressed the people who were still eating their salads. “I’m delighted to do the honors this evening and propose a toast to your friend and mine, Bill Jones. Bill, good luck and best wishes in your new job in Washington.” And everyone sipped a bit of wine.

senses.definition: to do exactly what needs to be done.
examples: Push it just a little more to the left. There, that does the trick.
If you lend me five dollars, I’ll have enough to do the trick.

senses.definition: to manage to get through life without someone or something that you want or need.
examples: I guess I’ll just have to do without a car.
I don’t know how I can do without.
The boss can’t do without a secretary.

senses.definition: Do you understand what I am telling you?
senses.notes: Typically asked of someone receiving a radio communication, such as from an airplane or an airport control tower. Also used as an emphatic way of asking if one is understood.
examples: This is Delta heavy 54. Do you read me?
I have said no twenty times already! The answer is still no! Do you read me?

senses.definition: a display, demonstration, or exhibition of something— such as something one is selling.
senses.notes: Refers to a circus act where trained dogs leap onto and off of trained ponies, in exactly the same sequence each time the show is performed.
examples: Gary was there with his dog and pony show, trying to sell his ideas to whomever would listen to him.
Don’t you get tired of running through the same old dog and pony show, week after week?

senses.definition: a situation in which one has to act ruthlessly in order to survive or succeed; ruthless competition.
examples: It is dog-eat-dog in the world of business these days.
Universities are not quiet peaceful places. It’s dog-eat-dog to get a promotion.

senses.definition: one who prevents other people from doing or having what one does not wish them to do or have.
senses.notes: From one of Aesop’s fables in which a dog— which cannot eat hay—lay in the hayrack [manger] and prevented the other animals from eating the hay.
examples: Jane is a real dog in the manger. She cannot drive, but she will not lend anyone her car.
If Martin were not such a dog in the manger, he would let his brother have that dinner jacket he never wears.

senses.definition: considering the amount of money involved; considering the cost.
examples: Dollar for dollar, you cannot buy a better car.
