Dollar for dollar, this laundry detergent washes cleaner and brighter than any other product on the market.

senses.definition: tired; exhausted; terminated; killed.
examples: I am really done in after all that exercise.
The project was done in by a vote of the board.
The witness was afraid he would be done in by the mobsters.

senses.definition: cooked just right.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also fit someone to a T; suit someone to a T.
examples: Yummy! This meat is done to a T.
I like it done to a turn, not too done and not too raw.

senses.definition: Do not stop breathing (while waiting a long time for something to happen).
examples: You think he’ll get a job? Ha! Don’t hold your breath.
I’ll finish building the fence as soon as I have time, but don’t hold your breath.

headword: Don’t let it go any further.
altForms: Don’t let it out of this room.

senses.definition: Don’t tell this secret to anyone else.
examples: This is a strict secret. Don’t let it go any further.
I’ll tell you what you what to know, but don’t let it go any further.

headword: Don’t let someone or something get you down.

senses.definition: Do not allow yourself to be overcome by someone or something.
examples: Don’t let their constant teasing get you down.
Don’t let Tom get you down. He’s not always unpleasant.

senses.definition: You are not very good at what you are doing, so don’t quit your regular job in hopes that you can support yourself doing this.
examples: I saw your comedy act at the nightclub. Don’t quit your day job!
So, you laid the bricks in this wall. Well, don’t quit your day job.

senses.definition: certain to fail, usually because of some obvious flaw.
examples: This project was doomed to failure from the very beginning.
The play is doomed to failure because there is not a good story line.

senses.definition: having to do with movement from one door to another or from one house to another.
senses.notes: See also from door to door.
examples: John is a door-to-door salesman.
We spent two weeks making a door-to-door survey.

senses.definition: by moving from one door to another or one house to another.
examples: Anne is selling books door-to-door.
We went door-to-door, collecting money.

headword: a dose of one’s own medicine

senses.definition: the same kind of treatment that one gives to other people.
examples: Sally never is very friendly. Someone is going to give her a dose of her own medicine someday.
He didn’t like getting a dose of his own medicine.

senses.definition: to reverse motion, moving toward someone or something rather than away from someone or something.
examples: The deer doubled back on the hunter.
The robber doubled back on the police, and they lost track of him.
He doubled back on his trail.

senses.definition: to betray someone by doing the opposite of what was promised; to betray a person by not doing what was promised.
examples: If you double-cross me again, I’ll kill you.
Tom is mad at Jane because she double-crossed him on the sale of his car.

senses.definition: to serve two purposes; to be useful for two different things.
senses.notes: Refers to a musician who can play a trumpet or trombone, etc., in addition to some other instrument.
examples: The English teacher also doubles in brass as the football coach.
The drummer doubles in brass as a violinist.

senses.definition: to share something with someone.
examples: We don’t have enough books. Tom, will you double up with Jane?
When we get more books, we won’t have to double up anymore.
We’ll share hotel rooms to save money. Tom and Bill will double up.

senses.definition: someone who will not easily believe something without strong proof or evidence.
examples: Mary won’t believe that I have a dog until she sees him. She’s such a doubting Thomas.
This school is full of doubting Thomases. They want to see Jimmy’s new bike with their own eyes.

senses.definition: sneaky, unfair, low-down, and nasty.
examples: The boys played a real down-and-dirty trick on the teacher.
A political campaign provides a lot of down-and-dirty speeches that only confuse the voters.

senses.definition: having no money or means of support.
examples: There are many young people down-and-out in Los Angeles just now.
John gambled away all his fortune and is now completely down-and-out.

senses.definition: shabby; poorly dressed.
senses.notes: Refers to shoes that are worn down at the heels.
examples: The hobo was really down-at-the-heels.
Tom’s house needs paint. It looks down-at-the-heels.

senses.definition: having a score that is lower, by the specified amount, than someone else’s score or the other team’s score.
examples: At halftime, the home team was down by 14 points.
Down by one run, the team scored two runs in the ninth inning and won the game.

senses.definition: finished for the time being.
senses.notes: From boxing, where a fallen fighter remains down [resting] until the last count, or even beyond.
examples: After the professor rebuked me in class, I knew I was down for the count.
I am down for the count, but I’ll try again tomorrow.

senses.definition: sad or depressed.
examples: I’ve been down in the dumps for the past few days.
Try to cheer Jane up. She’s down in the dumps for some reason.

senses.definition: sad-faced; depressed and unsmiling.
examples: Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth.
Bob has been down in the mouth since the car wreck.

senses.definition: without any money; unlucky.
examples: Can you lend me twenty dollars? I’ve been down on my luck lately.
The gambler had to get a job because he had been down on his luck and didn’t earn enough money to live on.

senses.definition: against someone or something; negative about someone or something.
examples: I’ve been down on red meat lately. It’s better to eat chicken or fish.
The teacher was down on Tom because he’s always talking in class.

senses.definition: to or in the southeastern United States.
senses.notes: See also back East; out West; up North.
examples: I used to live down South.
We are going down South for the winter.

senses.definition: lost forever; wasted.
examples: I just hate to see all that money go down the drain.
Well, there goes the whole project, right down the drain.

senses.definition: swallow (something).
senses.notes: [to] Informal or slang. Sometimes said when someone takes a drink of alcohol.
examples: Come on, Billy. Eat your dinner. Down the hatch!
John raised his glass of beer and said, “Down the hatch.”

senses.definition: a short distance away on this same street.
examples: Sally lives just down the street.
There is a drugstore down the street. It’s very convenient.

senses.definition: ruined; wasted.
examples: His political career went down the tubes after the scandal. He’s lost his job.
The business went down the tubes.

senses.definition: direct, frank, and honest.
examples: You can depend on Ann. She’s very down-to-earth.
It’s good that she’s down-to-earth and will give us a frank response.

senses.definition: practical; not theoretical; not fanciful.
examples: Her ideas for the boutique are always very down-to-earth.
The committee’s plans for the village are anything but down-to-earth.

senses.definition: considering all of the details.
examples: Jean planned the party very carefully, down to the last detail.
Mary wanted to be in charge of everything right down to the last detail.

senses.definition: at the very last minute; up to the very last instant.
senses.notes: Refers to a wire that marks the end of a horse race.
examples: I have to turn this in tomorrow, and I’ll be working down to the wire.
When we get down to the wire, we’ll know better what to do.

senses.definition: ill; sick at home.
senses.notes: Can be said about many diseases.
examples: Tom isn’t here. He’s down with a cold.
Sally is down with the flu.
The whole office has come down with something.

senses.definition: easy all the way.
examples: Don’t worry about your algebra course. It’s downhill all the way.
The mayor said that the job of mayor is easy— in fact, downhill all the way.

senses.definition: easy from this point on.
examples: The worst part is over. It’s downhill from here on.
The painful part of this procedure is over. It’s downhill from here on.

senses.definition: to act very slowly, often deliberately.
examples: The government is dragging its feet on this bill because it costs too much.
If the planning department had not dragged their feet, the building would have been built by now.

senses.definition: a burden to someone; a bore.
senses.notes: Slang. Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Mr. Franklin seems like a drag on Mrs. Franklin.
Yes, I’d expect him to be a drag.

headword: draw a bead on someone or something

senses.definition: to aim at someone or something; to pick out someone or something for special treatment.
examples: Ann wants a new car, and she has drawn a bead on a red convertible.
Jane wants to get married, and she has drawn a bead on Tom.

senses.definition: to get no response; to find nothing.
examples: I asked him about Tom’s financial problems, and I just drew a blank.
We looked in the files for an hour, but we drew a blank.

senses.definition: to fail to remember (something).
examples: I tried to remember her telephone number, but I could only draw a blank.
It was a very hard test with just one question to answer, and I drew a blank.

headword: draw a line between something and something else
altForms: draw the line between something and something else

senses.definition: to separate two things; to distinguish or differentiate between two things.
senses.notes: See also draw the line (at something).
examples: It’s necessary to draw a line between bumping into people and striking them.
It’s very hard to draw the line between slamming a door and just closing it loudly.

senses.definition: to make a wound that bleeds.
examples: The dog chased me and bit me hard, but it didn’t draw blood.
The boxer landed just one punch and drew blood immediately.

senses.definition: to anger or insult a person.
examples: Sally screamed out a terrible insult at Tom. Judging by the look on his face, she really drew blood.
Tom started yelling and cursing, trying to insult Sally. He wouldn’t be satisfied until he had drawn blood, too.

senses.definition: to appear interesting and get (someone’s) attention.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples below.
examples: This kind of event isn’t likely to draw a lot of interest.
What kind of thing will draw interest?

senses.definition: to earn interest while on deposit.
examples: Put your money in the bank so it will draw interest.
The cash value of some insurance policies also draws interest.

senses.definition: to choose from a group of things to determine who will do something.
senses.notes: Typically, to choose a straw from a bundle of straws. The person with the shortest straw is selected.
examples: We drew lots to decide who would wash the dishes.
The players drew straws to determine who would go first.

senses.definition: to coax someone to speak or answer; to bring someone into a conversation or other social interaction.
examples: Jane is usually very shy with older men, but Tom really drew her out last evening.
John drew out Mr. Smith on the question of tax increases.

senses.definition: to make something longer in length or time.
examples: Jane drew out the conversation for more than twenty minutes.
Bill drew the taffy candy out into a long string.

headword: draw (someone’s) fire (away from someone or something)

senses.definition: to make oneself a target in order to protect someone or something.
examples: The mother bird drew fire away from her chicks.
The hen drew the hunter’s fire away from her nest.
Birds draw fire by flapping their wings to get attention.
The president drew fire away from Congress by proposing a compromise.

senses.definition: to make something end.
examples: It is now time to draw this evening to a close.
What a lovely vacation. It’s a shame that we must draw it to a close.

senses.definition: to put something into writing; to prepare a written document; to put plans on paper.
senses.notes: Used especially with legal documents prepared by a lawyer.
examples: You should draw a will up as soon as you can.
I went to see my lawyer this morning about drawing up a will.
The architect is drawing up plans for the new city hall.

senses.definition: to set a limit at something; to decide when a limit has been reached.
senses.notes: See also hold the line (at someone or something).
examples: You can make as much noise as you want, but I draw the line at fighting.
It’s hard to keep young people under control, but you have to draw the line somewhere.

senses.definition: to end; to come to an end.
examples: This evening is drawing to a close.
It’s a shame that our vacation is drawing to a close.

senses.definition: dealt with very severely.
senses.notes: Refers to a practice of torturing someone guilty of treason, usually a male, by disemboweling and dividing the body into four parts.
examples: Todd was practically drawn and quartered for losing the Wilson contract.
You were much too harsh with Jean. No matter what she did, she didn’t need to be drawn and quartered for it!

senses.definition: a wish or a dream that has become real.
examples: Going to Hawaii is like a dream come true.
Having you for a friend is a dream come true.

senses.definition: What you are expecting or wanting to happen is nothing but fantasy, so enjoy yourself and create as many fantasies as you want.
examples: You want to get promoted to general manager? Dream on.
You, an opera singer? Dream on.

senses.definition: to bawl someone out; to give someone a good scolding.
examples: The sergeant dressed the soldier down severely.
I know they’ll dress me down when I get home.

senses.definition: dressed in fancy or stylish clothes.
examples: Wow, look at Sally! She’s really dressed to kill.
A person doesn’t go to church dressed to kill.

senses.definition: dressed very well.
senses.notes: What nines means is not known.
examples: Tom showed up at the dance dressed to the nines.
Sally is even dressed to the nines at the office.

senses.definition: in small irregular quantities.
examples: The checks for the charity are coming in in dribs and drabs.
The members of the orchestra arrived by dribs and drabs.
All her fortune was spent in dribs and drabs on silly things—like clothes and fine wines.

senses.definition: to drink too much alcohol; to drink alcohol continually.
examples: Mr. Franklin drinks to excess.
Some people drink to excess only at parties.

senses.definition: to work hard to negotiate prices or agreements in one’s own favor.
examples: I saved $200 by driving a hard bargain when I bought my new car.
All right, sir, you drive a hard bargain. I’ll sell you this car for $12,450.
You drive a hard bargain, Jane, but I’ll sign the contract.

senses.definition: to be making a point; to be approaching the making of a point.
examples: I do not understand what you are telling me. What are you driving at?
She was driving at how important it is to get an education.

senses.definition: to make someone insane.
examples: He’s so strange that he actually drove his wife crazy.
Doctor, there are little green people following me around trying to drive me mad.

senses.definition: to annoy or irritate someone.
examples: This itch is driving me crazy.
All these telephone calls are driving me mad.

senses.definition: to make someone insane.
examples: Mr. Franklin drove his wife up the wall.
All my problems will drive me up the wall someday.

senses.definition: to annoy or irritate someone.
examples: Stop whistling that tune. You’re driving me up the wall.
All his talk about moving to California nearly drove me up the wall.

senses.definition: to make something clearly understood.
examples: Why do I always have to shout at you to drive something home?
Sometimes you have to be forceful to drive home a point.

senses.definition: a person or a thing that motivates or directs someone or something.
examples: Money is the driving force behind most businesses.
Ambition is the driving force behind Tom.
Love can also be a driving force.

senses.definition: to announce shocking or startling news.
senses.notes: Also literal for bomb and brick. Informal or slang.
examples: They really dropped a bombshell when they announced that the mayor had cancer.
Friday is a good day to drop a bomb like that. It gives the business world the weekend to recover.
They must speak very carefully when they explode a bombshell like that.
They really dropped a brick when they told the cause of her illness.

senses.definition: to come and visit at some future time.
examples: Nice to see you, Mary. You and Bob must drop around sometime.
Please do drop around when you’re out driving.
We’d love to have you drop by.

senses.definition: to die suddenly.
examples: I understand that Tom Anderson dropped dead at his desk yesterday.
No one knows why Uncle Bob suddenly dropped dead.

senses.definition: Go away and stop bothering me.
examples: If you think I’m going to put up with your rudeness all afternoon, you can just drop dead!
Drop dead! I’m not your slave!

senses.definition: to stop doing whatever one is doing.
examples: Drop everything and go outside. The house is on fire.
Do you expect me to drop everything and come and pick you up at school?

senses.definition: to stop or collapse from exhaustion; to die suddenly.
examples: If I keep working this way, I’ll drop in my tracks.
Uncle Bob was working in the garden and dropped in his tracks. We are all sorry that he’s dead.

senses.definition: to pay someone a casual visit, perhaps a surprise visit.
examples: I hate to drop in on people when they aren’t expecting me.
You’re welcome to drop in at any time.
We won’t stay a minute. We just dropped in to say hello.

senses.definition: just a little bit; not enough of something to make a difference.
examples: But one dollar isn’t enough! That’s just a drop in the ocean.
At this point your help is nothing more than a drop in the ocean. I need far more help than twenty people could give.
I won’t accept your offer. It’s just a drop in the bucket.

senses.definition: to mention the names of important or famous people as if they were personal friends.
examples: Mary always tries to impress people by dropping the names of well-known film stars.
Bill’s such a snob. Leave it to him to drop the names of all the local gentry.

senses.definition: to go to sleep without difficulty; to fall asleep.
examples: I sat in the warm room for five minutes, and then I dropped off to sleep.
After I’ve eaten dinner, I can drop off with no trouble at all.

senses.definition: to stop being a member of something; to stop attending or participating in something.
examples: I’m working part time so that I won’t have to drop out of college.
I don’t want to drop out at this time.

senses.definition: to stop being friends with someone, especially with one’s boyfriend or girlfriend.
examples: Bob finally dropped Jane. I don’t know what he saw in her.
I’m surprised that she didn’t drop him first.

senses.definition: to write a letter or a note to someone.
senses.notes: Line refers to lines of writing.
examples: I dropped Aunt Jane a line last Thanksgiving.
She usually drops me a few lines around the first of the year.

senses.definition: to mention the name of an important or famous person as if the person were a personal friend.
examples: Mary always tries to impress people by dropping a well-known movie star’s name.
Joan is such a snob. Leave it to her to drop some social leader’s name.

senses.definition: to make a blunder; to fail in some way.
senses.notes: Refers to dropping the ball in a ball game.
examples: Everything was going fine in the election until my campaign manager dropped the ball.
You can’t trust John to do the job right. He’s always dropping the ball.

senses.definition: to do the deed that completes something; to do the expected remaining part of something.
senses.notes: Refers to the removal of shoes at bedtime. One shoe is dropped, and then the process is completed when the second shoe drops.
examples: Mr. Franklin has left his wife. Soon he’ll drop the other shoe and divorce her.
Tommy has just failed three classes in school. We expect him to drop the other shoe and quit altogether any day now.

senses.definition: to stop talking about whatever is being talked about.
examples: This is a disgusting conversation. Let’s drop the subject.
He had heard enough about my operation, so I just dropped the subject.

senses.definition: to try to forget one’s problems by drinking a lot of alcohol.
examples: Bill is in the bar, drowning his troubles.
Jane is at home, drowning her sorrows.

senses.definition: to make so much noise that someone or something cannot be heard.
examples: I can’t hear what you said. The radio drowned you out.
We couldn’t hear all the concert because the airplanes drowned out the quiet parts.

senses.definition: on the market in great abundance; a glut on the market.
examples: Right now, small computers are a drug on the market.
Ten years ago, small transistor radios were a drug on the market.

senses.definition: to stimulate people to buy what you are selling.
examples: I need to do something to drum some business up.
A little bit of advertising would drum up some business.

senses.definition: to expel or send someone away from something, especially in a formal or public fashion.
senses.notes: From the military use of drums on such occasions.
examples: The officer was drummed out of the regiment for misconduct.
I heard that he was drummed out of the country club for cheating on his golf score.

senses.definition: to make someone learn something through persistent repetition.
examples: Yes, I know that. They drummed it into me as a child.
Now I’m drumming it into my own children.
I will drum it into their heads day and night.

senses.definition: a criminal charge for public drunkenness accompanied by bad or offensive behavior.
examples: The judge fined Max for being drunk and disorderly.
In addition to being convicted for driving while intoxicated, Max was found guilty of being drunk and disorderly.

senses.definition: an attempt; a rehearsal.
examples: We had better have a dry run for the official ceremony tomorrow.
The children will need a dry run before their procession in the pageant.

senses.definition: to help a drunk person get sober.
examples: We had to call the doctor to help dry Mr. Franklin out.
It takes time to dry out someone who has been drinking for a week.

senses.definition: to become silent; to stop talking.
examples: The young lecturer was so nervous that he forgot what he was going to say and dried up.
Actors have a fear of drying up on stage.
Oh, dry up! I’m sick of listening to you.

senses.definition: to dodge something, such as an issue or a difficult question, and attempt to shield oneself against similar issues or questions.
senses.notes: Refers to ducking down and taking cover to protect oneself.
examples: The candidate’s first reaction to the question was to duck and cover.
The debaters were ducking and covering throughout the evening.

senses.definition: dodging something, such as an issue or a difficult question, and attempting to shield oneself against similar issues or questions.
examples: These politicians are experts at duck-and-cover.
When in doubt, turn to duck-and-cover.

senses.definition: an auction or sale that starts off with a high asking price that is then reduced until a buyer is found.
examples: Dutch auctions are rare—most auctioneers start with a lower price than they hope to obtain.
My real estate agent advised me to ask a reasonable price for my house rather than get involved with a Dutch auction.

senses.definition: unusual or artificial courage arising from the influence of alcohol.
examples: It was Dutch courage that made the football fan attack the policeman.
It will take a bit of Dutch courage to make an after-dinner speech.

senses.definition: a social occasion where one pays for oneself.
examples: “It’s nice of you to ask me out to dinner,” she said, “but could we make it a Dutch treat?”
The office outing is always a Dutch treat.

senses.definition: a man who gives frank and direct advice to someone in the manner of a parent or relative.
examples: I would not have to lecture you like a Dutch uncle if you were not so extravagant.
He acts more like a Dutch uncle than a husband. He’s forever telling her what to do in public.

senses.definition: forced by a sense of duty and honor to do something.
examples: Good evening, madam. I’m duty bound to inform you that we have arrested your husband.
No one made me say that. I was duty bound.

senses.definition: permanent; indelible; stubborn.
examples: My uncle was a dyed-in-the-wool farmer. He wouldn’t change for anything.
Sally is a dyed-in-the-wool socialist.

senses.definition: very anxious to do something.
examples: I’m just dying to go sailing in your new boat.
After a long hot day like this one, I’m just dying for a cool drink of water.

senses.definition: someone who is very enthusiastic; someone who works very hard.
examples: New volunteers are always eager beavers.
The young assistant gets to work very early. She’s a real eager beaver.

senses.definition: careful attention; an intently watchful eye.
senses.notes: From the sharp eyesight of the eagle.
examples: The students wrote their essays under the eagle eye of the headmaster.
The umpire kept his eagle eye on the tennis match.

senses.definition: someone who gets up or arrives early or starts something very promptly, especially someone who gains an advantage of some kind by so doing.
senses.notes: See also The early bird gets the worm.
examples: The members of the Smith family are all early birds. They caught the first bus to town.
I was an early bird and got the best selection of flowers.

headword: The early bird gets the worm.

senses.definition: The early person will get the reward or benefit.
examples: Don’t be late again! Don’t you know that the early bird gets the worm?
I’ll be there before the sun is up. After all, the early bird gets the worm.

headword: Early to bed, early to rise(, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise).

senses.definition: Going to bed early and getting up early is good for you.
senses.notes: Proverb. Sometimes said to explain why a person is going to bed early. The last part of the saying is sometimes left out.
examples: Tom left the party at ten o’clock, saying, “Early to bed, early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.”
I always get up at dawn. After all, early to bed, early to rise.

senses.definition: to reduce the urgency with which one deals with someone or something; to put less pressure on someone or something.
examples: Ease off on John. He has been yelled at enough today.
Yes, please ease off. I can’t stand any more.
Tell them to ease up on the horses. They are getting tired.
Tell them to ease up now! They are making the horses work too hard.

senses.definition: a phrase used when accepting the loss of something that required only a small amount of effort to get in the first place.
examples: Ann found twenty dollars in the morning and spent it foolishly at noon. “Easy come, easy go,” she said.
John spends his money as fast as he can earn it. With John it’s easy come, easy go.

senses.definition: Act with care.
examples: Be careful with that glass vase. Easy does it!
Now, now, Tom. Don’t get angry. Easy does it.

senses.definition: easily found; easily purchased; readily available.
examples: Please be careful with that phonograph record. It was not easy to come by.
A good dictionary is very easy to come by.

senses.definition: to eat a meal or a snack and then leave.
examples: Well, I hate to eat and run but I have to take care of some errands.
I don’t invite John to dinner anymore because he always has some excuse to eat and run.

headword: eat away at someone or something

senses.definition: to remove parts, bit by bit.
examples: John’s disease was eating away at him.
The acid in the rain slowly ate away at the stone wall.

senses.definition: to bother or worry someone.
examples: Her failure to pass the exam was eating away at her.
Fear of appearing in court was eating away at Tom.

senses.definition: to eat good or expensive food.
senses.notes: Folksy. Compare this with live high on the hog. Note the so in the second example. See also live high off the hog.
examples: The Smith family has been eating pretty high on the hog since they had a good corn harvest.
John would have more money to spend on clothing if he didn’t eat so high on the hog.

senses.definition: to act very humbly when one is shown to be wrong.
examples: I think I’m right, but if I’m wrong, I’ll eat humble pie.
You think you’re so smart. I hope you have to eat humble pie.

senses.definition: to accept insults and humiliation.
examples: John, stand up for your rights. You don’t have to eat humble pie all the time.
Beth seems quite happy to eat humble pie. She should stand up for her rights.

senses.definition: to eat only small amounts of food; to peck at one’s food.
examples: Jane is very slim because she eats like a bird.
Bill is trying to lose weight by eating like a bird.

senses.definition: to eat large amounts of food.
examples: No wonder he’s so fat. He eats like a horse.
John works like a horse and eats like a horse, so he never gets fat.

senses.definition: a phrase telling the kind of thing that one would do if a very unlikely event really happens.
senses.notes: Informal. Always used with an if-clause.
examples: If we get there on time, I’ll eat my hat.
I’ll eat my hat if you get a raise.
He said he’d eat his hat if she got elected.

senses.definition: to be very sad (about someone or something).
examples: Bill spent a lot of time eating his heart out after his divorce.
Sally ate her heart out when she had to sell her house.

senses.definition: to be envious (of someone or something).
examples: Do you like my new watch? Well, eat your heart out. It was the last one in the store.
Don’t eat your heart out about my new car. Go get one of your own.

senses.definition: to have to take back one’s statements; to confess that one’s predictions were wrong.
examples: You shouldn’t say that to me. I’ll make you eat your words.
John was wrong about the election and had to eat his words.

senses.definition: to do what someone else wants; to obey someone eagerly.
examples: Just wait! I’ll have everyone eating out of my hands. They’ll do whatever I ask.
The president has Congress eating out of his hands.
A lot of people are eating out of his hands.

headword: eat someone out of house and home

senses.definition: to eat a lot of food (in someone’s home); to eat all the food in the house.
examples: Billy has a huge appetite. He almost eats us out of house and home.
When the kids come home from college, they always eat us out of house and home.

senses.definition: to enjoy, absorb, or appreciate.
examples: The audience loved the comedian. They ate his act up and demanded more.
The children ate up Grandfather’s stories. They listened to him for hours.

senses.definition: to decrease and then increase, as with tides; a decrease followed by an increase, as with tides.
examples: The fortunes of the major political parties tend to ebb and flow over time.
The ebb and flow of democracy through history is a fascinating subject.

senses.definition: to remove a person from a job, office, or position, usually by beating the person in competition.
examples: The vice president edged the president out during the last election.
Tom edged out Bob as the new cook at the restaurant.

senses.definition: to encourage, urge, or dare someone to continue doing something, usually something unwise.
examples: John wouldn’t have done the dangerous experiment if his brother hadn’t egged him on.
The two boys kept throwing stones because the other children were egging them on.

senses.definition: either too much (of something) or not enough (of something).
examples: This month is very dry, and last month it rained almost every day. Our weather is either feast or famine.
Sometimes we are busy, and sometimes we have nothing to do. It’s feast or famine.

senses.definition: to force or pressure someone out of something, such as an office, post, or status.
senses.notes: Also literal when attempting to use one’s elbows to move the person beside oneself away.
examples: The old head of the company was elbowed out of office by a young vice president.
They tried to elbow me out, but I held on to what was mine.

senses.definition: a decision made at the last possible minute.
senses.notes: See also at the eleventh hour.
examples: Eleventh-hour decisions are seldom satisfactory.
The president’s eleventh-hour decision was made in a great hurry, but it turned out to be correct.

senses.definition: for its own sake; toward its own ends; toward no purpose but its own.
examples: For Bob, art is an end in itself. He doesn’t hope to make any money from it.
Learning is an end in itself. Knowledge does not have to have a practical application.

senses.definition: the end; the end of the whole process; death.
senses.notes: Line originally referred to railroad tracks.
examples: Our house is at the end of the road.
We rode the train to the end of the line.
When we reach the end of the road on this project, we’ll get paid.
You’ve come to the end of the line. I’ll not lend you another penny.
When I reach the end of the road, I wish to be buried in a quiet place, near some trees.

senses.definition: to conclude something by doing something.
senses.notes: Compare this with end up doing something.
examples: We ended up by going back to my house.
They danced until midnight and ended up by having pizza in the front room.

senses.definition: to have to do something that one had not planned to do.
senses.notes: Compare this with end up by doing something.
examples: We ended up going back to my house after all.
Todd wound up inviting everyone to his house, even though he planned to spend the evening at home alone.

senses.definition: to finish at a certain place.
examples: If you don’t get straightened out, you’ll end up in jail.
I fell and hurt myself, and I wound up in the hospital.

senses.definition: to talk only about minor matters rather than important or personal matters.
examples: All the people at the party were engaging in small talk.
They chatted about the weather and otherwise engaged in small talk.

senses.definition: a polite phrase said by a waiter or waitress when delivering food to the table.
examples: There you go. Enjoy your meal.
Do you have the medium steak? Enjoy your meal.

senses.definition: That is enough, and there should be no more.
examples: Stop asking for money! Enough is enough!
I’ve heard all the complaining from you that I can take. Stop! Enough is enough!

senses.definition: a supply adequate to serve everyone.
examples: Don’t take too much. There’s not enough to go around.
I cooked some extra potatoes, so there should be enough to go around.

senses.definition: to come to one’s mind; [for an idea or memory] to come into one’s consciousness.
examples: Leave you behind? The thought never even entered my mind.
A very interesting idea just entered my mind. What if I ran for Congress?

senses.definition: able to handle or deal with someone or something.
examples: I’m afraid that I’m not equal to Mrs. Smith’s problem right now. Please ask her to come back later.
That’s a very difficult task, but I’m sure Bill is equal to it.

senses.definition: to go unnoticed; to be overlooked.
senses.notes: Usually a way to point out that someone has failed to see or respond to something.
examples: I suppose my earlier request escaped your notice, so I’m writing again.
I’m sorry. Your letter escaped my notice.

headword: even in the best of times

senses.definition: even when things are good; even when things are going well.
examples: It is hard to get high-quality leather even in the best of times.
John had difficulty getting a loan even in the best of times because of his poor credit record.

senses.definition: even (with someone or something).
senses.notes: Informal or slang. Preceded by be or seem.
examples: Bill hit Tom; then Tom hit Bill. Now they are even steven.
Mary paid Ann the $100 she owed her. Ann said, “Good, we are even steven.”

senses.definition: now and then; occasionally.
examples: Ever and anon the princess would pay a visit to the sorcerer in the small walled garden directly behind the castle.
We eat swan ever and anon, but not when we can get wild boar.

headword: Every cloud has a silver lining.

senses.definition: There is something good in every bad thing.
examples: Jane was upset when she saw that all her flowers had died from the frost. But when she saw that the weeds had died too, she said, “Every cloud has a silver lining.”
Sally had a sore throat and had to stay home from school. When she learned she missed a math test, she said, “Every cloud has a silver lining.”

senses.definition: Everyone will get a chance.
examples: Don’t worry, you’ll get chosen for the team. Every dog has its day.
You may become famous someday. Every dog has his day.

senses.definition: completely; in every way.
examples: Mary is every inch the schoolteacher.
Her father is every inch a gentleman.

senses.definition: every one; every single one.
examples: You must eat all your peas! Every last one!
Each of you—every last one—has to take some medicine.

senses.definition: every person.
examples: I expect every living soul to be there and be there on time.
This is the kind of problem that affects every living soul.

senses.definition: time is very important.
examples: Doctor, please try to get here quickly. Every minute counts.
When you take a test, you must work rapidly because every minute counts.
When you’re trying to meet a deadline, every moment counts.

senses.definition: every small, out-of-the-way place where something can be hidden.
examples: We looked for the tickets in every nook and cranny. They were lost. There was no doubt.
The decorator had placed flowers in every nook and cranny.

senses.definition: occasionally; infrequently.
examples: We eat lamb every now and then.
We eat pork now and then.
I read a novel every now and again.
We don’t go to the movies except maybe every now and then.
I drink coffee every once in a while.
I drink tea once in a while.

senses.definition: every second person or thing; alternating.
examples: The magician turned every other card over.
Every other table had an ashtray on it.

senses.definition: frequently; at every turn; with annoying frequency.
examples: Somebody asks me for money every time I turn around.
Something goes wrong with Bill’s car every time he turns around.

senses.definition: everyone, without discrimination; ordinary people.
examples: The golf club is very exclusive. They don’t let any Tom, Dick, and Harry join.
Mary’s sending out very few invitations. She doesn’t want every Tom, Dick, and Harry turning up.

senses.definition: in all directions.
examples: The children were all running every which way.
The wind scattered the leaves every which way.

senses.definition: almost everything one can think of.
examples: When Sally went off to college, she took everything but the kitchen sink.
John orders everything but the kitchen sink when he goes out to dinner, especially if someone else is paying for it.

senses.definition: almost everything one can think of.
examples: For dinner we had everything from soup to nuts.
In college I studied everything from soup to nuts.
She mentioned everything from A to Z.

senses.definition: everything that is in the range of human powers.
examples: The rescuers did everything humanly possible to find the lost campers.
The doctor tried everything humanly possible to save the patient.

senses.definition: Everything is really just excellent.
examples: Life is wonderful. Everything is coming up roses.
Q: How are things going? A: Everything’s coming up roses.

headword: the exception that proves the rule

senses.definition: a saying identifying an exception to a rule or guideline as emphasizing the existence of the rule.
examples: Sixth-graders do not have to wear school uniforms, but they’re the exception that proves the rule.
The youngest dog is allowed in the house. He’s the exception that proves the rule.

headword: exchange more than some number of words with someone

senses.definition: to say hardly anything to someone.
examples: I know Tom was there, but I am sure that I didn’t exchange more than three words with him before he left.
We hardly exchanged more than two words the whole evening.
Sally and Liz didn’t have enough time to exchange more than five words.

senses.definition: to make polite apologies or explanations before leaving a place.
examples: Please excuse me. I must leave.
I will have to excuse myself from this meeting since I have a vested interest in the outcome.

senses.definition: to forgive someone.
senses.notes: Usually with me. Said when interrupting or when some other minor offense has been committed. There are many mannerly uses of this expression.
examples: John came in late and said, “Excuse me, please.”
John said “excuse me” when he interrupted our conversation.
When John made a strange noise at the table, he said quietly, “Excuse me.”
John suddenly left the room saying, “Excuse me. I’ll be right back.”

senses.definition: to permit someone to leave; to permit someone to remain away from an event.
examples: The coach excused John from practice yesterday.
The teacher excused John, and he ran quickly from the room.

senses.definition: pregnant.
examples: Tommy’s mother is expecting a child.
Oh, I didn’t know she was expecting.

senses.definition: to give a good explanation for something; to explain something so that it seems less important; to make excuses for something.
examples: This is a very serious matter, and you cannot just explain it away.
John couldn’t explain away his low grades.

senses.definition: to allow a release or expression of anger, such as through angry words.
examples: Don’t keep your emotions inside of you. You have to learn to express your anger.
Bob expresses his anger by yelling at people.

senses.definition: to allow someone to purchase something on credit.
examples: I’m sorry, Mr. Smith, but because of your poor record of payment, we are no longer able to extend credit to you.
Look at this letter, Jane. The store won’t extend credit anymore.
We are unable to extend that company credit any longer.

senses.definition: to express sympathy to someone.
senses.notes: A very polite and formal way to tell someone that you are sorry about a misfortune.
examples: Please permit me to extend my sympathy to you and your children. I’m very sorry to hear of the death of your husband.
Let’s extend our sympathy to Bill Jones, who is in the hospital with a broken leg. We should send him some flowers.

senses.definition: special circumstances that account for an irregular or improper way of doing something.
examples: Mary was permitted to arrive late because of extenuating circumstances.
Due to extenuating circumstances, the class will not meet today.

senses.definition: the center of a problem; the center of a commotion or a disturbance.
examples: Tom, finding himself at the eye of the storm, tried to blame someone else for the problem.
The manager’s office was known as the eye of the storm since all the major problems ended up there.

senses.definition: person to person; face to face.
examples: The discussions will have to be eyeball-to-eyeball to be effective.
Telephone conversations are a waste of time. We need to talk eyeball-to-eyeball.

senses.definition: to overcome someone by being bold; to disconcert someone by displaying great confidence.
examples: The teacher faced the angry student down without saying anything.
The mayor couldn’t face down the entire city council.

senses.definition: to receive punishment; to accept the unpleasant results of one’s actions.
examples: Mary broke a dining-room window and had to face the music when her father got home.
After failing a math test, Tom had to go home and face the music.

senses.definition: in person; in the same location.
senses.notes: Said only of people. An adverb.
examples: Let’s talk about this face-to-face. I don’t like talking over the telephone.
Many people prefer to talk face-to-face.

senses.definition: facing one another; in the same location.
examples: I prefer to have a face-to-face meeting.
They work better on a face-to-face basis.

senses.definition: the facts of sex and reproduction, especially human reproduction.
senses.notes: See also birds and the bees.
examples: My parents told me the facts of life when I was nine years old.
Bill learned the facts of life from his classmates.

senses.definition: the truth about the unpleasant ways that the world works.
examples: Mary really learned the facts of life when she got her first job.
Tom couldn’t accept the facts of life in business, so he quit.

senses.definition: fair and unbiased.
senses.notes: Usually referring to some aspect of the legal system, such as a jury, a hearing, or a judge.
examples: Gary felt that he had not received a fair and impartial hearing.
We demand that all of our judges be fair and impartial in every instance.

senses.definition: completely fair(ly).
examples: She won the game fair and square.
The division of the money should be fair and square.

senses.definition: someone or something that it is quite permissible to attack.
examples: I don’t like seeing articles exposing people’s private lives, but politicians are fair game.
Journalists always regard movie stars as fair game.

senses.definition: a favored person.
examples: The teacher’s fair-haired boy always does well on tests.
The supervisor’s son was the fair-haired boy on the construction site.

senses.definition: only fair or okay; a little better than acceptable.
examples: I don’t feel sick, just fair to middling.
The play wasn’t really good. It was just fair to middling.

senses.definition: someone who is your friend only when things are going well for you.
senses.notes: This person will desert you when things go badly for you. Compare this with A friend in need is a friend indeed.
examples: Bill wouldn’t help me with my homework. He’s just a fair-weather friend.
A fair-weather friend isn’t much help in an emergency.

headword: fall afoul of someone or something
altForms: run afoul of someone or something

senses.definition: to get into a situation where one is opposed to someone or something; to get into trouble with someone or something.
examples: Dan fell afoul of the law at an early age.
I hope that you will avoid falling afoul of the district manager. She can be a formidable enemy.
I hope I don’t run afoul of your sister. She doesn’t like me.

senses.definition: to behave awkwardly and eagerly when doing something.
senses.notes: See also fall over backwards (to do something).
examples: Tom fell all over himself trying to make Jane feel at home.
I fall over myself when I’m doing something that makes me nervous.

senses.definition: to give a lot of attention, affection, or praise to someone.
examples: My aunt falls all over me whenever she comes to visit.
I hate for someone to fall all over me. It embarrasses me.

senses.definition: to break into pieces; to fall apart; [for material that is sewn together] to separate at the seams.
senses.notes: [for something] Literal for cloth, otherwise figurative. See also come apart at the seams.
examples: My new jacket fell apart at the seams.
This old car is about ready to fall apart at the seams.

senses.definition: to go to sleep.
examples: The baby cried and cried and finally fell asleep.
Tom fell asleep in class yesterday.

headword: fall back on someone or something

senses.definition: to turn to someone or something for help.
examples: Bill fell back on his brother for help.
John ran out of ink and had to fall back on his pencil.

senses.definition: to come somewhere between two possibilities and so fail to meet the requirements of either.
examples: The material is not suitable for an academic book or for a popular one. It falls between two stools.
He tries to be both teacher and friend, but falls between two stools.

senses.definition: to give up and quit before the end (of something).
senses.notes: Refers to being too exhausted to finish a footrace.
examples: John fell by the wayside and didn’t finish college.
Many people start out to train for a career in medicine, but some of them drop by the wayside.
All of her projects fall by the wayside when she tires of them.

senses.definition: to fail to do something properly; to fail to do one’s job adequately.
senses.notes: Also literal referring to an accident while one is working.
examples: The team kept losing because the coach was falling down on the job.
Tom was fired because he fell down on the job.

senses.definition: to be completely unsuccessful.
examples: I fell flat on my face when I tried to give my speech.
The play fell flat on its face.
My jokes fall flat most of the time.

senses.definition: to cease to be held in favor, especially because of some wrong or foolish action.
examples: He was the teacher’s pet until he fell from grace by failing the history test.
Mary was the favorite grandchild until she fell from grace by running away from home.

senses.definition: to fall down, perhaps turning over or rolling.
examples: Fred tripped on the rug and fell head over heels into the center of the room.
Slow down or you will fall down—head over heels.

headword: fall head over heels in love (with someone)

senses.definition: to fall deeply in love with someone, perhaps suddenly.
examples: Roger fell head over heels in love with Maggie, and they were married within the month.
Very few people actually fall head over heels in love with each other.
She fell head over heels in love and thought she was dreaming.

senses.definition: to become ill.
examples: Tom fell ill just before he was to perform.
We both fell ill after eating the baked fish.

senses.definition: to line up in a row, standing shoulder to shoulder.
senses.notes: Also literal, meaning “to collapse.” Usually refers to people in scouting or the military. Compare this with fall in(to) line and fall out.
examples: The Boy Scouts were told to fall in behind the scoutmaster.
The soldiers fell in quickly.

senses.definition: to develop the emotion of love for someone.
examples: Tom fell in love with Mary, but she only wanted to be friends.
John is too young to really fall in love.

senses.definition: to become caught in someone’s scheme; to be deceived into doing or thinking something.
examples: We fell into a trap by asking for an explanation.
I fell into his trap when I agreed to drive him home.
We fell into the trap of thinking he was honest.

senses.definition: to line up with each person (except the first person) standing behind someone.
examples: The teacher told the students to fall in line for lunch.
Hungry students fall into line very quickly.

senses.definition: to conform; to fall in(to) place.
examples: All the parts of the problem finally fell into line.
Bill’s behavior began to fall in line.

senses.definition: to fit together; to become organized.
examples: After we heard the whole story, things began to fall in place.
When you get older, the different parts of your life begin to fall into place.

headword: fall in with someone or something

senses.definition: to meet someone by accident; to join with someone.
examples: John has fallen in with a strange group of people.
We fell in with some people from our hometown when we went on vacation.

senses.definition: to agree with someone or something.
examples: Bill was not able to fall in with our ideas about painting the house red.
Bob fell in with Mary’s plans to move to Texas.

senses.definition: to decline or diminish.
examples: Business falls off during the summer months.
My interest in school fell off when I became twenty.

senses.definition: to be ignored by the persons they were intended for.
examples: Her pleas for mercy fell on deaf ears.
All of Sally’s good advice fell on deaf ears. Walter had made up his own mind.

senses.definition: to happen; to result.
examples: As things fell out, we had a wonderful trip.
What fell out of our discussion was a decision to continue.

senses.definition: to leave one’s place in a formation when dismissed.
senses.notes: Usually in scouting or the military. The opposite of fall in.
examples: The scouts fell out and ran to the campfire.
All the soldiers fell out and talked among themselves.

senses.definition: to quarrel or disagree about something.
examples: Bill fell out with Sally over the question of buying a new car.
Bill fell out with John about who would sleep on the bottom bunk.
They are always arguing. They fall out about once a week.

senses.definition: to do everything possible to please someone.
senses.notes: Informal. See also fall (all) over oneself.
examples: The taxi driver fell over backwards to be helpful.
The teacher bent over backwards to help the students understand.
The principal said that it was not necessary to bend over backwards.
You don’t have to lean over backwards to get me to help. Just ask.

senses.definition: to lack something; to lack enough of something.
examples: We fell short of money at the end of the month.
When baking a cake, the cook fell short of eggs and had to go to the store for more.

senses.definition: to fail to achieve a goal.
examples: We fell short of our goal of collecting a thousand dollars.
Ann ran a fast race, but fell short of the record.

senses.definition: not to happen; to come to nothing.
examples: Our plans fell through, and we won’t be going to Texas after all.
The party fell through at the last minute.

senses.definition: to begin (to do something).
examples: The hungry children took their knives and forks and fell to.
The carpenter unpacked his saw and hammer and fell to.
The boys wanted to fight, so the coach put boxing gloves on them and told them to fall to.
John fell to and cleaned up his room after he got yelled at.

headword: fall to someone to do something

senses.definition: to become the responsibility of someone.
examples: It always falls to me to apologize first.
Why does it fall to me to answer the telephone every time it rings?

senses.definition: to attack someone or something.
examples: The cat fell upon the mouse and killed it.
The children fell on the birthday cake and ate it all.

senses.definition: [for a task] to become the duty of someone.
examples: The task of telling Mother about the broken vase fell upon Jane.
The job of cleaning up the spill fell upon Tom.

senses.definition: having a good knowledge of someone or something.
examples: Are you familiar with changing a flat tire?
I’m can’t speak German fluently, but I’m somewhat familiar with the language.

senses.definition: Knowing a person closely for a long time leads to bad feelings.
examples: Bill and his brothers are always fighting. As they say: “Familiarity breeds contempt.”
Mary and John were good friends for many years. Finally they got into a big argument and became enemies. That just shows that familiarity breeds contempt.

senses.definition: a follower of someone; someone who idolized someone.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: My mother is still a fan of the Beatles.
I’m a great fan of the mayor of the town.

senses.definition: to make something more intense; to make a situation worse.
examples: The riot fanned the flames of racial hatred even more.
The hostility in the school is bad enough without anyone fanning the flames.

senses.definition: unquestionably the best.
examples: This soap is far and away the best.
Sally is good, but Ann is far and away the best.

senses.definition: an appearance on one’s face of having one’s mind in another place.
examples: Dave had a far-away look in his eyes, so I touched him to get his attention.
Katherine’s face had a far-off look indicating that she was daydreaming.

headword: far be it from me to do something

senses.definition: it is not really my place to do something.
senses.notes: Always with but, as in the examples below.
examples: Far be it from me to tell you what to do, but I think you should buy the book.
Far be it from me to attempt to advise you, but you’re making a big mistake.

senses.definition: a thing that is very different from something else.
examples: What you did was a far cry from what you said you were going to do.
The song they played was a far cry from what I call music.

senses.definition: not it at all; not at all.
examples: Do I think you need a new car? Far from it. The old one is fine.
BILL: Does this hat look strange? TOM: Far from it. It looks good.

senses.definition: late into the night; late.
examples: She sat up and read far into the night.
The party went on far into the night.

senses.definition: to send someone (somewhere) for care or development.
examples: When my mother died, they farmed me out to my aunt and uncle.
The team manager farmed out the baseball player to the minor leagues until he improved.

senses.definition: to send something (elsewhere) to be dealt with.
examples: Bill farmed his chores out to his brothers and sisters and went to a movie.
I farmed out various parts of the work to different people.

senses.definition: very rapidly and with unrestrained energy.
examples: Her work in the kitchen was fast and furious, and it looked lovely when she finished.
Everything was going so fast and furious at the store during the Christmas rush that we never had time to eat lunch.

senses.definition: at an increasing rate of speed; fast and then even faster.
examples: The car went faster and faster and I was afraid we would crash.
The cost of education goes up faster and faster every year.

senses.definition: well-fed and content.
examples: Since all the employees were fat and happy, there was little incentive to improve productivity.
You look fat and happy. Has life been treating you well?

senses.definition: very little likelihood.
examples: Fat chance he has of getting a promotion.
You think she’ll lend you the money? Fat chance!

headword: feast one’s eyes (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to look at someone or something with pleasure, envy, or admiration.
examples: Just feast your eyes on that beautiful, juicy steak!
Yes, feast your eyes. You won’t see one like that again for a long time.

senses.definition: an honor; a reward for something.
examples: Getting a new client was really a feather in my cap.
John earned a feather in his cap by getting an A in physics.

senses.definition: to decorate and furnish one’s home in style and comfort.
senses.notes: Birds line their nests with feathers to make them warm and comfortable.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Simpson have feathered their nest quite comfortably.
It costs a great deal of money to feather one’s nest these days.

senses.definition: to use power and prestige to provide for oneself selfishly.
senses.notes: Said especially of politicians who use their offices to make money for themselves.
examples: The mayor seemed to be helping people, but she was really feathering her own nest.
The building contractor used a lot of public money to feather his nest.

headword: fed up (to somewhere) (with someone or something)

senses.definition: bored with or disgusted with someone or something.
senses.notes: Informal. The somewhere can be here, the teeth, the gills, or other places.
examples: I’m fed up with Tom and his silly tricks.
I’m fed up to here with high taxes.
They are fed up to the teeth with screaming children.
I’m really fed up!

senses.definition: to eat; to eat a regular meal.
examples: Come on, everyone. It’s time to feed your faces.
Bill, if you keep feeding your face all the time, you’ll get fat.

senses.definition: to contribute money to a special, voluntary collection.
examples: Please feed the kitty. Make a contribution to help sick children.
Come on, Bill. Feed the kitty. You can afford a dollar for a good cause.

senses.definition: a feeling of contentment, happiness, satisfaction, peace, etc.
examples: Anne felt a glow of happiness as she held her new baby.
Sitting by the lake, the lovers felt a warm glow of contentment.

senses.definition: to feel as if one belongs; to feel as if one were in one’s home; to feel accepted.
senses.notes: See also at home with someone or something.
examples: I liked my dormitory room. I really felt at home there.
We will do whatever we can to make you feel at home.

senses.definition: to feel exhausted.
examples: What a day! I really feel dragged out.
If he runs too much, he ends up feeling dragged out.

senses.definition: to feel well and healthy.
examples: If you want to feel fit, you must eat the proper food and get enough rest.
I hope I still feel fit when I get old.

senses.definition: to feel like one is permitted to do something or take something.
examples: Please feel free to stay for dinner.
If you see something you want in the refrigerator, please feel free.

headword: feel it beneath one (to do something)

senses.definition: to feel that one would be lowering oneself to do something.
examples: Ann feels it beneath her to carry her own luggage.
I would do it, but I feel it beneath me.

senses.definition: to feel well and healthy, both physically and mentally.
examples: A quick swim in the morning makes me feel like a million dollars.
What a beautiful day! It makes you feel like a million.

senses.definition: to feel refreshed and renewed, especially after getting well or getting dressed up.
examples: I bought a new suit, and now I feel like a new person.
Bob felt like a new person when he got out of the hospital.

senses.definition: to want to do something; to be in the mood to do something.
examples: Do you feel like stopping work to eat something?
I feel like going on a vacation.

senses.definition: to feel well enough to do something.
examples: I believe I’m getting well. I feel like getting out of bed.
I don’t feel like going to the party. I have a headache.

senses.definition: to want to have something or do something.
examples: I feel like having a nice cool drink.
I feel like a nice swim.

senses.definition: to sense that one is getting very angry.
examples: I felt my gorge rise and I knew I was going to lose my temper.
Bob could feel his gorge rise as he read his tax bill.

headword: feel on top of the world

senses.definition: to feel very good, as if one were ruling the world.
examples: I feel on top of the world this morning.
I do not actually feel on top of the world, but I have felt worse.

senses.definition: to feel that one does not belong in a place.
examples: I feel out of place at formal dances.
Bob and Ann felt out of place at the picnic, so they went home.

senses.definition: to feel taken advantage of or exploited.
examples: Bill refused to help because he felt put-upon.
Sally’s mother felt put-upon, but she took each of the children home after the birthday party.

senses.definition: to sense something; to have an intuition about something.
examples: The train will be late. I feel it in my bones.
I failed the test. I know it in my bones.

senses.definition: to experience hardship because of having too little money.
examples: The Smiths used to go abroad every year, but now that he’s retired, they’re really feeling the pinch.
You’re bound to feel the pinch a bit when you’re a student.

senses.definition: drunk.
examples: Bob’s on his eighth beer and feeling no pain.
At midnight when we were all feeling no pain, the landlord comes up and tells us to be quiet.

senses.definition: to restrict someone in some way.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also hem someone or something in.
examples: I don’t want to fence you in, but you have to get home earlier at night.
Don’t try to fence me in. I need a lot of freedom.

senses.definition: very few; few and widely scattered.
examples: Get some gasoline now. Service stations on this highway are few and far between.
Some people think that good movies are few and far between.

headword: a few cards shy of a full deck
altForms: a few cards short of a deck
two bricks shy of a load

senses.definition: not very smart or clever.
examples: Bob’s nice, but he’s a few cards shy of a full deck.
You twit! You’re two bricks shy of a load!

senses.definition: to tease, annoy, or play with someone; to waste someone’s time.
senses.notes: [with someone] See also mess around (with someone or something).
examples: All right, stop fiddling around with me and tell me how much you will give me for my car.
Now it’s time for all of you to quit fiddling around and get to work.
Tom, you have to stop spending your time fiddling about with your friends. It’s time to get serious with your studies.

senses.definition: to play with something; to tinker with something ineptly.
examples: My brother is outside fiddling around with his car engine.
He should stop fiddling around and go out and get a job.
Stop fiddling about with that stick. You’re going to hurt someone.

senses.definition: to do nothing or something trivial while knowing that something disastrous is happening.
senses.notes: From a legend that the emperor Nero played the lyre while Rome was burning.
examples: The lobbyists don’t seem to be doing anything to stop this tax bill. They’re fiddling while Rome burns.
The doctor should have sent for an ambulance right away instead of examining the woman. In fact, he was just fiddling while Rome burned.

senses.definition: to answer a series of questions, especially from reporters.
examples: After her speech, Jane fielded questions from reporters.
The president’s press agents field questions from the newspaper.

senses.definition: to hurry to meet a deadline or to do something quickly.
examples: The ambulance sped through the city to reach the accident, fighting against time.
All the students fought against time to complete the test.

headword: fight someone or something hammer and tongs
altForms: fight someone or something tooth and nail
go at it hammer and tongs
go at it tooth and nail

senses.definition: to fight against someone or something energetically and with great determination.
examples: They fought against the robber tooth and nail.
The dogs were fighting each other hammer and tongs.
The mayor fought the new law hammer and tongs.
We’ll fight this zoning ordinance tooth and nail.

senses.definition: a good possibility of success, especially if every effort is made.
examples: They have at least a fighting chance of winning the race.
The patient could die, but he has a fighting chance since the operation.

senses.definition: to play a role in something.
examples: Tom figures in our plans for a new building.
I don’t wish to figure in your future.

senses.definition: to plan on something; to make arrangements for something.
examples: We figured on twenty guests at our party.
I didn’t figure on so much trouble.

senses.definition: to understand someone or something; to find an explanation for someone or something.
examples: It’s hard to figure John out. I don’t know what he means.
I can’t figure out this recipe.

headword: fill someone in (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to inform someone about someone or something.
examples: Please fill me in on what is happening in Washington.
Please fill me in on Ann. How is she doing?
Sit down, and I’ll fill you in.
Later, I’ll fill in everyone else.

senses.definition: to take the place of some other person and do that person’s work satisfactorily.
senses.notes: Refers to the notion of taking on someone else’s problems by wearing the other person’s shoes.
examples: I don’t know how we’ll be able to do without you. No one can fill your shoes.
It’ll be difficult to fill Jane’s shoes. She did her job very well.

senses.definition: to be exactly the thing that is needed.
examples: Ah, this steak is great. It really fills the bill.
I think that this book will fit the bill just right.

senses.definition: filled all the way full; filled up to the top edge.
examples: I like my coffee cup filled to the brim.
If the glass is filled to the brim, I can’t drink without spilling the contents.

senses.definition: the last act or period of enjoyment before a change in one’s circumstances or life-style.
examples: You might as well have a final fling before the baby’s born.
Mary’s going out with her girlfriends for a final fling. She’s getting married next week.

senses.definition: to find things wrong with someone or something.
examples: We were unable to find fault with the meal.
Sally’s father was always finding fault with her.
Some people are always finding fault.

headword: find it in one’s heart (to do something)

senses.definition: to have the courage or compassion to do something.
examples: She couldn’t find it in her heart to refuse to come home to him.
I can’t do it! I can’t find it in my heart.

senses.definition: to end up in a place.
senses.notes: [for something] This expression avoids accusing someone of moving the thing to the place.
examples: The money found its way into the mayor’s pocket.
The secret plans found their way into the enemy’s hands.

senses.definition: to discover what one’s talents and preferences are.
examples: Bill did better in school after he found himself.
John tried a number of different jobs. He finally found himself when he became a cook.

senses.definition: to become used to a new situation or experience.
examples: She was lonely when she first left home, but she is finding her feet now.
It takes time to learn the office routine, but you will gradually find your feet.

senses.definition: to find the position or rank to which one is best suited.
examples: You cannot force clerks to be ambitious. They will all find their own level.
The new student is happier in the beginning class. It was just a question of letting her find her own level.

senses.definition: to be able to talk.
examples: Tom was speechless for a moment. Then he found his tongue.
Ann was unable to find her tongue. She sat there in silence.

senses.definition: to be able to move about an area satisfactorily.
examples: I can go downtown by myself. I can find my way around.
I know the area well enough to find my way.
He can find his way around when it comes to car engines.

senses.definition: to discover the route to a place.
examples: Mr. Smith found his way to the museum.
Can you find your way home?

senses.definition: to decide guilt or innocence and deliver a verdict in a court of law.
examples: The judge found the defendant not guilty by reason of insanity.
The jury found the defendant innocent.

senses.definition: to discover facts about someone or something; to learn a fact.
examples: I found something out that you might be interested in.
We found out that the Smiths are going to sell their house.

senses.definition: to discover something bad about someone.
examples: John thought he could get away with smoking, but his mother found him out.
Jane was taking a two-hour lunch period until the manager found her out.

senses.definition: a phrase said when something is found.
senses.notes: The person who finds something gets to keep it. The person who loses it can only be sorry.
examples: John lost a quarter in the dining room yesterday. Ann found the quarter there today. Ann claimed that since she found it, it was hers. She said, “Finders keepers, losers weepers.”
John said, “I’ll say finders keepers when I find something of yours!”

senses.definition: all right; okay; really fine.
examples: Everything is fine and dandy at work. No special problems at the present time.
I feel fine and dandy. The new medicine seems to be working.

senses.definition: a predicament.
examples: What a mess! This is a fine how-do-you-do!
Here’s a fine how-de-do!

senses.definition: a real mess; an unsatisfactory situation.
examples: The dog has eaten the steak we were going to have for dinner. This is a fine kettle of fish!
This is a fine kettle of fish. It’s below freezing outside, and the furnace won’t work.

senses.definition: to shoot a gun; to discharge a gun.
examples: The police caught the robber who had fired the gun.
Jane fired the gun and hit the target.

headword: fire away at someone or something

senses.definition: to shoot at someone or something.
examples: The hunters fired away at the ducks.
On television, somebody is always firing away at somebody else.

senses.definition: to ask many questions of someone; to criticize someone severely.
examples: When it came time for questions, the reporters began firing away at the mayor.
Members of the opposite party are always firing away at the president.

senses.definition: working at full strength; making every possible effort.
senses.notes: Refers to an internal combustion engine.
examples: The team is firing on all cylinders under the new coach.
The factory is hitting on all cylinders to finish the orders on time.

senses.definition: first and most important.
examples: First and foremost, I think you should work harder on your biology.
Have this in mind first and foremost: Keep smiling!

senses.definition: the first down [of four] with ten yards needed to earn another first down.
examples: It is first and ten on the forty-yard line, and Army has the ball.
There will be no first and ten on the last play because there was a flag on the play.

senses.definition: The first people to arrive will be served first.
examples: They ran out of tickets before we got there. It was first come, first served, but we didn’t know that.
Please line up and take your turn. It’s first come, first served.

senses.definition: the very first thing; before anything else.
examples: First of all, put your name on this piece of paper.
First of all, we’ll try to find a place to live.

senses.definition: before anything else in the morning.
examples: Please call me first thing in the morning. I can’t help you now.
I’ll do that first thing.

senses.definition: the most important things must be taken care of first.
examples: It’s more important to get a job than to buy new clothes. First things first!
Do your homework now. Go out and play later. First things first.

senses.definition: to try to get someone to pay you a compliment.
examples: When she showed me her new dress, I could tell that she was fishing for a compliment.
Tom was certainly fishing for a compliment when he modeled his fancy haircut for his friends.

senses.definition: to try to get information (from someone).
examples: The lawyer was fishing for evidence.
The teacher spent a lot of time fishing for the right answer from the students.

senses.definition: to involve oneself in a difficult, confused, or dangerous situation, especially in order to gain an advantage.
examples: Frank is fishing in troubled waters by buying more shares of that company. They are supposed to be in financial difficulties.
The company could make more money by selling armaments abroad, but they would be fishing in troubled waters.

senses.definition: either do the task you are supposed to be doing or quit and let someone else do it.
examples: Mary is doing much better on the job since her manager told her to fish or cut bait.
The boss told Tom, “Quit wasting time! Fish or cut bait!”

senses.definition: slim and in good physical shape.
examples: Jean tried to keep herself fit and trim at all times.
For some people, keeping fit and trim requires time, effort, and self-discipline.

senses.definition: totally suitable.
examples: What a delicious meal. It was fit for a king.
Our room at the hotel was fit for a king.

senses.definition: to be comfortable with someone or something; to be in accord or harmony with someone or something.
examples: I really feel as if I fit in with that group of people.
It’s good that you fit in.
This chair doesn’t fit in with the style of furniture in my house.
I won’t buy it if it doesn’t fit in.

senses.definition: to fit very well; to fit tightly or snugly.
examples: My new shoes fit like a glove.
My new coat is quite snug. It fits like a glove.

senses.definition: to manage to put someone into a schedule.
examples: The doctor is busy, but I can fit you into the schedule.
Yes, here’s an opening in the schedule. I can fit you in.

headword: fit someone or something out (with something)

senses.definition: to provide or furnish someone or something with something.
examples: They fitted the camper out with everything they needed.
They fitted them out for only $140.
He fitted his car out with lots of chrome.

senses.definition: to fit a person very well.
examples: His new jacket fits him to a T.
My new shoes fit me to a T.

senses.definition: very angry and excited.
senses.notes: Folksy. To be so angry that one has to be restrained with ropes.
examples: If I’m not home on time, my parents will be fit to be tied.
When Ann saw the bill, she was fit to be tied.

senses.definition: dressed up to look very fancy or sexy.
examples: Mary put on her best clothes and looked fit to kill.
John looked fit to kill in his tuxedo.

senses.definition: to punish someone; to get even with someone; to plot against someone.
examples: If you ever do that again, I’ll fix your wagon!
Tommy! You clean up your room this instant, or I’ll fix your wagon!
He reported me to the boss, but I fixed his wagon. I knocked his lunch on the floor.

headword: fix someone up (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to supply a person with something.
examples: The usher fixed us up with seats at the front of the theater.
We fixed up the visitors with a cold drink.

senses.definition: and line someone up with someone to supply a person with a date or a companion.
examples: They lined John up with my cousin, Jane.
John didn’t want us to fix him up.
We fixed up Bob with a date.

senses.definition: to die out; to come to a stop shortly after starting; to fail.
examples: It started to rain, and the fire fizzled out.
The car started in the cold weather, but it fizzled out before we got very far.
My attempt to run for mayor fizzled out.
She started off her job very well, but fizzled out after about a month.

senses.definition: to grow intense suddenly.
senses.notes: [for emotions or a chronic disease] Refers to a fire, suddenly burning brighter or with more vigor.
examples: Just when we thought we had put the fire out, it flared up again.
Mr. Jones always flares up whenever anyone mentions taxes.
My hay fever usually flares up in August.

senses.definition: someone or something that draws a lot of attention for a very brief time.
senses.notes: Refers to a small grease fire in a frying pan. Informal.
examples: I’m afraid that my success as a painter was just a flash in the pan.
Tom had hoped to be a singer, but his career was only a flash in the pan.

senses.definition: completely broke; with no money at all.
examples: I spent my last dollar, and I’m flat broke.
The bank closed its doors to the public. It was flat broke!

senses.definition: clearly and definitely; holding nothing back.
examples: I told her flat out that I didn’t like her.
They reported flat out that the operation was a failure.

senses.definition: at top speed, with the accelerator pedal flat on the floor.
examples: How fast will this car go flat out?
This car will hit about 110 miles per hour flat out.

senses.definition: You can praise me, but I’m not going to give you what you want.
examples: I am glad to hear that I am beautiful and talented, but flattery will get you nowhere.
Flattery will get you nowhere, but that doesn’t mean you should stop flattering me!
