senses.definition: a living human body, especially with reference to its natural limitations; a human being.
examples: This cold weather is more than flesh and blood can stand.
Carrying 300 pounds is beyond mere flesh and blood.

senses.definition: the quality of being alive.
examples: The paintings of this artist are lifeless. They lack flesh and blood.
This play needs flesh and blood, not the mumbling of intensely dull actors.

senses.definition: one’s own relatives; one’s own kin.
examples: That’s no way to treat one’s own flesh and blood.
I want to leave my money to my own flesh and blood.
Grandmother was happier living with her flesh and blood.

senses.definition: to make something more detailed, bigger, or fuller.
senses.notes: As if one were adding flesh to a skeleton.
examples: This is basically a good outline. Now you’ll have to flesh it out.
The play was good, except that the author needed to flesh out the third act. It was too short.

senses.definition: an idea or suggestion that is out of touch with reality or possibility.
examples: What is the point in indulging in flights of fancy about foreign vacations when you cannot even afford the rent?
We are tired of her flights of fancy about marrying a millionaire.

senses.definition: to suddenly become angry, crazy, or enthusiastic.
examples: Whenever anyone mentions taxes, Mr. Jones absolutely flips his wig.
Stop whistling. You’re going to make me flip my lid.
When I saw that brand-new car and learned it was mine, I just flipped my wig.

headword: flirt with the idea of doing something

senses.definition: to think about doing something; to toy with an idea; to consider something, but not too seriously.
examples: I flirted with the idea of going to Europe for two weeks.
Jane flirted with the idea of quitting her job.

senses.definition: to get a loan; to arrange for a loan.
examples: I couldn’t afford to pay cash for the car, so I floated a loan.
They needed money, so they had to float a loan.

senses.definition: plants and animals.
examples: The magazine story described the flora and fauna of Panama.
We went for a hike in the Finnish wilderness hoping to learn all about the local flora and fauna.

senses.definition: worthless matter; worthless encumbrances.
senses.notes: Refers to the floating wreckage of a ship and its cargo or to floating cargo deliberately cast overboard to stabilize a ship in a rough sea.
examples: His mind is burdened with the flotsam and jetsam of many years of poor instruction and lax study habits.
Your report would be better if you could get rid of a lot of the flotsam and jetsam and clean up the grammar a bit.

senses.definition: to speak one’s speech badly or forget one’s lines when one is in a play.
examples: The actress fluffed her lines badly in the last act.
I was in a play once, and I muffed my lines over and over.
It’s okay to blow your lines in rehearsal.

senses.definition: to fail a course; to fail out of school.
examples: Tom didn’t study, and he finally flunked out.
Bill is about to flunk out of geometry.

senses.definition: to cause someone to leave school by giving a failing grade.
examples: The teacher flunked Tom out.
The professor wanted to flunk out the whole class.

senses.definition: even with something; sharing a surface with something.
examples: The edge of the sink is flush with the counter.
The wood flooring is flush with the carpet so people won’t trip.

senses.definition: having lots of something.
examples: Our garden is flush with fresh vegetables.
The committee was flush with helpful ideas.

senses.definition: irresponsible; untrustworthy.
senses.notes: Refers to a person who sneaks away secretly in the night.
examples: The carpenter we hired was a fly-by-night worker who did a very bad job.
You shouldn’t deal with a fly-by-night merchant.

headword: fly in the face of someone or something
altForms: fly in the teeth of someone or something

senses.definition: to disregard, defy, or show disrespect for someone or something.
examples: John loves to fly in the face of tradition.
Ann made it a practice to fly in the face of standard procedures.
John finds great pleasure in flying in the teeth of his father.

senses.definition: a small, unpleasant matter that spoils something; a drawback.
examples: We enjoyed the play, but the fly in the ointment was not being able to find our car afterward.
It sounds like a good idea, but there must be a fly in the ointment somewhere.

headword: fly into the face of danger

senses.definition: to take great risks; to threaten or challenge danger, as if danger were a person.
senses.notes: This may refer to flying, as in an airplane, but not necessarily.
examples: John plans to go bungee-jumping this weekend. He really likes flying into the face of danger.
Willard was not exactly the type to fly into the face of danger, but tonight was an exception, and he ordered enchiladas.

senses.definition: to lose one’s temper.
examples: Every time anyone mentions taxes, Mrs. Brown flies off the handle.
If she keeps flying off the handle like that, she’ll have a heart attack.

senses.definition: to escape; to get out or get away.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to a chicken escaping from a chicken coop.
examples: I couldn’t stand the party, so I flew the coop.
The prisoner flew the coop at the first opportunity.

senses.definition: to be very angry.
senses.notes: Informal. Related to a “mad dog”—a dog with rabies—which foams at the mouth.
examples: Bob was raving—foaming at the mouth. I’ve never seen anyone so angry.
Bill foamed at the mouth in anger.

senses.definition: to trick someone into accepting something that is worthless.
examples: The car dealer fobbed a car off on Tom.
He also fobbed off a bad car on Jane.
Some car dealers are always trying to fob something off.

senses.definition: to force someone to take something that they don’t want.
examples: Bill tried to foist the task of washing dishes off on his sister.
The city council foisted the new garbage dump on the poorest neighborhood in the city.

senses.definition: to bring one’s hands together, palm to palm, with the fingers interlocking; to grasp one’s hands together, palm to palm, perpendicular to one another.
examples: Please fold your hands and put them on the table while the teacher reads you a story.
Sue folded her hands to pray.

senses.definition: to put an end to something; to close something such as a business or some other enterprise.
examples: Mr. Jones was going broke, so he folded his business up.
The producer decided to fold up the play early. It was losing money.

senses.definition: to harm or disfigure a machine-readable document, such as a computer punch card.
senses.notes: Such a document, if folded, placed on a bill spike, or otherwise punctured, would no longer be machine-readable. Now rarely seen on a bill but the expression is sometimes used in a figurative sense.
examples: At the bottom of the bill, it said “do not fold, spindle, or mutilate,” and Jane, in her anger, did all three.
Look here, chum, if you don’t want to get folded, spindled, or mutilated, you had better do what you are told!

senses.definition: to close up; to end.
senses.notes: Alluding to something that folds closed or collapses along its folds.
examples: The play folded up after two days.
It’s time to fold up and go home.

senses.definition: to follow someone’s example; to assume someone else’s role or occupation.
examples: The vice president was following in the president’s footsteps when he called for budget cuts.
She followed in her father’s footsteps and went into medicine.

senses.definition: to act according to one’s feelings; to obey one’s sympathetic or compassionate inclinations.
examples: I couldn’t decide what to do, so I just followed my heart.
I trust that you will follow your heart in this matter.

senses.definition: to go straight ahead, the direction that one’s nose is pointing.
examples: The town that you want is straight ahead on this highway. Just follow your nose.
The chief’s office is right around the corner. Turn left and follow your nose.

senses.definition: to follow an odor to its source.
examples: The kitchen is at the back of the building. Just follow your nose.
There was a bad smell in the basement—probably a dead mouse. I followed my nose until I found it.

senses.definition: to do as one has been instructed.
examples: You have to learn to follow orders if you want to be a marine.
I didn’t do anything wrong. I was only following orders.

senses.definition: to do as someone else does; to accept someone’s guidance; to follow someone’s direction.
examples: Just follow my lead and you will not get lost.
John followed his father’s lead and became a lawyer.

senses.definition: to follow in the same pattern; to follow someone else’s example.
examples: Mary went to work for a bank, and Jane followed suit. Now they are both head cashiers.
The Smiths went out to dinner, but the Browns didn’t follow suit. They stayed home.

senses.definition: to do what everyone else is doing.
examples: I am an independent thinker. I could never just follow the crowd.
When in doubt, I follow the crowd. At least I don’t stand out like a fool.

senses.definition: to find out more about someone or something.
examples: Please follow up on Mr. Brown and his activities.
Bill, Mr. Smith has a complaint. Would you please follow up on it?
We can take care of that when we follow up.

senses.definition: to check (on something) and do what needs to be done.
examples: I will follow up on this matter and make sure it is settled.
There is a problem with the bank account. Will you please follow up?

senses.definition: to like someone or something.
examples: I’m fond of chocolate.
Mary isn’t fond of me, but I’m fond of her.

senses.definition: something to think about.
examples: I don’t like your idea very much, but it’s food for thought.
Your lecture was very good. It contained much food for thought.

headword: A fool and his money are soon parted.

senses.definition: A person who acts unwisely with money soon loses it.
senses.notes: Often said about a person who has just lost a sum of money because of poor judgment.
examples: When Bill lost a $400 bet on a horse race, Mary said, “A fool and his money are soon parted.”
When John bought a cheap used car that fell apart the next day, he said, “Oh, well, a fool and his money are soon parted.”

senses.definition: to fiddle, play, or mess with someone or something; to waste time with someone or something.
examples: John is out fooling around with his friends again.
That child spends most of his time fooling around.
Please don’t fool around with the light switch. You’ll break it.
There are lots of interesting things in here, but you must leave them alone. Don’t fool around.

headword: fools rush in (where angels fear to tread)

senses.definition: people with little experience or knowledge often get involved in difficult or delicate situations that wiser people would avoid.
examples: I wouldn’t ask Jean about her divorce, but Kate did. Fools rush in, as they say.
Only the newest member of the committee questioned the chairman’s decision. Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.

senses.definition: to pay the bill; to pay (for something).
examples: Let’s go out and eat. I’ll foot the bill.
If the bank goes broke, don’t worry. The government will foot the bill.

senses.definition: without responsibilities or commitments.
examples: All the rest of them have wives, but John is footloose and fancy-free.
Mary never stays long in any job. She likes being footloose and fancy-free.

senses.definition: for a joke; as something done for fun.
examples: For a lark, I wore a clown’s wig to school.
On a lark, I skipped school and drove to the beach.

senses.definition: I don’t care if (something happens).
examples: For all I care, the whole city council can go to the devil.
They can all starve for all I care.

senses.definition: according to the information I have; I think; probably.
examples: For all I know, the mayor has resigned already.
She may have gone to town for all I know.

senses.definition: virtually; practically speaking; in effect.
senses.notes: Sometimes this expression has very little meaning.
examples: He entered the room, looking for all intents and purposes as if he would burst into song.
She said that for all intents and purposes she had completed her assignment.

senses.definition: if it has any value.
examples: My idea—for all it’s worth—is to offer them only $300.
Here is my thinking, for whatever it’s worth.
Ask her to give us her opinion, for what it’s worth.

senses.definition: as might be reasonably expected; essentially.
examples: For all practical purposes, this is simply a matter of right and wrong.
This should be considered final, for all practical purposes.

senses.definition: exactly; precisely.
examples: She sat there looking for all the world as if she was going to cry.
It started out seeming for all the world like a beautiful day. Then a storm came up.

senses.definition: everything.
examples: I wouldn’t give up my baby for all the world.
They wouldn’t sell their property for all the world.

senses.definition: under any conditions; no matter what happens.
examples: I married you for better or for worse.
For better or for worse, I’m going to quit my job.

senses.definition: for nearly nothing; for very little money.
examples: Bob doesn’t get paid much. He works for chicken feed.
You can buy an old car for chicken feed.
I won’t do that kind of work for peanuts!

senses.definition: For heaven’s sake!; I am amazed!
senses.notes: An exclamation of surprise and mild shock.
examples: For crying out loud! I didn’t expect to see you here.
For crying out loud! What a time to call someone on the telephone.

senses.definition: for many days.
examples: We kept on traveling for days on end.
Doctor, I’ve had this pain for days on end.

senses.definition: for no charge or cost; free of any cost.
examples: They let us into the movie for free.
I will let you have a sample of the candy for free.

senses.definition: forever; permanently.
examples: I finally left home for good.
They tried to repair it many times before they fixed it for good.

senses.definition: as extra; (adding) a little more to make sure there is enough.
examples: When I bought a pound of nails, the clerk threw in a few extra nails for good measure.
I always put a little extra salt in the soup for good measure.

senses.definition: for many hours.
examples: We sat and waited for the doctor for hours on end.
We listened to the speaker for hours on end.

senses.definition: for example.
examples: I’ve lived in many cities, for instance, Boston, Chicago, and Detroit.
Jane is very generous. For instance, she volunteers her time and gives money to charities.

senses.definition: forever; permanently.
senses.notes: Informal. See also play for keeps. Compare this with for good.
examples: When I get married, it’ll be for keeps.
We’ve moved around a lot. Now I think we’ll stay here for keeps.

senses.definition: for fun; just for entertainment; for no good reason.
examples: They didn’t mean any harm. They just did it for kicks.
We drove over to the next town for kicks.

senses.definition: for the remainder of one’s life.
examples: The accident caused me to become blind for life.
She will stay in prison for life.

senses.definition: as far as one is concerned; from one’s point of view.
examples: For my own part, I wish to stay here.
For her part, she prefers chocolate.

senses.definition: for one’s good or benefit; in honor of someone.
examples: I have to earn a living for my family’s sake.
I did it for my mother’s sake.
I didn’t do it for my own sake.

senses.definition: to start with.
examples: For openers, they played a song everyone knows.
For starters, I’ll serve a delicious soup.

senses.definition: authentic; genuine; really.
examples: Is this diamond for real?
Are you for real?
Are we there for real?

senses.definition: for the purpose of keeping someone or something safe.
examples: I put my jewelry in the vault for safekeeping.
I checked my fur coat at the entrance to the bar for safekeeping.

senses.definition: available for purchase; buyable.
examples: Is this item for sale?
How long has this house been for sale?
My car is for sale. Are you interested?

senses.definition: in a short form.
senses.notes: Usually refers to names of people or things.
examples: My name is William. They call me Bill for short.
Almost everyone who is named Robert is called Bob for short.

senses.definition: certainly; surely.
examples: MARY: Do you like my new jacket? JANE: For sure.
For sure, I want to go on the picnic.

senses.definition: besides; in addition.
examples: If you’re hungry, take one of my doughnuts. For that matter, take two.
I don’t like this house. The roof leaks. For that matter, the whole place is falling apart.
Tom is quite arrogant. So is his sister, for that matter.

senses.definition: better; an improvement.
senses.notes: See also take a turn for the better.
examples: A change of government would be for the better.
A new winter coat would certainly be for the better.

senses.definition: worthless; undesirable.
examples: This television program is for the birds.
Winter weather is for the birds.

senses.definition: just for fun; because it is slightly evil; for no good reason.
examples: We filled their garage with leaves just for the devil of it.
Tom tripped Bill for the heck of it.
John picked a fight with Tom just for the hell of it.

senses.definition: for the whole time that something continues; for the entire period of time required for something to be completed; for as long as something takes.
examples: We are in this war for the duration.
However long it takes, we’ll wait. We are here for the duration.

headword: for the good of someone or something

senses.definition: for the benefit, profit, or advantage of someone or something.
examples: The president said the strict drug laws were for the good of the country.
David took a second job for the good of his family.

senses.definition: for the present; for now; temporarily.
examples: This will have to do for the moment.
This is all right for the time being. It’ll have to be improved next week, however.
This good feeling will last only for the time being.
This solution is satisfactory for the moment.

senses.definition: mostly; in general.
examples: For the most part, the class is enjoying geometry.
I like working here for the most part.

headword: for the odds to be against one

senses.definition: for things to be against one generally; for one’s chances of success to be slim.
examples: You can give it a try, but the odds are against you.
I know the odds are against me, but I wish to run in the race anyway.

senses.definition: so that (one’s own version of) the facts will be known; so there will be a record of a particular fact.
senses.notes: This often is said when there are reporters present.
examples: I’d like to say—for the record— that at no time have I ever accepted a bribe from anyone.
For the record, I’ve never been able to get anything done around city hall without bribing someone.

headword: for the sake of someone or something

senses.definition: for the good of someone or something; for the honor or recognition of someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with for one’s own sake.
examples: I did it for the sake of all those people who helped me get through school.
I’m investing in a house for the sake of my children.
For the sake of honesty, Bill shared all the information he had.

senses.definition: someone or something that one finds attractive or desirable partly because having the person or thing is immoral or illegal.
senses.notes: From the fruit in the Garden of Eden that was forbidden to Adam by God.
examples: Jim flirts with his sister-in-law only because she’s forbidden fruit.
The boy watches that program only when his parents are out. It’s forbidden fruit.

senses.definition: to pressure someone to leave an elective office.
examples: The city council forced the mayor out of office.
Please resign immediately, or I’ll have to drive you out.

senses.definition: to force a person to reveal plans, strategies, or secrets.
senses.notes: Refers to a handful of cards in card playing.
examples: We didn’t know what she was doing until Tom forced her hand.
We couldn’t plan our game until we forced the other team’s hand in the last play.

senses.definition: to push someone to an extreme position; to put someone into an awkward position.
examples: He wouldn’t tell the truth until we forced him to the wall.
They don’t pay their bills until you drive them to the wall.

headword: a force to be reckoned with

senses.definition: someone or something that is important and powerful and must not be ignored.
examples: Walter is a force to be reckoned with. Be prepared to deal with him.
The growing discontent with the political system is a powerful force to be reckoned with.

senses.definition: at the front and the back, usually of a boat or ship.
examples: They had to attach new lights fore and aft because the old ones were not bright enough to meet the new regulations.
The captain ordered a watch stationed fore and aft.

senses.definition: a conclusion already reached; an inevitable result.
examples: That the company was moving to California was a foregone conclusion.
That the mayor will win reelection is a foregone conclusion.

senses.definition: forever.
examples: I will love you forever and ever.
This car won’t keep running forever and ever. We’ll have to get a new one sometime.
We have enough money to last forever and a day.

senses.definition: to forgive someone (for something) and forget that it ever happened.
examples: I’m sorry, John. Let’s forgive and forget. What do you say?
It was nothing. We’ll just have to forgive and forget.

senses.definition: to pay (perhaps unwillingly) for something.
senses.notes: Informal. Often mention is made of the amount of money. See the examples below.
examples: Do you think I’m going to fork twenty dollars out for that book?
Forking money out to everyone is part of life in a busy economy.
I like that stereo, but I don’t want to fork out a lot of money.

senses.definition: to give something to someone.
senses.notes: Refers to handing over money. Slang. Usually used in a command.
examples: Now! Fork it over now!
Okay, Joe. Fork over that twenty dollars you owe me.

senses.definition: meaningful content; structure and meaningful content.
examples: The first act of the play was one screaming match after another. It lacked form and substance throughout.
Jane’s report was good. The teacher commented on the excellent form and substance of the paper.

senses.definition: to think up or decide on an opinion.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: I don’t know enough about the issue to form an opinion.
Don’t tell me how to think! I can form my own opinion.
I don’t form opinions without careful consideration.

senses.definition: a short sleep; a nap.
senses.notes: Informal. See also catch forty winks.
examples: I had forty winks on the plane.
If you’re lucky you’ll get forty winks while the children are out.

senses.definition: to harm one’s own interests; to bring disadvantage upon oneself.
examples: He tried to discredit a fellow senator with the president, but just succeeded in fouling his own nest.
The boss really dislikes Mary. She certainly fouled her own nest when she spread those rumors about him.

senses.definition: illegal activity; bad practices.
examples: The police investigating the death suspect foul play.
Each student got an A on the test, and the teacher imagined it was the result of foul play.

senses.definition: to cause disorder and confusion for someone or something; to tangle up someone or something; to mess someone or something up.
examples: Go away! Don’t foul me up any more.
You’ve fouled up my whole day.
Watch out! You’re going to foul up my kite strings.
Stay off the field. You’re going to foul up the coach.

senses.definition: to do (something) badly; to mess something up.
examples: At the last minute, he fouled up and failed the course.
Take your time. Plan your moves, and don’t foul up.

senses.definition: messed up; in disorder.
examples: My fishing line is all fouled up.
The football team got fouled up and lost the game.

senses.definition: full of something dangerous or unpleasant.
examples: The spy’s trip to Russia was fraught with danger.
My escape from the kidnappers was fraught with danger.

senses.definition: without encumbrance, particularly in regard to the ownership of something.
examples: After the last payment, Jane owned the car free and clear.
If you can’t prove that you own the house and the land it stands on free and clear, you can’t sell it.

senses.definition: casual.
examples: John is so free and easy. How can anyone be so relaxed?
Now, take it easy. Just act free and easy. No one will know you’re nervous.

senses.definition: a disorganized fight or contest involving everyone; a brawl.
examples: The picnic turned into a free-for-all after midnight.
The race started out in an organized manner, but ended up being a free-for-all.

senses.definition: a translation that is not completely accurate and not well thought out.
examples: John gave a free translation of the sentence, which did not help us at all.
Anne gave a very free translation of the poem.

senses.definition: just now having sold or used up the last of something.
examples: Sorry, I can’t serve you scrambled eggs. We are fresh out of eggs.
We are fresh out of nails. I sold the last box just ten minutes ago.
Lettuce? Sorry. I’m fresh out.
Sorry. We are clean out of dried beans.

headword: A friend in need is a friend indeed.

senses.definition: A true friend is a person who will help you when you really need someone.
examples: When Bill helped me with geometry, I really learned the meaning of “A friend in need is a friend indeed.”
“A friend in need is a friend indeed” sounds silly until you need someone very badly.

senses.definition: a friend or an enemy.
examples: I can’t tell whether Jim is friend or foe.
“Who goes there? Friend or foe?” asked the sentry.

senses.definition: to frighten someone severely.
examples: The dentist always frightens me to death.
She scared me to death when she screamed.

headword: frighten the wits out of someone
altForms: frighten the (living) daylights out of someone
scare the (living) daylights out of someone
scare the wits out of someone

senses.definition: to frighten someone very badly.
examples: We nearly had an accident. It frightened the living daylights out of me.
The incident scared the wits out of me.

senses.definition: severely frightened.
examples: I don’t want to go to the dentist today. I’m frightened to death.
I’m frightened to death of dogs.
She’s scared to death she’ll fail algebra.

senses.definition: to waste something little by little, especially time or money.
examples: Don’t stand around and fritter the whole day away.
Stop frittering away my hard-earned money!

senses.definition: during the period of the day when there is light; from the rising of the sun to the setting of the sun.
examples: I have to work from dawn to dusk on the farm.
The factory runs from dawn to dusk to produce hats and gloves.

senses.definition: on a daily basis; one day at a time; occasionally.
examples: We face this kind of problem from day to day.
I’ll have to check into this matter from day to day.
When you’re very poor, you live from day to day.

senses.definition: moving from one door to another—typically, from one house to another.
examples: Anne went from door to door, selling books, to earn money for college.
The children went from door to door, saying “Trick or treat!” at each one.

senses.definition: from all around, both close by and farther away.
senses.notes: Reversible, but with a preference for from far and near.
examples: All the young people from far and near gathered at the high school for the game.
The eagles gathered from near and far at the river where the salmon were spawning.

senses.definition: from one person to a series of other persons.
examples: The book traveled from hand to hand until it got back to its owner.
By the time the baby had been passed from hand to hand, it was crying.

senses.definition: from the top of one’s head to one’s feet; all over the body.
senses.notes: See also from tip to toe.
examples: She was decked out in flowers from head to toe.
The huge parka covered the small child from head to toe, assuring that she would be well protected against the cold.

senses.definition: from a location on the other side of the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, according to the point of view of someone located in the U.S.
examples: The latest word from overseas is that the treaty has been signed.
Is there any news from overseas about the war?

senses.definition: from one place to a series of other places; (figuratively) from person to person, as with gossip.
examples: My father was in the army, and we moved from pillar to post year after year.
After I told one person my secret, it went quickly from pillar to post.

senses.definition: from poverty to wealth; from modesty to elegance.
examples: The princess used to be quite poor. She certainly moved from rags to riches.
After I inherited the money, I went from rags to riches.

senses.definition: moving first to one side and then to the other, repeatedly.
examples: The pendulum of the clock swings from side to side.
The singers swayed from side to side as they sang.

senses.definition: from the beginning to the end; throughout.
examples: I disliked the whole business from start to finish.
Mary caused problems from start to finish.

senses.definition: from one end to another.
senses.notes: Refers to the front and back ends of a ship.
examples: Now, I have to clean the house from stem to stern.
I polished my car carefully from stem to stern.

headword: from the bottom of one’s heart

senses.definition: sincerely.
senses.notes: Compare this with with all one’s heart and soul.
examples: When I returned the lost kitten to Mrs. Brown, she thanked me from the bottom of her heart.
Oh, thank you! I’m grateful from the bottom of my heart.

headword: from the cradle to the grave

senses.definition: from birth to death; throughout one’s life.
examples: The government promised to take care of us from the cradle to the grave.
You can feel secure and well protected from the cradle to the grave.

senses.definition: from the beginning; from start to finish.
senses.notes: Refers to the building of a house or other building.
examples: We must plan our sales campaign carefully from the ground up.
Sorry, but you’ll have to start all over again from the ground up.

senses.definition: from a deep and sincere emotional source.
examples: I know that your kind words come from the heart.
We don’t want your gift unless it comes from the heart.

senses.definition: holding attitudes or ideas that were popular and important in the past, but which are no longer considered relevant or in line with modern trends.
examples: Grammar was not taught much in my son’s school, but fortunately he had a teacher from the old school.
Aunt Jane is from the old school. She never goes out without wearing a hat and gloves.

senses.definition: from the beginning.
examples: We had problems with this machine from the outset.
We knew about the unfriendly judge from the outset of our trial.

senses.definition: from the beginning of something, such as a song or a script.
examples: Okay, let’s try it again from the top.
Play it from the top one more time.

senses.definition: from the beginning.
examples: I knew about the problem from the word go.
She was failing the class from the word go.

senses.definition: from today into the future.
examples: We’ll live in love and peace from this day on.
I’ll treasure your gift from this day forward.

senses.definition: occasionally.
examples: We have pizza from time to time.
From time to time, a visitor comes to our door.

senses.definition: from the top to the bottom.
senses.notes: Not necessarily of a person. See also from head to toe.
examples: She is wearing all new clothes from tip to toe.
The house needs to be cleaned thoroughly from tip to toe.

senses.definition: from the highest point to the lowest point; throughout.
senses.notes: Compare this with from stem to stern.
examples: I have to clean the house from top to bottom today.
We need to replace our elected officials from top to bottom.

senses.definition: from far in the past; from an earlier time.
examples: Grandfather comes from way back.
This antique clock is from way back.

senses.definition: the results of one’s work.
examples: We displayed the fruits of our labor at the convention.
What have you accomplished? Where is the fruit of your labors?

senses.definition: full of nonsense; talking nonsense.
examples: Oh, shut up, Mary. You’re full of hot air.
Don’t pay any attention to Bill. He’s full of beans.
My English professor is full of bull.
You’re full of it.
She doesn’t know what she’s talking about. She’s just full of prunes.

senses.definition: conceited; self-important.
examples: Mary is very unpopular because she’s so full of herself.
She doesn’t care about other people’s feelings. She’s too full of herself.

senses.definition: always making mischief.
senses.notes: Informal. Old Nick is another name for the devil.
examples: Tom is a lot of fun, but he’s sure full of the devil.
I’ve never seen a child get into so much mischief. He’s really full of Old Nick.

senses.definition: forward at the greatest speed possible; with as much energy and enthusiasm as possible.
senses.notes: From an instruction given to engineers on steamships.
examples: It will have to be full steam ahead for everybody if the factory gets this order.
It’s going to be full steam ahead for me this year. I take my final exams.

senses.definition: playing around; doing worthless things.
examples: All right, Bill, the fun and games are over. It’s time to get down to work.
This isn’t a serious course. It’s nothing but fun and games.

senses.definition: trickery or deception; illegal activity.
examples: From the silence as she entered the room, the teacher knew there was some funny business going on.
There’s some funny business going on at the warehouse. Stock keeps disappearing.

senses.definition: amusing; comical.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with funny peculiar.
examples: I didn’t mean that Mrs. Peters is funny ha-ha. She’s weird—funny peculiar, in fact.
Mike thinks his jokes are funny ha-ha, but we laugh because they are so silly.

senses.definition: odd; eccentric.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with funny ha-ha.
examples: I didn’t mean that Mary is funny ha-ha. She’s weird—funny peculiar, in fact.
His face is sort of funny—funny peculiar, that is.

senses.definition: to make progress; to advance; to become more important or popular.
examples: Our new product is gaining ground against that of our competitor.
Since the government announced the new policies, the stock market is gaining ground.

senses.definition: The deception is over.; The illegal activity has come to an end.
examples: When the police were waiting for them inside the bank vault, the would-be robbers knew that the game was up.
“The jig is up!” said the cop as he grabbed the shoulder of the pickpocket.

headword: a game that two can play

senses.definition: a manner of competing that two competitors can use; a strategy that competing sides can both use.
examples: The mayor shouted at the city council, “Politics is a game that two can play.”
“Flattery is a game that two can play,” said John as he returned Mary’s compliment.

senses.definition: to form into a group and attack someone.
senses.notes: Usually a physical attack, but it can also be a verbal attack.
examples: We can’t win against the robber unless we gang up on him.
All right, you guys, don’t gang up on me. Play fair!

senses.definition: wild or funny.
examples: You should have been at Susan’s party last night. It was a gas.
That movie was such a gas. I haven’t laughed so hard in ages.

senses.definition: to prepare for something; to get into shape for something.
examples: We are gearing up for a very busy summer season.
We are not ready yet. We have to gear up.
Tom is gearing himself up for his exams.

senses.definition: too generous; overly generous.
examples: My favorite uncle is generous to a fault.
Sally—always generous to a fault—gave away her sandwiches.

headword: get a bee in one’s bonnet

senses.definition: to get an idea or a thought that remains in one’s mind; to get an obsession.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also put a bee in someone’s bonnet.
examples: I have a bee in my bonnet that you’d be a good manager.
I got a bee in my bonnet about swimming. I couldn’t stop wanting to go swimming.

senses.definition: to receive or enjoy a happy celebration before departing.
senses.notes: Note: Get can be replaced with have. Note the variation in the examples. Get usually means “to become, to acquire, or to cause.” Have usually means “to possess, to be, or to have resulted in.” See also give someone a big send-off.
examples: I had a wonderful send-off before I left.
John got a fine send-off as he left for Europe.

senses.definition: to get a bruise near the eye from being struck.
senses.notes: The area around the eye is darkened, not black. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I got a black eye from walking into a door.
I have a black eye where John hit me.

senses.definition: to have one’s character or reputation harmed.
examples: Mary got a black eye because of her complaining.
The whole group now has a black eye.

senses.definition: to have good fortune; to receive a bit of luck.
senses.notes: Often with lucky, nice, etc. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Mary is going to get a break.
I wish I’d get a lucky break.
Why don’t I have a lucky break when I need one?
She’s got a lucky break and doesn’t even know it.

senses.definition: for a clever thought or idea to occur (to someone).
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Now and then I get a bright idea.
John hardly ever gets a bright idea.
Listen here! I have a bright idea!

headword: get a charge out of someone or something
altForms: get a bang out of someone or something
get a kick out of someone or something

senses.definition: to receive special pleasure from someone or something.
examples: Tom is really funny. I always get a kick out of his jokes.
Bill really got a bang out of the present we gave him.
Mary got a charge out of Bob’s visit.

senses.definition: to develop a cramp in the arm or leg, usually from strain.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Don’t work too hard or you’ll get a charley horse.
Poor Tom is always getting a charley horse in his leg.
Sally can’t play. She has a charley horse.

senses.definition: to have a physical examination by a physician.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: She got a checkup yesterday.
I going to have a checkup in the morning. I hope I’m okay.

headword: get a clean bill of health

senses.definition: to be pronounced healthy by a physician.
senses.notes: [for someone] Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Sally got a clean bill of health from the doctor.
Now that Sally has a clean bill of health, she can go back to work.

senses.definition: to become infatuated with someone.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Mary thinks she’s getting a crush on Bill.
Sally says she’ll never get a crush on anyone again.
John has a crush on Mary.

headword: get a dirty look from someone

senses.definition: to get frowned at by someone.
examples: I stopped whistling when I got a dirty look from Ann.
I got a dirty look from the teacher. I don’t know why.

senses.definition: to find out the exact location of something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone a fix on something.
examples: I can’t get a fix on your location. Where are you?
We are trying to get a fix on your radio transmission.
I have a fix on them now.

senses.definition: to begin to understand the direction of a discussion.
examples: I can’t quite get a fix on what you’re trying to say.
I can’t get a fix on where you’re going with this argument.

senses.definition: an initial position of support; a starting point.
examples: It’s difficult to get a foothold in the education market when schools are laying off teachers.
Max’s father helped him get a toehold in the textile industry.

headword: get a free hand (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to be granted complete control over something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone a free hand (with something).
examples: I didn’t get a free hand with the last project.
John was in charge then, but he didn’t have a free hand either.
I demand to have a free hand with my own child!

headword: get a frog in one’s throat

senses.definition: to get soreness or something else in one’s throat that prevents one from talking well.
senses.notes: This often leads to one clearing one’s throat. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The speaker got a frog in his throat and had to stop talking for a while.
Excuse me. I have a frog in my throat.

senses.definition: to remind, scold, or nag someone (to do something).
senses.notes: Informal. See also keep after someone.
examples: John hasn’t taken out the garbage. I’ll have to get after him.
Mary’s mother will get after her if she doesn’t do the dishes.

senses.definition: to understand something.
senses.notes: Also with good, solid, and sound, as in the examples. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Try to get a grasp of the basic rules.
You don’t have a good grasp of the principles yet.
John was unable to get a solid grasp of the methods used in his work, and we had to let him go.

senses.definition: to receive assistance with something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Mary would really like to get a hand with that. It’s too much for one person.
I’d like to have a hand with this.

senses.definition: to do or say something sooner than it ought to be done so that the proper explanation or preparations have not been made.
examples: I have to stick to my notes or I will get ahead of myself in my lecture.
When he bought a new little bicycle before the baby was born, he was getting ahead of himself.

headword: get a head start (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to start (something) earlier than someone else.
senses.notes: [with someone] Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Bill always gets there first because he gets a head start on everybody else.
I’m doing well in my class because I have a head start.

senses.definition: to start something earlier (than someone else).
examples: I was able to get a head start on my reading during the holidays.
If I hadn’t had a head start, I’d be behind in my reading.

senses.definition: to make contact with someone; to call someone on the telephone.
senses.notes: [with someone] See also get one’s hands on someone or something; get in touch (with someone). Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’ll try to get hold of you in the morning.
It’s very hard to get hold of John. He’s so busy.

senses.definition: to obtain something.
examples: I’m trying to get hold of a glass jar. I need it for school.
Does anyone know where I can get hold of a spare tire?
I have hold of a very large piece of land.

senses.definition: to start to hurry.
examples: We are going to leave in five minutes, Jane. Get a hurry on!
Mary! Get a move on! We can’t wait all day.

senses.definition: to get a spanking; to get beat in a fight.
examples: Billy, you had better get in here if you don’t want to get a licking.
Bob took a real licking in the stock market.
Tom took a licking in the fight he was in.

senses.definition: Don’t act so stupid!; Get a purpose for existing!
examples: Hey, stupid! You want to get run over? Get a life!
You worthless jerk! Get a life!

headword: get a line on someone or something

senses.definition: to get an idea on how to locate someone or something; to find out about someone who can help find someone or something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I got a line on a book that might help explain what you want to know.
Sally has a line on someone who could help you fix up your apartment.

senses.definition: to dress (oneself) up.
examples: I have to get all dolled up for the dance tonight.
I just love to get dolled up in my best clothes.

headword: get a load off one’s feet
altForms: take a load off one’s feet

senses.definition: to sit down; to enjoy the results of sitting down.
examples: Come in, John. Sit down and take a load off your feet.
Yes, I need to get a load off my feet. I’m really tired.

headword: get a load off one’s mind

senses.definition: to say what one is thinking; to talk about what is troubling one; to speak one’s mind.
examples: He sure talked a long time. I guess he had to get a load off his mind.
You aren’t going to like what I’m going to say, but I have to get a load off my mind.

headword: get a load of someone or something

senses.definition: look at someone or something.
examples: Get a load of that guy. Have you ever seen such arrogance?
Get a load of that car. It’s got real wire wheels.

senses.definition: to grow older.
examples: Grandfather is getting along in years.
Yes, he’s really getting along.

senses.definition: to be able to afford to live on very little money.
examples: For the last two years, we have had to get along on a shoestring.
With so little money, it’s hard to get along.

senses.definition: to manage without someone or something; to do without someone or something.
examples: I don’t think I can get along without my secretary.
My secretary just quit, and I don’t think I will be able to get along.
I like steak, but I can’t afford it. I guess I’ll have to get along without.

headword: get a lump in one’s throat

senses.definition: to have the feeling of something in one’s throat—as if one were going to cry.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Whenever they play the national anthem, I get a lump in my throat.
I have a lump in my throat because I’m frightened.

senses.definition: to hear or listen to a great amount of discussion, criticism, or complaint.
examples: She was really mad about something, and I sure got an earful.
Sue was standing around the corner while Jim and Mary were arguing and got an earful.

headword: get an eyeful (of someone or something)

senses.definition: to see everything; to see a shocking or surprising sight.
examples: The office door opened for a minute and I got an eyeful of the interior.
Mary got an eyeful of the company’s extravagant spending when she peeked into the conference room.

senses.definition: to have to rethink something because one was wrong the first time.
senses.notes: Folksy. Think is a noun here. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: She’s quite wrong. She’s got another think coming if she wants to walk in here like that.
You have another guess coming if you think you can treat me like that!

senses.definition: to become nervous and agitated.
senses.notes: Refers to the agitation caused by ants crawling into one’s pants. Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I always get ants in my pants before a test.
I wonder if all actors get ants in their pants before they go on stage.

senses.definition: to accept a piece of paper allowing one to see an event—which has been canceled—at a later time.
senses.notes: Originally said of sporting events that had to be canceled because of rain. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The game was canceled because of the storm, but we all got rain checks on it.
I didn’t take a rain check because I’m leaving town for a month.

senses.definition: to accept (or request) a reissuance of an invitation at a later date.
senses.notes: Said to someone who has invited you to something that you cannot attend now, but would like to attend at a later time.
examples: We would love to come to your house, but we are busy next Saturday. Could we take a rain check on your kind invitation?
Oh, yes. You have a rain check that’s good anytime you can come by and visit.

senses.definition: to accept a piece of paper that allows one to purchase an item on sale at a later date.
senses.notes: Stores issue these pieces of paper when they run out of specially priced sale merchandise.
examples: The store was all out of the shampoo they advertised, but I got a rain check.
Yes, you should always take a rain check so you can get it at the sale price later when they have more.

senses.definition: to receive unfair or bad treatment.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone a raw deal.
examples: Mary got a raw deal on her traffic ticket. She was innocent, but she had to pay a big fine.
I bought a used TV that worked for two days and then quit. I sure got a raw deal.
You sure had a raw deal.

senses.definition: to become recognized for being something.
senses.notes: Can be a good or a bad reputation. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: You’ll get a reputation as a cheater.
She once had a reputation as a singer.
Behave yourself, or you’ll get a reputation.
Unfortunately, Tom’s got a reputation.

senses.definition: to become recognized for doing something.
senses.notes: Often a bad reputation, as in the examples. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: You’ll get a reputation for cheating.
I don’t want to get a reputation.
He’s got a bad reputation.
I have a reputation for being honest.

headword: get a rise out of someone

senses.definition: to get a reaction from someone, usually anger or laughter.
examples: Mary really liked my joke. I knew I could get a rise out of her.
I got a rise out of him by telling him to go home.

senses.definition: to receive a general idea; to receive an estimate.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I need to get a rough idea of how many people will be there.
I don’t need to know exactly. Just get a rough idea.
Judy has got a rough idea about who’ll be there.
I have a rough idea. That’s good enough.

senses.definition: to be experienced; to know a lot about life.
senses.notes: Informal. Use with caution—especially with females—since this can also refer to sexual experience. See also have been around.
examples: That’s a hard question. I’ll ask Jane. She gets around.
John knows a lot about New York City. He gets around.

senses.definition: to find time to do something; to do something after a long delay.
senses.notes: Compare this with get (around) to something.
examples: I finally got around to buying a new coat.
It takes Sally years to get around to visiting her aunt.
I finally got around to doing the breakfast dishes.

headword: get a run for one’s money

senses.definition: to receive what one deserves, expects, or wants.
senses.notes: See also give one a run for one’s money.
examples: I get a run for my money at a high school football game.
I get a run for my money in the stock market.

senses.definition: to receive a challenge.
examples: Bob got a run for his money when he tried to convince Mary to go to college.
Bill got a run for his money playing cards with John.

senses.definition: to receive a beating.
examples: The boxer took a shellacking and lost the fight.
I got a shellacking when I broke the window.

senses.definition: to be beaten—as in sports.
examples: Our team played well, but got a shellacking anyway.
I practiced my tennis game so I wouldn’t take a shellacking in the tournament.

headword: get a slap on the wrist

senses.definition: to get a light punishment (for doing something wrong).
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone a slap on the wrist.
examples: He created quite a disturbance, but he only got a slap on the wrist.
I thought I’d get a slap on the wrist for speeding, but I got fined $200.
She had a slap on the wrist about that before.

senses.definition: to receive help starting one’s car.
examples: My car is stalled. I need to get a start.
I got my car going. I got a jump from John.

senses.definition: to receive training or a big opportunity in beginning one’s career.
senses.notes: The same as get one’s start. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: She got a start in show business in Cincinnati.
She had a start when she was only four.

headword: get a taste of one’s own medicine

senses.definition: to receive difficulties of the same kind that one has been causing other people.
senses.notes: [for one] Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also dose of one’s own medicine.
examples: Now you see how it feels to have someone call you names! You are getting a taste of your own medicine!
John, who is often rude and abrupt with people, was devastated when the teacher treated him rudely. He doesn’t like having a taste of his own medicine.

senses.definition: to receive a severe scolding.
senses.notes: Folksy. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone a tongue-lashing.
examples: I really got a tongue-lashing when I got home.
Ted will have a tongue-lashing at home.
I never had a tongue-lashing like that before.

senses.definition: to do something bad and not get punished or found out.
examples: Tom did it again and didn’t get punished. He’s always getting away with murder.
Just because she’s so popular, she thinks she can get away with anything.
You’ll never get away with it.

senses.definition: to learn about someone almost accidentally.
examples: The boss got a whiff of the problems in the accounting department.
No one will get a whiff of your trouble with the police. I’ll see to that.

senses.definition: to manage to say something when other people are talking and ignoring you.
examples: It was such an exciting conversation that I could hardly get a word in edgewise.
Mary talks so fast that nobody can get a word in edgeways.

senses.definition: to repay one for a bad deed; to get even (with someone).
senses.notes: Have back at someone is informal or folksy. Compare this with have at someone or something at get at someone or something.
examples: Tom called me a jerk, but I’ll get back at him.
I don’t know how I’ll get back, but I will.
Just wait. I’ll have back at you!

senses.definition: to start being social with people again after a period of being by oneself; to start dating again, especially after a divorce or breakup with a lover.
examples: Sally is anxious to get back into circulation after the nasty divorce she went through.
Todd could not bring himself to get back into circulation after the death of his wife.

senses.definition: to return to one’s workplace, such as after a vacation or a period of illness.
senses.notes: Refers to harnessing a horse so it can return to work.
examples: I am not at all anxious to get back into harness after spending two weeks in Mexico.
Tom was eager to get back into harness after his illness.

senses.definition: to become independent again; to become able to get around again.
senses.notes: Note the variations with own and two in the examples.
examples: He was sick for a while, but now he’s getting back on his feet.
My parents helped a lot when I lost my job. I’m glad I’m back on my own feet now.
It feels great to be back on my own two feet again.

senses.definition: to continue talking with someone (at a later time); to find out information and tell it to a person (at a later time).
examples: I don’t have the answer to that question right now. Let me find out and get back to you.
Okay. Please try to get back early tomorrow.

senses.definition: to improve.
examples: I had a bad cold, but it’s getting better.
Business was bad last week, but it’s getting better.
I’m sorry you’re ill. I hope you get better.

senses.definition: to start working; to work harder or faster.
examples: The boss is coming. You’d better get busy.
I’ve got to get busy and clean this house up.
Come on, everybody. Let’s get busy and get this job done.

senses.definition: to get a nervous feeling in one’s stomach.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give one butterflies in one’s stomach.
examples: Whenever I have to go on stage, I get butterflies in my stomach.
She always has butterflies in her stomach before a test.

senses.definition: to be overcome by emotion or enthusiasm (in one’s thinking or actions).
senses.notes: Also literal when someone or something is transported away.
examples: Calm down, Jane. Don’t get carried away.
Here, Bill. Take this money and go to the candy store, but don’t get carried away.

senses.definition: to be close friends with someone; to get to know someone well.
examples: I would really like to get close to Jane, but she’s so unfriendly.
We talked for hours and hours, but I never felt that we were getting close.
It’s very hard to get next to someone who won’t talk to you.

senses.definition: to almost equal something; to be almost as good as something.
examples: I practiced and practiced, but my bowling couldn’t get close to Mary’s.
Her performance was so good that I couldn’t get close.

senses.definition: to become timid or frightened; to have one’s feet seem to freeze with fear.
examples: I usually get cold feet when I have to speak in public.
John got cold feet and wouldn’t run in the race.

senses.definition: to get moving; to get busy.
examples: Let’s go. Come on, get cracking!
Move it! We don’t have all day. Let’s get cracking!
We’ll never get finished if you don’t get cracking.

senses.definition: to receive praise or recognition for one’s role in something.
senses.notes: Especially with a lot of, much, etc., as in the examples below.
examples: Mary should get a lot of credit for the team’s success.
Each of the team captains should get credit.

senses.definition: to begin to talk about important things; to get down to business.
examples: Let’s get down to brass tacks. We’ve wasted too much time chatting.
Don’t you think that it’s about time to get down to brass tacks?

senses.definition: to begin to get serious; to begin to negotiate or conduct business.
examples: All right, everyone. Let’s get down to business. There has been enough playing around.
When the president and vice president arrive, we can get down to business.
They’re here. Let’s get down to work.

senses.definition: to begin to discuss specific matters; to get down to business.
examples: When we’ve finished the general discussion, we’ll get down to cases.
Now that everyone is here, we can get down to cases.

senses.definition: to begin doing some kind of work in earnest.
examples: I have to get down to my typing.
John, you get in here this minute and get down to that homework!

senses.definition: to begin to talk about things that matter; to get to the truth.
examples: The judge told the lawyer that the time had come to get down to the facts.
Let’s get down to the facts, Mrs. Brown. Where were you on the night of January 16?

senses.definition: to get down to the facts; to get down to cases.
examples: Stop fooling around. Get down to the nitty-gritty.
Let’s stop wasting time. We have to get down to the nitty-gritty.

senses.definition: to repay someone’s bad deed; to get back (at someone).
examples: Bill hit Bob, and Bob got even with Bill by hitting him back.
Some people always have to get even.

senses.definition: to become overly bold or impertinent with someone.
examples: When I tried to kiss Mary, she slapped me and shouted, “Don’t get fresh with me!”
I can’t stand people who get fresh.

senses.definition: to feel prickly or become bumpy due to cold, fear, or excitement.
senses.notes: [for one’s skin] Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: When he sings, I get goose bumps.
I never get goose pimples.
That really scared her. Now she’s got goose pimples.

senses.definition: to have one’s hair turn gray from stress or frustration.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’m getting gray hair because I have three teenage boys.
Oh, Tom, stop it! I’m going to get gray hairs.
I have gray hairs from raising four kids.

senses.definition: to bother or irritate someone.
examples: Billy is always getting in his mother’s hair.
I wish you’d stop getting in my hair.

senses.definition: to get into difficulty or confusion.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with get out of a mess.
examples: Try to keep from getting into a mess.
“Hello, Mom,” said John on the telephone. “I’m at the police station. I got into a jam.”

senses.definition: to begin to argue with someone.
examples: Let’s try to discuss this calmly. I don’t want to get into an argument with you.
Tom got into an argument with John.
Tom and John got into an argument.
Let’s not get into an argument.

senses.definition: to move into the peak of activity; to start moving fast or efficiently.
examples: In the summer months, things really get into full swing around here.
We go skiing in the mountains each winter. Things get into high gear there in November.

senses.definition: to get into trouble or difficulty; to get involved in something that is complicated or troublesome.
examples: When you start trying to build your own computer, you are getting into hot water.
When Fred was caught cheating on his exam, he got into hot water.

senses.definition: to try to be part of whatever is going on.
senses.notes: Refers to someone trying to get on stage and participate in a performance.
examples: I can do this by myself. There is no need for you to get into the act.
Everyone wants to get into the act. Please let us do it. We don’t need your help!

headword: get into the swing of things

senses.definition: to join into the routine or the activities.
examples: Come on, Bill. Try to get into the swing of things.
John just couldn’t seem to get into the swing of things.

senses.definition: to communicate with someone; to telephone or write to someone.
senses.notes: See also keep in touch (with someone).
examples: I have to get in touch with John and ask him to come over for a visit.
Yes, you must try to get in touch.

senses.definition: to become associated with someone.
examples: Sally is getting involved with Bill. They’ve been seeing a lot of each other.
I hope they don’t get too involved.
He didn’t want his son involved with the gangs.

senses.definition: to become fit or organized; to organize one’s thinking; to become relaxed and rational.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Bill seems to be acting more normal now. I think he’s getting it all together.
I hope he gets it together soon. His life is a mess.
When Jane has it all together, she really makes sense.
Sally is a lovely person. She really has it together.

senses.definition: to receive something bad, such as punishment or criticism.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with get it.
examples: I don’t know why I should get it in the neck. I didn’t break the window.
Bill got it in the neck for being late.

senses.definition: to become lost; to lose one’s way.
examples: We got lost on the way home.
Follow the path, or you might get lost.

senses.definition: Go away!; Stop being an annoyance!
examples: Stop bothering me. Get lost!
Get lost! I don’t need your help.
Stop following me. Get lost!

senses.definition: to become angry at someone or something.
examples: Don’t get mad at me. I didn’t do it.
I got mad at my car. It won’t start.
I get mad every time I think about it.

senses.definition: to muster all one’s physical and mental resources in order to do something.
examples: Come on, Bill. If you’re going to lift your end of the piano, you’re going to have to get mad at it.
The sergeant keep yelling, “Work, work! Push, push! Come on, you guys, get mad!”

senses.definition: to become united as husband and wife.
examples: Bill and Sally got married when they were in college.
We got married in Texas just after we graduated from college.

senses.definition: to get confused.
examples: I get mixed-up easily whenever I take a test.
Sorry, I didn’t say the right thing. I got mixed-up.

senses.definition: not to make progress; to get nowhere.
examples: I can’t seem to make any progress. No matter what I do, I’m just getting nowhere fast.
Come on. Speed up this car. We’re getting nowhere fast.

senses.definition: to receive very little punishment (for doing something wrong).
senses.notes: See also get a slap on the wrist.
examples: It was a serious crime, but Mary got off easy.
Billy’s punishment was very light. Considering what he did, he got off lightly.

headword: get off on the wrong foot
altForms: get off to a bad start

senses.definition: to start something (such as a friendship) with negative factors.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also get off; be off on the wrong foot; be off to a bad start; start off on the wrong foot.
examples: Bill and Tom got off on the wrong foot. They had a minor car accident just before they were introduced.
Let’s work hard to be friends. I hate to get off on the wrong foot.
Bill is getting off to a bad start in geometry. He failed the first test.

senses.definition: Leave someone alone!; Stop picking on someone!
examples: I’m tired of your criticism, Bill. Get off my case!
Quit picking on her. Get off her back!
Leave me alone! Get off my tail!

senses.definition: to free oneself from an obligation.
examples: They have asked you to lead the parade, and I don’t think you can get off the hook.
I couldn’t get off the hook no matter how much I pleaded.

headword: get off to a flying start

senses.definition: to have a very successful beginning to something.
examples: The new business got off to a flying start with those export orders.
We shall need a large donation from the local citizens if the charity is to get off to a flying start.

senses.definition: to become less haughty.
examples: You should get off your high horse and pay attention more to what people think.
If she would get off her high horse and try to be human, everyone would like her better.

senses.definition: to get oneself organized, especially mentally.
senses.notes: Slang. Originally from theatrical use. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’m so confused about life. I have to get my act together.
Bill Smith had a hard time getting his act together after his mother’s death.
Mary really has her act together. She handles herself very well.

senses.definition: to determine where one is; to determine how one is oriented to one’s immediate environment.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: After he fell, it took Ted a few minutes to get his bearings.
I don’t have my bearings yet. Wait a minute.

senses.definition: to get a reprimand; to get the punishment one deserves.
examples: Tom is always insulting people, but he finally got his comeuppance. Bill hit him.
I hope I don’t get my comeuppance like that.

headword: get one’s ducks in a row

senses.definition: to get something into order or into line; to put one’s affairs in order; to get things ready.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. Refers to a mother duck leading a row of ducklings.
examples: Jane is organized. She really has all her ducks in a row.
You can’t hope to go into a company and sell something until you get your ducks in a row.
As soon as you people get your ducks in a row, we’ll leave.

headword: get (oneself) into a stew (over someone or something)

senses.definition: to be worried or upset about someone or something.
examples: Please don’t get yourself into a stew over Walter.
Liz is the kind of person who gets into a stew over someone else’s business.

headword: get one’s feet on the ground
altForms: have one’s feet on the ground

senses.definition: to get firmly established or reestablished.
examples: He’s new at the job, but soon he’ll get his feet on the ground.
Her productivity will improve after she gets her feet on the ground again.

senses.definition: to begin something; to have one’s first experience of something.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Of course he can’t do the job right. He’s hardly got his feet wet yet.
I’m looking forward to learning to drive. I can’t wait to get behind the steering wheel and get my feet wet.
I’ve only been at this job for a month, and I don’t have my feet wet yet.

senses.definition: to have a bad experience.
senses.notes: Also literal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I had my fingers burned the last time I did this.
I tried that once before and got my fingers burned. I won’t try it again.
If you go swimming and get your fingers burned, you won’t want to swim again.

headword: get one’s foot in the door

senses.definition: to achieve a favorable position (for further action); to take the first step in a process.
senses.notes: Refers to people selling things from door to door who block the door with a foot so it cannot be closed on them. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I think I could get the job if I could only get my foot in the door.
It pays to get your foot in the door. Try to get an appointment with the boss.
I have a better chance now that I have my foot in the door.

senses.definition: to become involved with something illegal; to do a shameful thing; to do something that is beneath one.
examples: The mayor would never get his hands dirty by giving away political favors.
I will not dirty my hands by breaking the law.
Sally felt that to talk to the hobo was to soil her hands.

headword: get one’s hands on someone or something
altForms: lay one’s hands on someone or something

senses.definition: to get (a)hold of someone or something; to get someone or something in one’s grasp.
senses.notes: Informal. Sometimes said in anger, as if one may wish to do harm.
examples: Just wait until I get my hands on Tom. I’ll really give him something to think about.
When I lay my hands on my book again, I’ll never lend it to anyone.

senses.definition: to get ahead of one’s problems; to catch up with one’s work or responsibilities.
senses.notes: Also literal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I can’t seem to get my head above water. Work just keeps piling up.
I’ll be glad when I have my head above water.

senses.definition: to get what one deserves.
examples: I feel better now that Jane got her just deserts. She really insulted me.
Bill got back exactly the treatment that he gave out. He got his just deserts.

senses.definition: to get something as bad as one deserves.
examples: The criminal who was sent to prison got his just rewards.
I am sure that when he died, he got his just reward.

senses.definition: to receive punishment.
senses.notes: Also literal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I got my knuckles rapped for whispering too much.
You will have your knuckles rapped if you are not careful.

senses.definition: to get everything that has been paid for; to get the best quality for the money paid.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Weigh that package of meat before you buy it. Be sure you’re getting your money’s worth.
I didn’t get my money’s worth with my new camera, so I took it back.
I will stay here and watch the movie over and over until I get my money’s worth.

headword: get one’s nose out of someone’s business

senses.definition: to stop interfering in someone else’s business; to mind one’s own business.
senses.notes: See also keep one’s nose out of someone’s business.
examples: Go away! Get your nose out of my business!
Bob just can’t seem to get his nose out of other people’s business.

headword: get one’s (own) way (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to have someone or something follow one’s plans; to control someone or something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The mayor got his way with the city council.
He seldom gets his own way.
How often do you have your way with your own money?
Parents usually have their way with their children.

senses.definition: to become accustomed to the movement of a ship at sea; to be able to walk steadily on the constantly rolling and pitching decks of a ship.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Jean was a little awkward at first, but in a few days she got her sea legs and was fine.
You may feel a little sick until you get your sea legs.
I will feel better when I have my sea legs.

senses.definition: for one’s breathing to become stabilized after exerting oneself for a short time.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: John was having a hard time running until he got his second wind.
Bill had to quit the race because he never got his second wind.
“At last,” thought Ann, “I have my second wind. Now I can really swim fast.”

senses.definition: to become more active or productive (after starting off slowly).
examples: I usually get my second wind early in the afternoon.
Mary is a better worker now that she has her second wind.

senses.definition: to receive the first major opportunity of one’s career.
examples: I had my start in painting when I was thirty.
She helped me get my start by recommending me to the manager.

senses.definition: to start on something seriously, especially a difficult task.
senses.notes: Informal. See also sink one’s teeth into something.
examples: Come on, Bill. You have to get your teeth into your biology.
I can’t wait to get my teeth into this problem.

senses.definition: to get fired.
senses.notes: Informal. See also give one one’s walking papers.
examples: Well, I’m through. I got my walking papers today.
They are closing down my department. I guess I’ll get my walking papers soon.

senses.definition: to get confused about something.
senses.notes: Informal. As if one’s brain were an electrical circuit. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: You don’t know what you are talking about. You really have your wires crossed!
Joan got her wires crossed about who arrived first. It was Bob, not Gary.

senses.definition: to pull oneself together for action; to set one’s mind to work, especially in a time of stress.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Let me get my wits about me so I can figure this out.
I don’t have my wits about me at this time of the morning.

senses.definition: to irritate someone.
examples: Please stop whistling. It’s getting on my nerves.
All this arguing is getting on their nerves.

senses.definition: to join the popular side (of an issue); to take a popular position.
examples: You really should get on the bandwagon. Everyone else is.
Jane has always had her own ideas about things. She’s not the kind of person to jump on the bandwagon.

headword: get on the good side of someone

senses.definition: to get in someone’s favor.
examples: You had better behave properly if you want to get on the good side of Mary.
If you want to get on the good side of your teacher, you must do your homework.

headword: get out from under someone or something

senses.definition: to get free of someone’s control.
examples: Mary wanted to get out from under her mother.
We started our own business because we needed to get out from under our employer.

senses.definition: to get free of a burdensome problem.
examples: I can’t go out tonight until I get out from under this pile of homework.
There is so much work to do! I don’t know when I’ll ever get out from under it.

senses.definition: to get free from a problem or a bad situation.
examples: Would you lend me five dollars? I need it to get out of a jam.
I need some help getting out of a jam.

senses.definition: to get free of a bad situation.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with this, such a, etc. See the examples. Compare this with get into a mess.
examples: How can anyone get out of a mess like this?
Please help me get out of this mess!

senses.definition: to move out of the path or route.
examples: Will you please get out of the way?
The dog got out of Jane’s way just before she stepped on it.

headword: get out while the getting is good

senses.definition: to leave a place while it is still possible to do so; to withdraw from a place, position, or some organization at an opportune time.
examples: The party was getting noisy enough that one of the neighbors was bound to call the police, so we left. We always get out while the getting is good.
Everyone at my office was being required to do more and more work. I decided to get out while the getting was good. I quit.

senses.definition: to use physical force against someone.
examples: The coach got in trouble for getting physical with some members of the team.
When the suspect wouldn’t cooperate, the police were forced to get physical.

senses.definition: to touch someone in lovemaking.
examples: I’ve heard that Bill tends to get physical with his dates.
I don’t care if he gets physical—within reason.

senses.definition: to prepare to do something.
examples: Get ready to jump!
It’s time to get ready to go to work.
It’s time to get ready.

senses.definition: to become serious (about something), usually after a powerful experience; to develop a strong religious belief.
senses.notes: Folksy. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’ve always had religion. I don’t need a crisis to make me get it.
When I had an automobile accident, I really got religion. Now I’m a very safe driver.
Soldiers often say they got religion in the midst of a battle.

headword: get rid of someone or something

senses.definition: to get free of someone or something; to dispose of or destroy someone or something.
examples: I’m trying to get rid of Mr. Smith. He’s bothering me.
I’ll be happy when I get rid of my old car.

senses.definition: to do something immediately.
examples: I know it has to be done to-day. I’ll get right on it.
Please get right on these reports as soon as possible.

senses.definition: to get started.
examples: Come on. It’s time to leave. Let’s get rolling!
Bill, it’s 6:30. Time to get up and get rolling!

headword: get second thoughts about someone or something

senses.definition: to have new doubts about someone or something.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’m beginning to get second thoughts about Tom.
Tom is getting second thoughts about it, too.
We now have second thoughts about going to Canada.

senses.definition: get ready; get organized.
senses.notes: Also with be, as in the examples below.
examples: We are going to start. Please get set.
We are set. Let’s go.
Hurry up and get set!

senses.definition: to become ill (perhaps with vomiting).
examples: I got sick and couldn’t go to school.
My whole family got sick with the flu.

senses.definition: to vomit.
examples: Mommy, the dog just got sick on the carpet.
Bill got sick in the hallway.
