senses.definition: to become diverted from one’s task; to start off on a second task before the first one is finished.
examples: I’m sorry the work is not completed. I got sidetracked.
Pay attention to what you are doing and don’t get sidetracked.

senses.definition: to depress someone; to make someone sad.
examples: Try not to let all your problems get you down.
She is very cheerful and practically nothing gets her down.

senses.definition: to free someone from an obligation.
senses.notes: Informal. When someone is omitted, this refers to oneself.
examples: Thanks for getting me off the hook. I didn’t want to attend that meeting.
I couldn’t get off the hook by myself.

senses.definition: to manage to swallow something, especially something large or unpleasant.
examples: The pill was huge, but I got it down.
It was the worst food I have ever had, but I got it down somehow.

senses.definition: to depress a person; to make a person very sad.
senses.notes: [with someone] Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: My dog ran away, and it really got me down.
Oh, that’s too bad. Don’t let it get you down.
All my troubles really have me down.

headword: get someone out of a jam

senses.definition: to free someone from a problem or a bad situation.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with in a jam.
examples: I like John. He got me out of a jam once.
I would be glad to help get you out of a jam.

senses.definition: to be put at the mercy of someone; to get control over someone.
senses.notes: [for someone] Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: He got me over a barrel, and I had to do what he said.
Ann will do exactly what I say. I’ve got her over a barrel.
All right, John. You’ve got me under your thumb. What do you want me to do?

senses.definition: to make someone get angry.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Now, don’t get your dander up. Calm down.
I insulted him and really got his hackles up.
Bob had his Irish up all day yesterday. I don’t know what was wrong.
She really got her back up when I asked her for money.
Now, now, don’t get your hackles up. I didn’t mean any harm.

senses.definition: to get someone to listen (to you).
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. Compare this with bend someone’s ear.
examples: He got my ear and talked for an hour.
While I have your ear, I’d like to tell you about something I’m selling.

senses.definition: to irritate someone; to annoy and arouse someone to anger.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to get your goat.
Jean got Sally’s goat and Sally made quite a fuss about it.
Tom really had her goat for a while.

senses.definition: to convey information to someone; to teach someone.
examples: I’m trying to get this across to you. Please pay attention.
I’ll keep trying until I get it across.

senses.definition: to tell something that has been bothering you.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I have to get this off my chest. I broke your window with a stone.
I knew I’d feel better when I had that off my chest.

headword: get something out in the open

senses.definition: to make something public; to stop hiding a fact or a secret.
examples: We had better get this out in the open before the press gets wind of it.
I’ll feel better when it’s out in the open. I can’t stand all of this secrecy.

headword: get something out of one’s system

senses.definition: to get something like food or medicine out of one’s body, usually through natural elimination.
examples: He’ll be more active once he gets the medicine out of his system.
My baby, Mary, ate applesauce and has been crying for three hours. She’ll stop when she gets the applesauce out of her system.

senses.definition: to be rid of the desire to do something; to do something that you have been wanting to do so that you aren’t bothered by wanting to do it anymore.
examples: I bought a new car. I’ve been wanting to for a long time. I’m glad I finally got that out of my system.
I can’t get it out of my system! I want to go back to school and earn a degree.

senses.definition: to have something settled or finished.
senses.notes: See also wrap something up. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’ll take the contract to the mayor tomorrow morning. I’ll get the whole deal sewed up by noon.
Don’t worry about the car loan. I’ll have it sewed up in time to make the purchase.
I’ll get the loan wrapped up, and you’ll have the car this week.

senses.definition: to understand something clearly.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Now get this straight. You’re going to fail history.
Let me get this straight. I’m supposed to go there in the morning?
Let me make sure I have this straight.

headword: get something through someone’s thick skull
altForms: get something into someone’s thick head

senses.definition: to manage to get someone, including oneself, to understand something.
examples: He can’t seem to get it through his thick skull.
If I could get this into my thick head once, I’d remember it.

senses.definition: to eat or drink something.
senses.notes: This means the food goes into one’s stomach and is under one’s belt. Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’d feel a lot better if I had a cool drink under my belt.
Come in out of the cold and get a nice warm meal under your belt.

senses.definition: to learn something well; to assimilate some information.
examples: I have to study tonight. I have to get a lot of algebra under my belt.
Now that I have my lessons under my belt, I can rest easy.

senses.definition: to get something started.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The time has come to get this meeting under way.
Now that the president has the meeting under way, I can relax.

senses.definition: to be obsessed with show business; to be stage-struck.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Many young people get stars in their eyes at this age.
Ann has stars in her eyes. She wants to go to Hollywood.

senses.definition: to achieve a position superior to someone else.
senses.notes: The word the can be replaced with an. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also take advantage of someone or something.
examples: Toward the end of the race, I got the advantage over Mary.
She’d had an advantage over me since the start of the competition.
I got an edge on Sally, too, and she came in second.
It’s speed that counts. You can have the edge over everyone, but if you don’t have speed, you lose.

senses.definition: to be ignored or sent away.
senses.notes: See also give someone the air.
examples: Whenever I get around Tom, I end up getting the air.
I hate to get the air. It makes me feel unwanted.

senses.definition: to start something; to get some process going.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: If I could just get the ball rolling, then other people would help.
Who else would start the ball rolling?
I had the ball rolling, but no one helped me with the project.
Ann set the ball rolling, but didn’t follow through.

headword: get the benefit of the doubt

senses.definition: to receive a judgment in your favor when the evidence is neither for you nor against you.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone the benefit of the doubt.
examples: In my math course, I was right between a B and an A. I got the benefit of the doubt—an A.
I thought I should have had the benefit of the doubt, but the judge made me pay a fine.

senses.definition: to win out over someone in a competition or bargain.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Bill got the best of John in the boxing match.
I tried to get the better of John, but he won anyway.
I set out to have the better of Sally, but I didn’t have enough skill.

senses.definition: to become sad or depressed.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: You’ll have to excuse Bill. He has the blues tonight.
I get the blues every time I hear that song.

senses.definition: to be sent away (from somewhere); to be dismissed from one’s employment; to be kicked out (of a place).
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the sack; give someone the boot.
examples: I guess I wasn’t dressed well enough to go in there. I got the boot.
I’ll work harder at my job today. I nearly got the boot yesterday.

senses.definition: to be ignored or sent away; to be rejected.
examples: Don’t talk to Tom. You’ll just get the brush-off.
I went up to her and asked for a date, but I got the brush-off.

senses.definition: to be ignored; to be rejected.
senses.notes: Informal. See also give someone the cold shoulder.
examples: If you invite her to a party, you’ll just get the cold shoulder.
I thought that Sally and I were friends, but lately I’ve been getting the cold shoulder.

senses.definition: to become frightened; to become uneasy.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I get the creeps when I see that old house.
I really had the willies when I went down into the basement.

senses.definition: to have a day free from working.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also take the day off.
examples: The next time I get a day off, we’ll go to the zoo.
I have the day off. Let’s go to the zoo.

senses.definition: to receive a severe scolding.
examples: Bill is always getting the devil about something.
I’m late. If I don’t get home soon, I’ll catch hell!
I caught the devil yesterday for being late.

senses.definition: to understand the general idea of something.
examples: I knew enough German to get the drift of this article.
I don’t get the drift of what you’re trying to tell me.

senses.definition: to get a good understanding of the facts; to make sure that all the facts are accurate and properly stated.
examples: Ask a lot of questions and get all of the facts straight.
Please be sure you get the facts straight before you make a decision.

senses.definition: to receive official permission to address the audience.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: When I get the floor, I’ll make a short speech.
The last time you had the floor, you talked for an hour.

senses.definition: to be sent away; to be rejected.
senses.notes: Slang. See also give someone the gate.
examples: I thought he liked me, but I got the gate.
I was afraid I’d get the gate, and I was right.

senses.definition: to receive an overly friendly welcome; to receive insincere attention.
examples: Whenever I go into that store, I get the glad hand.
I hate to go to a party and get the glad hand.

senses.definition: to receive a signal to start or continue.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone the go-ahead.
examples: We have to wait here until we have the go-ahead.
I hope we get the green light on our project soon.

senses.definition: to find out something potentially damaging or embarrassing about someone.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: John beat me unfairly in tennis, but I’ll get even. I’ll get the goods on him and his cheating.
The authorities have the goods on Mr. Smith. He has been selling worthless land again.

senses.definition: to learn how to do something; to learn how something works.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: As soon as I get the hang of this computer, I’ll be able to work faster.
Now that I have the hang of starting the car in cold weather, I won’t have to get up so early.

senses.definition: to receive considerable pressure to buy or accept (something).
examples: I won’t go to that store again. I really got the hard sell.
You’ll probably get the hard sell if you go to a used-car dealer.

senses.definition: to receive a prearranged signal.
senses.notes: Often refers to a hand signal or some other visual signal.
examples: When I got the high sign, I pulled cautiously out into the roadway.
The train’s engineer got the high sign and began to move the train out of the station.

senses.definition: to get the advantage (over someone) because of special connections, special knowledge, or favoritism.
senses.notes: The inside track is the shortest track in an oval race track that is divided into tracks. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: If I could get the inside track, I could win the contract.
The boss likes me. Since I have the inside track, I’ll probably be the new office manager.

senses.definition: to do something before someone; to get ahead of someone.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I got the jump on Tom and got a place in line ahead of him.
We’ll have to work hard to get the contract, because they have the jump on us.

senses.definition: to laugh at or ridicule someone who has laughed at or ridiculed you; to put someone in the same bad position that you were once in; to turn the tables (on someone).
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also He who laughs last, laughs longest.
examples: John laughed when I got a D on the final exam. I got the last laugh, though. He failed the course.
Mr. Smith said I was foolish when I bought an old building. I had the last laugh when I sold it a month later for twice what I paid for it.

senses.definition: to get to make the final point (in an argument); to get to make the final decision (in some matter).
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The boss gets the last word in hiring.
Why do you always have to have the final word in an argument?

senses.definition: to hurry; to move faster.
senses.notes: Slang. This means to get the lead weights out of your pants so you can move faster.
examples: Come on, you guys. Get the lead out!
If you’re going to sell cars, you’re going to have to shake the lead out.

headword: get the low-down (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to receive the full story about someone or something.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone the low-down (on someone or something).
examples: I need to get the low-down on John. Is he still an accountant?
Sally wants to get the low-down on the new expressway. Please tell her all about it.
Now I have the low-down on the princess!

senses.definition: to get chosen.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: The manager is going to pick the new sales manager. I think Ann will get the nod.
I had the nod for captain of the team, but I decided not to do it.

senses.definition: to get thrown out (of a place); to get dismissed (from one’s employment).
senses.notes: Informal. From nautical use, where sailors used heave-ho to coordinate hard physical labor. One sailor called “Heave-ho,” and all the sailors would pull at the same time on the ho. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone or something the (old) heave-ho.
examples: I went there to buy a record album, but I got the old heave-ho. That’s right. They threw me out!
They fired a number of people today, but I didn’t get the heave-ho.
John had the old heave-ho last week. Now he’s unemployed.

senses.definition: to receive a quick visual examination.
senses.notes: Note the variations in the examples. See also give someone the once-over.
examples: Every time John walks by I get the once-over. Does he like me?
I went to the doctor yesterday, but I only had a once-over.
I wanted a complete examination, not just a once-over.

senses.definition: to understand the whole situation.
examples: Okay, Bob. That’s the whole explanation. You get the picture?
Yes, I got the picture.

senses.definition: to receive very special treatment; to receive royal treatment.
senses.notes: This refers—sometimes literally—to the rolling out of a clean red carpet for someone to walk on. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off. See also give someone the red-carpet treatment; roll out the red carpet for someone.
examples: I love to go to fancy stores where I get the red-carpet treatment.
The queen expects to get the red-carpet treatment wherever she goes.

senses.definition: to receive a series of excuses, delays, and referrals.
examples: You’ll get the runaround if you ask to see the manager.
I hate it when I get the runaround.

senses.definition: to get fired; to be dismissed (from one’s employment).
senses.notes: Slang. See also give someone the ax.
examples: I got the sack yesterday. Now I have to find a new job.
I tried to work harder, but I got the ax anyway.

headword: get the shock of one’s life

senses.definition: to receive a serious (emotional) shock.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I opened the telegram and got the shock of my life.
I had the shock of my life when I won $5,000.

headword: get the short end of the stick
altForms: end up with the short end of the stick

senses.definition: to end up with less (than someone else); to end up cheated or deceived.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Why do I always get the short end of the stick? I want my fair share!
She’s unhappy because she has the short end of the stick again.
I hate to end up with the short end of the stick.

headword: get the show on the road

senses.definition: to get (something) started.
examples: Hurry up, you guys. Let’s get the show on the road.
If you don’t get the show on the road right now, we’ll never finish today.

senses.definition: to elude or escape (someone).
examples: We followed her for two blocks, and then got the slip.
The police got the slip, and the criminal got away.

senses.definition: to be questioned in great detail for a long period.
senses.notes: Slang. See also give someone the third degree.
examples: Why is it I get the third degree from you every time I come home late?
Poor Sally spent all night at the police station getting the third degree.

senses.definition: to get into a position superior to someone; to get the advantage of someone.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: John is always trying to get the upper hand on someone.
He never ends up having the upper hand, though.

senses.definition: to receive an explanation; to receive the final and authoritative explanation.
examples: I’m sorry, I didn’t get the word. I didn’t know the matter had been settled.
Now that I have gotten the message, I can be more effective in answering questions.

senses.definition: to receive a lot of something.
senses.notes: Slang. The works can be a lot of food, good treatment, bad treatment, etc. See also give someone the works.
examples: BILL: Shall we order a snack or a big meal? JANE: I’m hungry. Let’s get the works.
But, your honor. I shouldn’t get the works. I only drove too fast!

senses.definition: to reach someone; to manage to communicate to someone.
examples: I called her on the telephone time after time, but I couldn’t get through to her.
I tried every kind of communication, but I couldn’t get through.

senses.definition: to pass through (something).
examples: The crowd was so thick that I couldn’t get through to him.
I tried, but I couldn’t get through. The crowd was too heavy.

senses.definition: to make someone understand something; to get something through someone’s thick skull.
examples: Why don’t you try to understand me? What do I have to do to get through to you?
Can anybody get through, or are you just stubborn?
Ann is still too sick to understand what I’m saying. Maybe I can get through to her tomorrow.

senses.definition: to get finished with something.
senses.notes: Compare this with get through something.
examples: You can use this pencil when I get through with it.
Can I have the salt when you get through with it?

senses.definition: to receive a period of time that is free from employment.
senses.notes: Compare this with get the day off. See also take time off. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: I’ll have to get time off for jury duty.
I got time off to go downtown and shop.
I don’t have time off from work very often.

headword: get time off for good behavior

senses.definition: to have one’s prison sentence shortened because of good behavior.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Bob will get out of jail tomorrow rather than next week. He got time off for good behavior.
I know I will have time off for good behavior.

headword: get time to catch one’s breath

senses.definition: to find enough time to relax or behave normally.
senses.notes: Also literal. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: When things slow down around here, I’ll get time to catch my breath.
Sally was so busy she didn’t even have time to catch her breath.

headword: get to first base (with someone or something)
altForms: reach first base (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to make a major advance with someone or something.
senses.notes: Informal. First base refers to baseball.
examples: I wish I could get to first base with this business deal.
John adores Sally, but he can’t even reach first base with her. She won’t even speak to him.
He smiles and acts friendly, but he can’t get to first base.

senses.definition: to stand up.
examples: On a signal from the director, the singers got to their feet.
I was so weak, I could hardly get to my feet.

headword: get to the bottom of something

senses.definition: to get an understanding of the causes of something.
examples: We must get to the bottom of this problem immediately.
There is clearly something wrong here, and I want to get to the bottom of it.

headword: get to the heart of the matter
altForms: get at the heart of the matter

senses.definition: to get to the essentials of a matter.
examples: We have to stop wasting time and get to the heart of the matter.
You’ve been very helpful. You really seem to be able to get to the heart of the matter.

headword: get to the root of the problem

senses.definition: to gain an understanding of the causes or basis of a problem and propose a solution; to get to the bottom of something.
examples: It will take a little more study to get to the root of the problem.
Let’s stop avoiding the issue and get to the root of the problem.

senses.definition: to become firm with someone; to use physical force against someone.
senses.notes: Compare this with get physical (with someone).
examples: The teacher had to get tough with the class because the students were acting badly.
I’ve tried to get you to behave, but it looks like I’ll have to get tough.

senses.definition: to get a number of things against one; to be in a position where success is unlikely.
senses.notes: From baseball where one is “out” after three strikes. Also with have. See the note at get a big send-off.
examples: Poor Bob got two strikes against him when he tried to explain where he was last night.
I can’t win. I’ve got two strikes against me before I start.

senses.definition: to bother or irritate someone.
examples: John is so annoying. He really gets under my skin.
I know he’s bothersome, but don’t let him get under your skin.

senses.definition: to start going; to start.
senses.notes: The word get can be replaced with be. Compare this with get something under way.
examples: The ship is leaving soon. It’s about to get under way.
Let us get our journey under way.
I’m glad our project is under way.

headword: get up enough nerve (to do something)

senses.definition: to get brave enough to do something.
examples: I could never get up enough nerve to sing in public.
I’d do it if I could get up enough nerve, but I’m shy.

headword: get up on the wrong side of the bed
altForms: get out of the wrong side of the bed

senses.definition: to get up in the morning in a bad mood.
examples: What’s wrong with you? Did you get up on the wrong side of the bed today?
Excuse me for being grouchy. I got out of the wrong side of the bed.

headword: get used to someone or something

senses.definition: to become accustomed to someone or something.
examples: I got used to being short many years ago.
John is nice, but I really can’t get used to him. He talks too much.

senses.definition: to become healthy again.
examples: Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well.
Hurry up and get well!

senses.definition: to become soaked with water.
examples: Get out of the rain or you’ll get wet.
Don’t get wet, or you’ll catch a cold.

senses.definition: to get what one deserves.
senses.notes: See also give one what’s coming to one.
examples: If you cheat, you’ll get in trouble. You’ll get what’s coming to you.
Billy got what was coming to him.

senses.definition: to hear about something; to receive information about something.
examples: I just got wind of your marriage. Congratulations.
Wait until the boss gets wind of this. Somebody is going to get in trouble.

senses.definition: to find out about someone or something; to see through the deception of someone or something.
examples: Watch out, John. Your friends are getting wise to your tricks.
John’s friends are getting wise. He had better watch out.

senses.definition: to get excited or emotionally distressed about something.
senses.notes: See also all worked up (over something).
examples: Please don’t get worked up over this matter.
They get worked up about these things very easily.
I try not to get worked up.

senses.definition: even the slightest chance; even the most insubstantial chance.
examples: She can’t do it. She doesn’t have a ghost of a chance.
There is just a ghost of a chance that I’ll be there on time.

senses.definition: to add ornament or decoration to something that is pleasing in its original state; to attempt to improve something that is already fine the way it is.
senses.notes: Often refers to flattery or exaggeration.
examples: Your house has lovely brickwork. Don’t paint it. That would be gilding the lily.
Oh, Sally. You’re beautiful the way you are. You don’t need makeup. You would be gilding the lily.

senses.definition: to get ready; to prepare oneself (for something).
examples: Well, I guess I had better gird up my loins and go to work.
Somebody has to do something about the problem. Why don’t you gird your loins and do something?

headword: give a good account of oneself

senses.definition: to do (something) well or thoroughly.
examples: John gave a good account of himself when he gave his speech last night.
Mary was not hungry, and she didn’t give a good account of herself at dinner.

headword: give (an) ear to someone or something
altForms: give one’s ear to someone or something

senses.definition: to listen to someone or to what someone is saying.
senses.notes: Compare this with get someone’s ear.
examples: I gave an ear to Mary so she could tell me her problems.
She wouldn’t give her ear to my story.
He gave ear to the man’s request.

headword: give as good as one gets

senses.definition: to give as much as one receives; to pay someone back in kind.
examples: John can take care of himself in a fight. He can give as good as he gets.
Sally usually wins a formal debate. She gives as good as she gets.

headword: give birth to someone or some creature

senses.definition: to bring a baby or other offspring into the world through birth.
examples: Mary gave birth to a lovely baby girl.
The raccoon gave birth to 6 little raccoons.

senses.definition: to give rise to or start something.
examples: The composer gave birth to a new kind of music.
They gave birth to a new view of language.

senses.definition: to chase someone or something.
examples: The dogs gave chase to the fox.
A mouse ran by, but the cat was too tired to give chase.
The police gave chase to the robber.

senses.definition: to believe something; to consider something believable.
examples: He tells lies. Don’t give credence to what he says.
Please don’t give credence to Mary. She doesn’t know what she’s talking about.

headword: give credit where credit is due

senses.definition: to give credit to someone who deserves it; to acknowledge or thank someone who deserves it.
examples: We must give credit where credit is due. Thank you very much, Sally.
Let’s give credit where credit is due. Mary is the one who wrote the report, not Jane.

senses.definition: to allow someone to be completely in charge (of something).
senses.notes: See also get a free hand (with someone or something).
examples: The boss gave the manager free rein with the new project.
The principal gave free rein to Mrs. Brown in her classes.

senses.definition: to retreat (literally or figuratively).
examples: When I argue with Mary, she never gives ground.
I approached the barking dog, but it wouldn’t give ground.

senses.definition: Stop talking and give your mouth a rest.
examples: Shut up, Bob! Give it a rest!
Give it a rest. You talk too much.

senses.definition: to make a motor or engine run faster; to rev up an engine.
senses.notes: Informal or slang. The her is often pronounced “er.”
examples: BILL:
How fast will this thing go? BOB: I’ll give it the gun and see.
Hurry up, driver. Give’er the gun. I’ve got to get there immediately.

senses.definition: Be patient.; In time, things will change for the better or for the worse.
examples: Things will get better. Don’t worry. Give it time.
Of course, things will improve. Give it time.

headword: Give one an inch, and one will take a mile.

senses.definition: A person who is granted a little of something (such as a reprieve or lenience) will want more.
examples: I told John he could turn in his paper one day late, but he turned it in three days late. Give him an inch, and he’ll take a mile.
First we let John borrow our car for a day. Now he wants to go on a two-week vacation. If you give him an inch, he’ll take a mile.

headword: give one a run for one’s money

senses.definition: to give one what one deserves, expects, or wants.
senses.notes: See also get a run for one’s money.
examples: High school football gives me a run for my money.
I invest in the stock market, and that really gives me a run for my money.

senses.definition: give one a challenge.
examples: That was some argument. Bill gave John a run for his money.
Tom likes to play cards with Mary because she always gives him a run for his money.

senses.definition: to set someone free; to divorce someone.
examples: Mrs. Brown wanted to give her husband his freedom.
Well, Tom, I hate to break it to you this way, but I have decided to give you your freedom.

senses.definition: to fire someone; to give someone the sack.
senses.notes: Informal. See also get one’s walking papers.
examples: Tom has proved unsatisfactory. I decided to give him his walking papers.
We might even give Sally her walking papers, too.

senses.definition: to cause something.
examples: The bad performance gave rise to many complaints.
The new law gave rise to violence in the cities.

senses.definition: to give someone a bit of excitement.
examples: John always gives me a bang.
The whole afternoon, with all its silliness, gave me a charge anyway.

senses.definition: to see someone off on a journey with celebration and encouragement.
senses.notes: See also get a big send-off.
examples: When I left for college, all my brothers and sisters came to the airport to give me a big send-off.
When the sailors left, everyone went down to the docks and gave them a big send-off.

senses.definition: to hit someone near the eye so that a dark bruise appears.
examples: John became angry and gave me a black eye.
The door began to swing closed as I approached and it gave me a black eye.

senses.definition: to harm the character or reputation of someone.
senses.notes: See also get a black eye
examples: The constant complaining gave the whole group a black eye.
His behavior gave him a black eye with the manager.

altForms: give a blank check to someone

senses.definition: to give someone freedom or permission to act as one wishes or thinks necessary.
senses.notes: Refers to a signed bank check with the amount left blank.
examples: He’s been given a blank check with regard to reorganizing the work force.
The manager has been given no instructions about how to train the staff. The owner just gave him a blank check.
Jean gave the decorator a blank check and said she wanted the whole house done.

senses.definition: to give someone a chance; to give someone another chance or a second chance.
examples: I’m sorry. Don’t send me home. Give me a break!
They gave me a nice break. They didn’t send me home.

senses.definition: to give someone a clever thought or idea.
examples: That gives me a bright idea!
Thank you for giving me a bright idea.

senses.definition: to give someone misleading instructions or guidance; to make a misleading suggestion.
senses.notes: Slang. Bum = false; phony. Steer = guidance, as in the steering of a car.
examples: Max gave Ted a bum steer and Ted ended up in the wrong town.
Someone gave me a bum steer and I paid far more than I needed to for a used car.

headword: give someone a clean bill of health

senses.definition: to pronounce someone well and healthy.
examples: The doctor gave Sally a clean bill of health.
I had hoped to be given a clean bill of health, but there was something wrong with my blood test results.

senses.definition: to frown or make an angry face at someone.
examples: Ann gave me a dirty look.
I gave her a dirty look back.

senses.definition: to give someone fair treatment.
examples: He’s unpleasant, but we have to give him a fair shake.
We give all our people a fair shake.

headword: give someone a fix on something

senses.definition: to tell someone the location of something.
senses.notes: See also get a fix on something.
examples: Please give me a fix on your location.
If you give the tower a fix on where you are, they can advise you on runway selection.

headword: give someone a free hand (with something)

senses.definition: to give someone complete control over something.
senses.notes: See also get a free hand (with someone or something).
examples: They gave me a free hand with the project.
I feel proud that they gave me a free hand. That means that they trust my judgment.

senses.definition: a scolding.
examples: After that dressing-down I won’t be late again.
The boss gave Fred a real dressing-down for breaking the machine.

senses.definition: to applaud someone for something.
examples: After she sang, they gave her a nice hand.
Come on, give them a hand. They did very well.

headword: give someone a hand (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to help someone with someone or something, often with the hands.
examples: Will somebody please give me a hand with this?
Can you give me a hand with the baby?

senses.definition: to give someone unnecessary difficulty.
examples: Please don’t give me a hard time.
The clerk gave me a hard time, so I walked out.

headword: give someone a head start (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to allow someone to start (something) earlier than someone else.
examples: They gave Bill a head start on everyone else, so he arrived early.
Please give me a head start on Charles. He is too fast!

senses.definition: to allow someone to start something earlier (than someone else).
examples: We’ll give you a head start on the project.
I need a head start on the test because I lost my glasses.

senses.definition: to beat someone.
examples: Bill give Tom a licking in a fight.
I’ll give you a good licking if you don’t leave me alone.

senses.definition: to lead someone on; to deceive someone with false talk.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to John. He gives everybody a line.
He’s always feeding us a line.

senses.definition: to scold someone.
examples: I was so mad at her! I really gave her an earful.
When I find that little jerk I’m going to give him an earful.

senses.definition: to tell someone a lot of gossip; to give someone a lot of information.
examples: I just talked to Margaret. Boy did she give me an earful.
She always gives me an earful. Otherwise I’d never know what’s going on.

senses.definition: to annoy or bother someone.
examples: Here comes Sally. Oh, she gives me a pain.
She’s such a pest. She really gives me a pain.

headword: give someone a piece of one’s mind

senses.definition: to bawl someone out; to tell someone off; to rebuke someone.
examples: I’ve had enough from John. I’m going to give him a piece of my mind.
Sally, stop it, or I’ll give you a piece of my mind.

headword: give someone a rain check (on something)

senses.definition: to give someone a piece of paper allowing admission to an event—which has been canceled—at a later time.
examples: The game was canceled because of the rain, but they gave everyone rain checks.
They were not able to show the film, so everyone was given a rain check.

senses.definition: to tell someone that an invitation to a social event will be reissued at a later date.
examples: We couldn’t go to the Smiths’ party, so they gave us a rain check.
We are sorry we cannot attend, but we would love for you to give us a rain check on another date.

senses.definition: to issue a piece of paper that allows one to purchase an item on sale at a later date.
examples: If you have no more of the sale shampoo, will you give me a rain check on it, please?
Can I have a rain check on this item? You don’t have enough of it in stock.

senses.definition: to treat someone unfairly or badly.
senses.notes: See also get a raw deal.
examples: The judge gave Mary a raw deal.
The students think that the teacher gave them a raw deal.

headword: give someone a reputation (as a something)

senses.definition: to cause someone to be known for being something.
examples: That evening gave him a reputation as a flirt.
Yes, it gave him a reputation.

headword: give someone a reputation (for doing something)

senses.definition: to cause someone to be known for doing something.
examples: Her excellent parties gave Jane a reputation for entertaining well.
You had better be careful or your behavior will give you a reputation.

senses.definition: to call someone on the telephone.
examples: Nice talking to you. Give me a ring sometime.
Give me a buzz when you’re in town.

headword: give someone a rough idea (about something)
altForms: give someone a rough idea (of something)

senses.definition: to give someone a general idea or an estimate about something.
examples: I don’t need to know exactly. Just give me a rough idea about how big it should be.
Let me give you a rough idea about my plan.

senses.definition: to beat someone.
examples: My dad gave me a shellacking when I broke his fishing rod.
If you do that again, I will give you a shellacking.

senses.definition: to beat someone (in a contest).
examples: The other team gave us a shellacking.
The Bears gave the Packers a shellacking.

headword: give someone a slap on the wrist

senses.definition: to give someone a light punishment (for doing something wrong).
senses.notes: See also get a slap on the wrist.
examples: The judge gave her a slap on the wrist for speeding.
The judge should have done more than slap her wrist.
They should do more than just slap his wrist.

senses.definition: to make someone conceited.
examples: Fame gave John a swelled head.
Don’t let this success give you a swelled head.

senses.definition: to give someone a severe scolding.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also get a tongue-lashing.
examples: I gave Bill a real tongue-lashing when he got home late.
I will give you a real tongue-lashing if you ever do that again.

senses.definition: to give someone freedom or permission to act as one wishes or thinks necessary.
senses.notes: Almost the same as give someone a blank check.
examples: He’s been given carte blanche with the reorganization of the work force.
The manager has been given no instructions about how to train the staff. The owner just gave him carte blanche.
Jean gave carte blanche to the decorator and said she wanted the whole house done.

senses.definition: to praise or recognize someone for doing something.
examples: The coach gave Mary a lot of credit.
The director gave John much credit for his fine performance.

senses.definition: to cause someone to have prickly or bumpy skin owing to excitement or fear.
examples: It was a scary movie and it gave me goose bumps.
I hate being in that old house. It gives me goose pimples.

senses.definition: to cause someone’s hair to turn gray from stress or frustration.
senses.notes: Usually an expression of fear that one’s hair will turn gray.
examples: My three teenage boys are giving me gray hair.
Your behavior is giving me gray hairs.

headword: give someone or something a wide berth

senses.definition: to keep a reasonable distance from someone or something; to steer clear (of someone or something).
examples: The dog we are approaching is very mean. Better give it a wide berth.
Give Mary a wide berth. She’s in a very bad mood.

headword: give someone or something the (old) heave-ho

senses.definition: to throw someone or something out; to get rid of someone or something; to fire someone.
senses.notes: Informal. See also get the (old) heave-ho.
examples: We gave Jane the old heave-ho today.
John was behaving badly at our party, so my father gave him the heave-ho.
This chair is completely worn out. Shall I give it the old heave-ho?

senses.definition: to cause someone to stop and think.
examples: When I see a golden sunrise, it gives me pause.
Witnessing an accident is likely to give all of us pause.

senses.definition: to touch two hands together in a special greeting, like a handshake.
senses.notes: [for two people] Slang. One hand may be slapped down on top of the other, or they may be slapped together palm to palm with the arms held vertically. Usually said as a command.
examples: Hey, Bob, give me some skin!
Come over here, you guys. I want you to meet my brother and give him some skin!

senses.definition: to ignore someone; to dismiss someone.
examples: Tom always gives me the air. Is there something wrong with me?
Why is she giving him the air? What did he do?

senses.definition: to fire someone; to terminate someone’s employment.
examples: I gave Tom the sack, and he has to find a new job.
I had to give three people the ax yesterday. We are having to reduce our office staff.

headword: give someone the benefit of the doubt

senses.definition: to make a judgment in someone’s favor when the evidence is neither for nor against the person.
senses.notes: See also get the benefit of the doubt.
examples: I’m glad the teacher gave me the benefit of the doubt.
Please, judge. Give me the benefit of the doubt.

senses.definition: to dismiss someone; to kick someone out (of a place).
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the boot.
examples: You had better behave, or they’ll give you the boot.
I will give him the boot if he doesn’t straighten up.

senses.definition: to send someone away; to reject someone.
examples: Tom wouldn’t talk to her. He just gave her the brush-off.
Please don’t give me the brush-off!

senses.definition: to hurry someone into leaving; to usher someone out of a place quickly.
senses.notes: As someone might quickly escort a vagrant from a fancy restaurant.
examples: The young customer in the jewelry store was being given the bum’s rush, so he pulled out an enormous roll of bills and the clerk became much more helpful.
The doorman gave Bill the bum’s rush at the restaurant because Bill did not have a tie on.

senses.definition: to harass someone; to give someone a bad time.
examples: The people in that office can’t answer your question. They just give you the business.
I’ll get rid of her. I’ll give her the business.

senses.definition: to ignore someone; to reject someone.
senses.notes: Informal. See also get the cold shoulder.
examples: She gave me the cold shoulder when I asked her to the party.
Sally has been giving me the cold shoulder.

senses.definition: to make someone uneasy; to frighten someone.
senses.notes: Informal. See also get the creeps.
examples: That old house gives me the creeps.
That strange old man gives him the willies.

senses.definition: to scold someone severely.
examples: I’m going to give Bill hell when he gets home. He’s late again.
Bill, why do I always have to give you the devil?

senses.definition: to look at someone in a way that communicates romantic interest.
senses.notes: Informal. See also catch someone’s eye.
examples: Ann gave John the eye. It really surprised him.
Tom kept giving Sally the eye. She finally left.

senses.definition: to send someone away; to reject someone.
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the gate.
examples: Not only was he not friendly, he gave me the gate.
He was rude, so we gave him the gate.

senses.definition: to give someone an overly friendly welcome; to give someone insincere attention.
examples: Here comes Tom. Watch him give us the glad hand and leave.
These politicians give you the glad hand and ignore you after they are elected.

senses.definition: to give someone the signal to start or continue.
examples: It’s time to start work. Give everybody the go-ahead.
They gave us the green light to start.

senses.definition: to put pressure on someone to buy or accept (something).
examples: They gave me the hard sell, but I still wouldn’t buy the car.
The clerk gave the customer the hard sell.

senses.definition: to give someone a prearranged signal.
examples: As the robber walked past me, I gave the police officer a high sign. Then the officer arrested the robber.
Things got started when I gave the conductor the high sign.

headword: give someone the low-down (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to tell someone the full story about someone or something.
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the low-down (on someone or something).
examples: Please give Sally the low-down on the new expressway.
I do not know what’s going on. Please give me the low-down.

senses.definition: to visually examine someone quickly.
examples: John gives me the once-over every time he walks by me.
Why does he just give me the once-over? Why doesn’t he say hello?

senses.definition: to give someone very special treatment; to give someone royal treatment.
senses.notes: See also get the red-carpet treatment.
examples: We always give the queen the red-carpet treatment when she comes to visit.
They never give me the red-carpet treatment.

senses.definition: to give someone a series of excuses, delays, and referrals.
examples: If you ask to see the manager, they’ll give you the runaround.
Stop giving me the runaround!

headword: give someone the shirt off one’s back

senses.definition: to be very generous or solicitous to someone.
examples: Tom really likes Bill. He’d give Bill the shirt off his back.
John is so friendly that he’d give anyone the shirt off his back.

senses.definition: to escape from or elude someone.
examples: We followed her for two blocks, and then she gave us the slip.
Max gave Lefty the slip.

senses.definition: to question someone in great detail for a long period.
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the third degree.
examples: The police gave Sally the third degree.
Stop giving me the third degree. I told you what I know.

senses.definition: to give someone the full amount or the full treatment.
senses.notes: Slang. See also get the works.
examples: The judge gave her the works for driving too fast.
I want everything on my hamburger. Give me the works.

senses.definition: to give someone something equal to what was given you; to exchange a series of things, one by one, with someone.
examples: They gave me the same kind of difficulty that I gave them. They gave me tit for tat.
He punched me, so I punched him. Every time he hit me, I hit him. I just gave him tit for tat.

senses.definition: to explain something to someone; to imply something to someone.
senses.notes: This may mislead someone, accidentally or intentionally.
examples: Mr. Smith gave Sally to understand that she should be home by midnight.
The mayor gave the citizens to understand that there would be no tax increase. He didn’t promise, though.

headword: give something a lick and a promise

senses.definition: to do something poorly—quickly and carelessly.
examples: John! You didn’t clean your room! You just gave it a lick and a promise.
This time, Tom, comb your hair. It looks as if you just gave it a lick and a promise.

senses.definition: to try something.
examples: I have never dived before, but I will give it a shot.
Tom decided to take a shot at writing a poem.

senses.definition: make a try at doing something.
examples: If at first you don’t succeed, give it another whirl.
John gave bowling a whirl last night.

senses.definition: to accompany the bride to the groom in a wedding ceremony.
examples: Mr. Brown is ill. Who’ll give the bride away?
In the traditional wedding ceremony, the bride’s father gives the bride away.

senses.definition: to give your foe proper credit (for something).
senses.notes: This usually refers to a person who has been evil—like the devil.
examples: She’s generally impossible, but I have to give the devil her due. She bakes a terrific cherry pie.
John may cheat on his taxes and yell at his wife, but he keeps his car polished. I’ll give the devil his due.

senses.definition: to reveal a plan or strategy.
examples: Now, all of you have to keep quiet. Please don’t give the game away.
If you keep giving out hints, you’ll give the game away.

senses.definition: to die; to release one’s spirit.
examples: The old man sighed, rolled over, and gave up the ghost.
I’m too young to give up the ghost.

senses.definition: to express anger; to release one’s anger, irritation, emotion, etc.
senses.notes: The something is usually anger, ire, irritation, etc.
examples: John gave vent to his anger by yelling at Sally.
Bill couldn’t give vent to his frustration because he had been warned to keep quiet.

senses.definition: to express a feeling or an opinion in words; to speak out about something.
examples: The bird gave voice to its joy in the golden sunshine.
All the people gave voice to their anger at Congress.

senses.definition: a fact that is taken for granted; a fact that is assumed.
examples: That Mary will go to college is a given. The question is what she is going to study.
It is a given that the earth revolves around the sun.

senses.definition: likely to do something; inclined to do something habitually.
examples: Mary is given to singing in the shower.
Bob is given to shouting when things don’t go his way.

senses.definition: made to believe.
examples: They were given to understand that there would be no tax increase, but after the election taxes went up.
She was given to understand that she had to be home by midnight.

senses.definition: to cover up or conceal an error; to make something appear right by minimizing or concealing the flaws.
examples: When I asked him not to gloss the flaws over, he got angry.
When Mr. Brown was selling me the car, he tried to gloss over its defects.

senses.definition: someone who seems to like doing or seeking out difficult, unpleasant, or badly paid tasks.
examples: If you want to work for this charity, you’ll have to be a glutton for punishment and work long hours for nothing.
Jane must be a real glutton for punishment. She’s typing Bill’s manuscript free of charge, and he doesn’t even thank her.

senses.definition: to slash about with the teeth.
examples: Bill clenched his fists and gnashed his teeth in anger.
The wolf gnashed its teeth and chased after the deer.

senses.definition: to go against the natural direction or inclination.
senses.notes: Refers to the grain of wood. See also rub someone(‘s fur) the wrong way.
examples: You can’t expect me to help you cheat. That goes against the grain.
Would it go against the grain for you to call in sick for me?

senses.definition: to have sexual intercourse with someone.
examples: If you go all the way, you stand a chance of getting pregnant.
I’ve heard that they go to bed all the time.

senses.definition: to accompany (someone) for the pleasure of riding along.
examples: Join us. You can go along for the ride.
I don’t really need to go to the grocery store, but I’ll go along for the ride.

headword: go a long way toward doing something
altForms: go a long way in doing something

senses.definition: almost to satisfy specific conditions; to be almost right.
examples: This machine goes a long way toward meeting our needs.
Your plan went a long way in helping us with our problem.

senses.definition: to agree to something.
senses.notes: [with something] Also literal, meaning “to accompany someone.”
examples: All right. I’ll go along with your plan.
I’m sure that John won’t want to go along with it.

senses.definition: to agree with someone.
examples: I go along with Sally. I’m sure she’s right.
I can’t go along with John. He doesn’t know what he’s talking about.

senses.definition: to become very excited and enthusiastic about someone or something.
examples: I really go ape over chocolate ice cream.
Tom really goes ape over Mary.

senses.definition: to keep going over the same ideas or repeating the same actions, often resulting in confusion, without reaching a satisfactory decision or conclusion.
examples: We’re just going round in circles discussing the problems of the party. We need to consult someone else to get a new point of view.
Fred’s trying to find out what’s happened but he’s going round in circles. No one will tell him anything useful.

senses.definition: to be or act confused.
examples: I’m so busy I’m going around in circles.
I can’t work anymore. I’m so tired that I’m going round in circles.

senses.definition: to go around a turn or a curve; to make a turn or a curve.
examples: You’ll see the house you’re looking for as you go round the bend.
John waved to his father until the car went round the bend.

senses.definition: to go crazy; to lose one’s mind.
examples: If I don’t get some rest, I’ll go round the bend.
Poor Bob. He has been having trouble for a long time. He finally went around the bend.

senses.definition: to leave the proper path (literally or figuratively).
examples: Stay right on the road. Don’t go astray and get lost.
Follow the rules I’ve given you and don’t go astray. That’ll keep you out of trouble.

senses.definition: to depart with nothing.
senses.notes: Compare this with come away empty-handed.
examples: I hate for you to go away empty-handed, but I cannot afford to contribute any money.
They came hoping for some food, but they had to go away empty-handed.

senses.definition: to become absent without leave.
examples: Private Smith went AWOL last Wednesday. Now he’s in a military prison.
Tom went AWOL once too often.

senses.definition: to break a promise that one has made.
examples: I hate to go back on my word, but I won’t pay you $100 after all.
Going back on your word makes you a liar.

senses.definition: to become rotten, undesirable, evil, etc.
examples: I’m afraid that this milk has gone bad.
Life used to be wonderful. Now it has gone bad.

senses.definition: to go crazy or become silly.
examples: Whenever I see Sally, I just go bananas! She’s fantastic.
This was a horrible day! I almost went bananas.

senses.definition: to be unwanted or unused.
senses.notes: As if an object were begging for an owner or a user.
examples: There is still food left. A whole lobster is going begging. Please eat some more.
There are many excellent books in the library just going begging because people don’t know they are there.

senses.definition: to completely run out of money and other assets.
examples: This company is going to go broke if you don’t stop spending money foolishly.
I made some bad investments last year, and it looks as if I may go broke this year.

senses.definition: to get ruined or lost.
senses.notes: This is a nautical expression meaning “to fall or be washed overboard.”
examples: I hate to see good food go by the board. Please eat up so we won’t have to throw it out.
Your plan has gone by the board. The entire project has been canceled.

senses.definition: to follow the rules exactly.
senses.notes: Refers to a book of rules.
examples: The judge of the contest went by the book and disqualified us in the first round.
Everyone insisted that the chairman go by the book and rule against the questionable motion.

senses.definition: to go away (and stop being a bother).
examples: He was bothering me, so I told him to go chase himself.
Get out, you pest! Go chase yourself!

senses.definition: Go away and stop bothering me!
examples: Go away and stop bothering me. Go climb a tree!
Go climb a tree! You are a pain in the neck.

senses.definition: to stop (doing something) without tapering off.
senses.notes: Slang. Originally drug slang. Now concerned with breaking any habit.
examples: I had to stop smoking, so I went cold turkey. It’s awful!
When heroin addicts go cold turkey, they get terribly sick.

senses.definition: to become crazy, disorientated, or frustrated.
examples: It is so busy here that I think I will go crazy.
Bob went crazy because his car got a flat tire.

senses.definition: to continue the struggle until one is completely defeated.
examples: I won’t give up easily. I’ll go down fighting.
Sally, who is very determined, went down fighting.

senses.definition: to decline and grow worse and worse.
examples: This industry is going downhill. We lose money every year.
As one gets older, one tends to go downhill.

senses.definition: to be remembered as historically important.
examples: Bill is so great. I’m sure that he’ll go down in history.
This is the greatest party of the century. I bet it’ll go down in history.

senses.definition: to share the cost of a meal or some other event.
examples: JANE: Let’s go out and eat. MARY: Okay, but let’s go Dutch.
It’s getting expensive to have Sally for a friend. She never wants to go Dutch.

senses.definition: to be kind or gentle with someone or something.
senses.notes: See also take it easy (on someone or something).
examples: Go easy on Tom. He just got out of the hospital.
Go easy on the cat. It doesn’t like to be roughed up.
Okay, I’ll go easy.

senses.definition: to use something sparingly.
examples: Go easy on the mustard. That’s all there is.
When you make my sandwich, please go easy on the onions. I don’t like them very well.

senses.definition: to divide the cost of something in half with someone.
examples: Todd and Jean decided to go fifty-fifty on dinner.
The two brothers went fifty-fifty on a replacement for the broken lamp.

senses.definition: to risk everything; to try as hard as possible.
examples: Okay, this is my last chance. I’m going for broke.
Look at Mary starting to move in the final hundred yards of the race! She is really going for broke.

senses.definition: to progress from a bad state to a worse state.
examples: This is a terrible day. Things are going from bad to worse.
My cold is awful. It went from bad to worse in just an hour.

senses.definition: to go fast or energetically.
examples: I’m over my cold and going great guns.
Business is great. We are going great guns selling ice cream.

senses.definition: to go wrong; to malfunction; to break down.
examples: I was talking to Mary when suddenly the telephone went haywire. I haven’t heard from her since.
There we were, driving along, when the engine went haywire. It was two hours before the tow truck came.

senses.definition: to behave wildly.
examples: Have a good time at the party, but don’t go hog-wild.
The teacher cannot control a class that is going hog-wild.

senses.definition: to move in a group.
examples: The whole team went in a body to talk to the coach.
Each of us was afraid to go alone, so we went in a body.

headword: go in one ear and out the other

senses.definition: to be heard and then forgotten.
senses.notes: [for something] See also in one ear and out (of) the other.
examples: Everything I say to you seems to go in one ear and out the other. Why don’t you pay attention?
I can’t concentrate. Things people say to me just go in one ear and out the other.

senses.definition: to start doing something.
examples: I usually get to work at 7:45, and I go into action at 8:00.
When the ball is hit in my direction, you should see me swing into action.

senses.definition: suddenly to dive toward the ground, nose first.
examples: It was a bad day for flying, and I was afraid we’d go into a nosedive.
The small plane took a nosedive. The pilot was able to bring it out at the last minute, so the plane didn’t crash.

senses.definition: to go into a rapid emotional or financial decline, or a decline in health.
examples: Our profits took a nosedive last year.
After he broke his hip, Mr. Brown’s health went into a nosedive, and he never recovered.

senses.definition: to lose control and spin to the earth, nose first.
examples: The plane shook and then suddenly went into a tailspin.
The pilot was not able to bring the plane out of the tailspin, and it crashed into the sea.

senses.definition: to become disoriented or panicked; [for someone’s life] to fall apart.
examples: Although John was a great success, his life went into a tailspin. It took him a year to get straightened out.
After her father died, Mary’s world fell apart, and she went into a tailspin.

senses.definition: to give all the details; to present and discuss the details.
examples: The clerk went into detail about the product with the customer.
I just want a simple answer. Don’t go into detail.

senses.definition: to become effective; to start to function.
examples: When does this new law go into effect?
The new tax laws won’t go into effect until next year.
This law takes effect almost immediately.

senses.definition: to conceal oneself in a hidden place for a period of time.
examples: The political dissident went into hiding.
After robbing the bank, the bandits went into hiding for months.

senses.definition: go into debt.
examples: We will have to go into hock to buy a house.
I go further into hock every time I use my credit card.

headword: go into one’s song and dance (about something)

senses.definition: to start giving one’s explanations and excuses about something.
senses.notes: One’s can be replaced by the same old.
examples: Please don’t go into your song and dance about how you always tried to do what was right.
John went into his song and dance about how he won the war all by himself.
He always goes into the same old song and dance every time he makes a mistake.

senses.definition: to get very excited; to be in ecstasy.
examples: When I got a letter from my boyfriend in England, I almost went into orbit.
Tom goes into orbit every time the football team scores.

senses.definition: to do something by oneself.
examples: Do you need help, or will you go it alone?
I think I need a little more experience before I go it alone.

senses.definition: to progress with regularity and dependability.
examples: The building project is progressing nicely. Everything is going like clockwork.
The elaborate pageant was a great success. It went like clockwork from start to finish.

senses.definition: to proceed without proper preparation; to speak (about something) without adequate knowledge.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to what John says. He’s always going off half-cocked.
Get your facts straight before you make your presentation. There is nothing worse than going off half-cocked.

senses.definition: to go off suddenly in another direction; suddenly to change one’s line of thought, course of action, etc.
examples: Please stick to one subject and don’t go off on a tangent.
If Mary would settle down and deal with one subject she would be all right, but she keeps going off on tangents.

senses.definition: to become deeply involved (with someone or something) before one is ready; to follow one’s emotions into a situation.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to going into a swimming pool at the deep end—rather than the shallow end—and finding oneself in deep water. Applies especially to falling in love.
examples: Look at the way Bill is looking at Sally. I think he’s about to go off the deep end.
Now, John, I know you really want to go to Australia, but don’t go jumping off the deep end. It isn’t all perfect there.

senses.definition: to do too much of something.
senses.notes: Slang. Especially to drink too much.
examples: Jane went on a binge last night and is very sick this morning.
Bill loves to spend money on clothes. He’s out on a binge right now—buying everything in sight.

senses.definition: to attempt to discover information.
examples: We are going to have to go on a fishing expedition to try to find the facts.
One lawyer went on a fishing expedition in court, and the other lawyer objected.

senses.definition: to have a rampage.
examples: The angry bull went on a rampage and broke the fence.
My boss went on a rampage because the report wasn’t finished.

headword: go on to a better land

senses.definition: to die.
examples: After a long illness, Reggie went on to a better land.
When I finally go on to a better land, I hope there is enough money for a proper funeral.

senses.definition: to become unfashionable; to become obsolete.
examples: That kind of furniture went out of style years ago.
I hope this kind of thing never goes out of fashion.

headword: go out of one’s way (to do something)

senses.definition: to travel an indirect route in order to do something.
examples: I’ll have to go out of my way to give you a ride home.
I’ll give you a ride even though I have to go out of my way.

senses.definition: to make an effort to do something; to endure and accept the bother of doing something.
examples: We went out of our way to please the visitor.
We appreciate anything you can do, but don’t go out of your way.

senses.definition: to quit working at their jobs until certain demands are met.
examples: If we don’t have a contract by noon tomorrow, we’ll go out on strike.
The entire work force went on strike at noon today.

senses.definition: to be very much appreciated by someone.
examples: Your jokes did not exactly go over big with my parents.
We hope that the musical will go over big with the audience.

senses.definition: to do too much; to be extravagant.
senses.notes: Also literal as on a ship.
examples: Look, Sally, let’s have a nice party, but don’t go overboard. It doesn’t need to be fancy.
Okay, you can buy a big comfortable car, but don’t go overboard.

headword: go over like a lead balloon

senses.definition: to fail; to go over badly.
senses.notes: Slang. See also go over with a bang.
examples: Your joke went over like a lead balloon.
If that play was supposed to be a comedy, it went over like a lead balloon.
Her suggestion went over like a lead balloon.

senses.definition: to be too difficult for someone to understand.
examples: All that talk about computers went over my head.
I hope my lecture didn’t go over the students’ heads.

headword: go over something with a fine-tooth comb
altForms: search something with a fine-tooth comb

senses.definition: to search through something very carefully.
examples: I can’t find my calculus book. I went over the whole place with a fine-tooth comb.
I searched this place with a fine-tooth comb and didn’t find my ring.

senses.definition: to succeed spectacularly.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with go over like a lead balloon.
examples: The play was a success. It really went over with a bang.
That’s a great joke. It went over with a bang.

senses.definition: to have a good future.
examples: Sally shows great promise as a scholar. She’s really going to go places.
Tom is as good as we thought. He’s certainly going places now.

senses.definition: to pass through and out of the body very rapidly.
examples: Those little apples go right through me, but I love them.
I can’t eat onions. They go right through me.

senses.definition: to go unpunished; to be acquitted of a crime.
senses.notes: This scot is an old word meaning “tax” or “tax burden.”
examples: The thief went scot-free.
Jane cheated on the test and got caught, but she got off scot-free.

senses.definition: to go very high, as with a price or a measurement.
examples: Prices go sky-high whenever there is inflation.
Oh, it’s so hot. The temperature went sky-high about noon.

headword: go so far as to say something

senses.definition: to put something into words; to risk saying something.
examples: I think that Bob is dishonest, but I wouldn’t go so far as to say he’s a thief.
Red meat may be harmful, but I can’t go so far as to say it causes cancer.

senses.definition: to do something superior to what someone else has done; to top someone.
examples: That was a great joke, but I can go you one better.
Your last song was beautifully sung, but Mary can do you one better.

senses.definition: to travel by foot; to go somewhere on foot.
examples: The car wouldn’t start so I had to go to work by shank’s mare.
We enjoy walking and go by shank’s mare whenever we can.

senses.definition: to go to an event (which is meant for couples) without a member of the opposite sex.
senses.notes: Informal. Originally referred only to males.
examples: Is Tom going to take you, or are you going stag?
Bob didn’t want to go stag, so he took his sister to the party.

senses.definition: to date someone on a regular basis.
examples: Mary is going steady with John.
Bill went steady for two years before he got married.

senses.definition: to become anxious because one is confined.
senses.notes: Slang. Stir is an old criminal word for “prison.”
examples: If I stay around this house much longer, I’m going to go stir-crazy.
John left school. He said he was going stir-crazy.

senses.definition: to begin to obey the law; to become law-abiding.
senses.notes: Also literal. Slang. Primarily criminal slang.
examples: When John got out of prison, he decided to go straight.
I promised the teacher that I would go straight and that I would never cheat again.

senses.definition: to do the whole amount; to play the entire game; to run the whole race.
examples: That horse runs fast. I hope it can go the distance.
This is going to be a long, hard project. I hope I can go the distance.

senses.definition: to try harder to please someone or to get the task done correctly; to do more than one is required to do to reach a goal.
examples: I like doing business with that company. They always go the extra mile.
My teacher goes the extra mile to help us.

senses.definition: to do as much as possible.
senses.notes: Compare this with go whole hog.
examples: What do I want on my hamburger? Go the limit!
Don’t hold anything back. Go the limit.

senses.definition: to proceed by consulting the proper persons or offices.
examples: If you want an answer to your questions, you’ll have to go through channels.
If you know the answers, why do I have to go through channels?

senses.definition: to examine something.
examples: Give me a day or two to go through this contract, and then I’ll call you with advice.
Don’t go through it too fast. Read it carefully, or you might miss something.

senses.definition: to experience something; to endure something unpleasant; to get through something.
examples: It was a terrible thing. I don’t know how I went through it.
It’ll take four years to go through college.

senses.definition: to experience a rough period in one’s life.
examples: Sally’s pretty upset. She’s really going through the changes.
Most teenagers spend their time going through the changes.

senses.definition: to make a feeble effort to do something; to do something insincerely.
examples: Jane isn’t doing her best. She’s just going through the motions.
Bill was supposed to be raking the yard, but he was just going through the motions.

senses.definition: to go very high; to reach a very high degree (of something).
examples: It’s so hot! The temperature is going through the roof.
Mr. Brown got so angry he almost went through the roof.

senses.definition: to decide to do something; to finish something.
examples: We decided to go through with the new highway.
I can’t do it. I just can’t go through with it.

senses.definition: to do whatever is necessary.
examples: I’ll go to any length to secure this contract.
I want to get a college degree, but I won’t go to any length to get one.

senses.definition: to support or help someone.
senses.notes: Informal. From baseball. See pinch-hit (for someone).
examples: I tried to go to bat for Bill, but he said he didn’t want any help.
I heard them gossiping about Sally, so I went to bat for her.

senses.definition: to go to where one’s bed is, get into it, and go to sleep.
examples: It’s time for me to go to bed.
I want to go to bed, but there is too much work to do.

headword: go to bed with the chickens

senses.definition: to go to bed at sundown; to go to bed very early (when the chickens do).
examples: Of course I get enough sleep. I go to bed with the chickens.
Mr. Brown goes to bed with the chickens and gets up with them, too.

senses.definition: to go to the bottom of the sea.
senses.notes: Thought of as a nautical expression.
examples: My camera fell overboard and went to Davy Jones’s locker.
My uncle was a sailor. He went to Davy Jones’s locker during a terrible storm.

senses.definition: to look, sound, or taste good together.
examples: Do you think that this pink one and this purple one go together?
Milk and grapefruit don’t go together.

senses.definition: to date each other regularly.
examples: Bob and Ann have been going together for months.
Tom and Jane want to go together, but they live too far apart.

headword: go to hell in a handbasket

senses.definition: to become totally worthless; to go to (hell).
senses.notes: Informal. Use caution with hell. Not used as a command.
examples: The whole country is going to hell in a handbasket.
Look at my lawn—full of weeds. It’s going to hell in a handbasket.

senses.definition: to do more than is acceptable.
examples: I didn’t mind at first, but now you’ve gone too far.
If you go too far, I’ll slap you.

senses.definition: to break into pieces; to fall apart.
examples: My old winter coat is going to pieces.
I don’t want to see a nice vase like that go to pieces.

senses.definition: to break out in tears; to break down mentally.
examples: On hearing of the death, we just went to pieces.
I couldn’t talk about it any longer. I went to pieces.

senses.definition: to go to ruin; to deteriorate.
examples: My whole life seems to be going to pot.
My lawn is going to pot. I had better weed it.
The government is going to the dogs.

senses.definition: to go to ruin.
senses.notes: The words rack and wrack mean “wreckage” and are found only in this expression.
examples: That lovely old house on the corner is going to go to rack and ruin.
My lawn is going to wrack and ruin.

senses.definition: to make someone conceited; to make someone overly proud.
examples: You did a fine job, but don’t let it go to your head.
He let his success go to his head, and soon he became a complete failure.

senses.definition: to go into a rest room, bathroom, or toilet.
examples: BILL: Where is Bob? JANE: He went to the bathroom.
John went to the bathroom to brush his teeth.

senses.definition: to eliminate bodily wastes through defecation and urination.
examples: Mommy! The dog went to the bathroom on the carpet!
Billy’s in there going to the bathroom. Don’t disturb him.

headword: go to the expense (of doing something)

senses.definition: to pay the (large) cost of doing something.
examples: I hate to have to go to the expense of painting the house.
It needs to be done, so you’ll have to go to the expense.

senses.definition: to go somewhere and use a toilet.
examples: Bob requested to leave the room to go to the lavatory.
Please stop the car. I have to go to the lavatory.

senses.definition: to do as much as is possible to do.
senses.notes: Compare this with go the limit.
examples: Okay, we can’t afford it, but we’ll go to the limit.
How far shall I go? Shall I go to the limit?

senses.definition: to use a toilet for defecation or urination.
examples: Jimmy washed his hands after he went to the toilet.
Excuse me, I have to go to the toilet.

headword: go to the trouble (of doing something)
altForms: go to the trouble (to do something)

senses.definition: to endure the bother of doing something.
examples: I really don’t want to go to the trouble to cook.
Should I go to the trouble of cooking something for her to eat?
Don’t go to the trouble. She can eat a sandwich.

senses.definition: to be defeated; to fail in business.
examples: We really went to the wall on that deal.
The company went to the wall because of that contract. Now it’s broke.

senses.definition: to work hard or fast.
examples: Look at all those ants working. They are really going to town.
Come on, you guys. Let’s go to town. We have to finish this job before noon.

senses.definition: to be wasted; to be unused (and therefore thrown away).
examples: Eat your potatoes! Don’t let them go to waste.
We shouldn’t let all those nice flowers go to waste. Let’s pick some.

senses.definition: to fail.
examples: The company was weak from the start, and it finally went under.
Tom had a lot of trouble in school, and finally he went under.

senses.definition: to have a surgical operation.
examples: Mary didn’t want to go under the knife, but the doctor insisted.
If I go under the knife, I want to be completely asleep.

senses.definition: to burn up.
examples: The whole museum went up in flames.
My paintings—my whole life’s work—went up in flames.
What a shame for all that to go up in smoke.

senses.definition: to do everything possible; to be extravagant.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with go the limit.
examples: Let’s go whole hog. Order steak and lobster.
Show some restraint. Don’t go whole hog all the time.

senses.definition: to go about looking at goods in store windows without actually buying anything.
examples: The clerks usually go window-shopping in their lunch hour, looking for things to buy when they get paid.
Joan said she was just going window-shopping, but she bought a new coat.

senses.definition: to manage to get along without something.
senses.notes: Compare this with do without (someone or something).
examples: I went without food for three days.
Some people have to go without a lot longer than that.

senses.definition: to proceed easily and cooperatively in the same manner that other people or processes are moving.
examples: John is very easy to get along with. He just goes with the flow.
I try to cooperate. I go with the flow where possible.

senses.definition: to fail; [for something bad] to happen.
examples: The project failed. I don’t know what went wrong.
I’m afraid that everything will go wrong.

senses.definition: serves to prove a point to you.
examples: It just goes to show you that too much sugar is bad for you.
Of course you shouldn’t have married her. It goes to show you that your parents are always right.

senses.definition: is so obvious that it need not be said.
examples: It goes without saying that you are to wear formal clothing to dinner each evening.
Of course. That goes without saying.

senses.definition: the condition of a path of travel or progress.
examples: The going was rough through the mountains.
