I decided to sell my stock while the going was still good.

senses.definition: the current rate.
examples: The going interest rate for your account is 10 percent.
Our babysitter charges us the going rate.

senses.definition: someone or something that is full of information.
examples: Grandfather is a gold mine of information about World War I.
The new encyclopedia is a positive gold mine of useful information.

senses.definition: gone or dead but still remembered.
examples: The good days we used to have together are gone, but not forgotten.
Uncle Harry is gone but not forgotten. The stain where he spilled the wine is still visible in the parlor carpet.

senses.definition: someone or something that has departed or run away.
examples: Surely, the burglar is a gone goose by now.
The child was a gone goose, and we did not know where to look for him.

senses.definition: died.
examples: My husband, Tom—he’s gone on, you know—was a great one for golf.
Let us remember those who have gone on before.

senses.definition: died.
examples: Poor old Bob has gone to meet his Maker.
After a long illness, Reggie went to meet his Maker.

senses.definition: gone; mysteriously gone.
senses.notes: A phrase made famous by the Margaret Mitchell novel and film Gone with the Wind. The phrase is used to make gone have a stronger force.
examples: Everything we worked for was gone with the wind.
Jean was nowhere to be found. She was gone with the wind.

senses.definition: dead or finished; as good as dead or nearly dead.
senses.notes: Informal. Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: The boy brought the sick fish back to the pet store to get his money back. “This one is a goner,” he said.
John thought he was a goner when his parachute didn’t open.

senses.definition: very something.
senses.notes: The something can be ready, mad, tired, worn-out, etc.
examples: Now I’m good and mad, and I’m going to fight back.
I’ll be there when I’m good and ready.
He’ll go to bed when he’s good and tired.

headword: good enough for someone or something

senses.definition: adequate for someone or something.
examples: This seat is good enough for me. I don’t want to move.
I’m happy. It’s good enough for me.
That table is good enough for my office.

senses.definition: worthless.
examples: Here comes that good-for-nothing boy now.
Where is that good-for-nothing pen of mine?

senses.definition: a worthless person.
examples: Tell that good-for-nothing to go home at once.
Bob can’t get a job. He’s such a good-for-nothing.

senses.definition: back in an earlier time, which everyone remembers as a better time, even if it really wasn’t.
examples: Back in the good old days, during WWII, they used real cactus needles in record players.
The good old days didn’t start until they had indoor bathrooms.

senses.definition: good to be rid (of worthless persons or things).
examples: She slammed the door behind me and said, “Good riddance to bad rubbish!”
“Good riddance to you, madam,” thought I.

senses.definition: all ready to go; all checked and pronounced ready to go.
examples: I’ve checked everything and we are good to go.
Everything’s good to go and we will start immediately.

senses.definition: to waste time.
examples: John is always goofing off.
Quit goofing off and get to work!

senses.definition: undeniable.
examples: The witness swore he was telling the gospel truth.
I told my parents the gospel truth about how the vase broke.

senses.definition: to get something to eat; to get food that can be eaten quickly.
examples: I need a few minutes to grab a bite to eat.
Bob often tries to grab a bite between meetings.

senses.definition: made elegant by means of some ornament or decoration.
examples: The altar was graced with lovely white flowers.
The end of the beautiful day was graced with a beautiful sunset.

senses.definition: even the smallest amount of truth.
examples: The attorney was unable to find a grain of truth in the defendant’s testimony.
If there were a grain of truth to your statement, I would trust you.

senses.definition: to depend on something that is useless; to make a futile attempt at something.
examples: John couldn’t answer the teacher’s question. He was just grasping at straws.
There I was, grasping at straws, with no one to help me.

senses.definition: to annoy someone; to bother someone.
examples: My obnoxious brother is grating on my nerves.
Your whining really grates on me.

senses.definition: an area of a subject or question that is difficult to put into a particular category because it is not clearly defined and may have connections or associations with more than one category.
examples: The responsibility for social studies in the college is a gray area. Several departments are involved.
Publicity is a gray area in that firm. It is shared between the marketing and design divisions.

senses.definition: intelligence; brains; power of thought.
senses.notes: Brain tissue is grayish in color.
examples: Use your gray matter and think what will happen if the committee resigns.
Surely they’ll come up with an acceptable solution if they use a bit of gray matter.

senses.definition: to bribe someone.
examples: If you want to get something done around here, you have to grease someone’s palm.
I’d never oil a police officer’s palm. That’s illegal.

senses.definition: much; a lot.
examples: You can learn a great deal about nature by watching television.
This is a serious problem and it worries me a great deal.

headword: the greatest thing since sliced bread

senses.definition: the best thing there ever was.
examples: To hear her talk, you would think she had found the greatest thing since sliced bread.
Todd thinks he is the greatest thing since sliced bread.

senses.definition: envious; jealous.
examples: When Sally saw me with Tom, she turned green with envy. She likes him a lot.
I feel green with envy whenever I see you in your new car.

senses.definition: to endure something unpleasant in good humor.
examples: There is nothing you can do but grin and bear it.
I hate having to work for rude people. I guess I have to grin and bear it.

senses.definition: to slow to a stop; to run down.
examples: By the end of the day, the factory had ground to a halt.
The car ground to a halt, and we got out to stretch our legs.

senses.definition: to attract and hold someone’s attention.
examples: The scary movie gripped my attention.
The professor’s interesting lecture gripped the attention of all the students.

senses.definition: something that can be put to good use or that can bring advantage or profit.
examples: Some of the jobs that we are offered are more interesting than others, but each one is grist for my mill.
The company is having to sell some tacky-looking dresses, but they are grist for their mill and keep the company in business.

senses.definition: to grind one’s teeth together in anger or determination.
examples: I was so mad, all I could do was stand there and grit my teeth.
All through the race, Sally was gritting her teeth. She was really determined.

headword: groan under the burden of something

senses.definition: to suffer under the burden or domination of someone or something.
examples: John groaned under the burden of his new responsibilities.
The servant groaned under the burden of a cruel master.

senses.definition: to revolt someone; to make someone sick.
examples: Oh, look at his face. Doesn’t it gross you out?
That teacher is such a creep. He grosses out the whole class.

senses.definition: to take away someone’s privileges.
senses.notes: Informal. Usually said of a teenager.
examples: My father said that if I didn’t get at least C’s, he’d ground me.
Guess what! He grounded me!

senses.definition: based on facts.
examples: This movie is grounded in fact.
The stories in this book are all grounded in actual fact.

senses.definition: a basis or cause for legal action, such as a lawsuit.
examples: Your negligence is grounds for a lawsuit.
Is infidelity grounds for divorce in this state?

senses.definition: to become commonplace and comfortable to a person.
senses.notes: [for someone or something] The someone is usually one, someone, a person, etc., not a specific person.
examples: That music is strange, but it grows on you.
I didn’t think I could ever get used to this town, but after a while it grows on one.

senses.definition: to abandon something as one matures.
examples: I used to have a lot of allergies, but I grew out of them.
She grew out of the habit of biting her nails.

senses.definition: to gradually begin to do certain things, using verbs such as feel, know, like, need, respect, sense, suspect, think, want, wonder, etc.
examples: I grew to hate Bob over a period of years.
As I grew to know Bob, I began to like him.

senses.definition: work that is hard and thankless.
examples: During the summer, I earned money doing grunt work.
I did all of the grunt work on the project, but my boss got all of the credit.

senses.definition: to take care to avoid someone or something.
examples: Try to guard against getting a cold.
You should guard against pickpockets.

senses.definition: a guest who gets special attention from everyone; the person for whom a party, celebration, or ceremony is held.
examples: Bob is the guest of honor, and many people will make speeches about him.
The guest of honor sits at the front of the room on the dais.

senses.definition: to eagerly or desperately try to get air or a breath.
examples: Tom gulped for air after trying to hold his breath for three minutes.
Mary came up out of the water, gulping for air.

senses.definition: to make something inoperable; to ruin someone’s plans.
examples: Please, Bill, be careful and don’t gum up the works.
Tom sure gummed it up.
Tom sure gummed up the whole plan.

senses.definition: to be looking for someone, presumably to harm them.
senses.notes: Refers to a sheriff or outlaw seeking a person with the intention of shooting him. Originally from western and gangster movies.
examples: The coach is gunning for you. I think he’s going to bawl you out.
I’ve heard that the sheriff is gunning for me, so I’m getting out of town.

senses.definition: a personal, intuitive feeling or response.
examples: I have a gut feeling that something bad is going to happen.
My gut reaction is that we should hire Susan for the job.

senses.definition: to deceive someone in order to get something of value.
examples: The salesclerk gypped me out of a dollar.
The taxi driver tried to gyp me out of a fortune by driving all over town.

senses.definition: to endure something; to deal with something.
senses.notes: Slang. The something is usually it.
examples: I don’t know if I can hack it.
John works very hard, but he can’t seem to hack it.

senses.definition: ought to do something.
senses.notes: Informal. Almost the same as the following entry.
examples: You had best get that fixed right away.
You had best be at school on time every day.

senses.definition: ought to do something (or face the consequences).
senses.notes: Almost the same as the previous entry.
examples: I had better get home for dinner, or I’ll get yelled at.
You had better do your homework right now.

senses.definition: would prefer to do something else; would be content to do something.
senses.notes: The would or had is usually’d. Also with just, as in the examples below.
examples: They want me to go into town. I’d as soon stay home.
If you’re cooking stew tonight, we’d as soon eat somewhere else.
I would just as soon stay home as see a bad movie.
If that’s what we’re having for dinner, I’d just as soon starve.

senses.definition: would prefer to do something.
senses.notes: The had is usually expressed in a contraction,’d.
examples: I’d rather go to town than sit here all evening.
They’d rather not.
I’d sooner not make the trip.

senses.definition: friendly to everyone; falsely friendly to everyone.
senses.notes: Usually said of males. See also get the glad hand.
examples: Yes, he’s friendly, sort of hail-fellow-well-met.
He’s not a very sincere person. Hail-fellow-well-met—you know the type.
What a pain he is. Good old Mr. Hail-fellow-well-met. What a phony!

senses.definition: to come originally from somewhere.
examples: I’m from Kansas. Where do you hail from?
I hail from the Southwest.

headword: the hair of the dog that bit one

senses.definition: a drink of liquor taken when one has a hangover; a drink of liquor taken when one is recovering from drinking too much liquor.
examples: Oh, I’m miserable. I need some of the hair of the dog that bit me.
That’s some hangover you’ve got there, Bob. Here, drink this. It’s some of the hair of the dog that bit you.

senses.definition: well and healthy.
examples: Doesn’t Ann look hale and hearty?
I don’t feel hale and hearty. I’m really tired.

headword: Half a loaf is better than none.

senses.definition: Having part of something is better than having nothing.
examples: When my raise was smaller than I wanted, Sally said, “Half a loaf is better than none.”
People who keep saying “Half a loaf is better than none” usually have as much as they need.

senses.definition: a liquid that is half milk and half cream.
examples: Harry would always pour half-and-half on his breakfast cereal in spite of what his doctor told him.
There is less fat in half-and-half than there is in cream.

senses.definition: a substance composed half of one thing and half of another.
examples: This coffee is half-and-half, so there isn’t quite as much caffeine as in regular coffee.
I can’t decide between a chocolate sundae and a pineapple sundae, so make mine half-and-half.

senses.definition: unenthusiastic about someone or something.
examples: Ann was halfhearted about the choice of Sally for president.
She didn’t look halfhearted to me. She looked angry.

senses.definition: to make a performance seem silly by showing off or exaggerating one’s part.
senses.notes: Informal. A show-off actor is known as a ham.
examples: Come on, Bob. Don’t ham it up!
The play was going fine until Bob got out there and hammed up his part.

senses.definition: to keep trying to accomplish something with someone or something.
senses.notes: Refers to repeated pounding with a hammer.
examples: John, you’ve got to keep hammering away at your geometry.
They hammered away at the prisoner until he confessed.

senses.definition: to try extremely hard to make someone understand or realize something.
examples: The teacher hammered the dates home.
I tried to hammer home to Anne the fact that she would have to get a job.
The boss hopes to hammer home the company’s precarious financial position to the staff.

senses.definition: to work hard at writing up an agreement; to work hard at writing something.
senses.notes: Literally to pound something flat with a hammer or mallet. This refers to hammering at the keys of a typewriter.
examples: I’m busy hammering my latest novel out.
The lawyers sat down to hammer out a contract.

senses.definition: to play something on the piano.
examples: She hammered the song out loudly and without feeling.
Listen to John hammer out that song on the piano.

senses.definition: very close to someone.
examples: John is really hand in glove with Sally.
The teacher and the principal work hand in glove.

senses.definition: holding hands.
examples: They walked down the street hand in hand.
Bob and Mary sat there quietly, hand in hand.

senses.definition: together, one with the other.
senses.notes: Said of two things where the presence of one implies the other.
examples: Cookies and milk seem to go hand in hand.
Teenagers and back talk go hand in hand.

senses.definition: Give it to me.
examples: It’s mine. Hand it over!
Come on. Give me the box of jewels. Hand it over!

senses.definition: to give credit to someone.
senses.notes: Informal. Often with have to or must.
examples: I’ll hand it to you. You did a fine job.
We must hand it to Sally. She helped us a lot.

senses.definition: something, such as an article of used clothing, that has been handed down from someone.
senses.notes: See also hand something down (to someone).
examples: Why do I always have to wear my brother’s hand-me-downs? I want some new clothes.
This is a nice shirt. It doesn’t look like a hand-me-down at all.

senses.definition: very rapidly.
senses.notes: [for money and merchandise to be exchanged]
examples: What a busy day. We took in money hand over fist.
They were buying things hand over fist.

senses.definition: one hand after the other (again and again).
examples: Sally pulled in the rope hand over hand.
The man climbed the rope hand over hand.

senses.definition: to give something to a younger person.
senses.notes: Either at death or during life. See also hand-me-down.
examples: John handed his old shirts down to his younger brother.
I hope my uncle will hand down his golf clubs to me when he dies.

senses.definition: to announce or deliver a (legal) verdict or indictment.
examples: The grand jury handed down seven indictments last week.
The jury handed down a guilty verdict.

senses.definition: to be very careful with a touchy person.
examples: Bill has become so sensitive. You really have to handle him with kid gloves.
You don’t have to handle me with kid gloves. I can take it.

senses.definition: without a doubt.
senses.notes: Usually regarding a choice or a winner.
examples: Jean was our choice for the new manager hands down.
Todd won the race hands down.
Sharon was the favorite librarian of all the people there hands down.

senses.definition: Do not touch [someone or something]!
examples: Careful! Don’t touch that wire. Hands off!
The sign says, “Hands off!” and you had better do what it says.

senses.definition: Put your hands in the air!
senses.notes: Slang. Said by robbers and police officers. Hands that are in the air cannot reach or draw a weapon.
examples: All right, you, hands up!
Stick’em up! I got you covered.

senses.definition: to turn to the left.
senses.notes: Slang. See also the following entry.
examples: Hang a left up at that light.
Go three blocks and hang a left.

senses.definition: to turn to the right.
examples: At the next corner, hang a right.
Hang a right at the stop sign.

senses.definition: to spend a lot of time with someone; to waste away time with someone.
senses.notes: See also run around with someone.
examples: John hangs around with Bill a lot.
They’ve been going around with the Smiths.
I’ve asked them all to stop hanging around.

senses.definition: to stay behind (the others); to hold back (from the others).
examples: Walk with the group, Bob. Don’t hang back. You’ll get left behind.
Three of the marchers hung back and talked to each other.

senses.definition: to be in an uncertain position; to depend on something very insubstantial; to hang in the balance.
examples: Your whole argument is hanging by a thread.
John isn’t failing geometry, but his passing grade is just hanging by a hair.

senses.definition: to delay or wait.
examples: I think we should hang fire and wait for other information.
Our plans have to hang fire until we get planning permission.

senses.definition: to be in an undecided state; to be between two equal possibilities.
examples: The prisoner stood before the judge with his life hanging in the balance.
This whole issue will have to hang in the balance until Jane gets back from her vacation.

senses.definition: to keep trying; to persevere.
examples: I know things are tough, John, but hang in there.
I know if I hang in there, things will come out okay.

senses.definition: to relax; to remain calm.
examples: I know I can pass this test if I just hang loose.
Hang loose, Bob. Everything is going to be all right.

senses.definition: to take up residence somewhere.
examples: George loves Dallas. He’s decided to buy a house and hang his hat up there.
Bill moves from place to place and never hangs his hat up anywhere.

senses.definition: to listen with complete attention to everything someone says.
examples: He gave a great lecture. We hung on his every word.
Look at the way John hangs on Mary’s every word. He must be in love with her.

senses.definition: to remember someone or something for a long time; to be affected very much by someone or something in the past.
senses.notes: Also literal meaning grasping or holding someone or something.
examples: That’s a nice thought, Bob. Hang on to it.
You’ve been holding on to those bad memories for too long. It’s time to let them go.
Yes, I can’t keep hanging on.

senses.definition: to spend time somewhere; to waste time somewhere.
examples: I wish you guys wouldn’t hang out around the bowling alley.
Why do you have to hang out near our house?

senses.definition: to waste time in the company of someone.
examples: I hope Bob isn’t hanging out with the wrong people.
He needs to spend more time studying and less time hanging out.

senses.definition: to hang a dummy or some other figure of a hated person.
senses.notes: See also burn someone in effigy.
examples: They hanged the dictator in effigy.
The angry mob hanged the president in effigy.

senses.definition: to be firm in one’s position; to stick to one’s position.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with hang in there.
examples: I know that your parents don’t want you to go out tonight, but hang tough. They may change their minds.
Hang tough, Mary. You’ll get your way!

senses.definition: to replace the telephone receiver; to terminate a telephone call.
examples: If you have called a wrong number, you should apologize before you hang up.
When you hear the busy signal, you’re supposed to hang up.

senses.definition: to meet someone, or find something unexpectedly.
examples: I happened on this nice little restaurant on Elm Street yesterday.
Mr. Simpson and I happened on one another in the bank last week.

headword: a harbinger of things to come
altForms: a portent of things to come

senses.definition: a sign of things to come; a taste of things to come a sample of the events that are to occur in the future.
examples: The first cuts in our budget are a harbinger of things to come.
Today’s visit from the auditors is a portent of things to come.

senses.definition: rigid or strict, especially when applied to rules, laws, or regulations.
examples: The rule isn’t hard-and-fast, but we expect you to obey it anyway.
The company has a hard-and-fast rule about the use of radios, even in private offices.

senses.definition: difficult person or thing to deal with.
examples: This problem is getting me down. It’s a hard nut to crack.
Tom sure is a hard nut to crack. I can’t figure him out.
He sure is a tough nut to crack.

senses.definition: unable to hear well; partially deaf.
examples: Please speak loudly. I am hard of hearing.
Tom is hard of hearing, but is not totally deaf.

senses.definition: following someone very closely; following very closely to someone’s heels.
examples: I ran as fast as I could, but the dog was still hard on my heels.
Here comes Sally, and John is hard on her heels.

senses.definition: able to do something only with great difficulty.
examples: I’m hard put to come up with enough money to pay the rent.
I get hard put like that about once a month.

senses.definition: greatly in need of something.
examples: Ann was hard up for cash to pay the bills.
I was so hard up, I couldn’t afford to buy food.

senses.definition: to be very busy.
examples: This was such a busy day. I hardly had time to breathe.
They made him work so hard that he hardly had time to breathe.

senses.definition: so busy that one can hardly think properly; very busy.
examples: I’ve been so busy that I hardly have time to think.
I hardly have time to think in the job that I do. We are just too busy.

senses.definition: to have originated as something; to have started out as something.
senses.notes: Harken is an older word meaning “pay heed to.”
examples: The word icebox harks back to refrigerators that were cooled by ice.
Our modern breakfast cereals hark back to the porridge and gruel of our ancestors.

senses.definition: to remind one of something.
examples: Seeing a horse and buggy in the park harks back to the time when horses drew milk wagons.
Sally says it harkens back to the time when everything was delivered by a horse-drawn wagon.

senses.definition: to keep talking or complaining about something; to refer to something again and again.
examples: Mary’s always harping on being poor, but she has more than enough money.
Jack has been harping on high taxes for years.

senses.definition: to discuss something in great detail.
examples: Okay, we can hash it over this afternoon.
Why don’t you come to my office so we can hash over this contract?

senses.definition: Time gained in doing something rapidly and carelessly will be lost when one has to do the thing over again correctly.
examples: Now, take your time. Haste makes waste.
Haste makes waste, so be careful as you work.

senses.definition: to hate someone very much.
examples: Oh, Bob is terrible. I hate his guts!
You may hate my guts for saying so, but I think you’re getting gray hair.

senses.definition: to arrest someone; [for a police officer] to take someone to the police station.
examples: The cop hauled the crook in.
They hauled in the suspects.
The traffic officer said, “Do you want me to haul you in?”

senses.definition: to stop somewhere; to come to rest somewhere.
examples: The car hauled up in front of the house.
My hat blew away just as the bus pulled up.
The attackers hauled up at the city gates.

headword: have a bad effect (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to be bad for someone or something.
examples: Aspirin has a bad effect on me.
Cold weather has a bad effect on roses.

senses.definition: have a really great time.
senses.notes: Slang. This ball is a formal, social dancing party.
examples: The picnic was fantastic. We had a ball!
Hey, Mary! Have a ball at the party tonight!

headword: have a bee in one’s bonnet

senses.definition: to have an idea or a thought remain in one’s mind; to have an obsession.
examples: I have a bee in my bonnet that you’d be a good manager.
I had a bee in my bonnet about swimming. I couldn’t stop wanting to go swimming.

senses.definition: to be a gossiper; to be a person who tells secrets.
examples: Mary has a big mouth. She told Bob what I was getting him for his birthday.
You shouldn’t say things like that about people all the time. Everyone will say you have a big mouth.

senses.definition: to burst.
examples: I had a blowout on the way here. I nearly lost control of the car.
If you have a blowout in one tire, you should check the other tires.

senses.definition: to have a big, wild party; to enjoy oneself at a big party.
examples: Mary and Bill had quite a blowout at their house Friday night.
Fred and Tom had quite a blowout last night.

headword: have a bone to pick (with someone)

senses.definition: to have a disagreement to discuss with someone; to have something to argue about with someone.
examples: Hey, Bill. I’ve got a bone to pick with you. Where is the money you owe me?
I had a bone to pick with her, but she was so sweet that I forgot about it.
You always have a bone to pick.

senses.definition: to have a brief contact with something; to have a brief experience with something.
senses.notes: Especially with the law. Sometimes a close brush. Compare this with have a scrape (with someone or something).
examples: Ann had a close brush with the law. She was nearly arrested for speeding.
When I was younger, I had a brush with scarlet fever, but I got over it.

senses.definition: to have much evidence that can be used against someone.
senses.notes: See also build a case (against someone).
examples: Do the police have a case against John?
No, they don’t have a case.

senses.definition: to change one’s attitude or decision, usually from a negative to a positive position.
examples: I had a change of heart at the last minute and gave the old lady some money.
Since I talked to you last, I have had a change of heart. I now approve of your marrying Sam.

headword: have a chip on one’s shoulder

senses.definition: to be tempting someone else to an argument or a fight; to seem willing to instigate conflict.
examples: Who are you mad at? You always seem to have a chip on your shoulder.
John has had a chip on his shoulder ever since he got his speeding ticket.

headword: have a clear conscience (about someone or something)
altForms: have a clean conscience (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to be free of guilt about someone or something.
examples: I’m not sorry that John got the blame. I have a clean conscience about the whole affair.
I have a clear conscience about John and his problems.
I didn’t do it. I have a clean conscience.
She can’t sleep at night because she doesn’t have a clear conscience.

senses.definition: to have a narrow escape from something dangerous.
senses.notes: See also have a brush with something.
examples: What a close shave I had! I nearly fell off the roof when I was working there.
I almost got struck by a speeding car. It was a close shave.

senses.definition: to know anything about something; to have even a hint about something.
examples: I don’t have a clue about where to start looking for Jim.
Why do you think I have a clue about Tom’s disappearance?

senses.definition: to get angry or hysterical.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also have a fit.
examples: I got so mad I thought I was going to have a conniption.
My father had a conniption fit when I got home this morning.

senses.definition: to sound familiar.
examples: Your excuse has a familiar ring. Have you done this before?
This term paper has a familiar ring. I think it has been copied.

senses.definition: to have a premonition that [something might happen]; to have an intuition about something.
examples: I had a feeling that you might be dropping by this afternoon.
I didn’t have any facts to support it. I just had a feeling.

senses.definition: to experience freedom from one’s usual work schedule; to have a wild time.
senses.notes: Refers to a day when children are released from classes to take part in sports and athletic contests.
examples: The boss was gone and we had a field day to-day. No one got anything done.
The air was fresh and clear, and everyone had a field day in the park during the lunch hour.

headword: have a finger in the pie
altForms: have one’s finger in the pie

senses.definition: to have a role in something; to be involved in something.
examples: Tess wants to have a finger in the pie. She doesn’t think we can do it by ourselves.
Sally always wants to have a finger in the pie.

senses.definition: to be very angry.
examples: The teacher had a fit when the dog ran through the classroom.
John had a fit when he found his car had been damaged.

headword: have a foot in both camps

senses.definition: to have an interest in or to support each of two opposing groups of people.
examples: The shop steward had been promised a promotion and so had a foot in both camps during the strike—workers and management.
Mr. Smith has a foot in both camps in the parent-teacher dispute. He teaches math, but he has a son at the school.

headword: have a frog in one’s throat

senses.definition: to have a feeling of hoarseness.
examples: I cannot speak more clearly. I have a frog in my throat.
I had a frog in my throat, and the telephone receptionist couldn’t understand me.

senses.definition: to be susceptible to collapsing when struck on the head.
senses.notes: Informal. Said only of boxers who are frequently knocked down by a blow to the head.
examples: When the prizefighter was knocked out in his third fight, the newspapers said he had a glass jaw.
Once a fighter has a glass jaw, he’s finished as a boxer.

headword: have a good command of something

senses.definition: to know something well.
examples: Bill has a good command of French.
Jane has a good command of economic theory.

headword: have a good head on one’s shoulders

senses.definition: to have common sense; to be sensible and intelligent.
examples: Mary doesn’t do well in school, but she’s got a good head on her shoulders.
John has a good head on his shoulders and can be depended on to give good advice.

headword: have a (good) mind to do something

senses.definition: to be tempted to do something; to be on the verge of doing something that one has thought about.
examples: I have a good mind to tell her just exactly what I think of her.
She had a mind to leave the room right then and there.

senses.definition: to have something arranged for one’s benefit.
examples: Sally paints pictures and sells them at art fairs. She has a good thing going, and she makes good money.
John inherited a fortune and doesn’t have to work for a living anymore. He’s got a good thing going.

senses.definition: to have the ability to grow plants well.
examples: Just look at Mr. Simpson’s garden. He has a green thumb.
My mother has a green thumb when it comes to houseplants.

senses.definition: to play a part in (doing) something.
examples: I had a hand in the picnic plans.
I want to have a hand in any revision of the script.

senses.definition: to have or get control of something; to have or get an understanding of something.
examples: Get a handle on your temper and calm down.
The police chief had a handle on the potential riot situation.

senses.definition: to experience unnecessary difficulties.
examples: I get a hard time every time I come to this store.
I never have a hard time at the store across the street.

senses.definition: have the mental capacity for something.
examples: Jane has a good head for directions and never gets lost.
Bill doesn’t have a head for figures and should never become an accountant.

senses.definition: to be compassionate; to be generous and forgiving.
examples: Oh, have a heart! Give me some help!
If Ann had a heart, she’d have made us feel more welcome.

senses.definition: to be generous, sincere, and friendly.
examples: Mary is such a lovely person. She has a heart of gold.
You think Tom stole your watch? Impossible! He has a heart of gold.

senses.definition: to be cold and unfriendly.
examples: Sally has a heart of stone. She never even smiles.
The villain in the play had a heart of stone. He was an ideal villain.

senses.definition: to have a sincere and intimate talk.
examples: I had a heart-to-heart talk with my father before I went off to college.
I have a problem, John. Let’s sit down and have a heart-to-heart.

senses.definition: to have a strong and secure influence on someone.
examples: The strange religion seemed to have a strong hold on its followers.
The drug has a hold on the minds of those who use it.

headword: have a hunch (that) something will happen

senses.definition: to have an idea about what did, will, or should happen; to have a feeling that something will or should happen.
examples: I had a hunch that you would be here when I arrived.
I have a hunch about the way things will happen.

headword: have a keen interest in something

senses.definition: to have a strong interest in something; to be very interested in something.
examples: Tom had always had a keen interest in music, so he started a band.
The children have a keen interest in having a pet, so I bought them a cat.

senses.definition: to have many things working to one’s benefit.
examples: Jane is so lucky. She has a lot going for her.
She has a good job and a nice family. She has a lot going.

senses.definition: to be very promising; to have a good future ahead.
examples: Sally is quite young, but she has a lot of promise.
This bush is small, but it has a lot of promise.

headword: have a lot on one’s mind

senses.definition: to have many things to worry about; to be preoccupied.
examples: I’m sorry that I’m so grouchy. I have a lot on my mind.
He forgot to go to his appointment because he had a lot on his mind.

senses.definition: to anger easily.
examples: Be nice to John. He’s upset and has a low boiling point.
Mr. Jones sure has a low boiling point. I hardly said anything, and he got angry.

headword: have a mind like a steel trap

senses.definition: to have a very sharp and agile mind; to have a mind capable of fast, incisive thought.
examples: Sally can handle the questioning. She has a mind like a steel trap.
If I had a mind like a steel trap, I wouldn’t have so much trouble concentrating.

senses.definition: to experience something that was not foreseen or intended.
examples: Traffic is very bad. I almost had an accident.
Drive carefully. Try to avoid having an accident.

senses.definition: to lose control of the bowels or the bladder.
senses.notes: Euphemistic. Usually said of a young child.
examples: “Oh, Ann,” cried Mother. “It looks like you’ve had an accident!”
Mother asked Billy to go to the bathroom before they left so that he wouldn’t have an accident in the car.

headword: have an ace up one’s sleeve

senses.definition: to have a secret or concealed means of accomplishing something.
senses.notes: Refers to being prepared to cheat in a card game.
examples: I think that Liz has an ace up her sleeve and will surprise us with success at the last minute.
I have done all I can do. I have no idea what to do next. I don’t have an ace up my sleeve, and I can’t work miracles.

headword: have an ax to grind (with someone)

senses.definition: to have something to complain about.
examples: Tom, I need to talk to you. I have an ax to grind with you.
Bill and Bob went into the other room to argue. They had an ax to grind.

senses.definition: to have the ability to learn music or languages.
examples: Bill doesn’t have an ear for music. He can’t carry a tune.
Mary has a good ear for languages.

senses.definition: to nearly crash or collide.
examples: The airplanes—flying much too close—had a near miss.
I had a near miss while driving over here.

headword: have an eye for someone or something

senses.definition: to have a taste or an inclination for someone or something.
examples: Bob has an eye for beauty.
He has an eye for color.
Ann has an eye for well-dressed men.

headword: have an eye on someone or something
altForms: keep an eye on someone or something

senses.definition: to keep watch on someone or something; to keep track of someone or something.
senses.notes: The an can be replaced by one’s.
examples: I have my eye on the apple tree. When the apples ripen, I’ll harvest them.
Please keep an eye on the baby.
Will you please keep your eye on my house while I’m on vacation?

headword: have an eye out (for someone or something)
altForms: keep an eye out (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to watch for the arrival or appearance of someone or something.
senses.notes: The an can be replaced by one’s.
examples: Please try to have an eye out for the bus.
Keep an eye out for rain.
Have your eye out for a raincoat on sale.
Okay. I’ll keep my eye out.

senses.definition: to have a desire for something.
examples: I have an itch for a nice cool glass of lemonade.
Who besides me has an itch for pizza?

headword: have an itch to do something

senses.definition: to have a desire to do something.
examples: I have an itch to see a movie tonight.
Tom has an itch to go swimming.

senses.definition: to be in need of a tip; to tend to ask for tips.
senses.notes: As if placing money in the palm would stop the itching.
examples: All the waiters at that restaurant have itchy palms.
The cabdriver was troubled by an itching palm. Since he refused to carry my bags, I gave him nothing.

senses.definition: to have the talent for finding something.
examples: Police dogs have a good nose for drugs.
The reporter has a nose for news.

senses.definition: to have a mind that thinks entirely or almost entirely about one subject, often sex.
examples: Adolescent boys often have one-track minds. All they’re interested in is the opposite sex.
Bob has a one-track mind. He can only talk about football.

headword: have a passion for someone or something

senses.definition: to have a strong feeling of need or desire for someone, something, or some activity.
examples: Mary has a great passion for chocolate.
John has a passion for fishing, so he fishes as often as he can.

senses.definition: to look quickly, sometimes through a small hole.
examples: Have a peep into the refrigerator and see if we need any milk.
I took a peep at the comet through the telescope.

headword: have a penchant for doing something

senses.definition: to have a taste, desire, or inclination for doing something.
examples: John has a penchant for eating fattening foods.
Ann has a penchant for buying clothes.

senses.definition: to eat or drink something stimulating.
senses.notes: The have can be replaced with need, want, etc. The me does not change.
examples: I’d like to have a pick-me-up. I think I’ll have a bottle of pop.
You look tired. You need a pick-me-up.

headword: have a price on one’s head

senses.definition: to be wanted by the authorities, who have offered a reward for one’s capture.
senses.notes: Informal or folksy. Usually limited to western and gangster movies.
examples: We captured a thief who had a price on his head, and the sheriff gave us the reward.
The crook was so mean, he turned in his own brother, who had a price on his head.

headword: have a right to do something
altForms: have the right to do something

senses.definition: to have the freedom to do something; to possess legal or moral permission or license to do something.
examples: You don’t have the right to enter my home without my permission.
I have a right to grow anything I want on my farmland.

senses.definition: to experience a difficult period.
examples: Since his wife died, Mr. Brown has been having a rough time of it.
Be nice to Bob. He’s been having a rough time.

senses.definition: to reach a position of power, authority, or prominence.
examples: Jane saw her picture on the cover of the magazine and felt that she had finally arrived.
When I got an office with a window, I knew that I had arrived.

senses.definition: to have an unpleasant and troublesome encounter with someone.
examples: I had a run-in with Anne at the party, so I left early.
David had a small run-in with the law last night.

headword: have a run of bad luck

senses.definition: to have bad luck repeatedly; to have bad things happen a number of times.
examples: I have had a run of bad luck, and I have no more money to spend.
The company had a run of bad luck over the last few years.

senses.definition: to have a continuous series of events.
examples: The city had a run of serious crimes that angered the citizens.
We had a run of very hot days last July.

headword: have a score to settle (with someone)

senses.definition: to have a problem to clear up with someone; to have to get even with someone about something.
senses.notes: See also settle a score with someone.
examples: I have a score to settle with John.
John and I have a score to settle.

headword: have a scrape (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to come into contact with someone or something; to have a small battle with someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with have a brush with something.
examples: I had a scrape with the county sheriff.
John and Bill had a scrape, but they are friends again now.

senses.definition: to act silly or crazy.
examples: John is such a clown. He acts as if he has a screw loose.
What’s the matter with you? Do you have a screw loose or something?

senses.definition: to smoke a cigarette, cigar, or pipe.
senses.notes: The have can be replaced with need, want, etc.
examples: Can I have a smoke? I’m very nervous.
Do you have a cigarette? I need a smoke.

headword: have a snowball’s chance in hell

senses.definition: to have no chance at all; to have a chance no greater than that of a snowball in hell.
senses.notes: A snowball would melt in hell and have no chance of surviving. Use caution with hell.
examples: He has a snowball’s chance in hell of passing the test.
You don’t have a snowball’s chance in hell of her agreeing to marry you.

headword: have a soft spot in one’s heart for someone or something

senses.definition: to be fond of someone or something.
examples: John has a soft spot in his heart for Mary.
I have a soft spot in my heart for chocolate cake.

senses.definition: to get angry or hysterical; to have a conniption (fit).
examples: Relax, Bob. Don’t have a spaz.
My father had a spaz when I came in late last night.

senses.definition: to experience sudden unconsciousness or paralysis due to an interruption in the blood supply to the brain.
senses.notes: Also used as an exaggeration. See the last two examples below.
examples: The patient who received an artificial heart had a stroke two days after the operation.
My great-uncle Bill—who is very old— had a stroke last May.
Calm down, Bob. You’re going to have a stroke.
My father almost had a stroke when I came home at three o’clock this morning.

senses.definition: to desire to eat many sweet foods—especially candy and pastries.
examples: I have a sweet tooth, and if I don’t watch it, I’ll really get fat.
John eats candy all the time. He must have a sweet tooth.

senses.definition: a desire for a particular food, drink, or experience.
examples: The Smiths have a taste for adventure and take exotic vacations.
When she was pregnant, Mary often had a taste for pickles.

senses.definition: to have a romance or a love affair with someone.
examples: John and Mary have a thing going.
Bill has a thing going with Ann.
They have something going.

headword: have a vested interest in something

senses.definition: to have a personal or biased interest, often financial, in something.
examples: Margaret has a vested interest in wanting her father to sell the family firm. She has shares in it and would make a large profit.
Jack has a vested interest in keeping the village traffic-free.

senses.definition: to have a part in making a decision.
examples: I’d like to have a voice in choosing the carpet.
John wanted to have a say in the issue also.
He says he seldom gets to have a say.

headword: have a way with someone or something

senses.definition: to handle or deal well with someone or something.
examples: John has a way with hamburger. It’s always delicious.
Mother has a way with Father. She’ll get him to paint the house.

headword: have a weakness for someone or something

senses.definition: to be unable to resist someone or something; to be fond of someone or something; to be (figuratively) powerless against someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with have a soft spot in one’s heart for someone or something.
examples: I have a weakness for chocolate.
John has a weakness for Mary. I think he’s in love.

headword: have a whale of a time

senses.definition: to have an exciting time; to have a big time.
senses.notes: Slang. Whale is a way of saying big.
examples: We had a whale of a time at Sally’s birthday party.
Enjoy your vacation! I hope you have a whale of a time.

senses.definition: to speak to someone, usually privately.
examples: The manager asked to have a word with me when I was not busy.
John, could I have a word with you? We need to discuss something.

senses.definition: to be slightly crazy.
examples: Poor old Tom has bats in his belfry.
Don’t act so silly, John. People will think you have bats in your belfry.

senses.definition: to apply to something; to affect or influence something.
examples: The worker’s opinion has no bearing on the boss’s decision.
Does this information have any bearing on the question?

senses.definition: to be experienced in life.
senses.notes: Informal. Use with caution—especially with females—since this can also refer to sexual experience. See also get around.
examples: Ask Sally about how the government works. She’s been around.
They all know a lot about life. They’ve been around.

senses.definition: to have been mistreated; to have been been cheated or dealt with badly.
examples: They were cheated out of a thousand dollars. They’ve really been had.
Look what they did to my car. Boy, have I been had.

senses.definition: have been badly treated; have become exhausted.
examples: This has been a rough day. I’ve really been through the mill.
This old car is banged up, and it hardly runs. It’s been through the mill.

headword: have been to hell and back

senses.definition: to have survived a great deal of trouble.
examples: What a terrible day! I feel like I have been to hell and back.
After a day of shopping, I feel like I have been to hell and back.

senses.definition: to have the ability to take on unpleasant responsibilities; to have the ability to accept criticism or rebuke.
senses.notes: Refers to the apparent strength of broad shoulders to support a heavy burden.
examples: No need to apologize to me. I can take it. I have broad shoulders.
Karen may have broad shoulders, but she can’t endure endless criticism.

senses.definition: to be guiltless.
senses.notes: Refers to the blood on the hands of a murderer.
examples: Don’t look at me. I have clean hands.
The police took him in, but let him go again because he had clean hands.

senses.definition: to have accomplished much; to have advanced much.
examples: My, how famous you are. You’ve come a long way.
Tom has come a long way in a short time.

senses.definition: a link to someone resulting in communication.
examples: I have had no contact with Bill since he left town.
Tom had contact with a known criminal last month.

headword: have designs on someone or something

senses.definition: to have plans for someone or something.
examples: Mrs. Brown has designs on my apple tree. I think she’s going to cut off the part that hangs over her fence.
Mary has designs on Bill. I think she’ll try to date him.

senses.definition: to reserve something for oneself; to claim something for oneself.
senses.notes: Informal. See also put (one’s) dibs on something.
examples: I have dibs on the last piece of cake.
John has dibs on the last piece again. It isn’t fair.

senses.definition: to be embarrassed because of an error that is obvious to everyone.
examples: Bob has egg on his face because he wore jeans to the party and everyone else wore formal clothing.
John was completely wrong about the weather for the picnic. It snowed! Now he has egg on his face.

headword: have eyes bigger than one’s stomach

senses.definition: to have a desire for more food than one could possibly eat.
senses.notes: See also one’s eyes are bigger then one’s stomach.
examples: I know I have eyes bigger than my stomach, so I won’t take a lot of food.
Todd has eyes bigger than his stomach.

headword: have eyes in the back of one’s head

senses.definition: to seem to be able to sense what is going on outside of one’s vision.
examples: My teacher seems to have eyes in the back of her head.
My teacher doesn’t need to have eyes in the back of his head. He watches us very carefully.

senses.definition: to have a defect of character.
examples: All human beings have feet of clay. No one is perfect.
Sally was popular and successful. She was nearly fifty before she learned that she, too, had feet of clay.

senses.definition: to embarrass oneself through a silly blunder.
senses.notes: Informal. This is a parody on foot-and-mouth disease or hoof-and-mouth disease, which affects cattle and deer. See also put one’s foot in one’s mouth.
examples: I’m sorry I keep saying stupid things. I guess I have foot-in-mouth disease.
Yes, you really have foot-in-mouth disease tonight.

senses.definition: to have pains—which are attributed to growth—in the muscles and joints.
examples: The doctor said that all Mary had were growing pains and that nothing was really wrong.
Not everyone has growing pains.

senses.definition: to have difficulties in its growth.
examples: The banker apologized for losing my check and said the bank was having growing pains.
Governments have terrible growing pains.

senses.definition: to have had as much of something as is needed or will be tolerated.
senses.notes: Compare this with have had it (up to here).
examples: Stop yelling at me. I’ve had enough.
No more potatoes, please. I’ve had enough.
I’m leaving you, Bill. I’ve had enough!

senses.definition: to be no longer useful or successful.
examples: Streetcars have had their day in most American cities.
Some people think that radio has had its day, but others prefer it to television.

senses.definition: to have reached the end of one’s endurance or tolerance.
examples: Okay, I’ve had it. You kids go to bed this instant.
We’ve all had it with you, John. Get out!
I’ve had it. I’ve got to go to bed before I drop dead.
Tom is disgusted. He said that he has had it up to here.

headword: have half a notion to do something
altForms: have half a mind to do something

senses.definition: to have almost decided to do something, especially something unpleasant.
examples: I have half a mind to go off and leave you here.
The cook had half a notion to serve cold chicken.

senses.definition: Do you understand exactly what I am telling you?
examples: I don’t intend to warn you again. Have I made myself clear?
I do not want you to go there! Have I made myself clear?

senses.definition: to have both of two incompatible things.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also have one’s cake and eat it too.
examples: John wants the security of marriage and the freedom of being single. He wants to have it both ways.
John thinks he can have it both ways—the wisdom of age and the vigor of youth.

senses.definition: to have a purpose in what one is doing, even though it seems to be mad.
examples: What I’m doing may look strange, but there is method in my madness.
Wait until she finishes; then you’ll see that there is method in her madness.

headword: have mixed feelings (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to be uncertain about someone or something.
examples: I have mixed feelings about Bob. Sometimes I think he likes me; other times I don’t.
I have mixed feelings about my trip to England. I love the people, but the climate upsets me.
Yes, I also have mixed feelings.

senses.definition: to have lots of money; to have more money than one needs.
senses.notes: See also Money burns a hole in someone’s pocket.
examples: Look at the way Tom buys things. You’d think he had money to burn.
If I had money to burn, I’d just put it in the bank.

senses.definition: have never had so much good fortune.
examples: No, I’m not complaining. I’ve never had it so good.
Mary is pleased with her new job. She’s never had it so good.

senses.definition: to be wrong to do something; to be extremely unwise to do something.
examples: You have no business bursting in on me like that!
You have no business spending money like that!

senses.definition: to tolerate or endure no amount of something.
examples: I’ll have none of your talk about quitting school.
We’ll have none of your gossip.
I wish to have none of the sweet potatoes, please.

senses.definition: to lack endurance; not to be able to last.
examples: Sally can swim fast for a short distance, but she has no staying power.
That horse can race fairly well, but it has no staying power.

headword: have nothing on someone or something

senses.definition: to lack evidence against someone.
examples: The police had nothing on Bob, so they let him loose.
You’ve got nothing on me! Let me go!

senses.definition: to have no information about someone or something.
examples: The dictionary had nothing on the word I looked up.
The librarian said that the library has nothing on the Jones brothers.

headword: have one foot in the grave

senses.definition: to be near death, either because of old age or because of illness.
examples: Fred’s uncle is ninety. He has one foot in the grave and may not live another two months.
Terry has one foot in the grave and will perish unless he receives treatment soon.

senses.definition: to have a drink just before leaving.
examples: I think I’ll have one for the road, bartender.
Forget having one for the road if you are driving.

headword: have one’s back to the wall

senses.definition: to be in a defensive position.
senses.notes: Informal. See also push someone to the wall.
examples: He’ll have to give in. He has his back to the wall.
How can I bargain when I’ve got my back to the wall?

headword: have one’s cake and eat it too
altForms: eat one’s cake and have it too

senses.definition: to enjoy both having something and using it up; to have it both ways.
examples: Tom wants to have his cake and eat it too. It can’t be done.
Don’t buy a car if you want to walk and stay healthy. You can’t eat your cake and have it too.

senses.definition: to get one’s choice; to be permitted to have one’s preference.
senses.notes: Folksy. The druthers is from would rather.
examples: If I had my druthers, I’d go to France.
Tom said that if he had his druthers, he’d choose to stay home.

headword: have one’s ear to the ground
altForms: keep one’s ear to the ground

senses.definition: to listen carefully, hoping to get advance warning of something.
senses.notes: Refers to holding one’s ear against the ground to listen for approaching horses or a train.
examples: John had his ear to the ground, hoping to find out about new ideas in computers.
His boss told him to keep his ear to the ground so that he’d be the first to know of a new idea.

headword: have one’s finger in too may pies

senses.definition: to be involved in too many things; to have too many tasks going to be able to do any of them well.
examples: I’m too busy. I have my finger in too may pies.
She never gets anything done because she has her finger in too many pies.

headword: have one’s hand in the till

senses.definition: to be stealing money from a company or an organization.
senses.notes: The till is a cash box or drawer.
examples: Mr. Jones had his hand in the till for years before he was caught.
I think that the new clerk has her hand in the till. There is cash missing every morning.

headword: have one’s hands full (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to be busy or totally occupied with someone or something.
senses.notes: Literal when one cannot hold anything else in one’s hands.
examples: I have my hands full with my three children.
You have your hands full with the store.
We both have our hands full.

senses.definition: to be prevented from doing something.
examples: I can’t help you. I was told not to, so I have my hands tied.
John can help. He doesn’t have his hands tied.

headword: have one’s head in the clouds

senses.definition: to be unaware of what is going on.
examples: “Bob, do you have your head in the clouds?” said the teacher.
She walks around all day with her head in the clouds. She must be in love.

headword: have one’s heart go out to someone

senses.definition: to have compassion for someone.
examples: I can’t have my heart go out to everyone.
To have compassion is to have one’s heart go out to those who are suffering.

headword: have one’s heart in the right place

senses.definition: to have good intentions, even if there are bad results.
senses.notes: See also one’s heart is in the right place.
examples: I don’t always do what is right, but my heart is in the right place.
Good old Tom. His heart’s in the right place.
It doesn’t matter if she lost the game. She has her heart in the right place.

headword: have one’s heart set against something

senses.definition: to be totally against something.
senses.notes: Also with dead, as in the example. See also dead set against someone or something; set one’s heart against something.
examples: Jane has her heart dead set against going to Australia.
John has his heart set against going to college.

headword: have one’s heart set on something

senses.definition: to be desiring and expecting something.
examples: Jane has her heart set on going to London.
Bob will be disappointed. He had his heart set on going to college this year.
She had her heart set on it.

senses.definition: an expression said when one’s heart (figuratively) stops beating because one is feeling strong emotions.
examples: I had my heart stand still once when I was overcome with joy.
Lovers—at least the ones in love songs— usually have their hearts stand still.

senses.definition: for one’s good luck to stop; for one’s good fortune to come to an end.
examples: I had my luck run out when I was in South America. I nearly starved.
I hate to have my luck run out just when I need it.

headword: have one’s nose in a book

senses.definition: to be reading a book; to read books all the time.
examples: Bob has his nose in a book every time I see him.
His nose is always in a book. He never gets any exercise.

headword: have one’s nose in the air

senses.definition: to be conceited or aloof.
senses.notes: See also one’s nose is in the air.
examples: Mary always seems to have her nose in the air.
I wonder if she knows that she has her nose in the air.

headword: have one’s words stick in one’s throat

senses.definition: to be so overcome by emotion that one can hardly speak.
examples: I sometimes have my words stick in my throat.
John said that he never had his words stick in his throat.

headword: have one’s work cut out for one

senses.definition: to have a large and difficult task prepared for one.
senses.notes: See also one’s work is cut out for one.
examples: They sure have their work cut out for them, and it’s going to be hard.
There is a lot for Bob to do. He has his work cut out for him.

altForms: have more important fish to fry

senses.definition: to have other things to do; to have more important things to do.
examples: I can’t take time for your problem. I have other fish to fry.
I won’t waste time on your question. I have bigger fish to fry.

headword: have precedence over someone or something
altForms: take precedence over someone or something

senses.definition: have the right to come before someone or something else.
examples: Ambulances have precedence over regular cars at intersections.
My manager’s concerns take precedence over mine.

senses.definition: to have influence with someone.
senses.notes: Slang. Also with some, much, lots, etc.
examples: Let’s ask Ann to help us. She has pull with the mayor.
Do you know anyone who has some pull with the bank president? I need a loan.

senses.definition: to be silly or crazy.
examples: John is a real nut. He has rocks in his head.
I don’t have rocks in my head—I’m just different.

headword: have second thoughts about someone or something

senses.definition: to have doubts about someone or something.
examples: I’m beginning to have second thoughts about Tom.
We now have second thoughts about going to Canada.

senses.definition: to be worn or worn out.
examples: This coat has seen better days. I need a new one.
Oh, my old legs ache. I’ve seen better days, but everyone has to grow old.

senses.definition: to have proven someone unquestionably guilty.
examples: The police burst in on the robbers while they were at work. They had the robbers dead to rights.
All right, Tom! I’ve got you dead to rights! Get your hand out of the cookie jar.

senses.definition: to have control over someone.
examples: Don’t worry about the mayor. She’ll cooperate. I’ve got her in my pocket.
John will do just what I tell him. I’ve got him and his brother in my pocket.

senses.definition: to have someone waiting for your decision.
examples: Sally has John on the string. He has asked her to marry him, but she hasn’t replied yet.
Yes, it sounds like she has him on the string.

headword: have someone or something in one’s hands

senses.definition: to have control of or responsibility for someone or something.
examples: You have the whole project in your hands.
The boss put the whole project in your hands.
I have to leave the baby in your hands while I go to the doctor.

headword: have someone or something on one’s hands

senses.definition: to be burdened with someone or something.
examples: I run a record store. I sometimes have a large number of unwanted records on my hands.
She the all the children on her hands today.

headword: have someone’s blood on one’s hands

senses.definition: to be responsible for someone’s death; to be guilty of causing someone’s death.
examples: The teenager’s blood was on the policeman’s hands.
The king’s blood was on the hands of the murderer who killed him.

senses.definition: to scold or punish someone.
senses.notes: Refers to skinning an animal. Informal. Compare this with skin someone alive.
examples: If you ever do that again, I’ll have your hide.
He said he’d have my hide if I entered his garage again.

senses.definition: to have something within (one’s) reach.
senses.notes: Have can be replaced with keep.
examples: I have a dictionary at my fingertips.
I try to have everything I need at hand.
I keep my medicine at my fingertips.

senses.definition: to deserve punishment (for something).
examples: Bill broke a window, so he has a spanking coming to him.
That’s it, Bill. Now you’ve got it coming!

senses.definition: to have plans for a particular time.
senses.notes: Informal. Note the variation with anything in the examples below.
examples: BOB: Are you busy Saturday night? BILL: Yes, I’ve got something doing.
I don’t have anything doing Sunday night.
I have something on almost every Saturday.

senses.definition: to have learned or memorized something perfectly.
examples: I have practiced my speech until I have it down pat.
Tom has his part in the play down pat. He won’t make any mistakes.

senses.definition: to have a business deal with someone.
examples: Sally has a new business project going with Ann. They’ll announce a new product in the spring.
John and Tom work as stockbrokers. I’ve heard that they have a business deal going.

headword: have something hanging over one’s head

senses.definition: to have something bothering or worrying one; to have a deadline worrying one.
examples: I keep worrying about getting drafted. I hate to have something like that hanging over my head.
I have a history paper that is hanging over my head.

headword: have something in common (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to resemble one another in specific ways.
examples: Bill and Bob both have red hair. They have that in common with each other.
Bob and Mary have a lot in common. I can see why they like each other.

senses.definition: to have something in one’s hand or close by.
senses.notes: Compare this with have something at hand.
examples: I have your letter of May tenth in hand.
I have my pen in hand, and I’m ready to write.

senses.definition: to have merchandise available and ready for sale.
examples: Do you have extra large sizes in stock?
Of course, we have all sizes and colors in stock.

senses.definition: to have something planned for one’s future.
examples: Tom has a large inheritance in store for him when his uncle dies.
I wish I had something like that in store.

senses.definition: to hire someone to make something.
examples: Isn’t it a lovely coat? I had to have it made because I couldn’t find one I liked in a store.
We had the cake made at the bakery. Our oven isn’t big enough for a cake that size.

senses.definition: to have achieved a successful state.
examples: Mary really has it made. She inherited one million dollars.
I wish I had it made like that.

senses.definition: to have a written record of something in storage.
examples: I’m sure I have your letter on file. I’ll check again.
We have your application on file somewhere.

senses.definition: to have a particular amount of smartness or cleverness.
examples: Both John and Mary have a lot on the ball. They should go far.
I think I’d do better in school if I had more on the ball. I learn slowly.

senses.definition: to be obsessed with something.
examples: Bob has chocolate on the brain.
Mary has money on the brain. She wants to earn as much as possible.

headword: have something on the tip of one’s tongue

senses.definition: to be on the verge of remembering a specific fact, such as someone’s name; to have just forgotten a specific fact.
senses.notes: See also on the tip of one’s tongue.
examples: Just give me a minute. I have her name on the tip of my tongue!
I had her name on the tip of my tongue, but you made me forget it when you called.

headword: have something stick in one’s craw

senses.definition: to have something irritate or displease someone.
examples: I don’t like to have Bill’s words stick in my craw.
He meant to have the problem stick in my craw and upset me.

senses.definition: to have more than enough of something.
senses.notes: Informal. See also and something to spare.
examples: Ask John for some firewood. He has firewood to spare.
Do you have any candy to spare?

senses.definition: to have a secret or surprise plan or solution (to a problem).
senses.notes: Slang. Refers to cheating at cards by having a card hidden in one’s sleeve.
examples: I’ve got something up my sleeve, and it should solve all your problems. I’ll tell you what it is after I’m elected.
The manager has something up her sleeve. She’ll surprise us with it later.

senses.definition: to have a tendency to steal.
examples: The clerk—who had sticky fingers—got fired.
The little boy had sticky fingers and was always taking his father’s small change.

headword: have the ball in one’s court

senses.definition: to be responsible for the next move in some process; to have to make a response to something that someone else has started.
examples: You have the ball in your court now. You have to answer the attorney’s questions.
There was no way that Liz could avoid acting. She had the ball in her court.

headword: have the best of both worlds

senses.definition: to be in a situation where one can enjoy two different opportunities.
examples: When Donna was a fellow at the university, she had the privileges of a professor and the freedom of a student. She definitely had the best of both worlds.
Don hated to have to choose between retirement and continuing working. He wanted to do both so he could have the best of both worlds.

headword: have the cards stacked against one
altForms: have the deck stacked against one

senses.definition: to have one’s chance at future success limited by factors over which one has no control; to have luck against one.
examples: You can’t get very far in life if you have the deck stacked against you.
I can’t seem to get ahead. I always have the cards stacked against

headword: have the courage of one’s convictions

senses.definition: to have enough courage and determination to carry out one’s goals.
examples: It’s fine to have noble goals in life and to believe in great things. If you don’t have the courage of your convictions, you’ll never reach your goals.
Jane was successful because she had the courage of her convictions.

senses.definition: to have a great deal of trouble.
examples: If you cheat on your income taxes, you’ll have the devil to pay.
I came home after three in the morning and had hell to pay.

headword: have the gall to do something

senses.definition: to have sufficient arrogance to do something.
examples: I bet you don’t have the gall to argue with the mayor.
Only Jane has the gall to ask the boss for a second raise this month.

senses.definition: to have a great facility with language; to be able to use language very effectively.
examples: My brother really has the gift of gab. He can convince anyone of anything.
If I had the gift of gab like you do, I’d achieve more in life.

senses.definition: to possess the qualities that are needed for something.
examples: The young boy had the makings of a fine baseball player.
My boss has all the makings of a prison warden.

senses.definition: to have the ability to be successful, especially the ability to make money easily.
senses.notes: From the name of a legendary king whose touch turned everything to gold.
examples: Bob is a merchant banker and really has the Midas touch.
The poverty-stricken boy turned out to have the Midas touch and was a millionaire by the time he was twenty-five.

headword: have them rolling in the aisles

senses.definition: to make an audience roll in the aisles with laughter.
examples: I have the best jokes you’ve ever heard. I’ll have them rolling in the aisles.
What a great performance. We had them rolling in the aisles.

headword: have the patience of a saint

senses.definition: to be very patient.
senses.notes: Refers to the “patience” that someone experiencing martyrdom might have.
examples: I don’t know how she puts up with all those stupid questions. She has the patience of a saint.
Hurry up, please. I am late and you are working too slow. I don’t have the patience of a saint.

headword: have the presence of mind to do something

senses.definition: to have the calmness and the ability to act sensibly in an emergency or difficult situation.
examples: Jane had the presence of mind to phone the police when the child disappeared.
The child had the presence of mind to take note of the car’s license number.

senses.definition: to possess the legal right to occupy a particular space on a public roadway.
examples: I had a traffic accident yesterday, but it wasn’t my fault. I had the right-of-way.
Don’t pull out onto a highway if you don’t have the right-of-way.

headword: have the shoe on the other foot

senses.definition: to experience the opposite situation (from a previous situation).
senses.notes: Informal. Also with be instead of have. See the examples. See the proverb The shoe is on the other foot. Compare this with in someone else’s shoes.
examples: I used to be a student, and now I’m the teacher. Now I have the shoe on the other foot.
You were mean to me when you thought I was cheating. Now that I have caught you cheating, the shoe is on the other foot.

headword: have the time of one’s life

senses.definition: to have a very good time; to have the most exciting time in one’s life.
examples: What a great party! I had the time of my life.
We went to Florida last winter and had the time of our lives.

senses.definition: to have the means to do something, especially energy or money.
examples: He has good ideas, but he doesn’t have the wherewithal to carry them out.
I could do a lot if only I had the wherewithal.

senses.definition: to have to endure something.
senses.notes: See also learn to live with something.
examples: I have a slight limp in the leg that I broke last year. The doctor says I’ll have to live with it.
We don’t like the new carpeting in the living room, but we’ll have to live with it.

headword: have too many irons in the fire

senses.definition: to be doing too many things at once.
examples: Tom had too many irons in the fire and missed some important deadlines.
It’s better if you don’t have too many irons in the fire.

senses.definition: to have passed a critical point in a process.
examples: The patient has turned the corner. She should begin to show improvement now.
The project has turned the corner. The rest should be easy.

senses.definition: to have several things against one; to be in a position where success is unlikely.
examples: Poor Bob had two strikes against him when he tried to explain where he was last night.
I can’t win. I have two strikes against me before I start.

senses.definition: to have the ability, courage, or stamina (to do something).
examples: Bill has what it takes. He can swim for miles.
Tom won’t succeed. He doesn’t have what it takes.

senses.definition: a vague greeting inquiry asking about how someone has been occupied.
senses.notes: Really just a way to say hello and open a conversation.
examples: How are you? Have you been keeping busy?
What’ve you been doing? Have you been keeping busy?

senses.definition: to make a guess.
examples: Even if you don’t know, please hazard a guess.
If you don’t know the answer, hazard a guess.

senses.definition: to give an opinion.
examples: Anne asked the attorney to hazard an opinion about the strength of her lawsuit.
Don’t feel like you have to hazard an opinion on something you know nothing about.

headword: He who laughs last, laughs longest.
altForms: He laughs best who laughs last.

senses.definition: Whoever succeeds in making the last move or pulling the last trick has the most enjoyment.
examples: Bill had pulled many silly tricks on Tom. Finally Tom pulled a very funny trick on Bill and said, “He who laughs last, laughs longest.”
Bill pulled another, even bigger, trick on Tom and said, laughing, “He laughs best who laughs last.”

headword: He who pays the piper calls the tune.

senses.definition: The person who is paying for something has control over how the money is used.
examples: Fred’s father is paying his way through college, and wants to help him choose his courses. He says that he who pays the piper calls the tune.
The bride’s parents should have a say in where the wedding is held since they’re paying for it. He who pays the piper calls the tune.

senses.definition: a person; [for] an individual.
examples: How much do you charge per head for dinner?
It costs four dollars a head.

headword: head and shoulders above someone or something

senses.definition: clearly superior to someone or something.
senses.notes: Often with stand, as in the example.
examples: This wine is head and shoulders above that one.
John stands head and shoulders above Bob.

senses.definition: to aim for or move toward someone or something.
examples: She waved good-bye as she headed for the door.
Ann came in and headed for her mother.

senses.definition: to reach the end of something.
senses.notes: Originally said of a dying cowboy.
examples: This ballpoint pen is headed for the last roundup. I have to get another one.
I am so weak. I think I’m headed for the last roundup.

senses.definition: deeply in debt.
examples: Finally, when she was head over heels in debt, she tore up her credit cards.
I couldn’t stand being head over heels in debt, so I always pay off my bills immediately.

headword: head over heels in love (with someone)

senses.definition: very much in love with someone.
senses.notes: See also fall head over heels in love (with someone).
examples: John is head over heels in love with Mary.
They are head over heels in love with each other.
They are head over heels in love.

senses.definition: to prevent someone or something from arriving.
examples: The doctors worked round the clock to head the epidemic off.
Bill headed his mother off so that we had time to clean up the mess before she saw it.
The farmer headed off the herd of sheep before it ruined our picnic.

senses.definition: to serve as leader or head of something.
examples: I had already agreed to head the fund-raising campaign up.
They asked me to head up the meeting.

senses.definition: the face of a coin or the other side of a coin.
senses.notes: Often used in an act of coin tossing, where one circumstance is valid if the front of a coin appears and another circumstance is valid if the other side appears.
examples: Jim looked at Jane as he flipped the coin into the air. “Heads or tails?” he asked.
It doesn’t matter whether the result of the toss is heads or tails. I won’t like the outcome in any case.

senses.definition: Raise your head from work and look around you carefully for information, danger, or warnings that you need to see!
examples: Heads up! Watch out for that door!
Heads up! There is a car coming.

senses.definition: someone will get into severe trouble.
examples: When the company’s year-end results are known, heads will roll.
Heads will roll when the principal sees the damaged classroom.

headword: hear a peep out of someone

senses.definition: to get some sort of a response from someone; to hear the smallest word from someone.
examples: I don’t want to hear another peep out of you.
I didn’t know they were there. I didn’t hear a peep out of them.
