senses.definition: to tolerate something; to permit something.
examples: No, you cannot go to the movies! I won’t hear of it!
My mother wouldn’t hear of my marrying Bill.

senses.definition: to listen to everything that someone has to say and to not interrupt or go away.
examples: Please, hear me out. This is important.
He had a good idea, but the committee would not hear him out.

senses.definition: the central core [of someone or something].
examples: My very heart and soul was made sad by her hurtful attitude.
Now we are getting to the heart and soul of the matter.
This feature is the heart and soul of my invention.

senses.definition: difficult to do, understand, or make progress with.
examples: Jim finds math heavy going.
Talking to Mary is heavy going. She has nothing to say.

senses.definition: to reduce one’s loss on a bet or on an investment by counterbalancing the loss in some way.
examples: Bob bet Ann that the plane would be late. He usually hedges his bets. This time he called the airline and asked about the plane before he made the bet.

John bought some stock and then bet Mary that the stock would go down in value in one year. He has hedged his bets perfectly. If the stock goes up, he sells it, pays off Mary, and still makes a profit. If it goes down, he reduces his loss by winning the bet he made with Mary.

senses.definition: moving or behaving recklessly; riding a horse fast and recklessly.
senses.notes: Informal. Typically found in western movies.
examples: They took off after the horse thief, riding hell-bent for leather.
Here comes the boss. She’s not just angry; she’s hell-bent for leather.

senses.definition: a very unpleasant situation, as if one were in hell.
examples: That man made my life hell on earth!
The whole time I was there was just hell on earth.

senses.definition: to assist [someone to] do something.
examples: Bill can help load the truck.
I am too tired to help mow the grass.
Bill can help us load the truck.
I am too tired to help you mow the grass.

senses.definition: to take whatever one wants or needs.
examples: Please have some candy. Help yourself.
When you go to a cafeteria, you help yourself to the food.
Bill helped himself to dessert.

headword: help (someone or something) out (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to assist (someone or something) with a person or a thing.
examples: Can you help me out with my geometry?
Yes, I can help out.
Please help out my son with his geometry.
Please help me out around the house.
We helped out the school with its fund-raising.

senses.definition: to be uncertain about something; to be evasive; to say “ah” and “eh” when speaking—avoiding saying something meaningful.
examples: Stop hemming and hawing around. I want an answer.
Don’t just hem and haw around. Speak up. We want to hear what you think.

senses.definition: to trap or enclose someone or something.
examples: The large city buildings hem me in.
Don’t hem in the bird. Let it have a way to escape.

senses.definition: the present, as opposed to the past or the future.
examples: I don’t care what’s happening tomorrow or next week! I care about the here and now.
The past is dead. Let’s worry about the here and now.

senses.definition: I am beginning to do something that will probably fail or be poorly done.
examples: Sally stood on the diving board and said, “Here goes nothing.”
As Ann walked onto the stage, she whispered, “Here goes nothing.”

senses.definition: Something is going to start.; I will start now.; I will do it now.
examples: I’m ready to start now. Here goes.
Okay, it’s my turn to kick the ball. Here it goes!

senses.definition: everywhere; at all points.
senses.notes: See also hither, thither, and yon. Compare this with here and there.
examples: Fred searched here, there, and everywhere, frantically looking for the lost check.
She did not rest until she had been here, there, and everywhere, shopping for just the right gift.

senses.definition: Drink up.
examples: Here’s look at you, Tom.
Thanks for the drink. Here’s looking at you.

senses.definition: Drink up!
senses.notes: A simple and jocular drinking toast.
examples: Here’s mud in your eye, Tom.
Thanks for the drink. Here’s mud in your eye.

senses.definition: an expression used as a toast to someone or something to wish someone or something well.
examples: Here’s to Jim and Mary! May they be very happy!
Here’s to your new job!

senses.definition: a guessing game where one has to find something or figure out something that is concealed or disguised.
senses.notes: Refers to a game where a person hides and another person tries to find the hidden person.
examples: I am tired of running up against a game of hide-and-seek every time I ask to see the financial records of this company.
I have been trying to see the manager for two days. Where is she? I refuse to play hide-and-seek any longer. I want to see her now!

senses.definition: to cover one’s face because of shame or embarrassment.
examples: Mary was so embarrassed. She could only hide her face in shame.
When Tom broke Ann’s crystal vase, he wanted to hide his face in shame.

headword: hide one’s light under a bushel

senses.definition: to conceal one’s good ideas or talents.
examples: Jane has some good ideas, but she doesn’t speak very often. She hides her light under a bushel.
Don’t hide your light under a bushel. Share your gifts with other people.

senses.definition: safe; unbothered by difficulties; unscathed.
senses.notes: Refers to being safe from a flood.
examples: While the riot was going on, I was high and dry in my apartment.
Liz came out of the argument high and dry.

senses.definition: abandoned; unsupported and helpless.
senses.notes: See also leave someone high and dry.
examples: Everyone else on the committee quit, leaving me high and dry.
The company moved to Chicago, and I was left high and dry in Dallas.

senses.definition: self-important and arrogant.
examples: I don’t know why Albert is so high-and-mighty. He’s no better than the rest of us.
The boss acts high-and-mighty because he can fire us all.

headword: high man on the totem pole

senses.definition: the person at the top of the hierarchy; the person in charge of an organization.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with low man on the totem pole.
examples: I don’t want to talk to a secretary. I demand to talk to the high man on the totem pole.
Who’s in charge around here? Who’s high man on the totem pole?

senses.definition: intoxicated with some drug.
examples: He got thrown out of the movie because he was high on something.
Bill was high on marijuana and was singing loudly.

senses.definition: enthusiastic about something.
examples: Jane quit eating red meat. She’s really high on fish, however.
Bob is high on meditation. He sits and meditates for an hour each day.

senses.definition: a person who is ambitious or who is very likely to be successful.
examples: Jack was one of the highfliers of our university year, and he is now in the foreign office.
Tom is a highflier and has applied for the post of managing director.

senses.definition: to run or ride a horse away from somewhere fast.
senses.notes: Folksy. Typically heard in western movies.
examples: Here comes the sheriff. We’d better hightail it out of here.
Look at that guy go. He really hightailed it out of town.

senses.definition: roads; the major and minor roads and routes.
examples: I hope I meet you again some day on life’s highways and byways.
The city council voted to plant new trees along all the highways and byways of the town.

senses.definition: to depend on something.
examples: This all hinges on how much risk you’re willing to take.
Whether we have the picnic hinges on the weather.

senses.definition: carelessly; aimlessly; without plan or direction.
examples: There was no planning. It was just hit-and-miss.
We handed out the free tickets hit-or-miss. Some people got one; others got five or six.

senses.definition: an accident where the driver of a car strikes a person or another vehicle and speeds away without admitting to the deed or stopping to help.
examples: Fred was injured in a hit-and-run accident.
The state passed a law making any kind of hit-and-run accident a felony.

senses.definition: to reach a higher level of activity, sales, production, output, etc., and then stop and remain unchanged.
examples: When my sales hit a plateau, my boss gave me a pep talk.
When production hit a plateau, the company built a new factory.

senses.definition: to run into a problem.
examples: We’ve hit a snag with the building project.
I stopped working on the roof when I hit a snag.

senses.definition: to reach the lowest or worst point.
examples: Our profits have hit bottom. This is our worst year ever.
When my life hit bottom, I began to feel much better. I knew that if there was going to be any change, it would be for the better.

senses.definition: to really make sense; [for a comment] to make a very good point.
examples: Mary’s criticism of my clothes hit home, so I changed.
The teacher’s comment struck home and the student vowed to work harder.

senses.definition: to quickly become good friends with someone.
examples: Look how John hit it off with Mary.
Yes, they really hit it off.

senses.definition: to affect one personally and intimately.
examples: Her comments really hit me where I live. Her words seemed to apply directly to me.
I listened carefully and didn’t think she hit close to home at all.

senses.definition: to discover something of value.
senses.notes: Slang. Refers to discovering valuable ore.
examples: Sally tried a number of different jobs until she hit pay dirt.
I tried to borrow money from a lot of different people. They all said no. Then when I went to the bank, I hit pay dirt.

senses.definition: to do something unfair or unsporting to someone.
senses.notes: Informal. From boxing, where a blow below the belt line is not permitted.
examples: You really hit me below the belt when you told the boss about my tax problems.
In business Bill is difficult to deal with. He hits below the belt.

senses.definition: to affect someone’s emotions strongly.
examples: The death of his friend hit John hard.
The investor was hit hard by the falling stock prices.

headword: hit (someone) like a ton of bricks

senses.definition: to surprise, startle, or shock someone.
examples: Suddenly, the truth hit me like a ton of bricks.
The sudden tax increase hit like a ton of bricks. Everyone became angry.

senses.definition: to become completely apparent; to surprise or impress someone.
examples: Suddenly, it hit me right between the eyes. John and Mary were in love.
Then—as he was talking—the exact nature of the evil plan hit me between the eyes.

senses.definition: to ask someone for something.
examples: John hit me up for a loan.
I told him to go hit up someone else.

senses.definition: to begin to study; to study.
examples: Well, time to hit the books.
John, if you don’t start hitting the books, you’re going to fail.

senses.definition: to drink alcohol to excess.
senses.notes: As if drinking directly from the bottle, that is, taking a hit from the bottle. Slang.
examples: Fred goes home and hits the bottle every night.
Bill has been hitting the bottle a lot lately. I think he has a problem.

senses.definition: to start walking; to go out into the streets.
examples: If you want to get a job, you had better get out there and hit the bricks.
I got fired today. The boss came by and told me to hit the bricks.

senses.definition: to achieve a goal perfectly.
senses.notes: Refers to hitting the center of a circular target. Informal.
examples: Your idea really hit the bull’s-eye. Thank you!
Jill has a lot of insight. She knows how to hit the bull’s-eye in discussions.

senses.definition: to become very angry.
examples: My father hit the ceiling when I damaged the car.
Our employer hit the ceiling when we lost an important contract.

senses.definition: to go to bed and get some sleep.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with sack out.
examples: Look at the clock. It’s time to hit the hay.
I like to hit the sack before midnight.

senses.definition: to do only the important, obvious, or good things.
examples: I won’t discuss the entire report. I’ll just hit the high spots.
First, let me hit the high spots; then I’ll tell you about everything.

senses.definition: to win at gambling.
senses.notes: Refers to the “jack” in playing cards.
examples: Bob hit the jackpot three times in one night.
I’ve never hit the jackpot even once.

senses.definition: to have a success.
examples: I hit the jackpot on a business deal.
I really hit the jackpot in the library. I found just what I needed.

headword: hit the nail (right) on the head

senses.definition: to do exactly the right thing; to do something in the most effective and efficient way; to identify the exact nature of something.
examples: You’ve spotted the flaw, Sally. You hit the nail on the head.
Bob doesn’t say much, but every now and then he hits the nail right on the head.

senses.definition: to depart; to begin one’s journey, especially on a road trip; to leave for home.
examples: It’s time to hit the road. I’ll see you.
We have to hit the road very early in the morning.

senses.definition: to decline; to decrease in value.
examples: Business usually hits the skids in the summer.
Tom hit the skids after he lost his job.

senses.definition: to be exactly right; to be refreshing.
examples: This cool drink really hits the spot.
That was a delicious meal, dear. It hit the spot.

senses.definition: to discover or think up something.
examples: Ann hit on the idea of baking lots of bread and freezing it.
John hit upon a new way of planting corn.

senses.definition: everywhere; here, there, and everywhere.
examples: The prince looked hither, thither, and yon for the beautiful woman who had lost the glass slipper.
The terrible wizard had sown the seeds of his evil vine hither, thither, and yon, and soon the evil, twisted plants began to sprout in all the land.

senses.definition: the location where things are very busy.
senses.notes: Refers to the activity around a beehive.
examples: The hotel lobby was a hive of activity each morning.
During the holidays, the shopping center is a hive of activity.

senses.definition: the choice between taking what is offered and getting nothing at all.
senses.notes: From the name of a stable owner in the seventeenth century who offered customers the hire of the horse nearest the door.
examples: We didn’t really want that particular hotel, but it was a case of Hobson’s choice. We booked very late and there was nothing else left.
If you want a yellow car, it’s Hobson’s choice. The garage has only one.

senses.definition: harmed or disadvantaged by an action of one’s own that was meant to harm someone else.
senses.notes: From a line in Shakespeare’s Hamlet.
examples: She intended to murder her brother but was hoist by her own petard when she ate the poisoned food intended for him.
The vandals were hoist with their own petard when they tried to make an emergency call from the pay phone they had broken.

senses.definition: to be in a favorable position; to be in a controlling position.
senses.notes: Slang. Refers to having possession of all four aces in a card game.
examples: How can I advance in my job when my enemy holds all the aces?
If I held all the aces, I’d be able to do great things.

senses.definition: to meet; to have a meeting (of an organization).
examples: We’ll have to hold a meeting to make a decision.
Our club held a meeting to talk about future projects.

senses.definition: ) to speak at length.
examples: I’ve never seen anyone who could hold forth so long.
The professor held forth on economic theory for nearly an hour.

headword: hold no brief for someone or something

senses.definition: not to care about someone or something; to dislike someone or something.
examples: I hold no brief for bad typists.
My father says he holds no brief for sweet potatoes.

senses.definition: to stop doing something and wait until something special happens.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Usually in the negative.
examples: BOB: The bus is going to come soon. BILL: Don’t hold your breath until it does.
I expect the mail to be delivered soon, but I’m not holding my breath.

headword: hold one’s end (of the bargain) up

senses.definition: to do one’s part as agreed; to attend to one’s responsibilities as agreed.
examples: If you don’t hold your end up, the whole project will fail.
Tom has to learn to cooperate. He must hold up his end of the bargain.

senses.definition: to refrain from shooting (a gun, etc.).
examples: The sergeant told the soldiers to hold their fire.
Please hold your fire until I get out of the way.

senses.definition: to postpone one’s criticism or commentary.
examples: Now, now, hold your fire until I’ve had a chance to explain.
Hold your fire, Bill. You’re too quick to complain.

senses.definition: to retain or display one’s dignity.
examples: I’ve done nothing wrong. I can hold my head up in public.
I’m so embarrassed and ashamed. I’ll never be able to hold up my head again.

senses.definition: to do as well as anyone else.
examples: I can hold my own in a footrace any day.
She was unable to hold her own, and she had to quit.

senses.definition: to remain silent.
examples: Bill was unable to hold his peace any longer. “Don’t do it!” he cried.
Quiet, John. Hold your peace for a little while longer.

senses.definition: to refrain from speaking; to refrain from saying something unpleasant.
senses.notes: See also the fixed phrase Hold your tongue!
examples: I felt like scolding her, but I held my tongue.
You must learn to hold your tongue, John. You can’t talk to people that way.

senses.definition: to insist on getting something; to refuse to accept less than something.
examples: The workers are holding out for a reasonable raise.
The teachers are holding out for a reduction in class size.

senses.definition: to offer to end a dispute and be friendly; to offer reconciliation.
senses.notes: The olive branch is a symbol of peace and reconciliation. A biblical reference.
examples: Jill was the first to hold out the olive branch after our argument.
I always try to hold out the olive branch to someone I have hurt. Life is too short for a person to bear grudges for very long.

senses.definition: to try to keep someone from succeeding.
examples: I still think you’re trying to hold him down.
I’m not trying to hold down my brother.

senses.definition: to keep someone as a hostage.
examples: The terrorists planned to hold everyone hostage in the airplane.
My neighbor was held hostage in his own home by a robber.

senses.definition: to have very great respect for someone or something; to admire someone or something greatly.
examples: We hold our employees in very high regard.
I do not hold Bob’s abilities in high regard.

senses.definition: to retain someone or something (for a period of time).
examples: The storm held John over for another day.
The manager held the movie over for another week.

senses.definition: to rob someone (figuratively or literally).
examples: I don’t eat at that restaurant any more. The food is too expensive. They really held me up the last time I ate there.
That’s the one who held me up at gunpoint.
The thug held up the old lady.

senses.definition: to detain someone or something; to make someone or something late.
senses.notes: Also literal meaning to keep someone or something upright.
examples: The traffic on the expressway held me up.
A storm in Boston held up our plane.

headword: hold someone or something up (as an example)

senses.definition: to point out someone or something as a good example.
senses.notes: See also make an example of someone.
examples: I was embarrassed when the boss held me up as an example.
I don’t like for anyone to hold me up like that.
The teacher held up the leaf as an example of a typical compound leaf.

senses.definition: to keep someone’s attention; to keep someone interested.
examples: The boring teacher could not hold the students’ attention.
The mystery novel held my attention and I couldn’t put it down.

senses.definition: to take care of a place, such as a store or one’s home.
senses.notes: Refers to defending a fort against attackers. Informal. From western movies.
examples: I’m going next door to visit Mrs. Jones. You stay here and hold the fort.
You should open the store at eight o’clock and hold the fort until I get there at ten.

headword: hold the line (at someone or something)

senses.definition: to limit the number of people or things; to limit (something) to someone or something.
senses.notes: See also draw the line (at something).
examples: The room will seat fifty, but I think you should hold the line at forty.
The Browns and the Smiths could be invited, but I think we ought to hold the line at the Browns.
Okay, we’ll hold the line.

senses.definition: to be true; [for something] to remain true.
examples: Does this rule hold true all the time?
Yes, it holds true no matter what.

senses.definition: to endure; to last a long time.
examples: How long will this cloth hold up?
I want my money back for this chair. It isn’t holding up well.

senses.definition: to delay doing something.
examples: Please hold up on the project. We’ve run out of money.
I have to hold up on my reading because I broke my glasses.

senses.definition: to accept or agree with something.
examples: My father doesn’t hold with fancy clothes.
I don’t hold with too many X rays.

senses.definition: Wait a minute and be reasonable!; Do not run off wildly!
examples: Now, hold your horses, John. Be reasonable for a change.
Don’t get so mad. Just hold your horses.

senses.definition: Be quiet!; Stop saying what you are saying!
examples: Hold your tongue! I’ve heard enough of your insults.
That’s enough rudeness for today! Hold your tongue!

senses.definition: to hide somewhere; to live in hiding somewhere.
senses.notes: Slang. Typically in western or gangster movies.
examples: The old man is holed up in the mountains, waiting for the war to end.
If we are going to hole up for the winter, we’ll need lots of food.

senses.definition: excessively pious; acting as though one is more virtuous than other people.
examples: Jack always adopts a holier-than-thou attitude to other people, but people say he has been in prison.
Jane used to be holier-than-thou, but she is marrying Tom, who is a crook.

senses.definition: to aim exactly at something and move toward it.
examples: The sheriff walked into the room and homed in on the horse thief.
The plane homed in on the beacon at the airport.
First, you must set your goal and then home in.

senses.definition: I speak the truth.
senses.notes: Some people may object to the use of God in this phrase.
examples: Did he really say that? Honest to goodness?
Honest to Pete, I’ve been to the moon.
I’ve been there, too—honest to God.

senses.definition: The early pleasant beginning has ended.
examples: Okay, the honeymoon is over. It’s time to settle down and do some hard work.
I knew the honeymoon was over when they started yelling at me to work faster.

senses.definition: to accept someone’s personal check.
examples: The clerk at the store wouldn’t honor my check. I had to pay cash.
The bank didn’t honor your check when I tried to deposit it. Please give me cash.

senses.definition: addicted to a drug or something similar.
examples: Jenny is hooked on cocaine.
She was not hooked on anything before that.
John is hooked on coffee.

senses.definition: enthusiastic about something; supportive of something.
examples: Mary is hooked on football. She never misses a game.
Jane is so happy! She’s hooked on life.

senses.definition: to shout in disapproval; to call and shout one’s displeasure.
examples: After the umpire rendered his decision, the spectators hooted and hollered their thoughts on the matter.
It’s hard to play a good game of basketball when the fans are hooting and hollering at everything you do.

headword: a hop, skip, and a jump

senses.definition: a short distance.
examples: Her house was just a hop, skip, and a jump away from mine, so we visited often.
Our town is just a hop, skip, and a jump from a big city, so we get the advantages of both city and country life.

senses.definition: Move fast!; Get started!
examples: Come on, you guys, move it! Hop to it!
Hop to it, Bill. You look like you’re loafing.

senses.definition: to have hope even when the situation appears to be hopeless.
examples: We hope against all hope that she’ll see the right thing to do and do it.
There is little point in hoping against hope, except that it makes you feel better.

senses.definition: incapable of doing something.
examples: Tom is hopeless at cooking.
Sally is hopeless at dusting. She hates it.

senses.definition: intoxicated with drugs or alcohol; stimulated by drugs or alcohol.
examples: The old man was hopped up again. He was addicted to opium.
John usually gets hopped up on the weekends.

senses.definition: excited; enthusiastic.
examples: What are you hopped up about now? You’re certainly cheery.
I always get hopped up when I think of mountain climbing.

senses.definition: to attempt to displace someone.
examples: I’m going to ask Sally to the party. Don’t you dare try to horn in on me!
I wouldn’t think of horning in.

senses.definition: to attempt to participate in something without invitation or consent.
examples: Are you trying to horn in on my conversation with Sally?
I hope you are not trying to horn in on our party.

senses.definition: a carriage pulled by a horse, as opposed to a modern automobile.
senses.notes: A symbol of old-fashionedness or out-ofdateness. Particularly with go out with, as in the examples below.
examples: That kind of clothing went out with the horse and buggy.
I thought suspenders went out with the horse and carriage, but I see them everywhere now.

senses.definition: to play around; to waste time in frivolous activities.
examples: Stop horsing around and get to work.
The children were on the playground horsing around when the bell rang.

altForms: a horse of a different color

senses.definition: another matter altogether.
examples: I was talking about trees, not bushes. Bushes are a horse of another color.
Gambling is not the same as investing in the stock market. It’s a horse of a different color.

senses.definition: common sense; practical thinking.
examples: Jack is no scholar but he has a lot of horse sense.
Horse sense tells me I should not be involved in that project.

senses.definition: excited; anxious.
examples: Now don’t get hot and bothered. Take it easy.
John is hot and bothered about the tax increase.

senses.definition: amorous; interested in romance or sex.
senses.notes: Informal and euphemistic. Use with caution.
examples: John gets hot and bothered whenever Mary comes into the room.
The dog seems hot and bothered. I think it’s that time of the year again.

senses.definition: referring to serious passion or emotions.
examples: Things were getting a little hot and heavy so Ellen asked to be taken home.
The movie had one hot and heavy scene after another. Pretty soon it got to be a joke.

senses.definition: enthusiastic about something; very much interested in something; knowledgeable about something.
examples: Meg’s hot on animal rights.
Jean is hot on modern ballet just now.

senses.definition: very angry.
examples: The boss was really hot under the collar when you told him you lost the contract.
I get hot under the collar every time I think about it.

senses.definition: to run away from a place.
senses.notes: Folksy. Compare this with high tail it out of somewhere.
examples: Did you see Tom hotfoot it out of the office when the boss came in?
Things are looking bad. I think we had better hotfoot it out of here.

senses.definition: Hello, how are you?
examples: Hi, Mary. How goes it with you?
How goes it, Bill?

senses.definition: How are you?
examples: Hi, Bob. How’s it going?
How’s it going? Everything all right?

senses.definition: How are you?
examples: Hi, Jane, How’s the world treating you?
How’s the world been treating you, Bill?

senses.definition: a loud public protest or opposition.
examples: There was a hue and cry when the city government tried to build houses on the playing field.
The decision to close the local school started a real hue and cry.

senses.definition: to breathe very hard; to pant as one exerts effort.
examples: John came up the stairs huffing and puffing.
He huffed and puffed and finally got up the steep hill.

senses.definition: obsessed with someone or something; devoted to someone or something.
examples: John is really hung up on Mary.
She’s hung up, too. See how she smiles when he enters the room.

senses.definition: to have a strong desire for something.
examples: All her life, Mary has had a hunger for affection.
The prisoner was consumed with a hunger for freedom.

senses.definition: desiring something.
examples: The orphan was hungry for the warmth of a family.
Bill is hungry for knowledge and always studying.

senses.definition: a slow “system” of typing where one searches for a letter and then presses it.
senses.notes: From the movement used by fowls when feeding.
examples: I never learned to type right. All I do is hunt-and-peck.
I can’t type. I just hunt-and-peck, but I get the job done—eventually.

headword: hunt high and low (for someone or something)
altForms: look high and low (for someone or something)
search high and low (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to look carefully in every possible place for someone or something.
examples: We looked high and low for the right teacher.
The Smiths are searching high and low for the home of their dreams.

senses.definition: to direct an insult at someone; to say something insulting directly to someone.
examples: Anne hurled an insult at Bob that made him very angry.
If you two would stop hurling insults, we could have a serious discussion.

headword: a hush fell over someone or something

senses.definition: a sudden silence enveloped something, someone, or a group.
examples: As the conductor raised his arms, a hush fell over the audience.
The coach shouted and a hush fell over the locker room.

senses.definition: money paid as a bribe to persuade someone to remain silent and not reveal certain information.
examples: Bob gave his younger sister hush money so that she wouldn’t tell Jane that he had gone to the movies with Sue.
The crooks paid Fred hush money to keep their whereabouts secret.

senses.definition: Please be quiet!
examples: I’ve heard enough of that talk. Hush your mouth!
Now, hush your mouth! You know you really should not talk about other people’s problems like that!

senses.definition: confusion, hurry, and bother.
examples: The hustle and bustle of the big city is especially annoying in the hot days of summer.
Fred seems to enjoy the hustle and bustle of traffic during rush hour, so he is a very happy bus driver.

senses.definition: No one told me your name [or I have forgotten it].
senses.notes: A carrying on of a conversation that has just started—if one hasn’t been introduced properly—or simply finding out someone’s name.
examples: I’m sorry, but I didn’t catch your name.
I’m Wally Ott. I didn’t catch your name.

senses.definition: I have a premonition about this; I have a strange feeling about this.
examples: I really don’t know that something is wrong. I just have this feeling.
I just have this feeling that she is not telling us the truth.

senses.definition: a catch phrase said when someone makes a frown at someone or when someone casts a dirty look.
examples: Did you see the way she looked at me? If looks could kill....
If looks could kill. What a nasty glare.

senses.definition: if that is not [the case]; if that is not so.
examples: If not cleaned, the clock will stop running.
He should be here at noon. If not, we will eat without him.

senses.definition: if the situation really becomes difficult; if matters escalate into a strong argument.
senses.notes: See also when push comes to shove.
examples: If push comes to shove, I am ready to be more aggressive.
If push comes to shove, I am sure that our senator will help out.

senses.definition: if that is [the case]; if that is so.
examples: She might be late. If so, we will eat without her.
She is supposed to be all right. If so, we have nothing to worry about.

headword: If the shoe fits, wear it.

senses.definition: You should pay attention to advice or criticism if it applies to you.
examples: Some people here need to be quiet. If the shoe fits, wear it.
This doesn’t apply to everyone. If the shoe fits, wear it.

senses.definition: in the worst possible situation; if things really get bad.
examples: If worst comes to worst, we’ll hire someone to help you.
If worst comes to worst, I’ll have to borrow some money.

senses.definition: uneasy; anxious.
examples: I feel ill at ease about the interview.
You look ill at ease. Please relax.

senses.definition: not friendly; not favorable; not well disposed.
examples: I am ill-disposed to doing hard labor.
The police chief was ill-disposed to discussing the details of the case to the news reporters.

senses.definition: I agree with that!
senses.notes: Informal. As if joining in with drinks following a toast.
examples: Great idea! I’ll drink to that.
That’s a fine suggestion. I’ll drink to that.

senses.definition: money or other possessions acquired in a dishonest or illegal fashion.
examples: Fred cheated at cards and is now living on his ill-gotten gains.
Mary is also enjoying her ill-gotten gains. She deceived an old lady into leaving her money in her will.

senses.definition: I will try to talk with you or meet with you at some future time.
examples: I don’t have time to talk to you now. I’ll try to catch you later.
Hi, I’m leaving. I’ll catch you later.

senses.definition: hostile feelings or intentions.
examples: I hope you do not have any ill will toward me because of our argument.
Dave felt such ill will toward his family that he left his fortune to his best friend.

headword: I’m damned if I do and damned if I don’t.

senses.definition: There are problems if I do something and problems if I don’t do it.
examples: I can’t win. I’m damned if I do and damned if I don’t
No matter whether I go or stay, I am in trouble. I’m damned if I do and damned if I don’t.

senses.definition: an expression used to excuse oneself politely or apologize, especially when one has collided with someone, when one has offended someone, or to ask someone to repeat what has been said.
examples: “I’m sorry,” I said to the woman I bumped into.
I’m sorry, what did you say? I couldn’t hear you.

senses.definition: I can’t seem to remember anyone’s name.
senses.notes: Said as an apology to someone whose name you have forgotten.
examples: I’m terrible at names. Please tell me yours again.
Haven’t we met already? I’m awful at names.

senses.definition: Is that so?; How interesting and strange!
senses.notes: Said when one hears something that is interesting. Often sarcastic.
examples: Fell out of bed. Imagine that!
She’s late again. Imagine that!

senses.definition: ready to be moved into at this moment.
examples: This house is for immediate occupancy. You can move in today if you want.
It’s empty, so that means immediate occupancy.

senses.definition: to suggest that someone is involved in something.
examples: The mayor was implicated in the murder.
Jane’s essay implicated her teacher in the cheating scandal.

senses.definition: sad; depressed; grouchy; with low spirits.
examples: He’s in a bad mood. He may yell at you.
Please try to cheer me up. I’m in a bad mood.

senses.definition: in a critical or bad state.
senses.notes: Can refer to health, finances, mood, etc.
examples: Mr. Smith is in a bad way. He may have to go to the hospital.
My bank account is in a bad way. It needs some help from a millionaire.
My life is in a bad way, and I’m depressed about it.

senses.definition: in reserve.
examples: Until the judge determined that the evidence could be used in the trial, it was held in abeyance.
I kept my opinion in abeyance.

senses.definition: in a tight or difficult situation; stuck on a problem.
senses.notes: Note: In can be replaced with into to show movement toward or into the state described by bind or jam. Especially get into. See the examples below.
examples: I’m in a bind. I owe a lot of money.
Whenever I get into a jam, I ask my supervisor for help.
When things get busy around here, we get in a bind. We could use another helper.

senses.definition: in agreement with; in conformity with.
examples: In accordance with our discussion, I have prepared a contract.
I did this in accordance with your request.

senses.definition: in a very long time.
senses.notes: Folksy. Usually negative. The coon is a raccoon.
examples: How are you? I haven’t seen you in a coon’s age.
I haven’t had a piece of apple pie this good in a coon’s age.
John hasn’t seen a movie in a month of Sundays.

senses.definition: additionally; further; moreover; as an additional thing or person.
examples: In addition, I would like for you to sweep the kitchen floor.
I put the books away, and in addition, I cleaned up my desk.

senses.definition: at exactly the same time; tied.
examples: The two horses finished the race in a dead heat.
They ended the contest in a dead heat.

senses.definition: before it is due.
examples: The bill isn’t due for a month, but I paid it in advance.
I want my pay in advance.

senses.definition: pregnant.
examples: I’ve heard that Mrs. Smith is in a family way.
Our dog is in the family way.

senses.definition: in a bad situation.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I really got myself into a fix. I owe a lot of money on my taxes.
John is in a fix because he lost his wallet.
John got into a fix.

senses.definition: quickly; immediately.
examples: I’ll be there in a flash.
It happened in a flash. Suddenly my wallet was gone.

senses.definition: preoccupied; not paying attention to what is going on around one; not alert.
examples: Jane always seems to be in a fog.
When I get up, I’m in a fog for an hour.

senses.definition: in a condition of seeming happiness that will not last because it is based on false assumptions.
examples: They think they can live on love alone, but they are living in a fool’s paradise.
The inhabitants of the island feel politically secure, but they are living in a fool’s paradise. They could be invaded at any time.

senses.definition: in harmony; agreeing.
examples: The business partners were never in agreement about marketing strategies.
Because the partners were not in agreement, the business failed.

senses.definition: in a state of confusion.
examples: After being hit in the head by the bat, Bill was in a haze.
After surgery, I was in a haze until the anesthetic wore off.

senses.definition: in an angry or offended manner.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: He heard what we had to say, then left in a huff.
She came in a huff and ordered us to bring her something to eat.
She gets into a huff very easily.

senses.definition: very fast; very soon.
examples: Just wait a minute. I’ll be there in a jiffy.
I’ll be finished in a jiffy.

senses.definition: flustered; excited and agitated.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Now, calm down. Don’t be in a lather.
I always get in a lather when I’m late.
I get into a lather easily.

senses.definition: in a small amount of time; soon.
examples: I will be there in a little bit. Please wait.
In a little bit, we can go outside and play.

senses.definition: having good motives; displaying motives that will not result in a guilty conscience.
examples: In all good conscience, I could not recommend that you buy this car.
In good conscience, she could not accept the reward. She had only been acting as any good citizen should.

senses.definition: ever; in all one’s life.
examples: I’ve never been so angry in all my born days.
Have you ever heard such a thing in all your born days?

senses.definition: very likely; almost certainly.
examples: He’ll be here on time in all probability.
In all probability, they’ll finish the work today.

senses.definition: in a hurry; frantically.
examples: I ran around all day today in a mad rush, looking for a present for Bill.
Why are you always in a mad rush?

senses.definition: itself; considering it alone.
examples: The idea in and of itself is not bad, but the side issues introduce many difficulties.
Her action, in and of itself, caused us no problem.

senses.definition: in a few words; briefly; concisely.
examples: I don’t have time for the whole explanation. Please give it to me in a nutshell.
Well, in a nutshell, we have to work late.

senses.definition: no matter what happens.
examples: I intend to be home by supper time, but in any case by eight o’clock.
In any event, I’ll see you this evening.

senses.definition: in a situation where there is but one choice; in a situation where there is not time to locate another choice.
examples: I don’t care for this kind of paint, but it will do in a pinch.
Tom is not the best choice around, but he will have to do in a pinch.

senses.definition: in very good order; very well organized.
senses.notes: Folksy. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Please put everything in apple-pie order before you leave.
I always put my desk in apple-pie order every evening.
I’ve put my entire life into apple-pie order.

senses.definition: in a mess; in trouble.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John has gotten himself into a pickle. He has two dates for the party.
Now we are in a real pickle. We are out of gas.

senses.definition: uncertain about what to do; confused.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Mary was in a quandary about what college to go to.
I couldn’t decide what to do. I was in such a quandary.
I got myself into a quandary.

senses.definition: overdue; late, especially in reference to bills and money.
examples: This bill is three months in arrears. It must be paid immediately.
I was in arrears on my car payments, so the bank threatened to take my car away.

senses.definition: in a way; sort of.
examples: In a sense, cars make life better.
But, in a sense, they also make life worse.

senses.definition: in a fit of anger or irritation.
senses.notes: Slang. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Mrs. Smith threw on her coat and left in a snit.
Here comes John—in a snit again—as usual.
Don’t get into a snit.

senses.definition: in just an instant.
examples: The lightning struck, and in a split second the house burst into flames.
Just wait. I’ll be there in a split second.

senses.definition: in a loud whisper that everyone can hear.
examples: John said in a stage whisper, “This play is boring.”
“When do we eat?” asked Billy in a stage whisper.

headword: in a stew (about someone or something)

senses.definition: upset or bothered about someone or something.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I’m in such a stew about my dog. She ran away last night.
Now, now. Don’t be in a stew. She’ll be back when she gets hungry.
I hate to get into a stew about my friends.

senses.definition: in a dazed condition; in a condition in which one cannot concentrate or think.
examples: The drunk driver walked away from the car accident in a stupor.
In the morning, Mary remains in a stupor until she drinks coffee.

senses.definition: caught in a problem; in a jam.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Look, John, I’m in a tight spot. Can you lend me twenty dollars?
I’m in a spot too. I need $300.
I have never gotten into a tight spot.

senses.definition: in an excited and confused condition.
examples: John is in a tizzy because we’re an hour late.
Mary was in a tizzy when she couldn’t find her keys.

senses.definition: in a situation in which the solution of one problem leads to a second problem, and the solution of the second problem brings back the first problem, etc.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Life is so strange. I seem to be in a vicious circle most of the time.
I put lemon in my tea to make it sour, then sugar to make it sweet. I’m in a vicious circle.
Don’t let your life get into a vicious circle.

senses.definition: fearful and respectful of someone or something.
examples: Everyone in the country was in awe of the king and queen.
I love my new car. In fact, I’m in awe of it.
When I first saw the house, I just stood there in awe.

senses.definition: said simply; concisely said.
examples: Mrs. Smith is—in a word—haughty.
In a word, the play flopped.

headword: in a world of one’s own

senses.definition: aloof; detached; self-centered.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John lives in a world of his own. He has very few friends.
Mary walks around in a world of her own, but she’s very intelligent.
When she’s thinking, she drifts into a world of her own.

senses.definition: without sincerity; with bad or dishonest intent; with duplicity.
senses.notes: Compare this with in good faith.
examples: It appears that you acted in bad faith and didn’t live up to the terms of our agreement.
If you do things in bad faith, you’ll get a bad reputation.

senses.definition: in a bad humor; in a bad mood.
examples: Bill is in bad sorts today. He’s very grouchy.
I try to be extra nice to people when I’m in bad sorts.

senses.definition: rude; vulgar; obscene.
examples: Mrs. Franklin felt that your joke was in bad taste.
We found the play to be in poor taste, so we walked out in the middle of the second act.

senses.definition: having someone against you; having gotten into trouble with someone.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with in good (with someone).
examples: Sally is in bad with her parents for failing algebra.
She’s really in bad. She has real trouble.

senses.definition: as someone’s agent; [doing something] in place of someone; for the benefit of someone.
examples: I’m writing in behalf of Mr. Smith, who has applied for a job with your company.
I’m calling on behalf of my client, who wishes to complain about your actions.
I’m calling in her behalf.
I’m acting on your behalf.

senses.definition: located in the middle of two things, states, or possibilities.
examples: It’s not hot or cold. It’s in between.
A sandwich consists of two slices of bread with some other food in between.

senses.definition: official, in writing or printing.
senses.notes: Said of something, such as an agreement or a statement, which has been recorded in writing. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I have it in black and white that I’m entitled to three weeks of vacation each year.
It says right here in black and white that oak trees make acorns.
Please put the agreement into black and white.

senses.definition: with many flowers; at the peak of blooming.
examples: The garden is beautiful when it is in bloom.
The roses are in bloom and they smell so sweet!

senses.definition: with many flowers opening; in bloom.
examples: The peonies are in blossom early this spring.
If the daffodils are in blossom, spring is on the way.

senses.definition: briefly; concisely.
examples: The whole story, in brief, is that Bob failed algebra because he did not study.
Please tell me in brief why you want this job.

senses.definition: publicly visible in the daytime.
examples: The thief stole the car in broad daylight.
There they were, selling drugs in broad daylight.

senses.definition: in large quantities or amounts, rather than smaller, more convenient quantities or amounts.
examples: Jane always bought office supplies in bulk to save money.
Dave purchased cereal in bulk because his family used so much of it.

senses.definition: in conspiracy with someone; in league with someone.
examples: The mayor is in cahoots with the construction company that got the contract for the new building.
Those two have been in cahoots before.

senses.definition: through someone or by way of someone.
senses.notes: [to be delivered to someone] Indicates that mail is to be delivered to a person at some other person’s address.
examples: Bill Jones is living at his father’s house. Address the letter to Bill in care of Mr. John Jones.
Bill said, “Please send me my mail in care of my father at his address.”

senses.definition: in the event (that).
examples: What do we do in case the building catches fire?
We should close the windows just in case it rains.

senses.definition: in the event of something.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the case of someone or something; in case something happens.
examples: Please leave the building at once in case of fire.
Please take your raincoat in case of rain.

senses.definition: in the event that something takes place.
senses.notes: Compare this with in case of something.
examples: She carries an umbrella in case it rains.
I have some aspirin in my office in case I get a headache.

senses.definition: typical of someone’s behavior.
examples: For Tom to shout that way wasn’t at all in character. He’s usually quite pleasant.
It was quite in character for Sally to walk away angry.

senses.definition: with good fortune; in a very good situation, especially financially.
examples: If I get this contract, I’ll be in clover for the rest of my life.
I have very little money saved, so when I retire I won’t exactly be in clover.

senses.definition: without feeling; with cruel intent.
senses.notes: Informal or slang. Frequently said of a crime, especially murder.
examples: The killer walked up and shot the woman in cold blood.
How insulting! For a person to say something like that in cold blood is just horrible.

senses.definition: stored away for future use; in an out-of-the-way place.
examples: I have had this special gift in cold storage for an occasion such as this.
Todd had been keeping himself in cold storage, trying to study for his exams.

senses.definition: in cooperation with someone; with the aid of someone.
examples: Mrs. Smith planned the party in concert with her sister.
In concert they planned a lovely event.

senses.definition: in good health; strong and healthy.
senses.notes: Used only with people. Compare this with in good shape. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Bob exercises frequently, so he’s in condition.
If I were in shape, I could run faster and farther.
I’m not healthy. I have to try to get into shape.

senses.definition: as a result of something; because of something.
examples: In consequence of the storm, there was no electricity.
The wind blew down the wires. In consequence, we had no electricity.

senses.definition: in return for something; as a result of something.
senses.notes: Compare this with out of consideration (for someone or something).
examples: In consideration of your many years of service, we are pleased to present you with this gold watch.
In consideration of your efforts, here is a check for $3,000.

senses.definition: disrespect for a judge or for courtroom procedures.
examples: The bailiff ejected the lawyer who was held in contempt.
The judge found the juror in contempt of court when she screamed at the attorney.

headword: in custody of someone or something

senses.definition: the condition of being kept guarded by someone or some group.
examples: The suspect was in the sheriff’s custody awaiting a trial.
The prisoner is in the custody of the state.

senses.definition: having debts; having much debt; owing money.
examples: Mary is deeply in debt.
I am in debt to the bank for my car loan.

senses.definition: deeply involved.
examples: John and Mary have been seeing each other for months now. They are really in deep.
Bill loves the theater. He’s definitely in deep. He tries out for all the plays and gets into many of them.

senses.definition: deeply in debt.
examples: Bill owes a lot of money to the bank. He’s really in deep.
John is in deep with his stockbroker.

senses.definition: in a dangerous or vulnerable situation; in a serious situation; in trouble.
senses.notes: Refers to swimming in or falling into water that is over one’s head. See also go off the deep end. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John is having trouble with his taxes. He’s in deep water.
Bill is in deep water in algebra class. He’s almost failing.
He really got himself into deep water.

senses.definition: against someone’s will or against instructions; in bold resistance to someone or someone’s orders.
examples: Jane spent the afternoon in the park, in defiance of her mother’s instructions.
She did it in defiance of her mother.
She has done a number of things in defiance lately.

senses.definition: in a state of refusing to believe something that is true.
examples: Mary was in denial about her illness and refused treatment.
Tom doesn’t think he’s an alcoholic because he’s still in denial.

senses.definition: with lots of details; giving all the details.
examples: I explained the policy to the customer in detail.
We planned the entire project in great detail.

senses.definition: hidden behind a disguise; looking like something else.
examples: Santa Claus was really the little child’s father in disguise.
What I thought was terrible turned out to be a blessing in disguise!

senses.definition: in the clothing of the opposite sex.
senses.notes: Usually refers to a man wearing women’s clothing.
examples: The actor played the woman’s part in drag.
We all went to the costume party dressed in drag.

senses.definition: in a normal or expected amount of time.
examples: The roses will bloom in due course.
The vice president will become president in due course.
I’ll retire in due time.
Just wait, my dear. All in good time.
It’ll all work out in the course of time.
In time, things will improve.

senses.definition: in trouble with someone.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I’m in Dutch with my parents for my low grades.
You’re in Dutch quite a bit.
Don’t get into Dutch with anyone.

senses.definition: sincerely.
examples: This time I’ll try in earnest.
She spoke in earnest, and many people believed her.

senses.definition: in existence; applicable.
examples: A reduced rate at the hotel is in effect until the end of the year.
The curfew is in effect for all minors.

senses.definition: producing a particular effect; effectively.
examples: In effect, this new law will raise taxes for most people.
This policy harms domestic manufacturers. In effect, all our clothing will be made in foreign countries.

senses.definition: basically; essentially.
examples: I have lots of detailed advice for you, but in essence, I want you to do the best you can.
In essence, lightning is just a giant spark of electricity.

senses.definition: in return for someone or something.
examples: They gave us two of our prisoners in exchange for two of theirs.
I gave him chocolate in exchange for some licorice.
John gave Mary a book and got a sweater in exchange.

senses.definition: now existing; currently and actually being.
examples: The tiger may not be in existence in a few decades.
All the oil in existence will not last the world for another century.

senses.definition: in reality; really; actually.
examples: I’m over forty. In fact, I’m forty-six.
This is a very good computer. In fact, it’s the best.

senses.definition: fitting in well with the clothing that has been designed for a particular season of a particular year; fashionable.
examples: I understand that long skirts are in fashion this year.
I always want to find out what styles are in fashion so I can avoid them.

senses.definition: approving, supporting, or endorsing someone or something.
examples: Are you in favor of lower taxes?
Of course, I’m in favor.

senses.definition: with anxiety or fear; with dread.
examples: In fear and trembling, I went into the room to take the test.
The witness left the courtroom in fear and trembling.

senses.definition: in good humor; in good health.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Hello, John. You appear to be in fine feather.
Of course I’m in fine feather. I get lots of sleep.
Good food and lots of sleep put me into fine feather.

senses.definition: while flying.
examples: A passenger became ill in flight and the pilot had to return to the airport.
I really don’t care to eat in flight. I am too nervous.

senses.definition: in constant change; changing.
examples: I can’t describe my job because it’s in a constant state of flux.
The price of gold is in flux.

senses.definition: in a very large group.
examples: The entire group arrived in force.
The mosquitoes will attack in force this evening.

senses.definition: in progress; operating or running without restraint.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: We can’t leave now! The party is in full swing.
Our program to help the starving people is in full swing. You should see results soon.
Just wait until our project gets into full swing.

senses.definition: referring to the entire class being discussed; speaking of the entire range of possibilities; in most situations or circumstances.
examples: I like vegetables in general, but not beets.
In general, I prefer a hotel room on a lower floor, but will take a higher room if it’s special.

senses.definition: with good and honest intent; with sincerity.
senses.notes: Compare this with in bad faith.
examples: We are convinced you were acting in good faith, even though you made a serious error.
I think you didn’t sign the contract in good faith. You never intended to carry out our agreement.

senses.definition: in the safe, competent care of someone.
examples: Don’t worry. Your children are in good hands. Sally is a good babysitter.
Your car is in good hands. My mechanics are factory-trained.

senses.definition: in good condition; operating well; well taken care of.
senses.notes: Usually said of a thing rather than a person.
examples: The house is in good repair and ought to attract a number of potential buyers.
If the car were in good repair, it would run more smoothly.

senses.definition: physically and functionally sound and sturdy.
senses.notes: Used for both people and things. Compare this with in condition. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: This car isn’t in good shape. I’d like to have one that’s in better condition.
Mary is in good condition. She works hard to keep healthy.
You have to make an effort to get into good shape.

senses.definition: happy and cheerful; positive and looking toward the future, despite unhappy circumstances.
examples: The patient is in good spirits and that will speed her recovery.
Tom wasn’t in very good spirits after he heard the bad news.

senses.definition: quickly; in a short amount of time.
examples: We traveled from Mexico to Texas in good time.
I’ve never been able to make that trip in good time.

senses.definition: in someone’s favor; to have pull with someone.
senses.notes: Compare this with in bad (with someone).
examples: I can ask Mary a favor. I’m in good with her.
Well, I’m not in good with her.
I don’t know Mary. How do I go about getting in good?

senses.definition: wanted by many people; eagerly sought after.
examples: Liz is in great demand as a singer.
Mary’s paintings are in great demand.

senses.definition: very fast; in a big hurry.
examples: John always did his homework in great haste.
Why not take time and do it right? Don’t do everything in great haste.

senses.definition: controlled; under control.
examples: I thought I had my destiny in hand, but then fate played a trick on me.
Don’t worry about me. I have everything in hand.

senses.definition: in a period of sexual excitement; in estrus.
senses.notes: Estrus is the period of time in which females are most willing to breed. This expression is usually used for animals. It has been used for humans in a joking sense. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: She goes into heat every year at this time.
When my dog is in heat, I have to keep her locked in the house.

senses.definition: in a state of absolute bliss or happiness.
examples: Lisa was in heaven after winning the lottery.
Resting in his hammock, John was simply in heaven.

senses.definition: dead.
senses.notes: A polite euphemism, and perhaps used more when speaking to children.
examples: Mary’s daddy is in heaven. He was in a car accident.
I am afraid that she is not just sleeping. She is in heaven.

senses.definition: feeling or exhibiting great resentment; taking great offense at something.
examples: After the rude remarks, the person who was insulted left in high dudgeon.
Dennis strode from the room in high dudgeon, and we knew he would get his revenge eventually.

senses.definition: very fast and active.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Don’t leave now. The party is just now in high gear.
When Jane is in high gear, she’s a superb athlete.
When Jane moved into high gear, I knew she’d win the race.

senses.definition: in debt.
examples: After buying the luxury car, Bob was in hock for years.
I am deeply in hock and have to pay off my debts.

headword: in honor of someone or something

senses.definition: showing respect or admiration for someone or something.
examples: Our club gave a party in honor of the club’s president.
I wrote a poem in honor of John and Mary’s marriage.

senses.definition: expecting something.
senses.notes: Also with high, as in the example.
examples: I was in hopes of getting there early.
We are in high hopes that John and Mary will have a girl.

senses.definition: with intense shock or disgust.
examples: Mike stepped back from the rattlesnake in horror.
The jogger recoiled in horror when she came upon a body in the park.

senses.definition: in trouble.
senses.notes: Slang. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John got himself into hot water by being late.
I’m in hot water at home for coming in late last night.
I get into hot water a lot.

senses.definition: written or signed with a pen that uses ink.
examples: You should write your report in ink.
You must sign your checks in ink.

senses.definition: in a state of completeness.
examples: I watched the basketball game in its entirety.
My friends and I ate the two large pizzas in their entirety.

senses.definition: in danger; at risk; at hazard.
examples: John puts himself in jeopardy every time he goes skydiving.
I was in jeopardy when my car broke down on the deserted road.

senses.definition: in a very short period of time.
examples: I’ll be there in a second.
I’ll be with you in just a minute. I’m on the phone.

senses.definition: in accord or harmony with something; following the rules of something.
examples: In keeping with your instructions, I’ve canceled your order.
I’m disappointed with your behavior. It really wasn’t in keeping.
It was not in line with the kind of behavior we expect here.

senses.definition: in goods rather than in money.
examples: The country doctor was usually paid in kind. He accepted two pigs as payment for an operation.
Do you have to pay tax on payments made in kind?

senses.definition: similarly; [giving] something similar to what was received.
examples: John punched Bill, and Bill gave it back in kind.
She spoke rudely to me, so I spoke to her in kind.

senses.definition: experiencing the pains and exertion of childbirth.
examples: Susan was in labor for nearly eight hours.
As soon as she had been in labor for an hour, she went to the hospital.

senses.definition: in cooperation with someone; in a conspiracy with someone.
examples: The mayor is in league with the city treasurer. They are misusing public money.
Those two have been in league for years.

senses.definition: very quickly.
examples: I’ll be there in less than no time.
Don’t worry. This won’t take long. It’ll be over with in less than no time.

senses.definition: in place of something; instead of something.
senses.notes: The word lieu occurs only in this phrase.
examples: They gave me roast beef in lieu of beefsteak.
We gave money to charity in lieu of sending flowers to the funeral.

senses.definition: because of certain knowledge; considering something.
senses.notes: As if knowledge or enlightenment were like light shone on ignorance.
examples: In light of what you have told us, I think we must abandon the project.
In light of the clerk’s rudeness, we didn’t return to that shop.

senses.definition: a region on the border of hell.
senses.notes: In some Christian religions, there is a limbo set aside for souls that do not go to either heaven or hell. This sense is used only in this religious context. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The baby’s soul was in limbo because she had not been baptized.
Considering all things, getting into limbo is probably better than going to hell.

senses.definition: in a state of neglect; in a state of oblivion; in an indefinite state.
examples: We’ll have to leave the project in limbo for a month or two.
After I got hit on the head, I was in limbo for about ten minutes.

senses.definition: standing and waiting in a line of people.
senses.notes: On line is used typically by New Yorkers.
examples: I’ve been in line for an hour.
Get in line if you want to buy a ticket.
We waited on line to see the movie.

senses.definition: feeling love for someone or something; experiencing a strong affectionate emotion for someone or something.
examples: Mary was in love with her new car! It was perfect for her.
John is deeply in love with Mary.
Those two are really in love.

senses.definition: fortunate; lucky.
examples: You want a red one? You’re in luck. There is one red one left.
I had an accident, but I was in luck. It was not serious.

senses.definition: in a point high in the air.
examples: The planes crashed in midair.
Extra fuel was released from the plane in midair.

senses.definition: in perfect condition.
senses.notes: Refers to the perfect state of a coin that has just been minted. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: This is a fine car. It runs well and is in mint condition.
We went through a house in mint condition and decided to buy it.
We put our house into mint condition before we sold it.

senses.definition: nominally; not actual, only by terminology.
examples: The president is head of the country in name only. Congress makes the laws.
Mr. Smith is the boss of the Smith Company in name only. Mrs. Smith handles all the business affairs.

senses.definition: requiring basic things like food, clothing, and housing.
examples: Please contribute some money for those who are in need.
The charity works with old people who are in need.

senses.definition: requiring something.
examples: We are in need of a new car.
The company is in need of a larger building to hold all its employees.

senses.definition: with the shift lever of a vehicle in the position where the motor is running but is not powering the wheels or other moving parts.
examples: The car rolled down the hill because I’d left it in neutral and left the brake off.
If you are moving and in neutral, you do not have control of your vehicle.

headword: in no mood to do something

senses.definition: not to feel like doing something; to wish not to do something.
examples: I’m in no mood to cook dinner tonight.
Mother is in no mood to put up with our arguing.

senses.definition: in exactly no time at all.
examples: Of course I can get there in a hurry. I’ll be there in nothing flat.
We covered the distance between New York and Philadelphia in nothing flat.

senses.definition: very quickly.
senses.notes: Compare this with in less than no time.
examples: I’ll be there in no time.
It won’t take long. I’ll be finished in no time at all.

senses.definition: in very specific and direct language.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I was so mad. I told her in no uncertain terms to leave and never come back.
I told him in no uncertain terms to stop it.
He put his demands into no uncertain terms, and then they listened to him.

headword: in one ear and out (of) the other

senses.definition: ignored; [for something to be] unheard or unheeded.
senses.notes: [for something to be] In can be replaced with into. See the explanation at in a bind and the examples. See also go in one ear and out the other.
examples: Bill just doesn’t pay attention. Everything is in one ear and out the other.
I told Billy to be home by dinnertime, but I am sure it’s just in one ear and out the other.

senses.definition: naked; nude.
senses.notes: Informal. In the “clothes” in which one was born. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I’ve heard that John sleeps in his birthday suit.
We used to go down to the river and swim in our birthday suits.
You have to get into your birthday suit to bathe.

senses.definition: according to one’s own opinion.
examples: He’s okay in my book.
In my book, this is the best that money can buy.

senses.definition: drunk.
examples: She doesn’t make much sense when she’s in her cups.
The speaker—who was in his cups—could hardly be understood.

senses.definition: in a natural or comfortable situation or environment.
senses.notes: Compare this with out of one’s element. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Sally is in her element when she’s working with algebra or calculus.
Bob loves to work with color and texture. When he’s painting, he’s in his element.
He’s most comfortable when he can get into his element.

senses.definition: at one’s happiest or best.
examples: When I go to the beach on vacation, I’m in my glory.
Sally is a good teacher. She’s in her glory in the classroom.

senses.definition: in one’s mind.
senses.notes: Refers to visualizing something in one’s mind.
examples: In my mind’s eye, I can see trouble ahead.
In her mind’s eye, she could see a beautiful building beside the river. She decided to design such a building.

senses.definition: according to one’s belief or judgment.
examples: In my opinion, that is a very ugly picture.
That isn’t a good idea in my opinion.

senses.definition: very close to one.
examples: That kind of thing is quite rare. Imagine it happening right in your backyard.
You always think of something like that happening to someone else. You never expect to find it in your own backyard.

senses.definition: to one’s advantage; as a benefit to oneself.
examples: It is not in your own interests to share your ideas with Jack. He will say that they are his.
Jane thought it was in the best interest of her friend to tell his mother about his illness.

senses.definition: at one’s or its peak or best time.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the prime of life.
examples: Our dog—which is in its prime—is very active.
The program ended in its prime when we ran out of money.
I could work long hours when I was in my prime.

senses.definition: sane; rational and sensible.
examples: That was a stupid thing to do. You’re not in your right mind.
You can’t be in your right mind! That sounds crazy!

senses.definition: in one’s youth.
senses.notes: Usually formal or literary. Comparing the greenness of a salad with the greenness, or freshness and inexperience, of youth.
examples: I recall the joys I experienced in the warm summer air in my salad days.
In our salad days, we were apt to get into all sorts of mischief on the weekends.

senses.definition: interested in things or people that normally interest children.
examples: My father bought himself a toy train, and my mother said he was in his second childhood.
Whenever I go to the river and throw stones, I feel as if I’m in my second childhood.

senses.definition: in one’s extra time; in the time not reserved for doing something else.
examples: I write novels in my spare time.
I’ll try to paint the house in my spare time.

senses.definition: in one’s best Sunday clothes; in the clothes one wears to church.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: All the children were dressed up in their Sunday best.
I like to be in my Sunday best whenever I go out.
Let’s get into our Sunday best and go out for dinner.

senses.definition: present at the end of some activity, usually an activity with negative results.
senses.notes: Refers to being present when a hunted animal is put to death. Informal when used about any other activity.
examples: Congress was due to defeat the bill, and I went to Washington so I could be in on the kill.
The judge will sentence the criminal today, and I’m going to be in at the kill.

senses.definition: to circle a heavenly body.
senses.notes: [for something] Planets, moons, and stars are heavenly bodies. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The moon is in orbit around the earth.
They put the satellite into orbit.

senses.definition: ecstatic; thrilled; emotionally high.
examples: Jane is in orbit about her new job.
John went into orbit when he got the check in the mail.

senses.definition: for the purpose of doing something; as a means of doing something.
examples: I went to college in order to further my education.
I gave John three dollars in order to buy lunch.

senses.definition: said in another, simpler way.
examples: BOB: Cease! Desist! BILL: In other words, you want me to stop?
Our cash flow is negative, and our assets are worthless. In other words, we are broke.

senses.definition: having more difficulties than one can manage.
senses.notes: Informal. As if being in water that is too deep. See also in deep; in deep water.
examples: Calculus is very hard for me. I’m in over my head.
Ann is too busy. She’s really in over her head.

senses.definition: having the gears locked so the automobile cannot move.
examples: The driver stopped the car and placed it in park.
You have to be in park in order to start this car.

senses.definition: partly; to a lesser degree or extent.
examples: I was not there, in part because of my disagreement about the purpose of the meeting. I also had a previous appointment.
I hope to win, in part because I want the prize money.

senses.definition: specifically; especially.
examples: I’m not going anywhere in particular.
Of the three ideas, there is one I like in particular.

senses.definition: casually; as an aside.
senses.notes: See also mention someone or something in passing.
examples: I just heard your name in passing. I didn’t hear more than that.
The lecturer referred to George Washington in passing.

senses.definition: written or signed with a pencil.
examples: Why did you write your report in pencil?
You can’t sign a check in pencil!

senses.definition: for an indefinitely long period of time; eternally.
examples: My trust fund generates income in perpetuity.
My family has owned this land for generations and will continue to do so in perpetuity.

senses.definition: actually present in a place rather than appearing in a film, on a television screen, on a telephone, or through a radio broadcast.
examples: All the famous movie stars were there in person.
You must appear in the office in person to collect the money that is due to you.

senses.definition: in (someone’s or something’s) proper place or location.
senses.notes: See also out of place. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The maid came into the room and put everything into place.
It’s good to see everything in place again.

senses.definition: proper.
examples: Your remark was not in place.
The presentation was quite in place and nicely done.

headword: in place of someone or something

senses.definition: instead of someone or something.
examples: John went in place of Mary.
We had vegetables in place of meat.

senses.definition: in simple, clear, and straightforward language.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: That’s too confusing. Please say it again in plain English.
Tell me again in plain language.
Please put it into plain language.

senses.definition: in an application (of a principle, etc.); in the actual doing of something.
examples: Our policy is to be very particular, but in practice we don’t care that much.
The instructions say not to set it too high. In practice I always set it as high as possible.

senses.definition: well-rehearsed; wellpracticed; well-exercised.
examples: The swimmer was not in practice and almost drowned.
I play the piano for a living, and I have to keep in practice.

senses.definition: available for sale from the publisher.
senses.notes: [of a book, magazine, newspaper, or other written material] Compare this with out of print. See also put something into print.
examples: I think I can get that book for you. It’s still in print.
This is the only book in print on this subject.

senses.definition: privately.
examples: I’d like to speak to you in private.
I enjoy spending the evening in private.

senses.definition: happening now; taking place at this time.
examples: You can’t go into that room. There is a meeting in progress.
Please tell me about the work you have in progress.

senses.definition: showing the right or wrong proportion relative to something else.
examples: That man’s large head is out of proportion to his small body.
The cartoonist drew the dog in proportion to its surroundings.

senses.definition: in a place or way so that other people can see or know about something.
examples: It’s illegal to walk naked in public.
John always tries to embarrass me whenever we’re in public.

senses.definition: chasing after something.
examples: Bill spends most of his time in pursuit of money.
Every year Bob goes into the countryside in pursuit of butterflies.

headword: in quest of someone or something
altForms: in search of someone or something

senses.definition: seeking or hunting something; trying to find something.
examples: They went into town in quest of a reasonably priced restaurant.
Monday morning I’ll go out in search of a job.

senses.definition: in worn-out and torn clothing.
examples: Oh, look at my clothing. I can’t go to the party in rags!
I think the new casual fashions make you look as if you’re in rags.

senses.definition: viewing things realistically; really.
examples: Jane dreamed it was snowing, but in reality, it was very warm.
John looks happy, but in reality, he is miserable.

senses.definition: the recent period of time in which things happened that can be remembered.
examples: Never in recent memory has there been this much snow!
I haven’t been this happy in recent memory!
