senses.definition: a stage of development in the production of a play, opera, or concert, involving many rehearsals.
examples: The play is in rehearsal now and will open next month.
While the opera was still in rehearsal, the star developed a hatred for the director.

senses.definition: not as bad or seeming to be getting better.
examples: While the disease was in remission, John got to leave the hospital.
The doctor said my cancer was in remission.

senses.definition: reconsidering the past with the knowledge one now has.
examples: In retrospect, I would have gone to a better college.
David realized, in hindsight, that he should have finished school.

senses.definition: by way of giving something back; as a way of paying someone back for something; as part of an exchange.
examples: I helped Tom yesterday, and he helped me in return for my efforts.
I paid $20 and received four tickets in return.

senses.definition: as an estimated number; a figure that has been rounded off.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Please tell me in round numbers what it’ll cost.
I don’t need the exact amount. Just give it to me in round figures.

senses.definition: a state of having been destroyed.
examples: The enemy army left the cities they attacked in ruin.
The crops laid in ruin after the flood.

senses.definition: currently available for selling.
senses.notes: Some foods and other things are available only at certain seasons. Compare this with out of season. In can be replaced with into, especially when used with come. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Oysters are available in season.
Strawberries aren’t in season in January.
When do strawberries come into season?

senses.definition: legally able to be caught or hunted.
examples: Catfish are in season all year round.
When are salmon in season?

senses.definition: secretly.
examples: They planned in secret to blow up the bridge.
I will tell her in secret so no one else will hear.

senses.definition: operating or functioning.
senses.notes: [of a court, congress, or other organization]
examples: Smoking is forbidden while the meeting is in session.
The spectators must remain quiet while court is in session.

senses.definition: in a very happy state.
examples: Ann was really in seventh heaven when she got a car of her own.
I’d be in seventh heaven if I had a million dollars.

senses.definition: in a messy state; destroyed.
examples: After the earthquake, the town lay in shambles.
The TV set was in shambles after John tried to fix it.

senses.definition: stated briefly.
examples: At the end of the financial report, the board president said, “In short, we are okay.”
My remarks, in short, indicate that we are in good financial shape.

senses.definition: very quickly.
examples: I can straighten out this mess in short order.
The people came in and cleaned the place up in short order.

senses.definition: scarce.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Fresh vegetables are in short supply in the winter.
Yellow cars are in short supply because everyone likes them and buys them.
At this time of the year, fresh vegetables go into short supply.

senses.definition: able to be seen.
examples: I hear birds, but there are none in sight.
The locusts ate everything in sight.

senses.definition: lined up, one behind the other; in a line, one person or one thing wide.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Have you ever seen ducks walking in single file?
No, do they usually walk single file?
Please march in single file.
Please get into single file.

senses.definition: exactly; explicitly; literally.
examples: I told her in so many words to leave me alone.
He said yes, but not in so many words.

headword: in some neck of the woods

senses.definition: in some vicinity or neighborhood; in some remote place.
senses.notes: Folksy. The some is usually this, that, your, their, etc.
examples: I think that the Smiths live in your neck of the woods.
What’s happening over in that neck of the woods?

senses.definition: seeing or experiencing something from someone else’s point of view.
senses.notes: See the note at in a bind and the examples. See also put oneself in someone else’s place.
examples: You might feel different if you were in her shoes.
Pretend you’re in Tom’s place, and then try to figure out why he acts the way he does.

senses.definition: to someone’s advantage or credit.
senses.notes: Especially in sports scores, as in the examples below.
examples: The score was ten to twelve in our favor.
At the end of the second half, the score was forty to three in the other team’s favor.

senses.definition: liked by someone; approved of by someone.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John might be able to help me. I hope I’m currently in his favor.
My mother is mad at me. I’m certainly not in her favor.
I’ll try to get into her favor.

senses.definition: to someone, as when writing a check.
examples: Please make out a check for $300 in Tom’s favor.
I’m making out the check in favor of Mr. Brown.

senses.definition: in someone’s ownership; as someone’s property.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The house is in my name. I own all of it.
I put the house into my husband’s name.
The car is in our names.

senses.definition: remembered and called by name when someone prays.
examples: I am sorry to hear of your sickness. You will be in our prayers.
The whole family is in my prayers because they have suffered so much.

senses.definition: with regard to some or many details.
examples: In some respects, Anne’s comments are similar to yours.
The three proposals are quite different in many respects.

headword: in spite of someone or something

senses.definition: regardless of someone or something; in defiance of someone or something.
examples: In spite of what you said, I still like you.
He went to the concert in spite of his parents.

senses.definition: [marching or dancing] in cadence with another person; marching with the same rhythm as someone else.
senses.notes: [with someone] In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Please keep in step with Jane.
You two, back there. You aren’t in step.
Get into step!

senses.definition: keeping in rhythm or cadence with music.
examples: John, your marching isn’t in step with the beat.
I’m trying to play in time.

senses.definition: as up to date as someone or something.
examples: Bob is not in step with the times.
We try to keep in step.

senses.definition: readily available, as with goods in a store.
examples: I’m sorry, I don’t have that in stock. I’ll have to order it for you.
We have all our Christmas merchandise in stock now.

senses.definition: in a place where things are stored or kept.
examples: Mary placed her winter clothes in storage during the summer.
John’s furniture is in storage while he is in the army.

senses.definition: in fashion; fashionable.
senses.notes: Compare this with out of style. In can be replaced with into, especially with come. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: This old coat isn’t in style anymore.
I don’t care if it’s not in style. It’s warm.
I hope this coat comes into style again.

senses.definition: in elegance; in luxury.
examples: If I had a million dollars, I could really live in style.
If he saves his money, someday he’ll be able to live in style.

senses.definition: involved in surgery.
examples: Dr. Smith is in surgery now.
The patient is still in surgery.

senses.definition: in single file.
examples: We marched to the door in tandem.
They rode along in tandem.

senses.definition: in torn pieces of cloth.
examples: The poor man’s clothes hung in tatters.
The flag was in tatters after the storm.

senses.definition: relating to something; with regard to something.
examples: In terms of value to this company, how much do you think you are worth?
Is this a good paint job on my car—in terms of the quality, not the color?

headword: in the absence of someone or something

senses.definition: while someone or something isn’t here; without someone or something.
examples: In the absence of the cook, I’ll prepare dinner.
In the absence of opposition, she won easily.

senses.definition: while doing something.
senses.notes: See also catch someone in the act (of doing something).
examples: There he was, in the act of opening the door.
I tripped while in the act of climbing.
It happened in the act, not before or after.

senses.definition: in the form of an answer that means yes.
examples: The soldier answered in the affirmative by nodding his head “yes.”
My manager’s response was in the affirmative.

senses.definition: everywhere; all about.
examples: There is such a feeling of joy in the air.
We felt a sense of tension in the air.

senses.definition: naked; nude.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: We often went swimming in the altogether down at the creek.
The museum has a painting of some ladies in the buff.
Mary felt a little shy about getting into the altogether.
Bill says he sleeps in the raw.

senses.definition: in an undecided state.
senses.notes: See also hang in the balance.
examples: He stood on the edge of the cliff, his life in the balance.
With his fortune in the balance, John rolled the dice.

senses.definition: in addition to what was agreed on.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I bought a car, and they threw an air conditioner into the bargain.
When I bought a house, I asked the seller to include the furniture in the bargain.

senses.definition: very healthy.
examples: Bill is in the best of health. He eats well and exercises.
I haven’t been in the best of health. I think I have the flu.

senses.definition: not in debt; in a financially profitable condition.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the red. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I wish my accounts were in the black.
Sally moved the company into the black.

senses.definition: built into one’s personality or character.
examples: John’s a great runner. It’s in his blood.
The whole family is very athletic. It’s in the blood.

senses.definition: in a special place near a baseball playing field, warming up to pitch.
senses.notes: [for a baseball pitcher to be] In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: You can tell who is pitching next by seeing who is in the bullpen.
Our best pitcher just went into the bullpen. He’ll be pitching soon.

senses.definition: in the future.
examples: Well, what do you think is in the cards for tomorrow?
I asked the boss if there was a raise in the cards for me.

senses.definition: in the keeping of someone.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I left the baby in the care of my mother.
I placed the house into the care of my friend.
Bill left the office in the charge of his assistant.

headword: in the case of someone or something

senses.definition: in the matter of someone or something; in the instance of someone or something.
senses.notes: See also in case of something. Compare this with in the event of something.
examples: In the case of John, I think we had better allow his request.
In the case of this woman, we’ll not grant permission.

senses.definition: in the legal proceedings relating to someone.
senses.notes: [with someone] The someone may be contained in the official name of a legal case.
examples: I recall a similar situation in the case of Ohio v. Jane Smith.
Have they found any new facts in the case of Bill Wilson?

senses.definition: wealthy; with much money.
senses.notes: Slang. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John is a stock trader, and occasionally he’s in the chips.
Bill really came into the chips when his uncle died.

senses.definition: not obstructed; not enclosed.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: You’re in the clear. Go ahead and back up.
Once the deer got into the clear, it ran away.

senses.definition: innocent; not guilty.
examples: Don’t worry, Tom. I’m sure you’re in the clear.
I’ll feel better when I get into the clear.

senses.definition: in the circumstances under which something has happened.
examples: In the context of a funeral, laughing loudly is inappropriate.
In the context of an argument, it is fine to speak firmly.

headword: in the dark (about someone or something)

senses.definition: uninformed about someone or something; ignorant about someone or something.
examples: I’m in the dark about who is in charge around here.
I can’t imagine why they are keeping me in the dark.
You won’t be in the dark long. I’m in charge.
She’s in the dark about how this machine works.

senses.definition: in trouble; in (someone’s) disfavor.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I’m really in the doghouse. I was late for an appointment.
I hate being in the doghouse all the time. I don’t know why I can’t stay out of trouble.

senses.definition: sluggish; inactive; in low spirits.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: He’s usually in the doldrums in the winter.
I had some bad news yesterday, which put me into the doldrums.

senses.definition: in control.
senses.notes: Refers to driving and controlling a vehicle.
examples: Now that Fred is in the driver’s seat, there is a lot less criticism about how things are being done.
Joan can’t wait to get into the driver’s seat and do what she can to turn things around.

senses.definition: if something happens.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the case of someone or something.
examples: In the event of fire, please leave quickly and quietly.
The picnic will be canceled in the event of rain.

senses.definition: in truth; when all the facts are known; when the truth becomes known.
senses.notes: Usually used when someone is speculating about what the final truth is.
examples: In the final analysis, it is usually the children who suffer most in a situation like this.
In the last analysis, you simply do not want to do as you are told!

senses.definition: initially; to begin with.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the second place.
examples: In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one. In the second place, you don’t need one.
In the first instance, I don’t have the time. In the second instance, I’m not interested.

senses.definition: really present; in person.
examples: I’ve heard that the queen is coming here in the flesh.
Is she really here? In the flesh?
I’ve wanted a color television for years, and now I’ve got one right here in the flesh.

senses.definition: in a low state; depraved.
senses.notes: [for a person to be] Also literal. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: You had better straighten out your life, or you’ll end in the gutter.
His bad habits put him into the gutter.

senses.definition: in debt.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into with go. See in a bind and the examples.
examples: I’m $200 in the hole.
Our finances end in the hole every month.
We went into the hole on that deal.

senses.definition: in the meantime; in the time between the ending of something and the beginning of something else.
examples: In the interim between her morning and afternoon classes, Susan rushed home to get a book she had forgotten.
My favorite show starts in five minutes, but I’ll talk to you in the interim.

senses.definition: knowledgeable.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Let’s ask Bob. He’s in the know.
I have no knowledge of how to work this machine. I think I can get into the know very quickly, though.

senses.definition: in luxurious surroundings.
senses.notes: See the explanation at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: John lives in the lap of luxury because his family is very wealthy.
When I retire, I’d like to live in the lap of luxury.

senses.definition: with the clothes that are waiting to be washed.
examples: Is my blue shirt clean or is it in the laundry?
All my socks are in the laundry. What shall I do?

senses.definition: at the center of attention.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples. Limelight refers to an obsolete type of spotlight, and the word occurs only in this phrase.
examples: John will do almost anything to get himself into the limelight.
I love being in the spotlight.
All elected officials spend a lot of time in the limelight.

senses.definition: as part of the expected (military or police) duties.
examples: When soldiers fight people in a war, it’s in the line of duty.
Police officers have to do things they may not like in the line of duty.

senses.definition: over a long period of time; ultimately.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the short run.
examples: We’d be better off in the long run buying one instead of renting one.
In the long run, we’d be happier in the South.

senses.definition: following the current trends or styles that are popular or are considered normal.
examples: Bob is too old-fashioned to be in the mainstream of modern living.
Max likes to make fun of people in the mainstream.

senses.definition: wanting to buy something.
examples: I’m in the market for a video recorder.
If you have a boat for sale, we’re in the market.

senses.definition: the period of time between two things; the period of time between now and when something is supposed to happen.
examples: The movie starts at 6:00. In the meantime, let’s eat dinner.
My flight was at 8:00. In the meantime, I played solitaire.

senses.definition: in a very remote place.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: To get to my house, you have to drive into the middle of nowhere.
We found a nice place to eat, but it’s out in the middle of nowhere.

senses.definition: wealthy.
senses.notes: Informal. See also on the money.
examples: John is really in the money. He’s worth millions.
If I am ever in the money, I’ll be generous.

senses.definition: in the winning position in a race or contest.
senses.notes: Refers to winning the prize money.
examples: I knew when Jane came around the final turn that she was in the money.
The horses coming in first, second, and third are said to be in the money.

altForms: in the mood to do something

senses.definition: having the proper state of mind for a particular situation or for doing something.
examples: I’m not in the mood to see a movie tonight.
Are you in the mood for pizza?

senses.definition: in the time immediately ahead.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: I don’t plan to go to Florida in the near future.
Today’s prices won’t extend into the near future.
What do you intend to do in the near future?

senses.definition: in a state of nudity.
examples: Bill says he sleeps in the nude.
All the little boys swam in the nude in the creek.

senses.definition: happening at some time in the future.
senses.notes: See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: There is a big investigation in the offing, but I don’t know when.
It’s hard to tell what’s in the offing if you don’t keep track of things.

senses.definition: in the outdoors; in an area that is not closed in.
examples: John’s bike was stolen because he left it out in the open.
Mary loves gardening because she loves to be in the open.

senses.definition: according to a theory; theoretically.
examples: In theory, if I take my medicine regularly, I will get well.
How things work in theory doesn’t always match with how things work in reality.

senses.definition: in very good health; in very good condition, physically and emotionally.
senses.notes: Informal. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The garden is lovely. All the flowers are in the pink of condition.
Jane has to exercise hard to get into the pink of condition.
I’d like to be in the pink, but I don’t have the time.

senses.definition: in the best and most productive and healthy period of life.
senses.notes: See also in one’s prime. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The good health of one’s youth can carry over into the prime of life.
He was struck down by a heart attack in the prime of life.

senses.definition: publicly; visible to all; conspicuous.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Elected officials find themselves constantly in the public eye.
The mayor made it a practice to get into the public eye as much as possible.

senses.definition: located in the space or area behind someone or something.
examples: The waiter told me that the bathrooms were in the rear.
All deliveries must be made in the rear.

senses.definition: in debt.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the black and out of the red. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: My accounts are in the red at the end of every month.
It’s easy to get into the red if you don’t pay close attention to the amount of money you spend.

senses.definition: trying very hard.
examples: Bob is always in there pitching.
Just stay in there pitching. You’ll make some progress eventually.

senses.definition: on the moral or legal side of an issue; on the right side of an issue.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the wrong.
examples: I felt I was in the right, but the judge ruled against me.
It’s hard to argue with Jane. She always believes that she’s in the right.

headword: in the right place at the right time

senses.definition: in the location where something is to happen, exactly when it happens.
examples: I got a good deal on a car because I was in the right place at the right time.
Unless you are in the right place at the right time, you won’t get a chance to meet a movie star.

senses.definition: in competition; competing and having a chance to win.
senses.notes: Compare this with out of the running. In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Is Tom still in the running? Does he still have a chance to be elected?
I’m glad I didn’t get into the running.

senses.definition: in the same situation; having the same problem.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the explanation at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: TOM: I’m broke. Can you lend me twenty dollars? BILL: Sorry. I’m in the same boat.
Jane and Mary are both in the same boat. They have been called for jury duty.
I am in the same boat as Mary.

senses.definition: almost at the same time.
examples: He told me I was lazy, but then in the same breath he said I was doing a good job.
The teacher said that the students were working hard and, in the same breath, that they were not working hard enough.

senses.definition: secondly; in addition.
senses.notes: Usually said after one has said in the first place.
examples: In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one. In the second place, you don’t need one.
In the first place, I don’t have the time. In the second place, I’m not interested.

senses.definition: for the immediate future.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the long run.
examples: In the short run, we’d be better off saving our money.
We decided to rent an apartment in the short run. We can buy a house later.

senses.definition: in a bad situation.
senses.notes: Slang. In can be replaced with into. See in a bind and the examples below.
examples: Now I’m really in the soup. I broke Mrs. Franklin’s window.
I make a lot of mistakes. It’s easy for me to get into the soup.

senses.definition: involved in or participating in events or happenings.
senses.notes: The in can be replaced with into. See the explanation at in a bind and the examples. The opposite of out of the swim of things.
examples: I’ve been ill, but soon I’ll be back in the swim of things.
I can’t wait to settle down and get into the swim of things.

senses.definition: under the responsibility or in the care of someone.
examples: The state placed the orphan in the trust of the foster parents.
Our bonds are left in the trust of our broker.

headword: in the twinkling of an eye

senses.definition: very quickly.
examples: In the twinkling of an eye, the deer had disappeared into the forest.
I gave Bill ten dollars and, in the twinkling of an eye, he spent it.

headword: in the unlikely event of something
altForms: in the unlikely event that something happens

senses.definition: if something—which probably will not happen—actually happens.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the event of something.
examples: In the unlikely event of my getting the job, I’ll have to buy a car to get there every day.
In the unlikely event of a fire, please walk quickly to an exit.

senses.definition: just in time; at the last possible instant; just before it’s too late.
examples: The doctor arrived in the nick of time. The patient’s life was saved.
I reached the airport in the very nick of time.

senses.definition: after something; as a result of some event.
senses.notes: Refers to the wake of a boat.
examples: We had no place to live in the wake of the fire.
In the wake of the storm, there were many broken tree limbs.

senses.definition: as a kind of something; as a style of something.
examples: What do you have in the way of leather shoes?
We have nothing in the way of raincoats.
I’ve seen nothing in the way of nice weather in this part of the country.

senses.definition: about to happen.
examples: There are some major changes in the wind. Expect these changes to happen soon.
There is something in the wind. We’ll find out what it is soon.

senses.definition: being prepared; being planned; being done.
examples: There are some new laws in the works that will affect all of us.
I have some ideas in the works that you might be interested in.

senses.definition: very much.
examples: I want a new car in the worst way.
Bob wants to retire in the worst way.

senses.definition: on the wrong or illegal side of an issue; guilty or in error.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the right.
examples: I felt she was in the wrong, but the judge ruled in her favor.
It’s hard to argue with Jane. She always believes that everyone else is in the wrong.

headword: in the wrong place at the wrong time

senses.definition: in the location where something is to happen exactly when it happens.
examples: I always get into trouble. I’m just in the wrong place at the wrong time.
It isn’t my fault. I was just in the wrong place at the wrong time.

senses.definition: the fashionable thing to do.
examples: Eating low-fat food is the in thing to do.
Bob is very old-fashioned. He never does the in thing.

senses.definition: presently; currently; nowadays.
examples: You don’t expect people to be polite in this day and age.
Young folks don’t take care of their parents in this day and age.

senses.definition: before the deadline; before the last minute.
examples: Did you turn in your paper in time?
I didn’t go to Florida. I didn’t get to the airport in time.

senses.definition: long ago; in previous times.
examples: In times past, you would not have been able to wear casual clothing to work.
In times past, the air always seemed fresher and cleaner.

senses.definition: in very good physical condition.
examples: The runners are in top form, so this should be a good race.
I’m not in top form, but I’m not a physical mess either.

senses.definition: able to make witty remarks and clever statements quickly and easily.
examples: That was really funny, Bob. You are in top form tonight.

senses.definition: closely following; under someone’s control.
examples: The nanny walked into the park with three children in tow.
The manager went to the meeting with her staff in tow.

senses.definition: while in the process of being transported.
examples: Dave is in transit from London to Chicago.
The new stereo is now in transit from the manufacturer.

senses.definition: produced in three copies.
examples: Mr. Smith asked me to type up his notes in triplicate.
I completed each form in triplicate.

senses.definition: in danger; in difficulty; due for punishment.
examples: If you don’t be quiet, you’re going to be in trouble.
The company was in trouble for months, and then went bankrupt.

senses.definition: pregnant and unmarried.
examples: They had to get married. She was in trouble.
She’ll be in trouble before long, if she doesn’t quit running around like that.

senses.definition: in a state where musical notes are at their proper intervals so that none are flat or sharp.
senses.notes: Compare this with out of tune (with someone or something).
examples: Your piano is nicely in tune.
The choir members all sang in tune.

headword: in tune with someone or something

senses.definition: at the same or a harmonizing musical pitch.
senses.notes: In can be replaced with into. See the note at in a bind and the examples below.
examples: The violin isn’t in tune with the piano.
Bill, please get in tune with John.

senses.definition: keeping up with something.
examples: Tom, your clothes are old-fashioned. You aren’t in tune with the times.
Come on, Sally. Get in tune with what’s going on around you.

senses.definition: one at a time in sequence.
examples: Each of us can read the book in turn.
We cut the hair of every child in turn.

headword: in two shakes of a lamb’s tail

senses.definition: very quickly.
examples: I’ll be there in two shakes of a lamb’s tail.
In two shakes of a lamb’s tail, the bird flew away.

senses.definition: having the same pitch.
examples: This part of the piece is performed in unison.
The twins sang in unison.

senses.definition: acting as one; together and at the same time.
examples: In unison, all of the workers voted “yes” for the new contract.
John and his wife responded to my question in unison.

senses.definition: in consideration of something; because of something.
examples: In view of the high cost of gasoline, I sold my car.
I won’t invite John to the meeting in view of his attitude.

senses.definition: one inch at a time; little by little.
examples: Traffic moved along inch by inch.
Inch by inch, the snail moved across the stone.

senses.definition: to tend to do something; to lean toward doing something.
examples: Tom is inclined to tell jokes when he is with a group of people.
I’m inclined to go to the beach tomorrow if it doesn’t rain.

headword: incumbent upon someone to do something

senses.definition: necessary for someone to do something.
senses.notes: Upon can be replaced with on.
examples: It’s incumbent upon you to do the work.
It was incumbent on me to make the presentation of the first prize.

senses.definition: the correct and successful way to do something; the special things that one needs to know to do something.
examples: I don’t understand the ins and outs of politics.
Jane knows the ins and outs of working with computers.

senses.definition: as if bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: An adverb. Compare this with outside the box.
examples: If you keep your discussions inside the box, you will be bound by traditional limitations.
Nothing can be accomplished inside the box to solve this problem. We have already tried every obvious solution.

senses.definition: bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
examples: You have some really inside-the-box ideas, Ralph. Why not be more creative?
After some long, tedious, inside-the-box discussions, we arrived at the same old conclusion that we always arrive at.

senses.definition: playing an important part in doing something.
examples: John was instrumental in getting the contract to build the new building.
Our senator was instrumental in defeating the bill.

senses.definition: determined to do something.
examples: The children were intent on making a snowman.
The prisoner was intent on escaping.

senses.definition: in(to) a difficult situation.
examples: Mary cannot keep track of the many times Dave got himself into a jam.
I found myself in a jam when my car overheated on the highway.

senses.definition: into existence.
examples: The new law brought more problems into being.
That idea came into being centuries ago.

senses.definition: in the control of someone who has power or authority over someone else.
examples: Snow White fell into the clutches of the evil witch.
Once you’re in my clutches, I’ll ruin you.

senses.definition: an intrusion that results in the loss of someone’s privacy.
examples: Your invasion of my privacy is not welcome!
The athlete complained about the invasion of his privacy by the press.

senses.definition: to endow someone with something, such as power or privilege.
examples: The Constitution invests the vice president with the authority to act on the president’s behalf in certain conditions.
The state has invested me with the authority to unite this couple in marriage.

senses.definition: to solve a problem; to straighten out a problem; to smooth out a difficulty.
examples: The principal had to iron a classroom problem out.
I just have to iron out this little problem; then I’ll be able to see you.

senses.definition: to make a public invitation or request for something.
examples: The prime minister issued a call for peace.
The person who organized the writing contest issued a call for entries.

headword: It behooves one to do something.

senses.definition: It is necessary for one to do something.; It is incumbent upon someone to do something.
examples: It behooves me to report the crime.
It behooves you to pay for the window that you broke.

headword: It never rains but it pours.

senses.definition: A lot of bad things tend to happen at the same time.
examples: The car won’t start, the stairs broke, and the dog died. It never rains but it pours.
More bad news? It never rains but it pours.

senses.definition: It is only reasonable to hold a certain opinion.
examples: It stands to reason that most people will not buy a new car if they don’t think they can pay for it.
I think he will come back to pick up his check. It only stands to reason.

senses.definition: It is very unpleasant, but when it is gotten used to, it will not be so bothersome.
senses.notes: Said in recognition of the unpleasantness of something.
examples: I never ate duck’s feet before. It takes some getting used to.
These hot Mexican dishes seem impossible at first. They take some getting used to, I agree. But it’s worth it.

senses.definition: It will never work!; It will never be approved!
senses.notes: Also literal. Refers to an evaluation of an unlikely-looking aircraft of some type.
examples: I have read your report and studied your proposal. It’ll never fly.
Your design for a new electric automobile is interesting, but it’ll never fly!

senses.definition: It is almost too late!; I’ve been waiting a long time!
senses.notes: Informal. See also the following entry.
examples: So you finally got here! It’s about time!
They finally paid me my money. It’s about time!

senses.definition: It is totally incomprehensible to me.
examples: Can you explain what this paragraph in the lease means? Legal language is all Greek to me.
I can’t figure out this diagram of how to assemble my bicycle. It’s all Greek to me.

senses.definition: It is past time [for someone or something]!; [Someone or something] is overdue!
senses.notes: Informal. See also the previous entry.
examples: It’s high time that you got recognition for what you do!
They sent me my check, and it’s high time, too.

headword: It’s not over till it’s over.

senses.definition: There is still hope for things to go the way I want until the entire event is over.
examples: They haven’t won the game yet. It’s not over till it’s over.
It looks bad for our side, but it’s not over till it’s over.

senses.definition: It is hopeless to do something.; It is pointless to do something.
examples: It’s no use trying to call on the telephone. The line is always busy.
They tried and tried, but it was no use.

senses.definition: someone who can do several different jobs instead of specializing in one.
examples: John can do plumbing, carpentry, and roofing—a real jack-of-all-trades. He isn’t very good at any of them.
Take your car to a trained mechanic, not a jack-of-all-trades.

senses.definition: to motivate someone; to stimulate someone to do something.
examples: The mail is late again today. We’ll have to jack those people up at the post office.
I guess I’ll have to jack up the carpenter again to repair my stairs.

senses.definition: to raise something up on a mechanical lifting device.
examples: Now I have to jack the car up so I can change the tire.
Please jack up the car.

senses.definition: to raise the price of something.
examples: The store keeps jacking prices up.
The grocery store jacked up the prices again last night.

senses.definition: to make something more exciting, colorful, or lively.
examples: When we play the music this time, let’s jazz it up a bit.
I think we need to jazz up this room. It looks so drab.

senses.definition: someone with both an evil and a good personality.
senses.notes: From the novel The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson.
examples: Bill thinks Mary is so soft and gentle, but she can be very cruel—she is a real Jekyll and Hyde.
Jane doesn’t know that Fred is a Jekyll and Hyde. She sees him only when he is being kind and generous, but he can be very cruel.

senses.definition: to try to push or maneuver one’s way into an advantageous position at the expense of others.
examples: All the workers in the company are jockeying for position. They all want the manager’s job.
It is unpleasant working for a company where people are always jockeying for position.

senses.definition: to stimulate someone’s memory to recall something.
examples: Hearing the first part of the song I’d forgotten really jogged my memory.
I tried to jog Bill’s memory about our childhood antics.

senses.definition: someone who joins in (something) after it is under way.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to Sally. She’s just a Johnny-come-lately and doesn’t know what she’s talking about.
We’ve been here for thirty years. Why should some Johnny-come-lately tell us what to do?

senses.definition: someone who is in the right place at the right time.
examples: Here I am, Johnny-on-the-spot. I told you I would be here at 12:20.
Bill is late again. You can hardly call him Johnny-on-the-spot.

senses.definition: to unite with someone.
examples: We joined forces with the police to search for the lost child.
The choirs joined forces to sing the song.

senses.definition: to hold hands so that each person is holding the hands of two other people; [for two people] to hold each other’s hands.
examples: Let us join hands and pray together.
The dancers joined hands and formed a circle that moved to the left.

senses.definition: an expression indicating that the person spoken to is in the same, or a similar, unfortunate state as the speaker.
examples: You don’t have anyplace to stay? Join the club! Neither do we.
Did you get fired too? Join the club!

senses.definition: to join the fight or argument.
examples: After listening to the argument, Mary decided to jump into the fray.
Tom joined the fray and immediately got knocked down.

senses.definition: to start or stop moving suddenly, causing a jolt.
examples: The truck jolted to a stop at the stop sign.
The little car jolted to a quick start and threw the passenger back in his seat.

headword: judge something on its own merit(s)

senses.definition: to judge or evaluate a thing on its own good points and usefulness.
examples: You have to judge each painting on its own merits. Not every painting by a famous painter is superior.
Each rose must be judged on its own merit.

senses.definition: considering something; using something as an indication (of something else).
examples: Judging by your wet clothing, it must be raining.
Judging by the looks of this house, I would guess there has been a party here.

senses.definition: trivial and uninteresting snacks or refreshments.
examples: The party was not much. They might as well have served juice and cookies.
After juice and cookies, we all went back into the meeting room for another hour of talk, talk, talk.

senses.definition: to scold someone severely.
examples: If I don’t get home on time, my parents will jump all over me.
Don’t jump on me! I didn’t do it!
Please don’t jump all over John. He wasn’t the one who broke the window.
Why are you jumping down my throat? I wasn’t even in the house when it happened.

senses.definition: to seize the opportunity to do something.
senses.notes: Usually with it. See also jump at the chance, from which this phrase comes.
examples: When I heard about John’s chance to go to England, I knew he’d jump at it.
If something you really want to do comes your way, jump at it.

senses.definition: to eagerly accept the opportunity to do something.
examples: John jumped at the chance to go to England.
I don’t know why I didn’t jump at the opportunity myself.
I should have leaped at the chance.

senses.definition: to fail to appear in court for trial and give up one’s bail bond.
examples: Not only was Bob arrested for theft, he skipped bail and left town. He’s in a lot of trouble.
I thought only criminals jumped bail.

senses.definition: to react strongly to a shock or a surprise.
senses.notes: Informal. Usually with nearly, almost, etc.
examples: Oh! You really scared me. I nearly jumped out of my skin.
Bill was so startled he almost jumped out of his skin.

senses.definition: to start before the starting signal.
senses.notes: Originally used in sports contests that are started by firing a gun.
examples: We all had to start the race again because Jane jumped the gun.
When we took the test, Tom jumped the gun and started early.

senses.definition: to fall or jump off the rails or guides.
senses.notes: [for something] Usually said about a train.
examples: The train jumped the track, causing many injuries to the passengers.
The engine jumped the track, but the other cars stayed on.

senses.definition: to change suddenly from one thing, thought, plan, or activity to another.
examples: The entire project jumped the track, and we finally had to give up.
John’s mind jumped the track while he was in the play, and he forgot his lines.

senses.definition: to do everything possible to obey or please someone; to bend over backwards (to do something).
senses.notes: Informal. Trained animals jump through hoops.
examples: She expects us to jump through hoops for her.
What do you want me to do—jump through a hoop?

senses.definition: to judge or decide something without having all the facts; to reach unwarranted conclusions.
examples: Now don’t jump to conclusions. Wait until you hear what I have to say.
Please find out all the facts so you won’t leap to conclusions.

senses.definition: a point or place from which to begin something.
examples: The local library is a logical jumping-off point for your research.
The office job in that company would be a good jumping-off place for a job in advertising.

headword: The jury is still out (on someone or something).

senses.definition: A decision has not been reached on someone or something.; The people making the decision on someone or something have not yet decided.
examples: The jury is still out on Jane. We don’t know what we are going to do about her.
The jury is still out on the question of building a new parking lot.

senses.definition: I thought so; I knew it would be this way.
examples: Just as I expected. The window was left open and it rained in.
As I expected, he left work early again.

senses.definition: if (something happens).
senses.notes: Compare this with in case something happens.
examples: All right. I’ll take the umbrella just in case it rains.
I’ll take along some aspirin, just in case.

senses.definition: just something that couldn’t have been prevented; some unfortunate event caused by fate.
examples: I’m sorry, too. It’s not your fault. It’s just one of those things.
I feel terrible that I didn’t pass the bar exam. I guess it was just one of those things.

senses.definition: in perfect order; neat and tidy.
examples: Her hair is always just so.
Their front yard is just so.

senses.definition: Precisely right!; Quite right!
examples: BILL: The letter should arrive tomorrow. TOM: Just so!
JANE: We must always try our best. MARTIN: Just so!

senses.definition: exactly what is required, especially for health or comfort.
examples: That meal was delicious, Bob. Just what the doctor ordered.
BOB: Would you like something to drink? MARY: Yes, a cold glass of water would be just what the doctor ordered.

senses.definition: to fall over or fall down in a faint or in death.
examples: Suddenly, Mr. Franklin keeled over. He had had a heart attack.
It was so hot in the room that two people just keeled over.

senses.definition: willing or eager to do something.
examples: Dave isn’t very keen on going to the opera.
The children are keen on swimming this afternoon. Shall I take them?

senses.definition: to be enthusiastic about someone or something.
examples: I’m not too keen on going to Denver.
Sally is fairly keen about getting a new job.
Mary isn’t keen on her new boss.

senses.definition: to keep informed about something; to keep up (with the times).
senses.notes: Also with be instead of keep, as in the examples below.
examples: I try to keep abreast of the financial markets.
I believe that I’m abreast of foreign events.
Yes, I try to keep abreast by reading the papers every day.

headword: keep a civil tongue (in one’s head)

senses.definition: to speak decently and politely.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at keep a straight face.
examples: Please, John. Don’t talk like that. Keep a civil tongue in your head.
John seems unable to keep a civil tongue.
He’d be welcome here if he had a civil tongue in his head.

senses.definition: to remind or nag someone over and over to do something.
examples: I’ll keep after you until you do it!
Mother stayed after Bill until he did the dishes.
She kept at him until he dried them and put them away.
She kept on him for forty minutes before he finally finished.

senses.definition: to know a secret and not tell anyone.
examples: Please keep our little secret private.
Do you know how to keep a secret?

senses.definition: to be calm and unmoved by unsettling events.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at keep a straight face.
examples: John always keeps a stiff upper lip.
Now, Billy, don’t cry. Keep a stiff upper lip.
Bill can take it. He has a stiff upper lip.

senses.definition: to make one’s face stay free from smiles or laughter.
senses.notes: Note: Keep can be replaced with have. Keep implies the exercise of effort, and have means that a state exists.
examples: It’s hard to keep a straight face when someone tells a funny joke.
I knew it was John who played the trick. He couldn’t keep a straight face.
John didn’t have a straight face.

headword: keep a tight rein on someone or something
altForms: keep a close rein on someone or something

senses.definition: to watch and control someone or something diligently.
examples: The office manager kept a tight rein on the staff.
Mary keeps a close rein on her children.

senses.definition: to feed, clothe, and house oneself.
examples: I hardly have enough money to keep body and soul together.
How the old man was able to keep body and soul together is beyond me.

senses.definition: to monitor someone or something; to observe someone or something.
examples: Keep close watch on Bill. I think he’s loafing.
Okay. I’ll keep watch, but I think he’s a good worker.

senses.definition: to guard or care for someone or something.
examples: I’m keeping watch over my children to make sure they have the things they need.
I think that an angel is keeping close watch over her to make sure nothing bad happens to her.
Angels don’t have much to do except to keep watch.

senses.definition: to spend much time with someone; to associate with or consort with someone.
senses.notes: Compare this with keep someone company.
examples: Bill has been keeping company with Ann for three months.
Bob has been keeping company with a tough-looking bunch of boys.

senses.definition: to stay calm and undisturbed.
examples: Relax man, keep cool!
If Sally could just keep cool before a race, she could probably win.

senses.definition: to be accurate.
senses.notes: [for a clock or watch] See also keep time.
examples: I have to return my watch to the store because it doesn’t keep good time.
My alarm clock really keeps good time.

senses.definition: to continue to talk or complain about something; to keep raising a topic of conversation.
examples: Why do you keep harping on the same old complaint?
You keep harping on my problems and ignore your own!

senses.definition: to manage a household.
examples: I hate to keep house. I’d rather live in a tent than keep house.
My grandmother kept house for nearly sixty years.

senses.definition: to remain in friendly communication with someone.
senses.notes: See also get in touch (with someone).
examples: I try to keep in touch with my cousins.
All our family tries to stay in touch.

senses.definition: to stay up or stay out until very late.
senses.notes: This can cause one to be late for appointments or responsibilities.
examples: I’m always tired because I keep late hours.
If I didn’t keep late hours, I wouldn’t sleep so late in the morning.

senses.definition: to remain cool and calm.
senses.notes: Originally nautical. See also keep something on an even keel.
examples: If Jane can keep on an even keel and not panic, she will be all right.
Try to keep on an even keel and not get upset so easily.

senses.definition: to keep one’s spirits high; to act brave and confident.
examples: Keep your chin up, John. Things will get better.
Just keep your chin up and tell the judge exactly what happened.

senses.definition: to remain calm, even when provoked.
examples: I have a hard time keeping my cool when someone is yelling at me.
Whatever you do, try to keep your cool.

headword: keep one’s eye on the ball

senses.definition: to watch or follow the ball carefully, especially when one is playing a ball game; to follow the details of a ball game very carefully.
examples: John, if you can’t keep your eye on the ball, I’ll have to take you out of the game.
“Keep your eye on the ball!” the coach roared at the players.

senses.definition: to remain alert to the events occurring around one.
examples: If you want to get along in this office, you’re going to have to keep your eye on the ball.
Bill would do better in his classes if he would just keep his eye on the ball.

headword: keep one’s eyes open (for someone or something)
altForms: keep one’s eyes peeled (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to remain alert and watchful for someone or something.
senses.notes: The entries with peeled are informal. Peel refers to moving the eyelids back.
examples: I’m keeping my eyes open for a sale on winter coats.
Please keep your eyes peeled for Mary. She’s due to arrive here any time.
Okay. I’ll keep my eyes open.

headword: keep one’s feet on the ground

senses.definition: to remain firmly established.
senses.notes: See also get one’s feet on the ground.
examples: Sally will have no trouble keeping her feet on the ground.
If you can keep your feet on the ground, there should be no problem.

headword: keep one’s fingers crossed (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to wish for luck for someone or something, often by crossing one’s fingers; to hope for a good outcome for someone or something.
examples: I hope you win the race Saturday. I’m keeping my fingers crossed for you.
I’m trying out for a play. Keep your fingers crossed!

senses.definition: to retain one’s control of something.
senses.notes: See also take a hand in something.
examples: I want to keep my hand in the running of the business.
Mrs. Johnson has retired from the library, but she still wants to keep her hand in.

headword: keep one’s hands off (someone or something)

senses.definition: to refrain from touching or handling someone or something.
examples: I’m going to put these cookies here. You keep your hands off them.
Get your hands off my book, and keep them off.

senses.definition: to remain calm and sensible when in an awkward situation that might cause a person to panic or go out of control.
examples: She was very angry. We had to calm her down and encourage her to keep her head.
Always try to keep your head when others are panicking.

senses.definition: to stay ahead of one’s responsibilities; to remain financially solvent.
examples: Now that I have more space to work in, I can easily keep my head above water.
While I was out of work, I could hardly keep my head above water.

headword: keep one’s mouth shut (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to keep quiet about someone or something; to keep a secret about someone or something.
examples: They told me to keep my mouth shut about the boss or I’d be in big trouble.
I think I’ll keep my mouth shut.

senses.definition: to keep out of trouble, especially trouble with the law.
examples: I’m trying to keep my nose clean by staying away from those rough guys.
John, if you don’t learn how to keep your nose clean, you’re going to end up in jail.

headword: keep one’s nose out of someone’s business

senses.definition: to refrain from interfering in someone else’s business.
senses.notes: See also get one’s nose out of someone’s business.
examples: Let John have his privacy, and keep your nose out of my business, too!
Keep your nose out of my business!

headword: keep one’s nose to the grindstone

senses.definition: to keep busy continuously over a period of time.
senses.notes: See also put one’s nose to the grindstone.
examples: The manager told me to keep my nose to the grindstone or be fired.
Keep your nose to the grindstone, and you will prosper.

senses.definition: to keep one’s thoughts and plans to oneself; not to tell other people about one’s thoughts and plans.
examples: Jane is very quiet. She tends to keep her own counsel.
I advise you to keep your own counsel.

senses.definition: to exhibit only the behavior appropriate to one’s position or status in life.
examples: When I complained about the food, they told me to keep my place!
I suggest you keep your place until you’re in a position to change things.

senses.definition: not to get angry; to hold back an expression of anger.
senses.notes: The opposite of lose one’s temper.
examples: She should have learned to keep her temper when she was a child.
Sally got thrown off the team because she couldn’t hold her temper.

senses.definition: to watch for something (to happen); to be on the alert (for something); to be on guard.
examples: Some trouble is brewing. Keep your weather eye open.
Try to be more alert. Learn to keep your weather eye open.

senses.definition: to keep one’s mind operating in a time of stress.
examples: If Jane hadn’t kept her wits about her during the fire, things would have been much worse.
I could hardly keep my wits about me.

senses.definition: to uphold one’s promise.
senses.notes: The opposite of break one’s word.
examples: I told her I’d be there to pick her up, and I intend to keep my word.
Keeping one’s word is necessary in the legal profession.

senses.definition: to stay alert and watchful.
examples: If you want to be a success at this job, you will have to keep on your toes.
Please keep on your toes and report anything strange that you see.

senses.definition: to move at the same speed as someone or something; to keep up (with someone or something).
examples: The black horse was having a hard time keeping pace with the brown one.
Bill can’t keep pace with the geometry class.
You’ve just got to keep pace.

senses.definition: not to reveal something about someone or something; to keep a secret about someone or something.
examples: Please keep quiet about the missing money.
Please keep still about Mr. Smith’s illness.
All right. I’ll keep still.

senses.definition: to sit or stay with someone, especially someone who is lonely.
examples: I kept my uncle company for a few hours.
He was very grateful for someone to keep him company. He gets very lonely.

senses.definition: to make certain that someone behaves properly.
examples: It’s very hard to keep Bill in line. He’s sort of rowdy.
The teacher had to struggle to keep the class in line.

senses.definition: to cause someone to laugh loud and hard, over and over.
senses.notes: Informal. Also with have. See the note at keep a straight face.
examples: The comedian kept us in stitches for nearly an hour.
The teacher kept the class in stitches, but the students didn’t learn anything.
She had us in stitches for ten minutes.

senses.definition: to keep someone anxious or in suspense.
senses.notes: Also with have. See the note at keep a straight face.
examples: Please tell me now. Don’t keep me on tenterhooks any longer!
Now that we have her on tenterhooks, shall we let her worry, or shall we tell her?

headword: keep someone or something in check
altForms: hold someone or something in check

senses.definition: to keep someone or something under control; to restrain someone or something.
examples: Hang on to this rope to keep the dog in check.
I was so angry I could hardly hold myself in check.

headword: keep someone or something in mind
altForms: bear someone or something in mind

senses.definition: to remember and think about someone or something.
examples: When you’re driving a car, you must bear this in mind at all times: Keep your eyes on the road.
As you leave home, keep your family in mind.

senses.definition: to make someone or something silent or less noisy.
examples: Can you please keep the baby quiet?
Keep that stereo still!

senses.definition: and keep something quiet to keep something a secret.
senses.notes: [with something] See also keep quiet (about someone or something).
examples: I’m quitting my job, but my boss doesn’t know yet. Please keep it quiet.
Okay. I’ll keep it still.

senses.definition: to restrain or control someone or something so that the person or thing cannot move.
examples: Please keep your foot still. It makes me nervous when you wiggle it.
You have to hold the nail still if you want to hit it.

headword: keep someone out in the cold

senses.definition: to prevent someone from being informed.
examples: Please don’t keep me out in the cold. Tell me what’s going on.
Don’t keep your supervisor out in the cold. Tell her what’s going on.

senses.definition: to keep someone informed (of what is happening); to keep someone up to date.
examples: If the price of corn goes up, I need to know. Please keep me posted.
Keep her posted about the patient’s status.

senses.definition: to keep food in one’s stomach (without vomiting it up).
examples: I don’t know how I managed to keep the pill down.
The food must have been spoiled. I couldn’t keep it down.
Sally is ill. She can’t keep solid food down.

headword: keep something on an even keel

senses.definition: to keep something in a steady and untroubled state.
senses.notes: See also keep on an even keel.
examples: The manager cannot keep the company on an even keel any longer.
When the workers are unhappy, it is difficult to keep the factory on an even keel.

senses.definition: to keep something a secret; to keep something in one’s mind (only).
senses.notes: Informal. If the secret stays under your hat, it stays in your mind. Note the use of but in the examples below.
examples: Keep this under your hat, but I’m getting married.
I’m getting married, but keep it under your hat.

senses.definition: to keep something concealed (until some future time).
examples: We kept the plan under wraps until after the election.
The automobile company kept the new model under wraps until most of the old models had been sold.

senses.definition: do not move.
examples: Quit wiggling. Keep still!
“Hold still. I can’t examine your ear if you’re moving,” said the doctor.

senses.definition: to monitor someone or something; to follow the activities of someone or something.
examples: I’m supposed to keep track of my books.
Try to keep tabs on everyone who works for you.
It’s hard to keep tabs when you have a lot of other work to do.
I can’t keep track of the money I earn. Maybe someone else is spending it.

senses.definition: to cause something that is in progress to continue.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also get the ball rolling.
examples: Tom started the project, and we kept the ball rolling.
Who will keep the ball rolling now that she is gone?

senses.definition: to keep things going at one’s home or other central location.
senses.notes: From a World War I song.
examples: My uncle kept the home fires burning when my sister and I went to school.
The manager stays at the office and keeps the home fires burning while I’m out selling our products.

senses.definition: to restrain something; to keep something quiet.
examples: The politician worked hard to keep the lid on the scandal.
The party was noisy because they weren’t trying to keep the lid on it. It got louder and louder.

headword: keep the wolf from the door

senses.definition: to maintain oneself at a minimal level; to keep from starving, freezing, etc.
examples: I don’t make a lot of money, just enough to keep the wolf from the door.
We have a small amount of money saved, hardly enough to keep the wolf from the door.

senses.definition: to maintain a musical rhythm.
examples: Bob had to drop out of the band because he couldn’t keep time.
Since he can’t keep time, he can’t march and he can’t play the drums.

senses.definition: to keep watch over the time in a game or an athletic contest.
examples: Ann kept time at all the basketball games.
Whoever keeps time has to watch the referee very carefully.

senses.definition: to keep track of time accurately.
senses.notes: [for a clock or a watch] See also keep good time.
examples: This watch doesn’t keep time.
My other watch kept time better.

senses.definition: to maintain a false front; to act in a special way that is different from one’s natural behavior.
examples: Most of the time John kept up an act. He was really not a friendly person.
He works hard to keep up his act.

senses.definition: to keep oneself looking calm or happy despite serious problems.
examples: Even with all the trouble Dave was having at home, he still managed to keep up appearances.
She was trained from childhood to keep up appearances no matter how bad she really felt.

senses.definition: Be patient!
examples: Hey, keep your shirt on! I’ll be with you in a minute.
I’ll bring you your hamburger when it’s cooked. Just keep your shirt on, friend.

senses.definition: anxious; tense and expectant.
examples: I don’t know why I’m so keyed up all the time. I can’t even sleep.
Ann gets keyed up before a test.

senses.definition: to break a habit.
examples: It’s hard to kick a habit, but it can be done. I stopped biting my nails.
I used to drink coffee every morning, but I kicked the habit.

senses.definition: to regret doing something.
examples: I could just kick myself for going off and not locking the car door. Now the car has been stolen.
Don’t kick yourself. It’s insured.

senses.definition: to treat someone or something badly.
examples: I finally quit my job. My boss wouldn’t stop kicking me around.
Stop kicking my car around. It does everything I ask it.

senses.definition: to discuss an idea or a proposal.
examples: That sounds like a good idea to me. Let’s kick it around in our meeting tomorrow.
We kicked around John’s idea for a while.

senses.definition: to send someone away from a place.
examples: I lived at home until I was eighteen and my father kicked me out.
He kicked out his own child?
Yes. He booted out my brother when he was twenty.

senses.definition: to contribute some money (to a cause).
senses.notes: Literal meaning to break something in by kicking. Informal.
examples: John kicked five dollars in.
I’d be happy to kick in a dollar, but no more.

senses.definition: to start something; to start off an event.
examples: They kicked the picnic off with a footrace.
We kicked off the party by singing rowdy songs.
That was a great way to kick off a weekend.

senses.definition: to cause trouble or discomfort.
examples: The ignition in my car is kicking up again. I will have to have it looked into.
Aunt Jane’s arthritis is kicking up. She needs to see the doctor again.

senses.definition: to become a nuisance; to misbehave and disturb (someone).
senses.notes: Informal. Row rhymes with cow. Note the variation in the examples.
examples: The customer kicked up such a fuss about the food that the manager came to apologize.
I kicked up such a row that they kicked me out.
Oh, what pain! My arthritis is kicking up a storm.

senses.definition: to act frisky; to be lively and have fun.
examples: I like to go to an old-fashioned square dance and really kick up my heels.
For an old man, your uncle is really kicking up his heels.

senses.definition: to tease and joke with someone.
examples: I like to kid around with John. We are great friends.
Yes, John and I used to kid around a lot.

senses.definition: a very easy task.
examples: Climbing that hill is kid stuff.
Driving an automatic car is kid’s stuff.

senses.definition: to prepare an elaborate banquet (in someone’s honor).
senses.notes: From the biblical story recounting the return of the prodigal son. Fatted is older English for fattened.
examples: When Bob got back from college, his parents killed the fatted calf and threw a great party.
Sorry this meal isn’t much, John. We didn’t have time to kill the fatted calf.

senses.definition: to waste time.
examples: Stop killing time. Get to work!
We went over to the record shop just to kill time.

headword: kill two birds with one stone

senses.definition: to solve two problems with one solution.
examples: John learned the words to his part in the play while peeling potatoes. He was killing two birds with one stone.
I have to cash a check and make a payment on my bank loan. I’ll kill two birds with one stone by doing them both in one trip to the bank.

senses.definition: killed immediately.
examples: The driver was killed outright in the accident.
Twenty people were killed outright in the explosion.

senses.definition: a variety of something that is fairly close to the real thing, even though it is not exactly the real thing.
examples: I used a folded newspaper as a kind of hat to keep the rain off.
Bill is serving as a kind of helper or assistant on this project.

senses.definition: a twisted place or a cramp in the neck that causes pain.
examples: I got a kink in my neck from sleeping in a draft.
When I read on the plane, I get a kink in my neck.

senses.definition: to forgive (someone) and be friends again.
examples: They were very angry, but in the end they kissed and made up.
I’m sorry. Let’s kiss and make up.

senses.definition: to participate in something secret and private, and then tell other people about it.
examples: The project was supposed to be a secret between Jane and me, but she spread it all around. I didn’t think she was the type to kiss and tell.
I am willing to discuss it with you, but only if you promise not to kiss and tell.

senses.definition: an act that puts an end to someone or something.
examples: The mayor’s veto was the kiss of death for the new law.
Fainting on stage was the kiss of death for my acting career.

senses.definition: to anticipate or experience the loss of something.
examples: If you leave your camera on a park bench, you can kiss it good-bye.
You kissed your wallet good-bye when you left it in the store.

senses.definition: the entire amount; everyone; everything.
examples: Everybody in the family was there—the whole kit and caboodle.
The sheriff came and threw the crook out of town, kit and caboodle.

senses.definition: friends and relatives; people known to someone.
senses.notes: Older English. Kith means “acquaintances or neighbors” here.
examples: I was delighted to find all my kith and kin waiting for me at the airport to welcome me home.
I sent cards to my kith and kin, telling them of my arrival.

senses.definition: not very tall; short and small, as a child.
examples: Hello, Billy. I haven’t seen you since you were knee-high to a grasshopper.
I have two grandchildren, both knee-high to a grasshopper.

senses.definition: aware in advance that something was to happen.
examples: I shouldn’t act surprised. I knew it was coming.
It’s his own fault. He should have known it was coming.

senses.definition: to wrinkle one’s brow, especially by frowning.
examples: The woman knit her brow and asked us what we wanted from her.
While he read his book, John knit his brow occasionally. He must not have agreed with what he was reading.

senses.definition: to travel around; to act as a vagabond.
examples: I’d like to take off a year and knock about Europe.
If you’re going to knock about, you should do it when you’re young.

senses.definition: a serious fight; a serious argument.
examples: Boy, they really had a knock-down-drag-out fight.
Stop calling each other names, or you’re going to end up with a real knock-down-drag-out fight.

senses.definition: to stop something; to cease something.
examples: Shut up, you guys. Knock it off!
Knock it off. I’ve heard enough of your music.

senses.definition: to quit work (for the day).
examples: It’s time to knock off work.
It’s too early to knock off work.

senses.definition: to go to a great deal of trouble to do something.
senses.notes: Informal. As if one had worked oneself into unconsciousness.
examples: I knocked myself out to prepare this meal for you, and you won’t even taste it!
I don’t know why I knock myself out to do these things for you. You are not at all appreciative.

senses.definition: a phrase said to cancel out imaginary bad luck.
senses.notes: The same as the British English “touch wood.”
examples: My stereo has never given me any trouble— knock on wood.
We plan to be in Florida by tomorrow evening—knock on wood.

senses.definition: to scold some people; to get some people to do what they are supposed to be doing.
examples: If you kids don’t quiet down and go to sleep, I’m going to come in your room and knock some heads together.
The government is in a mess. We need to go to Washington and knock some heads together.

senses.definition: to put on a stunning performance or display for someone.
senses.notes: Informal. Someone is often replaced by’em from them.
examples: This band is going to do great tonight. We’re going to knock them dead.
“See how your sister is all dressed up!” said Bill. “She’s going to knock’em dead.”

senses.definition: to mistreat someone or something physically.
examples: They knocked my baggage around on the flight to Mexico.
The tough guys knocked me around a little.
They knocked my brother about a bit also.

headword: knock someone over with a feather

senses.definition: to leave someone stunned or surprised by something extraordinary.
examples: I was so surprised you could have knocked me over with a feather.
When she heard the news, you could have knocked her over with a feather.

senses.definition: to strike someone hard, especially in the head.
senses.notes: Slang. The block is the head.
examples: If you touch me again, I’ll knock your block off.
John punched Bob so hard that he almost knocked his block off.

senses.definition: to drink down a drink of something, especially something alcoholic.
examples: I don’t see how he can knock that stuff down.
John knocked back two beers in ten minutes.

senses.definition: to finish something, especially in haste or carelessly.
examples: I knocked it off with the help of Bob.
I knocked off the last chapter of my book in four hours.

headword: knock the props out from under someone

senses.definition: to destroy someone’s emotional, financial, or moral underpinnings; to destroy someone’s confidence.
examples: When you told Sally that she was due to be fired, you really knocked the props out from under her.
I don’t want to knock the props out from under you, but the bank is foreclosing on your mortgage.

headword: know (all) the tricks of the trade

senses.definition: to possess the skills and knowledge necessary to do something.
examples: Tom can repair car engines. He knows the tricks of the trade.
If I knew all the tricks of the trade, I could be a better plumber.

headword: know a thing or two (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to be well informed about someone or something; to know something unpleasant about someone or something.
examples: I know a thing or two about cars.
I know a thing or two about Mary that would really shock you.

senses.definition: to know some special way of dealing with a problem.
examples: I think I can handle all of this with no trouble. I know a trick or two.
I may be a senior citizen, but I still know a trick or two. I think I can help you with this.

senses.definition: to be wise enough, experienced enough, or well trained enough not to have done something wrong.
examples: Mary should have known better than to accept a lift from a stranger.
Children should know better than to play in the road.

senses.definition: knowledge and skill.
examples: Peter doesn’t have the know-how to mend that car.
Mary hasn’t the know-how to work the computer.

senses.definition: to know the alphabet; to know the most basic things (about something).
examples: Bill can’t do it. He doesn’t even know his ABCs.
You can’t expect to a write letter when you don’t even know your ABCs.

senses.definition: to know the behavior appropriate to one’s position or status in life.
senses.notes: See also put one in one’s place.
examples: I know my place. I won’t speak unless spoken to.
People around here are expected to know their place. You have to follow all the rules.

senses.definition: to know what one is expected to know; to know what is needed.
senses.notes: Informal or slang. See also know the score.
examples: I know my stuff. I can do my job.
She can’t handle the assignment. She doesn’t know her onions.

senses.definition: to know the techniques of getting something done, especially in a bureaucracy.
examples: Sally can get the job done. She knows her way around.
Since Sally worked at city hall for a year, she really knows her way about.

senses.definition: to know the name and recognize the face of someone.
examples: I’ve never met the man, but I know him by sight.
BOB: Have you ever met Mary? JANE: No, but I know her by sight.

headword: know someone or something like the palm of one’s hand
altForms: know someone or something like the back of one’s hand
know someone or something like a book

senses.definition: to know someone or something very well.
examples: Of course I know John. I know him like the back of my hand.
I know him like a book.

senses.definition: to know something very well; to know a passage of language so well that one could recite it backwards as well as forwards.
examples: Of course I’ve memorized my speech. I know it backwards and forwards.
Todd knows the skeletal structure of the frog backwards and forwards.

senses.definition: to know something perfectly; to have memorized something perfectly.
examples: I know my speech by heart.
I went over and over it until I knew it by heart.

senses.definition: to have memorized something so that one does not have to consult a written version; to know something well from seeing it very often.
senses.notes: Almost the same as know something by heart.
examples: Mary didn’t need the script because she knew the play from memory.
The conductor went through the entire concert without music. He knew it from memory.

senses.definition: to know something thoroughly; to know about something thoroughly.
examples: I know my geometry inside out.
I studied and studied for my driver’s test until I knew the rules inside out.

senses.definition: to know something very well; to know something from unpleasant experience.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples below.
examples: I know the problem only too well.
I know only too well the kind of problem you must face.

senses.definition: to know how to do something.
senses.notes: Informal. See also learn the ropes.
examples: I can’t do the job because I don’t know the ropes.
Ask Sally to do it. She knows the ropes.

senses.definition: to know the facts; to know the facts about life and its difficulties.
examples: Bob is so naive. He sure doesn’t know the score.
I know what you’re trying to do. Oh, yes, I know what’s what.

headword: know when one is not wanted

senses.definition: to sense when one presence is not welcome; to know when one is not among friends.
senses.notes: Usually said when someone feels hurt by being ignored by people.
examples: I’m leaving this place! I know when I’m not wanted!
She doesn’t know when she’s not wanted. Can’t she tell she’s out of place?

headword: know where all the bodies are buried

senses.definition: to know all the secrets and intrigue; to know all the important details.
examples: He is a good choice for president because he knows where all the bodies are buried.
Since he knows where all the bodies are buried, he is the only one who can advise us.

senses.definition: to know well the subject that one is speaking about.
examples: You are wrong! You do not know whereof you speak.
He simply doesn’t know whereof he speaks.

headword: know where someone stands (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to know what someone thinks or feels about someone or something.
examples: I don’t know where John stands on this issue.
I don’t even know where I stand.

senses.definition: to be able to distinguish one person or thing from another person or thing.
examples: I have an old one and a new one, but I don’t know which is which.
I know that Bill and Bob are twins, but I can’t tell which is which.

headword: know which side one’s bread is buttered on

senses.definition: to know what is most advantageous for one.
examples: He’ll do it if his boss tells him to. He knows which side his bread is buttered on.
Since John knows which side his bread is buttered on, he’ll be there on time.

senses.definition: something that is generally recognized as a fact.
examples: That grass is green is a known fact.
It is a known fact that John was in Chicago on the night of the murder.

senses.definition: someone whose character, personality, and behavior are recognized and understood.
examples: We need not worry about how John will behave. He is a known quantity.
Lisa is a known quantity and I am sure she will not surprise us by voting with the opposition.

senses.definition: to get busy doing something; to get serious about one’s work.
examples: It’s time you knuckled down to your studies.
Sue must knuckle down if she wants to be successful at the office.
