senses.definition: to submit to someone or something; to yield or give in to someone or something.
examples: You have to knuckle under to your boss if you expect to keep your job.
I’m too stubborn to knuckle under.

senses.definition: a task that is either unpaid or badly paid and that one does simply for one’s own satisfaction or pleasure or to please someone whom one likes or loves.
examples: Jane made no money out of the biography she wrote. She was writing about the life of a friend and the book was a labor of love.
Mary hates knitting, but she made a sweater for her boyfriend. What a labor of love.

senses.definition: to attack, devour, or scold someone or something.
examples: We laced into a big meal of pork and beans.
The bully punched John once, and then John really laced into him.
John lit into him with both fists.
My father really lit into me when I came in late. He yelled at me for ten minutes.

senses.definition: relaxed and unperplexed by difficulties.
examples: John is so laid-back. Nothing seems to disturb him.
I wish I could be more laid-back. I get so tense.

senses.definition: immobilized for recuperation or repairs.
examples: I was laid up for two weeks after my accident.
My car is laid up for repairs.
I was laid up with the flu for a week.
Todd was laid up for a month.

senses.definition: sleep.
senses.notes: Humorous. Borrowed from the Bible, Gen. 4:16. From the fact that people sometimes nod when they are falling asleep.
examples: The baby is in the land of Nod.
Look at the clock! It’s time we were all in the land of Nod.

senses.definition: to recover satisfactorily from a trying situation or a setback.
senses.notes: Also literal. As if having fallen. Informal.
examples: Her first year was terrible, but she landed on both feet.
It’s going to be a hard day. I only hope I land on my feet.

senses.definition: to finish somehow or somewhere; to come to be in a certain state or place at the end.
senses.notes: Usually in the wrong place or in a bad situation. See also end up somewhere.
examples: We set out for Denver but landed up in Salt Lake City.
He’s so extravagant that he landed up in debt.

senses.definition: a victory by a large margin; a very substantial victory, particularly in an election.
examples: The mayor won a landslide victory in the election.
The younger man won a landslide victory in the presidential election.

senses.definition: to believe something, especially something untrue.
examples: Did she believe it? She just lapped it up.
I can’t imagine why she lapped up that ridiculous story.

senses.definition: to go into a coma.
examples: The survivor of the crash lapsed into a coma.
Aunt Mary lapsed into a coma and died.

senses.definition: last in sequence, but not last in importance.
senses.notes: A cliché. Often said when introducing people.
examples: The speaker said, “And now, last but not least, I’d like to present Bill Smith, who will give us some final words.”
And last but not least, here is the loser of the race.

senses.definition: a final effort; the last possible attempt.
examples: I made one last-ditch effort to get her to stay.
It was a last-ditch effort. I didn’t expect it to work.

senses.definition: the most unlikely person of whom one could think in a particular situation; the most unlikely person to do something.
senses.notes: Also literal. Preceded by be, become, or seem like.
examples: Bob seems like the last person for Tom to insult. He’s so hot-tempered.
Mary was the last person to ask to chair the meeting—she’s so shy.

senses.definition: when one is old.
examples: She injured her hip running. She’s exercising rather late in life.
Isn’t it sort of late in life to buy a house?

senses.definition: far along in a project or activity; too late in a project or activity for action, decisions, etc., to be taken.
examples: It was a bit late in the day for him to apologize.
It’s late in the day to try to change the plans.

headword: laugh all the way to the bank

senses.definition: to be very happy about money that has been earned by doing something that other people might think is unfair.
examples: He may not be in the nicest business, but he is doing well and can laugh all the way to the bank.
She makes tons of money doing what no one else will do and laughs all the way to the bank.

headword: laugh out of the other side of one’s mouth

senses.definition: to change sharply from happiness to sadness.
examples: Now that you know the truth, you’ll laugh out of the other side of your mouth.
He was so proud that he won the election. He’s laughing out of the other side of his mouth since they recounted the ballots and found out that he lost.

senses.definition: to dismiss something as ridiculous.
examples: The committee laughed the suggestion out of court.
Bob’s request for a large salary increase was laughed out of court.

senses.definition: to laugh secretly; to laugh quietly to oneself.
examples: Jane looked very serious, but I knew she was laughing up her sleeve.
I told Sally that her dress was darling, but I was laughing up my sleeve because it was too small.

senses.definition: one who makes one’s own laws or rules; one who sets one’s own standards of behavior.
examples: You can’t get Bill to follow the rules. He’s a law unto himself.
Jane is a law unto herself. She’s totally unwilling to cooperate.

headword: lay a finger on someone or something

senses.definition: to touch someone or something, even slightly.
senses.notes: Usually in the negative. Compare this with put one’s finger on something.
examples: Don’t you dare lay a finger on my pencil. Go get your own!
If you lay a finger on me, I’ll scream.

senses.definition: to give a bad performance.
senses.notes: [for someone] Literal with birds and most reptiles. Informal.
examples: The cast of the play really laid an egg last night.
I hope I don’t lay an egg when it’s my turn to sing.

headword: lay down one’s life (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to sacrifice one’s life for someone or something.
examples: Would you lay down your life for your country?
There aren’t many things for which I’d lay down my life.

senses.definition: to state firmly what the rules are (for something).
examples: Before the meeting, the boss laid down the law. We all knew exactly what to do.
The way she laid down the law means that I’ll remember her rules.

senses.definition: to scold someone for misbehaving.
examples: When the teacher caught us, he really laid down the law.
Poor Bob. He really got it when his mother laid down the law.

headword: lay hold of someone or something

senses.definition: to grasp someone or something with the hands.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with get one’s hands on someone or something; get (a)hold of someone or something.
examples: Just wait till I lay hold of Bill!
I can’t wait to lay hold of that fishing pole. I’m ready to catch a huge fish.

senses.definition: to attack, consume, or scold someone or something.
examples: Bob laid into the big plate of fried chicken.
The bear laid into the hunter.
My father really laid into me when I got home.

altForms: lay it on with a trowel

senses.definition: to exaggerate praise, excuses, or blame.
examples: Sally was laying it on thick when she said that Tom was the best singer she had ever heard.
After Bob finished making his excuses, Sally said that he was pouring it on thick.
Bob always spreads it on thick.

senses.definition: to leave someone or something alone; to stop bothering someone or something; to take it easy (on someone or something).
senses.notes: Slang. See also lay someone off.
examples: Lay off Bill. He didn’t mean any harm!
Hey! I said lay off!
Lay off the butter. Don’t use it all up.

senses.definition: the arrangement of features on an area of land.
examples: The surveyor mapped the lay of the land.
The geologist studied the lay of the land, trying to determine if there was oil below.

senses.definition: the arrangement or organization of something other than land.
examples: As soon as I get the lay of the land in my new job, things will go better.
The company’s corporate structure was complex, so understanding the lay of the land took time.

senses.definition: to pause somewhere during one’s journey.
examples: I had to lay over in San Antonio for a few hours before my plane left.
I want a bus that goes straight through. I don’t want to lay over.

senses.definition: to bury someone.
examples: They laid my uncle away last week.
They laid him away with a quiet ceremony.

senses.definition: to put an employee out of work, possibly temporarily.
examples: They even laid the president off.
The computer factory laid off two thousand workers.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be ill in bed.
examples: A broken leg laid me up for two months.
Flu laid up everyone at work for a week or more.

senses.definition: to get something and store it for future use.
examples: They laid a lot of food in for the holidays.
We always lay in a large supply of firewood each November.

senses.definition: to direct blame, guilt, or verbal abuse at someone.
senses.notes: Also literal. Slang. See also put the blame on someone or something.
examples: Don’t lay that stuff on me! It’s not my fault.
The boss is in the conference room laying a lot of anger on the sales staff.

senses.definition: to destroy an area (literally or figuratively).
examples: The invaders laid the village to waste.
The kids came in and laid waste to my clean house.

senses.definition: to lead a miserable life.
examples: Poor Jane really leads a dog’s life.
I’ve been working so hard. I’m tired of living a dog’s life.

senses.definition: to begin; to start (assuming that others will follow).
examples: We were waiting for someone to start dancing. Finally, Bob and Jane led off.
The hunter led off, and the dogs followed.
The first baseman will lead off as the first batter in the baseball game.

senses.definition: to force someone to go somewhere (with you); to lead someone by coercion.
examples: John had to lead Tom by the nose to get him to the opera.
I’ll go, but you’ll have to lead me by the nose.

headword: lead someone down the garden path

senses.definition: to deceive someone.
examples: Now, be honest with me. Don’t lead me down the garden path.
That cheater really led her down the garden path.

headword: lead someone on a merry chase

senses.definition: to lead someone in a purposeless pursuit.
examples: What a waste of time. You really led me on a merry chase.
Jane led Bill on a merry chase trying to find an antique lamp.

senses.definition: to cause someone to do something.
examples: This agent led me to purchase a worthless piece of land.
My illness led me to quit my job.

senses.definition: to live in luxury.
senses.notes: Informal. No one knows who Riley is.
examples: If I had a million dollars, I could live the life of Riley.
The treasurer took our money to Mexico, where he lived the life of Riley until the police caught him.

senses.definition: to prepare the way for something.
examples: His compliments were his way of leading up to asking for money.
What were his actions leading up to?

senses.definition: a question that suggests the kind of answer that the person who asks it wants to hear.
examples: The mayor was angered by the reporter’s leading questions.
“Don’t you think that the police are failing to stop crime?” is an example of a leading question.

senses.definition: to disclose special information to the press so that the resulting publicity will accomplish something.
senses.notes: Also literal. Usually said of government disclosures. Also used for accidental disclosures.
examples: Don’t leak that information out.
I don’t want to be the one to leak it.
They let it get out on purpose.

senses.definition: to try to make someone do something; to coerce someone to do something.
examples: If she refuses to do it, lean on her a bit.
Don’t lean on me! I don’t have to do it if I don’t want to.

senses.definition: to tend toward doing something; to favor doing something.
examples: The union is leaning toward accepting the proposal.
My friends leaned toward swimming instead of shopping.

senses.definition: to learn something so well that it can be written or recited without thinking; to memorize something.
examples: The director told me to learn my speech by heart.
I had to go over it many times before I learned it by heart.

senses.definition: to learn something by memorizing without giving any thought to what is being learned.
examples: I learned history by rote; then I couldn’t pass the test that required me to think.
If you learn things by rote, you’ll never understand them.

headword: learn something from the bottom up

senses.definition: to learn something thoroughly, from the very beginning; to learn all aspects of something, even the least important ones.
examples: I learned my business from the bottom up.
I started out sweeping the floors and learned everything from the bottom up.

senses.definition: to learn something by experience, especially by an unpleasant experience.
examples: She learned how to make investments the hard way.
I wish I didn’t have to learn things the hard way.
I found out the hard way that it’s difficult to work and go to school at the same time.
Investing in real estate is tricky. I found that out the hard way.

senses.definition: to learn how to do something; to learn how to work something.
senses.notes: Informal. See also know the ropes; show someone the ropes.
examples: I’ll be able to do my job very well as soon as I learn the ropes.
John is very slow to learn the ropes.

senses.definition: to learn to adapt to something unpleasant or painful.
senses.notes: See also have to live with something.
examples: Finally the doctor told Marion that she was going to have to learn to live with her arthritis.
The floor plan of the house we bought is not as handy as we had thought, but we will learn to live with it.

senses.definition: least; of smallest importance.
examples: There were many things wrong with the new house. Least of all, the water faucets leaked.
What a bad day. Many things went wrong, but least of all, I tore my shirt.

headword: leave a bad taste in someone’s mouth

senses.definition: to leave a bad feeling or memory with someone.
senses.notes: [for someone or something] Also literal. Informal.
examples: The whole business about the missing money left a bad taste in his mouth.
It was a very nice party, but something about it left a bad taste in my mouth.
I’m sorry that Bill was there. He always leaves a bad taste in my mouth.

headword: leave a lot to be desired

senses.definition: to be lacking something important; to be inadequate.
senses.notes: A polite way of saying that something is bad.
examples: This report leaves a lot to be desired.
I’m sorry to have to fire you, Mary, but your work leaves a lot to be desired.

senses.definition: to search in all possible places.
senses.notes: Refers to finding something under a rock.
examples: Don’t worry. We’ll find your stolen car. We’ll leave no stone unturned.
In searching for a nice place to live, we left no stone unturned.

headword: leave oneself wide open for something
altForms: leave oneself wide open to something

senses.definition: to invite criticism or joking about oneself; to fail to protect oneself from criticism or ridicule.
examples: Yes, that was a harsh remark, Jane, but you left yourself wide open to it.
I can’t complain about your joke. I left myself wide open for it.

senses.definition: to affect the behavior and performance of another person.
examples: The wise professor left her mark on her students.
My father left his mark on me, and I will always remember all his good advice.

senses.definition: to abandon someone to whatever may happen—possibly death or some other unpleasant event.
examples: We couldn’t rescue the miners, and we were forced to leave them to their fate.
Please don’t try to help. Just go away and leave me to my fate.

senses.definition: to fail to entertain or stimulate someone.
examples: Your joke left me flat.
We listened carefully to his lecture, but it left us flat.

senses.definition: to leave someone without any money—flat broke.
examples: Paying all my bills left me flat.
The robber took all my money and left me flat.

senses.definition: to leave someone completely alone.
examples: I was at the dance with Harry, but when he met Alice, he left me flat.
They just walked off and left us flat.

senses.definition: to abandon someone as being dead.
senses.notes: The abandoned person may actually be alive.
examples: He looked so bad that they almost left him for dead.
As the soldiers turned—leaving the enemy captain for dead—the captain fired at them.

senses.definition: to leave someone unsupported and unable to maneuver; to leave someone helpless.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also high and dry.
examples: All my workers quit and left me high and dry.
All the children ran away and left Billy high and dry to take the blame for the broken window.

senses.definition: to leave someone flat broke.
examples: Mrs. Franklin took all the money out of the bank and left Mr. Franklin high and dry.
Paying the bills always leaves me high and dry.

senses.definition: to leave someone to take all the blame; to leave someone appearing guilty.
examples: They all ran off and left me holding the bag. It wasn’t even my fault.
It was the mayor’s fault, but he wasn’t left holding the bag.

senses.definition: to stop bothering someone; to go away and leave someone alone.
senses.notes: Does not necessarily mean to go away from a person.
examples: Please go—leave me in peace.
Can’t you see that you’re upsetting her? Leave her in peace.

senses.definition: to leave someone waiting for or anticipating your actions.
examples: Where were you, John? You really left me in the lurch.
I didn’t mean to leave you in the lurch. I thought we had canceled our meeting.

headword: leave someone or something hanging in midair
altForms: keep someone or something hanging in midair

senses.definition: to suspend dealing with someone or something; to leave someone or something waiting to be finished or continued.
examples: She left her sentence hanging in midair.
She left us hanging in midair when she paused.
Tell me the rest of the story. Don’t leave me hanging in midair.
Don’t leave the story hanging in midair.

headword: leave someone or something in one’s hands

senses.definition: to give one control of or responsibility for someone or something.
examples: You left the whole project in my hands!
I have to leave the care of baby in your hands while I go to the doctor.

headword: leave someone out in the cold

senses.definition: to fail to inform someone; to exclude someone.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Compare this with the previous entry.
examples: I don’t know what’s going on. They left me out in the cold.
Tom wasn’t invited. They left him out in the cold.

senses.definition: to leave a date or time unscheduled.
examples: I left something open on Friday, just in case we want to leave work early.
Please leave an appointment open for Mrs. Wallace next week. She will be calling in to our office for an appointment.

senses.definition: to leave a message with someone (who will pass the message on to someone else).
examples: If you decide to go to the convention, please leave word with my secretary.
Leave word before you go.
I left word with your brother. Didn’t he give you the message?

senses.definition: to listen to someone.
examples: Lend an ear to John. Hear what he has to say.
I’d be delighted to lend an ear. I find great wisdom in everything John has to say.

senses.definition: to provide an interesting accompaniment for something.
examples: Your clever comments lent a great deal of color to the slide show of your vacation.
The excellent master of ceremonies will lend color to an otherwise dry and uninteresting dance recital.

headword: lend oneself or itself to something

senses.definition: to be adaptable to something; [for someone or something] to be useful for something.
examples: This room doesn’t lend itself to bright colors.
John doesn’t lend himself to casual conversation.

senses.definition: to give someone some help, not necessarily with the hands.
examples: Could you lend me a hand with this piano? I need to move it across the room.
Could you lend a hand with this math assignment?
I’d be happy to lend a hand.

senses.definition: displeased.
examples: We were less than pleased to learn of your comments.
Bill was less than pleased at the outcome of the election.

senses.definition: the smaller one (of two); the one having the least amount.
examples: The last two pieces of pie were not quite the same size, and I chose the lesser of the two.
Faced with a basket containing too much and one with too little, Tom chose the lesser.

senses.definition: the less bad thing, of a pair of bad things.
examples: I didn’t like either politician, so I voted for the lesser of two evils.
Given the options of going out with someone I don’t like and staying home and watching a boring television program, I chose the lesser of the two evils and watched television.

senses.definition: not to mention or think of someone or something; not even to take someone or something into account.
examples: Do I have a dollar? I don’t even have a dime, let alone a dollar.
I didn’t invite John, let alone the rest of his family.

senses.definition: One should forget the problems of the past.
examples: Okay, Sally, let bygones be bygones. Let’s forgive and forget.
Jane was unwilling to let bygones be bygones. She still won’t speak to me.

headword: let go of someone or something

senses.definition: to release someone or something.
examples: Please let go of me!
Don’t let go of the steering wheel.

senses.definition: to shout something out or expel something; to shout or express something wildly.
examples: The audience cut loose with a loud cheer.
The whole team let go with a loud shout.
John let loose with a horrendous belch.
I wish you wouldn’t let loose like that!

headword: let grass grow under one’s feet

senses.definition: to do nothing; to stand still.
examples: Mary doesn’t let the grass grow under her feet. She’s always busy.
Bob is too lazy. He’s letting the grass grow under his feet.

senses.definition: to go ahead and start something; let something begin.
senses.notes: Informal or slang. Her is usually’er.
examples: When Bill was ready for John to start the engine, he said, “Okay, John, let’er rip.”
When Sally heard Bob say “Let’er rip,” she let the anchor go to the bottom of the lake.
Let’s go, Bill. Let it roll!

senses.definition: to tell or reveal everything and hold back nothing (because one is relaxed or carefree).
examples: Sally has no secrets. She lets it all hang out all the time.
Relax, John. Let it all hang out.

senses.definition: Forget it.; Stop worrying about it.
examples: Don’t get so angry about it. Let it go.
Let it go. Stop fretting.

senses.definition: to release excess energy or anger.
senses.notes: [for someone] Also literal in the case of steam engines. Informal.
examples: Whenever John gets a little angry, he blows off steam.
Don’t worry about John. He’s just letting off steam.

senses.definition: to become less constrained; to get excited and have a good time.
examples: I love to dance and just let myself go.
Let yourself go, John. Learn to enjoy life.

senses.definition: to be emotional, especially where it is not appropriate.
examples: I’m sorry for the outburst. I didn’t mean to let my emotions show.
Please stop crying. You mustn’t let your emotions show.

senses.definition: to become more intimate and begin to speak frankly.
examples: Come on, Jane, let your hair down and tell me all about it.
I have a problem. Do you mind if I let down my hair?

headword: let out some kind of sound

senses.definition: to make some kind of a noise or sound.
examples: Be quiet. Don’t let out a sound!
Suddenly, Jane let out a shriek.

senses.definition: One should not search for trouble and one should leave well enough alone.
examples: Don’t mention that problem with Tom again. It’s almost forgotten. Let sleeping dogs lie.
You’ll never be able to reform Bill. Leave him alone. Let sleeping dogs lie.

senses.definition: to disappoint someone; to fail someone.
examples: I’m sorry I let you down. Something came up, and I couldn’t meet you.
I don’t want to let you down, but I can’t support you in the election.

senses.definition: to dismiss someone from employment; to fire someone.
examples: John was not working out as well as we had hoped, and we had to let him go.
They let a number of the older workers go and were faced with an age discrimination suit.

headword: let someone have it (with both barrels)

senses.definition: to strike someone or attack someone verbally.
senses.notes: Refers to firing a shotgun. Informal. With both barrels intensifies the phrase. Refers to the firing a doublebarreled shotgun.
examples: I really let Tom have it with both barrels. I told him he had better not do that again if he knows what’s good for him.
Bob let John have it—with both barrels.

senses.definition: to tell someone the secret.
senses.notes: Informal. The something can be a plan, arrangements, scheme, trick, or anything else that might be kept a secret.
examples: Should we let John in on the secret?
Please let me in on the plan.

senses.definition: to tell someone something; to inform someone of something.
examples: Please let me know about it soon.
Will you be coming to the picnic? Please let me know.

senses.definition: to release someone from a responsibility.
examples: Please let me off the hook for Saturday. I have other plans.
Okay, I’ll let you off.

senses.definition: to release or dismiss someone without punishment.
senses.notes: [with someone] See also get off easy.
examples: The judge didn’t let me off.
The judge let off Mary with a warning.

senses.definition: to permit someone to disembark or leave a means of transportation.
examples: The driver let Mary off the bus.
“I can’t let you off at this corner,” said the driver.

senses.definition: to release something; to give something off.
examples: The engine was letting off some kind of smoke.
The flower let off a wonderful smell.

senses.definition: to let something go unnoticed or unchallenged.
examples: Bob let Bill’s insult pass because he didn’t want to argue.
Don’t worry, I’ll let this little incident pass.

senses.definition: to allow something to continue or remain as it is.
examples: It isn’t the best plan, but we’ll let it ride.
I disagree with you, but I’ll let it ride.

senses.definition: to neglect something.
examples: John let his lessons slide.
Jane doesn’t let her work slide.

senses.definition: to forget or miss an important time or date.
examples: I’m sorry I just let your birthday slip by.
I let it slide by accidentally.

senses.definition: to waste a period of time.
examples: You wasted the whole day by letting it slip by.
We were having fun, and we let the time slide by.

senses.definition: to tell a secret by accident.
examples: I didn’t let it slip out on purpose. It was an accident.
John let the plans slip when he was talking to Bill.

senses.definition: The person who buys something should investigate the goods or property thoroughly for damage or suitability.
examples: Be careful when buying things from street vendors. Let the buyer beware.
It’s the purchaser’s job to make sure the goods are ok. Let the buyer beware.

headword: let the cat out of the bag

senses.definition: to reveal a secret or a surprise by accident.
examples: When Bill glanced at the door, he let the cat out of the bag. We knew then that he was expecting someone to arrive.
We are planning a surprise party for Jane. Don’t let the cat out of the bag.
It’s a secret. Try not to spill the beans.

senses.definition: to lose the opportunity (to do something).
examples: When I was younger, I wanted to become a doctor, but I let the chance slip by.
Don’t let the chance slip by. Do it now!

senses.definition: to ignore the things that one is supposed to do; to fall behind in the doing of one’s work.
examples: I am afraid that I have let things slide while I was recovering from my operation.
If I let things slide for even one day, I get hopelessly behind in my work.

senses.definition: to take the pressure off someone or something; to take it easy (on someone or something).
examples: Please let up on me. I can’t work any faster, and you’re making me nervous.
Let up on the project. You’re working too hard.
Yes, I guess I had better let up.

senses.definition: we will do something [together].
senses.notes: A gentle command. More formal than let’s.
examples: Let us go in peace.
Let us bow our heads in prayer.

senses.definition: to leave things as they are (and not try to improve them).
examples: There isn’t much more you can accomplish here. Why don’t you just let well enough alone?
This is as good as I can do. I’ll stop and leave well enough alone.

senses.definition: Let’s have lunch together sometime.
examples: Some time next week, let’s do lunch.
Can’t talk to you now. Let’s do lunch sometime.

senses.definition: to aim a remark at someone; to direct something at someone.
examples: John leveled a sarcastic comment at his teacher.
The editorial leveled its remarks at the mayor.

senses.definition: to be honest with someone.
examples: Come on, Bill. Level with me. Did you do it?
I’m leveling with you. I wasn’t even in town. I couldn’t have done it.

senses.definition: permission, right, or justification to do something.
examples: You have no license to behave in that manner!
Who granted you license to enter my house without knocking?

senses.definition: a bit of work.
examples: I couldn’t get her to do a lick of work all day long!
The boys didn’t do a lick of work while you were away.

senses.definition: to show one’s eagerness to do something, especially to eat something.
senses.notes: Refers to the licking of one’s lips in expectation of eating. Some animals, but not people, really do lick their chops.
examples: We could tell from the way the boys were licking their chops that they really wanted a turn at riding the motorcycle.
Fred started licking his chops when he smelled the turkey roasting in the oven.

senses.definition: to show eagerness or pleasure about a future event.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. From the habit of people licking their lips when they are about to enjoy eating something.
examples: The children licked their lips at the sight of the cake.
The author’s readers were licking their lips in anticipation of her new novel.
The journalist was licking his lips when he went off to interview the disgraced politician.

senses.definition: to put something into good condition.
examples: I have to lick this report into shape this morning.
Let’s all lend a hand and whip this house into shape. It’s a mess.

senses.definition: to do one’s job poorly or not at all.
senses.notes: Lay is a common error for lie.
examples: Tom was fired because he was laying down on the job.
You mean he was lying down on the job, don’t you?
Sorry, I was lying down on the job in English class.

senses.definition: to remain unused.
examples: Each year we let a different section of our farmland lie fallow.
The land that is lying fallow this year will be cultivated next year.

senses.definition: to remain unused and neglected.
examples: You should not let your talent lie fallow. Practice the piano before you forget how to play it.
His writing had lain fallow for so long that he could hardly write a proper sentence.

senses.definition: to be on display in a public place.
examples: The dead leader lay in state for three days in the country’s main city.
While the king lay in state, many people walked by and paid their respects.

senses.definition: to keep quiet and not be noticed; to avoid being conspicuous.
senses.notes: Informal. Lay is a common error for lie.
examples: I suggest you lie low for a few days.
The robber said that he would lay low for a short time after the robbery.

senses.definition: to lie boldly.
examples: I knew she was lying through her teeth, but I didn’t want to say so just then.
I’m not lying through my teeth! I never do!

senses.definition: life is short and there is no point in wasting it on things like worry, hatred, vengeance, etc.
examples: I am not going to spend any more time trying to get even with Wally. Life’s too short.
It’s a waste of time worrying about money. Life is too short for that.

senses.definition: the type of person who is lively and helps make a party fun and exciting.
examples: Bill is always the life of the party. Be sure to invite him.
Bob isn’t exactly the life of the party, but he’s polite.

senses.definition: I am grateful that I am doing well in life.
examples: I can’t complain. Life’s been good to me.
I doing fine. Life’s been good.

headword: lift a hand (against someone or something)
altForms: raise a hand (against someone or something)

senses.definition: to threaten (to strike) someone or something.
senses.notes: Often in the negative. The a hand can be replaced with one’s hand.
examples: She’s very peaceful. She wouldn’t lift a hand against a fly.
That’s right. She wouldn’t lift a hand.
Would you raise your hand against your own brother?

senses.definition: to depart in haste for somewhere.
examples: The bus pulled away and lit out for the next stop.
It’s time I lit out for home.
I should have lit out ten minutes ago.

senses.definition: to depart somewhere in haste.
examples: It’s time I lit out of here. I’m late for my next appointment.
Look at that horse go. He really lit out of the starting gate.

headword: Lightning never strikes twice (in the same place).

senses.definition: It is extremely unlikely that the same misfortune will occur again in the same set of circumstances or to the same people.
examples: Ever since the fire, Jean has been afraid that her house will catch fire again, but they say that lightning never strikes twice.
Supposedly lightning never strikes twice, but the Smiths’ house has been robbed twice this year.

headword: like a bat out of hell

senses.definition: with great speed and force.
examples: Did you see her leave? She left like a bat out of hell.
The car sped down the street like a bat out of hell.

headword: like a bolt out of the blue

senses.definition: suddenly and without warning.
senses.notes: Refers to a bolt of lightning coming out of a clear blue sky. See also out of a clear blue sky.
examples: The news came to us like a bolt out of the blue.
Like a bolt out of the blue, the boss came and fired us all.

headword: like a bump on a log

senses.definition: unresponsive; immobile.
examples: I spoke to him, but he just sat there like a bump on a log.
Don’t stand there like a bump on a log. Give me a hand!

headword: like a fish out of water

senses.definition: appearing to be completely out of place; in a very awkward manner.
examples: Vincent stood there in his rented tuxedo, looking like a fish out of water.
Whenever I am with your friends, I feel like a fish out of water. What on earth do you see in them—or me?
At a formal dance, John is like a fish out of water.

senses.definition: rapidly and with force.
examples: The truck came roaring down the road like a house on fire.
The crowd burst through the gate like a house afire.

senses.definition: like someone or something that is easy to understand.
examples: Jane’s an open book. I always know what she is going to do next.
The committee’s intentions are an open book. They want to save money.

senses.definition: unguarded; unsuspecting and unaware.
senses.notes: The second phrase is the plural form. See also be a sitting duck.
examples: He was waiting there like a sitting duck—a perfect target for a mugger.
The soldiers were standing at the top of the hill like sitting ducks. It’s a wonder they weren’t all killed.

senses.definition: chaotic; exciting and busy.
examples: Our household is like a three-ring circus on Monday mornings.
This meeting is like a three-ring circus. Quiet down and listen!

senses.definition: furiously; very much, fast, many, or actively.
examples: People are coming in here like crazy. There isn’t enough room for them all.
We sold ice cream like crazy. It was a very hot day.
When she stubbed her toe, she started screaming like mad.

senses.definition: very fast.
senses.notes: Folksy. Informal. See also (as) quick as greased lightning.
examples: He left the room like greased lightning.
They fled the burning building like greased lightning.

senses.definition: either accept it or drop dead.
examples: I don’t care whether you care for my attitude or not. You can just like it or lump it.
This is all the food you get. Like it or lump it!

headword: Like it’s such a big deal!

senses.definition: It really isn’t all that important!
examples: So I dropped the glass. Like it’s such a big deal.
Like it’s such a big deal. Who cares?

senses.definition: quietly and without seeming to realize or complain about the likely difficulties or dangers of a situation.
examples: Young men fighting in World War I simply went like lambs to the slaughter.
Our team went on the football field like lambs to the slaughter to meet the league-leaders.

headword: like looking for a needle in a haystack

senses.definition: engaged in a hopeless search.
examples: Trying to find a white dog in the snow is like looking for a needle in a haystack.
I tried to find my lost contact lens on the beach, but it was like looking for a needle in a haystack.

senses.definition: very untidy or very unattractive.
examples: Joan arrived at the office looking like nothing on earth. She had fallen in the mud.
Alice was like nothing on earth in that electric yellow dress.

senses.definition: very unusual; otherworldly.
examples: The new car models look like nothing on earth this year.
This cake is so good! It’s like nothing on earth!

senses.definition: as if someone (or a pet) were a member of one’s family.
examples: We treat our dog like one of the family.
We are very happy to have you stay with us, Bill. I hope you don’t mind if we treat you like one of the family.

senses.definition: to enjoy one’s talking more than other people enjoy listening to it.
examples: I guess I don’t really have anything to say. I just like to hear myself talk, I guess.
There he goes again. He just likes to hear himself talk.

senses.definition: very close or intimate.
senses.notes: Compare this with as alike as (two) peas in a pod.
examples: Yes, they’re close. Like two peas in a pod.
They’re always together. Like peas in a pod.

headword: like water off a duck’s back

senses.definition: easily; without any apparent effect.
examples: Insults rolled off John like water off a duck’s back.
The bullets had no effect on the steel door. They fell away like water off a duck’s back.

senses.definition: someone; anyone like someone.
senses.notes: Informal. Almost always in a negative sense.
examples: I don’t like Bob. I wouldn’t do anything for the likes of him.
Nobody wants the likes of him around.

senses.definition: the course of action that will cause least trouble or effort.
senses.notes: Compare this with path of least resistance.
examples: Jane won’t stand up for her rights. She always takes the line of least resistance.
Joan never states her point of view. She takes the line of least resistance and agrees with everyone else.

senses.definition: to make money for oneself in a greedy or dishonest fashion.
examples: When it was discovered that the sales manager was lining her own pockets with commissions, she was fired.
If you line your pockets while in public office, you’ll get in serious trouble.

headword: line someone or something up with something

senses.definition: to position someone or something (or a group) in reference to other things.
senses.notes: See also fix someone up (with someone or something).
examples: Please line the chairs up with the floor tiles.
Line up this brick with the bricks below and at both sides. That’s the way you lay bricks.
Line up the boys with the row of trees.

senses.definition: to schedule someone for something; to arrange for someone to do or be something.
examples: I lined gardeners up for the summer work on the gardens.
I lined up four of my best friends to serve as ushers at my wedding.

senses.definition: the larger share of something.
examples: The elder boy always takes the lion’s share of the food.
Jim was supposed to divide the cake in two equal pieces but he took the lion’s share.

senses.definition: to yield to a reasonable argument; to take the reasonable course.
examples: Please listen to reason, and don’t do something you’ll regret.
She got into trouble because she wouldn’t listen to reason.

senses.definition: a question or experiment that seeks to determine the state of one important factor.
examples: His performance on the long exam served as a litmus test to determine whether he would go to college.
The amount of white cells in my blood became the litmus test for diagnosing my disease.

senses.definition: learned from a mysterious or secret source.
senses.notes: Often given as an evasive answer to someone who asks how you learned something. Rude in some circumstances.
examples: “All right,” said Mary, “where did you get that information?” John replied, “A little bird told me.”
A little bird told me where I might find you.

senses.definition: a small amount; some.
examples: Can I have a little bit of candy?
I need a little bit of time to finish this essay.

senses.definition: slowly, a bit at a time.
examples: Little by little, he began to understand what we were talking about.
The snail crossed the stone little by little.

headword: A little (hard) work never hurt anyone.
altForms: A little (hard) work never killed anyone.

senses.definition: One should expect to do hard or difficult work and not avoid doing it.
examples: Go help your father with the yard work. A little hard work never hurt anyone.
Go ahead. Bring me some more bricks. A little work never killed anyone.

headword: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing.

senses.definition: Incomplete knowledge can embarrass or harm someone or something.
examples: The doctor said, “Just because you’ve had a course in first aid, you shouldn’t have treated your own illness. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing.”
John thought he knew how to take care of the garden, but he killed all the flowers. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing.

senses.definition: to have a life of a certain quality or style.
examples: The movie star lived a life of luxury.
After Anne won the lottery, she lived the life of a queen.

senses.definition: to increase one’s knowledge by experience.
senses.notes: Also informal and folksy. Usually said when one is surprised to learn something.
examples: I didn’t know that snakes could swim. Well, live and learn!
John didn’t know he should water his houseplants a little extra in the dry winter months. When they all died, he said, “Live and learn.”

senses.definition: not to interfere with other people’s business or preferences.
examples: I don’t care what they do! Live and let live, I always say.
Your parents are strict. Mine just live and let live.

senses.definition: to spend more money than one can afford.
senses.notes: Compare this with live within one’s means.
examples: The Browns are deeply in debt because they are living beyond their means.
I keep a budget so that I don’t live beyond my means.

senses.definition: to survive by being clever.
examples: When you’re in the kind of business I’m in, you have to live by your wits.
John was orphaned at the age of ten and grew up living by his wits.

senses.definition: to live without planning for the future.
examples: John has no health or life insurance. He lives only for the moment.
When you’re young, you tend to live for the moment and not plan for your future security.

senses.definition: to live in poor circumstances.
examples: When both my parents were out of work, we lived from hand to mouth.
We lived from hand to mouth during the war. Things were very difficult.

senses.definition: to live in happiness after a specific event.
senses.notes: Usually found at the end of fairy tales.
examples: The prince and the princess lived happily ever after.
They went away from the horrible haunted castle and lived happily ever after.

senses.definition: to live well and eat good food.
senses.notes: Folksy. Note the variation with pretty. See also eat high on the hog.
examples: After they discovered oil on their land, they lived pretty high on the hog.
Looks like we’re living high off the hog tonight. What’s the occasion?

senses.definition: to be aloof from the realities of living.
senses.notes: Live can be replaced by a number of expressions meaning “to dwell or spend time,” as in the first example.
examples: If you didn’t spend so much time in your ivory tower, you’d know what people really think!
Many professors are said to live in ivory towers. They don’t know what the real world is like.

senses.definition: to have an exciting time; to do what one pleases—regardless of cost—to please oneself.
examples: At the party, John was really living it up.
Come on! Have fun! Live it up!
They spent a week in Mexico living it up and then came home broke.

headword: live off the fat of the land

senses.definition: to grow one’s own food; to live on stored-up resources or abundant resources.
examples: If I had a million dollars, I’d invest it and live off the fat of the land.
I’ll be happy to retire soon and live off the fat of the land.
Many farmers live off the fat of the land.

senses.definition: to live longer than circumstances warrant.
examples: John has a terminal disease, and he’s living on borrowed time.
This project is living on borrowed time. It is overdue for completion.

senses.definition: to live briefly in a place, never unpacking one’s luggage.
examples: I hate living out of a suitcase. For my next vacation, I want to go to just one place and stay there the whole time.
We were living out of suitcases in a motel while they repaired the damage the fire caused to our house.

senses.definition: to overcome the shame or embarrassment of something.
examples: You’ll live it down someday.
Max will never be able to live down what happened at the party last night.

senses.definition: to endure something.
examples: I thought I’d never be able to live through the lecture. It was so boring.
I just can’t live through another day like this.

headword: live up to one’s end of the bargain

senses.definition: to carry though on a bargain; to do as was promised in a bargain.
examples: You can’t quit now. You have to live up to your end of the bargain.
Bob isn’t living up to his end of the bargain, so I am going to sue him.

senses.definition: to fulfill expectations; to satisfy a set of goals.
senses.notes: Often with one’s reputation, promise, word, standards, etc.
examples: I hope I can live up to my reputation.
The class lives up to its reputation of being exciting and interesting.
He never lives up to his promises.
She was unable to live up to her own high standards.

senses.definition: to spend no more money than one has.
senses.notes: Compare this with live beyond one’s means.
examples: We have to struggle to live within our means, but we manage.
John is unable to live within his means.

senses.definition: angry.
examples: He left here in a rage. He was really loaded for bear.
When I got home from work, I was really loaded for bear. What a horrible day!

senses.definition: drunk.
senses.notes: An elaboration of loaded, which means “drunk.” Slang and folksy.
examples: By the end of the party, Bill was loaded for bear.
The whole gang drank for an hour until they were loaded for bear.

senses.definition: to get into an argument with someone.
examples: Let’s settle this peacefully. I don’t want to lock horns with the boss.
The boss doesn’t want to lock horns either.

senses.definition: to make something, such as a rate of interest, permanent over a period of time.
examples: We locked in an 11 percent rate on our mortgage.
You should try to lock in a high percentage rate on your bonds.

senses.definition: everything.
examples: We had to move everything out of the house— lock, stock, and barrel.
We lost everything—lock, stock, and barrel—in the fire.

senses.definition: the whole story; all the necessary facts.
examples: I was late and I missed my train, and that’s the long and short of it.
Soon after the big green frog turned into a handsome prince, Princess Ellen and her newfound love went to live happily ever after in a kingdom by the sea, and that’s the long and the short of it.

senses.definition: I have not seen you for a long time.
examples: Hello, John. Long time no see.
When John and Mary met on the street, they both said, “Long time no see.”

headword: look as if butter wouldn’t melt in one’s mouth

senses.definition: to appear to be cold and unfeeling (despite any information to the contrary).
examples: Sally looks as if butter wouldn’t melt in her mouth. She can be so cruel.
What a sour face. He looks as if butter wouldn’t melt in his mouth.

senses.definition: to do something slightly provocative.
examples: Bob is very excitable. He’d lose his temper if anyone so much as looked at him cross-eyed.
Don’t even look cross-eyed at the boss this morning unless you want trouble.

senses.definition: to give someone a dirty look.
senses.notes: Compare this with look at someone cross-eyed.
examples: Tom must have been mad at Ann from the way he was looking daggers at her.
Don’t you dare look daggers at me! Don’t even look cross-eyed at me!

headword: look down on someone or something
altForms: look down one’s nose at someone or something

senses.definition: to regard someone or something with contempt or displeasure.
examples: I think that John liked Mary, although he did seem to look down on her.
Don’t look down your nose at my car just because it’s rusty and noisy.

senses.definition: to anticipate something with pleasure.
examples: I’m really looking forward to your visit next week.
We all look forward to your new book on gardening.

senses.definition: seems fine in theory, but not perhaps in practice; appears to be a good plan.
examples: The plan looks good on paper, but it may not work.
This looks good on paper. Let’s hope it works in the real world.

senses.definition: to see to the welfare of someone or something; to visit someone or something.
examples: I’ll stop by your house and look in on things while you’re on vacation.
Yes, just look in and make sure nothing is wrong.
I checked in on John yesterday. He’s almost over his illness.
He was glad I checked in.

senses.definition: to investigate something.
examples: I’ll have to look into that matter.
The police checked into her story.
Don’t worry about your problem. I’ll see into it.

senses.definition: to look very good.
examples: Oh, Sally, you look like a million dollars.
Your new hairdo looks like a million dollars.

senses.definition: to look quite ill; to look as pale as a dead person.
examples: Poor Tom had quite a shock. He looks like death warmed over.
After her long ordeal with chemotherapy, she looked like death warmed over.

senses.definition: to give the appearance of predicting (something).
examples: The sky looks like rain.
No, it looks like snow.
Oh, oh. This looks like trouble. Let’s go.

headword: look like something the cat dragged in

senses.definition: to look very shabby, worn, exhausted, or abused.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Sometimes with drug.
examples: That new sofa of theirs looks like something the cat dragged in.
Poor Dave looks like something the cat drug in. He must have been out late last night.

headword: look like the cat that swallowed the canary

senses.definition: to appear as if one had just had a great success.
examples: After the meeting John looked like the cat that swallowed the canary. I knew he must have been a success.
What happened? You look like the cat that swallowed the canary.

senses.definition: to view or think of someone as something.
examples: I look on you as a very thoughtful person.
Mary looked on Jane as a good friend.

senses.definition: to face someone directly.
senses.notes: Facing someone this way should assure sincerity.
examples: I don’t believe you. Look me in the eye and say that.
She looked him in the face and said she never wanted to see him again.
I dare you to stare him in the face and say that!

senses.definition: to examine someone or something carefully.
examples: She looked him over and decided to hire him.
Please look over this report.

senses.definition: to search for and find someone or something.
examples: I don’t know where the hammer is. I’ll have to hunt it up.
Ann looked the word up in the dictionary.
Would you please look up John? I need to talk to him.

senses.definition: to ignore (something) on purpose.
examples: John could have prevented the problem, but he looked the other way.
By looking the other way, he actually made the problem worse.

senses.definition: to take care not to lower or diminish one’s reputation or position, especially in relation to that of someone else potentially better.
examples: With the arrival of the new member of the football team, James will have to look to his laurels to remain as the highest scorer.
The older members of the team will have to look to their laurels when young people join.

headword: look to someone or something (for something)

senses.definition: to expect someone or something to supply something.
examples: Children look to their parents for help.
Tom looked to the bank for a loan.
Most people who need to borrow money look to a bank.

senses.definition: to examine the engine of a car; to check the oil and water associated with the engine of a car.
examples: I finished putting gas in. I need to look under the hood.
Do you want me to look under the hood, sir?

senses.definition: to view someone with respect and admiration.
examples: Bill really looks up to his father.
Everyone in the class looked up to the teacher.

senses.definition: to be of great importance, especially when referring to a possible problem, danger, or threat.
examples: The exams were looming large on the horizon.
Eviction was looming large when the students could not pay their rent.

senses.definition: to dominate someone; to direct and control someone.
examples: Mr. Smith seems to lord it over his wife.
The boss lords it over everyone in the office.

senses.definition: to lose status; to become less respectable.
examples: John is more afraid of losing face than losing money.
Things will go better if you can explain to him where he was wrong, without making him lose face.

senses.definition: to fall behind; to fall back.
examples: She was recovering nicely yesterday, but she lost ground last night.
We are losing ground in our fight against mosquitoes.

senses.definition: to lose one’s courage or confidence.
examples: Now, don’t lose heart. Keep trying.
What a disappointment! It’s enough to make one lose heart.

senses.definition: to lose one’s temper; to lose one’s nerve.
examples: Wow, he really lost his cool! What a tantrum!
Whatever you do, don’t blow your cool.

senses.definition: to become deeply involved in something (so that everything else is forgotten).
examples: Jane has a tendency to lose herself in her work.
I often lose myself in thought.
Excuse me, I lost myself for a moment.

senses.definition: to lose control of a situation.
examples: I can’t seem to run things the way I used to. I’m losing my grip.
They replaced the board of directors because it was losing its grip.

headword: lose one’s head (over someone or something)

senses.definition: to become confused or “crazy” about someone or something.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to execution by decapitation. Refers especially to emotional attachments.
examples: Don’t lose your head over John. He isn’t worth it.
I’m sorry. I got upset and lost my head.

senses.definition: to go crazy; to go out of one’s mind.
senses.notes: The first phrase is slang and can be literal. See also not have all one’s marbles.
examples: What a silly thing to say! Have you lost your marbles?
I can’t seem to remember anything. I think I’m losing my mind.

senses.definition: to lose one’s power of reasoning, possibly in anger.
examples: I was so confused that I almost lost my reason.
Bob seems to have lost his reason when he struck John.

senses.definition: to lose all of one’s assets (including one’s shirt).
examples: I almost lost my shirt on that deal. I have to invest more wisely.
No, I can’t loan you $200. I just lost my shirt at the racetrack.

senses.definition: to become angry.
examples: Please don’t lose your temper. It’s not good for you.
I’m sorry that I lost my temper.

headword: lose one’s touch (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to lose one’s ability to handle someone or something.
examples: I seem to have lost my touch with my children. They won’t mind me anymore.
We’ve both lost our touch as far as managing people goes.
Tom said that he had lost his touch with the stock market.

senses.definition: to forget what one was talking or thinking about.
examples: Excuse me, I lost my train of thought. What was I talking about?
You made the speaker lose her train of thought.

senses.definition: to worry about someone or something.
senses.notes: Literal when worry keeps one awake.
examples: I keep losing sleep over my son, who is in the army.
Do you lose sleep over your investments?
No, I don’t lose sleep, and I never worry.

senses.definition: to lose contact with someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with keep in touch (with someone).
examples: Poor Sally has lost touch with reality.
I’ve lost touch with all my relatives.
Jane didn’t mean to lose touch, but she did.

senses.definition: to forget where someone or something is; to lose or misplace someone or something.
examples: I’ve lost track of the time.
The mother lost track of her child and started calling her.
When I get tired, I tend to lose track.

senses.definition: an office or department that handles items that someone has lost that have been found by someone else.
examples: The lost-and-found office had an enormous collection of umbrellas and four sets of false teeth!
I found a book on the seat of the bus. I turned it in to the driver, who gave it to the lost-and-found office.

senses.definition: lost; permanently lost.
examples: My poor doggy is lost and gone forever.
My money fell out of my pocket, and I am sure that it is lost and gone forever.

senses.definition: a futile attempt; a hopeless matter.
examples: Our campaign to have the new party on the ballot was a lost cause.
Todd gave it up as a lost cause.

senses.definition: busy thinking.
examples: I’m sorry, I didn’t hear what you said. I was lost in thought.
Bill—lost in thought as always—went into the wrong room.

senses.definition: having no effect on someone; wasted on someone.
examples: The joke was lost on Jean. She didn’t understand it.
The humor of the situation was lost on Mary. She was too upset to see it.

headword: a lot of someone or something

senses.definition: a large number of people or things; much of something.
examples: I got a lot of presents for my birthday.
I ate lots of cookies after dinner.

senses.definition: clear and distinctly.
senses.notes: Originally said of radio reception that is heard clearly and distinctly.
examples: TOM: If I’ve told you once, I’ve told you a thousand times: Stop it! Do you hear me? BILL: Yes, loud and clear.
I hear you loud and clear.

senses.definition: to mess up or ruin something.
examples: I’ve worked hard on this. Please don’t louse it up.
You’ve loused up all my plans.

senses.definition: with something in abundance.
examples: This place is lousy with cops.
Our picnic table was lousy with ants.

senses.definition: love established when two people first see one another.
examples: Bill was standing at the door when Ann opened it. It was love at first sight.
It was love at first sight when they met, but it didn’t last long.

senses.definition: rainy weather.
examples: BOB: Not very nice out today, is it? BILL: It’s lovely weather for ducks.
I don’t like this weather, but it’s lovely weather for ducks.

headword: low man on the totem pole

senses.definition: the least important person.
senses.notes: Compare this with high man on the totem pole.
examples: I was the last to find out because I’m low man on the totem pole.
I can’t be of any help. I’m low man on the totem pole.

senses.definition: to bring oneself down to some lower level of behavior.
examples: I refuse to lower myself to your level.
Has TV news lowered itself to the level of the tabloids?

senses.definition: to set one’s goals lower than they were.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to aiming a weapon.
examples: Even though you get frustrated, don’t lower your sights.
I shouldn’t lower my sights. If I work hard, I can do what I want.

senses.definition: to speak more softly.
examples: Please lower your voice, or you’ll disturb the people who are working.
He wouldn’t lower his voice, so everyone heard what he said.

senses.definition: to scold or punish someone severely; to crack down on someone; to throw the book at someone.
examples: If Bob won’t behave better, I’ll have to lower the boom on him.
The teacher lowered the boom on the whole class for misbehaving.

senses.definition: a quiet period just before a period of great activity or excitement.
examples: It was very quiet in the cafeteria just before the students came in for lunch. It was the lull before the storm.
In the brief calm before the storm, the clerks prepared themselves for the doors to open and bring in thousands of shoppers.

headword: lull someone into a false sense of security

senses.definition: to lead someone into believing that all is well before attacking or doing someone bad.
examples: We lulled the enemy into a false sense of security by pretending to retreat. Then we launched an attack.
The boss lulled us into a false sense of security by saying that our jobs were safe and then let half the staff go.

senses.definition: to cause someone to fall asleep.
examples: The mother lulled her baby to sleep.
The boring professor lulled the students to sleep.

senses.definition: the more extreme members of a group.
examples: Most of the members of that religious sect are quite reasonable, but Lisa belongs to the lunatic fringe.
Many people try to avoid eating a lot of fat, but Mary is part of the lunatic fringe and will hardly eat anything.

senses.definition: angry enough to bite through metal nails.
examples: I am mad enough to chew nails! Who took my checkbook?
Her sudden tirade made him angry enough to chew nails.

senses.definition: to be very well suited romantically.
examples: Bill and Jane were made for each other.
Mr. and Mrs. Smith were not exactly made for each other. They really don’t get along.

senses.definition: made especially to fit the measurements of a particular person.
examples: Jack has his suits made to measure because he’s rather large.
Having clothes made to measure is rather expensive.

senses.definition: put together on request.
examples: This suit fits so well because it’s made to order.
His feet are so big that all his shoes have to be made to order.

senses.definition: the first voyage of a ship or boat.
examples: The liner sank on its maiden voyage.
Jim is taking his yacht on its maiden voyage.

senses.definition: great force; brute force.
examples: They finally got the piano moved in to the living room by main strength and awkwardness.
Lifting the table must be done carefully. This is not a job requiring main strength and awkwardness.

senses.definition: to arrange neatly the sheets and blankets of a bed.
examples: The hotel maid made our bed.
Billy had to make his bed before he went to school.

headword: make a beeline for someone or something

senses.definition: to head straight toward someone or something.
senses.notes: Refers to the way bees fly in a straight line. Informal.
examples: Billy came into the kitchen and made a beeline for the cookies.
After the game, we all made a beeline for John, who was serving cold drinks.

headword: make a break for something or somewhere

senses.definition: to move or run quickly to something or somewhere.
examples: Before we could stop her, she made a break for the door and got away.
The mouse got frightened and made a break for a hole in the wall.

senses.definition: to make a lot of money.
examples: John really made a bundle on that deal.
I’d like to make a pile and retire.

senses.definition: to write a check naming someone as payee.
examples: Please make a check out to John Jones.
Do you want cash, or should I make out a check?

headword: make a clean breast of something

senses.definition: to confess something; to get something off one’s chest.
examples: You’ll feel better if you make a clean breast of it. Now tell us what happened.
I was forced to make a clean breast of the whole affair.

senses.definition: to do something completely or thoroughly, with no exceptions.
examples: The boss decided to fire everybody, so he made a clean sweep.
They made a clean sweep through the neighborhood, repairing all the sidewalks.

senses.definition: to return to one’s former (successful) career.
examples: After ten years in retirement, the singer made a comeback.
You’re never too old to make a comeback.

headword: make a day of doing something

senses.definition: to spend the whole day doing something.
examples: We went to the museum to see the new exhibit and then decided to make a day of it.
They made a day of cleaning the attic.

senses.definition: to begin to consume or accomplish something.
examples: Bob, you’ve hardly made a dent in your dinner!
There is a lot of rice left. We hardly made a dent in it all week.
Get busy! You haven’t even made a dent in your work.

senses.definition: to twist one’s face into a strange expression in order to show one’s dislike, ridicule, etc., or in order to make someone laugh.
examples: The comedian made faces in order to amuse the children.
Jane made a face when she was asked to work late.

senses.definition: to make a face at someone in ridicule.
examples: Mother, Billy made a face at me!
The teacher sent Jane to the principal for making a face in class.

senses.definition: to attempt to communicate to someone through facial gestures, usually an attempt to say “no” or “stop.”
examples: I started to tell John where I was last night, but Bill made a face so I didn’t.
John made a face at me as I was testifying, so I avoided telling everything.

senses.definition: to make money with little effort.
examples: Tom is always ready to make a fast buck.
I made a quick buck selling used cars.

headword: make a federal case out of something
altForms: make a big deal about something

senses.definition: to exaggerate the seriousness of something.
senses.notes: The first entry head can be literal. Slang.
examples: Come on. It was nothing! Don’t make a federal case out of it.
I only stepped on your toe. Don’t make a big deal about it.

senses.definition: to establish a link of friendship with someone.
examples: I have never found it difficult to make friends.
Mary had to make new friends when she changed schools.

headword: make a fuss (over someone or something)

senses.definition: to worry about or make a bother about someone or something.
examples: Why do you fuss over a problem like that?
Please don’t make a fuss. Everything will be all right.
Don’t make over me so much!

senses.definition: to be very solicitous and helpful toward a person or a pet.
examples: How can anyone make a fuss over a cat?
Billy was embarrassed when his mother made a fuss over him.

senses.definition: to argue about someone or something.
examples: Please don’t make a fuss over who gets the last cookie.
Please discuss it. Don’t make a fuss over it!

headword: make a great show of something

senses.definition: to make something obvious; to do something in a showy fashion.
examples: Ann made a great show of wiping up the drink that John spilled.
Jane displayed her irritation at our late arrival by making a great show of serving the cold dinner.

headword: make a hit (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to please someone.
examples: The singer made a hit with the audience.
She was afraid she wouldn’t make a hit.
John made a hit with my parents last evening.

senses.definition: to have a great success, especially in making money.
examples: John has got a job selling insurance. He’s not exactly making a killing.
Bill made a killing at the racetrack yesterday.

headword: make a laughingstock of oneself or something
altForms: make oneself or something a laughingstock

senses.definition: to make oneself a source of ridicule or laughter; to do something that invites ridicule.
examples: Laura made herself a laughingstock by arriving at the fastfood restaurant in full evening dress.
The board of directors made the company a laughingstock by hiring an ex-convict as president.

senses.definition: to earn enough money to live on.
examples: I’ll be glad when I get a job and can make a living.
I can hardly make a living with the skills I have.

senses.definition: to allow time, space, food, etc., for someone or something.
examples: When planning the party, please make allowances for John and his family.
I’m making allowance for ten extra guests.

senses.definition: to make excuses or explanations for someone or something; to take into consideration the negative effects of someone or something.
examples: You’re very late even when we make allowance for the weather.
We have to make allowance for the age of the house when we judge its condition.

senses.definition: to bring a story to an end.
senses.notes: A formula that introduces a summary of a story or a joke.
examples: And— to make a long story short—I never got back the money that I lent him.
If I can make a long story short, let me say that everything worked out fine.

senses.definition: to do something as an act of restitution or to make up for some error, injury, or loss that one has caused.
examples: After the argument, Jane later called her friend to make amends.
After amends had been made, Jane took her friend to dinner.

headword: make a mountain out of a molehill

senses.definition: to make a major issue out of a minor one; to exaggerate the importance of something.
examples: Come on, don’t make a mountain out of a molehill. It’s not that important.
Mary is always making mountains out of molehills.

senses.definition: to make a thorough and energetic effort.
examples: Sally made an all-out effort to get to class on time.
In my job, I have to make an all-out effort every day.

senses.definition: to become famous.
examples: Sally wants to work hard and make a name for herself.
It’s hard to make a name without a lot of talent and hard work.

senses.definition: to appear; to appear in a performance.
senses.notes: Compare this with put in an appearance.
examples: We waited for thirty minutes for the professor to make an appearance, then we went home.
The famous singing star made an appearance in Detroit last August.

senses.definition: to schedule a meeting with someone.
examples: I made an appointment with the doctor for late today.
The professor wouldn’t see me unless I made an appointment.

senses.definition: to make a public issue out of someone’s bad behavior.
examples: The judge decided to make an example of John, so he fined him the full amount.
The teacher made an example of Mary, who had disturbed the class constantly with her whispering.

senses.definition: to suspend a rule or practice for someone in a single instance.
examples: Please make an exception just this once.
The rule is a good one, and I will not make an exception for anyone.

senses.definition: to embarrass oneself by showing off or doing something daring in public.
senses.notes: Sometimes under the influence of alcohol.
examples: You can be certain that Joan will have too much to drink and make an exhibition of herself.
Sit down and be quiet. Stop making an exhibition of yourself.

headword: make a night of doing something

senses.definition: to do something for the entire night.
examples: We partied until three in the morning and then decided to make a night of it.
Once or twice in the early spring we make a night of fishing.

senses.definition: to produce a memorable effect on someone.
senses.notes: Often with good, bad, or some other adjective.
examples: Tom made a bad impression on the banker.
I’m afraid that you haven’t made a very good impression on our visitors.
You made quite an impression on my father.

senses.definition: to write something down.
examples: Please make a note of this address.
This is important. Make a note of it.

senses.definition: to be a constant bother.
examples: I’m sorry to make a nuisance of myself, but I do need an answer to my question.
Stop making a nuisance of yourself and wait your turn.

senses.definition: to flirt with someone; to make a romantic advance at someone.
senses.notes: This often has sexual implications. Compare this with make a play (for someone).
examples: I was shocked when Ann made a pass at me.
I think Bob was making a pass at me, but he did it very subtly.

headword: make a pitch (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to say something in support of someone or something; to attempt to promote, sell, or advance someone or something.
examples: Bill is making a pitch for his friend’s new product again.
The theatrical agent came in and made a pitch for her client.
Every time I turn on the television set, someone is making a pitch.

senses.definition: to attempt to attract the romantic interest of someone.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with make a pass at someone.
examples: Ann made a play for Bill, but he wasn’t interested in her.
I knew he liked me, but I never thought he’d make a play.

senses.definition: to state an item of importance.
senses.notes: Also literal, as in sports and games.
examples: You made a point that we all should remember.
He spoke for an hour without making a point.

headword: make a point of doing something

senses.definition: to make an effort to do something.
examples: Please make a point of mailing this letter. It’s very important.
The hostess made a point of thanking me for bringing flowers.

headword: make a point of someone or something
altForms: make an issue of someone or something

senses.definition: to turn someone or something into an important matter.
examples: Please don’t make a point of John’s comment. It wasn’t that important.
I hope you make an issue of Tom’s success and the reasons for it.
Tom has a lot of problems. Please don’t make an issue of him.

senses.definition: to turn something into a habitual activity.
examples: Jane makes a practice of planting daisies every summer.
Her mother also made it a practice.

senses.definition: to reserve a seat, as in an airplane, restaurant, or theater in advance; to reserve a room, as in a hotel in advance.
examples: Did you make a reservation or are we just going to chance getting a table?
I made reservations for a flight at twelve noon.

senses.definition: to make plans for someone or something.
examples: I’m making arrangements for the convention.
It starts next week, and I hardly have time to make arrangements.

senses.definition: to plan accommodations for someone.
examples: John is coming for a visit next week. Please make arrangements for him at the hotel.
I will make arrangements for everyone when I call the hotel.

senses.definition: to run fast to get away or get somewhere.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with make a break for something or somewhere.
examples: When the guard wasn’t looking, the prisoner made a run for it.
In the baseball game, the player on first base made a run for it, but he didn’t make it to second base.

senses.definition: to make a public display or disturbance.
examples: When John found a fly in his drink, he started to create a scene.
Oh, John, please don’t make a scene. Just forget about it.

headword: make a silk purse out of a sow’s ear

senses.definition: to create something of value out of something of no value.
examples: Don’t bother trying to fix up this old bicycle. You can’t make a silk purse out of a sow’s ear.
My mother made a lovely jacket out of an old coat. She succeeded in making a silk purse out of a sow’s ear.

senses.definition: to make or accept bets on something.
examples: It looks as if it will rain, but I wouldn’t make book on it.
John’s making book on the football game this Saturday.

senses.definition: to manage to live on a small amount of money.
examples: It’s hard these days to make ends meet.
I have to work overtime to make both ends meet.

senses.definition: to talk or chatter.
examples: We sat around all evening making chin music.
You were making chin music when you should have been listening.

senses.definition: to ridicule or make jokes about someone or something.
examples: Please stop making cracks about my haircut. It’s the new style.
Some people can’t help making cracks. They are just rude.

senses.definition: to flirt with someone.
examples: Tom spent all afternoon making eyes at Ann.
How could they sit there in class making eyes?

headword: make free with someone or something

senses.definition: to take advantage of or use something as if it were one’s own.
senses.notes: [with something] Compare this with take liberties with someone or something.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t come into my house and make free with my food and drink.
Please make free with my car while I’m gone.

senses.definition: to ridicule someone or something.
examples: Please stop making fun of me. It hurts my feelings.
Billy teases and makes fun a lot, but he means no harm.

senses.definition: to succeed in a particular role.
examples: I hope I make good as a teacher.
John made good as a football player.

senses.definition: to succeed at something.
examples: Bob worked hard to make good at selling.
Jane was determined to make good.

senses.definition: to earn a large amount of money.
examples: Ann makes good money at her job.
I don’t know what she does, but she makes good money.

senses.definition: to fulfill a promise.
examples: Tom made good on his pledge to donate $1,000.
Bill refused to make good on his promise.

senses.definition: to repay a debt.
examples: I couldn’t make good on my debts, and I got in a lot of trouble.
If you don’t make good on this bill, I’ll have to take back your car.

senses.definition: to travel fast; to progress rapidly.
examples: I am making good time. My report is almost finished.
Now that we are clear of the city traffic, we can make good time.

headword: make hamburger out of someone or something
altForms: make mincemeat out of someone or something

senses.definition: to beat up or overcome someone or something.
senses.notes: Literal when referring to foodstuffs. Figurative with people. Slang.
examples: Stop acting silly, or I’ll make hamburger out of you.
Our team made mincemeat out of the other team.

senses.definition: to make things difficult for someone; to put someone under pressure.
examples: Maybe if we make it hot for them, they’ll leave.
John likes making it hot for people. He’s sort of mean.

headword: make it one’s business to do something

senses.definition: to do something on one’s own even if it means interfering in something that does not directly concern one.
senses.notes: As opposed to minding one’s own business. See also take it upon oneself to do something.
