examples: I know I doesn’t concern me, but I made it my business to call city hall because someone had to.
Jane made it her business to find out exactly what had happened to the old lady.

senses.definition: to make something profitable enough for someone to do.
examples: If you deliver this parcel for me, I’ll make it worth your while.
The boss said he’d make it worth our while if we worked late.

senses.definition: to make someone unhappy over a long period of time.
examples: My shoes are tight, and they are making life miserable for me.
Jane’s boss is making life miserable for her.

senses.definition: to treat something as if it were unimportant or humorous.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t make light of his problems. They’re quite serious.
I make light of my problems, and that makes me feel better.

senses.definition: to share physical or emotional love (or both) with someone.
senses.notes: This phrase usually has a sexual meaning.
examples: Tom and Ann turned out the lights and made love.
The actress refused to make love to the leading man on stage.

senses.definition: to have fun; to have an enjoyable time.
examples: The guests certainly made merry at the wedding.
The children were making merry in the backyard.

senses.definition: to cause trouble.
examples: Bob loves to make mischief and get other people into trouble.
Don’t believe what Mary says. She’s just trying to make mischief.

headword: Make no bones about it. Make no mistake (about it).

senses.definition: Do not doubt it.
examples: This is the greatest cake I’ve ever eaten. Make no bones about it.
Make no bones about it, Mary is a great singer.

senses.definition: not to matter to someone; for someone not to care (about something).
examples: It makes no difference to me what you do.
Do whatever you want. It really makes no difference.

senses.definition: without a doubt; certainly.
examples: This car is a great buy. Make no mistake about it.
We support your candidacy—make no mistake.

senses.definition: to ignore something as if it had not happened; to think no more about something.
examples: My father caught me throwing the snowball, but he made nothing of it.
I made nothing of the remark, even though it seemed quite rude.
I saw him leave, but I made nothing of it.

senses.definition: to attract attention to oneself.
examples: Please don’t make yourself conspicuous. It embarrasses me.
Ann makes herself conspicuous by wearing brightly colored clothing.

senses.definition: to go away.
examples: Hey, kid, go away. Make yourself scarce.
When there is work to be done, I make myself scarce.

senses.definition: to decide.
examples: Please make your mind up. Which do you want?
Would you help me make up my mind?

senses.definition: either to improve or ruin someone.
examples: The army will either make or break him.
It’s a tough assignment, and it will either make or break her.

senses.definition: to give hints about something; to present or suggest ideas.
examples: The company made overtures about hiring me.
Tom is making overtures about inviting us to his country home next month.

senses.definition: to end a quarrel with someone.
senses.notes: Compare this with kiss and make up.
examples: Don’t you think it’s time to make peace with your brother? There is no point in arguing anymore.
Yes, it’s time we made peace.

senses.definition: to gain favor with someone.
examples: Tom is trying to make points with Ann. He wants to ask her out.
He’s trying to make points by smiling and telling her how nice she looks.

senses.definition: to be understandable to someone.
examples: John doesn’t make sense.
What John says makes sense.

headword: make sense out of someone or something

senses.definition: to understand or interpret someone or something.
senses.notes: Also with some, as in the second example.
examples: I can hardly make sense out of John.
I’m trying to make some sense out of what John is saying.

headword: make short work of someone or something
altForms: make fast work of someone or something

senses.definition: to finish with someone or something quickly.
examples: I made short work of Tom so I could leave the office to play golf.
Billy made fast work of his dinner so he could go out and play.

senses.definition: to cause someone to retract a statement or admit an error.
examples: Because Mary was completely wrong, we made her eat crow.
They won’t make me eat crow. They don’t know I was wrong.

senses.definition: to cause someone to appear successful or competent (especially when this is not the case).
examples: John arranges all his affairs to make himself look good.
The manager didn’t like the quarterly report because it didn’t make her look good.

senses.definition: to make someone look foolish (not funny).
examples: This hat makes me look ridiculous.
Please make me look good. Don’t make me look ridiculous!

senses.definition: to make someone very angry.
examples: It just makes my blood boil to think of the amount of food that gets wasted around here.
Whenever I think of that dishonest mess, it makes my blood boil.

senses.definition: to shock or horrify someone.
examples: The terrible story in the newspaper made my blood run cold.
I could tell you things about prisons that would make your blood run cold.

senses.definition: to cause someone’s skin to feel funny or get goose pimples through fright.
examples: Just to hear the story of the killings made my flesh crawl.
The horror movie made our flesh crawl.

senses.definition: to cause someone to become very angry.
examples: The unnecessary accident made my gorge rise.
Getting his tax bill made Bob’s gorge rise.

headword: make someone’s hair stand on end

senses.definition: to cause someone to be very frightened.
senses.notes: Literal if referring to the effects of a charge of static electricity. Informal.
examples: The horrible scream made my hair stand on end.
The ghost story made our hair stand on end.

senses.definition: to make someone dizzy or disoriented.
examples: Riding in your car makes my head spin.
Breathing the gas made my head swim.

senses.definition: to confuse or overwhelm someone.
examples: All these numbers make my head swim.
The physics lecture made my head spin.

senses.definition: to disgust someone.
examples: I am really tired of your vile talk. You make me sick!
She screamed at him that he made her sick and then she ran out of the house.

senses.definition: to make someone hungry (for something).
senses.notes: Also literal for causing saliva to flow into someone’s mouth. Informal.
examples: That beautiful salad makes my mouth water.
Talking about food makes my mouth water.

senses.definition: to clarify where someone stands on an issue.
examples: I don’t think you understand what I said. Let me make my position clear.
I can’t tell whether you are in favor of or against the proposal. Please make your position clear.

headword: make someone the scapegoat for something

senses.definition: to make someone take the blame for something.
examples: They made Tom the scapegoat for the whole affair. It wasn’t all his fault.
Don’t try to make me the scapegoat. I’ll tell who really did it.

senses.definition: to make something by starting with the basic ingredients.
examples: We made the cake from scratch, using no prepared ingredients.
I didn’t have a ladder, so I made one from scratch.

senses.definition: to replace or restore something.
senses.notes: Informal. See also set something right.
examples: I know I owe you some money, but don’t worry, I’ll make it good.
I’m sorry I broke your window. I’ll make it right, though.

senses.definition: to make an issue of something of little importance.
senses.notes: See also make a mountain out of a molehill.
examples: Relax, John, you’re making a big problem out of nothing.
You have no evidence. You’re making a case out of nothing.

senses.definition: to create something of value from nearly worthless parts.
examples: My uncle—he sells sand—made a fortune out of nothing.
My model airplane won the contest even though I made it out of nothing.

senses.definition: to put something together only when someone requests it.
senses.notes: Usually said about clothing. See also build something to order.
examples: This store only makes suits to order.
Our shirts fit perfectly because we make each one to order.

headword: make something up out of whole cloth

senses.definition: to create a story or a lie from no facts at all.
examples: I don’t believe you. I think you made that up out of whole cloth.
Ann made up her explanation out of whole cloth. There was not a bit of truth in it.

senses.definition: to make something profitable enough for someone to do.
examples: If you deliver this parcel for me, I’ll make it worth your while.
The boss said he’d make it worth our while if we worked late.

senses.definition: to restore a bed to an unslept-in condition.
examples: I make my bed every morning.
The maid goes to all the rooms to make the beds.

senses.definition: to try to make a bad situation work out well.
senses.notes: Compare this with make the most of something.
examples: It’s not good, but we’ll have to make the best of it.
Ann is clever enough to make the best of a bad situation.

senses.definition: to cause a fight or an argument; to create an uproar (about something).
examples: When your mother gets home and sees what you’ve done, she’ll really make the fur fly.
When those two get together, they’ll make the feathers fly. They hate each other.

senses.definition: to be satisfactory; to be what is expected.
examples: I’m sorry, but your work doesn’t exactly make the grade.
This meal doesn’t just make the grade. It is excellent.

senses.definition: to make something appear as good as possible; to exploit something; to get as much out of something as is possible.
senses.notes: Compare this with make the best of something.
examples: Mary knows how to make the most of her talents.
They designed the advertisements to make the most of the product’s features.

senses.definition: to appear somewhere, especially at a social event.
examples: I hope I can make the scene Saturday night at the party.
The big race is tomorrow. Man, I’ve got to make the scene. The whole world will be there!

senses.definition: to schedule time to see someone or do something.
examples: I can make time for you tomorrow morning.
I am very busy, but I can make time.
You are going to have to start making time for balanced meals.

senses.definition: to flirt with, date, or hang around with someone.
examples: I hear that Tom’s been making time with Ann.
I hear they’ve been making time for months.

senses.definition: to do much of something; to do something fast.
examples: Because we took so long eating lunch, we have to drive faster to make up for lost time. Otherwise we won’t arrive on time.
At the age of sixty, Bill learned to play golf. Now he plays it every day. He’s making up for lost time.

senses.definition: to make trouble or difficulties.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Compare this with rock the boat.
examples: I don’t want to make waves, but this just isn’t right.
Why do you always have to make waves? Can’t you be constructive?

senses.definition: to make progress; to move ahead.
senses.notes: Originally nautical. See also make way (for someone or something).
examples: Is this project making way?
A sailboat can’t make way if there is no wind.

senses.definition: to clear a path for someone or something.
examples: Make way for the stretcher.
Please make way for the nurse.
Here comes the doctor—make way!

senses.definition: a fashionable man who leads a sophisticated life.
examples: He prefers wine bars to pubs—quite a man-about-town.
Jack’s too much of a man-about-town to go to a football game.

senses.definition: the ordinary person.
examples: Politicians rarely care what the man in the street thinks.
The man in the street has little interest in literature.

senses.definition: speaking frankly and directly, one person to another.
examples: Let’s discuss this man to man so we know what each other thinks.
The two mothers discussed their childraising problems woman to woman.

senses.definition: A lot of help will make a chore seem easier.
examples: Let’s all work together and get this finished. Many hands make light work.
Many hands make light work, so please lend a hand.

senses.definition: on many occasions.
examples: Many is the time I wanted to complain, but I just kept quiet.
Many is the time that we don’t have enough to eat.

headword: march to (the beat of) a different drummer

senses.definition: to believe in a different set of principles.
examples: John is marching to a different drummer, and he doesn’t come to our parties anymore.
Since Sally started marching to the beat of a different drummer, she has had a lot of great new ideas.

senses.definition: remember what I’m telling you.
examples: Mark my word, you’ll regret this.
This whole project will fail—mark my words.

senses.definition: to make a note about someone; to note a fact about someone.
examples: I’m going to the party. Please mark me down.
Mark me down, too.

senses.definition: [for a teacher] to give someone a low score.
examples: He’ll mark you down for misspelled words.
I marked down Tom for bad spelling.

senses.definition: to lower the price of something.
examples: Okay, we’ll mark it down.
Let’s mark down this price so it’ll sell faster.

senses.definition: someone or something quite exciting or wonderful to see.
examples: Our new house is a marvel to behold.
Mary’s lovely new baby is a marvel to behold.

senses.definition: businesslike; unfeeling.
senses.notes: See also as a matter of fact.
examples: Don’t expect a lot of sympathy from Ann. She’s very matter-of-fact.
Don’t be so matter-of-fact. It hurts my feelings.

headword: a matter of life and death

senses.definition: an issue of great urgency; a situation that will affect life or death.
examples: We must find a doctor. It’s a matter of life and death.
A matter of life and death demands that I return home at once.

senses.definition: the matter of how good or bad someone or something is; a question about which there are different opinions.
examples: It’s a matter of opinion how good the company is. John thinks it’s great and Fred thinks it’s poor.
How efficient the committee is is a matter of opinion.

senses.definition: to be very serious and determined about something.
examples: Billy, get into this house and do your homework, and I mean business.
We mean business when we say you must stop all this nonsense.

headword: mean for someone to do something

senses.definition: to intend for someone to do something.
examples: John meant for us to go with them to the zoo.
John meant for Jane to do the dishes.

senses.definition: not to make sense to someone.
examples: This sentence means nothing to me. It isn’t clearly written.
I’m sorry. This message means nothing.

senses.definition: not to have feeling for (someone or something).
examples: Do I mean nothing to you after all these years?
Do all those years mean nothing?

senses.definition: to make sense to someone.
examples: Does this line mean anything to you?
Yes, it means something.

senses.definition: for someone to have feeling for (someone or something).
examples: You mean a lot to me.
This job means a lot to Ann.

senses.definition: to plan or intend to do something.
examples: Did you mean to do that?
No, it was an accident. I didn’t mean to.

senses.definition: destined to exist.
examples: Our love was meant to be!
It was not meant to be.

senses.definition: destined or fated to be something.
examples: Jane was meant to be a chemist.
I was meant to be rich, but something didn’t work right!

senses.definition: to be equal to someone or something.
examples: Ann is good, but she doesn’t measure up to Mary.
Tom measures up to the job.

senses.definition: to be as good as one expects.
examples: This measures up to my standards quite nicely.
This meal doesn’t measure up to my expectations.

senses.definition: basic, sturdy, and hearty.
senses.notes: Often refers to a robust person, usually a man, with simple tastes in food and other things.
examples: Fred was your meat-and-potatoes kind of guy. No creamy sauces for him.
There is no point in trying to cook up something special for the Wilsons. They are strictly meat-and-potatoes.

senses.definition: a place that is frequently visited by a particular group of people because it is important to them for some reason.
senses.notes: From the city of Mecca, the religious center of Islam.
examples: New York City is a Mecca for theatergoers.
St. Andrews is a Mecca for golf enthusiasts because of its famous course.

senses.definition: to experience something, especially death or problems.
examples: After 20 years, my dog finally met his death when he got hit by a bus.
The sky diver met his end when his parachute didn’t open.

senses.definition: to meet one’s equal.
examples: John played tennis with Bill yesterday, and it looks as if John has finally met his match.
Listen to Jane and Mary argue. I always thought that Jane was loud, but she has finally met her match.

senses.definition: to meet one’s final and insurmountable challenge.
senses.notes: Refers to Napoleon’s defeat at Waterloo.
examples: The boss is being very hard on Bill. It seems that Bill has finally met his Waterloo.
John was more than Sally could handle. She has finally met her Waterloo.

senses.definition: to offer to compromise with someone.
examples: No, I won’t give in, but I’ll meet you halfway.
They settled the argument by agreeing to meet each other halfway.

senses.definition: to fulfill the requirements for something.
examples: Sally was unable to meet the requirements for the job.
Jane met the requirements and was told to report to work the next day.

senses.definition: the establishment of agreement; complete agreement.
examples: After a lot of discussion we finally reached a meeting of minds.
We struggled to bring about a meeting of minds on the issues.

senses.definition: to taste very good.
examples: This cake is so good it’ll melt in your mouth.
John said that the food didn’t exactly melt in his mouth.

senses.definition: to be very, very tender.
examples: My steak is so tender it could melt in my mouth.
This fillet will melt in your mouth!

senses.definition: to restore good relations (with someone).
examples: I think I had better get home and mend my fences. I had an argument with my daughter this morning.
Sally called up her uncle to apologize and try to mend fences.

senses.definition: to improve one’s behavior.
examples: John used to be very wild, but he’s mended his ways.
You’ll have to mend your ways if you go out with Mary. She hates people to be late.

senses.definition: to play with or waste time with someone or something.
examples: Will you please stop messing around with that old car!
Stop messing about! Get busy!
Tom wastes a lot of time messing around with Bill.
Don’t monkey around with my computer!
John is always screwing around with his stereo.

senses.definition: to rough someone up; to beat someone up.
examples: The robbers threatened to mess Bob up if he didn’t cooperate.
John messed up Bill a little, but no real harm was done.

senses.definition: to make something disorderly.
examples: You really messed this place up!
Who messed up my bed?

senses.definition: halfway between two extremes, especially political extremes.
examples: Jane is very left-wing, but her husband is politically middle-of-the-road.
I don’t want to vote for either the left-wing or the right-wing candidate. I prefer someone with more middle-of-the-road views.

senses.definition: great physical strength; great force.
examples: The huge warrior, with all his might and main, could not break his way through the castle gates.
The incredible might and main of the sea crushed the ship against the cliff.

senses.definition: a very important event or point in one’s life.
senses.notes: From the stone at the side of a road showing the distance to or from a place.
examples: Joan’s wedding was a milestone in her mother’s life.
The birth of a child is a milestone in every parent’s life.

senses.definition: natural kindness and sympathy shown to others.
senses.notes: From Shakespeare’s play Macbeth, I. v.
examples: Mary is completely hard and selfish—she has no milk of human kindness in her.
Roger is too full of the milk of human kindness and people take advantage of him.

senses.definition: to pressure someone into giving information or money.
examples: The reporter milked the mayor’s aide for information.
The thief milked me for $20.

senses.definition: a continual burden or handicap.
examples: This huge and expensive house is a millstone about my neck.
Bill’s inability to read is a millstone about his neck.

senses.definition: to attend only to the things that concern one.
examples: Leave me alone, Bill. Mind your own business.
I’d be fine if John would mind his own business.

senses.definition: to pay attention to small details of behavior, especially manners.
examples: When we go to the mayor’s reception, please mind your p’s and q’s.
I always mind my p’s and q’s when I eat at a restaurant with white tablecloths.

senses.definition: to take care of local matters.
examples: Please stay here in the office and mind the store while I go to the conference.
I had to stay home and mind the store when Ann went to Boston.

senses.definition: a phrase indicating that something should be taken into consideration.
examples: He’s very well dressed, but mind you, he’s got plenty of money to buy clothes.
Lisa is unfriendly to me, but mind you, she’s never very nice to anyone.

senses.definition: to be careful to use good manners.
examples: Mind your manners while we visit Aunt Mary’s house.
Jimmy! Mind your manners!

senses.definition: someone or something that is full of information.
examples: Grandfather is a mine of information about World War I.
The new encyclopedia is a positive mine of useful information.

senses.definition: the point in time at which an event happens.
examples: I’ll be inside the minute it rains.
Call me the minute you get to town.

senses.definition: a wrong or mistaken decision, especially one made in a court of law.
examples: Sentencing the old man on a charge of murder proved to be a miscarriage of justice.
Punishing the student for cheating was a miscarriage of justice. He was innocent.

senses.definition: to put trust in the wrong person; to put trust in someone who does not deserve it.
examples: The writer misplaced his trust in his editor.
The voters misplaced their trust in the corrupt politician.

senses.definition: to fail to participate in something; to fail to take part in something.
examples: I’m sorry I missed out on the ice cream.
I lost out on it, too.
We both missed out.

senses.definition: to fail to hit something by a great distance; to land wide of the mark.
examples: Ann shot the arrow and missed the target by a mile.
“Good grief, you missed by a mile,” shouted Sally.

senses.definition: to miss out (on something); to be ignorant (of something).
examples: Pay attention, John, or you’ll miss the boat.
Tom really missed the boat when it came to making friends.

senses.definition: to fail to understand the important part of something.
examples: I’m afraid you missed the point. Let me explain it again.
You keep explaining, and I keep missing the point.

senses.definition: to assemble a limited number of items, usually clothing, in a number of different ways.
examples: Alice was very good at mixing and matching her skirts, blouses, and sweaters so that she always could be attractively dressed on a limited budget.
Gary always bought black, blue, and gray trousers and shirts so he could mix and match without too many bad combinations.

senses.definition: to select a number of items from an assortment, often in order to get a quantity discount.
senses.notes: As opposed to getting a quantity discount for buying a lot of only one item.
examples: The candles were 25 percent off, and you could mix and match colors, sizes, and length.
I found a good sale on shirts. They were four for fifty dollars, and the store would let you mix and match.

senses.definition: to argue or fight.
examples: First they were just talking, then suddenly one of them got mad and they really began to mix it up.
Look at you, Bill! Your face is bleeding. Have you been mixing it up with John again?

senses.definition: to confuse two things or two people with each other.
examples: Please don’t mix these ideas up. They are quite distinct.
I always mix up Bill and Bob.
Why do you mix them up?

senses.definition: to cause someone to be confused or puzzled.
examples: I’m confused as it is. Don’t mix me up anymore.
They mixed up my uncle by giving him too many things to remember.

senses.definition: to blend the ingredients of something; to assemble and mix the parts of something.
senses.notes: [with something] Usually refers to fluid matter such as paint, gasoline, or milk.
examples: The glue will be ready to use as soon as I mix it up.
Now, mix up the eggs, water, and salt; then add the mixture to the flour and sugar.

senses.definition: a varied collection of people or things.
senses.notes: Refers to a bag of game brought home after a day’s hunting.
examples: The new students in my class are a mixed bag—some bright, some positively stupid.
The furniture I bought is a mixed bag. Some of it is valuable and the rest is worthless.

senses.definition: the point at which someone has to face the reality or facts of a situation.
examples: The moment of truth is here. Turn over your test papers and begin.
Now for the moment of truth when we find out whether we have got permission or not.

headword: Money burns a hole in someone’s pocket.

senses.definition: Someone spends as much money as possible.
senses.notes: Proverb. See also have money to burn.
examples: Sally can’t seem to save anything. Money burns a hole in her pocket.
If money burns a hole in your pocket, you never have any for emergencies.

senses.definition: It does not matter how much something costs.
examples: Please show me your finest automobile. Money is no object.
I want the finest earrings you have. Don’t worry about how much they cost because expense is no object.

headword: Money is the root of all evil.

senses.definition: Money is the basic cause of all wrongdoing.
senses.notes: Proverb. The full version is The love of money is the root of all evil.
examples: Why do you work so hard to make money? It will just cause you trouble. Money is the root of all evil.
Any thief in prison can tell you that money is the root of all evil.

senses.definition: money gives one power and influence to help get things done or get one’s own way.
examples: Don’t worry. I have a way of getting things done. Money talks.
I can’t compete against rich old Mrs. Jones. She’ll get her way because money talks.

senses.definition: playful or out of the ordinary activities; mischievous or illegal activities.
examples: There’s been some monkey business in connection with the bank’s accounts.
Bob left the company quite suddenly. I think there was some monkey business between him and the boss’s wife.

senses.definition: a tuxedo.
senses.notes: Jocular. Possibly alluding to the fancy suit worn by an organ grinder’s monkey.
examples: Do I have to wear a monkey suit to dinner?
All the men except me wore monkey suits at dinner on the cruise.

headword: mop the floor up with someone

senses.definition: to overwhelm and physically subdue someone; to beat someone.
senses.notes: Slang. See also wipe up the floor with someone.
examples: Stop talking like that, or I’ll mop the floor up with you!
Did you hear that? He threatened to mop up the floor with me!

senses.definition: to go about in a depressed state.
examples: Since her dog ran away, Sally mopes around all day.
Don’t mope around. Cheer up!

senses.definition: an increasing amount; additional amounts.
examples: As I learn more and more, I see how little I know.
Dad seems to be smoking more and more lately.

senses.definition: exhausted; in very bad condition; near death.
examples: We arrived at the top of the mountain more dead than alive.
The marathon runners stumbled one by one over the finish line, more dead than alive.

senses.definition: usually.
examples: These flowers will live through the winter more often than not.
This kind of dog will grow up to be a good watchdog more often than not.

senses.definition: to some extent; approximately; sort of.
examples: This one will do all right, more or less.
We’ll be there at eight, more or less.

headword: more someone or something than one can shake a stick at

senses.definition: a lot; too many to count.
examples: There were more snakes than you could shake a stick at.
There are lots of flowers in the field—more than one can shake a stick at.

senses.definition: more of something, such as trouble or something bad, than a person can endure.
examples: This news is more than I can bear!
I’ve heard enough of this horrid music. It’s more than I can stand.

senses.definition: more than one thought one would get.
senses.notes: Usually in reference to trouble or difficulty.
examples: When Betsy brought home the sweet little puppy for a companion, she got more than she bargained for. That animal has cost her hundreds of dollars in medical bills.
I got more than I bargained for when I took this job.

senses.definition: the more people there are, the happier they will be.
examples: Of course you can have a ride with us! The more the merrier.
The manager hired a new employee even though there’s not enough work for all of us now. Oh, well, the more the merrier.

headword: more (to something) than meets the eye

senses.definition: hidden values or facts in something.
examples: There is more to that problem than meets the eye.
What makes you think that there is more than meets the eye?

senses.definition: the morning after a night spent drinking, when one has a hangover.
examples: Oh, I’ve got a headache. Talk about the morning after the night before!
It looked like a case of the morning after the night before, and Frank asked for some aspirin.

headword: move heaven and earth to do something

senses.definition: to make a major effort to do something.
examples: “I’ll move heaven and earth to be with you, Mary,” said Bill.
I had to move heaven and earth to get there on time.
Your father and I had to move heaven and earth to pay for your braces and your college bills, and what thanks do we get?

senses.definition: to attempt to displace someone or take over someone’s property, interests, or relationships.
senses.notes: [with someone] Slang, especially criminal slang. Compare this with muscle in (on someone or something).
examples: Look here, pal, Sally’s my girl. Are you trying to move in on me?
It looks like the southside gang is trying to move in. We’ll have to teach them a lesson.

senses.definition: to move into someone’s household.
examples: My mother-in-law moved in on us for two months.
I wouldn’t move in on you without an invitation.

senses.definition: to move closer to someone or something, especially with a camera.
examples: Now, slowly move in on the cereal box. This will be a great advertisement.
Hold the camera very steady and move in on the baby.

senses.definition: to get started in a new enterprise, job, etc.
examples: I moved into a new job last week. It’s very exciting work.
John moved into a new line of work, too.

senses.definition: to advance (oneself) and become successful.
examples: The harder I work, the more I move up in the world.
Keep your eye on John. He’s really moving up.

senses.definition: people who get things done; people who are productive and cause other people to be productive; people who create and produce.
examples: The trouble with the ABC Company is that all the movers and shakers are leaving to take jobs elsewhere.
It seems as if all the movers and shakers of the world are employed by a very small number of large firms.

senses.definition: a lot of excitement about nothing.
senses.notes: This is the title of a play by Shakespeare. Do not confuse ado with adieu.
examples: All the commotion about the new tax law turned out to be much ado about nothing.
Your promises always turn out to be much ado about nothing.

senses.definition: very visible or evident.
examples: John was much in evidence during the conference.
Your influence is much in evidence. I appreciate your efforts.

senses.definition: wanted or desired very much; highly desirable.
examples: This kind of crystal is much sought after. It’s very rare.
Sally is a great singer. She’s much sought after.

senses.definition: to make something less clear; to make matters confusing; to create difficulty where there was none before.
examples: Things were going along quite smoothly until you came along and muddied the water.
The events of the past month have muddied the water as far as our proposed joint venture is concerned.

senses.definition: to think about something; to ponder or worry about something.
examples: That’s an interesting idea, but I’ll have to mull it over.
I’ll mull over your suggestions and report to you next week.

senses.definition: don’t spread the secret.
examples: Don’t tell anyone what I told you. Remember, mum’s the word.
Okay, mum’s the word. Your secret is safe with me.

senses.definition: very destructive or harmful to something.
examples: Running a marathon is murder on your knees.
This dry weather is murder on my crops.

senses.definition: to try forcefully to displace someone or take over someone’s property, interests, or relationships.
senses.notes: Slang, especially criminal slang. Compare this with move in (on someone or something).
examples: Are you trying to muscle in on my scheme?
If you try to muscle in, you’ll be facing big trouble.

senses.definition: something that you must do.
senses.notes: Informal. Preceded by be, become, or seem like.
examples: When you’re in San Francisco, see the Golden Gate Bridge. It’s a must.
It’s a must that you brush your teeth after every meal.

senses.definition: to build up one’s courage; to call or bring forth one’s courage.
examples: I mustered my courage and dove from the high diving board.
He had to muster up all his courage in order to attend the dance.

headword: my gut tells me (that) something is so

senses.definition: my instincts tell me that something is so.
senses.notes: This refers to one’s gut reaction or gut response, that is, the way someone feels about something.
examples: My gut tells me that her idea is a sound one.
This looks good on paper, but my gut tells me that it is all wrong.

senses.definition: one’s spouse.
senses.notes: Informal. See also the one and only.
examples: Look at the time. I’ve got to get home to my one and only.
You’re my one and only. There is no one else for me.

senses.definition: to get a firm and final decision from someone (on something).
examples: I want you to find Bob and get an answer from him. Nail him down one way or the other.
Please nail down John on the question of signing the contract.

senses.definition: to get a firm and final decision (from someone) on something.
examples: Find Bob and nail down an answer.
Let’s get in touch with John and nail down this contract.

senses.definition: the human eye, unassisted by optics, such as a telescope, microscope, or spectacles.
examples: I can’t see the bird’s markings with the naked eye.
The scientist could see nothing in the liquid with the naked eye, but with the aid of a microscope, she identified the bacteria.
That’s how it appears to the naked eye.

senses.definition: goal or purpose.
examples: The name of the game is sell. You must sell, sell, sell if you want to make a living.
Around here, the name of the game is look out for yourself.

senses.definition: to give someone (usually a baby) the name of another person.
examples: We named our baby after my aunt.
My parents named me for my grandfather.

senses.definition: close or handy (to someone).
senses.notes: See also at hand; close at hand.
examples: Do you have a pencil near at hand?
My dictionary isn’t near at hand.

senses.definition: exactly even, especially in a race or a contest.
examples: John and Tom finished the race neck and neck.
Mary and Ann were neck and neck in the spelling contest. Their scores were tied.

headword: need something like a hole in the head

senses.definition: not to need something at all.
examples: I need a housecat like I need a hole in the head!
She needs a car like she needs a hole in the head.

senses.definition: to require something in a very big hurry.
examples: Yes, I’m in a hurry! I need it yesterday!
When do I need it? Now! Now! No, I need it yesterday!

senses.definition: not any recognizable thing; not any recognizable category.
examples: The car that they drove up in was neither fish nor fowl. It must have been made out of spare parts.
This proposal is neither fish nor fowl. I can’t tell what you’re proposing.

senses.definition: of no consequence or meaning; irrelevant and immaterial.
examples: Whether you go to the movie or stay at home is neither here nor there.
Your comment—though interesting—is neither here nor there.

senses.definition: no sign or indication (of someone or something).
examples: We could find neither hide nor hair of him. I don’t know where he is.
There has been no one here—neither hide nor hair—for the last three days.

senses.definition: do not worry; have confidence.
examples: I’ll be there on time—never fear.
I’ll help you, never fear.

senses.definition: not in one’s experience.
examples: Never in my life have I been so insulted!
He said that never in his life had he seen such an ugly painting.

senses.definition: forget it; pay no more attention (to something).
examples: I wanted to talk to you, but never mind. It wasn’t important.
Never mind. I’m sorry to bother you.

senses.definition: never would have thought something to be the case.
examples: He was the one who did it? I never would have guessed.
I never would have guessed that he wanted the job. He kept it a very good secret.

senses.definition: knew it all the time because it was so obvious.
senses.notes: Sarcastic. Not used in other tenses.
examples: I never would have guessed that he wanted the job. He only begged and begged for it.
Now she wants to go back home? I never would have guessed! She has been homesick for days.

senses.definition: a person who has recently been hired; a newly employed person.
examples: Anne is our new hire who will begin work Tuesday.
The accounting department is full of new hires.

senses.definition: a renewed and revitalized outlook on life.
examples: Getting the job offer was a new lease on life.
When I got out of the hospital, I felt as if I had a new lease on life.

senses.definition: the person living in the house or apartment closest to one’s own.
examples: My next-door neighbor came over to borrow a shovel.
I will be visiting our next-door neighbor if you need me.

senses.definition: someone’s closest living relative or relatives.
examples: The police notified the dead man’s next of kin.
My next of kin lives 800 miles away.

senses.definition: hardly anything; almost nothing.
examples: This car’s worth next to nothing. It’s full of rust.
I bought this antique chair for next to nothing.

senses.definition: near to someone or something; adjacent to someone or something.
examples: I live next to a bank.
Please sit next to me.

senses.definition: enough of some quality; adequately; sufficiently.
examples: It is nice and cool this evening.
I think your steak is nice and done now and probably overcooked.

senses.definition: to charge someone many small amounts of money; to assess many small fees against someone.
examples: We will not stay at that resort again. They nickel and dime you to death in that place. There is a charge for everything.
Tuition at the university hasn’t gone up in two years but other small fees have. They really nickel and dime you there.

senses.definition: a night of celebrating (at one or more places in a town).
examples: Did you enjoy your night on the town?
After we got the contract signed, we celebrated with a night on the town.

senses.definition: someone who usually stays up very late.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Anne’s a real night owl. She never goes to bed before 2 and sleeps till noon.
Jack’s a night owl and is at his best after midnight.

senses.definition: something that is of interest to people only for a short time.
examples: Don’t worry about the story about you in the newspaper. It’ll be a nine days’ wonder, and then people will forget.
The elopement of Jack and Anne was a nine days’ wonder. Now people never mention it.

senses.definition: a job with regular and normal hours.
examples: I wouldn’t want a nine-to-five job. I like the freedom I have as my own boss.
I used to work nights, but now I have a nine-to-five job.

senses.definition: almost even; almost tied.
examples: The horses ran nip and tuck for the first half of the race. Then my horse pulled ahead.
In the football game last Saturday, both teams were nip and tuck throughout the game.

senses.definition: to put an end to something at an early stage.
examples: John is getting into bad habits, and it’s best to nip them in the bud.
There was trouble in the classroom, but the teacher nipped it in the bud.

senses.definition: Not a big problem!
examples: It didn’t hurt. No big deal!
It isn’t a problem. No big deal!

senses.definition: It can’t be done.; I can’t do it.
examples: Sorry, John. No can do. I can’t sell you this one. I’ve promised it to Mrs. Smith.
BILL: Please fix this clock today. BOB: No can do. It’ll take a week to get the parts.

senses.definition: I have nothing to say on this matter.
examples: Q: When did you stop beating your dog? A: No comment.
Q: Georgie, did you chop down the cherry tree? A: No comment.

senses.definition: surely; without a doubt; undoubtedly.
examples: He will be here again tomorrow, no doubt.
No doubt you will require a ride home?

senses.definition: lots of something.
examples: It was a wonderful banquet. They had no end of good food.
Tom is a real problem. He’s no end of trouble.

senses.definition: someone is not slow; someone is not wasting time.
senses.notes: Refers to a person moving too fast to allow flies to light.
examples: Of course I work fast. I go as fast as I can. There are no flies on me.
There are no flies on Robert. He does his work very fast and very well.

senses.definition: nothing important or worth noticing.
examples: It’s okay, but it’s no great shakes.
I like John, but he’s no great shakes when it comes to sports.

senses.definition: no anger or resentment.
senses.notes: Informal. No can be replaced with any.
examples: I hope you don’t have any hard feelings.
No, I have no hard feelings.

senses.definition: It is all right. No one or nothing has been harmed.
examples: It’s okay. No harm done.
A: I am sorry I stepped on your toe. B: No harm done.

senses.definition: with no restraints.
examples: I intend to argue it out with Mary, no holds barred.
When Ann negotiates a contract, she goes in with no holds barred and comes out with a good contract.

headword: no ifs, ands, or buts about it

senses.definition: absolutely no discussion, dissension, or doubt about something.
examples: I want you there exactly at eight, no ifs, ands, or buts about it.
This is the best television set available for the money, no buts about it.

senses.definition: a serious matter.
examples: It’s no joke when you miss the last train.
It’s certainly no joke when you have to walk home.

senses.definition: honestly; [someone is] not joking or lying.
examples: No kidding, you really got an A in geometry?
I really did, no kidding.

senses.definition: a serious matter.
examples: Be serious. This is no laughing matter.
This disease is no laughing matter. It’s quite deadly.

headword: no love lost (between someone and someone else)

senses.definition: no friendship wasted between someone and someone else (because they are enemies).
examples: Ever since their big argument, there has been no love lost between Tom and Bill.
You can tell by the way that Jane is acting toward Ann that there is no love lost.

senses.definition: in any event; without regard to what happens (in the future).
examples: We’ll be there on time, no matter what.
No matter what happens, we’ll still be friends.

senses.definition: If one has not had any information about someone or something for some time, it means that all is well, since one would have heard if anything bad or unfortunate had occurred.
examples: I haven’t heard from my son since he left for college, but I suppose no news is good news.
I think Joan would have heard by now if she hadn’t got the job. No news is good news.

senses.definition: no purpose in doing something.
examples: There is no point in locking the barn door now that the horse has been stolen.
There’s no point is crying over spilled milk.

senses.definition: no difficulty for someone; no concern of someone.
examples: It’s no skin off my nose if she wants to act that way.
She said it was no skin off her teeth if we wanted to sell the house.

senses.definition: an expression indicating that something has been done quickly and obediently.
examples: When Sally asked for someone to open the window, it was no sooner said than done.
As Jane opened the window, she said, “No sooner said than done.”

senses.definition: not young (anymore).
examples: I don’t get around very well anymore. I’m no spring chicken, you know.
Even though John is no spring chicken, he still plays tennis twice a week.

senses.definition: no difficulty; do not worry.
examples: Of course I can have your car repaired by noon. No sweat.
You’d like a red one? No problem.

senses.definition: do not enter.
senses.notes: Usually seen on a sign. Not usually spoken.
examples: The sign on the tree said, “No Trespassing.” So we didn’t go in.
The angry farmer chased us out of the field shouting, “Get out! Don’t you see the no trespassing sign?”

senses.definition: no choice about it; no other interpretation of it.
senses.notes: Folksy. Note the form there’s rather than there are.
examples: You have to go to the doctor whether you like it or not. There’s no two ways about it.
This letter means you’re in trouble with the tax people. There’s no two ways about it.

senses.definition: a situation where there is no correct or satisfactory solution.
examples: The general was too weak to fight and too proud to surrender. It was a no-win situation.
The huge dog my father gave us as a gift eats too much. If we get rid of the dog, my father will be insulted. If we keep it, we will go broke buying food for it. This is a classic no-win situation.

senses.definition: not surprising.
examples: No wonder the baby is crying. She’s wet.
It’s no wonder that plant died. You watered it too much.

senses.definition: a sensible and wise person who is not easily deceived.
examples: Mary’s nobody’s fool. She knows Jack would try to cheat her.
Anne looks as though she’s not very bright, but she’s nobody’s fool.

senses.definition: to fall asleep, usually while sitting up.
examples: Jack nodded off during the minister’s sermon.
Father always nods off after Sunday lunch.

senses.definition: not of someone’s concern.
examples: Q: When are you going to leave for home? A: None of your business.
How I manage to keep thin is none of your business.

senses.definition: the very person.
examples: The new building was opened by none other than the mayor.
Jack’s wife turned out to be none other than my cousin.

senses.definition: not knowing any more.
examples: I was none the wiser about the project after the lecture. It was a complete waste of time.
Anne tried to explain the situation tactfully to Jack, but in the end, he was none the wiser.

senses.definition: no worse because of use or effort.
examples: I lent my car to John. When I got it back, it was none the worse for wear.
I had a hard day today, but I’m none the worse for wear.

senses.definition: not very something; not at all something.
examples: The towels in the bathroom were none too clean.
It was none too warm in their house.

senses.definition: to investigate; to check (into something).
examples: I don’t have an answer to your question, but I’ll nose around and see what I can find out.
I’ll nose about, too. Who knows what we’ll find out?

senses.definition: to move into something, front end first.
examples: Slowly the car nosed into its parking place.
You must nose in very carefully.

senses.definition: to push someone away; to exclude someone.
examples: Where I work someone is always trying to nose me out. I’d hate to lose my job.
John nosed out Bill from the team.

senses.definition: none at all.
examples: Am I unhappy? Not a bit.
I don’t want any mashed potatoes. Not a bit!

headword: not able to call one’s time one’s own

senses.definition: too busy; so busy as not to be in charge of one’s own schedule.
senses.notes: Informal. Not able to is often expressed as can’t.
examples: It’s been so busy around here that I haven’t been able to call my time my own.
She can’t call her time her own these days.

senses.definition: unable to continue (doing something—even living).
senses.notes: Not able to is often expressed as can’t.
examples: I just can’t go on this way.
Before her death, she left a note saying she was not able to go on.

senses.definition: unable to prevent or control something.
senses.notes: Not able to is often expressed as can’t.
examples: I’m sorry about being late. I wasn’t able to help it.
Bob can’t help being boring.

headword: not able to see the forest for the trees

senses.definition: allowing many details of a situation to obscure the situation as a whole.
senses.notes: Not able to is often expressed as can’t.
examples: The solution is obvious. You missed it because you can’t see the forest for the trees.
She suddenly realized that she hadn’t been able to see the forest for the trees.

senses.definition: to have to go to the bathroom urgently.
senses.notes: Also literal in a general sense. Informal.
examples: Mom, I can’t wait.
Driver, stop the bus! My little boy can’t wait.

senses.definition: to make someone ill; [for something one has eaten] to give one minor stomach distress.
examples: Fried foods don’t agree with Tom.
I always have onions in my garden, but I never eat them. They just don’t agree with me.

senses.definition: nobody.
senses.notes: Informal. See also not tell a (living) soul.
examples: No one was there—not a living soul.
Not a living soul saw me leave.

headword: not all something is cracked up to be
altForms: not what something is cracked up to be

senses.definition: not as good as something is said to be.
senses.notes: Informal. Not always in the negative.
examples: This isn’t a very good pen. It’s not all it’s cracked up to be.
Is this one all it’s cracked up to be?
This restaurant isn’t what it’s cracked up to be.

senses.definition: just in time; with no extra time.
examples: Hurry, hurry! There’s not a moment to spare!
I arrived without a moment to spare.

senses.definition: to show no signs of distress even when something bad happens or something shocking is said.
examples: Sam didn’t bat an eyelid when the mechanic told him how much the car repairs would cost.
The pain of the broken arm must have hurt Sally terribly, but she did not bat an eyelid.

senses.definition: not to believe what one is seeing; to be shocked or dumbfounded at what one is seeing.
examples: I walked into the room and I couldn’t believe my eyes. All the furniture had been stolen!
When Jimmy opened his birthday present, he could hardly believe his eyes. Just what he wanted!

senses.definition: experienced; knowledgeable in the ways of the world.
examples: I know what’s going on. I wasn’t born yesterday.
Sally knows the score. She wasn’t born yesterday.

headword: not breathe a word (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to keep a secret about someone or something.
examples: Don’t worry. I won’t breathe a word about the problem.
Please don’t breathe a word about Bob and his problems.

headword: not breathe a word of it

senses.definition: not to tell something (to anyone).
examples: Don’t worry. I won’t breathe a word of it.
Tom won’t breathe a word of it.

senses.definition: not accept something (to be true).
examples: You may think so, but I don’t buy it.
The police wouldn’t buy his story.

senses.definition: not by a great amount; not.
examples: Did I win the race? Not by a long shot.
Not by a long shot did she complete the assignment.

headword: not care two hoots (about someone or something)
altForms: not give two hoots (about someone or something)
not give a hang (about someone or something)
not give a hoot (about someone or something)

senses.definition: not to care at all about someone or something.
examples: I don’t care two hoots about whether you go to the picnic or not.
She doesn’t give a hoot about me. Why should I care?
I don’t give a hang about it.

headword: not enough room to swing a cat

senses.definition: not very much space.
examples: Their living room was very small. There wasn’t enough room to swing a cat.
How can you work in a small room like this? There’s not enough room to swing a cat.

senses.definition: not at all; not even for a short amount of time; never.
examples: I don’t want you to leave. Not for a moment!
I could not wish such a horrible punishment on anyone. Not for a moment!

senses.definition: not for anything (no matter what its value).
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples. The order of love nor money is fixed.
examples: I won’t do it for love nor money.
He said he wouldn’t do it—not for the world.
She said no, not for anything in the world.
Me, go there? Not on your life!

senses.definition: not available to take new passengers.
examples: The taxi was going to pick someone up at a nearby hotel and was not for hire.
The taxi had a lighted sign that said it was not for hire.

senses.definition: not to be talked about openly; secret.
examples: Please tell no one about this. It’s not for publication.
This report is not for publication, so keep the results to yourself.

senses.definition: not to worry about something anymore.
senses.notes: A polite way of accepting someone’s apology.
examples: It’s okay. Please don’t give it another thought.
You should not give it another thought. No one was bothered at all.

headword: not give someone the time of day

senses.definition: to ignore someone (usually out of dislike).
examples: Mary won’t speak to Sally. She won’t give her the time of day.
I couldn’t get an appointment with Mr. Smith. He wouldn’t even give me the time of day.

senses.definition: okay; pretty good.
examples: Say, this roast beef isn’t half bad.
Hey, Sally! You’re not half bad!

headword: not hold a stick to someone or something
altForms: not hold a candle to someone or something

senses.definition: not to be nearly as good as someone or something.
examples: Sally is much faster than Bob. Bob doesn’t hold a stick to Sally.
This TV doesn’t hold a candle to that one. That one is much better.

senses.definition: to make no sense; to be illogical.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Said of ideas, arguments, etc., not people. It means that the idea has holes in it.
examples: Your argument doesn’t hold water.
This scheme won’t work because it can’t hold water.

senses.definition: not to harm anything or anyone, even a tiny insect.
senses.notes: Also with other forms of negation.
examples: Ted would not even hurt a flea. He could not have struck Bill.
Ted would never hurt a flea, and he would not hit anyone as you claim.

headword: not in the same league with someone or something

senses.definition: not anywhere nearly as good as someone or something.
examples: John isn’t in the same league with Bob and his friends.
This house isn’t in the same league with our old one.

headword: not know beans (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to know nothing about someone or something.
examples: Bill doesn’t know beans about flying an airplane.
When it comes to flying, I don’t know beans.
She doesn’t know beans about Bill.

headword: not know enough to come in out of the rain

senses.definition: to be very stupid.
examples: Bob is so stupid he doesn’t know enough to come in out of the rain.
You can’t expect very much from somebody who doesn’t know enough to come in out of the rain.

senses.definition: to be stupid, innocent, and naive.
senses.notes: Slang. This nothing is not replaced with something. Usually with don’t, as in the examples below.
examples: Old John—he don’t know from nothing.
What do you expect from somebody who don’t know from nothing?

senses.definition: not to realize how destructive or harmful one’s strength can be.
examples: I didn’t mean to hurt you. I guess I don’t know my own strength.
He might break the door down by accident. He doesn’t know his own strength and could end up pushing too hard against the door.

senses.definition: not to know someone at all.
examples: I wouldn’t recognize John if I saw him. I don’t know him from Adam.
What does she look like? I don’t know her from Adam.

altForms: not know which way to turn

senses.definition: to have no idea about what to do (about something).
examples: I was so confused I didn’t know where to turn.
We needed help, but we didn’t know which way to turn.

headword: not know whether one is coming or going
altForms: not know if one is coming or going

senses.definition: to be very confused.
examples: I’m so busy that I don’t know if I’m coming or going.
You look as if you don’t know whether you’re coming or going.

headword: not lift a finger (to help someone)
altForms: not lift a hand (to help someone)

senses.definition: to do nothing to help someone.
senses.notes: The someone is anyone in the negative.
examples: They wouldn’t lift a finger to help us.
Can you imagine that they wouldn’t lift a finger?
Sally refused to lift a hand to help her own sister.

senses.definition: to be about to die.
examples: Our dog is nearly twelve years old and not long for this world.
I’m so tired. I think I’m not long for this world.

senses.definition: not having a lot of money; not having an unlimited supply of money.
examples: I can’t afford a car like that. I’m not made of money you know.
There is only so much they can pay. They’re not made of money.

senses.definition: not to miss observing any part of what is going on.
senses.notes: Usually with do as in the examples below.
examples: Ted doesn’t miss much. He is very alert.
The puppy doesn’t miss a thing. He sees every move you make.

senses.definition: not to miss experiencing something that really was not worth experiencing anyway.
senses.notes: Sarcastic. Usually with do as in the examples below.
examples: I missed the big sales meeting last week, but I understand I didn’t miss much.
BILL: I didn’t see that new movie that is showing at the theater. TOM: You didn’t miss much.

senses.definition: to remain perfectly motionless.
examples: Be quiet. Sit there and don’t move a muscle.
I was so tired I couldn’t move a muscle.

senses.definition: not even a tiny bit.
examples: I won’t give you any at all! Not one iota!
I did not get one iota of encouragement from any of those people.

senses.definition: not one’s role to do something.
examples: It was not my place to criticize my boss.
It was Bill’s place to ask the questions, not yours.

senses.definition: not to say anything at all; not to tell something (to anyone).
examples: Don’t worry, I’ll keep your secret. I won’t even open my mouth.
Have no fear. I won’t utter a word.
I don’t know how they found out. I didn’t even open my mouth.

headword: not see farther than the end of one’s nose
altForms: not see past the end of one’s nose

senses.definition: not to care about what is not actually present or obvious; not to care about the future or about what is happening elsewhere or to other people.
senses.notes: Could be literal or an exaggeration in a heavy fog or in dim light.
examples: Mary can’t see past the end of her nose. She doesn’t care about what will happen in the future as long as she’s comfortable now.
Jack’s been accused of not seeing farther than the end of his nose. He refuses to expand the company and look for new markets.

senses.definition: not to go somewhere.
examples: I wouldn’t set foot in John’s room. I’m very angry at him.
He never set foot here.

senses.definition: not to appear (somewhere).
examples: After what she said, she had better not show her face around here again.
If I don’t say I’m sorry, I’ll never be able to show my face again.

senses.definition: not to sleep at all.
examples: I couldn’t sleep a wink last night.
Ann hasn’t been able to sleep a wink for a week.

senses.definition: not something one prefers.
examples: Playing cards isn’t her cup of tea.
Sorry, that’s not my cup of tea.

headword: not take no for an answer

senses.definition: not to accept someone’s refusal.
senses.notes: Informal. A polite way of being insistent.
examples: Now, you must drop over and see us tomorrow. We won’t take no for an answer.
I had to go. They just wouldn’t take no for an answer.

senses.definition: not to reveal something to anyone.
examples: You secret is safe with me. I won’t tell a living soul.
Promise you won’t tell a soul, but I’m engaged.

senses.definition: not adequate.
senses.notes: Informal. See also up to snuff; up to scratch.
examples: Sorry, your paper isn’t up to scratch. Please do it over again.
The performance was not up to snuff.

senses.definition: worthless.
examples: This land is all swampy. It’s not worth a dime.
This pen I bought isn’t worth a dime. It has no ink.
It’s not worth a red cent.

headword: not worth a hill of beans

senses.definition: worthless.
examples: Your advice isn’t worth a hill of beans.
This old cow isn’t worth a plugged nickel.

senses.definition: not important enough to require a comment.
examples: There are others, but they are not worth mentioning.
A small number of books hint at the phenomenon, but they aren’t worth mentioning.

senses.definition: not worth apologizing for.
examples: This isn’t a problem at all. It’s not worth mentioning.
No need to apologize to me. No harm done. It’s not worth mentioning.

senses.definition: not worth bothering with; not worth spending time on.
examples: It’s not worth my while to discuss it with you.
Don’t bother trying to collect money from them. It isn’t worth your while.

senses.definition: not important enough to require a comment.
examples: Don’t bother with it. It isn’t worth the trouble.
There is no point in trying to get the spot out of the carpet. It isn’t worth the trouble.

senses.definition: very thin or emaciated.
examples: Bill has lost so much weight. He’s nothing but skin and bones.
Look at Bill. He’s just skin and bones.
That old horse is all skin and bones. I won’t ride it.

senses.definition: only something; just something.
examples: Joan drinks nothing but milk.
Fred buys nothing but expensive clothes.

senses.definition: no.
examples: No, I won’t do that. Nothing doing.
BOB: Will you help me with this? BILL: Nothing doing.

senses.definition: no; absolutely not.
examples: I didn’t tear your jacket—nothing of the kind!
Did I break your vase? Nothing of the kind!

senses.definition: nothing like that.
examples: That’s not true. We did nothing of the kind!
She did nothing of the kind! She wasn’t even there!

senses.definition: more or less the same as something bad; as bad as something.
examples: His behavior was nothing short of criminal.
Climbing those mountains alone is nothing short of suicide.

senses.definition: no choice; no choice in the selection; not enough of something to make a choice.
examples: I went to the store looking for new shoes, but there was nothing to choose from.
By the time I got around to selecting a team of helpers, there was nothing to choose from.

senses.definition: all right.
senses.notes: Folksy. Said in answer to the question “How are you?”
examples: Bob said he has nothing to complain about.
BILL: How’re you doing, Bob? BOB: Nothing to complain about, Bill. Yourself?

senses.definition: it is easy; no difficulty involved.
examples: Driving a car is easy. There’s nothing to it.
Geometry is fun to learn. There’s nothing to it.

senses.definition: not small or unimportant.
examples: It’s not a lot of money, but it’s nothing to sneeze at.
Our house isn’t a mansion, but it’s nothing to sneeze at.

senses.definition: not many; not much.
examples: JOHN: What’s happening around here? BILL: Nothing to speak of.
MARY: Has there been any rain in the last week? SALLY: Nothing to speak of.

senses.definition: nothing exciting or interesting.
examples: I’ve been busy, but nothing to write home about.
I had a dull week—nothing to write home about.

senses.definition: You cannot achieve anything if you do not try.
examples: Come on, John. Give it a try. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.
I felt as if I had to take the chance. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.

senses.definition: Pay attention to what is going to be said!
senses.notes: In the manner of an announcement over the public address system, especially in the military.
examples: Now hear this! You have to turn off the television and go to bed!
Now hear this! Now hear this! Everyone is ordered to abandon ship.

senses.definition: at this time and no other.
examples: This is your only chance, John. It’s now or never.
I decided that it was now or never, and jumped.

senses.definition: I was interrupted, so please help me remember what I was talking about.
examples: Now, where was I! I think I lost my place.
Q: Where was I? A: You had just described the War of 1812.

senses.definition: not nearly.
examples: We have nowhere near enough wood for the winter.
They’re nowhere near ready for the game.

senses.definition: canceled; worthless.
examples: I tore the contract up, and the entire agreement became null and void.
The judge declared the whole business null and void.

headword: a number of things or people

senses.definition: some things or people, in an indefinite amount.
examples: I subscribe to a number of different magazines.
A number of people are here now.

senses.definition: to keep resenting and disliking someone over a period of time.
senses.notes: See also bear a grudge (against someone).
examples: Sally is still nursing a grudge against Mary.
How long can anyone nurse a grudge?

senses.definition: to provide medical care that will restore someone to good health.
examples: After my operation, my mother nursed me back to health.
Lots of good food and loving care will help nurse you back to health.

senses.definition: the basic facts about something; the practical details of something.
examples: Tom knows all about the nuts and bolts of the chemical process.
Ann is familiar with the nuts and bolts of public relations.

headword: nuzzle up to someone or something

senses.definition: to nestle against someone or something, especially if pressing with the nose or face.
examples: The puppy nuzzled up to its mother.
Tom nuzzled up to Jane and asked her for a kiss.

senses.definition: to come into someone’s mind.
examples: It occurred to me that you might be hungry after your long journey.
Would it ever occur to you that I want to be left alone?

altForms: an ocean of someone or something

senses.definition: a very large amount of something.
examples: The naughty student was in oceans of trouble.
After a week of vacation, there was an ocean of work to do.

senses.definition: an unusual or atypical person or thing.
examples: I’m odd man out because I’m not wearing a tie.
You had better learn to work a computer unless you want to be odd man out.

senses.definition: an extra or spare something.
examples: The tailor repaired the odd loose button on my shirt.
When I travel, I might buy the odd trinket or two, but I never spend much money.

senses.definition: small, miscellaneous things.
examples: There were lots of odds and ends in the attic, but nothing of real value.
I had the whole house cleaned up except for a few odds and ends that didn’t seem to belong anywhere.

senses.definition: an atmosphere of excessive holiness or piety.
examples: I hate their house. There’s such an odor of sanctity, with Bibles and religious pictures everywhere.
People are made nervous by Jane’s odor of sanctity. She’s always praying for people or doing good works and never has any fun.

senses.definition: old enough to marry or to sign legal agreements.
senses.notes: See also come of age. Preceded by be or seem.
examples: Now that Mary is of age, she can buy her own car.
When I’m of age, I’m going to get married and move to the city.

senses.definition: how shocking; how dare (someone).
senses.notes: Informal. The speaker is exclaiming that someone is being very cheeky or rude.
examples: How dare you talk to me that way! Of all the nerve!
Imagine anyone coming to a formal dance in jeans. Of all the nerve!

senses.definition: Can you imagine?; Imagine that!
examples: She wore jeans to the dance. Of all things!
Billy, stop eating the houseplant! Of all things!

senses.definition: serving someone well; to the good of someone.
examples: I can’t believe that this proposal is of benefit to anyone.
Oh, I’m sure it’s of benefit.

senses.definition: interesting to someone.
examples: This is no longer of any interest.
This is of little interest to me.

senses.definition: by one’s own choice, without coercion.
examples: I wish that Sally would choose to do it of her own accord.
I’ll have to order her to do it because she won’t do it of her own free will.

senses.definition: of the finest quality.
senses.notes: [someone] From the system of grading pearls for quality.
examples: She is a very fine lady—a pearl of the first water.
Tom is of the first water—a true gentleman.

senses.definition: holding attitudes or ideas that were popular and important in the past, but which are no longer considered relevant or in line with modern trends.
examples: Grammar was not much taught in my son’s school, but fortunately he had a teacher of the old school.
Aunt Jane is of the old school. She never goes out without wearing a hat and gloves.

senses.definition: started up and going.
senses.notes: Also literal, as in a footrace.
examples: The car was finally loaded by 9:30, and we were off and running.
The construction of the building was going to take two years, but we were off and running, and it appeared we would finish on schedule.

senses.definition: unrealistic; inexact; wrong.
examples: I’m afraid you’re off base when you state that this problem will take care of itself.
You’re way off base!

senses.definition: not located on the grounds of a college or university.
examples: Tom has an apartment off campus.
The dean is off campus and cannot be reached.

senses.definition: not exactly in the center or middle.
examples: The arrow hit the target a little off-center.
The picture hanging over the chair is a little off-center.

senses.definition: slight possibility.
examples: I need your phone number on the off chance I need more help.
There’s an off chance that we might be hiring next month.

senses.definition: not the exact color (that one wants).
examples: The book cover used to be red, but now it’s a little off-color.
The wall was painted off-color. I think it was meant to be orange.

senses.definition: in bad taste; rude, vulgar, or impolite.
examples: That joke you told was off-color and embarrassed me.
The nightclub act was a bit off-color.

senses.definition: not working at one’s job.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t talk to you until I’m off duty.
The police officer couldn’t help me because he was off duty.

senses.definition: away [from a place] very quickly.
examples: He finished his dinner and was off like a shot.
The thief grabbed the lady’s purse and was off like a shot.

senses.definition: forbidden.
examples: This area is off limits. You can’t go in there.
Don’t go there. It’s out of bounds.
That kind of behavior is off limits. Stop it!

senses.definition: crazy; silly.
examples: Sometimes, Bob, I think you’re off your rocker.
Good grief, John. You’re off your nut.
About this time of the day, I go off my trolley. I get so tired.

senses.definition: not in the busy time of the year.
examples: We don’t have much to do off season.
Things are very quiet around here off season.

senses.definition: someone or something is leaving.
senses.notes: Said on the departure of someone or something.
examples: It’s time to leave. Off I go.
Sally looked at the airplane taking off and said, “Off it goes.”

senses.definition: not broadcasting (a radio or television program).
examples: The radio audience won’t hear what you say when you’re off the air.
When the performers were off the air, the director told them how well they had done.

senses.definition: in an unfamiliar place; on a route that is not often traveled.
examples: Their home is in a quiet neighborhood, off the beaten track.
We like to stop there and admire the scenery. It’s off the track, but it’s worth the trip.

senses.definition: spontaneous; without preparation or rehearsal.
examples: Her remarks were off-the-cuff, but very sensible.
I’m not very good at making speeches off-the-cuff.

senses.definition: not quite exactly right.
examples: Her answer was a little off the mark.
You were off the mark when you said we would be a little late to the party. It was yesterday, in fact!

senses.definition: unofficial; informal.
examples: This is off the record, but I disagree with the mayor on this matter.
Although her comments were off the record, the newspaper published them anyway.

senses.definition: not concerned with the subject being discussed.
examples: I got off the subject and forgot what I was supposed to be talking about.
The speaker was off the subject, telling about his vacation in Hawaii.

headword: off the top of one’s head

senses.definition: quickly and without having to think or remember.
examples: I can’t think of the answer off the top of my head.
Jane can tell you the correct amount off the top of her head.

senses.definition: irrelevant and immaterial (comments).
examples: I’m afraid you’re off the track, John. Try again.
I’m sorry. I was thinking about dinner, and I got off the track.

senses.definition: odd; silly; unusual.
examples: Why are you so off-the-wall today?
This book is strange. It’s really off-the-wall.

senses.definition: with a good, fast beginning, possibly a head start.
examples: I got off to a running start in math this year.
The horses got off to a running start.

headword: old enough to be someone’s mother
altForms: old enough to be someone’s father

senses.definition: as old as someone’s parents.
senses.notes: Also literal. Usually a way of saying that a person is too old.
examples: You can’t go out with Bill. He’s old enough to be your father!
He married a woman who is old enough to be his mother.

senses.definition: It’s hard to stop doing things that are part of a habit, especially a habit that one is trying to break.
examples: A: My grandfather still uses hand signals when he turns right. B: Old habits die hard.
Old habits die hard and bad one’s last even longer.

headword: an old hand at doing something

senses.definition: someone who is experienced at doing something.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: I’m an old hand at fixing clocks.
He’s an old hand at changing diapers.

senses.definition: old-fashioned; outmoded.
senses.notes: Informal. Preceded by be, become, or seem.
examples: That’s a silly idea. It’s old hat.
Nobody does that anymore. That’s just old hat.

senses.definition: on a diagonal line; on a diagonal pathway or direction.
examples: The panels of the dress were cut on a bias.
The seamstress sewed the fabric on the bias.

senses.definition: on a debt.
examples: I paid twelve dollars on account last month. Wasn’t that enough?
I still have $100 due on account.

senses.definition: in battle or ready to go into battle.
examples: The soldier was on active duty for ten months.
That was a long time to be on active duty.

senses.definition: trying to lose weight by eating less food or specific foods.
examples: I didn’t eat any cake because I’m on a diet.
I’m getting too heavy. I’ll have to go on a diet.

senses.definition: knowing someone very well; good friends with someone.
examples: I’m on a first-name basis with John.
John and I are on a first-name basis.

senses.definition: involved in a useless journey or task.
examples: Bill went for an interview, but he was on a fool’s errand. The job had already been filled.
I was sent on a fool’s errand to buy some flowers. I knew the shop would be closed by then.

senses.definition: uncertain; indecisive.
examples: I don’t know about the picnic. It’s on again, off again. It depends on the weather.
Jane doesn’t know if she’s going to the picnic. She’s off again, on again about it.

senses.definition: on one’s hands and knees.
examples: I dropped a contact lens and spent an hour on all fours looking for it.
The baby can walk, but is on all fours most of the time anyway.

senses.definition: for any purpose; for any reason; no matter what.
senses.notes: Compare this with on no account.
examples: On any account, I’ll be there on time.
This doesn’t make sense on any account.

senses.definition: for examination, with the privilege of return.
examples: I ordered the merchandise on approval so I could send it back if I didn’t like it.
Sorry, you can’t buy this on approval. All sales are final.

senses.definition: with a very small amount of money.
examples: We lived on a shoestring for years before I got a good job.
John traveled to Florida on a shoestring.

senses.definition: an instance of extravagant spending.
examples: Bob went on a splurge and bought a new car.
Susan has been on another spending splurge! Look at that new furniture.

senses.definition: on a list of people waiting for an opportunity to do something.
senses.notes: [with one’s name] A can be replaced with the.
examples: I couldn’t get a seat on the plane, but I got on a waiting list.
There is no room for you, but we can put your name on the waiting list.

senses.definition: with great humility.
senses.notes: The form bended is obsolescent and occurs now only in this phrase.
examples: Do you expect me to come to you on bended knee and ask you for forgiveness?
The suitors came on bended knee and begged the attention of the princess.

senses.definition: aboard (on or in) a ship, bus, airplane, etc.
examples: Is there a doctor on board? We have a sick passenger.
When everyone is on board, we will leave.

senses.definition: employed by (someone); working with (someone).
examples: Our company has a computer specialist on board to advise us about automation.
Welcome to the company, Tom. We’re all glad you’re on board now.

senses.definition: located in the Broadway theater district of New York City; performed in the Broadway theater district.
examples: Our musical is the best thing on Broadway!
I want to be a star on Broadway someday.

senses.definition: ready to serve when called.
examples: I live a very hard life. I’m on call twenty hours a day.
I’m sorry, but I can’t go out tonight. I’m on call at the hospital.

senses.definition: located or being on the grounds of a college or university.
examples: Do you live on campus or off campus?
I don’t think that Lisa is on campus right now.

senses.definition: very happy.
examples: When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine.
When the check came, I was on cloud nine for days.
