senses.definition: having been placed in a store for sale, without transferring the title of the goods to the operator of the store.
examples: The artist placed his work in a gallery on consignment.
I will attempt to sell your clothing on consignment.

senses.definition: using credit; buying something using credit.
examples: I tried to buy a new suit on credit, but I was refused.
The Smiths buy everything on credit and are very much in debt.

senses.definition: at the exact center of something.
examples: The arrow hit the target on dead center.
When you put the flowers on the table, put them on dead center.

senses.definition: exactly correct.
examples: Mary is quite observant. Her analysis is on dead center.
My view isn’t on dead center, but it’s sensible.

senses.definition: on the deck of a boat or a ship.
examples: Everyone except the cook was on deck when the storm hit.
Just pull up the anchor and leave it on deck.

senses.definition: ready (to do something); ready to be next (at something).
examples: Ann, get on deck. You’re next.
Who’s on deck now?

senses.definition: at work; currently doing one’s work.
examples: I can’t help you now, but I’ll be on duty in about an hour.
Who is on duty here? I need some help.

senses.definition: really; indeed; in fact.
senses.notes: Used as an intensifier after who, what, when, where, how, nothing, nowhere.
examples: What on earth do you mean?
How in creation do you expect me to do that?
Who in the world do you think you are?
When on earth do you expect me to do this?

senses.definition: in luxury.
examples: If I had a million dollars, I’d be on easy street.
Everyone has problems, even people who live on easy street.

senses.definition: on (something’s own) edge.
examples: Can you stand a dime on edge?
You should store your records on edge, not flat.

senses.definition: nervous.
examples: I have really been on edge lately.
Why are you so on edge?

senses.definition: burning; being burned with flames.
examples: Help! My car is on fire!
That house on the corner is on fire!

senses.definition: by walking.
examples: My bicycle is broken, so I’ll have to travel on foot.
You can’t expect me to get there on foot! It’s twelve miles!

senses.definition: friendly with someone.
examples: I’m on good terms with Ann. I’ll ask her to help.
We’re on good terms now. Last week we were not.

senses.definition: waiting; temporarily halted.
senses.notes: See also put someone or something on hold.
examples: The building project is on hold while we try to find money to complete it.
We put our plans on hold until we finished school.

senses.definition: left waiting on a telephone line.
examples: I hate to call up someone and then end up on hold.
I waited on hold for ten minutes when I called city hall.

senses.definition: on the back of a horse.
examples: Anne rode on horseback across the field.
Because they loved horses, the couple decided to marry on horseback.

senses.definition: after having had an impulse or sudden thought.
examples: On impulse, Bob decided to buy a car.
I didn’t need a cellular telephone. I just bought it on impulse.

senses.definition: on the soil; on the land and not at sea.
examples: The flight was rough and I feel better now that I am back on land.
When I am at sea, I feel more relaxed than when I am on land.

senses.definition: connected to a remote computer.
examples: As soon as I get on line, I can check the balance of your account.
I was on line for an hour before I found out what I wanted to know.

senses.definition: a place, located in a place distant from the movie studio, where a movie is filmed.
examples: This movie was shot on location in Ontario.
The actress went on location in Spain for her latest film.

senses.definition: taking medicine for a current medical problem.
examples: I can’t drive the car since I am on medication.
He is on medication and hopes to be well soon.

senses.definition: for no reason; absolutely not.
examples: On no account will I lend you the money.
Will I say I’m sorry? Not on any account.

senses.definition: occasionally.
examples: We go out for dinner on occasion.
I enjoy going to a movie on occasion.

senses.definition: being as polite as possible.
examples: When we went out, the children were on their best behavior.
I try to be on my best behavior all the time.

senses.definition: standing up.
examples: Get on your feet. They are playing the national anthem.
I’ve been on my feet all day, and they hurt.

senses.definition: well and healthy, especially after an illness.
examples: I hope to be back on my feet next week.
I can help out as soon as I’m back on my feet.

senses.definition: cautious; watchful.
examples: Be on guard. There are pickpockets around here.
You had better be on your guard.

senses.definition: on one’s solemn oath; sincerely.
examples: On my honor, I’ll be there on time.
He promised on his honor that he’d pay me back next week.

senses.definition: occupying one’s thoughts; currently being thought about.
examples: You’ve been on my mind all day.
Do you have something on your mind? You look so serious.

senses.definition: not while one is at work.
examples: The boss made me write the report on my own time. That’s not fair.
Please make your personal telephone calls on your own time.

senses.definition: carried with one.
examples: Always carry identification on your person.
I’m sorry, I don’t have any money on my person.

senses.definition: alert.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also step on someone’s toes.
examples: You have to be on your toes if you want to be in this business.
My boss keeps me on my toes.

senses.definition: ordered with delivery expected.
examples: Your car is on order. It’ll be here in a few weeks.
I don’t have the part in stock, but it’s on order.

senses.definition: equal to someone or something.
examples: Your effort is simply not on par with what’s expected from you.
These two reports are right on par.

senses.definition: anxious; in suspense.
examples: I’ve been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news.
We were on pins and needles until we heard that your plane landed safely.

senses.definition: serving a period of probation.
examples: While Anne was on probation, she reported to the police regularly.
John was on probation for a year.

senses.definition: serving a trial period.
examples: All new members are on probation for a year.
I was on probation in my job for a full year before it became permanent.

senses.definition: intentionally; in a way that is meant or intended; not an accident.
examples: The bully stepped on my foot on purpose.
Jealously, Jimmy destroyed Billy’s sand castle on purpose.

senses.definition: offered for sale at a special low price.
examples: I won’t buy anything that’s not on sale.
I need a new coat, but I want to find a nice one on sale.

senses.definition: at the expected or desired time.
examples: The plane came in right on schedule.
Things have to happen on schedule in a theatrical performance.

senses.definition: having given something more thought; having reconsidered something.
examples: On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment.
On second thought, let’s not go to a movie.

senses.definition: because of someone.
examples: Don’t do it on my account.
They were late on Jane’s account.

senses.definition: constantly criticizing someone.
senses.notes: Slang. See also Get off someone’s case!
examples: I’m tired of your being on my case all the time.
It seems as if someone is always on his back.

senses.definition: on someone’s own self.
examples: All the blame fell on their heads.
I don’t think that all the criticism should be on my head.

headword: on someone’s or something’s last legs

senses.definition: to be almost worn out or finished.
examples: This building is on its last legs. It should be torn down.
I feel as if I’m on my last legs. I’m really tired.

senses.definition: on someone’s authority; with someone’s permission.
examples: I can’t do it on your say-so. I’ll have to get a written request.
BILL: I canceled the contract with the ABC Company. BOB: On whose say-so?

senses.definition: on someone’s own self.
examples: Why should all the responsibility fall on my shoulders?
She carries a tremendous amount of responsibility on her shoulders.

senses.definition: on friendly terms with someone.
senses.notes: Often in the negative. Compare this with on good terms (with someone).
examples: I’m not on speaking terms with Mary. We had a serious disagreement.
We’re not on speaking terms.

senses.definition: waiting for one’s turn, especially describing the status of travelers who wait near a train, plane, or bus, hoping that a seat will become available.
examples: The passenger waited on standby for an available seat.
The agent was able to seat all of the passengers on standby.

senses.definition: on schedule; exactly as predicted.
examples: Your estimate of the cost was right on target.
My prediction was not on target.

senses.definition: broadcasting (a radio or television program).
examples: The radio station came back on the air shortly after the storm.
We were on the air for two hours.

headword: on the alert (for someone or something)

senses.definition: watchful and attentive for someone or something.
examples: Be on the alert for pickpockets.
You should be on the alert when you cross the street in heavy traffic.

senses.definition: generally; usually.
examples: On the average, you can expect about a 10 percent failure rate.
This report looks okay, on the average.

senses.definition: alert, effective, and efficient.
examples: Sally has a lot on the ball.
You’ve got to be on the ball if you want to succeed in this business.

senses.definition: exactly right; thinking along the correct lines.
examples: That’s the right idea. Now you’re on the beam!
She’s not on the beam yet. Explain it to her again.

senses.definition: directing a session of court.
senses.notes: Also literal. Said of a judge.
examples: I have to go to court tomorrow. Who’s on the bench?
It doesn’t matter who’s on the bench. You’ll get a fair hearing.

senses.definition: sitting, waiting for a chance to play in a game.
senses.notes: In sports, such as basketball, football, soccer, etc.
examples: Bill is on the bench now. I hope he gets to play.
John played during the first quarter, but now he’s on the bench.

senses.definition: on a city block.
examples: John is the biggest kid on the block.
We had a party on the block last weekend.

senses.definition: on sale at auction; on the auction block.
examples: We couldn’t afford to keep up the house, so it was put on the block to pay the taxes.
That’s the finest painting I’ve ever seen on the block.

senses.definition: in an uncertain position between two statuses; undecided.
examples: Bill was on the borderline between an A and a B in biology.
Jane was on the borderline of joining the navy.

senses.definition: exactly right; in exactly the right place; at exactly the right time.
examples: That’s it! You’re right on the button.
He got here at one o’clock on the button.

senses.definition: as the opposite.
senses.notes: Compare this with to the contrary.
examples: I’m not ill. On the contrary, I’m very healthy.
She’s not in a bad mood. On the contrary, she’s as happy as a lark.

senses.definition: overly ready to defend oneself.
examples: John goes on the defensive when his athletic ability is questioned.
The child was on the defensive when questioned about cheating.

senses.definition: at exactly the right time.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Compare this with at sometime sharp.
examples: I’ll be there at noon on the dot.
I expect to see you here at eight o’clock on the dot.

senses.definition: very fast.
examples: Okay, you guys. Get over here on the double.
Get yourself into this house on the double.

senses.definition: superficially; from the way it looks.
examples: This looks like a serious problem on the face of it. It probably is minor, however.
On the face of it, it seems worthless.

senses.definition: undecided.
examples: Ann is on the fence about going to Mexico.
I wouldn’t be on the fence. I’d love to go.

senses.definition: not operating; not operating correctly.
examples: This vacuum cleaner is on the fritz. Let’s get it fixed.
How long has it been on the blink?

senses.definition: soon after something.
examples: There was a rainstorm on the heels of the windstorm.
The team held a victory celebration on the heels of their winning season.

senses.definition: soon to happen.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also in the offing.
examples: Do you know what’s on the horizon?
Who can tell what’s on the horizon?

headword: on the horns of a dilemma

senses.definition: bothered by having to decide between two things, people, etc.
examples: Mary found herself on the horns of a dilemma. She didn’t know which to choose.
I make up my mind easily. I’m not on the horns of a dilemma very often.

senses.definition: in a difficult position; subject to much criticism.
examples: I was really in the hot seat for a while.
Now that John is on the hot seat, no one is paying any attention to what I do.

senses.definition: at each hour on the hour mark.
examples: I have to take this medicine every hour on the hour.
I expect to see you there on the hour, not one minute before and not one minute after.

senses.definition: given away free by a merchant.
examples: “Here,” said the waiter, “have a cup of coffee on the house.”
I went to a restaurant last night. I was the 10,000th customer, so my dinner was on the house.

senses.definition: working; doing what one is expected to do.
examples: I’m always on the job when I should be.
I can depend on my furnace to be on the job day and night.

headword: on the lookout (for someone or something)

senses.definition: watchful for someone or something.
examples: Be on the lookout for signs of a storm.
I’m on the lookout for John, who is due here any minute.
Okay, you remain on the lookout for another hour.

senses.definition: running around free.
examples: Look out! There is a bear on the loose from the zoo.
Most kids enjoy being on the loose when they go to college.

senses.definition: available for sale; offered for sale.
senses.notes: Compare this with on the block.
examples: I had to put my car on the market.
This is the finest home computer on the market.

senses.definition: getting well; healing.
examples: My cold was terrible, but I’m on the mend now.
What you need is some hot chicken soup. Then you’ll really be on the mend.

senses.definition: in exactly the right place; in exactly the right amount (of money).
examples: That’s a good answer, Bob. You’re right on the money.
This project is going to be finished right on the nose.

senses.definition: moving; happening busily.
examples: What a busy day. Things are really on the move at the store.
When all the buffalo were on the move across the plains, it must have been very exciting.

senses.definition: because of a slight possibility that something may happen, might be the case; just in case.
examples: I went to the theater on the off-chance that there were tickets for the show left.
We didn’t think we would get into the stadium, but we went anyway on the off-chance.

senses.definition: from one point of view; as one side (of an issue).
examples: On one hand, I really ought to support my team. On the other hand, I don’t have to time to attend all the games.
On the one hand, I need Ann’s help. On the other hand, she and I don’t get along very well.

senses.definition: from another point of view; as the other side (of an issue). See the examples for on (the) one hand.

headword: on the point of doing something
altForms: at the point of doing something

senses.definition: ready to start doing something.
senses.notes: Compare this with on the verge (of doing something).
examples: I was just on the point of going out the door.
We were almost at the point of buying a new car.

senses.definition: quietly; secretly.
examples: The company president was making payments to his wife on the QT.
The mayor accepted a bribe on the QT.

senses.definition: following the right set of assumptions.
senses.notes: Refers to following the right trail.
examples: Tom is on the right track and will solve the mystery soon.
You are on the right track to find the answer.

senses.definition: in a state of destruction or wreckage.
senses.notes: Refers to a ship stranded on the rocks.
examples: I hear their marriage is on the rocks.
The company is on the rocks and may not survive.

senses.definition: onto ice cubes in a glass.
examples: Joan prefers her drinks on the rocks.
Could I have a scotch on the rocks?

senses.definition: at exactly the right place; at exactly the right time.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. See also Johnny-on-the-spot.
examples: It’s noon, and I’m glad you’re all here on the spot. Now we can begin.
I expect you to be on the spot when and where trouble arises.

senses.definition: in trouble; in a difficult situation.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with on the hot seat.
examples: There is a problem in the department I manage, and I’m really on the spot.
I hate to be on the spot when it’s not my fault.

headword: on the spur of the moment

senses.definition: suddenly; spontaneously.
examples: We decided to go on the spur of the moment.
I had to leave town on the spur of the moment.

senses.definition: because of the support of something, such as a promise or evidence; due to something.
examples: On the strength of your comment, I decided to give John another chance.
On the strength of my testimony, my case was dismissed.

headword: on the tip of one’s tongue

senses.definition: about to be said; almost remembered.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also have something on the tip of one’s tongue.
examples: It’s right on the tip of my tongue. I’ll think of it in a second.
The answer was on the tip of my tongue, but Ann said it first.

headword: on the trail of someone or something
altForms: on the track of someone or something

senses.definition: seeking someone or something; about to find someone or something.
examples: I’m on the trail of a new can opener that is supposed to be easier to use.
I spent all morning on the track of the new secretary, who got lost on the way to work.

senses.definition: just about to do something, usually something important.
senses.notes: Compare this with on the point of doing something.
examples: I’m on the verge of opening a shoe store.
Tom was on the verge of quitting school when he became interested in physics.
I haven’t done it yet, but I’m on the verge.

senses.definition: not drinking alcohol; no longer drinking alcohol.
examples: None for me, thanks. I’m on the wagon.
Look at John. I don’t think he’s on the wagon anymore.

senses.definition: angry and upset (at someone).
examples: Oh, oh. Here comes Mrs. Smith. She’s on the warpath again.
Why are you always on the warpath? What’s wrong?

senses.definition: along the route to somewhere.
examples: She’s now on the way to San Francisco.
Yes, she’s on the way.

headword: on the way to doing something
altForms: on one’s way to doing something

senses.definition: in the process of doing something.
examples: You’re on the way to becoming a very good carpenter.
She’s on her way to becoming a first-class sculptor.

senses.definition: generally; considering everything.
examples: On the whole, this was a very good day.
Your work—on the whole— is quite good.

senses.definition: while flying; while in flight.
senses.notes: Refers to birds, fowl, etc., not people or planes.
examples: There is nothing as pretty as a bird on the wing.
The hawk caught the sparrow on the wing.

senses.definition: going the wrong way; following the wrong set of assumptions.
examples: You’ll never get the right answer. You’re on the wrong track.
They won’t get it figured out because they are on the wrong track.

senses.definition: in a risky situation.
examples: If you try that you’ll really be on thin ice. That’s too risky.
If you don’t want to find yourself on thin ice, you must be sure of your facts.

senses.definition: at the scheduled time; at the predicted time.
examples: The plane landed right on time.
We’ll have to hurry to get there on time.

senses.definition: standing or walking on the front part of the feet (the balls of the feet) with no weight put on the heels.
senses.notes: This is done to gain height or to walk quietly.
examples: I had to stand on tiptoe in order to see over the fence.
I came in late and walked on tiptoe so I wouldn’t wake anybody up.

senses.definition: victorious over something; famous or notorious for something.
examples: I have to study day and night to keep on top.
Bill is on top in his field.

senses.definition: up-to-date on something; knowing about the current state of something.
examples: Ask Mary. She’s on top of this issue.
This issue is constantly changing. She has to pay attention to it to stay on top of things.

senses.definition: in addition to something.
examples: Jane told Bill he was dull. On top of that, she said he was unfriendly.
On top of being dull, he’s unfriendly.

senses.definition: being tried in court.
examples: My sister is on trial today, so I have to go to court.
They placed the suspected thief on trial.

senses.definition: away, taking a vacation; on holiday.
examples: Where are you going on vacation this year?
I’ll be away on vacation for three weeks.

senses.definition: visible; on public display.
examples: The painting will be on view at the museum.
I’ll pull the shades so that we won’t be on view.

senses.definition: finally and irreversibly.
examples: I want to get this problem settled once and for all.
I told him once and for all that he has to start studying.

senses.definition: very rarely.
examples: I seldom go to a movie—maybe once in a blue moon.
I don’t go into the city except once in a blue moon.

senses.definition: a chance that will never occur again in one’s lifetime.
examples: This is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. Don’t miss it.
She offered me a once-in-a-lifetime chance, but I turned it down.

senses.definition: a quick and careless treatment.
senses.notes: A noun. Said of an act of cleaning, studying, examination, or appraisal.
examples: Bill gave his geometry the once-over-lightly and then quit studying.
Ann, you didn’t wash the dishes properly. They only got a once-over-lightly.

senses.definition: cursory; in a quick and careless manner.
examples: Tom studied geometry once-over-lightly.
Ann washed the dishes once-over-lightly.

senses.definition: once in the past.
senses.notes: A formula used to begin a fairy tale.
examples: Once upon a time, there were three bears.
Once upon a time, I had a puppy of my own.

senses.definition: the famous and talented (person).
senses.notes: Used in theatrical introductions. See also my one and only.
examples: And now—the one and only—Jane Smith!
Let’s have a big hand for the one and only Bob Jones!

senses.definition: a recordbreaking act.
examples: What a dive! That’s one for the record books.
I’ve never heard such a funny joke. That’s really one for the books.

senses.definition: A good deed should be repaid with another good deed.
examples: If he does you a favor, you should do him a favor. One good turn deserves another.
Glad to help you out. One good turn deserves another.

senses.definition: unique; one of a very few.
examples: He’s a great guy. He’s one in million.
Mary’s one in a hundred—such a hard worker.

headword: one jump ahead (of someone or something)
altForms: one move ahead (of someone or something)

senses.definition: one step in advance of someone or something.
examples: Try to stay one jump ahead of the customer.
If you’re one move ahead, you’re well prepared to deal with problems. Then, nothing is a surprise.

senses.definition: any at all; at all.
examples: Jean could not be persuaded to change her mind one little bit.
I don’t want to hear anything more about it. Not even one little bit.

headword: One man’s meat is another man’s poison.

senses.definition: One person’s preference may be disliked by another person.
examples: John just loves his new fur hat, but I think it is horrible. Oh, well, one man’s meat is another man’s poison.
The neighbors are very fond of their dog even though it’s ugly, loud, and smelly. I guess one man’s meat is another man’s poison.

headword: One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.

senses.definition: Something that one person considers worthless may be considered valuable by someone else.
examples: Q: Why would anyone want to hang a picture like that on the wall? A: One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.
A: Bob’s uncle is always going through people’s garbage, looking for old stuff. B: One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.

senses.definition: an activity lasting one night.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to either a musical performance or a period of sexual activity.
examples: Our band has played a lot of one-night stands.
What we want is an engagement for a week, not just a one-night stand.

senses.definition: someday; in some situation like this one.
examples: One of these days, someone is going to steal your purse if you don’t take better care of it.
You’re going to get in trouble one of these days.

headword: one sandwich short of a picnic

senses.definition: not very smart; lacking sufficient intelligence.
examples: Poor Bob just isn’t too bright. He’s one sandwich short of a picnic.
She not stupid. Just one sandwich short of a picnic.

senses.definition: One event sets things up for another event and so on.
senses.notes: As an explanation of how little problems lead to big problems.
examples: I kept spending more and more money until I was broke. You know how one thing leads to another.
He bought a car, then a house, then a boat. One thing leads to another.

headword: one thing or person after another

senses.definition: a series of things or people that seems without limit.
examples: It’s just one problem after another.
One customer after another has been buying shoes today!

senses.definition: each person can have or receive only one.
senses.notes: Refers to sales restrictions where each customer is permitted to buy only one.
examples: “Only one to a customer!” said the chef as he handed out the hamburgers.
Is it one to a customer, or can I take two now?

senses.definition: somehow.
examples: I’ll do it one way or another.
One way or another, I’ll get through school.

headword: One’s bark is worse than one’s bite.

senses.definition: One may threaten, but not do much damage.
examples: Don’t worry about Bob. He won’t hurt you. His bark is worse than his bite.
She may scream and yell, but have no fear. Her bark is worse than her bite.

senses.definition: one’s spouse.
examples: I think we’d like to come for dinner, but I’ll have to ask my better half.
I have to go home now to my better half. We are going out tonight.

senses.definition: someone responsible for someone else.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: I can’t force these kids to go to school and get an education so they can get jobs. I am not my brother’s keeper.
You can’t expect me to be my brother’s keeper. Each of us should be responsible!

senses.definition: physical exercises done every day.
examples: My brother always feels better after his daily dozen.
She would rather do her daily dozen than go on a diet.

senses.definition: one faces death or dismissal.
examples: If I don’t get this contract, my days are numbered at this company.
Uncle Tom has a terminal disease. His days are numbered.

senses.definition: one’s very sincere sympathy.
examples: I am so sorry about the death of your father. You have my deepest sympathy.
She sent her deepest sympathy to the family.

senses.definition: one’s ears are red from embarrassment.
examples: I’m so embarrassed. Wow, are my ears red!
My ears are red! I can’t believe I said that.

senses.definition: one hears a ringing sound because of exposure to an explosion, very loud music, or some other very loud sound.
examples: After the explosion, my ears were ringing for hours.
My ears are ringing because I have a cold.

headword: One’s eyes are bigger than one’s stomach.

senses.definition: One has taken more food than one can eat.
examples: I can’t eat all this. I’m afraid that my eyes were bigger than my stomach.
Try to take less food. Your eyes are bigger than your stomach at every meal.

senses.definition: a share of something that is equal to what others get or in proportion to what is deserved.
examples: Let him take more. He didn’t get his fair share.
I want my fair share. You cheated me! Give me some more!

senses.definition: one’s property if one asks for it.
examples: I have a cherry pie here. A slice is yours for the asking if you want it.
Uncle Mac said we could have his old car if we wanted it. It was ours for the asking.

headword: one’s heart goes out to someone

senses.definition: one feels compassion for someone.
examples: My heart goes out to those starving children I see on television.
We are so sorry. Our hearts go out to you.

headword: one’s heart is (dead) set against something

senses.definition: one is totally against something.
examples: Jane’s heart is set against going there.
We are dead set against it.

headword: one’s heart is in one’s mouth

senses.definition: one feels strongly emotional (about someone or something).
examples: “Gosh, Mary,” said John, “my heart is in my mouth whenever I see you.”
My heart is in my mouth whenever I hear the national anthem.
It was a touching scene. My heart was in my mouth the whole time.

headword: one’s heart is in the right place

senses.definition: one has good intentions, even if the results are bad.
senses.notes: See also have one’s heart in the right place.
examples: She gave it a good try. Her heart was in the right place.
He is awkward, but his heart is in the right place.

headword: one’s heart is set on something

senses.definition: one desires and expects something.
examples: Jane’s heart is set on going to London.
My heart is set on returning home.

senses.definition: one’s heart skips a beat one’s heart is fluttering or palpitating.
examples: Whenever I’m near you, my heart skips a beat.
When the racehorse fell, my heart missed a beat.

senses.definition: one’s heart (figuratively) stops beating because of strong emotions.
examples: When I first saw you, my heart stood still.
My heart will stand still until you answer.

senses.definition: one’s good luck stops.
examples: My luck ran out, so I had to come home.
She will quit gambling when her luck runs out.

senses.definition: one is in trouble or humiliated.
examples: If I can’t get this contract signed, my name will be mud.
His name is mud ever since he broke the crystal vase.

headword: one’s nose is in the air

senses.definition: one is acting conceited or aloof.
senses.notes: Note the variation with always. See also have one’s nose in the air.
examples: Mary’s nose is always in the air.
Her mother’s nose was always in the air, too.

senses.definition: one’s time to die—or to suffer some other unpleasantness—has come.
examples: John is worried. He thinks his number is up.
When my number is up, I hope it all goes fast.

senses.definition: the place where one was raised or where one has spent a lot of time.
senses.notes: Folksy. There are variants with stomping and grounds.
examples: Ann should know about that place. It’s near her old stamping ground.
I can’t wait to get back to my old stomping grounds.

senses.definition: one’s lifestyle; one’s pattern of living.
examples: That kind of thing just doesn’t fit into my way of life.
Our way of life includes contributing to worthy causes.

senses.definition: to be loyal to only one person, in the context of romance.
examples: Oh, Jane! I only have eyes for you!
Don’t waste any time on Tom. He only has eyes for Ann.

senses.definition: to start a conversation.
senses.notes: See also strike up a conversation.
examples: I tried to open a conversation with him, but he had nothing to say.
She opened a conversation with an inquiry into my health, which got me talking about my favorite subject.

senses.definition: something, usually a legal matter, that is simple and straightforward without complications.
examples: The murder trial was an open-and-shut case. The defendant was caught with the murder weapon.
Jack’s death was an open-and-shut case of suicide. He left a suicide note.

senses.definition: someone or something that is easy to understand.
examples: Jane’s an open book. I always know what she is going to do next.
The council is an open book. It wants to save money.

senses.definition: to start (doing something, such as asking questions or criticizing).
senses.notes: Refers to starting to shoot at someone.
examples: The reporters opened fire on the mayor.
When the reporters opened fire, the mayor was smiling, but not for long.

senses.definition: operating and ready to do business.
examples: The store is now open for business and invites you to come in.
The construction will be finished in March, and we will be open for business in April.

senses.definition: to reveal one’s inmost thoughts to someone.
examples: I always open my heart to my spouse when I have a problem.
It’s a good idea to open your heart every now and then.

senses.definition: to uncover a lot of unsuspected problems.
examples: When I asked Jane about her problems, I didn’t know I had opened Pandora’s box.
You should be cautious with people who are upset. You don’t want to open Pandora’s box.

senses.definition: unrestricted hunting of a particular game animal.
examples: It’s always open season on rabbits around here.
Is it ever open season on deer?

senses.definition: a time when everyone is criticizing someone.
senses.notes: [with someone] Informal. See also open fire (on someone).
examples: It seems as if it’s always open season on politicians.
At the news conference, it was open season on the mayor.

senses.definition: something that is supposed to be secret but is known to a great many people.
examples: Their engagement is an open secret. Only their friends are supposed to know, but in fact, the whole town knows.
It’s an open secret that Max is looking for a new job.

senses.definition: to become aware of something.
examples: He finally opened his eyes to what was going on.
It was a long time before he opened his eyes and realized what had been happening.

senses.definition: to cause someone else to be aware of something.
examples: I opened his eyes to what was happening at the office.
Why can’t I make you understand? What do I have to do to open your eyes to the problem?

senses.definition: to permit or allow something to become a possibility.
examples: Your policy opens the door to cheating.
Your statement opens the door to John’s candidacy.

senses.definition: agreeable to hear or learn about new ideas and suggestions.
examples: The store owner was open to suggestions from her employees.
We are always open to new ideas.

senses.definition: to uncover a set of problems; to create unnecessary complications.
senses.notes: Informal. Can of worms means “mess.” Also with various modifiers such as new, whole, another, as in the examples. Compare this with open Pandora’s box.
examples: Now you are opening a whole new can of worms.
How about cleaning up this mess before you open up a new can of worms?

senses.definition: to attack someone or something; to fire a gun or other weapon at someone or something.
examples: The sergeant told the soldiers to open up on the enemy position.
“Okay, you guys,” shouted the sergeant. “Open up!”

senses.definition: to talk frankly, truthfully, or intimately.
examples: Finally Sally opened up to her sister and told her what the problem was.
Bill wouldn’t open up with me. He’s still keeping quiet.
At last, Sally opened up and told everything.

senses.definition: to start out with something.
senses.notes: Usually said of a performance of some type.
examples: We’ll open with a love song and then go on to something faster.
The play opened with an exciting first act, and then it became very boring.

senses.definition: an opening movement or statement that is made to secure a position that is to one’s advantage.
examples: The rebel army’s opening gambit was to bomb the city’s business district.
The prosecution’s opening gambit was to call a witness who linked the defendant to the scene of the crime.

senses.definition: males; [from the point of view of a male] females.
senses.notes: [from the point of view of a female] Also with member of, as in the example.
examples: Ann is crazy about the opposite sex.
Bill is very shy when he’s introduced to the opposite sex.
Do members of the opposite sex make you nervous?

senses.definition: or suffer the consequences.
examples: Do what I tell you, or else.
Don’t be late for work, or else!

senses.definition: or with other words that have about the same meaning.
examples: She told me I ought to read more carefully—or words to that effect.
I was instructed to go to the devil, or words to that effect.

senses.definition: something necessary or usual; an overriding necessity.
examples: Warm clothes are the order of the day when camping in the winter.
Going to bed early was the order of the day when we were young.

senses.definition: to give commands to someone.
examples: I don’t like for someone to order me about.
Don’t order me around!

headword: the other side of the tracks

senses.definition: the poorer section of town or the richer section of town, depending on perspective.
senses.notes: Also literal. Usually refers to the wrong side of the tracks.
examples: He is from a wealthy family and I am from a very humble background, but he is the first boy I have met from the other side of the tracks, and I want to marry him.
I hear he is dating someone from the other side of the tracks.

senses.definition: if things stay the way they are now; if there were no complications by other factors.
examples: Other things being equal, we should have no trouble getting your order to you on time.
I anticipate no problems, other things being equal.

senses.definition: the reverse; the opposite.
examples: No, it won’t fit that way. Try it the other way round.
It doesn’t make any sense like that. It belongs the other way round.

headword: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

senses.definition: It is easier and better to prevent something bad than to deal with the results.
examples: When you ride in a car, buckle your seat belt. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
Every child should be vaccinated against polio. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

senses.definition: unconscious.
examples: I fell and hit my head. I was out cold for about a minute.
Tom fainted! He’s out like a light!

senses.definition: free and clear of something; no longer bearing a (figurative) burden.
examples: I’ll feel much better when I’m out from under this project.
Now that I’m out from under, I can relax.

senses.definition: in the front of one’s house.
examples: Our mailbox is out front.
We have a spruce tree out front and a maple tree in the back.

senses.definition: appearing in great numbers.
examples: What a night! The mosquitoes are out in force.
The police were out in force over the holiday weekend.

senses.definition: offbeat; unusual and eccentric.
senses.notes: Literal in reference to a baseball field. Informal. See also come out of left field.
examples: Sally is a lot of fun, but she’s sort of out in left field.
What a strange idea. It’s really out in left field.

headword: out of a clear blue sky

senses.definition: suddenly; without warning.
senses.notes: See also like a bolt out of the blue.
examples: Then, out of a clear blue sky, he told me he was leaving.
Mary appeared on my doorstep out of the blue.

senses.definition: of an exaggerated proportion; of an unrealistic proportion compared to something else; (figuratively) lopsided.
examples: This problem has grown out of all proportion.
Yes, this thing is way out of proportion.

senses.definition: outside the boundaries of the playing area.
examples: The ball went out of bounds, but the referee didn’t notice.
The play ended when Sally ran out of bounds.

senses.definition: unreasonable.
examples: Your demands are totally out of bounds.
Your request for money is out of bounds.

senses.definition: breathing fast and hard.
examples: I ran so much that I got out of breath.
Mary gets out of breath when she climbs stairs.

senses.definition: unlike one’s usual behavior.
examples: Ann’s remark was quite out of character.
It was out of character for Ann to act so stubborn.

senses.definition: inappropriate for the character that an actor is playing.
examples: Bill went out of character when the audience started giggling.
Bill played the part so well that it was hard for him to get out of character after the performance.

senses.definition: no longer available for use or lending.
examples: I’m sorry, but the book you want is temporarily out of circulation.
How long will it be out of circulation?

senses.definition: not interacting socially with other people.
examples: I don’t know what’s happening because I’ve been out of circulation for a while.
My cold has kept me out of circulation for a few weeks.

senses.definition: to be not currently in use or under command.
examples: This vessel will remain out of commission for another month.
The ship has been out of commission since repairs began.

senses.definition: broken, unserviceable, or inoperable.
examples: My watch is out of commission and is running slow.
I can’t run in the marathon because my knees are out of commission.

headword: out of consideration (for someone or something)

senses.definition: with consideration for someone or something; with kind regard for someone or something.
examples: Out of consideration for your past efforts, I will do what you ask.
They let me do it out of consideration. It was very thoughtful of them.

senses.definition: uncontrollable; wild and unruly.
examples: The party got out of control about midnight, and the neighbors called the police.
We tried to keep things from getting out of hand.

senses.definition: in order to be polite to someone; out of consideration for someone.
examples: We invited Mary’s brother out of courtesy to her.
They invited me out of courtesy.

senses.definition: old-fashioned; out of style; obsolete.
senses.notes: See also go out of style.
examples: Isn’t that suit sort of out-of-date?
All my clothes are out-of-date.

senses.definition: too far from the source of a sound to hear the sound.
examples: I was out of earshot and could not hear the conversation.
Mary waited until her children were out of earshot before mentioning the party to Bill.

senses.definition: no longer desirable or preferred by someone.
examples: I can’t ask John to help. I’m out of favor with him.
That kind of thing has been out of favor for years.

senses.definition: having no gasoline (in a car, truck, etc.).
examples: We can’t go any farther. We’re out of gas.
This car will be completely out of gas in a few more miles.

senses.definition: tired; exhausted; worn out.
examples: What a day! I’ve been working since morning, and I’m really out of gas.
This electric clock is out of gas. I’ll have to get a new one.

senses.definition: immediately and without consulting anyone; without delay.
examples: I can’t answer that out of hand. I’ll check with the manager and call you back.
The offer was so good that I accepted it out of hand.

senses.definition: not following the rules of something; out of accord with something.
senses.notes: Compare this with in keeping (with something).
examples: The length of this report is out of keeping with your request.
I didn’t even read it because it was so much out of keeping.

senses.definition: out of balance; crooked or tilted.
examples: John, your tie is sort of out of kilter. Let me fix it.
Please straighten the picture on the wall. It’s out of kilter.

senses.definition: malfunctioning; on the fritz.
examples: My furnace is out of kilter. I have to call someone to fix it.
This computer is out of kilter. It doesn’t work.

senses.definition: improper.
examples: I’m afraid that your behavior was quite out of line. I do not wish to speak further about this matter.
Bill, that remark was out of line. Please be more respectful.

senses.definition: not properly lined up in a line of things.
examples: I told you not to get out of line. Now, get back in line.
One of those books on the shelf is out of line with the others. Please fix it.

senses.definition: unreasonable when compared to something (else).
examples: The cost of this meal is out of line with what other restaurants charge.
Your request is out of line.

senses.definition: without good luck; having bad fortune.
examples: If you wanted some ice cream, you’re out of luck.
I was out of luck. I got there too late to get a seat.

senses.definition: because of necessity; due to need.
examples: I bought this hat out of necessity. I needed one, and this was all there was.
We sold our car out of necessity.

senses.definition: not in a natural or comfortable situation.
senses.notes: Compare this with in one’s element.
examples: When it comes to computers, I’m out of my element.
Sally’s out of her element in math.

senses.definition: silly and senseless; crazy; irrational.
examples: Why did you do that? You must be out of your mind!
Good grief, Tom! You have to be out of your head!
She’s acting as if she were out of her senses.

senses.definition: not in the correct order.
examples: This book is out of order. Please put it in the right place on the shelf.
You’re out of order, John. Please get in line after Jane.

senses.definition: not following correct parliamentary procedure.
examples: I was declared out of order by the president.
Ann inquired, “Isn’t a motion to table the question out of order at this time?”

senses.definition: not operating; broken.
examples: The coffee machine is out of order. It takes your money and gives you no coffee.
We will have to use the stairs. The elevator is out of order.

senses.definition: not in a proper place.
examples: The salt was out of place in the cupboard, so I couldn’t find it.
Billy, you’re out of place. Please sit next to Tom.

senses.definition: improper and impertinent; out of line.
examples: That kind of behavior is out of place in church.
Your rude remark is quite out of place.

senses.definition: the actual amount of money spent.
senses.notes: Refers to the money one person pays while doing something on someone else’s behalf. One is usually paid back this money.
examples: My out-of-pocket expenses for the party were nearly $175.
My employer usually pays all out-of-pocket expenses for a business trip.

senses.definition: performing poorly due to a lack of practice.
examples: I used to be able to play the piano extremely well, but now I’m out of practice.
The baseball players lost the game because they were out of practice.

senses.definition: to be no longer available for sale from the publisher.
examples: The book you want is out of print, but perhaps I can find a used copy for you.
It was published nearly ten years ago, so it’s probably out of print.

senses.definition: not near enough to be reached or touched.
examples: Place the cookies out of reach, or Bob will eat them all.
The mouse ran behind the piano, out of reach. The cat just sat and waited for it.

senses.definition: unattainable.
examples: I wanted to be president, but I’m afraid that such a goal is out of reach.
I shall choose a goal that is not out of reach.

senses.definition: not now available for sale.
senses.notes: The opposite of in season. Compare this with off season.
examples: Sorry, oysters are out of season. We don’t have any.
Watermelon is out of season in the winter.

senses.definition: not now legally able to be hunted or caught.
examples: Are salmon out of season?
I caught a trout out of season and had to pay a fine.

senses.definition: inoperable; not now operating.
examples: Both elevators are out of service, so I had to use the stairs.
The washroom is temporarily out of service.

senses.definition: not in the best physical condition.
examples: I get out of breath when I run because I’m out of shape.
Keep exercising regularly, or you’ll get out of condition.

senses.definition: not visible.
senses.notes: Especially with get, keep, or stay.
examples: The cat kept out of sight until the mouse came out.
“Get out of sight, or they’ll see you!” called John.

senses.definition: very high.
examples: I won’t pay this bill. It’s out of sight.
The estimate was out of sight, so I didn’t accept it.

senses.definition: figuratively stunning, unbelievable, or awesome.
examples: Wow, this music is out of sight!
What a wild party—out of sight!

headword: Out of sight, out of mind.

senses.definition: If you do not see something, you will not think about it.
examples: When I go home, I put my schoolbooks away so I won’t worry about doing my homework. After all, out of sight, out of mind.
Jane dented the fender on her car. It’s on the right side, so she doesn’t have to look at it. Like they say, out of sight, out of mind.

senses.definition: not feeling well; grumpy and irritable.
examples: I’ve been out of sorts for a day or two. I think I’m coming down with something.
The baby is out of sorts. Maybe she’s getting a tooth.

senses.definition: with the desire to harm someone or something.
examples: Jane told some evil gossip about Bill out of spite.
That was not an accident! You did it out of spite.

headword: out of step (with someone or something)

senses.definition: out of cadence with someone else.
examples: You’re out of step with the music.
Pay attention, Ann. You’re out of time.
forms: out of time (with someone or something)

senses.definition: not as up-to-date as someone or something.
examples: John is out of step with the times.
Billy is out of step with the rest of the class.

senses.definition: not immediately available in a store; [for goods] to be temporarily unavailable.
examples: Those items are out of stock, but a new supply will be delivered on Thursday.
I’m sorry, but the red ones are out of stock. Would a blue one do?

senses.definition: not fashionable; old-fashioned; obsolete.
examples: John’s clothes are really out of style.
He doesn’t care if his clothes are out of fashion.

headword: out of the corner of one’s eye

senses.definition: at a glance; glimpsing (something).
examples: I saw someone do it out of the corner of my eye. It might have been Jane who did it.
I only saw the accident out of the corner of my eye. I don’t know who is at fault.

headword: out of the frying pan into the fire

senses.definition: from a bad situation to a worse situation.
examples: When I tried to argue about my fine for a traffic violation, the judge charged me with contempt of court. I really went out of the frying pan into the fire.
I got deeply in debt. Then I really got out of the frying pan into the fire when I lost my job.

senses.definition: out of debt.
examples: I get paid next week, and then I can get out of the hole.
I can’t seem to get out of the hole. I keep spending more money than I earn.

senses.definition: unusual.
examples: It was a good meal, but not out of the ordinary.
Your report was nicely done, but nothing out of the ordinary.

senses.definition: not possible; not permitted.
examples: I’m sorry, but it’s out of the question.
You can’t go to Florida this spring. We can’t afford it. It’s out of the question.

senses.definition: out of debt.
examples: This year our company is likely to get out of the red before fall.
If we can cut down on expenses, we can get out of the red fairly soon.

senses.definition: no longer being considered; eliminated from a contest.
senses.notes: Compare this with in the running.
examples: After the first part of the diving meet, three members of our team were out of the running.
After the scandal was made public, I was no longer in the running. I pulled out of the election.

headword: out of the swim of things

senses.definition: not in the middle of activity; not involved in things.
senses.notes: Informal. The opposite of in the swim of things.
examples: While I had my cold, I was out of the swim of things.
I’ve been out of the swim of things for a few weeks. Please bring me up to date.

senses.definition: not on the regular route; following a different, more awkward, route.
examples: They live on a quiet, out-of-the-way street.
I know an out-of-the-way little restaurant on Maple Street.

senses.definition: past a critical phase; out of the unknown.
examples: When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed.
I can give you a better prediction for your future health when you are out of the woods.

senses.definition: out of nowhere; out of nothing.
examples: Suddenly—out of thin air—the messenger appeared.
You just made that up out of thin air.

senses.definition: wonderful; extraordinary.
examples: This pie is just out of this world.
Look at you! How lovely you look—simply out of this world.

headword: out of touch (with someone or something)

senses.definition: no longer talking to or writing to someone; knowing no news of someone.
examples: I’ve been out of touch with my brother for many years.
We’ve been out of touch for quite some time.

senses.definition: not keeping up with the developments of something.
examples: I’ve been out of touch with automobile mechanics for many years.
I couldn’t go back into mechanics because I’ve been out of touch for too long.

senses.definition: temporarily not in one’s own town.
examples: I’ll be out of town next week. I’m going to a conference.
I take care of Mary’s cat when she’s out of town.

headword: out of tune (with someone or something)

senses.definition: not in musical harmony with someone or something.
examples: The oboe is out of tune with the flute.
The flute is out of tune with John.
They are all out of tune.

senses.definition: not in (figurative) harmony or agreement.
examples: Your proposal is out of tune with my ideas of what we should be doing.
Your ideas and mine are out of tune.

senses.definition: not at the proper time; not in the proper order.
senses.notes: See also speak out of turn.
examples: We were permitted to be served out of turn because we had to leave early.
Bill tried to register out of turn and was sent away.

senses.definition: crazy; silly; irrational.
examples: Why do you always act as if you’re out of whack?
I’m not out of wack. I’m eccentric.

senses.definition: out of adjustment; out of order.
examples: I’m afraid that my watch is out of whack.
The elevator is out of wack. We’ll have to walk up.

senses.definition: unemployed, temporarily or permanently.
examples: How long have you been out of work?
My brother has been out of work for nearly a year.

senses.definition: in a dangerous position; taking a chance.
examples: I don’t want to go out on a limb, but I think I’d agree to your request.
She really went out on a limb when she agreed.

senses.definition: out of jail because bail bond money has been paid.
senses.notes: The money will be forfeited if the person who is out on bail does not appear in court at the proper time. See also jump bail.
examples: Bob is out on bail waiting for his trial.
The robber committed another crime while out on bail.

senses.definition: out of jail but still under police supervision.
examples: Bob got out on parole after serving only a few years of his sentence.
He was out on parole because of good behavior.

senses.definition: away from a central location, watching over a distant area while moving through it.
examples: Officer Smith is out on patrol and cannot see you now.
The soldiers who are on patrol on this snowy night must be very cold.

senses.definition: celebrating at one or more places in a town.
senses.notes: See also night on the town.
examples: I’m really tired. I was out on the town until dawn.
We went out on the town to celebrate our wedding anniversary.

senses.definition: eating lunch away from one’s place of work or activity.
examples: I’m sorry, but Sally Jones is out to lunch. May I take a message?
She’s been out to lunch for nearly two hours. When will she be back?

senses.definition: not alert; giddy; uninformed.
examples: Bill is really out of it. Why can’t he pay attention?
Don’t be so out of it, John. Wake up!
Ann is really out to lunch these days.

senses.definition: in the western part of the United States.
senses.notes: See also back East, down South, up North.
examples: We lived out West for nearly ten years.
Do they really ride horses out West?

senses.definition: to get too big for something.
examples: Tom outgrew all his clothes in two months.
The plant outgrew its pot.

senses.definition: to become too mature for something.
examples: I outgrew my allergies.
The boys will outgrow their toys.

senses.definition: to guess what someone else might do; to predict what someone might do.
examples: I can’t outguess Bill. I just have to wait and see what happens.
Don’t try to outguess John. He’s too sharp and tricky.

senses.definition: except for something; besides something.
examples: Outside of the cost of my laundry, I have practically no expenses.
Outside of some new shoes, I don’t need any new clothing.

senses.definition: as if not bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: An adverb. Compare this with inside the box.
examples: You need to move your discussions outside the box and get away from silly limitations.
Nothing can be done outside the box in such a rigid intellectual environment.

senses.definition: not bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
examples: You have some really outside-the-box ideas, Ralph.
After some long, outside-the-box discussions, we arrived at a creative solution.

senses.definition: more than something; in addition to something.
examples: I’ll need another twenty dollars over and above the amount you have already given me.
You’ve been eating too much food—over and above what is required for good nutrition. That’s why you’re gaining weight.

senses.definition: finished.
examples: I’m glad that’s over and done with.
Now that I have college over and done with, I can get a job.

senses.definition: not if I can stop you.
senses.notes: Slang. It means that you’ll have to kill me to prevent me from keeping you from doing something.
examples: Over my dead body you’ll sell this house!
You want to quit college? Over my dead body!

senses.definition: too difficult or clever for someone to understand.
examples: The children have no idea what the new teacher is talking about. Her ideas are way over their heads.
She enrolled in a physics course, but it turned out to be miles over her head.

senses.definition: overage; too old to do something.
examples: Now that Mary’s forty, she thinks she’s over the hill.
My grandfather was over eighty before he felt as if he was over the hill.

senses.definition: over the difficult part.
examples: This is a difficult project, but we’re over the hump now.
I’m halfway through—over the hump—and it looks as if I may get finished after all.

senses.definition: for a relatively long period of time.
examples: Over the long haul, it might be better to invest in stocks.
Over the long haul, everything will turn out all right.

senses.definition: for the immediate future.
examples: Over the short haul, you’d be better off to put your money in the bank.
Over the short haul, you may wish you had done something different. But things will work out all right.

senses.definition: having gained more than one’s goal.
examples: Our fund-raising campaign went over the top by $3,000.
We didn’t go over the top. We didn’t even get half of what we set out to collect.

senses.definition: excessive; beyond the pale; overdone.
examples: Her imitation of the president was over the top and completely offensive.
This is not satire! It is cruel and over the top.

senses.definition: because of something; due to the fact of something.
examples: Owing to the lateness of the evening, I must go home.
We were late owing to the heavy traffic.

senses.definition: to provide a burst of energy, power, or excitement.
examples: Wow, this spicy food really packs a wallop.
I put a special kind of gasoline in my car because I thought it would pack a punch. It didn’t.

senses.definition: a series of lies.
examples: The thief told a pack of lies to cover up the crime.
John listened to Bill’s pack of lies about the fight and became very angry.

senses.definition: to draw a lot of people.
examples: It was a good night at the theater. The play really packed them in.
The circus manager knew he could pack them in if he advertised the lion tamer.

senses.definition: packed very tightly.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: It was terribly crowded there. We were packed in like sardines.
The bus was full. The passengers were packed like sardines.
They packed us in like sardines.

senses.definition: to put unnecessary items on a bill to make the total cost higher.
examples: The plumber had padded the bill with things we didn’t need.
I was falsely accused of padding the bill.

senses.definition: to do (something) by oneself.
examples: I’ve been left to paddle my own canoe too many times.
Sally isn’t with us. She’s off paddling her own canoe.

senses.definition: a bother; an annoyance.
examples: This assignment is a pain in the neck.
Your little brother is a pain in the neck.

senses.definition: to have a wild celebration during a night on the town.
examples: Let’s all go out and paint the town red!
Oh, do I feel awful. I was out all last night, painting the town red.

senses.definition: to be friends with someone; to be the companion of someone.
examples: Bill likes to pal around with Mary, but it’s nothing serious.
Ann and Jane still like to pal around.

senses.definition: looking sick.
senses.notes: Informal. The around can be replaced with about.
examples: John is looking a little pale around the gills. What’s wrong?
Oh, I feel a little green about the gills.

senses.definition: to try to get something accepted as good.
examples: The crook palmed a fake $50 bill off on me.
Bob palmed his research off as original work, but we all knew he plagiarized it.

senses.definition: to try to hide faults or difficulties, often in a hasty or not very successful way.
examples: The politician tried to paper over the cracks in his party’s economic policy.
Tom tried to paper over the cracks in his relationship with the boss, but it was not possible.
She didn’t explain it. She just papered over the cracks.

senses.definition: typical; about what one could expect.
senses.notes: This refers to golf courses, not school courses.
examples: So he went off and left you? Well that’s about par for the course. He’s no friend.
I worked for days on this project, but it was rejected. That’s par for the course around here.

senses.definition: a place on earth that is as lovely as paradise.
examples: The retirement home was simply a paradise on earth.
The beach where we went for our vacation was a paradise.

senses.definition: Excuse me for swearing or saying naughty words.
examples: Pardon my French, but get that damn cat out of here!
He slipped and fell on his butt, pardon my French.

senses.definition: part of something; an important part of something.
examples: This point is part and parcel of my whole argument.
Get every part and parcel of this machine out of my living room.
Come on! Move out—part and parcel!

senses.definition: to leave someone; to depart from someone.
examples: Tom finally parted company with his brother.
They parted company, and Tom got in his car and drove away.

senses.definition: to come very close to someone.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. Usually an exaggeration.
examples: That plane flew so low that it nearly parted my hair.
He punched at me and missed. He only parted my hair.

senses.definition: to take something; to eat or drink something.
examples: I don’t usually partake of rich foods, but in this instance I’ll make an exception.
Good afternoon, Judge Smith, would you care to partake of some wine?

senses.definition: favoring or preferring someone or something.
examples: The boys think their teacher is partial to female students.
I am partial to vanilla ice cream.

senses.definition: specific details about something.
examples: My boss stressed the important particulars of the project.
What are the particulars of your request?

senses.definition: a point at which people separate and go their own ways.
senses.notes: Often with come to a, arrive at a, reach a, etc.
examples: Jane and Bob finally came to a parting of the ways.
Bill and his parents reached a parting of the ways.

senses.definition: the official ideas and attitudes that are adopted by the leaders of a particular group and that the other members are expected to accept.
examples: Tom has left the club. He refused to follow the party line.
Many politicians agree with the party line without thinking.

senses.definition: A happy or fortunate time has come to an end.
examples: We go back to school tomorrow. The party’s over.
The staff hardly worked at all under the old management, but they’ll find the party’s over now.

senses.definition: to succeed in being accepted as someone or something.
examples: The spy was able to pass as a regular citizen.
You could pass for your twin brother.
The thief was arrested when he tried to pass as a priest.

senses.definition: to die.
examples: My aunt passed away last month.
When I pass away, I want to have lots of flowers and a big funeral.
When I pass on, I won’t care about the funeral.

senses.definition: to measure up to the required standards.
examples: I tried, but my efforts didn’t pass muster.
If you don’t wear a suit, you won’t pass muster at that fancy restaurant. They won’t let you in.

senses.definition: to faint; to lose consciousness.
examples: Oh, look! Tom has passed out.
When he got the news, he passed out.

senses.definition: to pass the blame (to someone else); to give the responsibility (to someone else).
examples: Don’t try to pass the buck! It’s your fault, and everybody knows it.
Some people try to pass the buck whenever they can.

senses.definition: to attempt to collect money for some (charitable) project.
senses.notes: Refers to a hat that is sometimes used to hold the collected cash.
examples: Bob is passing the hat to collect money to buy flowers for Ann.
He’s always passing the hat for something.

senses.definition: to fill up time (by doing something).
examples: I never know how to pass the time when I’m on vacation.
What do you do to pass the time?

headword: pass the time of day (with someone)

senses.definition: to chat or talk informally with someone.
examples: I saw Mr. Brown in town yesterday. I stopped and passed the time of day with him.
No, we didn’t have a serious talk; we just passed the time of day.

senses.definition: to come to mind briefly; for an idea to occur to someone.
senses.notes: Compare this with come to mind.
examples: Let me tell you what just crossed my mind.
As you were speaking, something passed through my mind that I’d like to discuss.

senses.definition: something that allows something good to happen.
examples: John’s new girlfriend is his passport to happiness.
Anne’s new job is a passport to financial security.

senses.definition: someone proven to be extremely good or skillful at an activity.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Mary is a past master at cooking omelets.
Pam is a past master at the art of complaining.

senses.definition: beyond the most useful or productive period.
examples: Joan was a wonderful singer, but she’s past her prime now.
This old car’s past its prime. I’ll need to get a new one.

altForms: give someone a pat on the back

senses.definition: to congratulate someone; to encourage someone.
senses.notes: Also literal when the recipient is actually patted on the back.
examples: We patted Ann on the back for a good performance.
When people do a good job, you should give them a pat on the back.

senses.definition: to doctor someone; to dress someone’s wounds.
examples: They patched John up in the emergency room.
I patched up Ann’s cuts with bandages and sent her home.

senses.definition: to (figuratively) repair the damage done by an argument or disagreement.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Smith are trying to patch things up.
We patched up our argument, then kissed and made up.

senses.definition: to do the easiest thing; to take the easiest route.
senses.notes: Often with follow the or take the. Compare this with line of least resistance.
examples: John will follow the path of least resistance.
I like challenges. I won’t usually take the path of least resistance.

headword: pave the way (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to prepare (someone or something) for someone or something.
examples: The public doesn’t understand the metric system. We need to pave the way for its introduction.
They are paving the way in the schools.

senses.definition: to visit someone.
examples: Grandmother always paid us a call on Sundays.
Let’s pay a call on Mary at the hospital.

senses.definition: to pay a great deal for something.
senses.notes: To pay an amount as large as one might have to pay to get back a king held for ransom.
examples: I would like to buy a nice watch, but I don’t want to pay a king’s ransom for it.
It’s a lovely house. I had to pay a king’s ransom, but it is worth it.

headword: pay an arm and a leg (for something)

senses.definition: to pay too much [money] for something.
examples: I hate to have to pay an arm and a leg for a tank of gas.
If you shop around, you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg.
Why should you pay through the nose?

senses.definition: to pay costs as they occur; to pay for goods as they are bought (rather than charging them).
senses.notes: Literal when it means to pay for goods or services as you leave.
examples: You ought to pay as you go. Then you won’t be in debt.
If you pay as you go, you’ll never spend too much money.

senses.definition: paying costs as they occur.
examples: There is no charging allowed here. This store is strictly pay-as-you-go.
I can’t buy this then. I didn’t know your policy was pay-as-you-go.

senses.definition: to be attentive to someone or something; to give one’s attention or concentration to someone or something.
examples: Pay attention to me!
I’m paying attention!

senses.definition: to praise, respect, and honor someone.
examples: My parents taught me to pay homage to my elders.
The widower paid homage to his dead wife by placing flowers on her grave.

senses.definition: to pay (for something) before it is received or delivered.
examples: I want to make a special order. Will I have to pay in advance?
Yes, please pay in advance.

senses.definition: to express loyalty, respect, or support for something insincerely.
examples: You don’t really care about politics. You’re just paying lip service to the candidate.
Don’t sit here and pay lip service. Get busy!

senses.definition: to serve a sentence for a crime, usually in prison.
examples: The judge said that Mr. Simpson had to pay his debt to society.
Mr. Brown paid his debt in state prison.

senses.definition: to have earned one’s right to something through hard work or suffering.
senses.notes: Literal when referring to paying the fees required to belong to an organization. Informal.
examples: He worked hard to get to where he is today. He paid his dues and did what he was told.
I have every right to be here. I paid my dues!

senses.definition: to attend the wake or funeral of someone; to approach the coffin containing someone in a final act of respect.
examples: I went to Bill’s wake to pay my last respects.
Everyone in town came to the mayor’s funeral to pay their last respects.

senses.definition: to give someone a false compliment that is really an insult.
examples: John said that he had never seen me looking better. I think he was paying me a left-handed compliment.
I’d prefer that someone insulted me directly. I hate it when someone pays me a back-handed compliment—unless it’s a joke.

senses.definition: to compliment someone.
examples: Sally thanked me for paying her a compliment.
When Tom did his job well, I paid him a compliment.

altForms: pay a visit to someone or something

senses.definition: to visit someone or something.
examples: Bill paid a visit to his aunt in Seattle.
Please pay a visit to our house whenever you are in town.

senses.definition: to honor someone; to have and show respect for someone.
examples: You really should pay your boss more respect.
We have to pay our parents a lot of respect.

senses.definition: to pay the costs (of something) for someone.
examples: I wanted to go to Florida this spring, but my parents say I have to pay my own way.
My aunt is going to pay my way to Florida—only if I take her with me!

senses.definition: to face the results of one’s actions; to receive punishment for something.
examples: You can put off paying your debts only so long. Eventually you’ll have to pay the piper.
You can’t get away with that forever. You’ll have to pay the piper someday.

senses.definition: to be beneficial to do something; to be profitable.
examples: It doesn’t pay to drive downtown when you can take the train.
It pays to take an umbrella with you if it’s supposed to rain.

senses.definition: to think of someone in a certain way.
examples: Susan pegged the new employee as a lazy worker.
I had you pegged as an angry rebel before I got to know you.

headword: A penny saved is a penny earned.

senses.definition: Money saved through thrift is the same as money earned by employment.
examples: “I didn’t want to pay that much for the book,” said Mary. “After all, a penny saved is a penny earned.”
Bob put his money in a new bank that pays more interest than his old bank, saying, “A penny saved is a penny earned.”

senses.definition: an expression meaning that it is foolish to lose a lot of money to save a little money.
senses.notes: This is the British pound sterling.
examples: Sally shops very carefully to save a few cents on food, then charges the food to a charge card that costs a lot in annual interest. That’s being penny-wise and pound-foolish.
John drives thirty miles to buy gas for three cents a gallon less than it costs here. He’s really penny-wise and pound-foolish.

senses.definition: to make someone or something more sprightly and active.
examples: I need a bottle of pop to pep me up.
The third act of this play needs something to pep it up. How about a few good jokes?

senses.definition: Do not even consider thinking of something.
examples: If you should become ill—perish the thought—I’d take care of you.
I’m afraid that we need a new car. Perish the thought.

senses.definition: to make someone or something more cheery.
examples: A nice cup of coffee would really perk me up.
Don’t you think that new curtains would perk up this room?

senses.definition: to continue, with determination, to do something.
examples: John persists in thinking that he’s always right.
Tom persists in demanding that I agree to his terms.

senses.definition: to continue the state of something; to extend an action or state.
examples: Please do not persist with your demands that I agree to your terms.
If you persist with this intrusion, I’m going to call the police.

senses.definition: a way of looking at a situation and determining what is important.
examples: The jury did not have a good perspective on the crime since some of the evidence had to be ignored.
Studying history gives one perspective on the present.

senses.definition: to die or dwindle away; [for something] to become exhausted gradually.
examples: When the fire petered out, I went to bed.
My money finally petered out, and I had to come home.

senses.definition: to open a lock without a key; to open a lock without using a key.
examples: The robber picked the lock with a nail file.
The thief picked the lock on the safe and stole the money.

senses.definition: to choose very carefully from a number of possibilities; to be selective.
examples: You must take what you are given. You cannot pick and choose.
Meg is so beautiful. She can pick and choose from a whole range of boyfriends.

senses.definition: to start an argument or fight with someone.
examples: Are you trying to pick a quarrel with me?
Max intended to pick a fight with Lefty.

senses.definition: to criticize something severely; to find all the flaws or fallacies in an argument.
examples: The lawyer picked holes in the witness’s story.
They will pick holes in your argument.
She picked my story to pieces.

senses.definition: the best of the group.
examples: This playful puppy is the pick of the whole lot.
These potatoes are the pick of the crop.

senses.definition: to work slowly and meticulously through written material.
senses.notes: Literal when referring to moving carefully through a route filled with obstacles.
examples: My teacher said he couldn’t even pick his way through my report. It was just too confusing.
I spent an hour picking my way through the state tax forms.

senses.definition: to criticize someone or something; to abuse someone or something.
examples: Stop picking on me!
Why are you always picking on your dog?
Don’t pick on our house. It’s old, but we love it.

headword: pick on someone your own size
altForms: pick on somebody your own size

senses.definition: to abuse someone who is big enough to fight back.
examples: Go pick on somebody your own size!
Max should learn to pick on someone his own size.

senses.definition: to kill someone or something with a carefully aimed gunshot.
examples: The hunter picked the deer off with great skill.
The killer tried to pick off the police officer.

senses.definition: to go to a place in a car, bus, etc., and take on a person as a passenger.
examples: Please come to my office and pick me up at noon.
I have to pick up Billy at school.

senses.definition: to stop one’s car, bus, etc., and offer someone a ride.
examples: Don’t ever pick a stranger up when you’re out driving!
I picked up a hitchhiker today, and we had a nice chat.

senses.definition: to attempt to become acquainted with someone for romantic or sexual purposes.
examples: Who are you anyway? Are you trying to pick me up?
No, I never picked up anybody in my life!

senses.definition: [for the police] to find and bring someone to the police station for questioning or arrest.
examples: I tried to pick her up, but she heard me coming and got away.
Sergeant Jones, go pick up Sally Franklin and bring her in to be questioned about the jewel robbery.

senses.definition: to tidy up or clean up a room or some other place.
examples: Let’s pick this room up in a hurry.
I want you to pick up the entire house.

senses.definition: to find, purchase, or acquire something.
examples: Where did you pick that up?
I picked up this tool at the hardware store.

senses.definition: to learn something.
examples: I pick languages up easily.
I picked up a lot of knowledge about music from my brother.
I picked up an interesting melody from a movie.

senses.definition: to cause something to go faster, especially music.
examples: All right, let’s pick this piece up and get it moving faster.
Okay, get moving. Pick it up!

senses.definition: to resume something.
examples: Pick it up right where you stopped.
I’ll have to pick up my work where I left off.

senses.definition: to receive radio signals; to bring something into view.
examples: I can just pick it up with a powerful telescope.
