I can hardly pick up a signal.
We can pick up a pretty good television picture where we live.

senses.definition: to find a trail or route.
examples: The dogs finally picked up the scent.
You should pick up Highway 80 in a few miles.

senses.definition: to talk with someone to find out information about something.
examples: I spent the afternoon with Donna, picking her brain for ideas to use in our celebration.
Do you mind if I pick your brains? I need some fresh ideas.

senses.definition: to sort through something; to rummage through something.
examples: They picked all the records over.
The shoppers quickly picked over the sale merchandise.

senses.definition: to tidy up.
examples: When you finish playing, you have to pick up.
Please pick up after yourself.

senses.definition: to get busy; to go faster.
examples: Things usually pick up around here about 8:00.
I hope things pick up a little later. It’s boring here.

senses.definition: to intercept and pay the charges for a meal, entertainment, or other goods or services.
senses.notes: Meaning that the one who picks up the check pays the charges listed on it. Informal.
examples: Whenever we go out, my father picks up the tab.
Order whatever you want. The company is picking up the check.

senses.definition: rejected; worn, dirty, or undesirable.
examples: This merchandise looks worn and picked over. I don’t want any of it.
Everything in the store is picked over by the end of the month.

senses.definition: the perfect example of something; an exact image of something.
examples: The young newlyweds were the picture of happiness.
Our family is just the picture of love and joy.
The doctor says I am the picture of health.

senses.definition: a future reward after death, considered as a replacement for a reward not received on earth.
examples: You expect to get rich from this scheme, but that’s just pie in the sky.
His promises are just pie in the sky! He is a liar if I ever saw one.

senses.definition: very easy.
examples: No, it won’t be any trouble. It’s a piece of cake.
It’s easy! Look here—piece of cake.

senses.definition: a share in a scheme or project; a degree of involvement.
examples: If you guys are going to bet on the football game, I want a piece of the action, too.
My brother wants in on it. Give him a piece of the action.

senses.definition: a very loud and shrill scream.
examples: Suddenly, there was a piercing scream from the next room.
Bob heard Susan’s piercing scream and ran to help her.

senses.definition: to climb into something or get into something roughly.
examples: Okay, kids, pile in!
The children piled into the car and slammed the door.

senses.definition: to get out of something roughly.
examples: Okay, kids, pile out!
The car door burst open, and the children piled out.

senses.definition: to crash or wreck something.
senses.notes: Also literal meaning “to heap something up.”
examples: Drive carefully if you don’t want to pile the car up.
The driver piled up the car against a tree.

senses.definition: to crash or wreck.
examples: The car piled up against the tree.
The bus piled up on the curve.

senses.definition: a tower of strength someone or something that consistently provides moral, emotional, or financial support as does a pillar.
examples: My parents are my pillars of support.
The minister looked to God as her pillar of strength.
Jack was a tower of strength during the time that his father was unemployed.

senses.definition: to force someone to make a decision or choice.
senses.notes: See also on pins and needles.
examples: The doctor tried to pin Jane Smith down for her next appointment.
I won’t make up my mind for a week so don’t try to pin me down now.

senses.definition: to force someone to explain or clarify something.
examples: Try to pin her down on the time.
Pin down Jane on exactly what she means.
Please find out exactly how much it costs. Pin them down on the price.

senses.definition: to scold someone severely; to beat someone.
examples: Tom pinned my ears back because I insulted him.
I got very mad at John and wanted to pin his ears back, but I didn’t.

senses.definition: to place the blame for something on someone.
examples: I didn’t take the money. Don’t try to pin it on me. I wasn’t even there.
The police managed to pin the crime on Bob.

senses.definition: to substitute for someone.
senses.notes: Originally from baseball, where it refers to a substitute batter.
examples: Will you pinch-hit for me at band practice?
Sorry, I can’t pinch-hit. I don’t have the time.

senses.definition: a tingling feeling in some part of one’s body, especially the arms and legs.
senses.notes: See also on pins and needles.
examples: I’ve got pins and needles in my legs.
Mary gets pins and needles if she crosses her arms for long.

senses.definition: to be quiet; to get quiet.
examples: Okay, you guys, pipe down!
I’ve heard enough out of you. Pipe down!

senses.definition: a wish or an idea that is impossible to achieve or carry out.
senses.notes: From the dreams or visions induced by the smoking of an opium pipe.
examples: Going to the West Indies is a pipe dream. We’ll never have enough money.
Your hopes of winning a lot of money are just a silly pipe dream.

senses.definition: to speak up and say something, especially with a highpitched voice.
examples: Billy piped up with a silly remark.
Did I hear somebody pipe up with an insult?

senses.definition: extremely hot.
examples: On a cold day, I like to eat piping hot soup.
Be careful! This coffee is piping hot!

senses.definition: to arouse interest; to arouse curiosity.
examples: The advertisement piqued my curiosity about the product.
The professor tried to pique the students’ interest in French literature.

headword: pit someone or something against someone or something

senses.definition: to set someone or something in opposition to someone or something.
examples: The rules of the tournament pit their team against ours.
John pitted Mary against Sally in the tennis match.
In an interesting plowing match, Bill pitted himself against a small tractor.

senses.definition: to erect a tent at a campsite.
examples: The campers pitched their tent in a clearing in the woods.
I pitched my tent next to a large oak tree.

senses.definition: very black; as black as pitch.
examples: The hearse was pitch-black.
The bandit rode on a pitch-black horse and wore black clothing.

senses.definition: to set up or arrange a campsite.
examples: We pitched camp near the stream.
Two campers went ahead of us to pitch camp while it was still light.

senses.definition: very dark; as dark as pitch.
examples: I couldn’t see anything outside because it was pitch-dark.
The room was pitch-dark, and I couldn’t find the light switch!

senses.definition: to get busy and help (with something).
examples: Pick up a paintbrush and pitch in and help.
Why don’t some of you pitch in? We need all the help we can get.

senses.definition: to surprise someone with an unexpected act or event.
senses.notes: Alluding to pitching a curve ball in baseball. It is the route of the ball that is curved, not the ball itself.
examples: You really pitched me a curve ball when you said I had done a poor job. I did my best.
You asked Tom a hard question. You certainly pitched him a curve.

senses.definition: the worst possible.
examples: John is such a boring person. He’s the pits.
This restaurant isn’t the best, but it’s not the pits either.

senses.definition: to submit an order.
examples: My secretary placed an order for a new computer.
I placed my order only yesterday.

senses.definition: to recall someone’s name; to recall the details about a person that would help you identify the person.
examples: I am sorry, I can’t seem to place you. Could you tell me your name again?
I can’t place her. Did I meet her once before?

senses.definition: to make a joke that tricks someone.
examples: The children played a joke on their teacher.
I don’t like it when you play jokes on me.

headword: play along with someone or something

senses.definition: to agree to cooperate or conspire with someone or someone’s plan; to pretend to agree to cooperate or conspire with someone or someone’s plan.
examples: I refused to play along with the treasurer when she outlined her plan.
It might be wise to play along with the kidnappers, at least for a little while.
I’ll play along with your scheme until the others get here, but I don’t like it.

senses.definition: to engage in some amusing activity with someone or something; to tease someone or something.
examples: Please don’t play around with that vase. You’ll break it.
Don’t play about with the parrot. It’ll bite you.
Bill and I were just playing around when we heard the sound of breaking glass.

senses.definition: to do a trick that affects someone.
examples: Somebody played a trick on me by hiding my shoes.
The little boys planned to play a trick on their teacher by turning up the heat in the classroom.

senses.definition: to cooperate with someone.
senses.notes: Literal when referring to playing a ball game. Informal.
examples: Look, friend, if you play ball with me, everything will work out all right.
Things would go better for you if you’d learn to play ball.

senses.definition: to scheme in a way that pits two sides against each other (for one’s own gain).
examples: I told my brother that Mary doesn’t like him. Then I told Mary that my brother doesn’t like her. They broke up, so now I can have the car this weekend. I succeeded in playing both ends against the middle.
If you try to play both ends, you’re likely to get in trouble with both sides.

senses.definition: a description of an event given as the event is taking place.
senses.notes: Usually in reference to a sporting event.
examples: And now here is Bill Jones with a play-by-play description of the baseball game.
John was giving me a play-by-play description of the argument going on next door.

senses.definition: to alternate between kinds of behavior when dealing with someone, often in matters of pursuit.
examples: The police played cat and mouse with the suspect until they had sufficient evidence to make an arrest.
Tom had been playing cat and mouse with Ann. Finally she got tired of it and broke up with him.

senses.definition: to do something by the rules; to play something in a fair and just manner.
examples: John won’t play with Bill anymore because Bill doesn’t play fair.
You moved the golf ball with your foot! That’s not playing fair!

headword: play fast and loose (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to act carelessly, thoughtlessly, and irresponsibly.
examples: I’m tired of your playing fast and loose with me. Leave me alone.
Bob got fired for playing fast and loose with the company’s money.
If you play fast and loose like that, you can get into a lot of trouble.

senses.definition: to be the leader of a section of instruments in an orchestra or a band.
examples: Sally learned to play the violin so well that she now plays first chair in the orchestra.
I’m going to practice my flute so I can play first chair.

senses.definition: to act as a leader.
examples: I need to get this job done. Who plays first chair around here?
You’re not the boss! You don’t play first chair.

senses.definition: to attract someone’s attention by touching feet under the table; to flirt with someone.
examples: Bill was trying to play footsie with Sally at the dinner table. The hostess was appalled.
They shouldn’t play footsie at a formal dinner.

senses.definition: to get involved with someone; to collaborate with someone.
examples: The treasurer got fired for playing footsie with the vice president.
When politicians play footsie, there is usually something illegal going on.

senses.definition: to take an action that is permanent or final.
examples: Mary told me that Tom wants to marry me. I didn’t know he wanted to play for keeps.
I like to play cards and make money, but I don’t like to play for keeps.

senses.definition: to be coy, shy, and fickle.
senses.notes: Usually refers to someone of the opposite sex.
examples: Why can’t we go out? Why do you play hard to get?
Sally annoys all the boys because she plays hard to get.

senses.definition: not to go to school or to some important meeting.
examples: Why aren’t you in school? Are you playing hooky?
I don’t have time for the sales meeting today, so I think I’ll just play hooky.

senses.definition: to pretend to be ignorant [of something].
examples: I played ignorant even though I knew about the surprise party.
John played ignorant when I asked him if he knew who had been on the telephone.

senses.definition: to pretend to be innocent and not concerned.
examples: There is no need to play innocent. I know you broke the lamp!
John is playing innocent, and he knows more than he is telling us.

senses.definition: to come under one’s control without realizing it.
senses.notes: [for a person one is scheming against]
examples: John is doing exactly what I hoped he would. He’s playing into my hands.
John played into my hands by taking the coins he found in my desk. I caught him and had him arrested.

senses.definition: to act calm and unconcerned.
examples: No one will suspect anything if you play it cool.
Don’t get angry, Bob. Play it cool.

senses.definition: to be or act safe; to avoid taking a risk.
examples: You should play it safe and take your umbrella.
If you have a cold or the flu, play it safe and go to bed.

headword: play one’s cards close to the chest
altForms: play one’s cards close to one’s vest
keep one’s cards close to one’s chest
keep one’s cards close to one’s vest

senses.definition: to work or negotiate in a careful and private manner.
senses.notes: [for someone] Literal when referring to concealing one’s cards in a card game.
examples: It’s hard to figure out what John is up to because he plays his cards close to his chest.
Don’t let them know what you’re up to. Keep your cards close to your vest.

senses.definition: to work or negotiate correctly and skillfully.
examples: If you play your cards right, you can get whatever you want.
She didn’t play her cards well, and she ended up with something less than what she wanted.

senses.definition: to use a special trick; to use one’s most powerful or effective strategy or device.
examples: I won’t play my trump card until I have tried everything else.
I thought that the whole situation was hopeless until Mary played her trump card and solved the whole problem.

senses.definition: to have an effect on something; to manage something for a desired effect.
examples: The clerk played on my sense of responsibility in trying to get me to buy the book.
See if you can get her to confess by playing on her sense of guilt.

senses.definition: to negotiate politically.
examples: Everybody at city hall is playing politics as usual.
If you’re elected as a member of a political party, you’ll have to play politics.

senses.definition: to allow politics to dominate in matters where principle should prevail.
examples: Look, I came here to discuss this trial, not play politics.
They’re not making reasonable decisions. They’re playing politics.

senses.definition: to pretend to be inactive, unobservant, asleep, or dead.
senses.notes: Folksy. The possum is an opossum.
examples: I knew that Bob wasn’t asleep. He was just playing possum.
I can’t tell if this animal is dead or just playing possum.

senses.definition: to be in a subordinate position to someone.
examples: I’m tired of playing second fiddle to John.
I’m better trained than he, and I have more experience. I shouldn’t play second fiddle.

senses.definition: to treat someone like (a) something.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with take someone for someone or something.
examples: Don’t play me for a fool! I know what’s going on.
They played her for a jerk, but were they surprised!

headword: play someone off against someone else

senses.definition: to scheme in a manner that pits two of your adversaries against one another.
examples: Bill wanted to beat me up and so did Bob. I did some fast talking, and they ended up fighting with each other. I really played Bill off against Bob.
The president played the House off against the Senate and ended up getting his own way.

senses.definition: to lessen the effect or importance of someone or something.
examples: John is a famous actor, but the director tried to play him down as just another member of the cast.
They tried to play down her earlier arrest.

senses.definition: to make someone or something seem to be more important.
examples: The director tried to play Ann up, but she was not really a star.
Try to play up the good qualities of our product.

senses.definition: to be able to play a piece of music after just listening to it a few times, without looking at the notes.
examples: I can play “Stardust” by ear.
Some people can play Chopin’s music by ear.

senses.definition: to play a musical instrument well, without formal training.
examples: John can play the piano by ear.
If I could play by ear, I wouldn’t have to take lessons—or practice!

senses.definition: to improvise; to decide what to do after one is already involved in a situation.
examples: When we get into the meeting we’ll have to play everything by ear.
He never prepared his presentations. He always played things by ear.

senses.definition: to put forward arguments against or objections to a proposition—which one may actually agree with—purely to test the validity of the proposition.
senses.notes: The devil’s advocate was given the role of opposing the canonization of a saint in the medieval Church in order to prove that the grounds for canonization were sound.
examples: I agree with your plan. I’m just playing the devil’s advocate so you’ll know what the opposition will say.
Mary offered to play devil’s advocate and argue against our case so that we would find out any flaws in it.

senses.definition: to date many different people rather than going steady.
senses.notes: Informal. See also go steady with someone.
examples: When Tom told Ann good-bye, he said he wanted to play the field.
He said he wanted to play the field while he was still young.

senses.definition: to act in a silly manner in order to amuse other people.
examples: The teacher told Tom to stop playing the fool and sit down.
Fred likes playing the fool, but we didn’t find him funny last night.

senses.definition: to invest in the stock market, perhaps recklessly.
senses.notes: Informal. As if it were a game or gambling.
examples: Would you rather put your money in the bank or play the market?
I’ve learned my lesson playing the market. I lost a fortune.

senses.definition: to perform in a manner that will get the strong approval of the audience; to perform in a manner that will get the approval of the ruder members of the audience.
examples: John is a competent actor, but he has a tendency to play to the gallery.
When he made the rude remark, he was just playing to the gallery.

senses.definition: to trick or confuse someone.
examples: I thought I saw a camel over there. I guess my eyes are playing tricks on me.
Please don’t play tricks on your little brother. It makes him cry.

senses.definition: to try to gain someone’s favor.
examples: Bill is always playing up to the teacher.
Ann played up to Bill as if she wanted him to marry her.

senses.definition: to take a big risk.
examples: If you accuse her of stealing, you’ll be playing with fire.
I wouldn’t try that if I were you—unless you like playing with fire.

senses.definition: worn out; spent; exhausted.
examples: This charcoal is just about played out.
The batteries in this flashlight are almost played out.

senses.definition: lots of something; an abundance of something; enough of something.
examples: I have plenty of candy. Do you want some?
This project is giving me plenty of trouble.

senses.definition: Things are becoming more complicated or interesting.
examples: The police assumed that the woman was murdered by her ex-husband, but he has an alibi. The plot thickens.
John is supposed to be going out with Mary, but I saw him last night with Sally. The plot thickens.

senses.definition: to crash into someone or something; to bump hard into someone or something.
senses.notes: Also literal if one is running a plow into someone or something.
examples: The car plowed into the ditch.
The runner plowed into another player.

senses.definition: to work through something with determination.
examples: She plowed through the book to learn everything she could.
Billy plowed through dinner and ran outside to play.

senses.definition: to increase one’s courage a bit.
examples: Come on, Ann, make the dive. Pluck up your courage and do it.
Pluck up your courage, Ann! You can do it!

senses.definition: to keep trying something; to keep working at something.
examples: John kept pegging away at the trumpet until he became pretty good at it.
I’m not very good at it, but I keep plugging away.

senses.definition: to stop or fill up a hole, crack, or gap.
examples: Take out the nail and plug the hole up with something.
You have to plug up the cracks to keep out the cold.

senses.definition: completely crazy.
examples: If you think you can stand up against Marshall Dillon, you’re plumb loco.
Bob is not just a little strange, he’s plumb loco.

senses.definition: the appropriate but chance receiving of rewards or punishments by those deserving them.
examples: It was poetic justice that Jane won the race after Mary tried to get her banned.
The car thieves stole a car with no gas. That’s poetic justice.

senses.definition: the halfway point; the point at which it is too late to turn back.
examples: The flight was past the point of no return, so we had to continue to our destination.
The entire project is past the point of no return; we will have to continue with it.

senses.definition: a way of thinking about something; [someone’s] viewpoint; an attitude or expression of self-interest.
examples: From my point of view, all this talk is a waste of time.
She has a strange point of view, but she has made some good observations about the problem.

senses.definition: to select or indicate someone or something (from a group).
examples: Everyone pointed the error out.
She pointed the thief out to the police officer.
She pointed out the boy who took her purse.

senses.definition: to emphasize something; to demonstrate a fact.
examples: I’d like to point your approach up by citing some authorities who agree with you.
This kind of incident points up the flaws in your system.

senses.definition: to blame someone; to identify someone as the guilty person.
senses.notes: See also put the finger on someone.
examples: Don’t point the finger at me! I didn’t take the money.
The manager refused to point the finger at anyone in particular and said that everyone was sometimes guilty of being late.

senses.definition: ready for something; in the right position and waiting for something.
examples: The cat stared at the mouse, poised for action.
The army was poised for battle.

senses.definition: ready to do something; in the right position to do something.
examples: The cat is poised to jump on the mouse.
The army is poised to attack at dawn.

senses.definition: to look or search around.
examples: I’ve been poking around in the library looking for some statistics.
I don’t mind if you look in my drawer for a paper clip, but please don’t poke about.

senses.definition: to make fun of someone; to ridicule someone.
examples: Stop poking fun at me! It’s not nice.
Bob is always poking fun.

senses.definition: to interfere with something; to be nosy about something.
examples: I wish you’d stop poking your nose into my business.
She was too upset for me to stick my nose in and ask what was wrong.

senses.definition: very different; far from coming to an agreement.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, grow, or seem.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Jones don’t get along well. They are poles apart.
They’ll never sign the contract because they are poles apart.

senses.definition: to finish something off.
examples: There is just a little bit of work left. It won’t take any time to polish it off.
Bob polished off the rest of the pie.

senses.definition: to quit; to wear out and stop.
examples: I’m so tired I could poop out right here.
My car sounded as if it were going to poop out.

senses.definition: exhausted.
senses.notes: [for a person or animal to be] Slang.
examples: The horse was pooped out and could run no more.
I can’t go on. I’m pooped out.

senses.definition: having little money but clean and of good habits, nonetheless.
senses.notes: Either extremely condescending or jocular. Some people would consider it offensive.
examples: My salary isn’t very high, and I only have two color TV sets. Anyway, I’m poor but clean.
When Fred uttered the phrase poor but clean in reference to some of the people working in the yard, Ellen went into a rage.

senses.definition: to make a wisecrack or smart-aleck remark.
examples: If you pop off one more time, you’ll have to stay after school.
Bob keeps popping off at the worst times.

senses.definition: to suddenly become mentally disturbed; to go crazy.
examples: I was so upset that I nearly popped my cork.
They put him away because he popped his cork.

senses.definition: to become very angry.
examples: My mother popped her cork when she heard about my grades.
Calm down! Don’t pop your cork.

senses.definition: to ask someone to marry one.
examples: I was surprised when he popped the question.
I’ve been waiting for years for someone to pop the question.

senses.definition: to hit a baseball that goes upward rather than outward.
examples: The catcher came to bat and popped up.
I hope I don’t pop up this time.

senses.definition: to fly upward rather than outward.
examples: The ball popped up and went foul.
The ball will always pop up if you hit it in a certain way.

senses.definition: to arise suddenly; to appear without warning.
examples: New problems keep popping up all the time.
Billy popped up out of nowhere and scared his mother.

senses.definition: to ask a question; to imply the need for asking a question.
examples: Genetic research poses many ethical questions.
My interviewer posed a hypothetical question.

senses.definition: to pretend to be someone.
examples: The impostor posed as the president of the company.
My twin posed as me while I went on vacation.

senses.definition: under the control of something; obsessed with something.
examples: She acted as if she were possessed by evil spirits.
He was possessed by a powerful sense of guilt.

senses.definition: having something.
examples: Bill was possessed of an enormous sense of self-worth.
The Smiths were possessed of a great deal of fine ranch land.

senses.definition: charges for sending [something] through the mail and for wrapping and handling the item.
examples: The cost of the book was quite reasonable, but the postage and handling was outrageous.
They did not charge postage and handling because I prepaid the order.

headword: the pot calling the kettle black

senses.definition: someone with a fault accusing someone else of having the same fault.
examples: Ann is always late, but she was rude enough to tell everyone when I was late. Now that’s the pot calling the kettle black!
You’re calling me thoughtless? That’s really a case of the pot calling the kettle black.

senses.definition: to walk a route.
senses.notes: Informal. Usually said of a police patrol officer.
examples: Officer Smith pounded the same beat for years and years.
I don’t want to pound a beat all my life.

senses.definition: to play something loudly on the piano.
senses.notes: Also literal. Slang. Compare this with belt something out.
examples: Don’t pound the music out! Just play it.
Listen to her pound out that song.

senses.definition: to type something on a typewriter.
examples: Please pound it out again. There are six errors.
It’ll take just a few minutes to pound out this letter.

senses.definition: to walk through the streets looking for a job.
examples: I spent two months pounding the pavement after the factory I worked for closed.
Hey, Bob. You’d better get busy pounding those nails unless you want to be out pounding the pavement.

senses.definition: to discourage doing something; to reduce enthusiasm for something.
examples: When my father said I couldn’t have the car, he poured cold water on my plans.
John threw cold water on the whole project by refusing to participate.
I hate to dash cold water on your party, but you cannot use the house that night.

senses.definition: to waste money; to spend money as if one were throwing it away.
examples: What a waste! You’re just pouring money down the drain.
Don’t buy any more of that lowquality merchandise. That’s just throwing money down the drain.

senses.definition: to calm things down.
senses.notes: If oil is poured onto rough seas during a storm, the water will become more calm.
examples: That was a good thing to say to John. It helped pour oil on troubled water. Now he looks happy.
Bob is the kind of person who pours oil on troubled waters.

senses.definition: to tell all one’s hopes, fears, and feelings to someone.
examples: She was so upset. She poured her heart out to Sally.
She sat there talking for over an hour—pouring out her heart.

senses.definition: very heavy rain.
examples: The children’s clothes were soaked after they played out in the pouring rain.
I waited in the pouring rain for the next bus.

senses.definition: the person who controls the person who is apparently in charge.
examples: Mr. Smith appears to run the shop, but his brother is the power behind the throne.
They say that the vice president is the power behind the throne.

senses.definition: the people who are in authority.
examples: The powers that be have decided to send back the immigrants.
I have applied for a license, and the powers that be are considering my application.

senses.definition: to praise or recommend something to someone who is already in favor of it.
examples: Mary was preaching to the converted when she tried to persuade Jean to become a feminist. She’s been one for years.
Bob found himself preaching to the converted when he was telling Jane the advantages of living in the country. She hates city life.

senses.definition: very few; very little.
senses.notes: Informal. Few with things that are countable, otherwise, little.
examples: We get precious few tourists here in the winter.
There’s precious little food in the house and there is no money.

senses.definition: an act or event that comes before and signals another act or event.
examples: Her rudeness to her boss was a prelude to her resignation.
The invasion of Poland was a prelude to World War II.

senses.definition: in a hurry.
examples: I am sorry. I can’t talk to you. I’m just too pressed for time.
If you are pressed for time, you might want to stop for some food somewhere on the highway.

senses.definition: You should do pleasant things if you wish to be considered pleasant.
examples: Now, Sally. Let’s be nice. Pretty is as pretty does.
My great-aunt always used to say “pretty is as pretty does” to my sister.

senses.definition: an unpleasant state of affairs.
senses.notes: See also fine kettle of fish.
examples: This is a pretty state of affairs, and it’s all your fault.
What a fine state of affairs you’ve got us into.

senses.definition: to ask or beg someone (for a favor).
examples: Can I prevail upon you to give me some help?
Perhaps you could prevail on my brother for a loan.

senses.definition: to listen more closely.
senses.notes: Alluding to animals that move their ears about to hear better.
examples: At the sound of my voice on the telephone, my sister pricked up her ears.
I pricked up my ears when I heard my name mentioned.

senses.definition: something or someone that one is very proud of.
senses.notes: Often in reference to a baby, a car, a house, etc.
examples: And this is our little pride and joy, Roger.
Fred pulled up in his pride and joy and asked if I wanted a ride.

senses.definition: Someone who behaves in an arrogant or vain way is likely to suffer misfortune.
examples: Bert was so busy admiring his reflection in a shop window that he stepped in a puddle. Pride goes before a fall.
Jean was boasting about how well she thought she’d done on her final exams, but she failed them all. You know what they say. Pride goes before a fall.

senses.definition: the force that sets something going; someone or something that starts something off.
examples: The manager was the prime mover in getting the clerk fired.
Discontent with his job was the prime mover in John’s deciding to go to Alaska.

senses.definition: uniquely knowledgeable about something.
examples: The reporter became privy to the senator’s evil plan.
Why are you privy to this secret information?

senses.definition: to make extravagant promises to someone.
examples: Bill will promise you the moon, but he won’t live up to his promises.
My boss promised the moon, but only paid the minimum wage.

senses.definition: likely to [do] something; apt to have something.
examples: My boss is prone to fits of anger when my work isn’t done.
My sister is prone to sneezing because of her allergies.

senses.definition: to make a toast before drinking.
examples: I’d like to propose a toast in honor of your birthday.
At the wedding reception, the bride’s father proposed a toast.

headword: prove to be someone or something

senses.definition: to be shown to be someone or something; to be found to be someone or something.
examples: Susan proved to be a good friend when she lent me some money.
The food proved to be spoiled when I smelled it.

senses.definition: on the condition that something is so.
examples: I will come, provided that I am invited.
I will help you, provided that you pay me.

senses.definition: to go wild or crazy; to become irrational.
senses.notes: Slang. Pronounced as if it were spelled sike.
examples: I don’t know what happened to me. Suddenly I psyched out and started yelling.
Max nearly psyched out when he saw the bill.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be enthusiastic about doing something.
senses.notes: Slang. Pronounced as if it were spelled sike.
examples: The coach psyched up the team before the game.
I need someone to psyche me up before I go on stage.

senses.definition: confused and disoriented.
senses.notes: Slang. Pronounced as if it were spelled siked.
examples: What an upsetting day! I’m really psyched out.
She is so psyched out she can’t see straight.

senses.definition: excited and enthusiastic.
senses.notes: Slang. Pronounced as if it were spelled siked.
examples: I can play a great tennis game if I’m psyched up.
She is really psyched up for the game.

senses.definition: to publish many books or articles in scholarly journals or get released from a university or fall into disfavor in a university.
senses.notes: [for a professor] Also occurs as other parts of speech. See the examples below.
examples: Alice knew she would have to publish or perish if she took the teaching job.
This is a major research university and publish or perish is the order of the day.
When Jane heard that publish or perish was the rule at her university, she was afraid that she would not get any professors who were interested in her intellectual advancement.

senses.definition: to do something stupid or silly.
examples: Boy, I really pulled a boner! I’m so dumb.
If you pull a boner like that again, you’re fired!

senses.definition: to succeed in an act of deception.
examples: She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home.
Don’t try to pull a fast one with me! I know what you’re doing.

senses.definition: to bring out a gun or knife suddenly so that it is ready for use against someone.
examples: I screamed when the mugger pulled a knife on me.
The police shot the thief when he pulled a gun.

senses.definition: to deceive someone.
examples: Let’s pull a trick on the teacher.
Don’t you dare pull a stunt like that!

senses.definition: to become emotionally stabilized; to regain one’s composure.
examples: Now, calm down. Pull yourself together.
I’ll be all right as soon as I can pull myself together.

headword: pull oneself up (by one’s own bootstraps)

senses.definition: to achieve (something) through one’s own efforts.
examples: They simply don’t have the resources to pull themselves up by their own bootstraps.
If I could have pulled myself up, I’d have done it by now.

senses.definition: to strike with light blows to enable the other boxer to win.
examples: Bill has been barred from the boxing ring for pulling his punches.
“I never pulled my punches in my life!” cried Tom.

senses.definition: to hold back in one’s criticism.
senses.notes: Slang. Usually in the negative. The one’s can be replaced with any.
examples: I didn’t pull any punches. I told her just what I thought of her.
The teacher doesn’t pull any punches when it comes to discipline.

senses.definition: to use all one’s energy and effort in order to achieve something.
senses.notes: From the stops of a pipe organ. The more that are pulled out, the louder it gets.
examples: You’ll have to pull out all the stops if you’re going to pass the course.
The doctors will pull out all the stops to save the child’s life.

senses.definition: to assert one’s rank, authority, or position over someone when making a request or giving an order.
examples: Don’t pull rank on me! I don’t have to do what you say!
When she couldn’t get her way politely, she pulled rank and really got some action.

senses.definition: to degrade someone; to humiliate someone.
examples: I’m afraid that your friends are pulling you down. Your manners used to be much better.
My bad habits are pulling me down.
There is no need to pull down everyone.

senses.definition: to earn a certain amount of money.
examples: She’s able to pull down $400 a week.
I wish I could pull down a salary like that.
How much is she pulling down?

senses.definition: to demolish something; to raze something.
examples: Why do they want to pull it down? Why not remodel it?
They are going to pull down the old building today.

senses.definition: to lower or reduce the amount of something.
examples: That last test pulled my grade down.
Let’s see if we can pull down your temperature.

senses.definition: to kid, fool, or trick someone.
examples: You don’t mean that. You’re just pulling my leg.
Don’t believe him. He’s just pulling your leg.

senses.definition: to reduce the power of someone or something.
senses.notes: Also literal in the case of someone. Informal.
examples: The mayor tried to pull the teeth of the new law.
The city council pulled the teeth of the new mayor.

senses.definition: to help someone survive something.
examples: With the help of the doctor, we pulled her through her illness.
With lots of encouragement, we pulled her through.

senses.definition: to manage to make something happen.
senses.notes: Also literal. Slang. See also carry something off.
examples: Yes, I can pull it off.
Do you think you can pull off this deal?

senses.definition: to play a trick on someone; to deceive someone with a trick.
examples: You wouldn’t pull a trick on me, would you?
Who would pull something like that on an old lady?

headword: pull something out of a hat
altForms: pull something out of thin air

senses.definition: to produce something as if by magic.
examples: This is a serious problem, and we just can’t pull a solution out of a hat.
I’m sorry, but I don’t have a pen. What do you want me to do, pull one out of thin air?

senses.definition: to organize something; to arrange something.
senses.notes: Compare this with scrape something together.
examples: How about a party? I’ll see if I can pull something together for Friday night.
This place is a mess. Please pull things together.

senses.definition: to use influence (with someone to get something done).
examples: I can get it done easily by pulling strings.
Is it possible to get anything done around here without pulling strings?

headword: pull the plug (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to cause someone or something to end; to reduce the power or effectiveness of someone or something.
examples: Jane pulled the plug on the whole project.
The mayor was doing a fine job until the treasurer pulled the plug because there was no more money.

senses.definition: to turn off someone’s life support system in a hospital.
senses.notes: [with someone] This results in the death of person whose life support has been terminated.
examples: They had to get a court order to pull the plug on their father.
Fred signed a living will making it possible to pull the plug on him without a court order.

headword: pull the rug out (from under someone)

senses.definition: to make someone ineffective.
examples: The treasurer pulled the rug out from under the mayor.
Things were going along fine until the treasurer pulled the rug out.

headword: pull the wool over someone’s eyes

senses.definition: to deceive someone.
examples: You can’t pull the wool over my eyes. I know what’s going on.
Don’t try to pull the wool over her eyes. She’s too smart.

senses.definition: to get better; to recover from a serious illness or other problem.
examples: She’s very ill, but I think she’ll pull through.
Oh, I hope she pulls through.

senses.definition: to move to another place.
senses.notes: Refers to pulling up tent stakes and moving to another campsite.
examples: I’ve been here long enough. It’s time to pull up stakes.
I hate the thought of having to pull up stakes.

senses.definition: to make a hole in something with something.
examples: John punched a hole in the wall with his fist.
Mary punched a hole in the paper with her pencil.

senses.definition: absolutely; without further complication or elaboration.
examples: I told you what you must do, and you must do it, pure and simple.
Will you kindly explain to me what it is, pure and simple, that I am expected to do?
Just tell me plain and simple, do you intend to go or don’t you?
I explained it to her plain and simple, but she still didn’t understand.

senses.definition: to go away.
examples: We told the children to push off.
Push off! We don’t want you here.

senses.definition: to expect continued good fortune; to expect to continue to escape bad luck.
examples: You’re okay so far, but don’t push your luck.
Bob pressed his luck too much and got into a lot of trouble.

senses.definition: to force someone into a position where there is only one choice to make; to put someone in a defensive position.
examples: There was little else I could do. They pushed me to the wall.
When we pressed him to the wall, he told us where the cookies were hidden.

senses.definition: to panic; to become anxious or panicky.
examples: I do okay taking tests as long as I don’t push the panic button.
Whatever you do, don’t press the panic button.

senses.definition: dead and buried.
examples: If you don’t drive safely, you’ll be pushing up daisies.
We’ll all be pushing up daisies in the long run.

headword: put a bee in someone’s bonnet

senses.definition: to give someone an idea (about something).
senses.notes: See also get a bee in one’s bonnet.
examples: Somebody put a bee in my bonnet that we should go to a movie.
Who put a bee in your bonnet?

senses.definition: to put a limit on something
examples: We need to put a cap on spending on every department.
The city put a cap on the amount each landlord could charge.

senses.definition: place a restriction on something to show that it is reserved, delayed, or inactivated.
examples: The bank put a hold on my credit card until I paid my bill.
The committee agreed to put a hold on the troublesome piece of business.

headword: put all one’s eggs in one basket

senses.definition: to risk everything at once.
examples: Don’t put all your eggs in one basket. Then everything won’t be lost if there is a catastrophe.
John only applied to the one college he wanted to go to. He put all his eggs in one basket.

senses.definition: to interpret an event to make it seem favorable or beneficial to oneself.
examples: The mayor tried to put a positive spin on the damaging polls.
The pundit’s spin on the new legislation was highly critical.

senses.definition: to bring something to an end.
examples: I want you to put a stop to all this bad behavior.
Please put an end to this conversation.

senses.definition: to suggest something—usually something bad—to someone (who would not have thought of it otherwise).
examples: Bill keeps getting into trouble. Please don’t put ideas into his head.
Bob would get along all right if other kids didn’t put ideas into his head.

headword: put in a good word (for someone)

senses.definition: to say something (to someone) in support of someone.
examples: I hope you get the job. I’ll put in a good word for you.
Yes, I want the job. If you see the boss, please put in a good word.

senses.definition: to appear (somewhere) for just a little while.
senses.notes: Compare this with make an appearance.
examples: I couldn’t stay for the whole party, so I just put in an appearance and left.
Even if you can’t stay for the whole thing, at least put in an appearance.

senses.definition: to try to appear happy or satisfied when faced with misfortune or danger.
examples: We’ve lost all our money, but we must put on a brave face for the sake of the children.
Jim has lost his job and is worried, but he’s putting on a brave face.

senses.definition: to act superior.
examples: Stop putting on airs. You’re just human like the rest of us.
Ann is always putting on airs. You’d think she was a queen.

senses.definition: to pretend that one is something other than what one is.
examples: Be yourself, Ann. Stop putting on an act.
You don’t have to put on an act. We accept you the way you are.

senses.definition: to rebuke someone; to remind one of one’s (lower) rank or station.
examples: The boss put me in my place for criticizing her.
Then her boss put her in her place for being rude.

senses.definition: to apply great physical effort to lift or move something.
examples: All right, you guys. Put your backs into moving this piano.
You can lift it if you put your back to it.

senses.definition: to apply a lot of mental or creative effort to doing something.
examples: If we put our backs to it, we can bake twelve dozen cookies to-day.
The artist put his back into finishing the picture on time.

senses.definition: to act or appear at one’s best; to try to make a good impression.
examples: When you apply for a job, you should always put your best foot forward.
I try to put my best foot forward whenever I meet someone for the first time.

headword: put one’s cards on the table
altForms: lay one’s cards on the table

senses.definition: to reveal everything; to be open and honest with someone.
examples: Come on, John, lay your cards on the table. Tell me what you really think.
Why don’t we both put our cards on the table?

senses.definition: to lay a claim to something; to state one’s claim to something.
senses.notes: Informal. See also have dibs on something.
examples: I put dibs on the last piece of cake.
Mary put her dibs on the book you are reading. She gets it next.

senses.definition: to identify something as very important.
examples: Ann put her finger on the cause of the problem.
Yes, she really put her finger on it.

senses.definition: to become adamant about something.
examples: Ann put her foot down about what kind of car she wanted.
She doesn’t put her foot down very often, but when she does, she really means it.

headword: put one’s foot in one’s mouth
altForms: stick one’s foot in one’s mouth

senses.definition: to say something that you regret; to say something stupid, insulting, or hurtful.
examples: When I told Ann that her hair was more beautiful than I had ever seen it, I really put my foot in my mouth. It was a wig.
I put my foot in it by telling John’s secret.

senses.definition: to locate and acquire something.
senses.notes: Compare this with get one’s hands on someone or something.
examples: I wish I could put my hands on a 1954 Chevrolet.
If I could put my hands on that book, I could find the information I need.

headword: put one’s hand to the plow

senses.definition: to begin to do a big and important task; to undertake a major effort.
examples: If John would only put his hand to the plow, he could do an excellent job.
You’ll never accomplish anything if you don’t put your hand to the plow.

headword: put one’s head on the block (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to take great risks for someone or something; to go to a lot of trouble or difficulty for someone or something; to attempt to gain favor for someone or something.
examples: I don’t know why I should put my head on the block for Joan. What has she ever done for me?

Sally tried to get me to put in a good word about her with the boss. You know, tell the boss what a great worker she is and how smart she is. The last time I put my head on the block for anyone, it all backfired, and when the person goofed up, I looked like an idiot!

senses.definition: to put one’s business or personal affairs into good order.
examples: There was some trouble at work and the manager was told to put his house in order.
Every now and then, I have to put my house in order. Then life becomes more manageable.

senses.definition: to give one’s complete attention to something.
examples: I could finish this job tonight if I put my mind to it.
Please put your mind to it and concentrate on getting it finished.

headword: put one’s nose to the grindstone

senses.definition: to keep busy doing one’s work.
senses.notes: Also with have and get, as in the examples. See also keep one’s nose to the grindstone.
examples: The boss told me to put my nose to the grindstone.
I’ve had my nose to the grindstone ever since I started working here.
If the other people in this office would get their noses to the grindstone, more work would get done.

senses.definition: to give help; to interfere by giving advice; to put one’s two cents’ worth in.
senses.notes: Refers to adding one’s efforts to rowing a boat.
examples: You don’t need to put your oar in. I don’t need your advice.
I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have put in my oar.

headword: put one’s shoulder to the wheel

senses.definition: to get busy.
examples: You won’t accomplish anything unless you put your shoulder to the wheel.
I put my shoulder to the wheel and finished the job quickly.

senses.definition: to start thinking in a serious manner.
examples: It’s time to put our thinking caps on, children.
All right now, let’s put on our thinking caps and do some arithmetic.

headword: put one’s two cents(‘ worth) in

senses.definition: to add one’s comments (to something).
examples: Can I put in my two cents’ worth?
Sure, go ahead—put your two cents in.

senses.definition: to make one demonstrate what one can do; to make one do one’s job thoroughly.
senses.notes: See also put something through its paces.
examples: The boss really put me through my paces today. I’m tired.
I tried out for a part in the play, and the director really put me through my paces.

senses.definition: to dress or entertain in an extravagant or showy manner.
examples: The Smiths really put on the dog at their party last Saturday.
They’re always putting on the dog.

senses.definition: to eat a meal.
senses.notes: Literal with horses. Folksy and slang.
examples: It’s noon—time to put on the feed bag.
I didn’t put on the feed bag until about eight o’clock last night.

senses.definition: to attempt to find out something without being too obvious.
senses.notes: Refers to what an insect does to sense what is happening around it.
examples: I wanted to get a new job, so I put out some feelers.
The manager was mean to everyone in the office, so everyone put out feelers in an attempt to find new jobs.

senses.definition: to kill someone.
examples: The gangster threatened to put me away if I told the police.
They’ve put away witnesses in the past.

senses.definition: to bury someone.
examples: My uncle died last week. They put him away on Saturday.

senses.definition: to have someone put into a mental institution.
examples: My uncle became irrational, and they put him away.
They put away my aunt the year before.

senses.definition: to put someone’s name on a list of people who volunteer to do something or give an amount of money.
examples: Can I put you down for ten dollars?
We’re having a picnic, and you’re invited. Everyone is bringing something. Can I put you down for potato salad?

senses.definition: to give someone all the necessary facts about something.
senses.notes: Literal for a painter or digital graphics artist.
examples: They put the police in the picture about how the accident happened.
Would someone put me in the picture about what went on in my absence?

senses.definition: to respect, admire, or worship a person.
examples: He has put her on a pedestal and thinks she can do no wrong.
Don’t put me on a pedestal. I’m only human.

senses.definition: to ask someone embarrassing questions; to demand that someone produce as expected.
examples: Don’t put me on the spot. I can’t give you an answer.
The boss put Bob on the spot and demanded that he do everything he had promised.

senses.definition: to present someone in a good way or a good light.
examples: I don’t want Tom to make the speech. He doesn’t put himself across well.
I get myself across in situations like this. I’ll do it.

senses.definition: to make a clear explanation of something; to explain oneself clearly.
examples: The teacher got the idea across with the help of pictures.
I’m taking a course in public speaking to help put myself across better.

senses.definition: to convince someone of something; to get a plan accepted.
examples: After many weeks of trying, we were unable to put our plan across. They refused to accept it.
We just couldn’t get it across.

senses.definition: to belittle or degrade someone or something.
examples: It’s an old car, but that’s no reason to put it down.
Please stop putting me down all the time. It hurts my feelings.
You put down everything you don’t understand!

senses.definition: to repress or (figuratively) crush something.
examples: The army was called to put down the rebellion.
The police used tear gas to put the riot down.

senses.definition: to write something down.
examples: I’ll give you the address. Please put it down.
I’ll put down the address in my address book.

senses.definition: to land an aircraft.
examples: The pilot put the plane down exactly on time.
I can’t put down this plane in the rain.

senses.definition: to take the life of an animal, such as a pet that is suffering.
senses.notes: [with something] This is usually done by a veterinarian.
examples: We had to put our dog down. She was suffering so.
It’s very difficult to put down one’s pet.

headword: put someone or something on hold

senses.definition: to stop all activity or communication with someone.
examples: John put Ann on hold and started dating Mary.
“You can’t just put me on hold!” cried Ann.

senses.definition: to leave someone waiting on a telephone call.
examples: Please don’t put me on hold. I’ll call back later when you aren’t so busy.
I’ll have to put you on hold while I look up the information.

senses.definition: to postpone something; to stop the progress of something.
examples: They put the project on hold until they got enough money to finish it.
Sorry, but we must put your plan on hold.

headword: put someone or something out to pasture

senses.definition: to retire someone or something.
senses.notes: Refers to a horse that is too old to work.
examples: Please don’t put me out to pasture. I have lots of good years left.
This car has reached the end of the line. It’s time to put it out to pasture.

headword: put someone or something to sleep

senses.definition: to kill someone or something.
examples: We had to put our dog to sleep.
The robber said he’d put us to sleep forever if we didn’t cooperate.

senses.definition: to cause someone or something to sleep, perhaps through drugs or anesthesia.
examples: The doctor put the patient to sleep before the operation.
I put the cat to sleep by stroking its tummy.

senses.definition: to bore someone.
examples: That dull lecture put me to sleep.
Her long story almost put me to sleep.

headword: put someone or something to the test

senses.definition: to see what someone or something can achieve.
examples: I think I can jump that far, but no one has ever put me to the test.
I’m going to put my car to the test right now, and see how fast it will go.

senses.definition: to puncture or harm someone’s eye causing blindness.
examples: Careful with that stick or you’ll put your eye out.
He fell and almost put his eye out!

headword: put someone’s nose out of joint

senses.definition: to offend someone; to cause someone to feel slighted or insulted.
examples: I’m afraid I put his nose out of joint by not inviting him to the picnic.
There is no reason to put your nose out of joint. I meant no harm.

senses.definition: to give someone a difficult time.
examples: They are really putting me through the wringer at school.
The boss put Bob through the wringer over this contract.

headword: put someone to bed with a shovel

senses.definition: to kill someone; to kill and bury someone.
examples: That guy’d better be careful, or somebody’s going to put him to bed with a shovel.
“Watch out, wise guy,” said the robber, “or I’ll put you to bed with a shovel.”

senses.definition: to increase the power of something.
examples: The mayor tried to put some teeth into the new law.
The statement is too weak. Put some teeth in to it.

headword: put something down in black and white

senses.definition: to write down the terms of an agreement; to draw up a written contract; to put the details of something down on paper.
senses.notes: Refers to black ink and white paper.
examples: We agree on all the major points. Now, let’s put it down in black and white.
I think I understand what you are talking about, but we need to put it down in black and white.

senses.definition: to explain something as being caused by something else.
examples: I put his bad humor down to his illness.
We set your failure down to your emotional upset.

senses.definition: to state an idea; to advance an idea.
examples: Toward the end of the meeting, Sally put an idea forward.
Now, I’d like to put something forward.
He put several suggestions forward.

senses.definition: to put something in storage.
senses.notes: Also literal in reference to clothing. Often said of battleships.
examples: The navy put the old cruiser in mothballs and no one ever expected to see it again.
Let’s just put this small bicycle in mothballs until we hear of a child who can use it.

senses.definition: to start using a scheme or plan.
examples: I hope we can put your idea into practice soon.
The mayor hopes to put the new plan into practice after the next election.

altForms: put something on the back burner

senses.definition: to delay or postpone something; to put something on hold.
examples: I’m afraid that we’ll have to put your project on ice for a while.
Just put your idea on ice and keep it there till we get some money.

senses.definition: to write something down; to type or otherwise record something important.
examples: You have a great idea for a novel. Now put it on paper.
I’m sorry, I can’t discuss your offer until I see something in writing. Put it on paper, and then we’ll talk.

senses.definition: to buy something on credit; to add to one’s credit balance.
examples: I’ll take two of those, and please put them on the cuff.
I’m sorry, Tom. We can’t put anything more on the cuff.

senses.definition: to speak very firmly and directly about something.
examples: She was very mad. She put it on the line, and we had no doubt about what she meant.
All right, you kids. I’m going to lay it on the line. Don’t ever do that again if you know what’s good for you.

senses.definition: to state something firmly and explicitly.
examples: To put it plainly, I want you out of this house immediately.
Thank you. I think you’ve put your feelings quite plainly.

senses.definition: to demonstrate how well something operates; to demonstrate all the things something can do.
senses.notes: Compare this with put one through one’s paces.
examples: I was down by the barn, watching Sally put her horse through its paces.
This is an excellent can opener. Watch me put it through its paces.

senses.definition: to consider some facts and arrive at a conclusion.
examples: I couldn’t put everything together to figure out the answer in time.
When I put together all the facts, I found the answer.

senses.definition: to put an end to a rumor; to finish dealing with something and forget about it.
examples: I’ve heard enough about Ann and her illness. I’d like to put the whole matter to rest.
I’ll be happy to lay it to rest, but will Jane?

senses.definition: to apply pressure to someone.
examples: John’s been putting the arm on Mary to get her to go out with him.
John has been putting the arm on Bill to get him to cooperate.

senses.definition: to try to get money from someone.
examples: Tom put the bite on me for ten dollars.
Bill put the touch on me, but I told him to drop dead.

headword: put the cart before the horse

senses.definition: to have things in the wrong order; to have things confused and mixed up.
examples: You’re eating your dessert! You’ve put the cart before the horse.
Slow down and get organized. Don’t put the cart before the horse!
John has the cart before the horse in most of his projects.

senses.definition: to restrain or restrict someone.
examples: Tom’s parents put the clamps on him. They decided he was getting out of hand.
They got mad and put on the clamps.

senses.definition: to accuse someone; to identify someone as the one who did something.
senses.notes: Slang. See also point the finger at someone.
examples: Tom put the finger on John, and John is really mad.
He’d better not lay the finger on me. I didn’t do it.

senses.definition: to put pressure on someone (to do something); to coerce someone.
examples: John wouldn’t talk, so the police were putting the heat on him to confess.
When they put the screws on, they can be very unpleasant.
The police know how to put the squeeze on.

senses.definition: to put an end to something; to veto something.
examples: The mayor put the kibosh on the project.
It’s a great idea, and I’m sorry that I had to put the kibosh on it.

senses.definition: to cause something to fail.
examples: They put the skids on the project when they refused to give us any more money.
That’s the end of our great idea! Somebody put the skids on.

senses.definition: to figure something out from the information available.
examples: Well, I put two and two together and came up with an idea of who did it.
Don’t worry. John won’t figure it out. He can’t put two and two together.

senses.definition: to appear to be brave (even if one is not).
examples: Mary is frightened, but she’s putting up a brave front.
If she weren’t putting on a front, I’d be more frightened than I am.

senses.definition: to be made use of to an unreasonable degree.
examples: My mother was always put upon by her neighbors. She was too nice to refuse their requests for help.
Jane feels put upon by her husband’s parents.
They’re always coming to stay with her.

senses.definition: a command to prove something or stop talking about it; to do something or stop promising to do it.
examples: I’m tired of your telling everyone how fast you can run. Now, do it! Put up or shut up!
Now’s your chance to show us that you can run as fast as you can talk. Put up or shut up!

senses.definition: a command to bet money in support of what one advocates.
senses.notes: See also Put your money where your mouth is!
examples: If you think that your horse is faster than mine, then make a bet. Put up or shut up!
You think you can beat me at cards? Twenty bucks says you’re wrong. Put up or shut up!

senses.definition: to gain weight; to grow fat.
examples: I have to go on a diet because I’ve been putting on a little weight lately.
The doctor says I need to put on some weight.

senses.definition: to speak for another person without permission.
examples: Stop putting words into my mouth. I can speak for myself.
The lawyer was scolded for putting words into the witness’s mouth.

headword: Put your money where your mouth is!

senses.definition: a command to stop talking big and make a bet.
examples: I’m tired of your bragging about your skill at betting. Put your money where your mouth is!
You talk about betting, but you don’t bet. Put your money where your mouth is!

senses.definition: easily influenced by someone else; excessively willing to do what someone else wishes.
examples: Bob’s wife is putty in his hands. She never thinks for herself.
Jane’s putty in her mother’s hands. She always does exactly what she is told.

senses.definition: to figure something out; to try to figure something out.
examples: I looked and looked at it, but I couldn’t puzzle it out.
See if you can puzzle out this confusing mess.

senses.definition: fast and carelessly; [done] fast and cheaply.
examples: I am not interested in a quick and dirty job. I want it done right.
The contractor made a lot of money on quick and dirty projects that would never last very long.

senses.definition: quick to draw a gun and shoot.
examples: Some of the old cowboys were known to be quick on the trigger.
Wyatt Earp was particularly quick on the draw.

senses.definition: quick to respond to anything.
examples: John gets the right answer before anyone else. He’s really quick on the trigger.
Sally will probably win the quiz game. She’s really quick on the draw.

senses.definition: quick to understand (something).
examples: Just because I’m not quick on the uptake, it doesn’t mean I’m stupid.
Mary understands jokes before anyone else because she’s so quick on the uptake.

senses.definition: much or many.
examples: Do you need one? I have quite a few.
I have quite a little—enough to spare some.
How many? Oh, quite a number.

senses.definition: definitely [something]; a good example of [something].
examples: The captain of the swim team is quite a swimmer.
That’s quite a bruise you have there.

senses.definition: to name or state in advance the charge for doing or supplying something.
examples: The mechanic quoted a price of $100 to repair my car.
The carpenter quoted a price for fixing up the stairs.

senses.definition: a rush; rushing to beat a deadline.
examples: We were in a race against time to beat the deadline.
It was a race against time, but we made it.

senses.definition: to hurry to beat a deadline.
examples: We had to race against time to finish before the deadline.
You don’t need to race against time. Take all the time you want.

senses.definition: to try very hard to think of something.
examples: I racked my brains all afternoon, but couldn’t remember where I put the book.
Don’t waste any more time racking your brain. Go borrow the book from the library.

senses.definition: suffering from severe pain.
examples: My body was racked with pain, and I nearly passed out.
I sat there racked with pain, waiting for the doctor.

senses.definition: to complain loudly or violently to someone about something.
examples: Jane railed at the treasurer about not having received her check.
I am not responsible for your problems. Don’t rail at me!

senses.definition: to rain very hard.
examples: It’s raining cats and dogs. Look at it pour!
I’m not going out in that storm. It’s raining cats and dogs.

senses.definition: to ruin someone’s planned event; to spoil someone’s plans or scheme.
examples: I hate to rain on your parade, but the guest of honor cannot come to the reception.
The boss rained on our parade by making us all work overtime.

senses.definition: no matter whether it rains or the sun shines.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll be there rain or shine.
We’ll hold the picnic—rain or shine.

senses.definition: to spoil something by raining.
examples: Oh, the weather looks awful. I hope it doesn’t rain the picnic out.
It’s starting to sprinkle now. Do you think it will rain out the ball game?

senses.definition: to mention an objection about someone or something.
examples: I hope your family won’t raise an objection to my staying for dinner.
I’m certain no one will raise objection. We are delighted to have you.

headword: raise havoc with someone or something
altForms: play havoc with someone or something

senses.definition: to create confusion or disruption for or among someone or something.
examples: Your announcement raised havoc with the students.
I didn’t mean to play havoc with them.

headword: raise hob with someone or something
altForms: play hob with someone or something

senses.definition: to do something devilish to someone or something; to cause trouble for someone or something.
senses.notes: A hob is a hobgoblin, a wicked little elf.
examples: Your sudden arrival is going to play hob with my dinner plans.
Sorry, I didn’t mean to raise hob with you.

senses.definition: to set higher goals for oneself.
examples: When you’re young, you tend to raise your sights too high.
On the other hand, some people need to raise their sights.

senses.definition: to speak loudly or shout at someone in anger.
examples: Don’t you dare raise your voice to me!
I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to raise my voice.

senses.definition: to shock or surprise people mildly (by doing or saying something).
senses.notes: Some can be replaced with a few, someone’s, a lot of, etc.
examples: What you just said may raise some eyebrows, but it shouldn’t make anyone really angry.
John’s sudden marriage to Ann raised a few eyebrows.

headword: raise the devil (with someone or something)
altForms: raise the dickens (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to act in some extreme manner; to make trouble; to behave wildly; to be very angry.
examples: John was out all night raising the devil.
Don’t come around here and raise hell with everybody.
That cheap gas I bought really raised the dickens with my car’s engine.

senses.definition: brought up to behave like a barnyard animal; behaving crudely.
examples: Close the door behind you! Were you raised in a barn?
Don’t wipe your nose on your sleeve. Were you raised in a barn?

senses.definition: to give someone a severe scolding.
examples: My mother hauled me over the coals for coming in late last night.
The manager raked me over the coals for being late again.

senses.definition: to steal or embezzle a portion of a payment.
examples: They claimed that no one was raking anything off and that the money was only mislaid.
The county treasurer was caught raking off some of the tax money.

senses.definition: to uncover something unpleasant and remind people about it.
examples: The young journalist raked up the old scandal about the president.
The politician’s opponents are trying to dredge up some unpleasant details about his past.

senses.definition: to come together to support someone or something.
examples: Everyone rallied around Jack when he lost his job.
Former students rallied round their college when it was in danger of being closed.

senses.definition: to talk aimlessly about someone or something.
examples: John is so talkative. He’s always rambling on about something.
You’re rambling on yourself.

senses.definition: regular soldiers, not the officers.
examples: I think there is some trouble with the rank and file, sir.
The rank and file usually do exactly as they are told.

senses.definition: the members of a group, not the leaders.
examples: The rank and file will vote on the proposed contract tomorrow.
The last contract was turned down by the rank and file last year.

headword: rant and rave (about someone or something)

senses.definition: to shout angrily and wildly about someone or something.
examples: Bob rants and raves when anything displeases him.
Bob rants and raves about anything that displeases him.
Father rants and raves if we arrive home late.

headword: rant (at someone) about someone or something

senses.definition: to talk in a loud, violent way, about someone or something.
examples: Anne ranted about the bad service she had received at the store.
On the bus, someone was ranting at me about the end of the world.

senses.definition: to punish someone slightly.
examples: She rapped his knuckles for whispering too much.
Don’t rap my knuckles. I didn’t do it.

senses.definition: to talk; to chat.
examples: I rapped with the school counselor for half an hour.
My neighbor rapped with me on my back porch all night.

senses.definition: to be extremely eager to act or do something.
examples: Jane can’t wait to start her job. She’s rarin’ to go.
Mary is rarin’ to go and can’t wait for her university term to start.

senses.definition: to report someone’s bad behavior; to tattle on someone.
examples: John ratted on me, and I got in trouble.
If he rats on me, I’ll hit him!

senses.definition: a fierce struggle for success, especially in one’s career or business.
examples: Bob got tired of the rat race. He’s retired and gone to the country.
The money market is a rat race, and many people who work in it die of the stress.

senses.definition: to be in someone’s favor; to be thought of highly by someone.
examples: Ann is great. She really rates with me.
She doesn’t rate with me at all.

senses.definition: to recite something quickly and accurately.
examples: She can really reel them off.
Listen to Mary rattle off those numbers.

senses.definition: made very happy or delighted; overcome with happiness or delight.
senses.notes: Men are less likely to be ravished with delight.
examples: Mary was ravished with delight by the dozen roses.
My parents were ravished with delight when I graduated from college.

senses.definition: to achieve a compromise; to make a compromise.
examples: After many hours of discussion, we finally reached a compromise.
We were unable to reach a compromise and quit trying.

senses.definition: to achieve an agreement; to make an agreement.
examples: We reached an agreement and signed a contract.
We could not reach an agreement, so we stopped negotiating.

senses.definition: to progress to the point that a barrier stops further progress.
examples: When negotiations with management reached an impasse, the union went on strike.
The discussion reached an impasse and no one was able to propose a compromise.

senses.definition: to aspire to something; to set one’s goals high.
examples: It’s a good idea to set high goals, but there is no point in reaching for the sky.
Go ahead, you can do it! Reach for the sky!

senses.definition: a command to put one’s hands up, as in a robbery.
examples: Reach for the sky! This is a stickup!
The sheriff told the bank robbers to reach for the sky.

senses.definition: to do something at one’s best level of ability.
examples: When I reach my stride, things will go faster, and I’ll be more efficient.
Now that I’ve hit my stride, I can work more efficiently.

senses.definition: to infer something (from something).
senses.notes: Usually figurative. Does not necessarily refer to written or printed information.
examples: After listening to what she said, if you read between the lines, you can begin to see what she really means.
Don’t believe everything you hear. Learn to read between the lines.

headword: read someone like a(n open) book

senses.definition: to understand someone very well.
examples: I’ve got John figured out. I can read him like a book.
Of course I understand you. I read you like an open book.

senses.definition: to expel someone from an organization, such as a political party.
examples: Because of her statement, they read her out of the party.
The officers tried to read me out of the society, but they didn’t succeed.

senses.definition: to guess what someone is thinking, as if one had special powers to sense someone else’s thoughts.
examples: You’ll have to tell me what you want. I can’t read your mind, you know.
If I could read your mind, I’d know what you expect of me.

senses.definition: to give someone a severe scolding.
examples: The manager read me the riot act for coming in late.
The teacher read the students the riot act for their failure to do their assignments.

senses.definition: to attach or attribute a new or different meaning to something.
examples: This statement means exactly what it says. Don’t try to read anything else into it.
Am I reading too much into your comments?

senses.definition: to read all of something.
examples: Take this home and read it through.
Read through this report and see if you can find any errors.

headword: read the handwriting on the wall

senses.definition: to anticipate what is going to happen by observing small hints and clues.
examples: I know I am going to be fired. I can read the handwriting on the wall.
Can’t you read the handwriting on the wall? Can’t you see what they are planning?

senses.definition: prepared and willing.
examples: Are you ready to leave for the airport?
If you need me, I’m ready to help.

senses.definition: eager or at least willing [to do something].
examples: If you need someone to help you move furniture, I’m ready, willing, and able.
Fred is ready, willing, and able to do anything you ask him.

senses.definition: something that is genuine and not an imitation.
examples: I don’t want frozen yogurt, I want the real thing! Yes, ice cream!
She hates plastic that looks like wood. She wants the real thing.

senses.definition: the truth or actuality of the situation; the way the situation really is.
examples: The reality of the situation is that we must act right now.
Let’s face the reality of the situation and go out and get jobs so we can buy food.

senses.definition: to appear or become obvious after lying hidden.
examples: Jealousy reared its ugly head and destroyed their marriage.
The question of money always rears its ugly head in matters of business.

senses.definition: to greet someone eagerly.
examples: I’m sure they wanted us to stay for dinner. They received us with open arms.
When I came home from school, the whole family welcomed me with open arms.

senses.definition: to deal with someone or something; to confront someone or something.
examples: Eventually you will have to reckon with getting a job.
I really don’t want to have to reckon with the manager when she’s mad.

headword: recognize something for what it is
altForms: recognize one for what one is

senses.definition: to see and understand exactly what someone or something is or represents.
examples: The disease represented a serious threat to all peoples, and Dr. Smith recognized it for what it was.
I recognize you for what you are, you scoundrel!

senses.definition: to grow to feel comfortable with an undesirable or challenging situation.
examples: John reconciled himself to living alone.
Anne reconciled herself to having to wear glasses.

senses.definition: a piece of information or suggestion introduced to draw attention away from the real facts of a situation.
senses.notes: A red herring is a type of strong-smelling smoked fish that was once drawn across the trail of a scent to mislead hunting dogs and put them off the scent.
examples: The detectives were following a red herring, but they’re on the right track now.
Jack and Mary were hoping their friends would confuse their parents with a red herring so that they wouldn’t realize that they had eloped.

senses.definition: embarrassed.
examples: After we found Ann hiding in the closet, she became red in the face.
The speaker kept making errors and became red in the face.
