senses.definition: over-strict attention to the wording and details of rules and regulations, especially by government workers.
senses.notes: From the color of the tape used by government departments in England to tie up bundles of documents.
examples: Because of red tape, Frank took weeks to get a visa.
Red tape prevented Jack’s wife from joining him abroad.

senses.definition: brought into a certain humble condition or state.
examples: The grieving family was reduced to tears.
The poor man was reduced to begging for food.

senses.definition: sell a second or subsequent set of doses of a medicine upon a doctor’s orders.
examples: The pharmacy refused to refill my prescription because it has expired.
If you want the drugstore to refill your prescription, just give them the prescription number over the telephone.

senses.definition: to become calm and composed.
examples: I found it difficult to regain my composure after the argument.
Here, sit down and relax so that you can regain your composure.

senses.definition: to stand up again after falling or stumbling.
examples: I fell on the ice and almost couldn’t regain my feet.
I helped my uncle regain his feet as he tried to get up from the chair.

senses.definition: to become independent after financial difficulties.
examples: I lent Bill $400 to help him regain his feet.
I’ll be able to pay my bills when I regain my feet.

senses.definition: without considering something; at any rate; whatever is done; whatever option is chosen.
examples: Regardless of what you say, I’m still going to the club tonight.
I still have to pay the bill, regardless of the facts.

senses.definition: concerning someone or something.
examples: I have something to say relative to Bill.
Do you have any information relative to the situation in South America?

senses.definition: in proportion to someone or something.
examples: My happiness is relative to yours.
I can spend an amount of money relative to the amount of money I earn.

senses.definition: trust and dependence on someone or something.
examples: John’s reliance on his family is holding him back.
Reliance on sleeping pills is dangerous.

senses.definition: strict about something; conscientious about something.
examples: Bob is religious about paying his bills on time.
Max tries to be religious about being polite to everyone.

senses.definition: a feeling of not wanting to do something; unwillingness to do something.
examples: Mary showed great reluctance to go bowling with me.
Because of John’s reluctance to make friends, he was lonely.

senses.definition: reminding someone about someone or something; seeming like or suggesting someone or something.
examples: This fragrance is reminiscent of fresh flowers.
Jane’s dress is reminiscent of the style worn in the 1920s.

senses.definition: thought to do, be, or have something.
examples: My boss is reputed to have cancer.
My neighbor was reputed to have been a spy during the war.

senses.definition: to accept something reluctantly.
examples: I finally resigned myself to going to Mexico even though I didn’t want to.
Mary resigned herself to her fate.

senses.definition: to appeal to someone or cause someone to relate to it.
examples: The concept of buying CDs at a clothing store seems to resonate with young people.
Your notion just doesn’t resonate with the public in general.

senses.definition: the person or organization responsible or liable for something.
examples: I intend to find the responsible party and get some answers to my questions.
Mary sued the responsible party in the car crash.

senses.definition: to be assured; to be certain.
examples: Rest assured that you’ll receive the best of care.
Please rest assured that we will do everything possible to help.

senses.definition: to lie dead peacefully for eternity.
examples: We prayed that the deceased would rest in peace.
The bodies of the soldiers will rest in peace.

senses.definition: to enjoy one’s success and not try to achieve more.
examples: Don’t rest on your laurels. Try to continue to do great things!
I think I’ll rest on my laurels for a time before attempting anything new.

senses.definition: to cause something to happen.
examples: The storm resulted in a lot of flooding.
Her fall resulted in a broken leg.

senses.definition: to pay a compliment to someone who has paid you a compliment.
senses.notes: See also pay someone a compliment.
examples: Mary told me that my hair looked nice, so I returned her compliment and told her that her hair was lovely.
When someone says something nice, it is polite to return the compliment.

senses.definition: to do a good deed for someone who has done a good deed for you.
examples: You helped me last week, so I’ll return the favor and help you this week.
There is no point in helping Bill. He’ll never return the favor.

senses.definition: to make an idling engine run very fast, in short bursts of speed.
examples: Hey! Stop revving it up!
I wish that Tom wouldn’t sit out in front of our house in his car and rev up his engine.

senses.definition: having valuable resources, characteristics, traditions, or history.
examples: The entire region is rich in historical churches.
Our soil is rich in important nutrients.

senses.definition: having a lot of something; not lacking; abundant.
examples: The beautiful book was rich with color illustrations.
The old town was rich with elegant Victorian houses.

headword: ride herd on someone or something

senses.definition: to supervise someone or something.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to a cowboy supervising cattle.
examples: I’m tired of having to ride herd on my kids all the time.
My job is to ride herd on this project and make sure everything is done right.

senses.definition: to behave in a totally confused manner; to try to do everything at once.
senses.notes: Folksy. Can be said of one or more people.
examples: Bill has a tendency to ride off in all directions. He’s not organized enough.
Now, calm down. There is no sense in riding off in all directions.

senses.definition: to make one’s good fortune or success depend on another person.
senses.notes: Also with else, as in the examples below.
examples: Bill isn’t very creative, so he rides on John’s coattails.
Some people just have to hang on somebody else’s coattails.

headword: ride roughshod over someone or something

senses.definition: to treat someone or something with disdain or scorn.
examples: Tom seems to ride roughshod over his friends.
You shouldn’t have come into our town to ride roughshod over our laws and our traditions.

senses.definition: to endure something unpleasant.
senses.notes: Originally referred to ships lasting out a storm.
examples: It was a nasty situation, but the mayor tried to ride it out.
The mayor decided to ride out the scandal.

senses.definition: to live in luxury.
examples: If I had a million dollars, I sure could ride the gravy train.
I wouldn’t like loafing. I don’t want to ride the gravy train.

senses.definition: risking failure or an accident, usually due to overconfidence.
examples: Tom drives too fast, and he seems too sure of himself. He’s riding for a fall.
Bill needs to eat better and get more sleep. He’s riding for a fall.

senses.definition: to both sides; on all sides; everywhere.
examples: I dropped the tennis balls, and they rolled right and left.
There were children everywhere—running right and left.

senses.definition: exactly or precisely at [a specific place or time].
examples: Meet me at this corner right at noon.
The restaurant is right at First and Main Streets.

senses.definition: immediately.
examples: Please do it right away!
I’ll be there right away. I’m leaving this instant.

senses.definition: ideally suited to one’s interests or abilities.
examples: Skiing is right down my alley. I love it.
This kind of thing is right up John’s alley.

senses.definition: immediately; first thing.
examples: When he was learning to ride a bicycle, he fell on his head right off the bat.
The new manager demanded new office furniture right off the bat.

senses.definition: at the correct time; no later than the specified time.
examples: Bill always shows up right on time.
If you get there right on time, you’ll get one of the free tickets.

senses.definition: with the correct side upwards, as with a box or some other container.
examples: Keep this box right side up, or the contents will be crushed.
Please set your coffee cup right side up so I can fill it.

senses.definition: right in front of someone.
examples: I thought I’d lost my purse, but it was sitting on the table under my very nose.
How did Mary fail to see the book? It was right under her nose.

senses.definition: in someone’s presence.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: The thief stole Jim’s wallet right under his nose.
The jewels were stolen from under the very noses of the security guards.

senses.definition: to cause someone to remember something or for it to seem familiar.
examples: I’ve never met John Franklin, but his name rings a bell.
Whenever I see a bee, it rings a bell. I remember when I was stung by one.

senses.definition: to bring something to an end; to declare something to be at an end.
examples: It’s time to ring down the curtain on our relationship. We have nothing in common anymore.
We’ve tried our best to make this company a success, but it’s time to ring down the curtain.
After many years the old man brought down the curtain and closed the restaurant.

senses.definition: to celebrate the beginning of the new year at midnight on December 31.
examples: We are planning a big party to ring in the New Year.
How did you ring in the New Year?

senses.definition: to record the cost of an item on a cash register.
examples: Please ring this chewing gum up first, and I’ll put it in my purse.
The cashier rang up each item and told me how much money I owed.

senses.definition: to sound or seem true or likely.
senses.notes: From testing the quality of metal or glass by striking it and evaluating the sound made.
examples: The student’s excuse for being late doesn’t ring true.
Do you think that Mary’s explanation for her absence rang true?

senses.definition: to attack someone or something, physically or verbally.
examples: The bear ripped into the deer.
The angry teacher ripped into the student.

senses.definition: to cheat or deceive someone; to steal from someone.
examples: That store operator ripped me off.
They shouldn’t rip off people like that.

senses.definition: to steal something.
examples: I bought it! I didn’t rip it off!
The crooks ripped off a car in broad daylight.

senses.definition: a very old age.
examples: Mr. Smith died last night, but he lived to a ripe old age—99.
All the Smiths seem to reach a ripe old age.

senses.definition: a series of quiet but excited murmurs.
examples: A ripple of excitement spread through the crowd.
As the president came near, a ripple of excitement indicated that people could really see him.

senses.definition: a few quiet remarks protesting something; a small amount of subdued protest.
examples: There was only a ripple of protest about the new tax law.
The rude comedian hardly drew a ripple of protest.

senses.definition: Get out of bed and be lively and energetic!
examples: Come on, children! Rise and shine! We’re going to the beach.
Father always calls “Rise and shine!” in the morning when we want to go on sleeping.

senses.definition: to be lured by some kind of bait.
senses.notes: Literal when referring to a fish.
examples: I threatened to take another job elsewhere, but the boss did not rise to the bait.
When I said I was leaving, Ted rose to the bait and asked why.

senses.definition: to meet the challenge of an event; to try extra hard to do a task.
examples: John was able to rise to the occasion and make the conference a success.
It was a big challenge, but he rose to the occasion.

senses.definition: a chance of precipitation or rain.
senses.notes: Used only in weather forecasting. There is no “risk” of hazard or injury involved.
examples: And for tomorrow, there is a slight risk of showers in the morning.
There is a 50 percent risk of rain tonight.

senses.definition: to risk physical harm in order to accomplish something.
examples: Look at that traffic! I refuse to risk my neck just to cross the street to buy a paper.
I refuse to risk my neck at all.

senses.definition: to keep someone’s attention fixed [on something].
examples: The movie riveted the audience’s attention.
Professor Jones’s lecture riveted the students’ attention.

senses.definition: someone who drives carelessly and selfishly.
examples: Look at that road-hog driving in the middle of the road and stopping other drivers from passing him.
That road-hog nearly knocked the children over. He was driving too fast.

senses.definition: to take from one in order to give to another.
examples: Why borrow money to pay your bills? That’s just robbing Peter to pay Paul.
There’s no point in robbing Peter to pay Paul. You will still be in debt.

senses.definition: to marry or date someone who is much younger than you are.
examples: I hear that Bill is dating Ann. Isn’t that sort of robbing the cradle? She’s much younger than he is.
Uncle Bill— who is nearly eighty—married a thirtyyear-old woman. That is really robbing the cradle.

senses.definition: to cause trouble where none is welcome; to disturb a situation that is otherwise stable and satisfactory.
examples: Look, Tom, everything is going fine here. Don’t rock the boat!
You can depend on Tom to mess things up by rocking the boat.

senses.definition: to come in large numbers or amounts.
examples: We didn’t expect many people at the party, but they just kept rolling in.
Money is simply rolling in for our charity appeal.

senses.definition: to get ready to do some work.
examples: Roll your sleeves up and get busy. This isn’t a picnic. This is work!
Come on, you guys, get busy. Roll up your sleeves and go to work.

headword: roll out the red carpet for someone

senses.definition: to provide special treatment for someone.
senses.notes: Literal when the special treatment actually includes a length of red carpeting.
examples: There’s no need to roll out the red carpet for me.
We rolled out the red carpet for the king and queen.

senses.definition: to reduce a price to a previous amount.
examples: The government forced the company to roll its prices back.
It wouldn’t have rolled back its prices if the government hadn’t forced it to.

senses.definition: having large amounts of something, usually money.
examples: That family is rolling in money.
Jack doesn’t need to earn money. He’s rolling in it.

headword: A rolling stone gathers no moss.

senses.definition: A person who keeps changing jobs or residences and, therefore, accumulates no possessions or responsibilities.
examples: “John just can’t seem to stay in one place,” said Sally. “Oh, well, a rolling stone gathers no moss.”
Bill has no furniture to bother with because he keeps on the move. He keeps saying that a rolling stone gathers no moss.

headword: Rome wasn’t built in a day.

senses.definition: Important things don’t happen overnight.
examples: Don’t expect a lot to happen right away. Rome wasn’t built in a day, you know.
Don’t be anxious about how fast you are growing. Rome wasn’t built in a day.

senses.definition: food to eat and a place to live; the cost of food and lodging.
examples: That college charges too much for room and board.
How much is your room and board?

senses.definition: to cheer and encourage someone or something.
examples: Are you rooting for anyone in particular, or are you just shouting because you’re excited?
I’m rooting for the home team.

senses.definition: to get rid of something completely; to destroy something.
examples: No government will ever root out crime completely.
The headmaster wants to root troublemakers out at the local school.

senses.definition: based on something; connected to a source or cause.
examples: The civil war was rooted in old ethnic hatred.
This fictional book was rooted in actual events.

senses.definition: unable to move because of fear or surprise.
examples: Joan stood rooted to the spot when she saw the ghostly figure.
Mary was rooted to the spot as the mugger snatched her bag.

senses.definition: to persuade or trick someone into doing something.
examples: I don’t know who roped me into this, but I don’t want to do it.
See if you can rope somebody into taking this to the post office.

senses.definition: completely no good and worthless.
senses.notes: Also literal in reference to apples or other edible things.
examples: Fred is rotten to the core. He will never be a good member of society.
I hope that just because I made one little mistake with my life that you don’t think I am rotten to the core.

senses.definition: strong, active, and ready for anything.
examples: John is not exactly rough-and-ready, but he is a moderately good athlete.
Ralph is very rough-and-ready, but his table manners are very bad.

senses.definition: rough; [of living creatures] overly active.
examples: The game got sort of rough-and-tumble, so I stopped playing.
Jane runs with a rough-and-tumble crowd that’s always involved in some sort of sport.

senses.definition: to live in discomfort; to live in uncomfortable conditions without the usual amenities, such as on a camping trip.
examples: The students are roughing it in a shack with no running water.
Bob and Jack had nowhere to live and so they had to rough it in a tent till they found somewhere.

senses.definition: to beat or physically harass someone.
examples: The gangsters roughed their victim up.
The police roughed up the suspect, and they got in trouble for it.

senses.definition: to change a number to the next higher or lower whole number.
examples: You should round 8.122 off.
I rounded off 8.789 to 9.

senses.definition: to finish something by doing something special.
examples: She rounded her schooling off with a trip to Europe.
I like to round out the day with a period of meditation.

senses.definition: to express a number in the nearest whole amount or nearest group of 1, 10, 100, 1,000, 1⁄10, 1⁄100, 1⁄1,000, etc.
examples: When doing taxes, Anne rounded her figures off to the nearest dollar.
These census figures are rounded up to the nearest million.

senses.definition: a ticket (for a plane, train, bus, etc.) that allows one to go to a destination and return.
examples: A round-trip ticket is usually cheaper than a one-way ticket.
How much is a round-trip ticket to San Francisco?

senses.definition: very good treatment; very good and thoughtful care of a person.
examples: I was well cared for. They gave me the royal treatment.
I had the royal treatment when I stayed at that expensive hotel.

senses.definition: to associate with someone; to work closely with someone.
examples: I don’t care to rub elbows with someone who acts like that!
I rub shoulders with John at work. We are good friends.

senses.definition: to seem to transfer to someone else.
senses.notes: [for a characteristic of one person] Also literal.
examples: I’ll sit by Ann. She has been lucky all evening. Maybe it’ll rub off on me.
Sorry. I don’t think that luck rubs off.

senses.definition: deliberately to make someone’s unhappiness, shame, or misfortune worse.
examples: Don’t rub salt in the wound by telling me how enjoyable the party was.
Jim is feeling miserable about losing his job, and Fred is rubbing salt into the wound by saying how good his replacement is.

senses.definition: to kill someone.
examples: The crook said, “Bill is getting to be a problem. We’re going to have to rub him out.”
The gangsters tried to rub out the witness.

headword: rub someone(‘s fur) the wrong way

senses.definition: to irritate someone.
senses.notes: From the rubbing of a cat’s or dog’s fur the wrong way.
examples: I’m sorry I rubbed your fur the wrong way. I didn’t mean to upset you.
Don’t rub her the wrong way!

senses.definition: to remind one of something one has done wrong; to remind one of something bad or unfortunate that has happened.
senses.notes: From a method of housebreaking pets.
examples: When Bob failed his exam, his brother rubbed his nose in it.
Mary knows she shouldn’t have broken off her engagement. Don’t rub her nose in it.

senses.definition: to keep reminding one of one’s failures; to nag someone about something.
examples: I like to rub it in. You deserve it!
Why do you have to rub in everything I do wrong?

senses.definition: to point its feathers outward.
examples: The bird ruffled its feathers when it was annoyed.
My parrot ruffles its feathers whenever it is ready to preen itself.

senses.definition: to upset or annoy someone.
senses.notes: See ruffle its feathers for an explanation.
examples: You certainly ruffled Mrs. Smith’s feathers by criticizing her garden.
Try to be tactful and not ruffle people’s feathers.

headword: the ruin of someone or something

senses.definition: the cause of destruction; a failure.
examples: Your bad judgment will be the ruin of this company!
The greedy politicians were the ruin of the old empire.

senses.definition: a rough or an inexact guide; a basic or accepted pattern or rule.
senses.notes: From the use of one’s thumb to make quick and rough measurements.
examples: It’s a rule of thumb that the bus will be late whenever I’m in a hurry.
As a good rule of thumb, prepare two large potatoes for each person.

senses.definition: to be the boss or manager, especially at home.
examples: Who rules the roost at your house?
Our new office manager really rules the roost.

senses.definition: a meeting held after a larger meeting.
examples: A rump session continued after the meeting was adjourned.
A lot of business was conducted in the rump session.

senses.definition: to have a body temperature higher than normal; to have a fever.
examples: I ran a fever when I had the flu.
The baby is running a temperature and is grouchy.

senses.definition: to chase someone of the opposite sex hoping for a date or some attention.
examples: Is John still running after Ann?
No, Ann is running after John.

senses.definition: to take a short trip to do a specific thing; to complete an errand.
senses.notes: The plural is with some errands.
examples: I’ve got to run an errand. I’ll be back in a minute.
John has gone on an errand. He’ll be back shortly.

senses.definition: to take a chance that something (bad) will happen.
examples: I don’t want to run the risk of losing my job.
Don’t worry. You won’t have to run a risk.

headword: run around like a chicken with its head cut off

senses.definition: to run around frantically and aimlessly; to be in a state of chaos.
examples: I spent all afternoon running around like a chicken with its head cut off.
If you run around in circles, you’ll never get anything done.
Get organized and stop running in circles.

senses.definition: to be friends with someone; to go places with regular friends.
examples: John and I were great friends. We used to run around with each other all the time.
Mary ran around with Jane for about a year.

senses.definition: to run a ship or an organization in an orderly and disciplined manner.
senses.notes: Taut and tight mean the same thing. Taut is correct nautical use.
examples: The new office manager really runs a tight ship.
Captain Jones is known for running a taut ship.

senses.definition: to outrun or outdo someone.
examples: John is a much better racer than Mary. He can run circles around her.
Mary can run rings around Sally.

senses.definition: to be in opposition to something; to run against something.
examples: Your proposal runs counter to what is required by the manager.
His idea runs counter to good sense.

senses.definition: to try to escape by running.
examples: The guard’s not looking. Let’s run for it!
The convict tried to run for it, but the guard caught him.

senses.definition: to run away to save one’s life.
examples: The dam has burst! Run for your life!
The captain told us all to run for our lives.

senses.definition: for a characteristic to appear in all (or most) members of a family.
examples: My grandparents lived well into their nineties, and it runs in the family.
My brothers and I have red hair. It runs in the family.

senses.definition: to come to a barrier against further progress.
examples: We’ve run into a stone wall in our investigation.
Algebra was hard for Tom, but he really ran into a stone wall with geometry.

senses.definition: to run very well; to progress very well.
examples: I want this office to run like clockwork—with everything on time and everything done right.
The plans for the party were made and we knew that we could depend on Alice to make sure that everything ran like clockwork.

senses.definition: to near the end of a supply of something.
examples: We are running low on salt. It’s time to buy more.
The car is running low on gas.

senses.definition: to talk excessively.
examples: Shut up, John. You’re always running off at the mouth.
There is no need to run off at the mouth. Stop talking so much for so long.

headword: run off with someone or something

senses.definition: to take something or someone away; to steal something or kidnap someone.
examples: The thief ran off with the lady’s purse.
The kidnapper ran off with the baby.

senses.definition: and run off to run away with someone, as in an elopement.
examples: Tom ran off with Ann.
Tom and Ann ran off and got married.

senses.definition: common or average; typical.
examples: The restaurant we went to was nothing special—just run-of-the-mill.
The service was good, but the food was run-of-the-mill or worse.

senses.definition: to use up all the gasoline in a car’s tank.
examples: I hope we don’t run out of gas.
I am sorry I am late. I ran out of gas.

senses.definition: to become annoyed after being patient for a while.
examples: I finally ran out of patience and lost my temper.
The boss ran out of patience with me and sent me back to my desk.

senses.definition: to use up all of something and have no more.
examples: We ran out of milk, so we will have to buy some more.
I usually run out of money at the end of the month.

senses.definition: to use up all the available time.
examples: I ran out of time and couldn’t finish.
I hope she answers the question before she runs out of time.

senses.definition: to run, develop, or grow out of control.
examples: The children ran rampant through the house.
Weeds have run rampant around the abandoned house.

senses.definition: to go out of control.
examples: The dandelions have run riot in our lawn.
The children ran wild at the birthday party and had to be taken home.

senses.definition: to behave as if one were going to fail.
senses.notes: Informal. Typically said of someone running for election.
examples: The mayor was running scared, but won anyway.
When we lost that big contract, everyone in the office was running scared. We thought we’d be fired.

senses.definition: to use up almost all of something; to have too little or few of something left.
examples: We are running short of milk. Please buy some on the way home.
When it comes to money, we are always running short.

senses.definition: to take someone to the police station and make an arrest.
examples: “Don’t run me in,” cried the driver. “I’m innocent.”
The police officer was angry and ran in the motorist.

senses.definition: to degrade physically or put wear on someone or something.
examples: All these years of hard work have run Mrs. Brown down severely.
Our neighbors ran down their house before they sold it.

senses.definition: to say bad things about someone or something.
examples: Why are you always running your friends down?
Don’t run down my paintings! You just don’t understand art!

senses.definition: to look for and finally find someone or something.
examples: I finally ran John Smith down. He had moved to another town.
I will see if I can run down the book that you want.

headword: run someone or something to earth

senses.definition: to find someone or something after a search.
examples: Lisa finally ran her long-lost cousin to earth in Paris.
After months of searching, I ran a copy of Jim’s book to earth.

senses.definition: to run someone hard and fast; to keep someone very busy.
examples: This busy season is running us all ragged at the store.
What a busy day. I ran myself ragged.

senses.definition: to carry something too far.
examples: It was a good joke at first, Tom, but you’ve run it into the ground.
Just because everyone laughed once, you don’t have to drive it into the ground.

senses.definition: to raise a flag.
examples: I run it up every day except when it’s raining.
We run up the flag every day.

senses.definition: to add to a bill; to add many charges to one’s account.
examples: He ran the bill up until they asked him to pay part of it.
Tom ran up a big tab at the hotel.

senses.definition: say that again.
examples: I didn’t hear you. Could you run that by me again?
Run that by again. I don’t believe my ears.

senses.definition: to cover the range [from one thing to another].
examples: She wants to buy the house, but her requests run the gamut from expensive new carpeting to completely new landscaping.
His hobbies run the gamut from piano repair to portrait painting.

senses.definition: to do the best that one could; to live life as well and as fully as possible.
examples: He didn’t get what he wanted, but he ran the good race.
Joan ran the good race, and she will be remembered by all of us.

senses.definition: to waste something; to use up something rapidly.
examples: Have you run through all those eggs already?
I ran through my allowance in one day.

senses.definition: to read through something rapidly.
examples: I ran through your report, and it looks okay.
I didn’t read the novel, I only ran through it.

headword: run to an amount of money

senses.definition: to amount to a certain amount of money.
examples: In the end, the bill ran to thousands of dollars.
His account ran to more than I expected.

senses.definition: to become worn-out and uncared for.
senses.notes: Said especially of a lawn that needs care.
examples: Look at that lawn. The whole thing has run to seed.
Pick things up around here. This place is going to seed. What a mess!

senses.definition: to be in a state of excitement or anger.
examples: Feelings were running high as the general election approached.
The mood of the crowd was running high when they saw the mother slap her child.

senses.definition: a large demand for something.
examples: There was a rush on bottled water during the drought.
During the hot summer, there was a rush on air conditioners.

senses.definition: to find and prepare some food.
examples: I’m sure he can rustle something up.
Just go out into the kitchen and ask Bill to rustle up some food.

senses.definition: to go to bed; to go to sleep.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with hit the sack at hit the hay.
examples: Look at the clock. It’s time to sack out.
John sacks out at about nine o’clock.

senses.definition: something that is regarded by some people with such respect and veneration that they do not like it being criticized by anyone in any way.
senses.notes: From the fact that the cow is regarded as sacred in India and is not eaten or mistreated.
examples: A university education is a sacred cow in the Smith family. Fred is regarded as a failure because he quit school at 16.
Don’t talk about eating meat to Pam. Vegetarianism is one of her sacred cows.

senses.definition: unhappy but educated [about someone or something—after an unpleasant event].
examples: After the accident, I was sadder but wiser, and would never make the same mistake again.
We left the meeting sadder but wiser, knowing that we could not ever come to an agreement with Becky’s aunt.

senses.definition: to give someone something undesirable, annoying, or difficult to deal with.
examples: Mary says she doesn’t want to be saddled with a baby, but her husband would just love one.
Jim saddled Eddie with the most boring jobs so that he would leave.

senses.definition: safe and whole or healthy.
examples: It was a rough trip, but we got there safe and sound.
I’m glad to see you here safe and sound.

senses.definition: safety achieved by being concealed in large numbers of people or other creatures.
examples: We stayed close together, thinking that there was safety in numbers.
The elderly people went out together for a walk, knowing that there was safety in numbers.

senses.definition: very good and wise advice.
senses.notes: Refers to a sage or wise man.
examples: My parents gave me some sage advice when I turned 18.
I asked my uncle for some of his sage advice.

senses.definition: to finish something quickly and easily.
examples: The test was not difficult. I sailed right through it.
Bob sailed through his homework in a short amount of time.

senses.definition: to pretend to be something that one is not.
senses.notes: Originally nautical, referring to a pirate ship disguised as an innocent merchant ship.
examples: John has been sailing under false colors. He’s really a spy.
I thought you were wearing that uniform because you worked here. You are sailing under false colors.

senses.definition: the most worthy of people; a very good or worthy person.
examples: Mrs. Jones is the salt of the earth. She is the first to help anyone in trouble.
Frank’s mother is the salt of the earth. She has five children of her own and yet fosters three others.

senses.definition: to store or save something.
senses.notes: Originally referred to preserving food and storing it.
examples: Mary salted some extra candy away for use during the holidays.
I salted away about $1,000 when I worked as a clerk in the grocery store.

headword: the same as someone or something

senses.definition: identical to someone or something.
examples: Can you build me a birdhouse the same as yours?
Have you noticed that Mary looks the same as her mother?

senses.definition: Me too!; I agree!
examples: BOB: I’ll have chocolate ice cream! BILL: Same here.
MARY: I’ll vote for the best candidate. TOM: Same here!

senses.definition: something that occurs or has occurred in the same way often.
examples: Jim’s got no money. It’s the same old story. He’s spent it all on clothing.
The company is getting rid of workers. It’s the same old story—a shortage of orders.

senses.definition: the same comment applies to you.
senses.notes: Informal. This can be a polite or a rude comment.
examples: BILL: Have a pleasant evening. BOB: Thank you. The same to you.
MARY: You’re the most horrible person I’ve ever met! JOHN: The same to you!

senses.definition: the accumulated tiny amounts of time; time represented by the sand in an hourglass.
examples: The sands of time will make you grow old like everyone else.
My only enemy is the sands of time.

senses.definition: Stop talking.; Shut up!; Tell it to me later.
examples: I’ve heard enough. Save it!
Save it! You talk too much!

senses.definition: to refrain from talking, explaining, or arguing.
examples: There is no sense in trying to convince her. Save your breath.
Tell her to save her breath. He won’t listen to her.

senses.definition: to preserve one’s good standing or high position (after a failure).
examples: The ambassador was more interested in saving his face than winning the argument.
Most diplomats are concerned with saving face.

senses.definition: to save someone from injury, embarrassment, or punishment.
examples: I saved my skin by getting the job done on time.
Thanks for saving my neck! I would have fallen down the stairs if you hadn’t held my arm.

headword: save something for a rainy day

senses.definition: to reserve something—usually money—for some future need.
senses.notes: Also literal. Save something can be replaced with put something aside, hold something back, keep something, etc.
examples: I’ve saved a little money for a rainy day.
Keep some extra candy for a rainy day.

senses.definition: to produce a good result when a bad result was expected.
examples: The team was expected to lose, but Sally made many points and saved the day.
Your excellent speech saved the day.

senses.definition: rescued from a difficult or dangerous situation just in time by something that brings the situation to a sudden end.
senses.notes: From the sounding of a bell marking the end of a round in a boxing match.
examples: James didn’t know the answer to the question but he was saved by the bell when the teacher was called away from the room.
I couldn’t think of anything to say to the woman at the bus stop, but I was saved by the bell when my bus arrived.

senses.definition: the one thing that saves or redeems someone or something that would otherwise be a total disaster.
examples: Her saving grace is that she has a lot of money.
The saving grace for the whole evening was the good music played by the band.

senses.definition: to say a lot; to say something very important or meaningful.
examples: When you said things were busy around here, you said a mouthful. It is terribly busy.
You sure said a mouthful, Bob. Things are really busy.

senses.definition: to say a prayer of gratitude before or after a meal.
examples: Grandfather always says grace at Thanksgiving.
A local preacher said grace at the banquet.

headword: say something in a roundabout way

senses.definition: to imply something without saying it; to say something indirectly; to speak using circumlocution.
examples: Why don’t you say what you mean? Why do you always say something in a roundabout way?
What did she mean? Why did she say it in a roundabout way?

senses.definition: to say something (unpleasant) directly to someone.
examples: She knew I thought she was rude because I said it right to her face.
I thought she felt that way about me, but I never thought she’d say it to my face.

senses.definition: to say something so softly that almost no one can hear it.
examples: John was saying something under his breath, and I don’t think it was very pleasant.
I’m glad he said it under his breath. If he had said it out loud, it would have caused an argument.

senses.definition: to assume something; to suppose that something were so.
examples: Say that x is equal to a whole number greater than 10.
Say that two trains leave two different cities at the same time.

senses.definition: to give a signal to begin; to say yes or okay.
examples: I’m ready to start any time you say the word.
We’ll all shout “Happy Birthday!” when I say the word.

senses.definition: to surrender; to give in.
examples: Ann held Bobby down on the ground until he said uncle.
Why isn’t it enough to win the argument? Why do you demand that I say uncle?

senses.definition: to make something smaller by a certain amount or proportion.
examples: I scaled down the guest list because I couldn’t invite so many people.
Jane’s salary was scaled down by 10 percent last year.

senses.definition: to search for and find someone or something.
examples: Go out in the kitchen and scare some food up.
I’ll see if I can scare up somebody to fix the broken chair.

senses.definition: to scare someone severely; to frighten someone to death.
senses.notes: See the explanation at scared stiff.
examples: That loud noise scared me stiff.
The robber jumped out and scared us stiff.

senses.definition: frightened very much.
examples: I was scared silly by the loud explosion.
We were scared silly to go into the park after dark.

senses.definition: badly frightened.
senses.notes: Frightened to the point of being petrified and unable to move.
examples: We were scared stiff by the robber.
I was scared stiff when the dog growled at me.

senses.definition: a particular philosophy or way of thinking about something.
examples: One school of thought holds that cats cause allergic reactions.
I come from the school of thought that believes people should always be polite.

headword: scout around for someone or something

senses.definition: to search here and there for someone or something.
examples: Tom is scouting around for a date for Friday night.
Please scout around for some ideas on what to cook for dinner.

senses.definition: to assemble something quickly, usually from a small supply of components.
examples: I’ll try to scrape something together for dinner.
We really should try to have a party to celebrate the boss’s birthday. Let’s try to scrape together a little something.

headword: scrape the bottom of the barrel

senses.definition: to select from among the worst; to choose from what is left over.
examples: You’ve bought a bad-looking car. You really scraped the bottom of the barrel to get that one.
The worker you sent over was the worst I’ve ever seen. Send me another—and don’t scrape the bottom of the barrel.

senses.definition: to look here and there for something.
examples: Let me scratch around for a better bargain. Maybe I can come up with something you like.
I’ll scratch around for a week or two and see what I come up with.

senses.definition: to do a favor for someone in return for a favor done for you.
examples: You scratch my back, and I’ll scratch yours.
We believe that the mayor has been scratching the treasurer’s back.

senses.definition: to just begin to find out about something.
examples: The investigation of the governor’s staff revealed some suspicious dealing. It is thought that the investigators have just scratched the surface.
We don’t know how bad the problem is. We’ve only scratched the surface.

senses.definition: to complain bitterly; to complain unduly.
senses.notes: Slang. See also cry bloody murder.
examples: When we put him in an office without a window, he screamed bloody murder.
There is something wrong next door. Everyone is screaming bloody murder.

senses.definition: to cause trouble for someone or something.
examples: Your advice about making a lot of money really screwed me up. Now I’m broke.
Your efforts screwed up the entire project.

senses.definition: to build up one’s courage.
examples: I guess I have to screw up my courage and go to the dentist.
I spent all morning screwing up my courage to take my driver’s test.

senses.definition: to be very thrifty; to live on very little money, often in order to save up for something.
examples: We had to scrimp and save in order to send the children to college.
The Smiths scrimp and save all year in order to go on a Caribbean cruise.

senses.definition: the most unpleasant or roughest aspect of life.
senses.notes: Informal. Refers to the inside of a garment where the seams show. Seamy occurs only in this expression.
examples: Doctors in that area really see the seamy side of life.
Mary saw the seamy side of life when she worked as a volunteer in the shelter.

senses.definition: easy and natural for someone.
examples: Swimming is second nature to Jane.
Driving is no problem for Bob. It’s second nature to him.

senses.definition: not of the best quality; inferior.
examples: Bill’s a second-rate tennis player compared with Bob.
The government is building second-rate housing.

senses.definition: better than everything.
examples: This is an excellent car—second to none.
Her suggestion was second to none, and the manager accepted it eagerly.

senses.definition: something that keeps something safe; something that protects; a protection.
examples: Insurance provides security against financial loss owing to theft, loss, or damage.
A good education is a security against unemployment.

senses.definition: to ask about something; to check on something.
examples: I’ll have to see about your request to leave early.
I must see about the cake I have in the oven.

headword: see a man about a dog

senses.definition: to leave for some unmentioned purpose.
senses.notes: Informal. Often refers to going to the rest room.
examples: I don’t know where Tom went. He said he had to see a man about a dog.
When John said he was going to see a man about a dog, I thought he would be gone for only a minute.

senses.definition: to see two of everything instead of one.
examples: When I was driving, I saw two people on the road instead of one. I’m seeing double. There’s something wrong with my eyes.
Mike thought he was seeing double when he saw Mary with her twin sister. He didn’t know she had a twin.

headword: see eye to eye (with someone) (about something)
altForms: see eye to eye (with someone) (on something)

senses.definition: to view something in the same way (as someone else).
examples: John and Ann see eye to eye about the new law. Neither of them likes it.
John sees eye to eye with Ann about it.
That’s interesting because they rarely see eye to eye.

senses.definition: to decide to do something.
examples: If I see fit to return, I’ll bring Bill with me.
She’ll do it if she sees fit.

senses.definition: not to think of any objection to something.
examples: I see no objection to your idea.
Do you see any objection?
I do not see any objection to anything you have done.

headword: see one’s way clear (to do something)

senses.definition: to find it possible to do something.
examples: I’d be happy if you could see your way clear to attend our meeting.
I wanted to be there, but I couldn’t see my way clear.

senses.definition: to be angry.
examples: Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red.
Bill really saw red when the tax bill arrived.

senses.definition: to accompany someone home.
examples: Bill agreed to see his aunt home after the movie.
You don’t need to see me home. It’s perfectly safe, and I can get there on my own.

senses.definition: to escort someone to a place; to make sure that someone gets somewhere safely; to accompany someone to a place.
examples: I saw Mary to her door, and then got back in my car and left.
Bill saw his cousin to the train station, and then they parted.

senses.definition: to follow through on something until it is completed.
senses.notes: Compare this with see through someone or something.
examples: Mary is prepared to see the project through.
It’s going to be an unpleasant experience, but I hope you’ll see it through.

senses.definition: to see flashing lights after receiving a blow to the head.
examples: I saw stars when I bumped my head on the attic ceiling.
The little boy saw stars when he fell headfirst onto the concrete.

headword: see the color of someone’s money

senses.definition: to verify that someone has money or has enough money.
examples: So, you want to make a bet? Not until I see the color of your money.
I want to see the color of your money before we go any further with this business deal.

senses.definition: to know that something is certain to happen.
examples: If you don’t improve your performance, they’ll fire you. Can’t you see the writing on the wall?
I know I’ll get fired. I can see the handwriting on the wall.

senses.definition: to understand something clearly at last.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also the following two entries.
examples: After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light.
I know that geometry is difficult. Keep working at it. You’ll see the light pretty soon.

headword: see the light (at the end of the tunnel)

senses.definition: to foresee an end to something, such as a problem or a task, after a long period of time.
examples: I had been horribly ill for two months before I began to see the light at the end of the tunnel.
I began to see the light one day in early spring. At that moment, I knew I’d get well.
When I got to the last chapter, I could see the light at the end of the tunnel.

senses.definition: to come to the end of a very busy time.
examples: Finally, when the holiday season was over, we could see the light of day. We had been so busy!
When business lets up for a while, we’ll be able to see the light.

senses.definition: to see the important things in a place; to see what tourists usually see.
examples: We plan to visit Paris and see the sights.
Everyone left the hotel early in the morning to see the sights.

senses.definition: to understand or detect the true nature of someone or something.
senses.notes: Compare this with see something through.
examples: You can’t fool me anymore. I can see through you and all your tricks.
This plan is designed to make money for you, not to help people. I can see through it! I’m not a fool!

headword: see (to it) that something is done

senses.definition: to make sure of something; to make certain of something; to be certain to do something.
examples: The manager saw to it that everyone began working on time.
The mayor should see that the potholes are repaired.

senses.definition: to take care of someone or something.
examples: Tom will see to the horses. Come to the house and freshen up.
I hear the doorbell. Will someone please see to the door?
This paper needs filling out. Will you please see to it?

headword: see which way the wind is blowing

senses.definition: to determine what is the most expedient thing to do.
examples: We studied the whole situation to see which way the wind was blowing and decided to avoid any conflict at that time.
Sam failed to see which way the wind was blowing and got himself caught up in an argument.

senses.definition: one must believe something that one sees.
examples: I never would have thought that a cow could swim, but seeing is believing.
I can hardly believe we are in Paris, but there’s the Eiffel Tower, and seeing is believing.

senses.definition: to imagine one sees someone or something that is not there.
examples: Lisa says that she saw a ghost, but she was just seeing things.
I thought I was seeing things when Bill walked into the room. Someone had told me he was dead.

senses.definition: to take advantage of an opportunity.
examples: My uncle offered me a trip to Europe, so I seized the opportunity.
Whenever you have a chance, you should seize the opportunity.

senses.definition: to (figuratively) take hold of something and make an issue of it.
examples: Whenever I mention money, you seize on it and turn it into an argument!
The lawyer seized upon one point and asked many questions about it.

senses.definition: to be sold very fast.
examples: The delicious candy sold like hotcakes.
The fancy new cars were selling like hotcakes.

headword: sell someone a bill of goods

senses.definition: to get someone to believe something that isn’t true; to deceive someone.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to what John says. He’s just trying to sell you a bill of goods.
I’m not selling you a bill of goods. What I say is true.

headword: sell someone on a plan or idea

senses.definition: to convince someone of something.
examples: You don’t have to sell me on the value of an education.
Try to sell John on going to Mexico for a vacation.

senses.definition: to underestimate someone or something; to fail to see the good qualities of someone or something.
examples: This is a very good restaurant. Don’t sell it short.
When you say that John isn’t interested in music, you’re selling him short. Did you know he plays the violin quite well?

senses.definition: to sell something for very little money.
senses.notes: As in trading something of value for the singing of a song.
examples: I had to sell my car for a song because I needed the money in a hurry.
I have two geometry books and I would sell one of them for a song.

senses.definition: to sell something now and let the purchaser pay for it later.
senses.notes: Compare this with buy something on credit.
examples: I’m sorry, we don’t sell groceries on credit. It’s strictly cash-and-carry.
There is a shop around the corner that sells clothing on credit.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be in a certain state or condition.
examples: The horrifying news sent our family into hysterics.
The clerk’s rude behavior sent the customer into a fit of anger.

senses.definition: to participate in saying good-bye to someone who is leaving.
examples: We had a party to send Tom off on his vacation.
Bob’s parents sent him off from the airport.

senses.definition: to ridicule or make fun of someone or something; to satirize someone or something.
examples: John is always sending Jane up by mocking the way she walks.
The drama group sent their leaders up.

senses.definition: to send someone out to do a specific task.
examples: Mother sent Billy out on an errand.
I’m late because Bill sent me on an errand.

senses.definition: to send someone away; to dismiss someone, possibly rudely.
examples: I couldn’t stand him anymore, so I sent him packing.
The maid proved to be so incompetent that I had to send her packing.

senses.definition: to send a player out of the game and off the field, court, etc.
examples: John played so badly that the coach sent him to the showers after the third quarter.
After the fistfight, the coaches sent both players to the showers.

senses.definition: to send someone to prison.
examples: The judge sent Bill up the river for ten years.
The same judge sent him up the river the last time.

senses.definition: to send merchandise to someone who will pay for it when it is delivered.
senses.notes: C.O.D. means “cash on delivery” or “collect on delivery.”
examples: I sent away for a special book and asked them to send it C.O.D.
This person has ordered a copy of our record. Send the record C.O.D.

senses.definition: to suggest something and see how people respond to it; to test public opinion.
examples: Mary had an excellent idea, but when we sent up a trial balloon, the response was very negative.
Don’t start the whole project without sending up a trial balloon.

senses.definition: segregated but of equal value or quality.
senses.notes: A doctrine once sanctioned by the U.S. Supreme Court regarding racial segregation.
examples: The separate but equal doctrine was abandoned years ago.
They were provided with facilities that were said to be separate but equal—but were really of a lower standard.

headword: separate the men from the boys

senses.definition: to separate the competent from those who are less competent.
examples: This is the kind of task that separates the men from the boys.
This project requires a lot of thinking. It’ll separate the men from the boys.

headword: separate the sheep from the goats

senses.definition: to divide people into two groups.
examples: Working in a place like this really separates the sheep from the goats.
We can’t go on with the game until we separate the sheep from the goats. Let’s see who can jump the farthest.

headword: the separation of church and state

senses.definition: the constitutional barrier that prevents government from establishing a state religion.
senses.notes: This refers to eliminating evidence of religion in connection with government as well as assuring that the U.S. government does not establish a state religion.
examples: The city council stopped beginning each meeting with a prayer because someone suggested that it violated the principle of the separation of church and state.
Many countries do not have the separation of church and state.

senses.definition: to be experimented on; to allow some sort of test to be performed on someone.
senses.notes: [for someone] A guinea pig was once the quintessential experimental animal.
examples: Try it on someone else! I don’t want to serve as a guinea pig!
Jane agreed to serve as a guinea pig. She’ll be the one to try out the new flavor of ice cream.

senses.definition: to announce (something) to someone.
examples: John served notice on his fellow workers that he would not prepare the coffee anymore.
I’m serving notice that I’ll resign as secretary next month.

senses.definition: to punish someone fairly [for doing something].
examples: John copied off my test paper. It would serve him right if he fails the test.
It’d serve John right if he got arrested.

senses.definition: to spend a certain amount of time imprisoned.
examples: The criminal served ten years in jail.
After the felon served his time, he was released from prison.

senses.definition: to establish a pattern; to set a policy that must be followed in future cases.
examples: I’ll do what you ask this time, but it doesn’t set a precedent.
We’ve already set a precedent in matters such as these.

senses.definition: to adjust and prepare a trap to catch an animal.
examples: Bill set a mousetrap and baited it with cheese.
The old man set a trap to catch an annoying squirrel.

headword: set eyes on someone or something
altForms: lay eyes on someone or something

senses.definition: to see someone or something for the first time.
examples: I knew when I set eyes on that car that it was the car for me.
Have you ever laid eyes on such a beautiful flower?

headword: set fire to someone or something
altForms: set someone or something on fire

senses.definition: to ignite someone or something; to put someone or something to flames.
examples: The thief set fire to the building.
The poor man accidentally set himself on fire.

senses.definition: to go or enter somewhere.
examples: If I were you, I wouldn’t set foot in that town.
I wouldn’t set foot in her house! Not after the way she spoke to me.

senses.definition: to start out on something.
examples: We intend to set forth on our journey very early in the morning.
What time will you launch forth?

senses.definition: to begin presenting a speech or an explanation.
examples: As soon as John set forth on his speech, three people walked out.
Every time he launches forth, somebody walks out.

headword: set great store by someone or something

senses.definition: to have positive expectations for someone or something; to have high hopes for someone or something.
examples: I set great store by my computer and its ability to help me in my work.
We set great store by John because of his quick mind.

senses.definition: to begin.
senses.notes: [for a kind of weather, especially winter] Often said of weather or climatic conditions.
examples: Winter set in very early this year.
We got the windows painted before winter set in.

senses.definition: leading a fixed lifestyle; living according to one’s own established patterns.
examples: At her age, she’s getting sort of set in her ways.
If you weren’t so set in your ways, you’d be able to understand young people better.

headword: set one back on one’s heels

senses.definition: to surprise, shock, or overwhelm someone.
examples: Her sudden announcement set us all back on our heels.
The manager scolded me, and that really set me back on my heels.

senses.definition: to turn against something; to become totally against something.
senses.notes: See also have one’s heart set against something.
examples: Jane set her heart against going to Australia.
I set my heart against her departure.

senses.definition: to become determined about something.
examples: Jane set her heart on going to London.
Todd had set his heart on returning.

senses.definition: to select something as one’s goal.
examples: I set my sights on a master’s degree from the state university.
Don’t set your sights on something you cannot possibly do.

senses.definition: to depart in a boat for somewhere.
examples: This ship sets sail for Japan in two days.
When do you set sail?

headword: set someone back (some amount of money)

senses.definition: to cost someone (an amount of money).
examples: This coat set me back about $250.
That dinner at the restaurant last night really set us back.

senses.definition: to release someone or something; to allow someone or something to leave, go away, depart, escape.
examples: Jimmy went outside and set his balloon free.
The army set the political prisoners free.

senses.definition: to get someone very excited and angry.
examples: Whenever I see someone mistreating an animal, it really sets me off.
The tax bill set off Bob. He raved for an hour!

senses.definition: to start something.
examples: Don’t set another discussion off, please!
The question of taxes set off an argument.

senses.definition: to explain (something) to someone.
senses.notes: [with someone] See also put something straight.
examples: I don’t think you understand about taxation. Let me set you straight.
Ann was confused, so I set her straight.

senses.definition: to explain something (to someone).
senses.notes: [with something] See also put something straight.
examples: This is very confusing, but with a little explaining I can set it straight.
We’ll set this matter straight in a short time.

senses.definition: to lead—by deception—a person to play a particular role in an event; to arrange an event—usually by deception—so that a specific person takes the consequences for the event; to frame someone.
examples: I had nothing to do with the robbery! I was just standing there. Somebody must have set me up!
John isn’t the one who started the fight. Somebody set up the poor guy.

senses.definition: to put something together; to erect something.
examples: My parents bought me a dollhouse, but I had to set it up myself.
It took nearly an hour to set up the tent.

senses.definition: to establish or found something.
examples: We set up a fund to buy food for the needy.
The business owners set a bank up in the small town.

senses.definition: to make plans for something.
examples: John and Mary are hard at work setting something up for the meeting.
Sally and Tom set up a party for Saturday night.

senses.definition: to irritate one’s mouth and make it feel funny.
examples: Have you ever eaten a whole lemon? It’ll set your teeth on edge.
I can’t stand food that sets my teeth on edge.

senses.definition: to be irritating or get on one’s nerves.
examples: Please don’t scrape your fingernails on the blackboard! It sets my teeth on edge!
Here comes Bob. He’s so annoying. He really sets my teeth on edge.

senses.definition: to establish someone as something.
senses.notes: Compare this with set someone up (in business).
examples: Bill set himself up as boss.
When Mary got her degree, she set herself up as a consultant.
My father set up my sisters as coowners of the family business.
He set them up with the help of a lawyer.

senses.definition: to help establish someone in business; to provide the money someone needs to start a business.
examples: My father set my sisters up in business.
He helped set them up so he could keep the business in the family.

senses.definition: to correct something; to alter a situation to make it more fair.
examples: This is a very unfortunate situation. I’ll ask the people responsible to set this matter right.
I’m sorry that we overcharged you. We’ll try to put it right.

senses.definition: to incorporate words into a piece of music; to write a piece of music to incorporate a set of words.
examples: The musician set my lyrics to music.
The rock band set the poem to music.

senses.definition: to prepare for something; to get all of the appropriate things in place for something.
senses.notes: Refers to arranging the scenery, properties, and lighting for a theater production.
examples: The events of the past week have set the stage for further negotiation with the other side.
Your comments set the stage for the next step—which is the hard one.

senses.definition: to place plates, glasses, napkins, etc., on the table before a meal.
senses.notes: The opposite of clear the table.
examples: Jane, would you please set the table?
I’m tired of setting the table. Ask someone else to do it.

senses.definition: to do exciting things that bring fame and glory.
examples: I’m not very ambitious. I don’t want to set the world on fire.
You don’t have to set the world on fire. Just do a good job.

senses.definition: to cause people to start gossiping.
examples: The affair between the boss and her accountant set tongues awagging.
If you don’t get the lawn mowed soon, you will set tongues wagging in the neighborhood.

senses.definition: to arrange type for printing, now usually on a computer.
examples: Have you finished setting the type for page one yet?
John sets type for a living.

senses.definition: to attack someone or something violently.
examples: The dogs set upon the bear and chased it up a tree.
Bill set upon Tom and struck him hard in the face.

senses.definition: to establish one’s place of work somewhere.
examples: Mary set up shop in a small office building on Oak Street.
The police officer said, “You can’t set up shop right here on the sidewalk!”

senses.definition: to clear up a problem with someone; to get even with someone.
senses.notes: Slang. See also have a score to settle (with someone).
examples: John wants to settle a score with his neighbor.
Tom, it’s time you and I settled the score.

senses.definition: to agree to accept something (even though something else would be better).
examples: We wanted a red one, but settled for a blue one.
Ask your grocer for Wilson’s canned corn—the best corn in cans. Don’t settle for less!

senses.definition: to decide on something.
examples: We’ve discussed the merits of all of them, and we’ve settled on this one.
I can’t settle on one or the other, so I’ll buy both.

senses.definition: to deal with one’s business matters; to manage the business affairs of someone who can’t.
examples: When my uncle died, I had to settle his affairs.
I have to settle my affairs before going to Mexico for a year.

senses.definition: to end a disagreement and reach an agreement without having to go through a court of justice.
examples: The plaintiff and defendant decided to settle before the trial.
Mary and Sue settled out of court before the trial.

senses.definition: to pay someone what one owes; to pay someone one’s share of something.
examples: I must settle up with Jim for the bike I bought for him.
Fred paid the whole restaurant bill and we all settled up with him later.

senses.definition: to end a relationship or agreement suddenly.
examples: The company severed its ties with the dishonest employee.
John has severed all ties with his parents.

senses.definition: to complete something; to secure something.
examples: The manager told me to sew the contract up, or else.
Let’s sew up this contract today.

senses.definition: to have a one-night stand with someone; to copulate (with someone).
examples: Those two just wanted to shack up for a while.
He only wanted to shack up with me.

senses.definition: to move in with someone temporarily, presumably for sexual purposes.
examples: They shacked up for over a year until her parents found out and stopped sending her money.

senses.definition: reminders of someone or something; reminiscent of someone or something.
examples: When I met Jim’s mother, I thought “shades of Aunt Mary.”
“Shades of grade school,” said Jack as the university lecturer rebuked him for being late.

senses.definition: someone or something that is not as strong, healthy, full, or lively as before.
examples: The sick man was a shadow of his former self.
The redecorated house was merely a shadow of its old self.

senses.definition: to clasp and shake the hand of someone as a greeting.
examples: His hands were full, and I didn’t know whether to try to shake hands with him or not.
He put down his packages, and we shook hands.

senses.definition: to be afraid; to shake from fear.
examples: I was shaking in my boots because I had to go see the manager.
Stop quaking in your boots, Bob. I’m not going to fire you.

senses.definition: to extort money from someone; to blackmail someone.
examples: The gang of criminals made a living from shaking people down.
Lefty was trying to shake down the storekeeper.

senses.definition: to try something out; to test something and give the flaws a chance to appear.
examples: We took the new car out for a trip to shake it down.
You need to shake down a complicated piece of machinery when you first get it. Then any problems will show up while the guarantee is still in effect.

senses.definition: to get rid of someone; to get free of someone who is bothering you.
examples: Stop bothering me! What do I have to do to shake you off?
I wish I could shake off John. He’s such a pest!

senses.definition: to avoid getting a disease, such as a cold; to fight something off.
examples: I thought I was catching a cold, but I guess I shook it off.
I hope I can shake off this cold pretty soon.

senses.definition: to shock or upset someone.
senses.notes: [with someone] Slang. See also shook up.
examples: The sight of the injured man shook me up.
Your rude remark really shook up Tom.

senses.definition: to jostle or knock someone or something around; to toss someone or something back and forth.
examples: We rode over a rough road, and that shook us up.
The accident shook up John quite a bit.

senses.definition: to reorganize something or a group of people.
examples: The new manager shook the office up and made things run a lot better.
The coach shook the team up before the last game and made them better organized.

senses.definition: Either improve one’s performance (or behavior) or leave.
examples: Okay, Tom. That’s the end. Shape up or ship out!
John was late again, so I told him to shape up or ship out.

senses.definition: with equal shares.
examples: I kept five and gave the other five to Mary—share and share alike.
The two roommates agreed that they would divide expenses—share and share alike.

senses.definition: to understand and sympathize with someone’s pain or emotional discomfort.
senses.notes: Said in order to sound sympathetic.
examples: I am sorry about the loss of your home. I share your pain.
We sympathize about the loss of your mother. We share your pain.

senses.definition: to grieve as someone else grieves.
examples: We all share your sorrow on this sad, sad day.
I am sorry to hear about the death in your family. I share your sorrow.

senses.definition: to shed false tears; to pretend that one is weeping.
examples: The child wasn’t hurt, but she shed crocodile tears anyway.
He thought he could get his way if he cried crocodile tears.

senses.definition: to reveal something about something; to clarify something.
examples: This discussion has shed some light on the problem.
Let’s see if Ann can throw any light on this question.

senses.definition: to pay money (out).
examples: You’ll have to shell plenty out to settle this bill.
The traffic ticket turned out to be very expensive. I had to shell out $150.

senses.definition: to get along by oneself; to support oneself.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t pay your rent anymore. You’ll just have to shift for yourself.
When I became twenty years old, I left home and began to fend for myself.

senses.definition: to try to gain someone’s favor by being extra nice.
examples: John is a nice guy, except that he’s always trying to shine up to the professor.
Mary never tries to shine up to the manager.

senses.definition: the costs of handling a product and transporting it.
examples: Shipping and handling charges were included in the price.
The cost of the goods is low and shipping and handling added only a few cents.

headword: ships that pass in the night

senses.definition: people who meet each other briefly by chance and who are unlikely to meet again.
examples: Mary wanted to see Jim again, but to him, they were ships that passed in the night.
When you travel a lot on business, you meet many ships that pass in the night.

senses.definition: to neglect one’s job or task.
examples: The guard was fired for shirking his duty.
You cannot expect to continue shirking your duty without someone noticing.

headword: The shoe is on the other foot.

senses.definition: One is experiencing the same things that one caused another person to experience.
senses.notes: Proverb. Note the variation in the examples. See also have the shoe on the other foot.
examples: The teacher is taking a course in summer school and is finding out what it’s like when the shoe is on the other foot.
When the policeman was arrested, he learned what it was like to have the shoe on the other foot.

senses.definition: upset; shocked.
senses.notes: Slang. See also shake someone or something up.
examples: Relax, man! Don’t get shook up!
I always get shook up when I see something like that.

senses.definition: to try to do something; to attempt to do something; to aim toward a goal.
examples: The industrious student shot for success.
The worker shot for a $2 per hour raise.

senses.definition: to fire a gun that is held at one’s side, against one’s hip.
senses.notes: This increases one’s speed in firing a gun.
examples: When I lived at home on the farm, my father taught me to shoot from the hip.
I quickly shot the snake before it bit my horse. I’m glad I learned to shoot from the hip.

senses.definition: to speak directly and frankly.
examples: John has a tendency to shoot from the hip, but he generally speaks the truth.
Don’t pay any attention to John. He means no harm. It’s just his nature to shoot from the hip.

senses.definition: to boast or talk too much; to tell someone’s secrets.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to Bob. He’s always shooting his mouth off.
Oh, Sally! Stop shooting off your mouth! You don’t know what you’re talking about.

senses.definition: to stick, throw, or thrust something outward.
examples: The diamond shot bright shafts of light out when the sun fell on it.
The little girl shot out her tongue at the teacher.

senses.definition: to settle a matter by the use of guns.
senses.notes: Slang. Typical of gangster or western movies.
examples: Bill and the cowboy—with whom he had been arguing—went out in the street and shot it out.
Don’t they know they can settle a problem by talking? They don’t need to shoot out the problem when they can talk it over.

senses.definition: to spend time chatting.
senses.notes: Slang. See also the following entry.
examples: I went over to Bob’s place and shot the breeze for about an hour.
Don’t spend so much time shooting the breeze. Get to work!

senses.definition: to spend time chatting about one’s accomplishments, especially with others who are doing the same.
senses.notes: Slang. See also the previous entry.
examples: Those guys out in the backyard are just sitting around shooting the bull.
It was raining, so everybody spent the day indoors drinking beer and shooting the bull.

senses.definition: to do everything; to use up everything; to bet everything.
examples: Shall I bet half our money, or shall I shoot the works?
We shot the works at the carnival—spent every cent we brought with us.

senses.definition: brief (and pleasant because of briefness).
examples: That was a good sermon—short and sweet.
I don’t care what you say, as long as you make it short and sweet.

senses.definition: not having enough of something.
examples: I wanted to bake a cake, but I was short of eggs.
Usually at the end of the month, I’m short of money.

senses.definition: a boost; something that gives someone energy.
examples: Thank you for cheering me up. It was a real shot in the arm.
Your friendly greeting card was just what I needed—a real shot in the arm.

senses.definition: a random or wild guess or try.
examples: I don’t know how I guessed the right answer. It was just a shot in the dark.
I was lucky to hire such a good worker as Sally. When I hired her, it was just a shot in the dark.

senses.definition: containing something; interwoven, intermixed, or filled with something.
examples: The rose was a lovely pink shot through with streaks of white.
John’s comments are often shot through with sarcasm.
I want a wellmarbled steak—one shot through with fat.

senses.definition: a forced wedding.
senses.notes: Informal. From imagery of the bride’s father having threatened the bridegroom with a shotgun to force him to marry.
examples: Mary was six months pregnant when she married Bill. It was a real shotgun wedding.
Bob would never have married Jane if she hadn’t been pregnant. Jane’s father saw to it that it was a shotgun wedding.

senses.definition: should have stayed in bed.
examples: What a horrible day! I should have stood in bed.
The minute I got up and heard the news this morning, I knew I should have stood in bed.

senses.definition: side by side; with a shared purpose.
examples: The two armies fought shoulder to shoulder against the joint enemy.
The strikers said they would stand shoulder to shoulder against the management.

senses.definition: to make a path through a crowd by pushing.
examples: The impatient man shoved his way through the crowd.
The reporter shoved her way to the front of the crowd.

headword: shove someone or something down someone’s throat
altForms: ram someone or something down someone’s throat
force someone or something down someone’s throat

senses.definition: to force someone or something on someone.
examples: I don’t want any more insurance, and I don’t want anyone to shove any insurance down my throat.
Mary isn’t invited to my party, and I don’t wish for anyone to ram her down my throat!
Someone is always trying to force some stupid propaganda down my throat.

senses.definition: a trivial presentation of something of little interest.
senses.notes: Refers to the name of a classroom period in the lower grades where children bring something interesting into the classroom and show it to the rest of the class.
examples: I wouldn’t call that meeting useful. It was sort of a grown-up show-and-tell.
After the show-and-tell session where the author talked about his book, we all went into the hall and had refreshments.

senses.definition: to demonstrate good intentions or good will.
examples: I’m certain that you showed good faith when you signed the contract.
Do you doubt that she is showing good faith?

senses.definition: to do things in a way that is meant to attract attention.
examples: Please stop showing off! You embarrass me.
John is always showing off to his girlfriend.

senses.definition: a display of raised hands [in a group of people] that can be counted for the purpose of votes or surveys.
examples: We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands.
Jack wanted us to vote on paper, not by a show of hands, so that we could have a secret ballot.

senses.definition: to reveal one’s intentions to someone.
examples: I don’t know whether Jim is intending to marry Jane or not. He’s not one to show his hand.
If you want to get a raise, don’t show the boss your hand too soon.

senses.definition: to show what one is really like or what one is really thinking.
examples: Whose side are you on, John? Come on. Show your colors.
It’s hard to tell what Mary is thinking. She never shows her true colors.

senses.definition: to show hints or indications of something.
examples: I let the horse run at full speed until it began to show signs of tiring.
Sally is showing signs of going to sleep.

senses.definition: to display someone or something so that the best features are apparent.
examples: Mrs. Williams was showing off her baby to the neighbors.
Bill drove around all afternoon showing his new car off.

senses.definition: to tell or show someone how something is to be done.
examples: Since this was my first day on the job, the manager spent a lot of time showing me the ropes.
Take some time and show the new boy the ropes.

senses.definition: to lead or direct someone to a place to sit.
examples: May I show you to your seat, sir?
The ushers showed us to our seats politely and efficiently.

senses.definition: to lead or take someone to the door or exit.
examples: After we finished our talk, she showed me to the door.
Bill and I finished our chat as he saw me to the door.

senses.definition: to make someone’s faults or shortcomings apparent.
examples: John’s excellent effort really showed up Bill, who didn’t try very hard at all.
John is always trying to show someone up to make himself look better.

senses.definition: to reveal that someone is really something (else).
examples: The investigation showed her up as a fraud.
The test showed the banker up as unqualified.
