senses.definition: to display the best features of something; to display something so that its best features are apparent.
examples: Put the vase in the center of the table and show it to good advantage.
Having and using a large vocabulary shows your intelligence to good advantage.

senses.definition: to die.
senses.notes: Often jocular or formal euphemism. Not often used in consoling someone.
examples: Cousin Fred shuffled off this mortal coil after drinking a jug full of rat poison.
When I shuffle off this mortal coil, I want to go out in style—bells, flowers, and a long, boring funeral.

senses.definition: to silence someone.
examples: Oh, shut yourself up!
Will you please shut up that crying baby!

headword: shut the door on someone or something
altForms: close the door on someone or something

senses.definition: to close the door in order to keep someone or something out.
examples: Bob opened the door, and when he saw it was Mary, he closed the door on her.
“Don’t shut the door on me!” screamed Mary.

senses.definition: to terminate, exclude, or obstruct something.
examples: Your bad attitude shuts the door on any future cooperation from me.
The bad service at that store closes the door on any more business from my company.

senses.definition: to avoid someone or something.
examples: The dog shies away from John since he kicked it.
I can understand why the dog would shy away.
I shy away from eating onions. I think I’m allergic to them.

headword: sick and tired of someone or something

senses.definition: disgusted and annoyed with someone or something.
examples: I’m sick and tired of Ann and her whistling.
We are all sick and tired of this old car.

senses.definition: remaining in bed while (one is) ill.
examples: Tom is sick in bed with the flu.
He’s been sick in bed for nearly a week.

senses.definition: to be against someone; to take sides against someone.
examples: I thought you were my friend! I never thought you would side against me!
The two brothers were always siding against their sister.

senses.definition: a welcome sight.
examples: Oh, am I glad to see you here! You’re a sight for sore eyes.
I’m sure hungry. This meal is a sight for sore eyes.

senses.definition: to do something (knowingly) that will most likely result in severe trouble.
senses.notes: As if one were ordering one’s own execution.
examples: I wouldn’t ever gamble a large sum of money. That would be signing my own death warrant.
The killer signed his own death warrant when he walked into the police station and gave himself up.

senses.definition: to place one’s signature on a contract or other important paper.
senses.notes: The line is usually straight and solid.
examples: This agreement isn’t properly concluded until we both sign on the dotted line.
Here are the papers for the purchase of your car. As soon as you sign on the dotted line, that beautiful, shiny automobile will be all yours!

senses.definition: formally and officially signed; [for a formal document to be] executed.
examples: Here is the deed to the property—signed, sealed, and delivered.
I can’t begin work on this project until I have the contract signed, sealed, and delivered.

senses.definition: the time of year, usually late in the summer, when there is a lack of important news and newspapers contain articles about unimportant or trivial things instead.
examples: It must be the silly season. There’s a story here about peculiarly shaped potatoes.
There’s a piece on the front page about people with big feet. Talk about the silly season!

senses.definition: to get quiet or calm.
examples: Hey, you guys! Simmer down! Stop all the noise and go to sleep!
I’m very busy now. Please come back in a few hours when things have simmered down a bit.

senses.definition: since a very long time ago.
examples: My hometown has had a big parade on the Fourth of July since time immemorial.
Since time immemorial, the trees have blossomed each spring.

senses.definition: to change one’s manner, usually from bad to good.
senses.notes: Almost the same as dance to another tune.
examples: When she learned that I was a bank director, she began to sing a different tune.
You will sing another tune as soon as you find out how right I am!

senses.definition: to praise someone highly and enthusiastically.
examples: The boss is singing the praises of his new secretary.
The theater critics are singing the praises of the young actor.

senses.definition: to be understood.
examples: I heard what you said, but it took a while for it to sink in.
I pay careful attention to everything I hear in class, but it usually doesn’t sink in.

senses.definition: to grieve or become depressed.
examples: After losing all my money, I sank into despair.
There is no need to sink into despair. Everything is going to be all right.

senses.definition: to take a bite of some kind of food, usually a special kind of food.
examples: I can’t wait to sink my teeth into a nice juicy steak.
Look at that chocolate cake! Don’t you want to sink your teeth into that?

senses.definition: to get a chance to do, learn, or control something.
examples: That appears to be a very challenging assignment. I can’t wait to sink my teeth into it.
Being the manager of this department is a big task. I’m very eager to sink my teeth into it.

senses.definition: to fail or succeed.
examples: After I’ve studied and learned all I can, I have to take the test and sink or swim.
It’s too late to help John now. It’s sink or swim for him.

senses.definition: to admire someone greatly; to be influenced by someone’s teaching; to be taught by someone.
examples: Jack sat at the feet of Picasso when he was studying in Europe.
Tom would love to sit at the feet of the musician Yehudi Menuhin.

headword: sit back and let something happen

senses.definition: to relax and not interfere with something; to let something happen without playing a part in it.
examples: I can’t just sit back and let you waste all our money!
Don’t worry. Just sit back and let things take care of themselves.

senses.definition: to sit up straight.
examples: Tony sat bolt upright and listened to what the teacher was saying to him.
After sitting bolt upright for almost an hour in that crowded airplane, I swore I would never travel again.

senses.definition: to take someone’s else’s place in a specific activity.
senses.notes: The activity usually involves being seated.
examples: I can’t be at the meeting Thursday. Will you sit in for me?
Sorry, I can’t sit in for you. John is also going to be absent, and I am sitting in for him.

senses.definition: to witness or observe something without participating.
examples: I can’t sign up for the history class, but I have permission to sit in on it.
I asked the professor if I could sit in.

senses.definition: to refuse to applaud.
examples: We saw a very poor performance of the play. The audience sat on its hands for the entire play.
The audience just sat on its hands.

senses.definition: to do nothing; to fail to help.
examples: When we needed help from Mary, she just sat on her hands.
We need the cooperation of everyone. You can’t sit on your hands!

senses.definition: to hold someone or something back; to delay someone or something.
examples: The project cannot be finished because the city council is sitting on the final approval.
Ann deserves to be promoted, but the manager is sitting on her because of a disagreement.

senses.definition: not to take sides in a dispute; not to make a clear choice between two possibilities.
examples: When Jane and Tom argue, it is well to sit on the fence and then you won’t make either of them angry.
No one knows which of the candidates Joan will vote for. She’s sitting on the fence.

senses.definition: not to participate in something; to wait until something is over before participating.
examples: Oh, please play with us. Don’t sit it out.
I’m tired of playing cards, so I think I’ll sit out this game.

senses.definition: to witness or endure all of something.
examples: The performance was so bad that I could hardly sit through it.
You can’t expect small children to sit through a long movie.

senses.definition: to wait; to wait patiently.
senses.notes: Informal. This does not necessarily refer to sitting.
examples: Just relax and sit tight. I’ll be right with you.
We were waiting in line for the gates to open when someone came out and told us to sit tight because it wouldn’t be much longer before we could go in.

senses.definition: to become alert and pay attention.
examples: A loud noise from the front of the room caused everyone to sit up and take notice.
The company wouldn’t pay any attention to my complaints. When I had my lawyer write them a letter, they sat up and took notice.

senses.definition: to stay with someone through the night, especially with a sick or troubled person or with someone who is waiting for something.
examples: I had to sit up with my younger sister when she was ill.
I sat up with Bill while he waited for an overseas telephone call.

senses.definition: someone or something vulnerable to attack, physical or verbal.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like. See also a sitting target.
examples: You are a sitting duck out there. Get in here where the enemy cannot fire at you.
The senator was a sitting duck because of his position on school reform.

senses.definition: in a risky or explosive situation; in a situation where something serious or dangerous may happen at any time.
senses.notes: Informal. A powder keg is a keg of gunpowder.
examples: Things are very tense at work. The whole office is sitting on a powder keg.
The fire at the oil field seems to be under control for now, but all the workers there are sitting on a powder keg.

senses.definition: feeling wonderful; glorious; ecstatic.
examples: Wow, I feel on top of the world.
Since he got a new job, he’s on top of the world.

senses.definition: living in comfort or luxury; in a good situation.
examples: My uncle died and left enough money for me to be sitting pretty for the rest of my life.
Now that I have a good-paying job, I’m sitting pretty.

senses.definition: someone or something that is in a position that is easily attacked.
examples: The old man was a sitting target for the burglars. He lived alone and did not have a telephone.
People recently hired will be sitting targets if the company needs to cut back.

headword: six of one and half a dozen of the other

senses.definition: about the same one way or another.
examples: It doesn’t matter to me which way you do it. It’s six of one and half a dozen of the other.
What difference does it make? They’re both the same—six of one and half a dozen of the other.

senses.definition: a supposed power to know or feel things that are not perceptible by the five senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
examples: I have a sixth sense that told me to avoid going home by my usual route. Later I discovered there had been a fatal accident on it.
Jane’s sixth sense demanded that she not trust Tom, even though he seemed honest enough.

senses.definition: to observe someone or something to get information; to check someone or something.
examples: The comedian sized the audience up and decided not to use his new material.
I like to size up a situation before I act.

senses.definition: to be in a risky situation.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also on thin ice.
examples: I try to stay well informed so I don’t end up skating on thin ice when the teacher asks me a question.
You are skating on thin ice when you ask me that!

senses.definition: a hidden and shocking secret.
examples: You can ask anyone about how reliable I am. I don’t mind. I don’t have any skeletons in the closet.
My uncle was in jail for a day once. That’s our family’s skeleton in the closet.

senses.definition: to be very angry with someone; to scold someone severely.
examples: I was so mad at Jane that I could have skinned her alive.
If I don’t get home on time, my parents will skin me alive.

senses.definition: to sneak away from someone or some event; to leave someone or an event in secret.
examples: I heard that Bill skipped out on his wife.
I’m not surprised. I thought he should have skipped out long ago.

senses.definition: to jump over an arc of rope that is passed beneath one’s feet then over one’s head, repeatedly.
examples: The children skipped rope on the playground.
The boxer skipped rope while training.

senses.definition: There is no limit to the success that can be achieved or the money that can be gained or spent.
examples: If you take a job with us, you’ll find the promotion prospects very good. The sky’s the limit, in fact.
The insurance salesmen were told that the sky was the limit when it came to potential earnings.

senses.definition: to taper off; to reduce gradually.
examples: Business tends to slack off during the winter months.
The storms begin to slack off in April.

senses.definition: to become less active; to become lazy or inefficient.
examples: Near the end of the school year, Sally began to slack off, and her grades showed it.
John got fired for slacking off during the busy season.

senses.definition: an insult; an act that causes disappointment or discouragement.
examples: Losing the election was a slap in the face for the club president.
Failing to get into a good college was a slap in the face to Tim after his years of study.

senses.definition: to rebuke or rebuff someone, possibly with actual slapping.
examples: You may disagree with her, but you needn’t slap her down like that.
I only asked you what time it was! There’s no need to slap me down! What a rotten humor you’re in!

senses.definition: scheduled for something.
senses.notes: Refers to a schedule written on a slate.
examples: John was slated for Friday’s game, but he couldn’t play with the team.
Ann is slated for promotion next year.

senses.definition: scheduled to do something.
examples: John was slated to play ball Friday.
Who is slated to work this weekend?

senses.definition: someone who is under the control of something; someone who is controlled by something.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Mary is a slave to her job.
Bill is a slave to his drug addiction.

senses.definition: to sleep very soundly.
examples: Everyone in our family sleeps like a log, so no one heard the fire engines in the middle of the night.
Nothing can wake me up. I usually sleep like a baby.

senses.definition: to think about something overnight; to weigh a decision overnight.
examples: I don’t know whether I agree to do it. Let me sleep on it.
I slept on it, and I’ve decided to accept your offer.

senses.definition: to share a bed with someone.
examples: Do I have to sleep with my little brother?
Many little boys have to sleep with their brothers.

senses.definition: to copulate with someone.
examples: I hear Sam’s sleeping with Sally now.
Whom did you say he slept with?

senses.definition: a share of something.
examples: There’s not much work around and so everyone must get a slice of the cake.
The company makes huge profits and the workers want a slice of the cake.

senses.definition: an error in speaking where a word is pronounced incorrectly, or where something that the speaker did not mean to say is said.
examples: I didn’t mean to tell her that. It was a slip of the tongue.
I failed to understand the instructions because the speaker made a slip of the tongue at an important point.

senses.definition: to be forgotten.
senses.notes: [for something that was to be remembered]
examples: I meant to go to the grocery store on the way home, but it slipped my mind.
My birthday slipped my mind. I guess I wanted to forget it.

senses.definition: to be revealed.
examples: I asked her to keep our engagement secret, but she let it slip out.
I didn’t mean to tell. It just slipped out.

senses.definition: to get away from someone; for someone to lose track (of something or someone).
examples: I had a copy of the book you want, but somehow it slipped through my fingers.
There was a detective following me, but I managed to slip through his fingers.

senses.definition: to make an error.
examples: Try as hard as you can to do it right and not slip up.
Everything was going fine until the last minute when I slipped up.

headword: Slow and steady wins the race.

senses.definition: Deliberateness and determination will lead to success, or (literally) a reasonable pace will win a race.
examples: I worked my way through college in six years. Now I know what they mean when they say, “Slow and steady wins the race.”

Ann won the race because she started off slowly and established a good pace. The other runners tried to sprint the whole distance, and they tired out before the final lap. Ann’s trainer said, “You see! I told you! Slow and steady wins the race.”

senses.definition: the rate of speed when one is making progress.
examples: It was slow going at first, but I was able to finish the project by the weekend.
Getting the heavy rocks out of the field is slow going.

senses.definition: slow in drawing a gun.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with quick on the draw. Cowboy and gangster talk.
examples: Bill got shot because he’s so slow on the draw.
The gunslinger said, “I have to be fast. If I’m slow on the draw, I’m dead.”

senses.definition: slow to figure something out; slow-thinking.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with quick on the draw.
examples: Sally didn’t get the joke because she’s sort of slow on the draw.
Bill— who’s slow on the uptake—didn’t get the joke until it was explained to him.

senses.definition: to cause someone or something to reduce speed.
senses.notes: The phrases with up are informal.
examples: I’m in a hurry. Don’t try to slow me down.
Please slow up the train. There are sheep near the track.

senses.definition: at a decreasing rate of speed; slow and then even slower.
examples: The car is going slower and slower and will stop soon.
The dog’s breathing got slower and slower as it went to sleep.

senses.definition: slowly but with a purpose; slowly and deliberately.
senses.notes: The expression without the -ly is informal.
examples: Slowly but surely, the little train reached the top of the mountain.
Progress was slow but sure. Someday we would be finished.

senses.definition: right in the middle.
examples: I want a big helping of mashed potatoes with a glob of butter smack-dab in the middle.
Tom and Sally were having a terrible argument, and I was trapped—smack-dab in the middle.

senses.definition: unimportant people.
senses.notes: Small fry are small, juvenile fish.
examples: The police have only caught the small fry. The leader of the gang is still free.
You people are just small fry! I want to talk to the boss.

senses.definition: children.
examples: Peter’s taking the small fry to the zoo.
We should take the small fry to the pantomime.

senses.definition: the hours immediately after midnight.
examples: The dance went on into the small hours of the night.
Jim goes to bed in the wee hours and gets up at lunchtime.

senses.definition: the part of a document that is not easily noticed, often because of the smallness of the print, and that often contains important information.
examples: You should have read the small print before signing the contract.
You should always read the fine print in an insurance policy.

senses.definition: small; on a small scale.
examples: Our business is small-time just now, but it’s growing.
He’s a small-time crook.

senses.definition: a campaign aimed at damaging someone’s reputation by making accusations and spreading rumors.
examples: The politician’s opponents are engaging in a smear campaign against him.
Jack started a smear campaign against Tom so that Tom wouldn’t get the manager’s job.

senses.definition: to suspect that something is wrong; to sense that someone has caused something wrong.
examples: I don’t think this was an accident. I smell a rat. Bob had something to do with this.
The minute I came in, I smelled a rat. Sure enough, I had been robbed.

senses.definition: to be favorable to someone or something.
examples: Fate smiled on me and I got the job.
Lady luck smiled on our venture and we made a profit.

senses.definition: deception and confusion.
senses.notes: Said of statements or more complicated rhetoric used to mislead people rather than inform. Refers to the way a magician uses optical illusion to create believability while performing a trick.
examples: Most people know that the politician was just using smoke and mirrors to make things look better than they really were.
Her report was little more than smoke and mirrors. No one will believe any of it.

senses.definition: to reduce the intensity of an argument or a misunderstanding; to try to make people feel better about something that has happened.
examples: Mary and John had a terrible argument, and they are both trying to smooth it over.
Let’s get everyone together and try to smooth things out. We can’t keep on arguing with one another.
We can smooth over the whole affair.

senses.definition: a low and deceitful person.
examples: Sally said that Bob couldn’t be trusted because he was a snake in the grass.
“You snake in the grass!” cried Sally. “You cheated me.”

senses.definition: to speak sharply or angrily to someone.
examples: Don’t snap at me. What did I do?
Why did you snap at me? What did I do?

senses.definition: to become suddenly freed from a state.
senses.notes: Informal. The state can be a depression, an illness, unconsciousness, etc.
examples: I was very depressed for a week, but this morning I snapped out of it.
It isn’t often that a cold gets me down. Usually I can snap out of it quickly.

senses.definition: to grab and buy something.
examples: I always snap bargains up whenever I go shopping.
I went to the store, and they had soup on sale, so I snapped up plenty.

senses.definition: to make something go faster.
examples: You’re playing this music too slowly. Snap it up!
This performance is getting slow and dull. Let’s snap up the whole thing!

senses.definition: to locate someone or something.
examples: I’ll see if I can sniff out the correct stylus for your stereo.
Billy was lost, but by looking around, we were able to sniff him out.

headword: so clean you could eat off the floor

senses.definition: very clean.
examples: Her kitchen is so clean you could eat off the floor!
It’s so clean here you could eat off the floor. I prefer a little mess, myself.

senses.definition: All is going well so far.
examples: We are half finished with our project. So far, so good.
The operation is proceeding quite nicely—so far, so good.

senses.definition: That is the kind of thing that happens.; That is life.
examples: Too bad about John and his problems. So it goes.
I just lost a twenty-dollar bill, and I can’t find it anywhere. So it goes.

senses.definition: good-bye.
examples: So long, see you later.
As John got out of the car, he said, “Thanks for the ride. So long.”

senses.definition: very mad.
examples: I am just so mad I could scream! Why is he such a jerk?
She makes me so made I could scream.

headword: so much for someone or something

senses.definition: that is the last of someone or something; there is no need to consider someone or something anymore.
examples: It just started raining. So much for our picnic this afternoon.
So much for John. He just called in sick and can’t come to work today.

senses.definition: even better; all to the better.
examples: Please come to the picnic. If you can bring a salad, so much the better.
The flowers look lovely on the shelf. It would be so much the better if you put them on the table.

senses.definition: early; before the regular time; ahead of schedule.
examples: I got there early because my bus arrived so soon.
Because the meeting ended so soon, I had some extra time.

headword: so still you could hear a pin drop
altForms: so quiet you could hear a pin drop

senses.definition: very quiet.
examples: When I came into the room, it was so still you could hear a pin drop. Then everyone shouted, “Happy birthday!”
Please be quiet. Be so quiet you can hear a pin drop.

senses.definition: as one might say; said a certain way, even though the words are not exactly accurate.
examples: John helps me with my taxes. He’s my accountant, so to speak.
I just love my little poodle. She’s my baby, so to speak.

senses.definition: with one’s clothing wet clear through to the skin.
examples: I was caught in the rain and got soaked to the skin.
Oh, come in and dry off! You must be soaked to the skin.

senses.definition: to store something in a safe place.
examples: While I worked in the city, I was able to sock $100 away every month.
At the present time, I can’t sock away that much.

senses.definition: to excrete waste into its diaper.
examples: The baby soiled his diapers.
I detect that someone has soiled his diaper.

senses.definition: new personnel; new members brought into a group to revive it.
examples: This company needs some new blood on its board to bring in new ideas.
We’re trying to get some new blood in the club. Our membership is falling.
Our club needs new blood. It has become boring.
The firm’s management has at last got a little new blood. Things should improve now.

senses.definition: someone or something is verified or authenticated.
examples: I spent all afternoon working with my checkbook, trying to get the figures to check out.
The police wouldn’t believe that I am who I say I am until they made a few telephone calls to see if my story checked out.

senses.definition: a person who is famous.
examples: We invited a speaker of note to lecture at the next meeting.
The baseball player of note was inducted into the Hall of Fame.

senses.definition: something or someone held (secretly) in reserve; anything that can help in an emergency.
senses.notes: Slang. Refers to an ace dealt facedown in poker.
examples: The hostages served as the terrorists’ ace in the hole for getting what they wanted.
The twenty-dollar bill in my shoe is my ace in the hole.

senses.definition: someone’s income; someone’s livelihood—the source of one’s food.
senses.notes: Work or a job leads to a paycheck that will buy bread and butter.
examples: I can’t miss another day of work. That’s my bread and butter.
I like to go to business conferences. That’s good because that’s my bread and butter.

senses.definition: one is finished; one has been found out and is in trouble.
examples: It’s over. His goose is cooked!
If I get caught, my goose is cooked.

senses.definition: a will; the last edition of someone’s will.
examples: The lawyer read Uncle Charles’s last will and testament to a group of expectant relatives.
Fred dictated his last will and testament on his deathbed.

senses.definition: one’s purpose for living; the reason for which one lives on the earth.
examples: Bob’s mission in life is to make money.
My mission in life is to help people live in peace.

senses.definition: something that is disliked intensely by someone and is a constant or repeated annoyance.
examples: My pet hate is being put on hold on the telephone.
Another pet hate of mine is having to stand in line.

senses.definition: one’s “favorite” or most often encountered annoyance.
examples: My pet peeve is someone who always comes into the theater after the show has started.
Drivers who don’t signal are John’s pet peeve.

senses.definition: a place where business is done; a factory or office.
examples: Our place of business opens at noon each day.
You will have to come to our place of business to make a purchase.

senses.definition: the last work or performance of a playwright, musician, actor, etc., before death or retirement.
examples: His portrayal of Lear was the actor’s swan song.
We didn’t know that her performance last night was the singer’s swan song.

senses.definition: someone’s pattern of thinking; someone’s sequence of ideas; what one was just thinking about.
senses.notes: See also lose one’s train of thought.
examples: My train of thought is probably not as clear as it should be.
I cannot seem to follow your train of thought on this matter. Will you explain it a little more carefully, please?

headword: someone wrote the book on something

senses.definition: to be very authoritative about something; to know enough about something to write the definitive book on it.
senses.notes: Also literal. Always in past tense.
examples: Ted wrote the book on unemployment. He’s been looking for work in three states for two years.
Do I know about misery? I wrote the book on misery!

senses.definition: something wonderful; something extra special.
examples: Did you see her new car? That’s really something else!
John hit a ball yesterday that went out of the stadium and kept on going. He’s something else!

senses.definition: something entirely different.
examples: Borrowing is one thing, but stealing is something else.
Skin diving is easy and fun, but scuba diving is something else again.

senses.definition: something of the kind just mentioned.
examples: This is a spruce tree, or something of the sort.
Jane has a cold or something of the sort.

senses.definition: something like what was just said.
examples: She said she wouldn’t be available until after three, or something to that effect.
I was told to keep out of the house—or something to that effect.

headword: (somewhere) in the neighborhood of an amount

senses.definition: approximately a particular measurement.
examples: I take somewhere in the neighborhood of ten pills a day for my various ailments.
My rent is in the neighborhood of $700 per month.

altForms: a place to hang one’s hat
a place to call one’s own

senses.definition: a place to live; a place to call one’s home.
examples: What I need is somewhere to hang up my hat. I just can’t stand all this traveling.
A home is a lot more than a place to hang your hat.

senses.definition: a very horrible person.
senses.notes: Informal. Use with caution. Usually intended as a strong insult. Never used casually.
examples: Bill called Bob a son of a bitch, and Bob punched Bill in the face.
This guy’s a son of a bitch. He treats everybody rotten.

senses.definition: a useless annoyance; something worthless.
examples: This car is a son of a bitch. It won’t ever start when it’s cold.
This bumpy old road needs paving. It’s a real son of a bitch.

senses.definition: a difficult task.
examples: This job is a son of a bitch.
I can’t do this kind of thing. It’s too hard— a real son of a bitch.

senses.definition: a horrible person.
senses.notes: Informal. A euphemism for son of a bitch. Use with caution.
examples: When is that plumber going to show up and fix this leak? The stupid son of a gun!
Bob is a rotten son of a gun if he thinks he can get away with that.

senses.definition: old (male) friend.
senses.notes: Informal. A friendly—male to male—way of referring to a friend. Use with caution.
examples: Why Bill, you old son of a gun, I haven’t seen you in three or four years.
When is that son of a gun John going to come visit us? He’s neglecting his friends.

senses.definition: a person, usually a male.
senses.notes: Sometimes a substitute for son of a bitch.
examples: Why, good to see you, you old son of a sea biscuit.
You son of a sea biscuit! You make me so mad I could slug you.

senses.definition: eventually; in the short term or in the long term.
examples: He’ll have to pay the bill sooner or later.
She’ll get what she deserves sooner or later.

senses.definition: almost something; somewhat; somehow.
examples: Isn’t it sort of cold out?
That was kind of a stupid thing to do, wasn’t it?

senses.definition: to clear up confusion; to straighten out something disorderly.
examples: Now that things are settled down, I can sort out my life.
This place is a mess. Let’s sort things out before we do anything else.

senses.definition: to seem, from what has been said, as if something were so.
examples: It sounds as if you had a good vacation.
You sound like you are angry.

senses.definition: to say the same thing over and over again.
senses.notes: From an earlier age when a crack in a 78 rpm record would cause the needle (or stylus) to stay in the same groove and play it over and over.
examples: He’s always complaining about the way she treats him. He sounds like a broken record!
I hate to sound like a broken record, but we just don’t have enough people on the payroll to work efficiently.

senses.definition: to seem like something.
examples: That sounds like a good idea.
Your explanation sounds like an excuse!

senses.definition: to speak loudly and freely about something, especially when complaining.
examples: The people at the bus stop were sounding off about the poor transportation services.
Bob was sounding off about the government’s economic policies.
Sam sounds off every chance he gets.

senses.definition: to try to find out what someone thinks (about something).
examples: I don’t know what Jane thinks about your suggestion, but I’ll sound her out.
Please sound out everyone in your department.

senses.definition: to make something (especially a car) more powerful.
examples: I wish someone would soup my car up. It’ll hardly run.
Bill spent all summer souping up that old car he bought.

senses.definition: to do wild and foolish things in one’s youth.
senses.notes: Often assumed to have some sort of sexual meaning.
examples: Dale was out sowing his wild oats last night, and he’s in jail this morning.
Mrs. Smith told Mr. Smith that he was too old to be sowing his wild oats.

senses.definition: dopey; giddy.
examples: I don’t see how Sally can accomplish anything. She’s so spaced-out!
She’s not really spaced-out. She acts that way on purpose.

senses.definition: to exempt someone from having to listen to or experience something.
examples: I’ll spare you the details and get to the point.
Please, spare me the story and tell me what you want.

senses.definition: not to need explaining; [for things] to have an obvious meaning.
examples: The evidence speaks for itself.
The facts speak for themselves. Tom is guilty.
Your results speak for themselves. You need to work harder.

headword: speak highly of someone or something

senses.definition: to say good things about someone or something.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples. See also think a lot of someone or something.
examples: Ann speaks quite highly of Jane’s work.
Everyone speaks very highly of Jane.

senses.definition: to say something bad about someone.
examples: I refuse to speak ill of any of my friends.
Max speaks ill of no one and refuses to repeat gossip.

senses.definition: to speak in public without preparation.
examples: I’m not too good at speaking off the cuff.
I need to prepare a speech for Friday, although I speak off the cuff quite well.

senses.definition: said when someone whose name has just been mentioned appears or is heard from.
examples: Well, speak of the devil! Hello, Tom. We were just talking about you.
I had just mentioned Sally when—speak of the devil—she walked in the door.

senses.definition: to say frankly what one thinks (about something).
examples: Please let me speak my mind, and then you can do whatever you wish.
You can always depend on John to speak his mind. He’ll let you know what he really thinks.

senses.definition: to say something unwise or imprudent; to say the right thing at the wrong time.
examples: Excuse me if I’m speaking out of turn, but what you are proposing is quite wrong.
Bob was quite honest, even if he was speaking out of turn.

senses.definition: to have similar ideas, tastes, etc.
examples: Jane and Jack get along very well. They really speak the same language about almost everything.
Bob and his father didn’t speak the same language when it comes to politics.

senses.definition: to tell lies; to try to deceive someone.
examples: Jean’s mother sounds very charming, but she speaks with a forked tongue.
People tend to believe Fred because he seems plausible, but we know he speaks with a forked tongue.

senses.definition: to signify future trouble; to mean trouble.
examples: This letter that came today spells trouble.
The sky looks angry and dark. That spells trouble.

senses.definition: very clean.
examples: I have to clean up the house and get it spick-and-span for the party Friday night.
I love to have everything around me spick-and-span.

senses.definition: to tell a tale.
examples: Grandpa spun an unbelievable yarn for us.
My uncle is always spinning yarns about his childhood.

senses.definition: to be in motion, but get nowhere.
examples: This is a terrible job. I’m just spinning my wheels and not getting anywhere.
Get organized and try to accomplish something. Stop spinning your wheels!

senses.definition: to create something as a by-product of something else.
examples: When the company reorganized, it spun its banking division off.
By spinning off part of its assets, a company gets needed capital.

senses.definition: to throw something up; to vomit something.
senses.notes: A little gentler than throw (something) up.
examples: I guess that the food didn’t agree with the dog, because he spit it up.
The baby has been spitting up all morning.
Bob spit up his whole dinner.

senses.definition: to quibble; to try to make petty distinctions.
examples: They don’t have any serious differences. They are just splitting hairs.
Don’t waste time splitting hairs. Accept it the way it is.

senses.definition: to laugh so hard that one’s sides almost split.
examples: The members of the audience almost split their sides with laughter.
When I heard what happened to Patricia, I almost split my sides.

senses.definition: to separate two or more people (from one another).
examples: If you two don’t stop chattering, I’ll have to split you up.
The group of people grew too large, so we had to split them up.
I will have to split up that twosome in the corner.

senses.definition: to divide the difference evenly (with someone else).
examples: You want to sell for $120, and I want to buy for $100. Let’s split the difference and close the deal at $110.
I don’t want to split the difference. I want $120.

senses.definition: to separate or leave one another; [for a couple] to divorce or spearate.
examples: I heard that Mr. and Mrs. Brown have split up.
Our little club had to split up because everyone was too busy.

senses.definition: taken; reserved (for someone).
examples: I’m sorry, but this one is already spoken for.
Pardon me. Can I sit here, or is this seat spoken for?

senses.definition: to startle or disorient someone or something.
examples: A snake spooked my horse, and I nearly fell off.
Your warning spooked me, and I was upset for the rest of the day.

senses.definition: to treat someone with too much care or help; to teach someone with methods that are too easy and do not stimulate the learner to independent thinking.
examples: The teacher spoon-feeds the students by dictating notes on the novel instead of getting the children to read the books.
You mustn’t spoon-feed the new recruits by telling them what to do all the time. They must use their initiative.

senses.definition: a reasonably good chance.
examples: If you hurry, you have a sporting chance of catching the bus.
The small company has only a sporting chance of getting the export order.

senses.definition: to talk too much about someone or something.
examples: Why do you always have to spout off about things that don’t concern you?
Everyone in our office spouts off about the boss.
There is no need to spout off like that. Calm down and think about what you’re saying.

senses.definition: to spread rapidly and without control.
examples: The epidemic is spreading like wildfire. Everyone is getting sick.
John told a joke that was so funny it spread like wildfire.

senses.definition: to do so many things that you can do none of them well.
examples: It’s a good idea to get involved in a lot of activities, but don’t spread yourself too thin.
I’m too busy these days. I’m afraid I’ve spread myself too thin.

senses.definition: to treat (someone) to something.
examples: John and I went out last night, and he sprang for dinner.
At the park Bill usually springs for ice cream.

senses.definition: to surprise someone with something.
examples: I’m glad you told me now, rather than springing it on me at the last minute.
I sprang the news on my parents last night. They were not glad to hear it.

senses.definition: to make someone or something clean and orderly.
examples: I’ll be ready to go as soon as I spruce myself up a bit.
I have to spruce up the house for the party.

senses.definition: to settle one’s financial accounts with someone.
examples: I have to square accounts with the bank this week, or it’ll take back my car.
I called the bank and said I needed to come in and square accounts.

senses.definition: to get even with someone; to straighten out a misunderstanding with someone.
examples: I’m going to square accounts with Tom. He insulted me in public, and he owes me an apology.
Tom, you and I are going to have to square accounts.

senses.definition: a fair and honest transaction; fair treatment.
examples: All the workers want is a square deal, but their boss underpays them.
You always get a square deal with that travel company.

senses.definition: a nourishing, filling meal.
examples: All you’ve eaten today is junk food. You should sit down to a square meal.
The poor old man hadn’t had a square meal in weeks.

senses.definition: to get ready for an argument or a fight.
examples: John was angry and appeared to be squaring off for a fight.
When those two square off, everyone gets out of the way.

headword: a square peg in a round hole

senses.definition: a misfit.
examples: John can’t seem to get along with the people he works with. He’s just a square peg in a round hole.
I’m not a square peg in a round hole. It’s just that no one understands me.

senses.definition: to get someone or something arranged or properly taken care of.
examples: See if you can square Bob away in his new office.
Please square away the problems we discussed earlier.

headword: square up to someone or something

senses.definition: to face someone or something bravely; to tackle someone or something.
examples: You’ll have to square up to the bully or he’ll make your life miserable.
It’s time to square up to your financial problems. You can’t just ignore them.

senses.definition: to pay someone what one owes; to pay one’s share of something to someone.
examples: I’ll square up with you later if you pay the whole bill now.
Bob said he would square up with Tom for his share of the gas.

senses.definition: arranged or properly taken care of.
examples: Is Ann squared away yet?
I will talk to you when I am squared away.

senses.definition: to just barely get by someone or something.
examples: The guard was almost asleep, so I squeaked by him.
I wasn’t very well prepared for the test, and I just squeaked by.

senses.definition: to hide or store something.
examples: Billy has been squirreling candy away in his top drawer.
I’ve been squirreling away a little money each week for years.

senses.definition: to betray someone.
examples: I thought we were friends! Why did you stab me in the back?
You don’t expect a person whom you trust to stab you in the back.

headword: stack the deck (against someone or something)
altForms: stack the cards (against someone or something)

senses.definition: to arrange things against someone or something.
examples: I can’t get ahead at my office. Someone has stacked the cards against me.
Do you really think that someone has stacked the deck? Isn’t it just fate?

senses.definition: to lay or make a claim for something.
examples: I want to stake a claim to that last piece of pie.
You don’t need to stake a claim. Just ask politely.

senses.definition: to put off or delay someone or something.
examples: The sheriff is at the door. I’ll stall him off while you get out the back door.
You can stall off the sheriff, but you can’t stall off justice.

senses.definition: to get rid of or kill someone.
examples: You just can’t stamp somebody out on your own!
The victim wanted to stamp out the robbers without a trial.

senses.definition: to extinguish something.
examples: Quick, stamp that fire out before it spreads.
Tom stamped out the sparks before they started a fire.

senses.definition: to eliminate something.
examples: The doctors hope they can stamp cancer out.
Many people think that they can stamp out evil.

senses.definition: to have a chance.
examples: Do you think I stand a chance of winning first place?
Everyone stands a chance of catching the disease.

senses.definition: to give up something to someone who demands it.
senses.notes: Originally used by highway robbers asking for passengers’ valuables. Now used figuratively.
examples: And when the tax agent says “Stand and deliver” you have to be prepared to pay what is demanded.
The robber stopped the coach and demanded of Lady Ellen, “Stand and deliver!”

altForms: stand (in) back of someone or something

senses.definition: to endorse or guarantee something or the actions of a person.
examples: Our company stands behind this product 100 percent.
I stand behind Bill and everything he does.

senses.definition: to wait and remain ready.
senses.notes: Generally heard in communication, such as broadcasting, telephones, etc.
examples: Your transatlantic telephone call is almost ready. Please stand by.
Is everyone ready for the telecast? Only ten seconds—stand by.

senses.definition: to support someone; to continue supporting someone even when things are bad.
senses.notes: Also literal. Compare this with stick by someone or something.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll stand by you no matter what.
I feel as though I have to stand by my brother even if he goes to jail.

senses.definition: to admit that one has been wrong.
examples: I realize that I accused him wrongly. I stand corrected.
We appreciate now that our conclusions were wrong. We stand corrected.

senses.definition: to endure something.
examples: The teacher won’t stand for any whispering in class.
We just can’t stand for that kind of behavior.

senses.definition: to signify something.
examples: In a traffic signal, the red light stands for “stop.”
The abbreviation Dr. stands for “doctor.”

senses.definition: to endorse or support an ideal.
examples: The mayor claims to stand for honesty in government and jobs for everyone.
Every candidate for public office stands for all the good things in life.

headword: stand in awe (of someone or something)

senses.definition: to be overwhelmed with respect for someone or something.
examples: Many people stand in awe of the president.
Bob says he stands in awe of a big juicy steak. I think he’s exaggerating.
When it comes to food, you can say that it’s delicious, but one hardly stands in awe.

senses.definition: to substitute for someone; to serve in someone’s place.
examples: The famous opera singer was ill, and an inexperienced singer had to stand in for her.
The new singer was grateful for the opportunity to stand in.

senses.definition: to be a barrier to someone’s desires or intentions.
examples: I know you want a divorce so you can marry Ann. Well, I won’t stand in your way. You can have the divorce.
I know you want to leave home, and I don’t want to stand in your way. You’re free to go.

senses.definition: to hold rigidly to protocol or formal manners.
examples: Please help yourself to more. Don’t stand on ceremony.
We are very informal around here. Hardly anyone stands on ceremony.

senses.definition: to stand up for one’s rights; to resist an attack.
examples: The lawyer tried to confuse me when I was giving testimony, but I managed to stand my ground.
Some people were trying to crowd us off the beach, but we held our ground.

headword: stand on one’s own two feet

senses.definition: to be independent and self-sufficient.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with get back on one’s feet.
examples: I’ll be glad when I have a good job and can stand on my own two feet.
When Jane gets out of debt, she’ll be able to stand on her own two feet again.

senses.definition: to be uniquely visible or conspicuous.
examples: This computer stands out as one of the best available.
Because John is so tall, he really stands out in a crowd.

senses.definition: to remain as is; to preserve the status quo.
examples: We can’t just stand pat! We have to keep making progress!
This company isn’t increasing sales. It’s just standing pat.

senses.definition: to be useful or beneficial to someone.
examples: This is a fine overcoat. I’m sure it’ll stand you in good stead for many years.
I did the mayor a favor that I’m sure will stand me in good stead.

senses.definition: to pay for food or drink for someone as a special favor.
examples: We went to the zoo, and my father stood us all to a treat. We had ice cream and soft drinks.
We went to a nice restaurant and had a fine meal. It was even better when Mr. Williams told us he’d stand us to a treat, and he picked up the bill.

senses.definition: to fail to meet someone for a date or an appointment.
examples: John and Jane were supposed to go out last night, but she stood him up.
If you stand up people very often, you’ll find that you have no friends at all.

senses.definition: to tolerate or endure something.
examples: I won’t stand still for that kind of behavior!
She won’t hold still for that kind of talk.

senses.definition: to seem reasonable.
examples: It stands to reason that it’ll be colder in January than it is in November.
It stands to reason that Bill left in a hurry, although no one saw him go.

senses.definition: to state one’s support (for someone or something); to come out for someone or something.
examples: If you believe in more government help for farmers, write your representative—stand up and be counted.
I’m generally in favor of what you propose, but not enough to stand up and be counted.

senses.definition: a subject that regularly and over a period of time causes amusement whenever it is mentioned.
examples: Uncle Jim’s driving was a standing joke. He used to drive incredibly slowly.
Their mother’s inability to make a decision was a standing joke in the Smith family all their lives.

senses.definition: totally insane; completely crazy; out of control.
examples: When she heard about what happened at the office, she went stark raving mad.
You must be stark raving mad if you think I would trust you with my car!

senses.definition: to start from the beginning; to start from nothing.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with make something from scratch.
examples: Whenever I bake a cake, I start from scratch. I never use a cake mix in a box.
I built every bit of my own house. I started from scratch and did everything with my own hands.

headword: start off on the wrong foot

senses.definition: to begin [something] by doing something wrong.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also be off on the wrong foot; get off on the wrong foot.
examples: I don’t want to start off on the wrong foot by saying something stupid. What should I say?
Poor Donna started off on the wrong foot when she arrived forty minutes late.

senses.definition: to start out again afresh; to ignore the past and start over again.
senses.notes: Refers to making marks on a [clean] slate with chalk.
examples: I plowed under all last year’s flowers so I could start with a clean slate next spring.
If I start off with a clean slate, then I’ll know exactly what each plant is.
When Bob got out of jail, he started over with a clean slate.

senses.definition: not to move; to stay where one is.
examples: We’ve decided to stay put and not to move to Florida.
If the children just stay put, their parents will come for them soon.

senses.definition: to sneak from one base to another in baseball.
examples: The runner stole second base, but he nearly got put out on the way.
Tom runs so slowly that he never tries to steal a base.

senses.definition: to get some sort of an advantage over someone without being noticed.
examples: I got the contract because I was able to steal a march on my competitor.
You have to be clever and fast—not dishonest—to steal a march.

senses.definition: to lessen someone’s force or authority.
examples: What do you mean by coming in here and stealing my thunder? I’m in charge here!
Someone stole my thunder by leaking my announcement to the press.

senses.definition: to give the best performance in a show, play, or some other event; to get attention for oneself.
examples: The lead in the play was very good, but the butler stole the show.
Ann always tries to steal the spotlight when she and I make a presentation.

senses.definition: angry.
examples: What Bob said really got me steamed up.
Why do you get so steamed up about nothing?

senses.definition: very angry; very mad; very upset.
examples: The steaming coach yelled at the clumsy players.
The principal was steaming mad when he found that his office had been vandalized.

senses.definition: to avoid someone or something.
examples: John is mad at me, so I’ve been steering clear of him.
Steer clear of that book. It has many errors in it.
Good advice. I’ll steer clear.

senses.definition: little by little, one step at a time.
senses.notes: Refers both to walking and following instructions.
examples: Just follow the instructions step-by-step, and everything will be fine.
The old man slowly moved across the lawn step-by-step.

senses.definition: to resign a job or a responsibility.
examples: The mayor stepped down from office last week.
It’s unusual for a mayor to step down.

senses.definition: to take over a job or some role from someone.
examples: I was prepared to step into the boss’s shoes, so there was no disruption when he left for another job.
There was no one who could step into Alice’s shoes when she left, so everything came to a stop.

senses.definition: to move into a space or vacancy; to assume the job of someone who has left it.
examples: When Ann resigned as president, I stepped into the breach.
A number of people asked me to step in and take her place.

senses.definition: to interfere with or offend someone.
examples: When you’re in public office, you have to avoid stepping on anyone’s toes.
Ann stepped on someone’s toes during the last campaign and lost the election.

senses.definition: hurry up.
examples: I’m in a hurry, driver. Step on it!
I can’t step on the gas, mister. There’s too much traffic.

senses.definition: to misbehave; to do something offensive.
examples: I’m terribly sorry. I hope I didn’t step out of line.
John is a lot of fun to go out with, but he has a tendency to step out of line.

senses.definition: to move forward, toward someone.
examples: Step up and get your mail when I call your name.
Come on, everybody. Step right up and help yourself to supper.

senses.definition: to cause something to go faster.
examples: The factory was not making enough cars, so they stepped up production.
The music was not fast enough, so the conductor told everyone to step it up.

senses.definition: to be left alone to suffer one’s anger or disappointment.
examples: John has such a terrible temper. When he got mad at us, we just let him go away and stew in his own juice.
After John stewed in his own juice for a while, he decided to come back and apologize to us.

senses.definition: to remain in a place.
examples: The kids stuck around for a time after the party was over.
Oh, Ann. Please stick around for a while. I want to talk to you later.

senses.definition: to support someone or something; to continue supporting someone or something when things are bad.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with stand by someone.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll stick by you no matter what.
I feel as if I have to stick by my brother even if he goes to jail.
I’ll stick by my ideas whether you like them or not.

senses.definition: someone who is stubbornly old-fashioned.
examples: Come on to the party with us and have some fun. Don’t be an old stick-in-the-mud!
Tom is no stick-in-the-mud. He’s really up-to-date.

headword: stick one’s neck out (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to take a risk.
examples: Why should I stick my neck out to do something for her? What’s she ever done for me?
He made a risky investment. He stuck his neck out for the deal because he thought he could make some money.

headword: stick out like a sore thumb

senses.definition: to be very prominent or unsightly; to be obvious and visible.
examples: Bob is so tall that he sticks out like a sore thumb in a crowd.
The house next door needs painting. It sticks out like a sore thumb.

senses.definition: to affix or attach something onto a wall, post, etc.
examples: This notice ought to be on the bulletin board. Please stick it up.
I’m going to stick up this poster near the entrance.

senses.definition: to rob someone or something.
examples: One robber stuck the cashier up first, but someone sounded the alarm before any money was taken.
The robbers came in and tried to stick up the bank, but they got caught first.

senses.definition: to endure something.
examples: The play was terribly boring, but I managed to stick it out.
College was very difficult for Bill, but he decided to stick it out.

senses.definition: to remain together as a group.
examples: Come on, you guys. Let’s stick together. Otherwise somebody will get lost.
Our group of friends has managed to stick together for almost twenty years.

senses.definition: to remain firm in one’s convictions; to stand up for one’s rights.
senses.notes: Informal. Compare this with stand one’s ground.
examples: I’ll stick to my guns on this matter. I’m sure I’m right.
Bob can be persuaded to do it our way. He probably won’t stick to his guns on this point.

senses.definition: to last long and fortify one well; [for food] to sustain one even in the coldest weather.
senses.notes: [for food] Refers to the inside of one’s ribs.
examples: This oatmeal ought to stick to your ribs. You need something hearty on a cold day like this.
I don’t want soup! I want something that will stick to my ribs.

headword: stick up for someone or something

senses.definition: to support someone or something; to speak in favor of someone or something.
examples: Everyone was making unpleasant remarks about John, but I stuck up for him.
Our team was losing, but I stuck up for it anyway.

senses.definition: elements of harm [directed at someone].
senses.notes: Part of a rhyme, “Sticks and stones may break my bones, but words will never hurt me.”
examples: I have had enough of your sticks and stones. I have enough trouble without your adding to it.
After the opposing candidate had used sticks and stones for a month, suddenly there were kind words heard.

senses.definition: to smell very bad.
examples: What happened? This place stinks to high heaven.
This meat smells to high heaven. Throw it away!

senses.definition: to make someone angry or excited; to make someone get active.
examples: I need a cup of hot coffee to stir me up in the morning.
Reading the newspaper always stirs up my father.

senses.definition: to cause trouble; to foment disagreement and difficulty.
examples: They stirred up quite a commotion.
Who stirred up this matter?

senses.definition: to create trouble or difficulties.
examples: What a mess you have made of things. You’ve really stirred up a hornet’s nest.
Bill stirred up a hornet’s nest when he discovered the theft.

senses.definition: to build up a supply of something.
examples: Before the first snow, we always stock up on firewood.
John drinks a lot of milk, so we stock up when we know he’s coming.

senses.definition: to degrade oneself or condescend to doing something; to do something that is beneath one.
examples: Whoever thought that the manager of the department would stoop to typing?
I never dreamed that Bill would stoop to stealing.

senses.definition: halting repeatedly; stopping and continuing repeatedly.
examples: This project has been stop-and-go since we began. Problems keep appearing.
The traffic was stop-and-go for miles. I thought I would never get here!

senses.definition: to do everything possible (to accomplish something); to be unscrupulous.
examples: Bill would stop at nothing to get his way.
Bob is completely determined to get promoted. He’ll stop at nothing.

senses.definition: to visit a place, usually briefly.
examples: I was coming home, but I decided to stop by my aunt’s on the way.
She was very glad that I stopped in.

senses.definition: to exercise caution at street corners and railroad crossings, by stopping, looking to the left and to the right, and listening for approaching vehicles or a train.
examples: Sally’s mother trained her to stop, look, and listen at every street corner.
It is a good practice to stop, look, and listen at a railroad crossing.

senses.definition: to break one’s journey somewhere, usually overnight or even longer.
examples: On our way to New York, we stopped over in Philadelphia for the night.
That’s a good place to stop over. There are some nice hotels in Philadelphia.

senses.definition: not to go as far as doing something; not to go as far as something.
examples: Fortunately Bob stopped short of hitting Tom.
The boss criticized Jane’s work, but stopped short of reprimanding her.
Jack was furious but stopped short of hitting Tom.
Jane wouldn’t stop short of telling lies in order to get a job.

senses.definition: There is going to be a storm.
examples: Look at the clouds. A storm is brewing.
A storm is brewing in the west.

senses.definition: There is going to be trouble or emotional upset.
examples: He looks angry. A storm is brewing.

senses.definition: a straight and law-abiding route through life.
senses.notes: Informal. From straight and narrow pathway.
examples: You should have no trouble with the police if you stick to the straight and narrow.
Roger was the kind who followed the straight and narrow every day of his life.

senses.definition: from an authoritative or dependable source.
examples: I know it’s true! I heard it straight from the horse’s mouth!
This comes from the horse’s mouth, so it has to be believed.

senses.definition: sincerely; frankly; holding nothing back.
examples: Sally always speaks straight from the shoulder. You never have to guess what she really means.
Bill gave a good presentation—straight from the shoulder and brief.

senses.definition: to make someone understand something.
examples: Jane was confused about the date, so I straightened her out.
I took a few minutes and straightened out everyone.

senses.definition: to reform someone.
examples: Most people think that jail never straightens anybody out.
The judge felt that a few years at hard labor would straighten out the thief.

senses.definition: to make a situation less confused.
examples: John made a mess of the contract, so I helped him straighten it out.
Please straighten out your checking account. It’s all messed up.

senses.definition: to put someone or something into an upright position.
examples: The fence is tilted. Please straighten up that post when you get a chance.
Bill, you’re slouching again. Straighten yourself up.

senses.definition: to tidy up someone or something.
examples: John straightened himself up a little before going on stage.
This room is a mess. Let’s straighten up this place, right now!

senses.definition: someone who is new to an area or place.
examples: Although John was no stranger to big cities, he did not enjoy visiting New York.
You are a stranger to our town, and I hope you feel welcome.

senses.definition: very much in need of money.
examples: I’m strapped for a few bucks. Can you loan me five dollars?
Sorry, I’m strapped, too.

senses.definition: to interpret a point flexibly and with great latitude.
examples: Would it be stretching a point to suggest that everyone is invited to your picnic?
To say that everyone is invited is stretching the point.

senses.definition: to walk around after sitting down or lying down for a time.
examples: We wanted to stretch our legs during the theater intermission.
After sitting in the car all day, the travelers decided to stretch their legs.

senses.definition: to exaggerate; to misrepresent the truth just a little bit.
examples: She was stretching the truth when she said everything was ready for the party.
I don’t want to stretch the truth. Our town is probably the wealthiest around here.

senses.definition: honest; dependably open and fair.
examples: How can I be sure you’re on the level?
You can trust Sally. She’s strictly on the level.

headword: strike a balance (between two or more things)

senses.definition: to find a satisfactory compromise between two extremes.
examples: The political party must strike a balance between the right wing and the left wing.
Jane is overdressed for the party and Sally is underdressed. What a pity they didn’t strike a balance.

senses.definition: to reach an agreement on a price (for something).
examples: They argued for a while and finally struck a bargain.
They were unable to strike a bargain, so they left.

senses.definition: to cause someone to remember something; to remind someone or something; to be familiar.
examples: The woman in the portrait struck a chord and I realized that it was my grandmother.
His name strikes a chord with me, but I don’t know why.

senses.definition: to find a compromise position; to arrive at a position halfway between two unacceptable extremes.
examples: Ann likes very spicy food, but Bob doesn’t care for spicy food at all. We are trying to find a restaurant that strikes a happy medium.
Tom is either very happy or very sad. He can’t seem to hit a happy medium.

senses.definition: to light a match.
examples: Mary struck a match and lit a candle.
When Sally struck a match to light a cigarette, Jane said quickly, “No smoking, please.”

senses.definition: to position oneself in a certain posture.
examples: Bob struck a pose in front of the mirror to see how much he had grown.
Lisa walked into the room and struck a pose, hoping she would be noticed.

senses.definition: to signify something unpleasant.
examples: Jane’s sad announcement struck a sour note at the annual banquet.
News of the crime hit a sour note in our holiday celebration.

senses.definition: to acquire wealth suddenly.
examples: If I could strike it rich, I wouldn’t have to work anymore.
Sally ordered a dozen oysters and found a huge pearl in one of them. She struck it rich!

headword: strike out at someone or something

senses.definition: to (figuratively or literally) hit at or attack someone or something.
examples: She was so angry she struck out at the person she was arguing with.
I was frantic. I wanted to strike out at everything and everybody.

senses.definition: to affect someone a certain way.
examples: John’s rude behavior struck me as odd.
Mary’s attitude struck me as childish.

senses.definition: to seem funny to someone.
examples: Sally has a great sense of humor. Everything she says strikes me funny.
Why are you laughing? Did something I said strike you funny?

senses.definition: to appeal to someone.
examples: I’ll have some ice cream, please. Chocolate strikes my fancy right now.
Why don’t you go to the store and buy a record album that strikes your fancy?

senses.definition: to achieve the desired effect; to do something suitable or pleasing.
examples: Meg struck the right note when she wore a dark suit to the interview.
The politician’s speech failed to strike the right note with the crowd.

senses.definition: to start a conversation (with someone).
examples: I struck up an interesting conversation with someone on the bus yesterday.
It’s easy to strike up a conversation with someone when you’re traveling.

senses.definition: to become friends (with someone).
examples: I struck up a friendship with John while we were on a business trip together.
If you’re lonely, you should go out and try to strike up a friendship with someone you like.

headword: strike while the iron is hot

senses.definition: to do something at the best possible time; to do something when the time is ripe.
examples: He was in a good mood, so I asked for a loan of $200. I thought I’d better strike while the iron was hot.
Please go to the bank and settle this matter now! They are willing to be reasonable. You’ve got to strike while the iron is hot.

senses.definition: to accompany someone; to run around with someone.
examples: Sally seemed to know where she was going, so I decided to string along with her.
She said it was okay if I strung along.

senses.definition: to draw something out (in time); to make something last a long time.
examples: The meeting was long enough. There was no need to string it out further with all those speeches.
They tried to string out the meeting to make things seem more important.

senses.definition: a bit of luck; a lucky happening.
examples: I had a stroke of luck and found Tom at home when I called. He’s not usually there.
Unless I have a stroke of luck, I’m not going to finish this report by tomorrow.

senses.definition: a bitter struggle either to success or failure.
examples: It was a struggle to the death, but I finally finished my report on time.
I had a terrible time getting my car started. It was a struggle to the death, but it finally started.

senses.definition: extended in time; overly long.
examples: Why was that lecture so strung out? She talked and talked.
It was strung out because there was very little to be said.

senses.definition: doped or drugged.
examples: Bob acted very strangely—as if he were strung out or something.
I’ve never seen Bob or any of his friends strung out.

senses.definition: kept in an established way of living that never changes.
examples: David felt like he was stuck in a rut, so he went back to school.
Anne was tired of being in a rut, so she moved to Los Angeles.

senses.definition: to be caught in a traffic jam.
examples: I am sorry I am late. I was stuck in traffic.
Our taxi was stuck in traffic, and I thought I would never get to the airport on time.

senses.definition: to be fond of or in love with someone.
examples: John was stuck on Sally, but she didn’t know it.
He always is stuck on the wrong person.

senses.definition: to be locked into an idea, cause, or purpose.
examples: Mary is really stuck on the idea of going to France this spring.
You’ve proposed a good plan, Jane, but you’re stuck on it. We may have to make some changes.

senses.definition: burdened with someone or something; left having to care for someone or something.
examples: Please don’t leave me stuck with your aunt. She talks too much.
My roommate quit school and left me stuck with the telephone bill.

senses.definition: nonsense.
examples: Come on! Don’t give me all that stuff and nonsense!
I don’t understand this book. It’s all stuff and nonsense as far as I am concerned.

senses.definition: to put fraudulent ballots into a ballot box; to cheat in counting the votes in an election.
examples: The election judge was caught stuffing the ballot box in the election yesterday.
Election officials are supposed to guard against stuffing the ballot box.

senses.definition: to find someone or something, usually by accident.
examples: I stumbled across an interesting book yesterday when I was shopping.
Guess who I stumbled into at the library yesterday?
I stumbled on a real bargain at the bookstore last week.

senses.definition: to bump into someone or something accidentally.
examples: I stumbled into John, and I apologized. It was my fault.
I stumbled into a post and hurt my arm.

senses.definition: to enter something or a place by stumbling.
examples: I tripped on the curb and stumbled into the car.
I stumbled into the house, exhausted and in need of a cool drink.

senses.definition: to trip over someone or something.
examples: There were three of us sleeping in the small tent. Each of us would stumble on the others whenever we went out or came in.
I stumbled on the curb and twisted my ankle.

senses.definition: something that prevents or obstructs progress.
examples: We’d like to buy that house, but the high price is the stumbling block.
Jim’s age is a stumbling block to getting another job. He’s over 60.

senses.definition: likely to have something, such as a physical disorder.
examples: The sick man was subject to dizzy spells.
I am subject to frequent headaches.

senses.definition: tentative, depending on something; vulnerable to something.
examples: I have made all the necessary plans, subject to your approval, of course.
My remarks are, of course, subject to your criticisms.

senses.definition: to have a standing order for a magazine or something similar.
examples: I usually buy my monthly magazines at the newsstand. I don’t subscribe to them.
I subscribe to all the magazines I read because it’s nice to have them delivered by mail.

senses.definition: someone or something whose name has been forgotten or should not be said.
examples: Mary said that such and such was coming to her party, but I forgot their names.
If you walk into a store and ask for such and such and they don’t have it, you go to a different store.

senses.definition: of a particular kind; of the sort that is; like.
examples: Where can I get a haircut such as yours?
I’d like to buy a vase such as the one in your display case.

senses.definition: for example.
examples: Bill enjoys many kinds of fruit, such as apples, pears, and plums.
Mary has many hobbies, such as swimming, bowling, and running.

senses.definition: in the imperfect state that one sees it; in the less-than-perfect condition in which one finds it.
examples: This is where I live. This is my glorious home—such as it is.
I’ve worked for days on this report, and I’ve done the best that I can do. It’s my supreme effort—such as it is.

senses.definition: That is the way things happen, even it isn’t the way I want it to be!
examples: Oh, well. Everything can’t be perfect. Such is life!
So I failed my test. Such is life! I can take it again some time.

senses.definition: to deceive someone.
senses.notes: The expression with suck is slang.
examples: I try to shop carefully so that no one can take me in.
I think that someone sucked in both of them. I don’t know why they bought this car.

senses.definition: reminiscent of something; seeming to suggest something.
examples: Bill’s homemade soup is suggestive of his mother’s.
The new movie was suggestive of an old one I had seen on TV.

senses.definition: to do something one’s own way; to do something to please oneself.
examples: If he doesn’t want to do it my way, he can suit himself.
Take either of the books that you like. Suit yourself. I’ll read the other one.

senses.definition: to be very appropriate for someone.
examples: This kind of job suits me to a T.
This is Sally’s kind of house. It fits her to a T.

senses.definition: a summary; the gist.
examples: Can you quickly tell me the sum and substance of your proposal?
In trying to explain the sum and substance of the essay, Thomas failed to mention the middle name of the hero.

senses.definition: one’s best clothes.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also in one’s Sunday best.
examples: John was all dressed up in his Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes.
I hate to be wearing my Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes when everyone else is casually dressed.

senses.definition: the availability of things or people as compared to the need to utilize the things or people; the availability of goods compared to the number of willing customers for the goods.
examples: Sometimes you can find what you want by shopping around and other times almost no store carries the items you are looking for. It depends entirely on supply and demand.

Sometimes customers ask for things we do not carry in stock and other times we have things in abundance that no one wants to buy. Whether or not we can make money off of a product depends entirely on supply and demand.

senses.definition: expected or intended to do something; obliged or allowed to do something.
examples: You’re supposed to say “excuse me” when you burp.
Mom says you’re supposed to come inside for dinner now.

senses.definition: fish and beef; lobster and beef.
senses.notes: A type of meal incorporating both expensive seafood and an expensive cut of beef. Refers to the sea and to the pasture.
examples: Walter ordered the surf and turf, but Alice ordered only a tiny salad.
No surf and turf for me. I want fish and fish alone.

senses.definition: the idea that the most able or fit will survive (while the less able and less fit will perish).
senses.notes: This is used literally as a part of the theory of evolution.
examples: In college, it’s the survival of the fittest. You have to keep working in order to survive and graduate.
I don’t give my houseplants very good care, but the ones I have are really flourishing. It’s the survival of the fittest, I guess.

senses.definition: easily persuaded; easily influenced.
examples: The students were susceptible to the allure of drugs.
The young revolutionaries were susceptible to propaganda.

senses.definition: likely to contract a sickness; likely to become sick.
examples: People with AIDS are susceptible to pneumonia.
Infants and the elderly are more susceptible to illness than other people.

senses.definition: to forget one’s pride and accept something humiliating.
examples: I had to swallow my pride and admit that I was wrong.
When you’re a student, you find yourself swallowing your pride quite often.

headword: swallow something, hook, line, and sinker

senses.definition: to believe something completely.
senses.notes: Slang. These terms refer to fishing and fooling a fish into being caught.
examples: I made up a story about why I was so late. The boss swallowed it, hook, line, and sinker.
I feel like a fool. I swallowed it, hook, line, and sinker.

senses.definition: to take an oath on someone or something.
examples: My uncle is sort of old-fashioned. He makes promises by swearing by his “sainted mother.”
He sometimes swears by his foot!

senses.definition: to have complete faith and confidence in someone or something.
examples: I’m willing to swear by John. He’s completely dependable.
This is an excellent brand of detergent. My sister swears by it.

headword: swear on a stack of Bibles

senses.definition: to state something very earnestly, pledging to tell the truth.
senses.notes: Stack of Bibles refers to swearing to tell the truth in court by placing one’s hand on a Bible.
examples: I swear on a stack of Bibles that I am telling the truth.
Of course, I’m telling the truth. I swear on my mother’s grave!

senses.definition: to be very anxious and tense.
examples: What a terrible test! I was really sweating blood at the last.
Bob is such a bad driver. I sweat blood every time I ride with him.

senses.definition: to endure or wait for something that causes tension or boredom.
examples: I had to wait for her in the reception area. It was a long wait, but I managed to sweat it out.
I took the test and then spent a week sweating out the results.

senses.definition: to knock someone down.
examples: The wind swept me off my feet.
Bill punched Bob playfully, and knocked him off his feet.

senses.definition: to overwhelm someone (figuratively).
examples: Mary is madly in love with Bill. He swept her off her feet.
The news was so exciting that it knocked me off my feet.

senses.definition: to move or leave in a flamboyant or theatrical way.
examples: The insulted customer swept out of the store.
The celebrity rose from his table and swept out of the restaurant.

senses.definition: to try to hide something unpleasant, shameful, etc., from the attention of others.
examples: The boss said he couldn’t sweep the theft under the carpet, that he’d have to call in the police.
