Roger had a tendency to sweep all the problems under the rug.

senses.definition: pleasing and quiet.
examples: Play me something that is sweet and low.
I like dance music that is sweet and low—not any of this rowdy, violent stuff.

senses.definition: a combination of fruity sweet and sour, but not necessarily salty, flavors.
senses.notes: Often refers to certain Chinese-American foods.
examples: I prefer sweet and sour pork to anything else on the menu.
Alice does not care for sweet and sour dishes, but she will usually eat whatever we serve her.

senses.definition: affectionate but unimportant or meaningless words spoken to a loved one.
examples: Jack was whispering sweet nothings in Joan’s ear when they were dancing.
The two lovers sat in the cinema exchanging sweet nothings.

senses.definition: fond of someone.
examples: Tom is sweet on Mary. He may ask her to marry him.
Mary’s sweet on him, too.

senses.definition: to talk convincingly to someone with much flattery.
examples: I didn’t want to help her, but she sweet-talked me into it.
He sweet-talked her for a while, and she finally agreed to go to the dance with him.

senses.definition: fast and certain.
senses.notes: As with the flight of a well-aimed arrow.
examples: The response of the governor to the criticism by the opposing party was swift and sure.
The boxer’s punch was swift and sure and resulted in a quick knockout and a very short match.

senses.definition: to do the opposite of everyone else; to go against the trend.
examples: Bob tends to do what everybody else does. He isn’t likely to swim against the tide.
Mary always swims against the current. She’s a very contrary person.

senses.definition: to make something happen.
examples: I hope I can swing a deal that will make us all a lot of money.
We all hope you can swing it.

senses.definition: to postpone the discussion of something during a meeting.
examples: Mary suggested that they should table the motion.
The motion for a new policy was tabled until the next meeting.

senses.definition: a situation where a small part is controlling the whole thing.
examples: John was just hired yesterday, and today he’s bossing everyone around. It’s a case of the tail wagging the dog.
Why is this small matter so important? Now we see the tail wagging the dog!

senses.definition: to defer to someone; to give control to someone.
examples: I decided to take a backseat to Mary and let her manage the project.
I had done the best I could, but it was time to take a backseat and let someone else run things.

senses.definition: to have large financial losses on an investment.
examples: I took a bath on all my oil stock. I should have sold it sooner.
I don’t mind losing a little money now and then, but I really took a bath this time.

senses.definition: to bow and receive credit for a good performance.
examples: At the end of the concerto, the pianist rose and took a bow.
The audience applauded wildly and demanded that the conductor come out and take a bow again.

senses.definition: to have a short rest period in one’s work.
examples: It’s ten o’clock—time to take a break.
I don’t usually take my break until 10:30.

senses.definition: to try something where failure or bad fortune is likely.
examples: Come on, take a chance. You may lose, but it’s worth trying.
I’m not reckless, but I don’t mind taking a risk now and then.

senses.definition: to enroll in a course and do the required work.
examples: I decided to take a course in history.
Bob drives into the city where he is taking a course.

senses.definition: to have a try at something; to give something a try.
examples: I don’t think I can convince her to leave, but I’ll take a crack at it.
Someone had to try to rescue the child. Bill said he’d take a crack at it.

senses.definition: to insult someone; to say something that will irritate a person.
examples: Jane took a dig at Bob for being late all the time.
Jane is always taking digs at Bob, but she never really means any harm.

headword: take a dim view of something

senses.definition: to regard something skeptically or pessimistically.
examples: My aunt takes a dim view of most things that young people do.
The manager took a dim view of my efforts on the project. I guess I didn’t try hard enough.

headword: take advantage of someone or something

senses.definition: to cheat or deceive someone.
examples: The store owner took advantage of me, and I’m angry.
You must be alert when you shop to make sure that someone doesn’t take advantage of you.

senses.definition: to utilize someone or something to one’s own benefit.
examples: Jane can be of great help to me, and I intend to take advantage of her.
Try to take advantage of every opportunity that comes your way.

headword: take a fancy to someone or something
altForms: take a liking to someone or something
take a shine to someone or something

senses.definition: to develop a fondness or a preference for someone or something.
examples: John began to take a fancy to Sally late last August at the picnic.
I’ve never taken a liking to cooked carrots.
I think my teacher has taken a shine to me.

senses.definition: to resemble a close, older relative.
examples: Don’t you think that Sally takes after her mother?
No, Sally takes after her Aunt Ann.

headword: take a gander (at someone or something)

senses.definition: to examine someone or something; to take a look (at someone or something).
examples: Hey, will you take a gander at that fancy car!
Drive it over here so I can take a gander.

senses.definition: to help plan or do something.
examples: I was glad to take a hand in planning the picnic.
Jane refused to take a hand in any of the work.

senses.definition: to be firm with someone; to have a firm policy for dealing with someone.
examples: The manager takes a hard line with people who show up late.
This is a serious matter. The police are likely to take a hard line.

senses.definition: to understand a hint and behave accordingly.
examples: I said I didn’t want to see you anymore. Can’t you take a hint? I don’t like you.
Sure I can take a hint, but I’d rather be told directly.

senses.definition: to get in control of someone or something.
examples: Take hold of yourself! Calm down and relax.
She took a few minutes to get hold of herself, and then she spoke.

senses.definition: to aim (something) at someone or something.
examples: The hunter took aim at the deer and pulled the trigger.
You must take aim carefully before you shoot.

senses.definition: to prepare to deal with someone or something.
examples: Now we have to take aim at the problem and try to get it solved.
He turned to me and took aim. I knew he was going to scold me severely.

headword: take a leaf out of someone’s book

senses.definition: to behave or to do something in the way that someone else would.
examples: When you act like that, you’re taking a leaf out of your sister’s book, and I don’t like it!
You had better do it your way. Don’t take a leaf out of my book. I don’t do it well.

headword: Take a long walk off a short pier.

senses.definition: Get out of here!; Go do something that will get you permanently out of here!
examples: Get out of here! Take a long walk off a short pier!
You bother me. Go play in the traffic.

headword: take a look (at someone or something)

senses.definition: to examine (briefly) someone or something.
senses.notes: Also with have, as in the example below.
examples: I asked the doctor to take a look at my ankle that has been hurting.
“So your ankle’s hurting,” said the doctor. “Let’s take a look.”
Please have a look at my car. It’s not running well.

senses.definition: to have a brief period of sleep.
examples: I took a short nap just after lunch.
The baby takes a long nap each afternoon.

senses.definition: to begin a new course or direction.
examples: When I received the telegram with the exciting news, my life took a new turn.
I began taking the medicine at noon, and by evening the disease had begun to take a new turn. I was getting better!

senses.definition: to develop an interest in something.
examples: I wish John would take an interest in his schoolwork.
We hoped you’d take an interest and join our club.

senses.definition: to make an oath; to swear to something.
examples: You must take an oath that you will never tell anyone about this.
When I was a witness in court, I had to take an oath that I would tell the truth.

headword: take a potshot at someone or something

senses.definition: to criticize someone or something; to include a criticism of someone or something in a broader or more general criticism.
examples: Daily, the media took potshots at the foolish politician.
John is taking potshots at me in his condemnation of office workers.

senses.definition: to leave (a place); to sneak out or run out (of a place).
examples: When the police came to the door, Tom decided it was time to take a powder. He left by the back door.
When the party got a little dull, Bill and his friend took a powder.

senses.definition: to strike or strike at someone with one’s fist.
examples: Mary got so angry at Bob that she took a punch at him.
She took a punch at him, but she missed.

senses.definition: to bathe.
examples: I take a shower every morning.
John takes a hot bath to relax.

senses.definition: to have a fall; to tip over.
senses.notes: Also with bad, nasty, quite, etc. Also with have.
examples: Ann tripped on the curb and took a nasty spill.
John had quite a spill when he fell off his bicycle.

headword: take a stand (against someone or something)

senses.definition: to take a position in opposition to someone or something; to oppose or resist someone or something.
examples: The treasurer was forced to take a stand against the board because of its wasteful spending.
The treasurer took a stand, and others agreed.

senses.definition: the damage or wear that is caused by using something or by hard living.
examples: Years of sunbathing took a toll on Mary’s skin.
Drug abuse takes a heavy toll on the lives of people.

senses.definition: to make a record of persons attending something.
examples: The teacher took attendance before starting the class.
I will take attendance each day.

headword: take a turn for the better

senses.definition: to start to improve; to start to get well.
senses.notes: The opposite of the following entry.
examples: She was very sick for a month; then suddenly she took a turn for the better.
Things are taking a turn for the better at my store. I may make a profit this year.

headword: take a turn for the worse

senses.definition: to start to get worse.
senses.notes: The opposite of the previous entry.
examples: It appeared that she was going to get well; then, unfortunately, she took a turn for the worse.
My job was going quite well; then last week things took a turn for the worse.

senses.definition: to go somewhere for a vacation; to stop work to have a vacation.
examples: Sue took a vacation at the Grand Canyon last year.
I need to take a vacation and relax.

headword: take a whack at someone or something

senses.definition: to hit at someone; to hit someone.
senses.notes: [with someone] Slang. Whack is sometimes spelled wack. Also with have, as in the examples below.
examples: He took a whack at me, so I punched him.
Don’t try to take a whack at me again!
I’ll have a wack at you!

headword: take care of someone or something

senses.definition: to deal with someone or something; to handle or manage someone or something.
examples: Would you please take care of this little problem?
This is an easy thing to take care of. I will fix it immediately.

senses.definition: to provide care for someone or something.
examples: John and Mary took care of their aged grandmother.
Please take care of my plants while I am on vacation.

senses.definition: to tip someone.
examples: I took care of the doorman as we left.
Did you remember to take care of the waiter?

senses.definition: to kill or dispose of someone.
examples: Max said he was going to take care of Lefty once and for all.
The crime king ordered Max to take care of a certain private detective.

senses.definition: to take (over) control of someone or something.
examples: The president came in late and took charge of the meeting.
When the new manager took charge, things really began to happen.

senses.definition: to disagree with something (that someone has said).
examples: I take exception to your remarks, and I would like to discuss them with you.
I’m sorry you take exception. Let’s discuss the matter.

senses.definition: to take a five-minute rest period.
examples: Okay, everybody. Take five!
Hey, Bob. I’m tired. Can we take five?

senses.definition: to make a great effort to do something.
examples: Tom took pains to decorate the room exactly right.
We took pains to get there on time.

senses.definition: to be brave; to have courage.
examples: Take heart, John. Things could be worse!
I told her to take heart and try again next time.

senses.definition: to be cautious.
examples: Take heed, and don’t get involved with the wrong kind of people.
Just take heed, and you’ll be safe.

senses.definition: to make an inventory list.
examples: They are taking inventory in the warehouse, counting each item and writing the number on a list.
The hardware store closed once a year in order to take inventory.

senses.definition: to argue with someone; to dispute a point with someone.
examples: I hate to take issue with you on such a minor point, but I’m quite sure you’re wrong.
I don’t mind if you take issue, but I’m sure I’m right.

senses.definition: to start up a performance.
senses.notes: Also literal. Typically a public announcement of the beginning of a musical performance. Slang.
examples: And now, here is the band playing “Song of Songs.” Take it away!
Sally will now sing us a song. Take it away, Sally!

senses.definition: Good-bye and take care of yourself.
examples: Bye, Tom. Take it easy.
Take it easy. I’ll see you later.

headword: take it easy (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to be gentle (with someone or something).
senses.notes: See also go easy (on someone or something).
examples: Take it easy on Mary. She’s been sick.
Please take it easy on the furniture. It has to last us many years.
Take it easy! You will break the chair!

senses.definition: to use less of something (rather than more).
examples: Take it easy on the soup. There’s just enough for one serving for each person.
Please take it easy! There are hardly any left.

senses.definition: to experience and endure a direct blow or assault.
examples: The bad news was a real shock, and John took it on the chin.
The worst luck comes my way, and I always end up taking it on the chin.

senses.definition: to accept something (the way it is) or forget it.
examples: This is my last offer. Take it or leave it.
It’s not much, but it’s the only food we have. You can take it or leave it.

senses.definition: to move or go slowly.
examples: The road is rough, so take it slow.
This book is very hard to read, and I have to take it slow.

senses.definition: to carry a secret with one until one dies.
examples: I will never tell anyone. I’ll take your secret to my grave.
She took the answer to the mystery to her grave.

senses.definition: to be agreeable to something.
examples: My father doesn’t take kindly to anyone using his tools.
I hope they’ll take kindly to our request.

senses.definition: to become irrational.
examples: What are you doing? Have you taken leave of your senses?
What a terrible situation! It’s enough to make one take leave of one’s senses.

headword: take liberties with someone or something
altForms: make free with someone or something

senses.definition: to use or abuse someone or something.
examples: You are overly familiar with me, Mr. Jones. One might think you were taking liberties with me.
I don’t like it when you make free with my lawn mower. You should at least ask when you want to borrow it.

senses.definition: to pay no attention to something; not to believe or accept something.
examples: I take no stock in anything John has to say.
He doesn’t take stock in your opinions either.

senses.definition: to observe and remember something.
examples: Please take note of the point I’m about to make.
Here is something else of which you should take note.

senses.definition: to observe something.
examples: I didn’t take notice of when he came in.
They say he came in late, but I didn’t take notice.

senses.definition: to become resentful of someone or something.
examples: Bill took offense at Mary for her thoughtless remarks.
Almost everyone took offense at Bill’s new book.
I’m sorry you took offense. I meant no harm.

senses.definition: to begin serving as an elected or appointed official.
examples: When did the mayor take office?
All the elected officials took office just after the election.

senses.definition: to offer praise for someone’s good accomplishments.
senses.notes: Refers to taking off one’s hat to show deference to someone.
examples: I have to take off my hat to Mayor Johnson. She has done an excellent job.
Yes, we all ought to take off our hats. She is our best mayor ever.

senses.definition: to believe what someone says and act accordingly.
examples: She told me to go jump in the lake, and I took her at her word.
You shouldn’t take her at her word. She frequently says things she doesn’t really mean.

senses.definition: to use someone else’s behavior or reactions as a guide to one’s own.
senses.notes: From the theatrical cue as a signal to speak, etc.
examples: If you don’t know which spoons to use at the dinner, just take your cue from John.
The other children took their cue from Tommy and ignored the new boy.

senses.definition: to say good-bye to someone and leave.
examples: I took leave of the hostess at an early hour.
One by one, the guests took their leave.

senses.definition: to accept the punishment or the bad fortune that one deserves.
examples: I know I did wrong, and I know I have to take my medicine.
Billy knew he was going to get spanked, and he didn’t want to take his medicine.

senses.definition: to kill oneself; to commit suicide.
examples: Bob tried to take his own life, but he was stopped in time.
Later, he was sorry that he had tried to take his own life.

senses.definition: to get a loan of money, especially from a bank.
examples: Mary took out a loan to buy a car.
We will have to take out a loan to pay the bills this month.

senses.definition: to participate in something.
examples: They invited me to take part in their celebration.
I was quite pleased to take part.

senses.definition: to feel sorry for someone or something.
examples: We took pity on the hungry people and gave them some warm food.
She took pity on the little dog and brought it in to get warm.
Please take pity! Please help us!

senses.definition: to happen.
examples: When will this party take place?
It’s taking place right now.

senses.definition: to begin to take hold or have effect.
examples: Things will begin to change when my new policies take root.
My ideas began to take root and influence other people.

senses.definition: to begin to be organized and specific.
senses.notes: [for something, such as plans, writing, ideas, arguments, etc.]
examples: My plans are beginning to take shape.
As my manuscript took shape, I started showing it to publishers.

senses.definition: to become ill.
examples: I took sick with a bad cold last week.
I hope I don’t take ill before final exams.

senses.definition: to choose one side of an argument.
examples: They were arguing, but I didn’t want to take sides, so I left.
I don’t mind taking sides on important issues.

senses.definition: to beat someone up.
examples: Don’t talk to me that way, or I’ll take you apart.
He was so mad that I thought he was going to take apart all of us.

headword: take someone down a peg (or two)
altForms: take someone down a notch (or two)

senses.definition: to reprimand someone who is acting too arrogant.
examples: The teacher’s scolding took Bob down a notch or two.
He was so rude that someone was bound to take him down a peg or two.

senses.definition: to assume that someone is stupid.
examples: I wouldn’t do anything like that! Do you take me for an idiot?
I don’t take you for a fool. I think you’re very clever.

senses.definition: to trick or deceive someone.
examples: Old people are being taken for a ride by bogus workmen.
Whoever sold Tom that car took him for a ride. It needs a new engine.

headword: take someone or something at face value

senses.definition: to take someone or something by its outward appearance; to take someone or something as it first appears to be.
examples: Don’t just accept her offer at face value. Think of the implications.
Jane tends to take people at face value and so she is always getting hurt.

senses.definition: to remove someone or something.
examples: I don’t want any more soup. Please take it away.
Take away Bill and John. They are bothering me.

headword: take someone or something by storm

senses.definition: to overwhelm someone or something; to attract a great deal of attention from someone or something.
examples: Jane is madly in love with Tom. He took her by storm at the office party, and they’ve been together ever since.
The singer took the world of opera by storm with her performance in La Boheme.

headword: take someone or something for granted

senses.definition: to accept someone or something—without gratitude—as a matter of course.
examples: We tend to take a lot of things for granted.
Mrs. Franklin complained that Mr. Franklin takes her for granted.

headword: take someone or something into account

senses.definition: to remember to consider someone or something.
examples: I hope you’ll take Bill and Bob into account when you plan the party.
I’ll try to take into account all the things that are important in a situation like this.

senses.definition: to misunderstand someone or something.
examples: Please don’t take me wrong, but I believe that your socks don’t match.
You’ll probably take this wrong, but I have to say that I’ve never seen you looking better.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be out of breath due to a shock or hard exercise.
examples: Walking this fast takes my breath away.
Mary frightened me and took my breath away.

senses.definition: to overwhelm someone with beauty or grandeur.
examples: The magnificent painting took my breath away.
Ann looked so beautiful that she took my breath away.

senses.definition: to take a side in an argument; to support someone in an argument.
examples: My sister took my mother’s part in the family argument.
You are always taking the part of underdog!

senses.definition: to scold or reprimand someone.
examples: The teacher took John to task for his bad behavior.
I lost a big contract, and the boss took me to task in front of everyone.

senses.definition: to abuse or damage someone.
examples: There was a real rough guy there who threatened to take me to the cleaners if I didn’t cooperate.
The crook said he’d take anybody who interfered to the cleaners.

senses.definition: to take over and care for a person.
examples: John wasn’t doing well in geometry until the teacher took him under her wing.
I took the new workers under my wings, and they learned the job in no time.

senses.definition: to understand something as wrong or insulting.
senses.notes: Compare this with take someone or something wrong.
examples: Would you take it amiss if I told you I thought you look lovely?
Why would anyone take such a nice compliment amiss?
I was afraid you’d take it the wrong way.

senses.definition: to accept something exactly the way it appears to be.
examples: I don’t know whether I can take her story at face value, but I will assume that she is not lying.
The committee took the report at face value and approved the suggested changes.

senses.definition: to withdraw or cancel one’s statement.
examples: I heard what you said, and I’m very insulted. Please take it back.
Take back your words, or I’ll never speak to you again!

senses.definition: to accept something as natural or expected.
examples: The argument surprised him, but he took it in stride.
It was a very rude remark, but Mary took it in stride.

senses.definition: to endure something unpleasant without fighting back.
examples: He insulted me publicly. You don’t expect me to take that lying down, do you?
I’m not the kind of person who’ll take something like that lying down.

senses.definition: to accept or believe something on the basis of little or no evidence.
examples: Please try to believe what I’m telling you. Just take it on faith.
Surely you can’t expect me to take a story like that on faith.

senses.definition: to experience and endure a direct (figurative or literal) blow or assault.
examples: The bad news was a real shock, but John took it on the chin.
The worst luck comes my way, and I always end up taking it on the chin.

senses.definition: to interpret a remark as if it were mean or critical about oneself.
examples: Don’t take it personally, but you really need a haircut.
I want to tell you something, but please don’t take it personally.

senses.definition: to take something very seriously.
examples: John took the criticism to heart and made an honest effort to improve.
I know Bob said a lot of cruel things to you, but he was angry. You shouldn’t take those things to heart.

headword: take something with a pinch of salt
altForms: take something with a grain of salt

senses.definition: to listen to a story or an explanation with considerable doubt.
examples: You must take anything she says with a grain of salt. She doesn’t always tell the truth.
They took my explanation with a pinch of salt. I was sure they didn’t believe me.

senses.definition: to do what is necessary to prevent something.
examples: I took steps to prevent John from learning what we were talking about.
I have to keep John from knowing what I’ve been doing. I can prevent it if I take steps.

senses.definition: to make an appraisal of resources and potentialities.
examples: I spent some time yesterday taking stock of my good and bad qualities.
We all need to take stock now and then.

headword: take the bit in one’s teeth
altForms: take the bit between the teeth

senses.definition: to put oneself in charge.
examples: Someone needed to direct the project, so I took the bit in my teeth.
If you want to get something done, you’ve got to take the bit between your teeth and get to work.

headword: take the bitter with the sweet

senses.definition: to accept the bad things along with the good things.
examples: We all have disappointments. You have to learn to take the bitter with the sweet.
There are good days and bad days, but every day you take the bitter with the sweet. That’s life.

headword: take the bull by the horns
altForms: seize the bull by the horns

senses.definition: to meet a challenge directly.
examples: If we are going to solve this problem, someone is going to have to take the bull by the horns.
This threat isn’t going to go away by itself. We are going to seize the bull by the horns and settle this matter once and for all.

senses.definition: to win the prize; to be the best or the worst.
examples: Look at those fireworks. If they don’t take the cake, I don’t know what does.
Well, Jane, this dinner really takes the cake! It’s delicious.
Tom really messed it up. What he did really takes the cake.

senses.definition: to choose not to go to work for one day.
senses.notes: Compare this with get the day off.
examples: The sun was shining, and it was warm, so I took the day off and went fishing.
Jane wasn’t feeling well, so she took the day off.

senses.definition: to remove the essence, power, or “bite” of something.
examples: I had to tell her some very sad things, so I spoke slowly and softly to take the edge off the news.
I put sugar in my coffee to take the edge off.

senses.definition: to activate oneself to do something even if one has not been asked to do it.
senses.notes: See also make it one’s business to do something.
examples: The door hinges squeak because no one will take the initiative to oil them.
Sometimes, in order to get things done, you have to take the initiative.

headword: take the law into one’s own hands

senses.definition: to attempt to administer the law; to act as a judge and jury for someone who has done something wrong.
examples: Citizens don’t have the right to take the law into their own hands.
The shopkeeper took the law into his own hands when he tried to arrest the thief.

headword: take the liberty of doing something

senses.definition: to assume the right to do something.
examples: Since I knew you were arriving late, I took the liberty of securing a hotel room for you.
May I take the liberty of addressing you by your first name?

headword: take the rap (for someone or something)

senses.definition: to take the blame (for something) for someone else.
examples: I don’t want to take the rap for you.
John robbed the bank, but Tom took the rap for him.

senses.definition: to take the blame for (doing) something.
examples: I won’t take the rap for the crime. I wasn’t even in town.
Who’ll take the rap for it? Who did it?

senses.definition: to go to and sit in the witness chair in a courtroom.
examples: I was in court all day, waiting to take the stand.
The lawyer asked the witness to take the stand.

headword: take the starch out of someone

senses.definition: to make someone less arrogant or stiff.
examples: I told a joke that made Mr. Jones laugh very hard. It really took the starch out of him.
John is so arrogant. I’d really like to take the starch out of him!

senses.definition: to make someone tired and weak.
examples: This hot weather really takes the starch out of me.
What a long day! It sure took the starch out of me.

senses.definition: to make an effort to do something (that one might not otherwise do).
examples: I wish I had taken the trouble to study this matter more carefully.
I just didn’t have enough time to take the trouble.

headword: take the wind out of someone’s sails

senses.definition: to challenge someone’s boasting or arrogance.
examples: John was bragging about how much money he earned until he learned that most of us make more. That took the wind out of his sails.
Learning that one has been totally wrong about something can really take the wind out of one’s sails.

headword: take the words out of one’s mouth

senses.definition: to say what you were going to say.
senses.notes: [for someone else] Informal. Also with right, as in the example.
examples: John said exactly what I was going to say. He took the words out of my mouth.
I agree with you, and I wanted to say the same thing. You took the words right out of my mouth.

senses.definition: not to work for a period of time—a few minutes or a longer period.
senses.notes: Compare this with get time off.
examples: I had to take time off to go to the dentist.
Mary took time off to have a cup of coffee.

senses.definition: to undertake to do too much work or too many tasks.
examples: Don’t take too much on, or you won’t be able to do any of it well.
Ann tends to take on too much and get exhausted.

senses.definition: to run away.
examples: The little boy said hello and then took to his heels.
The man took to his heels to try to get to the bus stop before the bus left.

senses.definition: to do something, one (person) at a time (rather than everyone all at once).
examples: Please take turns at reading the book.
Everyone is taking turns looking at the picture.
It’s more orderly when everyone takes turns.

senses.definition: to feel that one has been insulted by something.
examples: The employee took umbrage at not getting a raise.
Mary took umbrage at the suggestion that she was being unreasonable.

senses.definition: to collect money for a specific project.
examples: We wanted to send Bill some flowers, so we took up a collection.
The office staff took up a collection to pay for the office party.

headword: take up arms (against someone or something)

senses.definition: to prepare to fight against someone or something.
examples: Everyone in the town took up arms against the enemy.
They were all so angry that the leader convinced them to take up arms.

senses.definition: to fill or occupy space.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples.
examples: The piano is taking up too much room in our living room.
John, you’re not being any help at all. You’re just taking up space.

senses.definition: to require or fill time.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the examples. Also without up.
examples: This project is taking up too much time.
This kind of thing always takes up time.

headword: take up where one left off

senses.definition: to start up again in the very place that one has stopped.
examples: I had to leave the room for a minute, but when I got back, I took up where I left off.
It’s time to stop for lunch. After lunch, we will take up where we left off.

senses.definition: surprised and confused.
examples: When Mary told me the news, I was taken aback for a moment.
When I told my parents I was married, they were completely taken aback.

senses.definition: appearing to be dead; assumed to be dead.
examples: I was so ill with the flu that I was almost taken for dead.
The accident victims were so seriously injured that they were taken for dead at first.

senses.definition: to talk very much and very rapidly.
examples: Billy didn’t talk until he was six, and then he started talking a blue streak.
I can’t understand anything Bob says. He talks a blue streak, and I can’t follow his thinking.

senses.definition: to respond (to a rebuke) rudely or impertinently.
examples: John got in trouble for talking back to the teacher.
A student never gains anything by talking back.

senses.definition: to brag or boast; to talk in an intimidating manner.
examples: John is always talking big, but he hasn’t really accomplished a lot in life.
She talks big, but she’s harmless.

senses.definition: to speak to someone in a patronizing manner; to speak to someone in the simplest way.
examples: The manager insulted everyone in the office by talking down to them.
Please don’t talk down to me. I can understand almost anything you have to say.

senses.definition: to talk in a confusing or roundabout manner.
examples: I couldn’t understand a thing he said. All he did was talk in circles.
We argued for a long time and finally decided that we were talking in circles.

senses.definition: someone or something who is the subject of a conversation somewhere, especially the town.
examples: The handsome new teacher was the talk of the town.
John’s new car is the talk of the office.

senses.definition: to talk about business matters at a social event (where business talk is out of place).
examples: All right, everyone, we’re not here to talk shop. Let’s have a good time.
Mary and Jane stood by the punch bowl, talking shop.

senses.definition: to win out over someone in an argument; to convince someone by arguing.
examples: She loves to argue. She takes pleasure in talking someone down.
She tried to talk me down, but I held my ground.

senses.definition: to convince someone to lower the price.
examples: She wanted $2,000 for the car, but I talked her down.
This is my final offer. Don’t try to talk me down.

senses.definition: to overcome someone’s objections to doing something; to convince someone to do something.
examples: They talked me into going to the meeting, even though I didn’t really have the time.
No one can talk me into doing something illegal.

senses.definition: to promote or speak in support of someone or something.
examples: I’ve been talking up the party all day, trying to get people to come.
The mayor is running for reelection, and everyone at city hall is talking her up.

senses.definition: to convince someone not to do something.
examples: I tried to talk her out of going, but she insisted.
Don’t try to talk me out of quitting school. My mind is made up.

senses.definition: to convince someone to give something up.
examples: This is my candy, and you can’t talk me out of it.
I tried to talk her out of her property, but she didn’t want to sell.

senses.definition: to speak too much.
examples: Why does John always talk his head off? Doesn’t he know he bores people?
She talks her head off and doesn’t seem to know what she’s saying.

senses.definition: to talk to and bore someone.
examples: John is very friendly, but watch out or he’ll talk your head off.
My uncle always talked my ear off whenever I went to visit him.

senses.definition: to discuss something.
examples: Come into my office so we can talk this over.
We talked over the plans for nearly an hour.

senses.definition: to talk nonsense; to brag and boast.
examples: John isn’t really as good as he says. He’s just talking through his hat.
Stop talking through your hat and start being sincere!

senses.definition: to talk business; to talk frankly.
examples: Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss. Let’s talk turkey.
John wanted to talk turkey, but Jane just wanted to joke around.

headword: talk until one is blue in the face

senses.definition: to talk until one is exhausted.
examples: I talked until I was blue in the face, but I couldn’t change her mind.
She had to talk until she was blue in the face in order to convince him.

senses.definition: tired of talking; unable to talk more.
senses.notes: Folksy. See also talk oneself out.
examples: I can’t go on. I’m all talked out.
She was talked out in the first hour of discussion.

senses.definition: to attempt to alter or change something; to meddle with or damage something.
examples: Someone has tampered with my door lock.
Please don’t tamper with my stereo.

senses.definition: to spank someone.
examples: Billy’s mother said she’d tan Billy’s hide if he ever did that again.
“I’ll tan your hide if you’re late!” said Tom’s father.

senses.definition: to stop doing something gradually.
examples: My doctor told me to taper off smoking cigarettes.
I have to taper off because I can’t stop all at once.

senses.definition: to chastise someone severely.
examples: They threatened to tar and feather me if I ever came back into their town.
I don’t believe that they’d really tar and feather me, but they could be very unpleasant.

senses.definition: sharing the same characteristic(s); having the same good or bad points as someone else.
examples: Jack and his brother are tarred with the same brush. They’re both crooks.
The Smith children are tarred with the same brush. They’re all lazy.

senses.definition: an experience; an example.
examples: Bill gave Sue a taste of her own rudeness.
My friend used a parachute and got a taste of what it’s like to be a bird.

senses.definition: spending freely and taxing heavily.
senses.notes: Refers to a legislative body that repeatedly passes expensive new laws and keeps raising taxes to pay for the cost.
examples: I hope that people do not elect another tax-and-spend Congress this time.
The only thing worse than a tax-and-spend legislature is one that spends and runs up a worsening deficit.

senses.definition: a fancy or fussy meeting or reception where refreshments, especially sweet and insubstantial refreshments, are served.
senses.notes: Alluding to a genteel appointment where tea and some light pastries are served.
examples: I don’t have time to spend the afternoon having tea and crumpets with the office staff. I have work to do!
Almost every one of my Sunday afternoons is taken up with tea and crumpets for this cause and tea and crumpets for that cause! My rest and relaxation is the only cause I am interested in this Sunday!

headword: teach one’s grandmother to suck eggs

senses.definition: to try to tell or show someone more knowledgeable or experienced than oneself how to do something.
examples: Don’t suggest showing Mary how to knit. It will be teaching your grandmother to suck eggs. She’s an expert.
Don’t teach your grandmother to suck eggs. Bob has been playing tennis for years.

senses.definition: to get even with someone for bad behavior.
examples: John tripped me, so I punched him. That ought to teach him a lesson.
That taught me a lesson. I won’t do it again.

senses.definition: the teacher’s favorite student.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: Sally is the teacher’s pet. She always gets special treatment.
The other students don’t like the teacher’s pet.

senses.definition: to join with someone.
examples: I teamed up with Jane to write the report.
I had never teamed up with anyone else before. I had always worked alone.

senses.definition: to criticize and scold someone.
examples: Tom tore into John and yelled at him for an hour.
Don’t tear into me like that. You have no right to speak to me that way.

senses.definition: to attack or fight with someone or something.
examples: The boxer tore into his opponent.
The lion tore into the herd of zebras.

senses.definition: to leave or depart in a great hurry.
examples: Well, excuse me. I have to tear off.
Bob tore off down the street, chasing the fire engine.

senses.definition: to be anxious, frustrated, or angry.
examples: I was so nervous, I was about to tear my hair.
I had better get home. My parents will be tearing their hair out.

senses.definition: to criticize or degrade someone or something.
examples: Tom is always tearing Jane down. I guess he doesn’t like her.
It’s not nice to tear down the people who work in your office.
Why are you always tearing my projects down?

senses.definition: to dismantle or destroy something.
examples: They plan to tear the old building down and build a new one there.
They’ll tear down the building in about two weeks.

senses.definition: to cause someone much grief.
examples: The news of Tom’s death really tore Bill up.
Bad news tears up some people. Other people can take it calmly.

senses.definition: to make someone angry.
examples: That kind of talk really tees me off!
Don’t let him tee you off. He doesn’t mean any harm.

senses.definition: difficulties and problems experienced in the early stages of a project, activity, etc.
examples: There have been a lot of teething troubles with the new computer system.
We have finally gotten over the teething troubles connected with the new building complex.

senses.definition: to indicate clearly what has happened.
examples: The upturned boat told its own tale. The fisherman had drowned.
The girl’s tearstained face told its own story.

senses.definition: I do not believe you (maybe the marines will).
examples: That’s silly. Tell it to the marines.
I don’t care how good you think your reason is. Tell it to the marines!

senses.definition: to tell (something) to someone directly.
examples: I’m sorry that Sally feels that way about me. I wish she had told me to my face.
I won’t tell Tom that you’re mad at him. You should tell him to his face.

senses.definition: to report someone’s bad behavior; to tattle on someone.
examples: If you do that again, I’ll tell on you!
Please don’t tell on me. I’m in enough trouble as it is.

senses.definition: to distinguish one person or a group of people from another person or group of people.
examples: Tom and John are brothers, and you can hardly tell them apart.
Our team is wearing red, and the other team is wearing orange. I can’t tell them apart.

headword: tell someone a thing or two
altForms: tell someone where to get off

senses.definition: to scold someone; to express one’s anger to someone; to tell someone off.
examples: Wait till I see Sally. I’ll tell her a thing or two!
She told me where to get off and then started in scolding Tom.

senses.definition: to scold someone; to attack someone verbally.
senses.notes: This has a sense of finality about it.
examples: I was so mad at Bob that I told him off.
By the end of the day, I had told off everyone else, too.

senses.definition: to tell secrets or spread rumors.
examples: I wish that John would keep quiet. He’s telling tales out of school again.
If you tell tales out of school a lot, people won’t know when to believe you.

senses.definition: to distinguish one thing or a group of things from another thing or group of things.
examples: This one is gold, and the others are brass. Can you tell them apart?
Without their labels, I can’t tell them apart.

senses.definition: to keep or report the correct time.
examples: This clock doesn’t tell time very accurately.
My watch stopped telling time, so I had to have it repaired.

senses.definition: to be able to read time from a clock or watch.
examples: Billy is only four. He can’t tell time yet.
They are teaching the children to tell time at school.

senses.definition: an uproar about practically nothing.
examples: This isn’t a serious problem—just a tempest in a teapot.
Even a tempest in a teapot can take a lot of time to get settled.

senses.definition: to be thankful for one’s luck.
examples: You can thank your lucky stars that I was there to help you.
I thank my lucky stars that I studied the right things for the test.

senses.definition: a sarcastic remark made when someone tells something that is unpleasant, overly personal, disgusting, or otherwise annoying.
examples: Thank you for sharing. I really needed to hear about your operation.
Thank you for sharing, Bob. I hope your parents’ divorce goes well.

senses.definition: grateful for any small benefits or advantages one has, especially in a generally difficult situation.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, or seem.
examples: We have very little money, but we must be thankful for small blessings. At least we have enough food.
Bob was badly injured in the accident, but at least he’s still alive. Let’s be thankful for small blessings.

senses.definition: owing to someone or something; because of someone or something.
senses.notes: This does not refer to gratitude.
examples: Thanks to the storm, we have no electricity.
Thanks to Mary, we have tickets to the game. She bought them early before they were sold out.

senses.definition: That is not a small amount of money.
examples: I paid forty dollars for it, and that ain’t hay!
Bob lost his wallet with $200 in it—and that ain’t hay.

senses.definition: That is the last thing that is needed to force me to take action!
examples: That does it! I’m mad and I’m going home!
Well, that tears it! I have never been so insulted!

senses.definition: The same is true for me.
examples: So you’re going to the football game? That makes two of us.
BILL: I just passed my biology test. BOB: That makes two of us!

senses.definition: That is worthless.
examples: Yuck! That sucks!
This meat loaf is terrible. It sucks.

senses.definition: That is settled.
examples: That takes care of that, and I’m glad it’s over.
I spent all morning dealing with this matter, and that takes care of that.

senses.definition: I don’t believe that the day will ever come (when something will happen).
examples: Do you really think that John will pass geometry? That’ll be the day.
John graduate? That’ll be the day!

headword: That’s about the size of it.

senses.definition: It is final and correct.
examples: MARY: Do you mean that you aren’t going? TOM: That’s about the size of it.
At the end of his speech Bob said, “That’s about the size of it.”

senses.definition: Someone will get no more chances to do things correctly.
examples: That’s all for you, Tom. I’ve had all I can take from you. One disappointment after another.
You’ve gone too far, Mary. That’s all for you. Good-bye!

senses.definition: That is all.
examples: At the end of his informal talk, Tom said, “That’s all she wrote.”
Sally looked at the empty catsup bottle and said, “That’s all she wrote.”

senses.definition: That does it!; That’s the last straw!
examples: That’s it! I’m leaving! I’ve had enough!
Ok. That’s it! I’m going to report you to human resources!

senses.definition: That is the answer!
examples: That’s it! You are right.
That’s it! You got the right answer.

senses.definition: It is permanently settled and need not be dealt with again.
examples: I said no, and that’s that.
You can’t come back. I told you to leave, and that’s that.

senses.definition: That is exactly what is needed.
examples: That’s the ticket, John. You’re doing it just the way it should be done.
That’s the ticket! I knew you could do it.

headword: That’s the way the ball bounces.
altForms: That’s the way the cookie crumbles.

senses.definition: That is too bad.; Those things happen.
examples: Sorry to hear about your problems. That’s the way the ball bounces.
John wrecked his car and then lost his job. That’s the way the cookie crumbles.

senses.definition: Those are words that will start a fight.
senses.notes: Folksy. Note that them is is permissible in this expression.
examples: Better not talk like that around here. Them’s fighting words.
Them’s fighting words, and you’d better be quiet unless you want trouble.

senses.definition: right then.
examples: I asked him right then and there exactly what he meant.
I decided to settle the matter then and there and not wait until Monday.

headword: There aren’t enough hours in the day.

senses.definition: There are too many things to do and not enough time.
examples: I am behind in all my work. There aren’t enough hours in the day!
We can’t handle all the problems that come our way. There aren’t enough hours in the day.

headword: There are plenty of other fish in the sea.

senses.definition: There are other choices.
senses.notes: Proverb. Used to refer to persons.
examples: When John broke up with Ann, I told her not to worry. There are plenty of other fish in the sea.
It’s too bad that your secretary quit, but there are plenty of other fish in the sea.

senses.definition: one is not permitted to do something.
examples: There is no arguing with Bill.
There is no cigarette smoking here.

headword: There will be the devil to pay.

senses.definition: There will be lots of trouble.
senses.notes: Informal. See also have the devil to pay.
examples: If you damage my car, there will be the devil to pay.
Bill broke a window, and now there will be the devil to pay.

headword: There’s more than one way to skin a cat.

senses.definition: There is more than one way to do something.
examples: If that way won’t work, try another way. There’s more than one way to skin a cat.
Don’t worry, I’ll figure out a way to get it done. There’s more than one way to skin a cat.

senses.definition: There is no explanation for people’s preferences.
examples: Look at that purple and orange car! There’s no accounting for taste.
Some people seemed to like the music, although I thought it was worse than noise. There’s no accounting for taste.

headword: They don’t make them like they used to.

senses.definition: goods are not as well made now as they were in the past.
senses.notes: Often used as a catch phrase. Them is often’em.
examples: Look at this flimsy door! They don’t make’em like they used to.
Why don’t cars last longer? They just don’t make’em like they used to.

senses.definition: in large numbers or amounts and at a rapid rate.
examples: The enemy soldiers came thick and fast.
New problems seem to come thick and fast.

senses.definition: not easily upset or hurt; insensitive.
senses.notes: Also literal. The opposite of thin-skinned.
examples: Tom won’t worry about your insults. He’s completely thick-skinned.
Jane’s so thick-skinned she didn’t realize Fred was being rude to her.

senses.definition: balding.
examples: James is wearing a hat because he’s getting thin on top.
Father got a little thin on top as he got older.

senses.definition: easily upset or hurt; sensitive.
senses.notes: Also literal. The opposite of thick-skinned.
examples: You’ll have to handle Mary’s mother carefully. She’s very thin-skinned.
Jane weeps easily when people tease her. She’s too thin-skinned.

senses.definition: Conditions are looking better.
examples: Since I got a salary increase, things are looking up.
Things are looking up at school. I’m doing better in all my classes.

senses.definition: to remember and think about someone or something in one’s past.
examples: When I think back on Sally and the good times we had together, I get very sad.
I like to think back on my childhood and try to remember what it was like.

senses.definition: to reconsider something; to think again and decide not to do something.
examples: Jack was going to escape, but he thought better of it.
Jill had planned to resign, but thought better of it.

senses.definition: to think in traditional fashion, bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: As if thinking or creativity were confined or limited by a figurative box. See also inside the box. Compare this with think outside the box.
examples: You won’t come up with good ideas if you think only inside the box.
You guys only think inside the box and will never find a better solution.

headword: think little of someone or something
altForms: think nothing of someone or something

senses.definition: to have a low opinion of someone or something.
examples: Most experts think little of Jane’s theory.
People may think nothing of it now, but in a few years everyone will praise it.
The critics thought little of her latest book.

senses.definition: to think, reason, and plan while one is talking.
examples: If you want to be a successful teacher, you must be able to think on your feet.
I have to write out everything I’m going to say, because I can’t think on my feet too well.

senses.definition: to say one’s thoughts aloud.
examples: Excuse me. I didn’t really mean to say that. I was just thinking out loud.
Mr. Johnson didn’t prepare a speech. He just stood there and thought out loud. It was a terrible presentation.

senses.definition: to think freely, not bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: As if thinking or creativity were confined in or limited by a figurative box. See also outside the box. Compare this with think inside the box.
examples: You won’t come up with good ideas until you think outside the box.
Let’s think outside the box for a minute and try to find a better solution.

headword: think someone or something fit for something

senses.definition: to believe that someone or something is suitable for something.
examples: I don’t think John fit for the job.
Do you think this car fit for a long trip?

senses.definition: to contrive or invent something.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll find a way to do it. I can think something up in time to get it done.
John thought up a way to solve our problem.

headword: think the world of someone or something

senses.definition: to be very fond of someone or something.
examples: Mary thinks the world of her little sister.
The old lady thinks the world of her cats.

senses.definition: to consider carefully whether one should do something; to be cautious about doing something.
examples: You should think twice before quitting your job.
That’s a serious decision, and you should certainly think twice.

senses.definition: thinking traditionally, bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: Compare this with thinking outside the box.
examples: Thinking inside the box will seldom produce any creative solution for a serious problem.
Thinking inside the box is what got us into this mess in the first place.

senses.definition: thinking freely, not being bound by old, nonfunctional, or limiting structures, rules, or practices.
senses.notes: Compare this with thinking inside the box.
examples: Thinking outside the box will often produce some creative solutions to a complex problem.
Thinking outside the box is a popular way to encourage creative solutions, or it can waste a lot of valuable time.

senses.definition: a craving or desire for something.
examples: The tyrant had an intense thirst for power.
The actor’s thirst for fame caused him to become unscrupulous.

senses.definition: craving or desiring something.
examples: The students were thirsty for knowledge.
That evil tyrant is thirsty for power.

senses.definition: there and everywhere.
senses.notes: Archaic. See also hither, thither, and yon.
examples: I sent my résumé thither and yon, but no one responded.
The children are all scattered thither and yon, and it is difficult for them to get home for the holidays.

senses.definition: a constant bother or annoyance to someone.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: This problem is a thorn in my side. I wish I had a solution to it.
John was a thorn in my side for years before I finally got rid of him.

senses.definition: The days we have been referring to were the greatest of times.
examples: Ah, yes. The eighties. Those were the days!
Those were the days. Back when people knew right from wrong.

senses.definition: to discuss something thoroughly and solve any problems.
examples: The committee took hours to thrash the whole matter out.
Fred and Anne thrashed out the reasons for their constant disagreements.

senses.definition: to make a path for oneself through a crowded area; to make one’s way through a crowded area.
examples: The spy threaded his way through the crowd.
The joggers threaded through the shoppers on the sidewalks.

senses.definition: drunk.
senses.notes: These sheets are the ropes on a sailing vessel.
examples: I think that guy is three sheets to the wind. He can hardly stand up.
Bob and Bill are three sheets to the wind. You know, drunk.

senses.definition: to please or excite someone very much.
examples: John sent flowers to Ann and thrilled her to pieces.
Your wonderful comments thrilled me to death.

senses.definition: very excited; very pleased.
examples: She was thrilled to death to get the flowers.
I’m just thrilled to pieces to have you visit me.

senses.definition: thoroughly; completely.
examples: I’ve studied this report through and through trying to find the facts you’ve mentioned.
I was angry through and through, and I had to sit and recover before I could talk to anyone.

senses.definition: through all sorts of severe difficulties.
examples: I came through hell and high water to get to this meeting on time. Why don’t you start on time?
You’ll have to go through hell and high water to accomplish your goal, but it’ll be worth it.

senses.definition: through good times and bad times.
examples: We’ve been together through thick and thin, and we won’t desert each other now.
Over the years, we went through thick and thin and enjoyed every minute of it.

senses.definition: to become very angry; to put on a display of anger.
examples: Sally threw a fit when I showed up without the things she asked me to buy.
My dad threw a fit when I got home three hours late.

headword: throw a monkey wrench into the works

senses.definition: to cause problems for someone’s plans.
examples: I don’t want to throw a monkey wrench into the works, but have you checked your plans with a lawyer?
When John suddenly refused to help us, he really threw a monkey wrench into the works.

senses.definition: to give or hold a party (for someone).
examples: Mary was leaving town, so we threw a party for her.
Fred is having a birthday. Do you know a place where we could throw a party?

senses.definition: to become very careless.
examples: Jane, who is usually cautious, threw caution to the wind and went windsurfing.
I don’t mind taking a little chance now and then, but I’m not the type of person who throws caution to the wind.

senses.definition: to challenge (someone) to an argument or to (figurative) combat.
examples: When Bob challenged my conclusions, he threw down the gauntlet. I was ready for an argument.
Frowning at Bob is the same as throwing down the gauntlet. He loves to get into a fight about something.

senses.definition: to waste additional money after wasting money once.
examples: I bought a used car and then had to spend $300 on repairs. That was throwing good money after bad.
The Browns are always throwing good money after bad. They bought an acre of land that turned out to be swamp, and then had to pay to have it filled in.

senses.definition: to quit (doing something).
examples: When John could stand no more of Mary’s bad temper, he threw in the towel and left.
Don’t give up now! It’s too soon to throw in the sponge.

senses.definition: to give oneself willingly to someone else for romance.
examples: I guess that Mary really likes John. She practically threw herself at him when he came into the room.
Everyone could see by the way Tom flung himself at Jane that he was going to ask her for a date.

senses.definition: to behave in a very humble and contrite manner.
senses.notes: Refers to bowing down humbly at someone’s feet.
examples: Do I have to throw myself at your feet in order to convince you that I’m sorry?
I love you sincerely, Jane. I’ll throw myself at your feet and await your command. I’m your slave!

headword: throw one’s hands up in despair

senses.definition: to give up; to raise one’s hands making a sign of giving up.
examples: John threw his hands up in despair because they wouldn’t let him see his brother in the hospital.
There was nothing I could do to help. I threw up my hands in despair and left.

headword: throw one’s hands up in horror

senses.definition: to be shocked; to raise one’s hands as if one had been frightened.
examples: When Bill heard the bad news, he threw his hands up in horror.
I could do no more. I had seen more than I could stand. I just threw up my hands in horror and screamed.

senses.definition: to project one’s voice so that it seems to be coming from some other place.
examples: The ventriloquist threw his voice.
Jane can throw her voice, so I thought she was standing behind me.

senses.definition: to attempt to boss people around; to give orders.
examples: The district manager came to our office and tried to throw his weight around, but no one paid any attention to him.
Don’t try to throw your weight around in this office. We know who our boss is.

senses.definition: to confuse someone slightly.
senses.notes: See also throw someone for a loop.
examples: You threw me for a minute when you asked for my identification. I thought you recognized me.
The question the teacher asked was so hard that it threw me, and I became very nervous.

senses.definition: to pitch a curve ball to someone in baseball.
examples: The pitcher threw John a curve, and John swung wildly against thin air.
During that game, the pitcher threw everyone a curve at least once.

senses.definition: to confuse someone by doing something unexpected.
examples: When you said “house” you threw me a curve. The password was supposed to be “home.”
John threw me a curve when we were making our presentation, and I forgot my speech.

senses.definition: to confuse or shock someone.
senses.notes: Informal. This is more severe and upsetting than throw someone a curve or throw someone.
examples: When Bill heard the news, it threw him for a loop.
The manager knocked Bob for a loop by firing him on the spot.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be uncertain or confused.
examples: The stress of being in front of so many people threw Ann for a loss. She forgot her speech.
It was a difficult problem. I was thrown for a loss for an answer.

senses.definition: to cause one to lose one’s place in the sequence of things.
examples: The interruption threw me off the track for a moment, but I soon got started again with my presentation.
Don’t let little things throw you off the track. Concentrate on what you’re doing.

senses.definition: to cause someone to lose the trail (when following someone or something).
examples: The raccoon threw us off the track by running through the creek.
The robber threw the police off the trail by leaving town.

senses.definition: to confuse someone; to mislead someone.
examples: The interruption threw me off, and I lost my place in the speech.
Little noises throw me off. Please try to be quiet.
Your comment threw me off.

senses.definition: to resist or recover from a disease.
examples: It was a bad cold, but I managed to throw it off in a few days.
I can’t seem to throw off my cold. I’ve had it for weeks.

senses.definition: to emit or give off an odor.
examples: The small animal threw a strong odor off.
The flowers threw off a heavy perfume.

senses.definition: to force a person to leave a place or an organization.
examples: John behaved so badly that they threw him out of the party.
I was very loud, but they didn’t throw me out.
They threw Toni out of the club because she was so unpleasant.

senses.definition: to end a romance with someone.
examples: Jane threw Bill over. I think she met someone she likes better.
Bill was about ready to throw her over, so it’s just as well.

senses.definition: to impress people by saying you know a famous or influential person.
examples: You won’t get anywhere around here by throwing the mayor’s name around.
When you get to the meeting, just throw my name around a bit, and people will pay attention to you.

senses.definition: to (figuratively) sacrifice someone.
examples: The press was demanding an explanation, so the mayor blamed the mess on John and threw him to the wolves.
I wouldn’t let them throw me to the wolves! I did nothing wrong, and I won’t take the blame for their errors.

senses.definition: to include something in a deal.
examples: To encourage me to buy a new car, the car dealer threw a free radio into the bargain.
If you purchase three pounds of chocolates, I’ll throw one pound of salted nuts into the bargain.

senses.definition: to assemble or arrange something in haste.
examples: Don’t just slap something together! Use care and do it right.
You assembled this device very badly. It seems that you just slapped it together.
John went into the kitchen to throw together something for dinner.

senses.definition: to vomit something.
examples: The meat was bad, and I threw it up.
I hate to throw up.
Billy threw up his dinner.

senses.definition: to mention a shortcoming to someone repeatedly.
examples: I know I’m thoughtless. Why do you keep throwing it up to me?
Bill was always throwing Jane’s faults up to her.

headword: throw the baby out with the bath(water)

senses.definition: to dispose of the good while eagerly trying to get rid of the bad.
examples: In her haste to talk down the idea containing a few disagreeable points, she has thrown the baby out with the bathwater.
Hasty action will result in throwing out the baby with the bath.

senses.definition: to charge someone with, or convict someone of, as many crimes as is possible.
examples: I made the police officer angry, so he took me to the station and threw the book at me.
The judge threatened to throw the book at me if I didn’t stop insulting the police officer.

senses.definition: to enter into verbal combat [with someone]; to compete actively [with someone].
senses.notes: Refers to movements in the sport of fencing.
examples: I spent the entire afternoon thrusting and parrying with a committee of so-called experts in the field of insurance.
I do not intend to stand here and thrust and parry with you over a simple matter like this. Let’s get someone else’s opinion.

senses.definition: to get a ride from a passing motorist; to make a sign with one’s thumb that indicates to passing drivers that one is begging for a ride.
examples: My car broke down on the highway, and I had to thumb a ride to get back to town.
Sometimes it’s dangerous to hitch a ride with a stranger.

headword: thumb one’s nose at someone or something

senses.definition: to (figuratively or literally) make a rude gesture of disgust with one’s thumb and nose at someone or something.
examples: The tramp thumbed his nose at the lady and walked away.
You can’t just thumb your nose at people who give you trouble. You’ve got to learn to get along.

senses.definition: to look through a book, magazine, or newspaper, without reading it carefully.
examples: I’ve only thumbed through this book, but it looks very interesting.
I leafed through a magazine while waiting to see the doctor.

senses.definition: a short or small picture or description.
examples: The manager gave a thumbnail sketch of her plans.
The student wrote a thumbnail sketch of his project.

headword: thumbs down on someone or something

senses.definition: opposed to someone or something.
senses.notes: See also turn thumbs down (on someone or something).
examples: Bob is thumbs down on hiring anyone else.
I had hoped that she’d agree with our plan, but she’s thumbs down on it.

headword: thumbs up on someone or something

senses.definition: in favor of someone or something.
senses.notes: See also turn thumbs up (on someone or something).
examples: Bob is thumbs up on hiring Claude.
I never hoped she’d agree with our plan, but she’s totally thumbs up on it.

senses.definition: to please or entertain someone very much.
examples: Bill told a joke that really tickled us all pink.
I know that these flowers will tickle her to death.

senses.definition: to interest someone; to make someone curious.
examples: I have an interesting problem here that I think will tickle your fancy.
This doesn’t tickle my fancy at all. This is dull and boring.

senses.definition: very much pleased or entertained.
examples: I was tickled to death to have you visit us.
We were tickled pink when your flowers arrived.

senses.definition: to last until someone can get some more.
examples: I don’t get paid until next Wednesday. Could you lend me thirty dollars to tide me over?
Could I borrow some coffee to tide me over until I can get to the store tomorrow?

senses.definition: to connect to something.
examples: I’m trying to get my home computer to tie in with the big one at the university.
Could I tie into your water line while I’m waiting for mine to be repaired?
What you just told me ties into John’s version of the event.

senses.definition: to restrict or encumber someone.
examples: I’d like to go fishing every weekend, but my family ties me down.
I don’t want to tie you down, but you do have responsibilities here at home.

senses.definition: to keep someone busy or occupied.
examples: Sorry, this matter will tie me up for about an hour.
The same matter will tie up almost everyone in the office.

senses.definition: to conclude and finalize something.
examples: Let’s try to tie up this deal by Thursday.
We’ll manage to tie our business up by Wednesday at the latest.

senses.definition: to prevent someone from doing something.
senses.notes: Also literal. See also have one’s hands tied.
examples: I’d like to help you, but my boss has tied my hands.
Please don’t tie my hands with unnecessary restrictions. I’d like the freedom to do whatever is necessary.

senses.definition: to become anxious or upset.
examples: John tied himself in knots worrying about his wife during the operation.
This waiting and worrying really ties me up in knots.

senses.definition: to get married.
examples: Well, I hear that you and John are going to tie the knot.
My parents tied the knot almost forty years ago.

senses.definition: to cause road traffic to stop.
examples: If you tie traffic up for too long, you’ll get a traffic ticket.
Please don’t stop on the roadway. It’ll tie up traffic.

senses.definition: restricted by responsibilities.
examples: I love my home, but sometimes I don’t like being tied down.
I don’t feel tied down, even though I have a lot of responsibility.

headword: tied to one’s mother’s apron strings

senses.definition: dominated by one’s mother; dependent on one’s mother.
examples: Tom is still tied to his mother’s apron strings.
Isn’t he a little old to be tied to his mother’s apron strings?

senses.definition: busy.
examples: How long will you be tied up?
I will be tied up in a meeting for an hour.

senses.definition: to manage to spend less money; to use less of something.
examples: Things are beginning to cost more and more. It looks as if we’ll all have to tighten our belts.
Times are hard, and prices are high. I can tighten my belt for only so long.

senses.definition: very stingy with money.
examples: The manager is very closefisted with expenditures.
My parents are very tightfisted with money.

senses.definition: to fight battles with imaginary enemies; to fight against unimportant enemies or issues.
senses.notes: As with the fictional character, Don Quixote, who attacked windmills.
examples: Aren’t you too smart to go around tilting at windmills?
I’m not going to fight this issue. I’ve wasted too much of my life tilting at windmills.

senses.definition: repeatedly; over and over (again).
examples: You’ve made the same error time after time! Please try to be more careful!
I’ve told you time and again not to do that.
You keep saying the same thing over and over, time and time again. Stop it!
I have told you time and again: don’t put wet garbage in the trash can!

senses.definition: time passes very quickly.
examples: I didn’t really think it was so late when the party ended. Doesn’t time fly?
Time simply flew while the old friends exchanged news.

senses.definition: time is valuable, so don’t waste it.
examples: I can’t afford to spend a lot of time standing here talking. Time is money, you know!
People who keep saying that time is money may be working too hard.

senses.definition: Exactly the right time has come.
examples: I’ll tell her the good news when the time is ripe.
The time is ripe to ask the question again.

senses.definition: The allotted time has run out.
examples: You must stop now. Your time is up.
Time’s up! Turn in your tests whether you’re finished or not.

senses.definition: to find enough time to relax or behave normally.
examples: When things slow down around here, I’ll get time to catch my breath.
Sally was so busy she didn’t even have time to catch her breath.

senses.definition: there was a time when; at a time in the past.
examples: Time was when old people were taken care of at home.
Time was when people didn’t travel around so much.

senses.definition: Something will become known in the course of time.
examples: I don’t know if things will improve. Time will tell.
Who knows what the future will bring? Only time will tell.

senses.definition: to give someone a hint; to warn someone.
examples: I tipped John off that there would be a test in his algebra class.
I didn’t want to tip off everyone, so I only told John.

senses.definition: to weigh some amount.
examples: Tom tips the scales at nearly 200 pounds.
I’ll be glad when I tip the scales at a few pounds less.

senses.definition: a public display of [the human female] breasts and buttocks.
senses.notes: Refers to television, film, and stage performances in which women exhibit prominent and well-formed breasts and buttocks or in which these body parts are emphasized or made prominent. Slang. Use caution with the expression.
examples: We have a really fine choice on television tonight. There is brutal violence on channel 2, bloody horror on channel 5, and tits and ass on channel 10.
Without tits and ass, many Broadway musicals would flop.

senses.definition: mainly; largely.
examples: To a great extent, Mary is the cause of her own problems.
I’ve finished my work to a great extent. There is nothing important left to do.

senses.definition: toward and away from (something).
senses.notes: Compare this with back and forth.
examples: The puppy was very active— running to and fro—wagging its tail.
The lion in the cage moved to and fro, watching the people in front of the cage.

senses.definition: very much; very fast.
examples: The carpenter sawed and hammered to beat the band.
They baked cookies and pies to beat the band.

headword: to be on the safe side

senses.definition: to be safe; to be cautious; [to do something just] in case it is necessary; to be very well prepared.
examples: To be on the safe side, carry some extra money in your shoe.
I like to be on the safe side and stay in my hotel room at night.

senses.definition: to be cautious; to be careful; [to do something just] in case it is necessary; to be very well prepared.
examples: Just to be safe, you should take some clean water with you.
Other people like to drive over the speed limit, but I prefer to be safe.

senses.definition: in addition; besides.
examples: For breakfast I had my usual two eggs and a slice of ham to boot.
When I left for school, my parents gave me an airplane ticket and fifty dollars to boot.

senses.definition: to count people.
examples: I’ll tell you how many people are here after I count heads.
Everyone is here. Let’s count heads so we can order hamburgers.

senses.definition: up to the present time.
examples: How much have you accomplished to date?
I’ve done everything I’m supposed to have done to date.

senses.definition: very much gone; gone to hell.
examples: All my hard work is to hell and gone.
When you see everything you’ve planned to hell and gone, you get kind of angry.

senses.definition: with no effect; unsuccessful.
examples: All of my efforts were to no avail.
Everything I did to help was of no avail. Nothing worked.

senses.definition: as much as one wants.
examples: John wanted a week’s vacation so he could go to the lake and fish to his heart’s content.
I just sat there, eating chocolate to my heart’s content.

senses.definition: to understate something; to say something politely.
senses.notes: Note the variation in the example below.
examples: She was angry at almost everyone—to put it mildly.
To say she was angry is putting it mildly.
To put it mildly, she was enraged.

headword: to say nothing of someone or something

senses.definition: not to even mention the importance of someone or something.
examples: John and Mary had to be taken care of, to say nothing of Bill, who would require even more attention.
I’m having enough difficulty painting the house, to say nothing of the garage that is very much in need of paint.

senses.definition: at the very least; without dwelling on the subject; to put it mildly.
examples: We were not at all pleased with her work—to say the least.
When they had an accident, they were upset to say the least.

senses.definition: to some degree; in some amount; partly.
examples: I’ve solved this problem to some extent.
I can help you understand this to some extent.

senses.definition: in a way that pleases someone.
examples: I hope I’ve done the work to your liking.
Sally didn’t find the meal to her liking and didn’t eat any of it.

senses.definition: in someone’s opinion.
examples: This isn’t satisfactory to my way of thinking.
To my way of thinking, this is the perfect kind of vacation.

headword: to the best of one’s ability

senses.definition: as well as one is able.
examples: I did the work to the best of my ability.
You should always work to the best of your ability.

headword: to the best of one’s knowledge

senses.definition: as far as one knows; from one’s knowledge.
examples: This is the true story to the best of my knowledge.
To the best of my knowledge, John is the only person who can answer that question.

senses.definition: to the very end.
senses.notes: Originally nautical. This originally had nothing to do with bitterness.
examples: I kept trying to the bitter end.
It took me a long time to get through school, but I worked hard at it all the way to the bitter end.

senses.definition: as the opposite of what has been stated; contrary to what has been stated.
senses.notes: Compare this with on the contrary.
examples: The brown horse didn’t beat the black horse. To the contrary, the black one won.
Among spiders, the male is not the larger one. To the contrary, the female is larger.

senses.definition: all the way through; basically and essentially.
senses.notes: Usually with some negative sense, such as evil, rotten, etc.
