examples: Bill said that John is evil to the core.
This organization is rotten to the core.

headword: to the ends of the earth

senses.definition: to the remotest and most inaccessible points on the earth.
examples: I’ll pursue him to the ends of the earth.
We’ve explored almost the whole world. We’ve traveled to the ends of the earth trying to learn about our world.

senses.definition: to the end; to the conclusion.
examples: All of us kept trying to the last.
It was a very boring play, but I sat through it to the last.

senses.definition: exactly as instructed; exactly as written.
examples: I didn’t make an error. I followed your instruction to the letter.
We didn’t prepare the recipe to the letter, but the cake still turned out very well.

senses.definition: to the maximum amount.
examples: Jane is a perfectionist and tries to be careful to the nth degree.
This scientific instrument is accurate to the nth degree.

headword: to the tune of some amount of money

senses.definition: a certain amount of money.
examples: My checking account is overdrawn to the tune of $340.
My wallet was stolen, and I’m short of money to the tune of seventy dollars.

headword: To the victors belong the spoils.
altForms: To the victor belongs the spoils.

senses.definition: The winners achieve power over people and property.
examples: The mayor took office and immediately fired many workers and hired new ones. Everyone said, “To the victors belong the spoils.”
The office of president includes the right to live in the White House and at Camp David. To the victors belong the spoils.

senses.definition: to the person to whom this applies.
senses.notes: A form of address used when you do not know the name of the person who handles the kind of business you are writing about.
examples: The letter started out, “To whom it may concern.”
When you don’t know who to write to, just say, “To whom it may concern.”

senses.definition: namely; that is; that is to say.
examples: The criminal was punished; to wit, he received a 20-year sentence.
Many students, to wit Mary, Bill, Sue, and Anne, complained about their teacher.

senses.definition: to do what one is expected to do; to follow the rules.
examples: You’ll get ahead, Sally. Don’t worry. Just toe the mark, and everything will be okay.
John finally got fired. He just couldn’t learn to toe the line.

senses.definition: moving back and forth on an issue, first deciding one way and then changing to another.
examples: The boss spent most of the afternoon toing and froing on the question of who was to handle the Wilson account.
I wish you would stop toing and froing and make up your mind.

senses.definition: to make something less extreme.
examples: That yellow is too bright. Please try to tone it down.
Can you tone down your remarks? They seem quite strong for this situation.

senses.definition: mockingly; insincere; joking.
examples: Ann made a tongue-in-cheek remark to John, and he got mad because he thought she was serious.
The play seemed very serious at first, but then everyone saw that it was tongue-in-cheek, and they began laughing.

senses.definition: too haughty for one’s status or age.
senses.notes: Also literal. Folksy or informal. Britches are trousers.
examples: Bill’s getting a little too big for his britches, and somebody’s going to straighten him out.
You’re too big for your britches, young man! You had better be more respectful.

senses.definition: to be dangerously close.
senses.notes: [for a misfortune or a threat] See also close to home.
examples: That car nearly hit me! That was too close for comfort.
When I was in the hospital, I nearly died from pneumonia. Believe me, that was too close for comfort.

senses.definition: almost unbelievable; so good as to be unbelievable.
examples: The news was too good to be true.
When I finally got a big raise, it was too good to be true.

headword: Too many cooks spoil the stew.
altForms: Too many cooks spoil the broth.

senses.definition: Too many people trying to manage something simply spoil it.
examples: Let’s decide who is in charge around here. Too many cooks spoil the stew.
Everyone is giving orders, but no one is following them! Too many cooks spoil the broth.

headword: too much of a good thing

senses.definition: more of a good thing than is good or useful.
examples: I usually take short vacations. I can’t stand too much of a good thing.
Too much of a good thing can make you sick, especially if the good thing is chocolate.

senses.definition: to boast or praise oneself.
examples: Tom is always tooting his own horn. Is he really as good as he says he is?
I find it hard to blow my own horn, but I manage.

senses.definition: to do or be better than someone or something.
examples: Ann has done very well, but I don’t think she can top Jane.
Do you think your car tops mine when it comes to gas mileage?

senses.definition: to add to the difficulty of something.
examples: Jane lost her job, and to top that off, she caught the flu.
I had a bad day, and to top it off, I have to go to a meeting tonight.

headword: torn between choosing something or something else

senses.definition: troubled by a choice or dilemma.
examples: Jane was torn between two bad choices.
We were torn between telling our boss the bad news or keeping it a secret.

senses.definition: to mix the green of a salad together with dressing.
examples: The chef tossed the salad.
I tossed the salad just before my guests arrived.

senses.definition: to vomit.
examples: Don’t run too fast after you eat or you’ll toss your cookies.
Oh, I feel terrible. I think I’m going to toss my cookies.

headword: toss one’s hat into the ring

senses.definition: to announce that one is running for an elective office.
examples: Jane wanted to run for treasurer, so she tossed her hat into the ring.
The mayor never tossed his hat into the ring. Instead he announced his retirement.

senses.definition: to throw something off (of oneself).
examples: Bob coughed so hard he shook his blanket off.
Tom tossed off his jacket and sat down to watch television.

senses.definition: to ignore or resist the bad effects of something.
examples: John insulted Bob, but Bob just tossed it off.
If I couldn’t shake off insults, I’d be miserable.

senses.definition: very uncertain or critical.
examples: Things were touch and go at the office until a new manager was hired.
Jane had a serious operation, and everything was touch and go for two days after her surgery.

senses.definition: to refer to a sensitive matter that will upset someone.
examples: I seem to have touched a sore spot. I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to upset you.
When you talk to him, avoid talking about money. It’s best not to touch a sore point if possible.

senses.definition: to talk to someone; to confer with someone.
examples: I need to touch base with John on this matter.
John and I touched base on this question yesterday, and we are in agreement.

senses.definition: to mention something; to talk about something briefly.
examples: In tomorrow’s lecture I’d like to touch on the matter of taxation.
The teacher only touched on the subject. There wasn’t time to do more than that.

senses.definition: to ask someone for a loan of something, usually a sum of money.
examples: Fred’s always trying to touch people for money.
Jack touched John for ten dollars.

senses.definition: to make someone very angry.
examples: Your rude comments touched Mary off. She’s very angry at you.
I didn’t mean to touch off anyone. I was only being honest.

senses.definition: to ignite something; to start something.
examples: A few sparks touched all the fireworks off at once.
The argument touched off a serious fight.

senses.definition: to repair a paint job on something.
examples: We don’t need to paint the whole room. We can just touch the walls up.
You should touch up scratches on your car as soon as they occur.

senses.definition: emotionally affected or moved by someone or something.
examples: Sally was very nice to me. I was very touched by her.
I was really touched by your kind letter.

senses.definition: crazy.
examples: Sometimes Bob acts like he’s touched in the head.
In fact, I thought he was touched.

senses.definition: a good presentation or performance that is difficult to follow with one’s own performance.
examples: Bill’s speech was excellent. It was a tough act to follow, but my speech was good also.
In spite of the fact that I had a tough act to follow, I did my best.

senses.definition: a bit of bad fortune.
examples: I’m sorry to hear about your accident. Tough break.
John had a lot of tough breaks when he was a kid, but he’s doing okay now.

senses.definition: to endure a difficult situation.
examples: Geometry is very hard for John, but he managed to tough it out until the end of the year.
This was a very bad day at the office. A few times, I was afraid I wouldn’t be able to tough it out.

senses.definition: a difficult task to undertake.
examples: It was a tough row to hoe, but I finally got a college degree.
Getting the contract signed is going to be a tough row to hoe, but I’m sure I can do it.

senses.definition: the [poor] relations between a town and the university located within the town; the [poor] relations between university students and the nonstudents who live in a university town.
examples: There is another town-and-gown dispute in Adamsville over the amount the university costs the city for police services.
There was more town-and-gown strife reported at Larry’s Bar and Grill last Saturday night.

senses.definition: to tease someone; to deal lightly with someone’s emotions.
examples: Ann broke up with Tom because he was just toying with her. He was not serious at all.
Don’t toy with me! I won’t have it!

senses.definition: to play or fiddle with something.
examples: Stop toying with the radio, or you’ll break it.
John sat there toying with a pencil all through the meeting.

senses.definition: to use a fact or a situation to one’s advantage.
examples: Tom was able to trade on the fact that he had once been in the Army.
John traded on his poor eyesight to get a seat closer to the stage.

altForms: have one’s sights trained on something

senses.definition: to have something as a goal; to direct something or oneself toward a goal.
examples: You should train your sights on getting a promotion in the next year.
Lisa has her sights trained on a new car.

senses.definition: a miscarriage of justice; an act of the legal system that is an insult to the system of justice.
examples: The jury’s verdict was a travesty of justice.
The lawyer complained that the judge’s ruling was a travesty of justice.

senses.definition: trying repeatedly for success.
examples: I finally found the right key after lots of trial and error.
Sometimes trial and error is the only way to get something done.

senses.definition: problems and tests of one’s courage or perseverance.
examples: I suppose I have the normal trials and tribulations for a person of my background, but some days are just a little too much for me.
I promise not to tell you of the trials and tribulations of my day if you promise not to tell me yours!

senses.definition: Give me a treat of some kind or I will play a trick on you!
senses.notes: The formulaic expression said by children after they ring someone’s doorbell and the door is answered on Halloween. It is now understood to mean simply that the child is requesting a treat of some kind— candy, fruit, popcorn, etc.
examples: “Trick or treat!” cried Jimmy when the door opened.
Mr. Franklin opened the door to find four very small children dressed like flowers standing silently on his doorstep. After a moment, he said, “Isn’t anyone going to say, ‘Trick or treat’?”

senses.definition: to fool someone; to deceive someone; to cheat someone.
examples: The thief tricked John into giving him $10.
Mary tricked her friends into paying for her dinner.

senses.definition: tested by time and proven to be sound.
examples: I have a tried-and-true remedy for poison ivy.
All of her investment ideas are tried-and-true and you ought to be able to make money if you follow them.

senses.definition: to mention something regularly or habitually, without giving it much thought.
examples: Jack always trots the same excuses out for being late.
When James disagreed with Mary, she simply trotted out her same old political arguments.

senses.definition: Trouble is developing.
examples: Trouble’s brewing at the office. I have to get there early tomorrow.
There is trouble brewing in the government. The prime minister may resign.

senses.definition: to bother oneself to do something.
examples: He didn’t even trouble himself to turn off the light when he left.
No, thank you. I don’t need any help. Please don’t trouble yourself.

headword: trouble one’s head about someone or something

senses.definition: to worry about someone or something; to trouble oneself about someone or something that is none of one’s business.
senses.notes: Folksy. Usually in the negative. Also with pretty, as in the example. Usually in the negative, meaning “to mind one’s own business.”
examples: Now, now, don’t trouble your pretty head about all these things.
You needn’t trouble your head about Sally.

senses.definition: to ask someone to pass something or give something.
examples: Could I trouble you for the salt?
Could I trouble you for some advice?

senses.definition: to ask someone to do something.
examples: Could I trouble you to pass the salt?
Could I trouble you to give me some advice?

senses.definition: exactly as expected; following the usual pattern.
senses.notes: Often with running, as in the example.
examples: As usual, John is late. At least he’s true to form.
And true to form, Mary left before the meeting was adjourned.
This winter season is running true to form—miserable!

senses.definition: keeping one’s promise.
examples: True to his word, Tom showed up at exactly eight o’clock.
We’ll soon know if Jane is true to her word. We’ll see if she does what she promised.

senses.definition: false; fraudulently devised.
examples: They tried to have Tom arrested on a trumped-up charge.
Bob gave some trumped-up excuse for not being at the meeting.

senses.definition: eventually, the truth will become known; truth tends to become known, even when it is being concealed.
examples: The truth will out! Some day my name will be cleared.
We just found out about corruption in the mayor’s office. Like they say, “The truth will out.”

senses.definition: to take a try at something.
examples: Someday I’d like to try my hand at flying a plane.
Give me a chance. Let me try my hand!

senses.definition: to attempt to do something (where success requires luck).
examples: My great-grandfather came to California to try his luck at finding gold.
I went into a gambling casino to try my luck.

senses.definition: to test one’s fitness for a role in a play, a position on a sports team, etc.
examples: I sing pretty well, so I thought I’d try out for the chorus.
Hardly anyone else showed up to try out.

senses.definition: to try to do something one has recently become qualified to do.
senses.notes: Like a young bird uses its wings to try to fly.
examples: John just got his driver’s license and wants to borrow the car to try out his wings.
I learned to skin-dive, and I want to go to the seaside to try my wings.
She was eager to try out her wings.

senses.definition: to do something annoying that may cause someone to lose patience; to cause someone to be annoyed.
examples: Stop whistling. You’re trying my patience. Very soon I’m going to lose my temper.
Some students think it’s fun to try the teacher’s patience.

senses.definition: to test something on someone (to see how it works or if it is liked).
examples: I found a recipe for oyster stew and tried it out on my roommate.
I’m glad you didn’t try out that stuff on me!
I have a tremendous idea! Let me try it out on you.
I want to try out my plan on you. Please give me your honest opinion.

senses.definition: to eat something with hunger and enjoyment.
examples: The children really tucked into the ice cream.
Jean would like to have tucked into the chocolate cake, but she’s on a strict diet.

senses.definition: to ignore someone or something; to become unaware of someone or something.
examples: Sally annoys me sometimes, so I just tune her out.
Your radio doesn’t bother me. I just tune out the noise.

senses.definition: to set a radio or television control so as to receive something.
examples: Why don’t you try to tune the ball game in?
This is a cheap radio, and I can’t tune in distant stations.
Please try to tune in.

headword: turn a blind eye to someone or something

senses.definition: to ignore someone or something troublesome and pretend not to see it.
examples: The usher turned a blind eye to the little boy who sneaked into the theater.
How can you turn a blind eye to all those starving children?

headword: turn a deaf ear (to someone or something)

senses.definition: to ignore what someone requests; to ignore a cry for help.
examples: How can you just turn a deaf ear to their cries for food and shelter?
The government has turned a deaf ear.

senses.definition: to go to bed.
examples: It’s late. I think I’ll turn in.
We usually turn in at about midnight.

senses.definition: the end of one century and the beginning of another.
examples: It’s just a few years until the turn of the century.
People like to celebrate the turn of the century.

senses.definition: to turn in a very tight turn.
examples: This car handles very well. It can turn on a dime.
The speeding car turned on a dime and headed in the other direction.

headword: turn one’s back (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to abandon or ignore someone or something.
examples: Don’t turn your back on your old friends.
Bob has a tendency to turn his back on serious problems.
This matter needs your attention. Please don’t just turn your back.

headword: turn one’s nose up at someone or something

senses.definition: to sneer at someone or something; to reject someone or something.
examples: John turned his nose up at Ann, and that hurt her feelings.
I never turn up my nose at dessert, no matter what it is.

senses.definition: to begin to cry.
examples: Every time Billy got homesick, he turned on the waterworks.
Sally hurt her knee and turned on the waterworks for about twenty minutes.

senses.definition: to end satisfactorily.
senses.notes: Compare this with work out for the best.
examples: I hope everything turns out all right.
Oh, yes. It’ll all pan out.
Things usually work out, no matter how bad they seem.

senses.definition: to happen that; to end up that.
examples: After it was all over, it turned out that both of us were pleased with the bargain.
Have you heard how the game turned out?

senses.definition: to start or to rotate.
examples: My car engine was so cold that it wouldn’t even turn over.
The engine turned over a few times and then stopped for good.

senses.definition: to start again with the intention of doing better; to begin again, ignoring past errors.
senses.notes: Leaf is a page. This refers to starting a new page.
examples: Tom promised to turn over a new leaf and do better from now on.
After a minor accident, Sally decided to turn over a new leaf and drive more carefully.

senses.definition: to be shocked or horrified.
senses.notes: [for a dead person] Refers to something that would be so shocking to a person who is actually dead, that the dead person would quicken enough to turn over.
examples: If Beethoven heard Mary play one of his sonatas, he’d turn over in his grave.
If Aunt Jane knew what you were doing with her favorite chair, she would roll over in her grave.

senses.definition: to discourage or disgust someone.
examples: His manner really turns me off.
That man has a way of turning off everyone he comes in contact with.

senses.definition: to excite someone; to excite someone sexually.
examples: Sally said she preferred not to watch movies that attempted to turn people on.
The lecture was very good. It turned on the whole class.

senses.definition: to refuse or deny someone.
examples: I applied for a job with the city, but they turned me down.
They turned down Mary who also applied.

senses.definition: to deny someone’s request.
examples: I offered her some help, but she turned it down.
She had turned down John’s offer of help, too.

senses.definition: to fold part of something downward.
examples: The hotel maid turned the bed down while I was at dinner.
In the mail-order catalog, I always turn down a page that interests me.

senses.definition: to lower the volume or amount of something, such as heat, sound, water, air pressure, etc.
examples: It’s hot in here. Please turn down the heat.
Turn the stereo down. It’s too loud.

senses.definition: to send someone out of somewhere.
examples: I didn’t pay my rent, so the manager turned me out.
I’m glad it’s not winter. I’d hate to turn out someone in the snow.

senses.definition: to manufacture something; to produce something.
examples: John wasn’t turning enough work out, so the manager had a talk with him.
This machine can turn out two thousand items a day.

senses.definition: to search for and find someone or something.
examples: Let me try to see if I can turn someone up who knows how to do the job.
I turned up a number of interesting items when I went through Aunt Jane’s attic.

senses.definition: to distract someone; to cause someone not to be sensible.
examples: Don’t let our praise turn your head. You’re not perfect!
Her successes had turned her head. She was now quite arrogant.

senses.definition: to disgust someone.
senses.notes: Refers to an attack of nausea.
examples: Your rude remarks simply turn my stomach.
The play was so bad that it turned my stomach.

senses.definition: to use something in such a way that it is to one’s advantage; to make good use of a situation, experience, etc.
examples: Pam turned her illness to good account and did a lot of reading.
Many people turn their retirement time to good account and take up interesting hobbies.

senses.definition: to try to return to the past.
examples: You are not facing up to the future. You are trying to turn the clock back to a time when you were more comfortable.
Let us turn the clock back and pretend we are living at the turn of the century—the time that our story takes place.
No, you can’t turn back the clock.

senses.definition: to use force to persuade someone to do something; to increase the pressure on someone to do something.
examples: Management is turning the heat up to increase production.
The teacher really turned up the heat on the students by saying that everyone would be punished if the real culprit was not found.

senses.definition: to ignore abuse or an insult.
examples: When Bob got mad at Mary and yelled at her, she just turned the other cheek.
Usually I turn the other cheek when someone is rude to me.

senses.definition: to cause a reversal in someone’s plans; to make one’s plans turn back on one.
examples: I went to Jane’s house to help get ready for a surprise party for Bob. It turned out that the surprise party was for me! Jane really turned the tables on me!
Turning the tables like that requires a lot of planning and a lot of secrecy.

senses.definition: to cause a reversal in the direction of events; to cause a reversal in public opinion.
examples: It looked as if the team was going to lose, but near the end of the game, our star player turned the tide.
At first, people were opposed to our plan. After a lot of discussion, we were able to turn the tide.

headword: turn thumbs down (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to veto someone or something; to reject someone or something.
senses.notes: See also thumbs down on someone or something.
examples: The board of directors turned thumbs down on my proposal.
They turned thumbs down without even hearing my explanation.
The committee turned thumbs down on Carl and we did not hire him after all.

headword: turn thumbs up (on someone or something)

senses.definition: to accept someone or something; to approve someone or something.
senses.notes: See also thumbs up on someone or something.
examples: The board of directors turned thumbs up on my proposal and voted to fund the project.
The committee turned thumbs up on Carl as the new manager.
When the boss turned thumbs up, I knew everything was okay.

senses.definition: to begin to get busy.
examples: Come on, you guys! Turn to! Let’s get to work.
If you people will turn to, we can finish this work in no time at all.

headword: turn to someone or something (for something)

senses.definition: to seek something from someone or something.
examples: I turned to Ann for help.
Bill turned to aspirin for relief from his headache.

senses.definition: to turn upside down.
examples: The sailboat turned turtle, but the sailors only got wet.
The car ran off the road and turned turtle in the ditch.

senses.definition: to appear.
examples: We’ll send out invitations and see who turns up.
Guess who turned up at my door last night?

senses.definition: to die.
examples: When I turn up my toes, I want a big funeral with lots of flowers.
Our cat turned up his toes during the night. He was nearly ten years old.

senses.definition: to fill up time by playing with one’s fingers.
examples: What am I supposed to do while waiting for you? Sit here and twiddle my thumbs?
Don’t sit around twiddling your thumbs. Get busy!

headword: twist someone around one’s little finger

senses.definition: to manipulate and control someone.
examples: Bob really fell for Jane. She can twist him around her little finger.
Billy’s mother has twisted him around her little finger. He’s very dependent on her.

senses.definition: to force or persuade someone.
examples: At first she refused, but after I twisted her arm a little, she agreed to help.
I didn’t want to run for mayor, but everyone twisted my arm.

senses.definition: to restate someone’s words inaccurately when quoting them or trying to understand them.
examples: Stop twisting my words around! Listen to what I am telling you!
You are twisting my words again. That is not what I said!

senses.definition: people or things of the same type or that are similar in character, attitude, etc.
examples: Jack and Tom are two of a kind. They’re both ambitious.
The companies are two of a kind. They both pay their employees badly.

senses.definition: to cheat on or betray one’s spouse or lover by dating or seeing someone else.
examples: When Mrs. Franklin learned that Mr. Franklin was two-timing her, she left him.
Ann told Bob that if he ever two-timed her, she would cause him a lot of trouble.

senses.definition: Two people want to be alone and a third person will be in the way.
examples: Two’s company. I’m sure Tom and Jill won’t want his sister to go to the movies with them.
John has been invited to join Jane and Peter on their picnic, but he says, “Two’s company, three’s a crowd.”

senses.definition: not used to someone or something.
examples: The poor family was unaccustomed to going to fancy restaurants.
Bill was unaccustomed to typing his own letters.

senses.definition: to be suspected of (doing) something.
examples: Someone stole some money at work, and now everyone is under a cloud of suspicion.
Even the manager is under a cloud.

senses.definition: being or having been arrested and in the care of the police in preparation for the filing of a charge.
examples: Stop where you are! You are under arrest.
Am I under arrest, officer? What did I do?

senses.definition: depending on or influenced by something; because of something.
examples: Under certain conditions, you can see across the lake.
Under no circumstances are you to leave the house tonight.

senses.definition: being watched or examined closely.
examples: Under close scrutiny, the jeweler found a flaw in the diamond.
The suspect was kept under scrutiny throughout the investigation.

senses.definition: being built or repaired.
examples: We cannot travel on this road because it’s under construction.
Our new home has been under construction all summer. We hope to move in next month.

senses.definition: manageable; restrained and controlled; not out of control.
examples: We finally got things under control and functioning smoothly.
The doctor felt she had the disease under control and that I would get well soon.

senses.definition: during an attack.
examples: There was a scandal in city hall, and the mayor was forced to resign under fire.
John is a good lawyer because he can think under fire.

senses.definition: bound by an oath; having taken an oath.
examples: You must tell the truth because you are under oath.
I was placed under oath before I could testify in the trial.

senses.definition: by one’s own power or effort.
examples: I missed my ride to class, so I had to get there under my own steam.
John will need some help with this project. He can’t do it under his own steam.

senses.definition: experiencing something that causes an amount of stress or anxiety.
examples: I have a headache because I’m under a lot of pressure at work.
The professor’s children were under pressure to do well in school.

senses.definition: under the sponsorship of someone or some group; under the control or monitoring of someone or some group.
examples: The entire project fell under the aegis of Thomas.
The entire program is under the auspices of Acme-Global Paper Co., Inc.

senses.definition: in a particular situation; because of the circumstances.
examples: I’m sorry to hear that you’re ill. Under the circumstances, you may take the day off.
We won’t expect you to come to work for a few days, under the circumstances.

senses.definition: in secret or illegally.
examples: The drugstore owner was arrested for selling liquor under the counter.
The clerk sold dirty books under the counter.

senses.definition: drunk; nearly drunk; affected by alcohol.
examples: She behaves quite rudely when under the influence of alcohol.
Ed was stopped by a police officer for driving while under the influence.

senses.definition: experiencing the effects of something such as alcohol, drugs, or any controlling power or person.
senses.notes: See also under the influence (of alcohol).
examples: I think that guy is under the influence of drugs.
Bill has lived under the influence of his mother for too long.

senses.definition: anywhere on earth at all.
examples: This is the largest cattle ranch under the sun.
Isn’t there anyone under the sun who can help me with this problem?

senses.definition: in secret, as with the giving of a bribe.
examples: The construction company had been paying money to the mayor under the table.
Tom transferred the deed to the property to his wife under the table.

senses.definition: ill.
examples: I’m a bit under the weather today, so I can’t go to the office.
My head is aching, and I feel a little under the weather.

senses.definition: just barely in time or on time.
examples: I turned in my report just under the wire.
Bill was the last person to get in the door. He got in under the wire.

senses.definition: an area of knowledge unknown to the speaker.
examples: We are in unfamiliar territory and I don’t know the answer.
Astronomy is unfamiliar territory, and I cannot answer any questions about the stars.

senses.definition: a person or thing about which no one is certain.
senses.notes: Preceded by be, become, seem like, or act like.
examples: John is an unknown quantity. We don’t know how he’s going to act.
The new clerk is an unknown quantity. Things may not turn out all right.

headword: until all hours (of the day and night)

senses.definition: until very late.
examples: Mary is out until all hours, night after night.
If I’m up until all hours two nights in a row, I’m just exhausted.

senses.definition: until the last; until very late.
senses.notes: Folksy or informal. Refers to the end of the day, when the cows come home to be fed and milked.
examples: We were having so much fun that we decided to stay at school until the cows came home.
Where’ve you been? Who said you could stay out’til the cows come home?

senses.definition: at a dead end; on a route that leads nowhere.
examples: I have been trying to find out something about my ancestors, but I’m up a blind alley. I can’t find anything.
The police are up a blind alley in their investigation of the crime.

senses.definition: having trouble with something.
senses.notes: The something is often it, meaning facing trouble in general.
examples: Jane is up against a serious problem.
Yes, she really looks as if she’s up against it.

senses.definition: out of bed and moving about or able to move about.
senses.notes: Refers to a person who has just arisen for the day or to someone who has been sick in bed.
examples: When Tom is up and around, ask him to call me.
The flu put Alice into bed for three days, but she was up and around on the fourth.

senses.definition: to get up and go at people or things; to get active and get busy.
examples: Come on, Bob—up and at’em!
There is a lot of work to be done around here. Up and at’em, everybody!

senses.definition: up into the air and into flight.
senses.notes: Said of a bird or an airplane.
examples: After a few seconds of speeding down the runway, our flight to Tucson was up and away.
Just before the cat pounced on the sparrows, they were up and away and the cat was left with empty paws and jaws.

senses.definition: new, but enterprising and alert.
examples: Jane is a hard worker—really up-and-coming.
Bob is also an up-and-coming youngster who is going to become well known.

senses.definition: in a difficult situation and unable to get out; stymied and confused.
examples: I’m really up a tree on this problem.
Geometry is too hard for me. It’s got me up a tree.

senses.definition: available to anyone.
examples: Mary quit yesterday, and her job is up for grabs.
Who’s in charge around here? This whole organization is up for grabs.

senses.definition: sincere and open.
examples: Ann is a very up-front kind of person. Everyone feels easy around her.
It’s hard to tell what Tom is really thinking. He’s not very up-front.

senses.definition: in advance.
examples: I ordered a new car, and they wanted 20 percent up-front.
I couldn’t afford to pay that much up-front. I’d have to make a smaller deposit.

senses.definition: rising up in anger; very angry.
senses.notes: Also literal when actual weapons are involved.
examples: My father was really up in arms when he got his tax bill this year.
The citizens were up in arms, pounding on the gates of the palace, demanding justice.

headword: up in the air (about someone or something)

senses.definition: undecided about someone or something; uncertain about someone or something.
examples: I don’t know what Sally plans to do. Things were sort of up in the air the last time we talked.
Let’s leave this question up in the air until next week.

senses.definition: old; elderly.
examples: My uncle is up in years and can’t hear too well.
Many people lose their hearing somewhat when they are along in years.

senses.definition: to or at the northern part of the country or the world.
senses.notes: See also back East, down South, and out West.
examples: I don’t like living up North. I want to move down South where it’s warm.
When you say “up North,” do you mean where the polar bears live, or just in the northern states?

senses.definition: in a bad situation.
senses.notes: Slang. Use with caution. There is a taboo version of this phrase.
examples: What a mess I’m in. I’m really up the creek without a paddle.
I tried to prevent it, but I seem to be up the creek, too.

senses.definition: modern; up to the current standards of fashion; with the latest information.
examples: I’d like to see a more up-to-date report on Mr. Smith.
This is not an up-to-date record of the construction project.
I’m having my living room redecorated to bring it up-to-date.
I don’t care if my rooms are up-to-date. I just want them to be comfortable.

senses.definition: able to do something.
examples: Do you feel up to going back to work today?
She just isn’t up to staying up all night.

senses.definition: doing something bad.
examples: I could tell from the look on Tom’s face that he was up to no good.
There are three boys in the front yard. I don’t know what they are doing, but I think they are up to no good.

senses.definition: having a lot of something; very much involved in something.
examples: I can’t come to the meeting. I’m up to my neck in these reports.
Mary is up to her ears in her work.
I am up to my eyeballs in things to do! I can’t do any more!

senses.definition: as good as the standard or average; up to standard.
examples: I’m just not feeling up to par today. I must be coming down with something.
The manager said that the report was not up to par and gave it back to Mary to do over again.

senses.definition: as good as is required; meeting the minimum requirements.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with up to par.
examples: Sorry, Tom. Your performance isn’t up to snuff. You’ll have to improve or find another job.
My paper wasn’t up to scratch, so I got an F.

senses.definition: the very latest or most recent.
examples: I want to hear some up-to-the-minute news on the hostage situation.
I just got an up-to-the-minute report on Tom’s health.

senses.definition: at the place or time of making an impact.
examples: The car crumpled upon impact with the brick wall.
The man who fell from the top of the building died on impact.

senses.definition: the higher levels of society; the upper class.
senses.notes: Informal. From the top, as opposed to the bottom, crust of a pie.
examples: Jane speaks like that because she pretends to be from the upper crust, but her father was a miner.
James is from the upper crust, but he is penniless.

senses.definition: good fortune and bad fortune.
examples: I’ve had my ups and downs, but in general life has been good to me.
All people have their ups and downs.

senses.definition: to mess up or ruin something.
examples: Tom really upset the apple cart by telling Mary the truth about Jane.
I always knew he’d upset the apple cart.

senses.definition: the result or outcome of something.
examples: The upshot of my criticism was a change in policy.
The upshot of the argument was an agreement to hire a new secretary.

headword: use every trick in the book

senses.definition: to use every method possible.
examples: I used every trick in the book, but I still couldn’t manage to get a ticket to the game Saturday.
Bob tried to use every trick in the book, but he still failed.

senses.definition: to use one’s own intelligence.
senses.notes: Noggin and noodle are slang terms for “head.”
examples: You can do better in math if you’ll just use your head.
Jane uses her noggin and gets things done correctly and on time.
Yes, she sure knows how to use her noodle.

senses.definition: use some effort.
senses.notes: Slang. As if lubricating one’s elbow would make one more efficient. Note the variation in the examples.
examples: Come on, Bill. You can do it. Just use some elbow grease.
I tried elbow grease, but it doesn’t help get the job done.

headword: use someone or something as an excuse

senses.definition: to blame someone or something (for a failure).
examples: John used his old car as an excuse for not going to the meeting.
My husband was sick in bed, and I used him as an excuse.

senses.definition: to swear, threaten, or use abusive language.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t use strong language in front of the children.
If you feel that you have to use strong language with the manager, perhaps you had better let me do the talking.

senses.definition: to have done something [customarily] in the past.
examples: We used to go swimming in the lake before it became polluted.
I used to eat nuts, but then I became allergic to them.

senses.definition: accustomed to someone or something.
examples: I’m not used to Jane yet. She’s a bit hard to get along with.
How long does it take to get used to this weather?

senses.definition: the earth; mortal life on earth.
examples: When it comes time for me to leave this vale of tears, I hope I can leave some worthwhile memories behind.
Uncle Fred left this vale of tears early this morning.

senses.definition: to disappear without leaving a trace.
examples: My money gets spent so fast. It seems to vanish into thin air.
When I came back, my car was gone. I had locked it, and it couldn’t have vanished into thin air!

headword: Variety is the spice of life.

senses.definition: Differences and changes make life interesting.
examples: Mary reads all kinds of books. She says variety is the spice of life.
The Franklins travel all over the world so they can learn how different people live. After all, variety is the spice of life.

senses.definition: to get rid of one’s feelings of anger caused by someone or something by attacking someone or something else.
examples: Jack vented his spleen at his wife whenever things went badly at work.
Peter vented his spleen on his car by kicking it when he lost the race.

senses.definition: to be almost something.
examples: Your blouse is a lovely color. It seems to be blue verging on purple.
Sally has a terrible case of the flu, and they are afraid it’s verging on pneumonia.

senses.definition: the end; an absolute end of something.
examples: At the very last of the movie, the hero gets killed.
Bill stayed at the party until the very last.

senses.definition: the exact thing that is required.
examples: The vacuum cleaner is the very thing for cleaning the stairs.
I have the very thing to remove that stain.

senses.definition: someone or something that is responsible for something bad or wrong.
examples: I wondered who told the newspapers about the local scandal. I discovered that Joan was the villain of the piece.
We couldn’t think who had stolen the meat. The dog next door turned out to be the villain of the piece.

senses.definition: energy and enthusiasm.
examples: I just don’t seem to have the vim and vigor that I had a few years ago.
Alice appeared with all the vim and vigor of youth, and began to help carry in the packages.

senses.definition: to cast a ballot on which the votes are divided between two or more parties.
examples: I always vote a spilt ticket since I detest both parties.
Mary voted a split ticket for the first time in her life.

senses.definition: to cast a ballot with all the votes for members of the same political party.
examples: I’m not a member of any political party, so I never vote a straight ticket.
I usually vote a straight ticket because I believe in the principles of one party and not in the other’s.

senses.definition: a poll taken to discover whether or not a person, party, etc., still has the majority’s support.
examples: The government easily won the vote of confidence called for by the opposition.
The president of the club resigned when one of the members called for a vote of confidence in his leadership.

senses.definition: a speech expressing appreciation and thanks to a speaker, lecturer, organizer, etc., and inviting the audience to applaud.
examples: John gave a vote of thanks to Professor Jones for his talk.
Mary was given a vote of thanks for organizing the dance.

senses.definition: to express one’s dissatisfaction with something by leaving, especially by walking away.
examples: I think that the play is a total flop. Most of the audience voted with its feet during the second act.
I am prepared to vote with my feet if the meeting appears to be a waste of time.

senses.definition: to start in (doing) something immediately.
examples: I need some preparation. I can’t just wade into the job and start doing things correctly.
We don’t expect you to wade in. We’ll tell you what to do.

senses.definition: to chatter or chat with someone.
examples: We stood around and wagged our chins for almost an hour.
Don’t just wag your chin. Stop talking and get to work!

senses.definition: a skeptical attitude; an uncertain attitude where someone will just wait and see what happens.
examples: John thought that Mary couldn’t do it, but he took a wait-and-see attitude.
His wait-and-see attitude didn’t influence me at all.

headword: wait on someone hand and foot

senses.definition: to serve someone very well, attending to all personal needs.
examples: I don’t mind bringing you your coffee, but I don’t intend to wait on you hand and foot.
I don’t want anyone to wait on me hand and foot. I can take care of myself.

senses.definition: ready or prepared to do something, especially to take over someone else’s job or position.
senses.notes: Refers to a performer waiting at the side of the stage to go on.
examples: Mr. Smith retires as manager next year, and Mr. Jones is just waiting in the wings.
Jane was waiting in the wings, hoping that a member of the hockey team would drop out and she would get a place on the team.

senses.definition: to be so loud as to wake those who are “sleeping” the most soundly: the dead.
examples: You are making enough noise to wake the dead.
Stop hollering! You’ll wake the dead!

senses.definition: to treat someone badly.
examples: She’s so mean to her children. She walks all over them.
The manager had walked all over Ann for months. Finally she quit.

senses.definition: to be in a situation where one must be very cautious.
examples: I’ve been walking a tightrope all day. I need to relax.
Our business is about to fail. We’ve been walking a tightrope for three months.

senses.definition: to win something easily.
examples: John won the tennis match with no difficulty. He walked away with it.
Our team walked away with first place.

senses.definition: to take or steal something.
examples: I think somebody just walked off with my purse!
Somebody walked off with my daughter’s bicycle.

senses.definition: to be very happy; to be euphoric.
examples: Ann was walking on air when she got the job.
On the last day of school, all the children are walking on air.

senses.definition: to be very cautious.
examples: The manager is very hard to deal with. You really have to walk on eggs.
I’ve been walking on eggs ever since I started working here.

senses.definition: to abandon someone; to leave one’s spouse.
examples: Mr. Franklin walked out on Mrs. Franklin last week.
Bob walked out on Jane without saying good-bye.

senses.definition: to leave a performance (of something by someone).
examples: We didn’t like the play at all, so we walked out.
John was giving a very dull speech, and a few people even walked out on him.

senses.definition: to pace nervously while waiting.
examples: While Bill waited for news of the operation, he walked the floor for hours on end.
Walking the floor won’t help. You might as well sit down and relax.

senses.definition: to suffer punishment at the hand of someone.
senses.notes: From the image of pirates making their blindfolded captives commit suicide by walking off the end of a plank jutting out over the open sea.
examples: Fred may think he can make the members of my department walk the plank, but we will fight back.
Tom thought he could make John walk the plank, but John fought back.

senses.definition: covered with something in all places.
examples: The hallway is wall-to-wall with Jimmy’s toys.
The beach was wall-to-wall with tourists.

senses.definition: We may be overheard.
examples: Let’s not discuss this matter here. Walls have ears, you know.
Shhh. Walls have ears. Someone may be listening.

senses.definition: to lack nothing; to have everything one needs or wishes.
examples: The Smiths don’t have much money, but their children seem to want for nothing.
Jean’s husband spoils her. She wants for nothing.

senses.definition: to remain out of play during a game—seated on a bench.
examples: John spent the whole game warming the bench.
Mary never warms the bench. She plays from the beginning to the end.

headword: warm the cockles of someone’s heart

senses.definition: to make someone feel warm and happy.
examples: It warms the cockles of my heart to hear you say that.
Hearing that old song again warmed the cockles of her heart.

senses.definition: to become friendly with someone; to get used to a person and become friends.
examples: It took a while before John warmed up to me, but then we became good friends.
It’s hard to warm up to Sally. She’s very quiet and shy.

senses.definition: including all the faults and disadvantages.
examples: Jim has many faults, but Jean loves him, warts and all.
The place where we went on vacation had some dismal aspects, but we liked it, warts and all.

senses.definition: to do a little bit of laundry, such as socks and underclothing.
examples: I’m sorry I can’t go out tonight. I’ve got to wash a few things out.
I’ll be ready to leave in just a minute. I’ve just got to wash out a few things.

senses.definition: referring to clothing made out of a kind of cloth that looks presentable after washing without ironing.
examples: I always travel with wash-and-wear clothing.
All his shirts are wash-and-wear, and this makes his life much easier since he used to burn them when he ironed them.

headword: wash one’s hands of someone or something

senses.definition: to end one’s association with someone or something.
examples: I washed my hands of Tom. I wanted no more to do with him.
That car was a real headache. I washed my hands of it long ago.

senses.definition: exhausted; lacking energy.
examples: Pam was completely washed-out after the birth of the baby.
I feel washed-out. I need a vacation.

senses.definition: finished.
examples: “You’re through, Tom,” said the manager, “fired— washed-up!”
Max is washed-up as a bank teller.

senses.definition: to waste one’s time talking; to talk in vain.
examples: Don’t waste your breath talking to her. She won’t listen.
You can’t persuade me. You’re just wasting your breath.

senses.definition: to kill someone.
examples: The thief tried to waste the bank guard after the bank robbery.
The crook said, “Try that again, and I’ll waste you!”

senses.definition: to act with care and caution so as not to make a mistake or offend someone.
examples: John had better watch his step with the new boss. He won’t put up with his lateness.
Mary was told by the lecturer to watch her step and stop missing classes.

senses.definition: to monitor or guard someone or something.
examples: Please watch over my apartment while I am on vacation.
I am looking for someone to watch over my grandmother during the day.

headword: watch someone or something like a hawk

senses.definition: to watch someone very carefully.
examples: The teacher watched the students like a hawk to make sure they did not cheat on the quiz.
We have to watch our dog like a hawk in case he runs away.

senses.definition: to dilute a liquid, usually with water.
examples: The punch was good until someone watered it down.
This is too strong! Water it down.

senses.definition: to make something milder or less intense.
senses.notes: Refers to diluting as in sense 1.
examples: The language in the script was rude but realistic until someone watered it down.
Professor Jones sometimes waters down his lectures so people can understand them better.

senses.definition: past and forgotten.
senses.notes: [something] Refers to water that has already flowed under a bridge and has gone downstream.
examples: Please don’t worry about it anymore. It’s all water under the bridge.
I can’t change the past. It’s water under the bridge.

senses.definition: to increase and then decrease, especially with reference to the phases of the moon.
examples: As the moon waxes and wanes, so does the height of the tide change.
Voter sentiment about the tax proposal waxes and wanes with each passing day.

senses.definition: referring to the raising of money to pay for something.
senses.notes: Typically refers to a government committee or a committee of some organization charged with raising money.
examples: The suggestion was referred to the ways and means committee for discussion at the next meeting.
The proposed legislation is stalled in ways and means.

senses.definition: We really try to make people happy.
examples: We aim to please because we want you to be our customer.
I’m glad you like our food. We aim to please.

senses.definition: a large amount of something.
examples: There’s a wealth of information on parrots at the library.
The junkyard had a wealth of used car parts.

senses.definition: the process of wearing down or breaking down something.
examples: Driving in freezing weather means lots of wear and tear on your car.
I drive carefully and sensibly to avoid wear and tear.

senses.definition: to have more than one set of responsibilities; to hold more than one office.
examples: The mayor is also the police chief. She wears more than one hat.
I have too much to do to wear more than one hat.

senses.definition: to become less; to stop gradually.
examples: The effects of the painkiller wore off and my tooth began to hurt.
I was annoyed at first, but my anger wore off.

headword: wear one’s heart on one’s sleeve
altForms: have one’s heart on one’s sleeve

senses.definition: to display one’s feelings openly and habitually, rather than keep them private.
examples: John always has his heart on his sleeve so that everyone knows how he feels.
Because she wears her heart on her sleeve, it’s easy to hurt her feelings.

senses.definition: to bother or annoy someone.
examples: We stayed with them only a short time because my children seemed to wear on them.
Always being short of money wears on a person after a while.

senses.definition: to stay too long (at an event to which one has been invited); to visit somewhere too often.
examples: Tom visited the Smiths so often that he wore out his welcome.
At about midnight, I decided that I had worn out my welcome, so I went home.

senses.definition: to overcome someone’s objections; to persist until someone has been persuaded.
examples: John didn’t want to go, but we finally wore him down.
We were unable to wear down John, and when we left, he was still insisting on running away from home.

senses.definition: to exhaust someone; to make someone tired.
examples: The coach made the team practice until he wore them out.
If he wears out everybody on the team, nobody will be left to play in the game.

senses.definition: to get out or sneak out of something.
senses.notes: Refers to the ability of a weasel to move through tiny openings. Informal.
examples: I don’t want to go to the meeting. I think I’ll try to weasel out of it.
You had better be there! Don’t try to weasel out!

senses.definition: if the weather allows it.
examples: Weather permitting, we will be there on time.
The plane lands at midnight, weather permitting.

senses.definition: to move, drive, or walk in and out of something, such as traffic, a line, etc.
examples: The car was weaving in and out of traffic dangerously.
The deer ran rapidly through the forest, weaving in and out of the trees.

senses.definition: married to someone.
examples: The couple will have been wed to each other for fifty years next June.
Anne is wed to one of my cousins.

senses.definition: mentally attached to something; firmly committed to something.
examples: The manager was wedded to the idea of getting new computers.
The mayor was wedded to the new budget plan.

senses.definition: to remove someone or something unwanted or undesirable from a group or collection.
examples: We had to weed them out one by one.
The auditions were held to weed out the actors with the least ability.
I’m going through my books to weed out those that I don’t need anymore.

senses.definition: every week, week after week.
examples: We have the same old food, week in, week out.
I’m tired of this job. I’ve done the same thing—week in, week out—for three years.

senses.definition: to be in a person’s thoughts; [for something] to be bothering someone’s thinking.
examples: This problem has been weighing on my mind for many days now.
I hate to have things weighing on my mind. I can’t sleep when I’m worried.

senses.definition: to worry or depress someone.
senses.notes: [for a thought or worry] Also literal.
examples: All these problems really weigh me down.
Financial problems have been weighing down our entire family.

senses.definition: to consider carefully what someone says.
examples: I listened to what he said, and I weighed his words very carefully.
Everyone was weighing his words. None of us knew exactly what he meant.

senses.definition: to consider one’s own words carefully when speaking.
examples: I always weigh my words when I speak in public.
John was weighing his words with great care because he didn’t want to be misunderstood.

senses.definition: to be free to do something.
examples: You’re welcome to leave whenever you wish.
He’s welcome to join the club whenever he feels he’s ready.

senses.definition: feeling positively toward someone or something; favorable toward someone or something.
examples: I do not think I will get a raise since the boss is not well-disposed toward me.
The senators are well-disposed toward giving themselves a raise.

senses.definition: wealthy; with sufficient money.
examples: My uncle can afford a new car. He’s well-heeled.
Everyone in his family is well-off.

senses.definition: wealthy and of good social position.
senses.notes: Often with quite, as in the examples below.
examples: The Jones family is quite well-to-do.
There is a gentleman waiting for you at the door. He appears quite well-to-do.

senses.definition: aged; old.
examples: Jane’s husband is well up in years. He is nearly 75.
Joan’s well up in years but healthy.

senses.definition: young and inexperienced.
examples: John’s too young to take on a job like this! He’s still wet behind the ears!
He may be wet behind the ears, but he’s well trained and totally competent.
Tom is going into business by himself? Why, he’s hardly dry behind the ears.
That kid isn’t dry behind the ears. He’ll go broke in a month.

senses.definition: a dull or depressing person who spoils other people’s enjoyment.
examples: Jack’s fun at parties, but his brother’s a wet blanket.
I was with Anne and she was being a real wet blanket.

senses.definition: to take a drink of something.
examples: Wow, am I thirsty. I need something to wet my whistle.
Hey, Sally! Give her something to wet her whistle.

senses.definition: What are you implying?; What do you mean?
examples: What are you driving at? What are you trying to say?
Why are you asking me all these questions? What are you driving at?

senses.definition: I am at a loss for words.
examples: I’m sorry. I’ll pay for it. What can I say?
What can I say? I never meant it to end like this.

headword: What do you want me to say?

senses.definition: You caught me and I’m sorry, and I don’t know what more to say.
examples: What do you want me to say? I apologized. There is nothing more I can do.
Okay, so I’m wrong. What do you want me to say?

senses.definition: The results of things that one has done will someday have an effect on the person who started the events.
examples: So he finally gets to see the results of his activities. Whatever goes around, comes around.
Now he is the victim of his own policies. Whatever goes around comes around.

headword: What have you been up to?

senses.definition: I haven’t seen you for a long time, so tell me what you have been doing?
examples: Hi, Tom. Where have you been? What have you been up to?
What have you been up to? Busy, I am sure.

senses.definition: what would be the result if something were true?
examples: What if you had all the money you want?
What if everyone thought you were great?

senses.definition: something that motivates someone; something that makes someone behave in a certain way.
examples: William is sort of strange. I don’t know what makes him tick.
When you get to know people, you find out what makes them tick.

senses.definition: to cause something to run or function.
examples: I don’t know what makes it tick.
I took apart the radio to find out what made it tick.

headword: What one doesn’t know won’t hurt one.

senses.definition: Unknown facts cannot worry or upset a person.
examples: Don’t tell me that I have made a mistake. What I don’t know won’t hurt me.
Don’t tell him the truth about his missing dog. What he doesn’t know won’t hurt him.

senses.definition: Whatever will happen will just happen and there is little we can do about it.
examples: There is little I can do at this stage. Whatever will be, will be.
The doctors have done all they can. Whatever will be, will be.

senses.definition: It is final and in the past.
examples: It’s too late to change it now. What’s done is done.
What’s done is done. The past cannot be altered.

senses.definition: What is taking you so long?; Why are you still there and not here?
examples: Dinner is ready, and you are still at work. I telephoned to ask what’s keeping you.
What’s keeping you? I am ready to go and you are still in there dressing.

senses.definition: How are you? Tell me what you have been doing.
examples: Good to see you. What’s new?
What’s new? How are things down your way?

senses.definition: What is the point of something?; Why bother with something?
examples: What’s the good of my going at all if I’ll be late?
There is no need to get there early. What’s the good of that?

senses.definition: to take part in clever (but sometimes dishonest or immoral) business deals.
examples: John loves to wheel and deal in the money markets.
Jack got tired of all the wheeling and dealing of big business and retired to run a pub in the country.

headword: when all is said and done

senses.definition: when everything is finished and settled; when everything is considered.
senses.notes: See also after all is said and done.
examples: When all is said and done, this isn’t such a bad part of the country to live in after all.
When all is said and done, I believe I had a very enjoyable time on my vacation.

senses.definition: never.
senses.notes: The first entry is always affirmative and the second is always negative.
examples: I’ll say I’m sorry to you when hell freezes over!
I won’t apologize until hell freezes over.

headword: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

senses.definition: One should behave in the same way that the local people behave.
examples: I don’t usually eat lamb, but I did when I went to Australia. When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
I always carry an umbrella when I visit London. When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

headword: when it comes right down to it

senses.definition: all things considered; when one really thinks about something.
examples: When it comes right down to it, I’d like to find a new job.
When it comes right down to it, he can’t really afford a new car.

senses.definition: as for something; speaking about something.
examples: When it comes to fishing, John is an expert.
When it comes to trouble, Mary really knows how to cause it.

senses.definition: when one does not expect (something).
examples: An old car is likely to give you trouble when least expected.
My pencil usually breaks when least expected.

headword: when one is good and ready

senses.definition: when one is completely ready.
examples: I’ll be there when I’m good and ready.
Ann will finish the job when she’s good and ready and not a minute sooner.

senses.definition: when the situation becomes more difficult; when matters escalate.
senses.notes: See also if push comes to shove.
examples: When push comes to shove, I will take a stronger position.
When push comes to shove, I will come up with the money you need.

headword: When the cat’s away, the mice will play.

senses.definition: Some people will get into mischief when they are not being watched.
examples: The students behaved very badly for the substitute teacher. When the cat’s away, the mice will play.
John had a wild party at his house when his parents were out of town. When the cat’s away, the mice will play.

senses.definition: at the final, critical moment; when things really get difficult.
examples: When the chips are down, I know that I can depend on Jean to help out.
I knew you would come and help when the chips were down.

senses.definition: when things get extremely difficult; when it becomes difficult to proceed.
senses.notes: Also literal when referring to travel. A second line is sometimes added to the main entry phrase: When the going gets tough, the tough get going. This means that when things become difficult, strong people began to work or move faster and harder.
examples: When the going gets tough, I will be there to help you.
I appreciate the kind words you sent to us when the going got a little rough last month.

senses.definition: at exactly the right time.
examples: I’ll tell her the good news when the time is ripe.
When the time is ripe, I’ll bring up the subject again.

senses.definition: one’s point of view.
examples: I think I know what you mean. I know where you’re coming from.
Man, you don’t know where I’m coming from! You don’t understand a single word I say.

headword: Where there’s a will there’s a way.

senses.definition: One can do something if one really wants to.
examples: Don’t give up, Ann. You can do it. Where there’s a will there’s a way.
They told John he’d never walk again after his accident. He worked at it, and he was able to walk again! Where there’s a will there’s a way.

senses.definition: Evidence of a problem probably indicates that there really is a problem.
examples: There is a lot of noise coming from the classroom. There is probably something wrong. Where there’s smoke there’s fire.
I think there is something wrong at the old house on the corner. The police are there again. Where there’s smoke there’s fire.

senses.definition: Hello, I haven’t seen you in a long time.
examples: I haven’t seen you in a long time. Where’ve you been hiding yourself?
Where’ve you been hiding yourself? We missed you at the meeting.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be interested in something and to be eager to have, know, learn, etc., more about it.
examples: Seeing that film really whetted my sister’s appetite for horror films. She now sees as many as possible.
My appetite for theater was whetted when I was very young.

senses.definition: either if something is the case or if something is not the case; one way or the other.
examples: I’ll drive to New York tomorrow whether or not it rains.
I’m going to the mall whether you come with me or not.

senses.definition: to spend or waste time.
examples: I like to read to while away the time.
Jane whiles the time away by daydreaming.

senses.definition: to prepare, create, or put something together quickly.
examples: I haven’t written my report yet, but I’ll whip one up before the deadline.
Come in and sit down. I’ll go whip up something to eat.

senses.definition: something that is useless and which is either a nuisance or is expensive to keep up.
senses.notes: From the gift of a white elephant by the kings of Siam [Thailand] to courtiers who displeased them, knowing the cost of the upkeep would ruin them.
examples: Bob’s father-in-law has given him an old Rolls-Royce, but it’s a real white elephant. He has no place to park it and can’t afford the maintenance on it.
Those antique vases Aunt Mary gave me are white elephants. They’re ugly and take ages to clean.

headword: Who do you think you’re kidding?

senses.definition: I don’t believe you, and what makes you think you can deceive me?
examples: Who does he think he’s kidding? Nobody believes him.
A: You are the finest batter I’ve ever seen. B: Who do you think you’re kidding?

headword: Who do you think you’re talking to?

senses.definition: Do you know the importance of the person [me] you are talking to?
examples: Who do you think you’re talking to? I’m the boss here, you know!
Don’t talk to me that way! Who do you think you are talking to?

senses.definition: I would never have guessed that something so surprising could happen.
examples: So he’s run off with the maid. Who would have thought?
It turns out she robbed a bank when she was 18. Who would have thought?

senses.definition: the whole thing; the whole matter or affair; the entire affair or organization.
examples: John is not a good manager. Instead of delegating jobs to others, he runs the whole shooting match himself.
There’s not a hard worker in that whole shooting match.
I will be glad to be finished with this project. I want to be done with the whole ball of wax.
I am tired of this job. I am fed up with the whole ball of wax.

senses.definition: a new set of circumstances.
examples: It’s a whole new ball game since Jane took over the office.
You can’t do the things you used to do around here. It’s a new ball game.

senses.definition: to enjoy oneself in a lively and noisy manner.
examples: John’s friends really whooped it up at his bachelor party.
Jean wants to have a large party and whoop it up to celebrate her promotion.

headword: the whys and wherefores of something

senses.definition: the reason or causes relating to something.
examples: I refuse to discuss the whys and wherefores of my decision. It’s final.
Bob doesn’t know the whys and wherefores of his contract. He just knows that it means he will get a lot of money when he finishes the work.

senses.definition: completely awake.
examples: After the telephone rang, I was wide-awake for an hour.
I’m not very wide-awake at six o’clock in the morning.

senses.definition: far from the target.
examples: Tom’s shot was wide of the mark.
The pitch was quite fast, but wide of the mark.

senses.definition: inadequate; far from what is required or expected.
examples: Jane’s efforts were sincere, but wide of the mark.
He failed the course because everything he did was wide of the mark.

senses.definition: enthusiastic about someone or something.
examples: Bill is wild about chocolate ice cream.
Sally is wild about Tom and his new car.

senses.definition: a worthless hunt or chase; a futile pursuit.
examples: I wasted all afternoon on a wild-goose chase.
John was angry because he was sent out on a wild-goose chase.

senses.definition: nothing could force someone (to go somewhere).
examples: I refuse to go to that meeting! Wild horses couldn’t drag me.
Wild horses couldn’t drag her to that game.

senses.definition: will not tolerate or permit something.
examples: You mustn’t drive home alone. I won’t hear of it.
My parents won’t hear of my staying out that late.

senses.definition: to win by the slightest amount of difference.
senses.notes: Informal. As in a horse race where one horse wins with only its nose ahead of the horse that comes in second.
examples: I ran the fastest race I could, but I only won by a nose.
Sally won the race, but she only won by a nose.

senses.definition: to beat someone or something in a race or a contest.
examples: My horse won out over yours, so you lose your bet.
I knew I could win out if I just kept trying.

senses.definition: to succeed in gaining the support and sympathy of someone.
examples: Jane’s parents disapproved of her engagement at first, but she won them over.
I’m trying to win the boss over and get him to give us the day off.

senses.definition: to decrease or diminish.
examples: Things are very busy now, but they’ll wind down in about an hour.
I hope business winds down soon. I’m exhausted.

senses.definition: to conclude something.
examples: Today we’ll wind that deal up with the bank.
I have a few items of business to wind up; then I’ll be with you.

senses.definition: the habit or practice of looking at goods in shop windows or stores without actually buying anything.
examples: Mary and Jane do a lot of window-shopping in their lunch hour, looking for things to buy when they get paid.
Jane said she was just window-shopping, but she bought a new coat.

senses.definition: to treat someone to an expensive meal of the type that includes fine wines; to entertain someone lavishly.
examples: The lobbyists wined and dined the senators one by one in order to influence them.
We were wined and dined every night and given the best hotel accommodations in town.

senses.definition: to do the best that one can in a situation, especially when one is not prepared.
senses.notes: Compare this with play something by ear.
examples: I lost my notes before my speech, and I had to wing it.
The professor, it turned out, was winging it in every single lecture.

senses.definition: to ignore something.
examples: Billy caused me a little trouble, but I just winked at it.
This is a serious matter, and you can’t expect me just to wink at it.

senses.definition: to cause someone to be broke.
examples: They wiped me out in the poker game.
The crop failure wiped out all the farmers.

senses.definition: to exterminate someone or something.
examples: The hunters came and wiped all the deer out.
The crooks wiped out the two witnesses.

senses.definition: to erase someone’s (bad) record.
examples: I’d like to wipe my slate clean and start all over again.
Bob did badly in high school, but he wiped his slate clean and did a good job in college.

senses.definition: to remove something (from something else) by wiping or rubbing.
examples: There is mud on your shirt. Please wipe it off.
My shirt has catsup on it. I must wipe off the catsup.

senses.definition: to tidy or clean something by wiping (something else) off.
examples: Please wipe the table off. There’s water on it.
Wipe off your shirt. There’s catsup on it.

headword: wipe the floor up with someone

senses.definition: to beat or physically abuse someone.
senses.notes: Slang. Usually said as a threat. See also mop the floor up with someone.
examples: You say that to me one more time, and I’ll wipe the floor up with you.
Oh, yeah! You’re not big enough to wipe up the floor with anybody!

senses.definition: to begin to understand the truth about someone or something.
examples: It was almost a week before I began to wise up to John. He’s a total phony.
You had better stay hidden for a while. The police are beginning to wise up.

senses.definition: to pass something off onto someone else.
examples: I don’t want to have to deal with your problems. Don’t wish them off on me.
The storekeeper wished off the defective watch on the very next customer who came in.

senses.definition: believing that something is true or that something will happen just because one wishes that it were true or would happen.
examples: Hoping for a car as a birthday present is just wishful thinking. Your parents can’t afford it.
Mary thinks that she is going to get a big rise, but that’s wishful thinking. Her boss is so mean.

senses.definition: sadly.
examples: With a heavy heart, she said good-bye.
We left school on the last day with a heavy heart.

headword: with all one’s heart and soul

senses.definition: very sincerely.
examples: Oh, Bill, I love you with all my heart and soul, and I always will!
She thanked us with all her heart and soul for the gift.

senses.definition: with all the condiments that accompany a certain kind of food.
examples: For $5.99 you get a turkey dinner with all the fixings.
Max likes his hamburgers with all the fixings.

senses.definition: with determination and eagerness, as if angry.
examples: The angry soldier attacked the enemy with a vengeance.
Bill ate all his dinner and gobbled up his dessert with a vengeance.

headword: with a view to doing something
altForms: with an eye to doing something

senses.definition: with the intention of doing something.
examples: I came to this school with a view to getting a degree.
The mayor took office with an eye to improving the town.

senses.definition: with determination and enthusiasm.
examples: The children worked with a will to finish the project on time.
The workers set about manufacturing the new products with a will.

senses.definition: eagerly, willingly, and on time.
examples: Oh, yes! I’ll meet you at the restaurant. I’ll be there with bells on.
All the smiling children were there waiting for me with bells on their toes.

senses.definition: as days pass, one by one; day by day.
examples: Things grow more expensive with each passing day.
We are all growing older with each passing day.

senses.definition: without effort.
examples: The smart student passed the test with ease.
The gymnast did a back flip with ease.

senses.definition: repeatedly or continually.
examples: Bob was out in the yard, raking leaves and cursing with every other breath.
The child was so grateful that she was thanking me with every breath.

senses.definition: ordered with everything available on it, such as ketchup, mustard, onions, cheese, peppers, chili, lettuce, tomato, etc., as appropriate.
examples: Do you want it with everything?
Give me a cheeseburger with everything on it.

senses.definition: easily and excellently.
senses.notes: Flying colors refers to ships’ pennants.
examples: John passed his geometry test with flying colors.
Sally qualified for the race with flying colors.

senses.definition: with humility.
examples: She stormed off but came back with hat in hand when she ran out of money.
We had to go hat in hand to the committee to get a grant for our proposal.

senses.definition: without risk of punishment; with immunity from the negative consequences of an act; while being exempt from punishment.
examples: The diplomat parked in illegal parking spaces with impunity.
Bob used his brother’s property with impunity.

senses.definition: unconditionally; with no obligations attached.
examples: My parents gave me a computer without any strings attached.
I want this only if it comes with no strings attached.

headword: with one hand tied behind one’s back
altForms: with both hands tied behind one’s back

senses.definition: even under a severe handicap; easily.
examples: I could put an end to this argument with one hand tied behind my back.
John could do this job with both hands tied behind his back.

headword: with one’s tail between one’s legs

senses.definition: appearing frightened or cowardly, like a frightened or defeated dog; appearing threatened or humiliated.
examples: John seems to lack courage. When people criticize him unjustly, he just goes away with his tail between his legs and doesn’t tell them that they’re wrong.
The frightened dog ran away with its tail between its legs when the bigger dog growled.

headword: with regard to someone or something

senses.definition: concerning someone or something.
examples: What shall we do with regard to planning dinner?
With regard to Bill, I think he is working too hard.

senses.definition: with pleasure or enjoyment.
examples: John ate his juicy hamburger with great relish.
We sampled the excellent food with relish.

headword: with respect to someone or something

senses.definition: of or about someone or something.
examples: With respect to radiation, this power plant is very safe.
This article examines experiments with respect to ethical issues.

headword: with the best will in the world

senses.definition: however much one wishes to do something or however hard one tries to do something.
examples: With the best will in the world, Jack won’t be able to help Mary get the job.
With the best will in the world, they won’t finish the job in time.

senses.definition: to decline or fade away at an early stage of development.
senses.notes: [for something] Also literal in reference to grapes or other fruit.
examples: You have a great plan, Tom. Let’s keep it alive. Don’t let it wither on the vine.
The whole project died on the vine when the contract was canceled.

headword: within an inch of one’s life

senses.definition: very close to taking one’s life; almost to death.
examples: The accident frightened me within an inch of my life.
