When Mary was seriously ill in the hospital, she came within an inch of her life.

senses.definition: very close (to something).
senses.notes: Possibly as close as the distance one could throw a stone. It usually refers to a distance much greater than one could throw a stone.
examples: The police department was located within a stone’s throw of our house.
We live in Carbondale, and that’s just a stone’s throw from the Mississippi River.
Come visit. We live just a stone’s throw away.
John saw Mary across the street, just a stone’s throw away.
Philadelphia is a stone’s throw from New York City.

senses.definition: close enough to hear someone call out.
examples: When the boat came within hailing distance, I asked if I could borrow some gasoline.
We weren’t within calling distance, so I couldn’t hear what you said to me.

senses.definition: up to a certain point; with certain restrictions.
examples: You’re free to do what you want—within limits, of course.
You must try to keep behavior at the party within bounds.

senses.definition: reasonable; reasonably.
examples: You can do anything you want within reason.
I’ll pay any sum you ask—within reason.

senses.definition: almost in the possession of someone.
examples: My goals are almost within my reach, so I know I’ll succeed.
We almost had the contract within our grasp, but the deal fell through at the last minute.

senses.definition: close enough to walk to.
examples: Is the train station within walking distance?
My office is within walking distance from here.

senses.definition: casually; without showing alarm or response.
examples: I knew I had insulted her, but she turned to me and asked me to leave without batting an eye.
Right in the middle of the speech— without batting an eye—the speaker walked off the stage.

senses.definition: for certain; absolutely.
examples: I’ll be there at noon without fail.
The plane leaves on time every day without fail.

senses.definition: without further talk.
senses.notes: An overworked phrase usually heard in public announcements.
examples: And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr. Bill Franklin!
The time has come to leave, so without further ado, good evening and good-bye.

senses.definition: absolutely; certainly.
examples: She agreed to help without question.
She said, “I stand ready to support you without question.”

senses.definition: without purpose, order, or reason.
examples: The teacher said my report was disorganized. My paragraphs seemed to be without rhyme or reason.
Everything you do seems to be without rhyme or reason.
This procedure is without rhyme or reason.

headword: without so much as doing something

senses.definition: without even doing something.
examples: Jane borrowed Bob’s car without so much as asking his permission.
Mary’s husband walked out without so much as saying good-bye.

senses.definition: I am unfortunate!; I am unhappy!
examples: Woe is me! I have to work when the rest of the office staff is off.
Woe is me. I have the flu and my friends have gone to a party.

senses.definition: someone or something threatening that is disguised as someone or something kind.
examples: Beware of the police chief. He seems polite, but he’s a wolf in sheep’s clothing.
This proposal seems harmless enough, but I think it’s a wolf in sheep’s clothing.

senses.definition: one word at a time.
examples: We examined the contract word by word to make sure everything was the way we wanted.
We compared the stories word by word to see what made them different.

senses.definition: in the exact words; verbatim.
examples: I memorized the speech, word for word.
I can’t recall word for word what she told us.

senses.definition: a good piece of advice; a word of wisdom.
examples: If I can give you a word to the wise, I would suggest going to the courthouse about an hour before your trial.
Here is a word to the wise. Keep your eyes open and your mouth shut.

senses.definition: to work very hard.
examples: I’ve been working like a horse all day, and I’m tired.
I’m too old to work like a horse. I’d prefer to relax more.

headword: work one’s fingers to the bone

senses.definition: to work very hard.
examples: I worked my fingers to the bone so you children could have everything you needed. Now look at the way you treat me!
I spent the day working my fingers to the bone, and now I want to relax.

senses.definition: to manage to join or become a member of something.
examples: Ann worked her way into the club, and now she’s a member in good standing.
Bob worked his way into the top management of the company.

senses.definition: to hold a job that pays part of one’s college expenses.
examples: Tom couldn’t get a loan, so he had to work his way through college.
I worked my way through college, and that made college seem more valuable to me.

senses.definition: to advance in one’s job or position, from the beginning level to a higher level.
examples: I haven’t always been president of this bank. I started as a teller and worked my way up.
If I work my way up, can I be president of the bank?

senses.definition: to try to convince someone about something.
examples: We worked on Tom for nearly an hour, but we couldn’t get him to change his mind.
I’ll work on him for a while, and I’ll change his mind.

senses.definition: to give medical treatment to someone.
examples: The dentist was working on Mary while I waited for her in the other room.
The surgeon worked on the patient, trying to stop the bleeding.

senses.definition: to repair, build, or adjust something.
examples: The carpenter worked on the fence for three hours.
Bill is out working on his car engine.

senses.definition: to do a program of exercise.
examples: I have to work out every day in order to keep healthy.
Working out a lot gives me a big appetite.

senses.definition: to end up in the best possible way.
examples: Don’t worry. Things will work out for the best.
It seems bad now, but it’ll work out for the best.

senses.definition: to insert someone or something (into a schedule or a line).
examples: The doctor’s schedule was very busy, but the nurse agreed to try to work me in.
The mechanic had many cars to fix, but he said he’d work my car in.
I’m glad he could work in my car.

senses.definition: to get someone ready for something, especially medical treatment.
examples: The coach worked up the whole team before the game.
The doctor told the nurse to work Mr. Franklin up for surgery.

senses.definition: to create, cook, or arrange something.
examples: Bob is in the kitchen working up dinner.
Is there something planned for Friday night, or should we work something up?

senses.definition: to threaten, intimidate, or beat someone.
examples: I thought they were really going to work me over, but they only asked a few questions.
The police worked over Bill until he told where the money was hidden.

senses.definition: to get rid of something, such as fat, by doing physical exercise.
examples: Bob put on weight on his vacation and is trying to work it off by swimming regularly.
Jane tried to work off her depression by playing a game of tennis.

senses.definition: to settle a problem.
examples: It was a serious problem, but we managed to work it out.
I’m glad we can work out our problems without fighting.

senses.definition: to try to get something done by going through the proper procedures and persons.
examples: You can’t accomplish anything around here if you don’t work through channels.
I tried working through channels, but it takes too long. This is an emergency.

senses.definition: to be surprisingly beneficial to someone or something; to be very helpful with someone or something.
examples: This new medicine works wonders with my headaches.
Jean was able to work wonders with the office staff. They improved their efficiency as soon as she took over.

senses.definition: everything.
examples: They gave me everything I could possibly want. They gave me the works!
I want the works! Everything you have to offer!

senses.definition: Someone who is usually patient and humble has decided to stop being so.
examples: Jane used to be treated badly by her husband and she just accepted it, but one day she hit him. The worm turned all right.
Tom used to let the other boys bully him on the playground, but one day the worm turned and he’s now leader of their gang.

headword: worm one’s way out of something

senses.definition: to squeeze or wiggle out of a problem or a responsibility.
examples: This is your job, and you can’t worm your way out of it!
I’m not trying to worm my way out of anything!

senses.definition: to get some kind of information out of someone.
examples: He didn’t want to tell me the truth, but I finally wormed it out of him.
She succeeded in worming the secret out of me. I didn’t mean to tell it.

senses.definition: very valuable.
examples: This book is worth its weight in gold.
Oh, Bill. You’re wonderful. You’re worth your weight in gold.

senses.definition: worth one’s salary.
examples: Tom doesn’t work very hard, and he’s just barely worth his salt, but he’s very easy to get along with.
I think he’s more than worth his salt. He’s a good worker.

senses.definition: worth one’s time and trouble.
senses.notes: See also make it worth someone’s while.
examples: The job pays so badly it’s not worth your while even going for an interview.
It’s not worth Mary’s while going all that way just for a one-hour meeting.

senses.definition: deserving to be so called; good enough to enjoy a specific name.
examples: There was not an actor worthy of the name in that play.
Any art critic worthy of the name would know that painting to be a fake.

headword: would give one’s right arm (for someone or something)

senses.definition: would be willing to give something of great value in exchange for someone or something.
examples: I’d give my right arm for a nice cool drink.
I’d give my right arm to be there.

headword: would like (to have) someone or something

senses.definition: to want someone or something; to prefer someone or something.
examples: I would like to have three cookies.
I would like a piece of cake.

senses.definition: would prefer [something] more willingly; would prefer [something] more readily.
examples: I would rather have an apple than a pear. I don’t like pears.
I’d rather live in the north than the south, because I like snow.

senses.definition: would not even consider doing something.
examples: I wouldn’t dream of taking your money!
I’m sure that John wouldn’t dream of complaining to the manager.

headword: wouldn’t touch someone or something with a ten-foot pole

senses.definition: would not be involved with something under any circumstances.
examples: I know about the piece of vacant land for sale on Maple Street. I wouldn’t touch it with a ten-foot pole because there used to be a gas station there and the soil is polluted.
I wouldn’t touch that book with a ten-foot pole. It is nothing but gossip and scandal.

senses.definition: to terminate something; to bring something to an end.
senses.notes: Also literal. Informal. See also get something sewed up.
examples: It’s time to wrap this project up and move on to something else.
Let’s wrap up this discussion. It’s time to go home.

headword: wrapped up in someone or something

senses.definition: concerned and involved with someone or something.
examples: Sally is wrapped up in her work.
Ann is all wrapped up in her children and their activities.

senses.definition: to cause a lot of trouble with something; to ruin or damage something.
examples: Your attitude will wreak havoc with my project.
The weather wreaked havoc with our picnic plans.

senses.definition: to seek and get revenge on someone by harming someone or something.
examples: The thief wreaked his vengeance by destroying his rival’s house.
The general wanted to wreak vengeance on the opposing army for their recent successful attack.

senses.definition: to absorb a debt or a loss in accounting.
examples: The bill couldn’t be collected, so we had to write it off.
The bill was too large, and we couldn’t write off the amount. We decided to sue.

senses.definition: to drop someone or something from consideration.
examples: The manager wrote Tom off for a promotion.
I wrote off that piece of land as worthless. It can’t be used for anything.

senses.definition: to prepare a bill, order, or statement.
examples: Please write the order up and send me a copy.
As soon as I finish writing up your check, I’ll bring you some more coffee.

senses.definition: to write an article about someone or something.
examples: A reporter wrote me up for the Sunday paper.
I wrote up a local factory and sent the story to a magazine, but they didn’t buy the story.

senses.definition: to write something; to make a note of something.
examples: If I write it down, I won’t forget it.
I wrote down everything she said.

headword: the wrong side of the tracks

senses.definition: the poor part of a town.
senses.notes: Often with come from, be from, or live on, as in the examples. Compare this with the other side of the tracks.
examples: They said that Bob was from the wrong side of the tracks, but that it didn’t matter.
We went to a school that was on the wrong side of the tracks, and we all got a fine education.

senses.definition: this is the exact spot.
senses.notes: Can be used literally when someone draws an X to mark an exact spot.
examples: This is where the rock struck my car—X marks the spot.
Now, please move that table over here. Yes, right here—X marks the spot.

senses.definition: for many years, one after another.
examples: We go to the same place for our vacation year after year.
I seem to earn the same salary year after year.

headword: year in, year out year after year

senses.definition: all year long.
examples: I seem to have hay fever year in, year out. I never get over it.
John wears the same old suit, year in, year out.

senses.definition: to give the right to turn or move forward to another person or vehicle.
examples: When you’re driving, it’s better to yield the right-of-way than to have a wreck.
You must always yield the right-of-way when you’re making a left turn.

senses.definition: something that oppresses people; a burden.
examples: John’s greedy children are a yoke around his neck.
The Smiths have a huge mortgage that has become a yoke around their neck.

senses.definition: Surely!; Absolutely!
examples: BILL: Coming to the meeting next Saturday? BOB: You bet!
You bet your boots I’ll be there!

senses.definition: That is true!; You are correct!
senses.notes: Informal. The word that is emphasized.
examples: MARY: It sure is hot today. JANE: You can say that again!
BILL: This cake is yummy! BOB: You said it!

senses.definition: It is not possible to make everyone happy.
senses.notes: Said when dismissing a complaint or when someone has pointed out a flaw that cannot be fixed.
examples: When Jean complained about the choices on the dinner menu, the waiter said, “Sorry. You can’t please everyone.”
Jerry reported that many of his friends had noticed that the colors of the walls in the living room clashed. His mother said, “Oh, well. You can’t please everyone.”

headword: You can’t take it with you.

senses.definition: You should use your money now, because it is no good when you’re dead.
examples: My uncle is a wealthy miser. I keep telling him, “You can’t take it with you.”
If you have money, you should make out a will. You can’t take it with you, you know!

headword: You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.

senses.definition: Old people cannot learn anything new.
senses.notes: Proverb. Also used literally of dogs.
examples: “Of course I can learn,” bellowed Uncle John. “Who says you can’t teach an old dog new tricks?”
I’m sorry. I can’t seem to learn to do it right. Oh, well. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.

senses.definition: You really don’t see what people are trying to tell you!
examples: Everyone says that you are a bore, but you just don’t get it!
You just don’t get it! People avoid you because you offend them.

senses.definition: as you are aware, or should be aware.
senses.notes: Informal. This should not be overused.
examples: This is a very valuable book, you know.
Goldfish can be overfed, you know.

headword: You scared the hell out of me.
altForms: You scared the crap out of me.
You scared the dickens out of me.
You scared the devil out of me.
You scared me out of my wits.
You scared the pants off (of) me.

senses.definition: You frightened me very badly.
examples: He scared the hell out of all of us.
She really scared the pants off of me.

headword: You scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours.

senses.definition: You do a favor for me and I’ll do a favor for you.; If you do something for me that I cannot do for myself, I will do something for you that you cannot do for yourself.
examples: I’ll grab the box on the top shelf if you will creep under the table and pick up my pen. You scratch my back, and I’ll scratch yours.
Politicians are always saying to one another, “You scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours.”

senses.definition: You act as if you knew far more than you do!
examples: You think you’re so smart! You don’t know anything!
Boy! He thinks he’s so smart!

headword: Your guess is as good as mine.

senses.definition: Your answer is likely to be as correct as mine.
examples: I don’t know where the scissors are. Your guess is as good as mine.
Your guess is as good as mine as to when the train will arrive.

headword: Your secret is safe with me.

senses.definition: I will not tell your secret to anyone.
examples: Don’t worry. I won’t tell. Your secret’s safe with me.
Your secret is safe with me. I will carry it to my grave.

senses.definition: a polite closing phrase at the end of a letter, just before the signature.
examples: Yours truly, Tom Jones
Best wishes from yours truly, Bill Smith

senses.definition: oneself; I; me.
examples: There’s nobody here right now but yours truly.
Everyone else got up and left the table leaving yours truly to pay the bill.

senses.definition: to aim or focus directly on something.
examples: “Now,” said Mr. Smith, “I would like to zero in on another important point.”
Mary is very good about zeroing in on the most important and helpful ideas.

senses.definition: to pass out; to fall asleep.
examples: I was so tired after playing football that I almost zonked out on the floor.
I had a cup of coffee before the test to keep from zonking out in the middle of it.

senses.definition: to fly or move rapidly at someone or something.
examples: The hawk zoomed in on the sparrow.
The angry bees zoomed in on Jane and stung her.
When the door opened, the cat zoomed in.

senses.definition: to use a zoom lens to get a closer view of someone or something.
examples: Bill zoomed in on Sally’s face just as she grinned.
On the next shot I’ll zoom in for a close-up.

headword: arrange to do something with someone

senses.definition: to plan an event so as to include another person or persons.
examples: Jane arranged a meeting with Ann.
Bill arranged to go to the station with Tom and Mary.
forms: arrange to do something with someone

senses.definition: since; because.
examples: As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread.
So long as you’re here, please stay for dinner.

senses.definition: at one’s convenience.
examples: Choose one or the other at your leisure.
Please drop by at your leisure.

senses.definition: for quite a long time.
examples: He spoke on and on at some length.
He described the history of his village at length.

senses.definition: to determine through accounting that accounts are in balance, that all money is accounted for.
examples: The cashier was not allowed to leave the bank until the manager balanced the books.

senses.definition: to receive help starting one’s car.
examples: I got my car going. I got a jump from John.

senses.definition: to someone, as when writing a check.
examples: Please make out a check for $300 in Tom’s favor.
I’m making out the check in favor of Mr. Brown.

senses.definition: to make someone or something silent or less noisy.
examples: Can you please keep the baby quiet?

senses.definition: to restrain or control someone or something so that the person or thing cannot move.
examples: Please keep your foot still. It makes me nervous when you wiggle it.
You have to hold the nail still if you want to hit it.

senses.definition: do not move.
examples: Quit wiggling. Keep still!
“Hold still. I can’t examine your ear if you’re moving,” said the doctor.

senses.definition: to die.
examples: When I kick the bucket, I want a huge funeral with lots of flowers and crying.

senses.definition: to release or dismiss someone without punishment.
senses.notes: [with someone] See also get off easy.
examples: The judge didn’t let me off.
The judge let off Mary with a warning.

senses.definition: not to miss observing any part of what is going on.
senses.notes: Usually with do as in the examples below.
examples: The puppy doesn’t miss a thing. He sees every move you make.

headword: out of time (with someone or something)

senses.definition: out of cadence with someone else.
examples: Pay attention, Ann. You’re out of time.
forms: out of time (with someone or something)

senses.definition: to play a musical instrument well, without formal training.
examples: John can play the piano by ear.
If I could play by ear, I wouldn’t have to take lessons—or practice!

senses.definition: to finish something by doing something special.
examples: She rounded her schooling off with a trip to Europe.
I like to round out the day with a period of meditation.

senses.definition: slow to figure something out; slow-thinking.
senses.notes: Slang. Compare this with quick on the draw.
examples: Bill— who’s slow on the uptake—didn’t get the joke until it was explained to him.

senses.definition: to talk to and bore someone.
examples: My uncle always talked my ear off whenever I went to visit him.

senses.definition: to cause someone to lose the trail (when following someone or something).
examples: The robber threw the police off the trail by leaving town.

senses.definition: to wait for someone or something to catch up.
examples: Hold up! You’re going too fast.

senses.definition: to try to avoid a confrontation with someone or something.
examples: Look out for John. He’s looking for you, and he’s really mad.
Thanks. I’d better look out.
